column308:
The town of Sardis, in the eastern part of North Carolina, had been laid out by persons who believed that the Almighty had ordained a particular arrangement of society and that it was their province to preserve it, and the arrangement had survived the war, the surrender, and the brief and much-lamented interval of reconstruction with fewer alterations than might have been expected. The principal street still ran from the courthouse to the river, and the principal families still lived along it. The colored people, who made up somewhat more than half the population and paid somewhat less than a tenth of the taxes, lived for the most part beyond the railroad, in a quarter which the white people called by a name that need not be repeated here, and which the colored people themselves, with that adaptability which is perhaps the most serviceable of their virtues, had come to call Freedom Hill.

On the brow of this hill, where the ground rose high enough to catch whatever breeze came up from the river, stood the house of Jerome Haygood. It was a two-story frame dwelling with a porch across the front and green shutters at the windows, and it had been built by Haygood's own hands, for he was a carpenter and contractor by trade, and the best in the county, as even those who would not have said so in his hearing were obliged to admit when they wanted a staircase that would not creak or a cornice that would hang true. He had served his apprenticeship under a white master-builder in the old days, and had come out of slavery with a chest of tools, a reputation, and a degree of self-respect which some of his white neighbors regarded as the natural fruit of skill and others as a symptom of the general decay of manners since the war. He had prospered in a modest way. He owned his lot outright, but the house upon it was mortgaged to Colonel Ashby Tolliver, who held paper upon half the property on Freedom Hill and was accounted, by those who did not owe him money, a liberal and kindly man.

Mrs. Haygood had been, before her marriage, Miss Letitia Crane, a schoolteacher, and she had brought to her husband's house a set of Scott's novels, a melodeon, and a quiet conviction that the race would rise by the patient accumulation of property and character, and that it was the part of wisdom to give as little offense as possible while the accumulation was going forward. She was a comely woman of five-and-thirty, of a complexion which in another latitude would have excited no remark, and she had borne her husband three children, of whom the eldest, a girl of fourteen, was already spoken of as the most promising scholar in the colored school.

On a certain evening in the early autumn, Mrs. Haygood sat in the front room with her sewing, waiting for her husband to come home to supper. The children had eaten and gone up to their lessons; the lamp was lit; the kettle had been set back upon the stove to keep it from boiling dry. It was past eight o'clock when she heard his step upon the porch, and something in the sound of it, a certain heaviness and deliberation, caused her to lay down her needle before he had opened the door.

"You are late, Jerome," she said, when he came in. "Your supper has been waiting this hour."

"I am not hungry, Letty," he answered, and hung his hat upon the peg behind the door, and stood for a moment looking at it, as though he had never seen it before.

She regarded him in silence. Ten years of marriage had taught her that her husband's mind, like the timbers he worked in, would yield to pressure only along the grain, and that it was better to wait for him to speak than to force him. She took up her needle again, but she did not set a stitch.

"I have been to see Aunt Marthy Spence," he said at length.

The needle stopped altogether.

"I thought you might," she said. "I heard at the store this afternoon that you had been asked for at the jail."

"I was not asked for at the jail. I went there of my own accord. They would not let me see the boy, but I saw his mother afterwards, at her house."

Mrs. Haygood folded the garment in her lap with great care and laid it upon the table beside her.

"Jerome," she said, "sit down. You are standing there as if you meant to make a speech to me, and I would rather you did not."

He sat down in the chair opposite her, the lamp between them, and for some little time neither of them said anything. The clock upon the mantel, which had been a wedding present from the congregation of the African Methodist church, ticked with that solemn emphasis which clocks seem to reserve for the silences of married people.

The matter that lay between them was by this time known to every soul in Sardis, white and black, though it was known differently on the two sides of the railroad. On the Saturday night previous, a storehouse belonging to the Tolliver estate, standing near the river landing and containing some forty bales of cotton, had taken fire and burned to the ground. On the Monday a young colored man named Isom Spence, who had worked about the landing and had lately had some words with the Colonel's overseer concerning the matter of his wages, had been arrested upon the charge of having set it. The evidence against him consisted of the quarrel, of a statement by a white man named Pruitt that he had seen a negro running from the direction of the landing at about ten o'clock, and of the general and well-established principle that when anything goes wrong in a Southern town, and a negro is convenient, there is no particular need to look farther. The preliminary hearing was set for the following morning before the magistrate, and there had already been talk, in the barroom of the Planters' Hotel and elsewhere, of saving the county the expense of a trial.

What was not known on either side of the railroad, save to Jerome Haygood and his wife, was that at ten o'clock on the Saturday night in question Isom Spence had been in Haygood's own workshop, at the back of the lot, two miles from the landing, helping him to glue up the panels of a mahogany sideboard which was to be delivered on Monday morning to the house of Colonel Tolliver himself. The work had been behind time, and Haygood had sent for the young man, who was handy with clamps, and they had labored together by lantern light until near midnight. Mrs. Haygood had carried them out a pot of coffee at half past nine.

"Well," said Mrs. Haygood, when the clock had ticked long enough, "what did Aunt Marthy say?"

"She did not say much of anything. She sat there in her chair by the fireplace, with no fire in it, and rocked. She said, 'Brer Jerome, you know my boy wa'n't nowhar near dat lan'in'. You know it, 'caze he wuz wid you.' And I said, 'Yes, Aunt Marthy, I know it.' And she said, 'Den you gwine tell 'em?' And I did not answer her straight off, Letty, and she looked at me—" He stopped. "I would rather not tell you how she looked at me."

"You need not," said his wife. "I can imagine it."

"I told her I would be at the magistrate's office in the morning."

Mrs. Haygood rose from her chair, went to the window, and stood looking out into the darkness, where there was nothing whatever to be seen but the reflection of the lamp and of her own face in the glass. When she spoke again her voice was quite level, as it was in the schoolroom when a child had said something which required correction.

"Mr. Pruitt was here this afternoon," she said.

Her husband looked up quickly.

"Pruitt? Here?"

"He did not come in. He stood at the gate and asked for you, and when I said you were at work he said it did not signify, that he would leave a message. He said that the Colonel had been looking over his papers and found that the note on this house falls due at the first of the year, and that the Colonel had been thinking it might be well to have it settled, as money was likely to be close this winter. He said that of course the Colonel had always been willing to renew for a man who knew his place and kept to it, and that he had no doubt you would understand him. Then he lifted his hat to me, Jerome—he lifted his hat—and went away."

Haygood sat very still.

"How did he know?" he said at last. "Nobody knew that the boy was here but you and me."

"I have asked myself that all the afternoon. I suppose somebody saw the lantern in the shop. I suppose somebody saw Isom go in or come out. It does not matter how he knew. He knows, and the Colonel knows, and the message was plain enough for a child to read."

"It was plain enough," said Haygood. "It was a threat."

"It was a kindness," said his wife, turning from the window, "or it was meant to look like one, which in this town comes to very much the same thing. He might have said nothing at all and let you walk into the magistrate's office in the morning and find out afterwards. He has given you warning. That is more than most of them would do."

Haygood rose in his turn, and the two stood facing each other across the lamp. He was a tall man, broad in the shoulders, with the slight stoop of one who has spent his life bending over a workbench, and his wife, who was not tall, was obliged to lift her chin to meet his eyes; but she met them.

"Letty," he said, "do you mean to tell me that I should hold my tongue?"

"I mean to tell you what you already know, which is that if you go before the magistrate tomorrow and say that Isom Spence was in your shop on Saturday night, you will be contradicting the word of a white man in a matter concerning the property of Colonel Tolliver, and that the Colonel will call his note on the first of January, and that you have not the money to meet it, and that we shall be put out of this house that you built with your own hands. That is what I mean to tell you."

"And if I hold my tongue, they will hang that boy."

"You do not know that."

"I know it as well as I know my own name. You have heard the talk as well as I have. If they do not hang him from the courthouse oak, they will send him to the penitentiary for twenty years, and he will not live out ten of them. You know what the convict camps are."

"I know what they are," said Mrs. Haygood, and for the first time her voice faltered a little. "Do you think I have no heart, Jerome? Do you think I did not carry the coffee out to that boy with my own hands, and see him laugh when he burned his mouth on it? Do you think I have not been seeing his face all day, and his mother's face? I have prayed about it until I am ashamed to pray any more, for fear the Lord will grow tired of hearing me."

Her husband made a motion as if to go to her, but she put up her hand.

"No," she said; "let me finish. You will say that a man's duty is plain, and that he must do it and let the consequences take care of themselves. That is very fine, and it is what the preacher says on Sunday, and it is what the white folks say in their books when they are writing about Roman fathers and Scotch martyrs. But the Roman fathers had property that the law protected, and the Scotch martyrs were not colored people in Sardis, North Carolina, in the year eighteen hundred and ninety. Will your word save him? Will the magistrate take the word of a negro carpenter against the word of a white man, even if the white man is Pruitt, whom everybody knows to be a liar and a drunkard? You know he will not. You will lose the house, and Isom will hang just the same, and the only difference will be that our children will sleep in the street."

It was a strong argument, and Haygood knew it to be strong. He had made it to himself, in very nearly the same words, half a dozen times since Monday, and each time he had found it unanswerable, and each time he had found that his conviction remained precisely where it had been before. There are minds so constituted that they can be overcome in debate without being in the least degree persuaded, and it is perhaps fortunate for the progress of the world that such minds exist, though they are exceedingly inconvenient to live with.

"I do not know whether my word will save him," he said slowly. "Very likely it will not. But it will be said. It will be written down in the magistrate's book, and the lawyer that the Northern society sent down to help Aunt Marthy will have it to work with, if the thing goes to trial. And whether it saves him or not, Letty, he will know, and his mother will know, and every colored man on this hill will know, that there was one man among us who had seen the truth and was not afraid to tell it. That is something. It may not be much, but it is something."

"It will not feed the children."

"No. It will not feed them. But I have been thinking, all the way home, what I would say to Ellen when she is grown, and asks me—as she will ask me, for she is a sharp child, and she hears more than we think—what I did when they took Isom Spence. Shall I tell her that I kept the house? She would not thank me for it. She would despise me, and she would be right."

"She would be alive to despise you," said Mrs. Haygood, "and under a roof."

The words were hardly out of her mouth before she wished them unsaid, for she saw her husband's face change, and she understood that she had touched something which ten years of marriage had not taught her was there. He turned away from her and walked to the mantel and stood with his hand upon the clock, as though he would have stopped it if he could.

"Letty," he said, without turning round, "my father was sold away from my mother when I was six years old. I remember it. I remember the morning. He was a good man and a strong man, and he stood in the yard with the trader's hand on his arm, and he did not say anything at all. He could not say anything. There was nothing in the world that a man in his place could say that would have made any difference. I used to think, when I was a boy, that if ever I came to be a man, and free, and there was something to be said, I would say it. I have not had many chances. A colored man in this country does not get many. Mostly he must stand in the yard and hold his peace, as my father did. But this once—this once, Letty—the Lord has put a word into my mouth that is true, and that nobody else can say. And you are asking me to swallow it, for the sake of a house."

Mrs. Haygood did not answer at once. She sat down again in her chair by the table and took up the garment she had laid aside, and looked at it, and laid it down again. It was a dress she was making over for the second girl, from one of Ellen's that had been outgrown.

"I am not asking you for the sake of a house," she said presently, in a low voice. "I am asking you for the sake of your life. Do you suppose that the Colonel's note is the worst of it? Do you suppose that the men who are talking about the courthouse oak will be particular whether they hang one negro or two? You will be standing up in that office to say that a white man lied. There are men in this town who would kill you for less, and think they were doing God service."

"I know that," said Haygood.

"Then you have thought of it?"

"I have thought of nothing else since Monday."

"And you will go nevertheless?"

He turned and looked at her, and she saw in his face the answer which he did not trouble to put into words. She had married him, it may be, partly because of a certain quality which she had seen in him then, and which she had admired, without much considering what it might cost her; for young women, when they admire a quality in a lover, seldom pause to reckon the price of it in a husband. She was reckoning it now, and she found the sum a heavy one; and yet, when she had cast it up to the last figure, she discovered, somewhat to her own surprise, that she was not prepared to wish the quality away.

For a long while she sat with her hands in her lap. Then she rose, and went out into the kitchen, and came back with a plate of cold meat and bread and a cup of the coffee that had been keeping warm upon the stove, and set them down upon the table beside the lamp.

"Eat your supper," she said. "You cannot go before the magistrate on an empty stomach and stand up straight. And you cannot go in that coat, either. It has glue on the sleeve. I will brush your black one tonight, and you shall wear the shirt I ironed for Sunday."

Haygood looked at her, and then at the plate, and then at her again, and it seemed for a moment as though he would say something; but whatever it was, he did not say it. He sat down and ate, slowly, and his wife went to the closet under the stairs and brought out the black coat, and a brush, and sat down with it in the lamplight and began to work upon the nap with long, even strokes, as she had been taught to do by her mother, who had brushed the coats of a white family for forty years.

"Letty," said her husband, when he had finished, "if it should come to the worst—"

"If it should come to the worst," she said, without lifting her eyes from the coat, "my brother in Washington has a spare room, and the schools there are good, and Ellen will be glad enough of them. I have been thinking about it since this afternoon. I did not mean to tell you, because I did not want you to think I had given in. But I suppose I had given in before you came home, though I did not know it until just now."

He reached across the table and laid his hand upon hers, and the brush was still for a moment.

"I am obliged to you, Letty," he said.

"You need not be," she answered. "I should not have liked to explain to Ellen, either."

It may be recorded, for the satisfaction of those readers who prefer that a story should end somewhere, that Jerome Haygood went before the magistrate the next morning in his black coat and his Sunday shirt, and told what he knew, and that the magistrate, a cautious man with an election in the spring, wrote it down with every appearance of gravity and remanded the prisoner for trial at the next term of the superior court. What happened at that term, and what became of the Colonel's note, and whether the house on the brow of Freedom Hill continued to catch the breeze from the river for the family that had built it, belong to another chapter of the history of Sardis. It is sufficient for the present purpose to observe that the town was a good deal astonished, and that the more thoughtful of its white citizens, discussing the matter that evening upon the gallery of the Planters' Hotel, agreed among themselves that Haygood had always been a likely sort of negro, and that it was a great pity he should have been spoiled by too much education, when everybody knew perfectly well that his wife was the one who had been to school.

Mr. Edward Merrimon, of the city of Lakeport, in the State of Ohio, had for some fifteen years enjoyed that peculiar species of contentment which belongs to a man who has risen in the world and has had the good sense not to look too often over his shoulder. He was a dealer in real estate, with an office upon the second floor of a respectable building on Superior Avenue, where his name was lettered in gold upon the glass of the door. He had a brick house upon a quiet street, a wife who was admired for her complexion and her taste in furniture, and a pew in a church whose congregation was, if not altogether white, at least sufficiently pale to cherish the distinction. He was a member of a literary society which met fortnightly to read papers upon the English poets, and whose members, by a rule none the less binding for being unwritten, were drawn from that small and select circle of colored people whose features and fortunes alike entitled them to a certain consideration. Whether Mr. Merrimon would have been admitted to this society had his hair been less straight or his skin less fair is a question he had never found it necessary to put to himself, and it would be unkind to put it for him.

It was therefore with mixed emotions that Mr. Merrimon, one morning in the early part of May, opened a letter bearing the postmark of Wellsborough, North Carolina, and addressed in a hand which, though he had not seen it for many years, he recognized at once.

"Dear Cousin Edward," it ran, "I have been chosen by our conference as one of the delegates to the general meeting of the church, which is to be held in your city during the week of the twentieth. I should not like to pass through Lakeport without seeing you, if it is convenient, and I have some things to tell you that I would rather say than write. I shall arrive by the evening train on the nineteenth. If you are too much occupied, do not trouble yourself, for I have a place provided for me, and will understand. Your affectionate cousin, Silas Kinsey."

Mr. Merrimon laid the letter upon his desk and regarded it for some time with an expression in which affection, embarrassment, and a faint uneasiness contended for the mastery. He had been born in Wellsborough, and had been reared, after the death of his mother, in the house of his mother's sister, Aunt Phoebe Kinsey, whose son Silas was two years his senior. The two boys had slept in the same trundle-bed, had fished in the same mill-pond, had been whipped, upon occasion, with the same peach-tree switch, and had learned their letters from the same blue-backed speller by the light of the same pine-knot fire. When Edward was seventeen he had gone North with a few dollars in his pocket, the gift of his aunt, who had saved them out of her washing; and from that time forward his letters home, at first frequent, had grown less and less so, until, in the press of affairs and the gradual formation of new associations, they had ceased altogether. He had sent money once or twice, in the early years; but his aunt had returned the last remittance with a message, conveyed in Silas's hand, that she was "doin' very well, thank the Lord, and he had better keep it for his own needs"; and Edward, who was at that time making his first purchases of property, had been perhaps a little relieved to take her at her word.

It is one of the curious effects of prosperity that it lends to the past a certain unreality, as though the poor boy who once went barefoot in the red clay of a Southern road had been some other person, of whom one has heard, and toward whom one feels a vague but not very pressing benevolence. Mr. Merrimon had not denied his origin; he had merely ceased to mention it. Mrs. Merrimon, who had been born in Lakeport of parents who had come from Virginia before the war, and who had always been free, knew that her husband had kinspeople in the South, but she had never inquired very closely into their circumstances, and he had never volunteered the information. She had formed the impression, from his silence, that they were persons of humble station, and she had a well-bred woman's reluctance to pursue a subject that promised to be disagreeable.

"My cousin Silas is coming to the church conference," said Mr. Merrimon at dinner that evening, with an air of carelessness which did not entirely deceive his wife. "I shall meet him at the train. I suppose we ought to have him to supper."

"Your cousin?" said Mrs. Merrimon, lifting her eyebrows ever so slightly. "Is he—what is he like, Edward?"

The question was a perfectly natural one, and Mr. Merrimon understood it perfectly. He hesitated a moment before replying.

"He is a minister, I believe, or a teacher—or both. He was a good deal darker than I, as I remember him. His father was a black man."

"Oh," said Mrs. Merrimon. There was nothing in the monosyllable to which the most sensitive guest could have taken exception, and yet it conveyed a good deal. "Of course we must have him, Edward. Thursday would do very well. I had thought of asking the Dixons on Thursday, but it can just as well be another evening."

Mr. Merrimon thanked her, and was conscious, as he did so, of a feeling which he did not care to examine.

The evening train from the South was an hour late, as Southern trains are apt to be, and Mr. Merrimon, pacing the platform under the smoky glare of the gas-lamps, had ample time to consider what manner of man the years would have made of the boy he had left behind. He had pictured, without quite intending to, a figure somewhat rustic and ill at ease, in a coat of antiquated cut, with a carpet-bag and a manner too deferential or too familiar, he could not tell which. When at length the train came puffing into the station, and the passengers began to descend from the forward coach—the coach to which, south of the Ohio River, all persons of color were by law confined—he scanned their faces with an anxiety that surprised him.

He would not have known his cousin, had not his cousin known him. A tall, broad-shouldered man, very dark, with grizzled hair and a short beard touched with gray, stepped down from the car with a small valise in his hand and stood for a moment looking about him. His clothes were plain and of good quality, his bearing erect, his face grave and strong, with that settled composure which comes to men who have borne responsibility and have not been crushed by it. His eyes fell upon Mr. Merrimon, rested there a moment with a look of inquiry, and then lit up with a smile which transformed the whole countenance, and which Edward recognized, with a sudden contraction of the heart, as the smile of a boy who had once stood waist-deep in a mill-pond and dared him to come in.

"Edward," said the stranger, setting down his valise and holding out both hands. "You have not changed so much but I would know you anywhere. A little stouter, and a good deal more prosperous-looking; but the same."

"Silas," said Mr. Merrimon, and found that for the moment he could say nothing more.

They walked together to the street, where Mr. Merrimon's carriage was waiting, and on the way to the hotel at which the delegates were lodged they talked of the journey, of the weather, of the size of the city, and of all those indifferent matters with which men who have much to say to each other are wont to fill the first awkward moments of reunion. Silas declined, with quiet firmness, the invitation to stay at his cousin's house during the conference.

"I am obliged to you, Edward, but I had better be with the brethren. There will be committee meetings early and late, and I should only be a trouble to Mrs. Merrimon. But I shall come to supper Thursday with great pleasure, and I hope you will give me an hour or two this evening, if you are not too tired. I have come a long way to talk with you."

There was a small parlor off the hotel lobby, deserted at that hour, and thither the cousins repaired. Silas drew his chair near the window, through which the lights of the street threw a wavering glow upon his dark face, and for a little while he sat looking at Edward without speaking, as though he were comparing the man before him with some picture he had long carried in his mind.

"You must tell me about yourself," said Mr. Merrimon, to break a silence that was becoming oppressive. "I know nothing—I am ashamed to say how little I know. You are a minister?"

"A minister on Sundays," said Silas, smiling, "and a schoolmaster the rest of the week. We have a normal school at Wellsborough now, Edward—the Wellsborough Colored Normal and Industrial Institute, if you please, though the white folks call it 'Kinsey's school,' and some of them call it worse. It began in the old Methodist church on Back Street, with eleven scholars and one teacher, and the teacher was myself. We have three buildings now, and two hundred and forty pupils, and nine teachers, and we sent out thirty-two graduates last June to teach in the country schools. The State gives us something—not much, and grudgingly; the church gives us something; and the rest we have scraped together, a dollar at a time, from people who had very few dollars to spare."

"Thirty-two," repeated Mr. Merrimon, who dealt in figures and knew their value. "And how long has this been going on?"

"Eighteen years. I began it the year after Mother bought the lot behind the house."

"Aunt Phoebe bought a lot?"

"With her own money, out of her own savings. She was a remarkable woman, Edward. You knew that, of course, but I am not sure you knew how remarkable. She washed and ironed for the best families in Wellsborough for forty years, and she never in all that time spent a dollar she could save, except on me—and on you." He paused, and added, more gently, "She died in February."

Mr. Merrimon started as though he had been struck. He had not thought of his aunt as old; he had not, if the truth be told, thought of her very much at all; and now, at the news that she was gone, there rose up before him with a vividness that was almost painful the image of a little brown woman in a starched apron and a head-handkerchief, standing in the doorway of a whitewashed cabin with her hand shading her eyes, watching the road down which he had walked away twenty-five years before.

"I did not know," he said, in a low voice. "Why did no one write me?"

"I wrote," said Silas simply. "I directed the letter to the old address on Erie Street, which was the last we had. I suppose it did not reach you."

Mr. Merrimon remembered that he had left Erie Street eleven years ago, and that he had not sent the new address to Wellsborough. He said nothing, and his cousin, with a delicacy that did him honor, did not seem to expect him to say anything.

"She was not sick long," Silas went on. "A cold that settled on her chest, and she was past seventy-five. She was quite clear in her mind to the last, and she talked of you a great deal. That is one of the things I came to tell you."

"Of me?"

"Of you. You must not think, Edward, that because you stopped writing she stopped thinking of you. There was never a day, I believe, when she did not pray for you by name. She used to say, 'Ed'ard's gone 'mongst strangers, an' he's got mo' temptations than you is, Silas, an' he needs mo' prayin' for.' And she kept everything—every letter you ever wrote, and every scrap of news about you she could come by."

He opened his valise, which he had carried with him into the parlor, and took out a small parcel wrapped in brown paper and tied with a faded ribbon. This he placed in his cousin's hands.

Mr. Merrimon untied the ribbon with fingers that were not altogether steady. The parcel contained a bundle of letters, yellow with age, in his own boyish handwriting; and beneath these a number of newspaper clippings, carefully cut out and pasted upon sheets of brown wrapping-paper. There was the notice, from a Lakeport paper, of his first purchase of property; there was an account of a banquet given by a colored business league, at which he had responded to a toast; there was a paragraph from a church paper mentioning his election as a trustee; there was even the announcement of his marriage, cut from a society column, with the name of the bride and the description of her gown. How these things had found their way to a washerwoman's cabin in a little North Carolina town, Mr. Merrimon could not imagine.

"She could not read them herself," said Silas, answering the unspoken question. "She never learned to read more than her Bible, and that only the parts she knew by heart. But she got the colored papers from the North whenever she could, and she had me read them to her, and whenever your name was in them she made me cut it out. Some of these she got from the white people she worked for. Old Judge Bascom used to save her the Lakeport papers when he had them, and she would bring them home and say, 'See if they's anything in here 'bout Ed'ard.' Generally there wasn't; but sometimes there was, and then she was happier than if somebody had given her a dollar. She used to show these to the neighbors. You were a great man in Wellsborough, Edward, though you did not know it."

Mr. Merrimon turned over the brown sheets one by one, and the printed words blurred before his eyes. He was a man who had, in the course of his career, received a good many compliments, and had come to accept them with a comfortable complacency; but no tribute had ever been paid him that humbled him as this one did.

"I did not deserve it," he said at length.

"Perhaps not," said Silas, with the frankness of an old friend; "but love does not go by deserving, or most of us would get very little of it. There is one thing more."

He took from his pocket a folded paper, which proved to be a deed.

"Mother left a will—Judge Bascom drew it for her, and witnessed it himself, which made some talk in town. She left the house and the school lot to the trustees of the institute. That was understood between us. But there was a little piece of land she owned besides, down by the old mill-pond—you will remember it, the place where we used to fish. She bought it from the Mallard estate years ago for almost nothing, because nobody else wanted it. She left that to you."

Mr. Merrimon looked at the paper, and then at his cousin, with an expression of such bewilderment that Silas smiled.

"It is not worth much in money," he said. "Twelve acres of swamp and pine land, and the old mill-dam broke years ago. I doubt if it would bring two hundred dollars. But she wanted you to have it. She said—I will give you her words, as near as I can—'Ed'ard's got plenty o' land up yonder, I reckon, but he ain't got none at home. A man oughter own a piece o' de groun' he was bawn on, so's he'll know whar he b'longs.' I promised her I would bring it to you myself."

For a long time Mr. Merrimon sat silent, holding the deed in one hand and the bundle of letters in the other. The noises of the street came in through the window—the rumble of a passing car, the clatter of hoofs on the pavement, the voices of people going home from the theater—but he did not hear them. He was seeing instead a wide, still pond with cypress trees standing knee-deep at its edge, and dragon-flies darting over the water, and two small boys, one fair and one dark, sitting side by side upon a log with their bare feet dangling and their bent-pin hooks trailing in the brown water, talking, as boys will, of what they would do when they were men.

"Do you remember, Silas," he said at last, "the day we swore we would never leave each other? We cut our thumbs with your jack-knife, and mixed the blood, and said we would be brothers always."

"I remember," said Silas. "We were very young."

"And I was the one who broke it."

"No," said his cousin gravely. "It was not broken. It was only—mislaid. Things get mislaid, Edward, when a man moves into a large house with many rooms. I have never doubted that it would be found again."

There are moments in the lives of most men when the accumulated pretensions of years fall away from them like a garment, and they stand for an instant face to face with their own souls. Such a moment had come to Mr. Merrimon. He saw, with a clearness that was not comfortable, the meagerness of the ambitions which had filled his life; he measured his brick house and his gold-lettered door and his fortnightly papers upon the English poets against the eighteen years of patient labor which had planted two hundred and forty young people in three buildings on a washerwoman's lot; and he was not proud of the comparison. He perceived, too, that he had for a long time been ashamed of the wrong things, and proud of the wrong things, and that the dark man sitting before him, who had stayed behind in the land of the color line and borne its burdens without complaint, had grown in stature while he himself had merely grown in girth.

"Silas," he said abruptly, "I want to come down and see the school."

His cousin's face lit up with the old smile.

"Come, by all means. We should be glad to have you. Only I must warn you that you will have to ride in the forward car from Washington south, and that the hotel in Wellsborough will not take you if they know who you are, and that they will know, because I shall be at the station to meet you."

"Then I shall stay with you."

"You shall stay with me. I have a spare room, and a wife who is a better cook than her husband deserves, and three children who have heard about their Cousin Edward until they think he is a kind of prince. You must not disappoint them."

"I will try not to," said Mr. Merrimon humbly.

The supper on Thursday evening passed off better than Mrs. Merrimon had feared. Indeed, it passed off so well that she was somewhat at a loss to account for it. The guest, whose complexion had at first occasioned her a slight inward shiver, proved to be a man of excellent manners and considerable information, who talked of education and of the condition of the South with a quiet authority that commanded attention, and who complimented her upon her table in terms so simple and sincere that she was more pleased than by the more elaborate praises of her usual guests. When her husband announced, toward the close of the evening, that he intended to make a journey to North Carolina in the autumn, and that he hoped she would accompany him, she received the proposal with a composure which did her credit, though she privately resolved to discover, before committing herself, what the accommodations would be.

It is perhaps worth recording that Mr. Merrimon did go South that autumn, and that he rode in the forward car from Washington without complaint; that he spent a week in his cousin's house, and visited every classroom in the institute, and made a speech to the pupils which was remembered for a long time in Wellsborough; and that before he left he sat for an hour alone upon a fallen cypress log at the edge of what had once been the mill-pond, now grown up in rushes and young willows, with the deed to the land in his pocket. What he thought there is no business of ours. But the trustees of the Wellsborough Colored Normal and Industrial Institute found among their receipts, at the end of that year, a gift sufficient to build a fourth building, with the stipulation that it should be called the Phoebe Kinsey Hall; and the literary society of Lakeport, at its next fortnightly meeting, listened with polite astonishment to a paper by Mr. Edward Merrimon, not upon any of the English poets, but upon the subject of "Our Duty to Our Kin."

The paper was not considered one of the society's more successful efforts. Several of the members thought it in questionable taste, and one lady remarked, in the hearing of Mrs. Merrimon, that she had always supposed the society was organized for the cultivation of literature and not for the discussion of family affairs. Mrs. Merrimon, to her own surprise, found herself defending it.

column308:
I

Mr. Henry Merrick, carpenter and builder, of the town of Clarendon, in the State of North Carolina, was accounted by those of his own people who were competent to judge of such matters a man of substance and of character. He owned the neat frame house in which he lived, upon a quiet street that ran down toward the river, and two others which he rented. He had built, with his own hands and those of the three journeymen whom he employed, a good part of the new houses that had gone up in the town since the war. Among them was the residence of Judge Ballard, whose columned portico was the admiration of the county, and whose owner had been heard to remark, with that generosity toward the deserving individual which so often accompanies a firm conviction of the unworthiness of the class, that Merrick was "the best mechanic in the State, white or black, and a credit to his race."

Which race was meant, the Judge did not specify. Nor would it have been easy for a stranger to decide. Mr. Merrick was of that complexion which the census-taker, in the exercise of a discretion more confident than scientific, sets down as "mulatto," and which in the town of Clarendon was generally described as "bright." His features were regular. His hair, which he wore closely cut, had only so much of a wave as might have passed without comment upon a Spaniard. He had been born a slave, of a mother who was herself nearly white, and of a father concerning whom it was neither customary nor prudent to inquire. He had made his own way in the world by industry and thrift, and by a certain gravity of demeanor which commanded respect where it could not compel liking.

He was a member of the Methodist church, a trustee of the colored school, and a subscriber to two newspapers. If he had a fault, his neighbors would have said it was a kind of pride. It was not that he held himself aloof from those darker than himself, for his business and his church brought him daily among them. But he had a way of speaking of "our people" which suggested that he stood a little distance off, as a physician speaks of his patients. And in his household, which consisted of his wife Eliza, a comely woman of about his own shade, and their only child, a boy of seven named Lucius, there prevailed a standard of speech and manners from which the least departure was promptly corrected.

It is one of the anomalies of a society constituted as was that of Clarendon in those years, that a man situated like Mr. Merrick could hardly avoid some such attitude. The white people, while they rated him above the mass of his race, never for one moment permitted him to forget that he belonged to it. The black people, while they were proud of him, did not altogether trust him. He was like a man standing upon a narrow ledge between two precipices, and he had learned, as such men must, to walk carefully and to look neither to the right hand nor to the left. Whether he had also learned to look down upon those below him is a question which he would have answered with an indignant negative, and which the events of a certain afternoon in early October brought rather sharply home to him.

II

He had come in from his work somewhat earlier than usual, the lumber for a new job having failed to arrive, and was sitting upon his front piazza with the Clarendon Eagle in his hand, when he observed an old man coming slowly up the street. The old man pushed before him a small hand-cart, upon which were heaped a few sweet potatoes, a basket of chinquapins, and a bundle of fat-pine kindling. He was very black, very much bent, and very ragged, and he walked with the aid of a hickory staff. Mr. Merrick knew him well, as did everyone in Clarendon. He was called Uncle Ephraim, and had for many years gained a precarious living by the sale of such small wares from door to door.

Somewhat to Mr. Merrick's surprise, the old man did not pass by, but stopped before the gate, set down the handles of his cart, and, after a moment's hesitation, opened the gate and came up the walk. He removed his hat, which was of straw and had seen many summers, and stood at the foot of the steps.

"Evenin', Mist' Merrick," he said.

"Good evening, Uncle Ephraim," returned the carpenter, laying aside his paper. "I don't think we need any potatoes to-day. Mrs. Merrick bought a peck on Saturday."

"I ain' come ter sell no 'taters, suh," said the old man. "I come 'bout dat boy er yo'n."

Mr. Merrick's countenance grew grave. "What about him?"

The old man shifted his weight upon his staff, and seemed for a moment reluctant to proceed.

"Well, suh, it 'pears lak I got ter tell you, dough I'd ruther not. I wuz comin' 'long by de Jedge's place, 'bout two hours ago, an' dere wuz a passel er chilluns playin' in de road, de Jedge's two boys an' de Pettigrew boy an' some mo', an' yo' boy 'long wid 'em. An' w'en dey seed me comin' wid my cyart, dey all sot up a hollerin', an' one un 'em say, 'Yere come ole Crow,' an' de res' tuk it up. An' den dey commence' ter th'ow chinaberries, an' one un 'em hit my cyart an' upsot my chinquapins in de road. I ain' mindin' de white chilluns so much, suh. I done been called mo' names dan dat in my time, an' I reckon I'll be called some mo' befo' de good Lawd sen's fer me. But yo' boy wuz th'owin' too, an' hollerin' 'Crow' louder'n any un 'em, an' I 'lowed you'd want ter know it."

Mr. Merrick had risen from his chair. A deep flush had overspread his face, which in a man of his complexion was plainly visible.

"Are you sure it was Lucius?"

"Sho' ez I'm stan'in' yere, suh. I knowed him by dat little blue jacket wid de brass buttons. I's knowed dat chile sence he wuz bawn."

"Uncle Ephraim," said the carpenter, with some effort, "I am very much obliged to you for telling me, and I am more sorry than I can say. What did you lose by it?"

"Nothin' ter speak of, suh. I picked up mos' er de chinquapins. I ain' come fer no pay."

But Mr. Merrick had already taken out his purse, and the old man, after a decent show of reluctance, accepted a quarter, which he tucked away in some recess of his ragged clothing. Then he put on his hat, bowed with an old-fashioned courtesy which sat oddly upon his tatters, and went back down the walk to his cart.

Mr. Merrick stood for some moments looking after him. Then he went into the house.

III

Mrs. Merrick was in the kitchen, superintending the preparation of supper, when her husband appeared in the doorway.

"Eliza," he said, "where is Lucius?"

"He's in the back yard, I think, playing with the puppy. Why, Henry, what is the matter? You look as though you had seen a ghost."

"I have seen something worse than a ghost. Send him to me in the sitting-room, if you please."

He turned away without further explanation, and Mrs. Merrick, who knew her husband's moods, did not press him. She went to the back door and called the boy, who came running in, his face flushed with play and his jacket, the blue one with the brass buttons, considerably the worse for an afternoon in the road.

"Your father wants you in the sitting-room," she said, and something in her tone caused the boy's face to fall.

"What for, mamma?"

"He will tell you himself. Go along now, and wipe your feet first."

Lucius went, with lagging steps. He was a handsome child, fairer than either of his parents, with soft brown hair and the large, liquid eyes which are frequently the inheritance of mixed blood. He had been much indulged, as only children are apt to be, but he had also been taught to obey, and he presented himself before his father with a creditable effort at composure.

Mr. Merrick was standing by the mantel. He did not ask the boy to sit down.

"Lucius," he said, "where were you this afternoon?"

"Playing, papa."

"Where?"

"Up the street."

"With whom?"

The boy hesitated. "With Tom and Willie Ballard, and Jimmy Pettigrew, and some more."

"Did anything happen while you were playing?"

The boy looked down at the carpet, and was silent.

"I asked you a question, sir."

"Old Uncle Ephraim came by," said Lucius, in a low voice.

"And what did you do?"

"We—we threw chinaberries at his cart. But it was Tom Ballard who started it, papa. He said it would be fun."

"And did you think it was fun?"

The boy did not answer.

"What did you call him?"

There was a long pause. "Tom called him Old Crow," said Lucius, "and the other boys said it too, and so did I. But it was only a joke, papa. Tom says all the black people are crows, and that his father says so."

Mr. Merrick drew a long breath. He was not by nature a violent man, but there was in the corner of the room, behind the door, a slender switch cut from the peach tree in the yard, which had been placed there some months before against emergencies, and his eye went to it now. It had been the method of his own upbringing. He had been switched, in his childhood, for offenses far less grave than this. His mother, who was a gentle woman, had used the switch upon him with tears in her eyes, and he had never doubted that it was for his good. And it would have been a relief to him, at that moment, to lay it smartly about the legs of this small offender, and so be done with the matter.

But Mr. Merrick was a reflective man, and he was conscious that the feeling which moved him was not altogether a righteous anger. There was mingled with it a sense of personal humiliation which he did not care to examine too closely. It was not merely that his son had been cruel to an old man. It was that his son had been cruel to an old black man, in company with white boys, and at their instigation; and the father, standing there by the mantel, had a sudden and unwelcome vision of the Judge, upon his columned portico, laughing at the story over his evening cigar.

He turned away from the switch, and sat down in his armchair, and drew the boy to stand before him.

"Lucius," he said, "look at me."

The boy raised his eyes.

"Do you know what Tom Ballard's father calls you, when you are not by?"

Lucius looked puzzled. "He calls me Lucius, papa. He gave me a penny once."

"He calls you a little nigger," said Mr. Merrick quietly.

The boy stared. The word was one which was never spoken in that house, and he had perhaps never before heard it from his father's lips. A slow color mounted to his face.

"I am not!" he cried. "I'm not black, papa. I'm almost as white as Tom. Tom said so himself."

"Tom may have said so to-day. He will not say so many years longer. And when he is grown, and you are grown, he will not ask you to play in the road with him, nor to his house, nor to sit at his table. He will not care whether you are almost as white as he or as black as Uncle Ephraim. To him, and to his father, and to all the people of his kind, you and Uncle Ephraim are the same. You may as well learn that now as later. I learned it myself when I was not much older than you."

The boy's lip trembled. "But you said it was wrong to talk like the field hands, and to be dirty, and—"

"I said so, and I meant it. It is wrong to be dirty, and it is well to speak correctly, and to have good manners. But these things are not a matter of the color of the skin. Uncle Ephraim has better manners than Judge Ballard's sons, and he had them before you were born. He came to this house to-day and took off his hat to me, and he spoke to me like a gentleman, when he might have gone to the Judge and complained of the boys, and got nothing for his pains but a cursing. Do you think Tom Ballard would ever have done as much?"

Lucius was silent.

"Now listen to me, my son, for I am going to tell you something I have never told you before." Mr. Merrick's voice had grown somewhat less stern. "When I was a boy, no bigger than you, I belonged to old Colonel Merrick, who owned the plantation out on the Wilmington road, where the Sandersons live now. It was against the law, in those days, for a colored person to learn to read. A white man might be fined for teaching one, and a colored man might be whipped. My mother wanted me to learn, more than she wanted anything in the world, but she could not read herself, and there was no one to teach me. Now, there was a man on that plantation who had learned his letters from the Colonel's son, when they were boys together, and who had kept it to himself all those years. And one night he came to my mother's cabin, and said that if she would keep it secret, he would teach me. And he did. Every night for two winters, after the day's work was done, he sat by our fire with a piece of charcoal and a pine board, and showed me how to make the letters, and how to spell them out of an old almanac which he had hid under the floor of his cabin. He ran the risk of being whipped every night of those two winters, and he never took a penny for it, for he had none to take, and neither had we. Do you know who that man was?"

The boy shook his head; but there was already a dawning comprehension in his eyes.

"It was Uncle Ephraim," said his father. "If it were not for him, I should not be able to read the newspaper, nor to figure the cost of a house, nor to write a contract. I should be digging ditches for a dollar a day, and you would be running barefoot in the street, instead of going to school in a jacket with brass buttons. He is old now, and poor, and nobody remembers what he did, because the people he did it for are mostly dead or gone away. And to-day my son, my own son, stood in the road and threw chinaberries at him, and called him a crow, to please the son of a man who would not let Uncle Ephraim come to his front door."

He stopped. The boy's eyes had filled with tears, and he was struggling manfully to keep them from overflowing. It was a struggle in which he was not wholly successful.

"I didn't know, papa," he said, with a sob. "Nobody told me."

"No," said Mr. Merrick slowly, "nobody told you. That is partly my fault, and I am not going to pretend that it is not. But you knew that he was old, and that he was poor, and that he had done you no harm. You did not need to be told anything more than that to know that what you did was wrong."

IV

At this point Mrs. Merrick, who had been listening at the door with that solicitude which is the privilege of mothers, ventured to come into the room.

"Henry," she said, "I think the child understands. You won't whip him, will you?"

"No," replied her husband, "I am not going to whip him. I had thought of it, but I believe a whipping would teach him nothing except to be more careful whom he throws chinaberries at. He is going to do something harder than taking a whipping."

He rose, and went to the kitchen, and returned presently with a small basket, into which he had put a loaf of Mrs. Merrick's bread, a piece of bacon, and a paper of coffee. To these he added, from his own pocket, a silver half-dollar.

"Lucius," he said, "you know where Uncle Ephraim lives, down by the old brickyard?"

"Yes, papa."

"You are going to carry this basket to him, now, before supper. And when you get there, you are going to knock at the door, and take off your cap, and tell him that you are sorry for what you did, and that you ask his pardon. You are going to say it in your own words, and you are going to mean it. And then you are going to ask him whether he will let you come to see him on Saturday afternoons, and you are going to listen to anything he may choose to tell you about the old times. If he tells you to go away, you will thank him and come home. If he asks you to stay, you will stay until he is tired of you."

The boy looked up with something like dismay. To go alone, at dusk, to the cabin by the old brickyard, and to humble himself before the very person he had so lately derided, was an ordeal compared with which the peach switch seemed a light affliction.

"Must I go by myself, papa?"

"You went by yourself this afternoon," said his father, "when you threw the chinaberries. Tom Ballard did not throw them for you."

There was no answer to this, and Lucius did not attempt one. He took the basket, and his cap, and went out, his mother following him to the gate and watching his small figure until it disappeared around the corner, while Mr. Merrick resumed his chair upon the piazza and took up the Clarendon Eagle, which he did not read.

V

It was quite dark, and the lamps had been lit for some time, before the boy returned. His father, who had walked twice to the corner and back under one pretext or another, heard the gate click, and went into the house before his son should see him, so that when Lucius came up the steps he found only his mother waiting.

The boy's face was clean, for he had evidently washed it somewhere along the way, and it wore an expression of solemnity not usual to it.

"Well," said Mrs. Merrick, "did you see Uncle Ephraim?"

"Yes, ma'am. He was cooking his supper in the fireplace. He hasn't any stove, mamma. And he has only one chair, and he made me sit in it."

"Did you tell him you were sorry?"

"Yes, ma'am. He said he knowed I would be, when I studied 'bout it a little. He said boys is like puppies, they has ter be taught which way ter bite." The boy paused, for it was the first time he had ever reproduced the speech of the old man, and he did not know whether it would be permitted. His mother did not correct him. "And he told me about papa, mamma, when papa was little. He said papa was the smartest boy he ever saw, and learned his letters in two weeks, and used to cry when the fire went out because he couldn't see the board. Did papa cry, mamma?"

"I dare say he did," said Mrs. Merrick, with a smile which her son did not altogether understand.

"And he told me about grandmother. He said she was the handsomest woman in the county, and the kindest, and that she nursed him once when he had the fever and everybody else was afraid to come near him. And he said I had her eyes." Lucius was silent a moment. "He said I could come Saturday. He said he would show me how to make a trap for rabbits. Mamma, may I tell Tom Ballard about it?"

Mrs. Merrick hesitated, and glanced toward the sitting-room, where she knew her husband was listening.

"I would not tell Tom just yet," she said. "Tom would not understand."

From the sitting-room there came no sound; but Mr. Merrick, sitting in the lamplight with his paper upon his knee, was conscious of a certain discomfort which had nothing to do with his son. He had been reflecting, during the hour of the boy's absence, that it was a good many years since he himself had gone down to the cabin by the old brickyard; that he had passed Uncle Ephraim upon the street a hundred times with a nod and a "Good morning," and had bought his sweet potatoes with the condescending kindness which one extends to a deserving pensioner; and that he had never once, in all his prosperity, so much as asked the old man to sit down upon his piazza. He had taught his son to correct his speech and to keep his clothes clean, and he had supposed he was teaching him to be a gentleman. It had remained for Tom Ballard and a handful of chinaberries to show him what he had in fact been teaching.

When the family sat down to supper, Mr. Merrick asked the blessing, as was his custom. But he added to it, on that evening, a petition which his wife had not heard before, and which Lucius, being somewhat hungry, did not particularly remark. It was a brief petition for humility; and whether it was offered on behalf of the son or of the father, the record of the recording angel alone could show.

Here is an excerpt of Charles W. Chesnutt's writing, to show you their style:

Carteret fished from the depths of the waste-basket and handed to the general an eighteen by twenty-four sheet, poorly printed on cheap paper, with a "patent" inside, a number of advertisements of proprietary medicines, quack doctors, and fortune-tellers, and two or three columns of editorial and local news. Candor compels the admission that it was not an impressive sheet in any respect, except when regarded as the first local effort of a struggling people to make public expression of their life and aspirations. From this point of view it did not speak at all badly for a class to whom, a generation before, newspapers, books, and learning had been forbidden fruit.

"It's an elegant specimen of journalism, isn't it?" laughed the general, airily. "Listen to this 'ad':— "'Kinky, curly hair made straight by one application of our specific. Our face bleach will turn the skin of a black or brown person four or five shades lighter, and of a mulatto perfectly white. When you get the color you wish, stop using the preparation.' "Just look at those heads!—'Before using' and 'After using.' We'd better hurry, or there'll be no negroes to disfranchise! If they don't stop till they get the color they desire, and the stuff works according to contract, they'll all be white. Ah! what have we here? This looks as though it might be serious." Opening the sheet the general read aloud an editorial article, to which Carteret listened intently, his indignation increasing in strength from the first word to the last, while McBane's face grew darkly purple with anger. The article was a frank and somewhat bold discussion of lynching and its causes. It denied that most lynchings were for the offense most generally charged as their justification, and declared that, even of those seemingly traced to this cause, many were not for crimes at all, but for voluntary acts which might naturally be expected to follow from the miscegenation laws by which it was sought, in all the Southern States, to destroy liberty of contract, and, for the purpose of maintaining a fanciful purity of race, to make crimes of marriages to which neither nature nor religion nor the laws of other states interposed any insurmountable barrier. Such an article in a Northern newspaper would have attracted no special attention, and might merely have furnished food to an occasional reader for serious thought upon a subject not exactly agreeable; but coming from a colored man, in a Southern city, it was an indictment of the laws and social system of the South that could not fail of creating a profound sensation.

"Infamous—infamous!" exclaimed Carteret, his voice trembling with emotion. "The paper should be suppressed immediately."

"The impudent nigger ought to be horsewhipped and run out of town," growled McBane.

"Gentlemen," said the general soothingly, after the first burst of indignation had subsided, "I believe we can find a more effective use for this article, which, by the way, will not bear too close analysis,—there's some truth in it, at least there's an argument." "That is not the point," interrupted Carteret.

"No," interjected McBane with an oath, "that ain't at all the point. Truth or not, no damn nigger has any right to say it."

"This article," said Carteret, "violates an unwritten law of the South. If we are to tolerate this race of weaklings among us, until they are eliminated by the stress of competition, it must be upon terms which we lay down. One of our conditions is violated by this article, in which our wisdom is assailed, and our women made the subject of offensive comment. We must make known our disapproval."

"I say lynch the nigger, break up the press, and burn down the newspaper office," McBane responded promptly.

"Gentlemen," interposed the general, "would you mind suspending the discussion for a moment, while I mind Jerry across the street? I think I can then suggest a better plan." Carteret rang the bell for Jerry, who answered promptly. He had been expecting such a call ever since the gentlemen had gone in.

"Jerry," said the general, "step across to Brown's and tell him to send me three Calhoun cocktails. Wait for them,—here's the money."

"Yas, suh," replied Jerry, taking the proffered coin.

"And make has'e, charcoal," added McBane, "for we're gettin' damn dry." A momentary cloud of annoyance darkened Carteret's brow. McBane had always grated upon his aristocratic susceptibilities. The captain was an upstart, a product of the democratic idea operating upon the poor white man, the descendant of the indentured bondservant and the socially unfit. He had wealth and energy, however, and it was necessary to make use of him; but the example of such men was a strong incentive to Carteret in his campaign against the negro. It was distasteful enough to rub elbows with an illiterate and vulgar white man of no ancestry,—the risk of similar contact with negroes was to be avoided at any cost.
