column308:
The lamp had been lit in the front room of the little house on Mulberry Street for perhaps an hour before Edward Langley found courage to lay the letter upon the table. He had carried it in his breast pocket since noon, and it had seemed to grow heavier with every step he took between the schoolhouse and his own door. A man may bear a burden for a long while without complaint, if he bears it alone; it is when he must hand it to another that he first learns its true weight.

His wife sat opposite him, mending a small apron by the light which fell between them. She was a woman of perhaps six-and-twenty, of a warm brown complexion, with a face that might have been called handsome in any country where the standard of beauty was not fixed by the color of the skin. She had been a teacher in the same school before her marriage, and had given up the position, as the custom was, when she became a wife. Some vestiges of the schoolroom clung to her still, in a certain precision of speech and a habit of looking directly at whomever she addressed, which some of her neighbors thought proud and others merely unusual.

Langley himself was of so fair a complexion that a stranger, meeting him upon the street, would have hesitated to assign him to either side of that line which the laws of the state had drawn with such care, and which custom guarded with even greater vigilance. His hair was straight and brown, his eyes gray, and his features of the type which the novelists of the day were fond of describing as Saxon. That he was nevertheless a colored man, and principal of the colored graded school of Clarendon, was known to every one in the town, because every one in the town had known his mother. The knowledge of a man's antecedents is, in a small Southern community, a kind of public property, held in common and jealously preserved; and it is a property in which the man himself has the least interest of anybody.

"Lucinda," he said at length, "I have had a letter from Mr. Whitcomb."

She did not look up immediately, but her needle paused for the fraction of a second before it went on.

"The gentleman from Philadelphia," she said, "who came down to inspect the schools last spring?"

"The same. He has written to offer me a position."

"In Philadelphia?"

"In Philadelphia. In the offices of the Keystone Mutual Assurance Company, of which he is a director. The place is that of chief clerk in the actuarial department. The salary is eighteen hundred dollars a year, with the prospect of advancement."

Mrs. Langley laid down the apron upon her knee and looked at her husband. Eighteen hundred dollars was more than three times what the county paid him for teaching four hundred children, and keeping the schoolhouse in repair out of his own pocket, and enduring with what patience he could the visits of a school committee which regarded the education of colored children as, at best, a harmless indulgence, and at worst a dangerous experiment.

"That is very generous of Mr. Whitcomb," she said slowly. "I did not know that the insurance companies of Philadelphia employed colored men in such positions."

Langley did not answer at once. He took up the letter, unfolded it, and smoothed it upon the table with a care quite out of proportion to its need.

"They do not," he said.

There fell between them one of those silences which are more eloquent than speech, and in which two persons who know each other well may say more than they could utter in an hour of conversation. Mrs. Langley's face did not change, but something went out of it, as the light goes out of a window when a curtain is drawn.

"Then Mr. Whitcomb does not know," she said.

"Mr. Whitcomb does not know. He saw me at the schoolhouse, it is true, but he supposed, as the gentlemen from the North often do, that I was a white man engaged in missionary work among the freedmen. He spoke to me of my sacrifice, and praised my devotion, and I—" He hesitated.

"And you did not undeceive him."

"I did not think it necessary at the time. It seemed a matter of no consequence. He was here for an afternoon; he would never return. How was I to know that he would remember me, or that he would write?"

"And now?"

"And now," said Langley, rising and walking to the window, where he stood looking out into the darkness of the street, "and now I must decide."

Mrs. Langley took up her mending again, though it may be doubted whether she saw the stitches. When she spoke, her voice was even, with that careful evenness which betrays more feeling than a tremor.

"I think, Edward, that you have already decided. Otherwise you would have told me at dinner, as you tell me everything else, and we should have laughed together over Mr. Whitcomb's mistake. You have carried that letter about with you all day, and turned it over in your mind, and argued both sides of the question, and when you had reached a conclusion you brought it home to me. Is it not so?"

He turned from the window. "You do me an injustice, Lucinda. I have reached no conclusion. I have only considered."

"Then let us consider together," she said. "What is it that you would have to do?"

It was a simple question, but it struck at the very root of the matter, and Langley, who had rehearsed a dozen speeches upon the way home, found that none of them fitted it.

"I should go to Philadelphia," he said, "and take up the position. No one there would ask any questions. In a city of a million people, a man is what he appears to be. I should be simply Edward Langley, a clerk, of good education and correct habits, from somewhere in the South. In a year, or two years, I should be in a position to send for you."

"To send for me," she repeated. "And when I came, Edward, what should I be?"

He did not answer.

"I will tell you what I should be," she went on, still in that level voice. "I should be a colored woman from the South, married to a white man. Or I should be a servant in your house. Or I should not come at all. Those are the only three things that I could be. Which of them had you thought of?"

"You put it very harshly."

"I put it as the world would put it. You know very well that I could not pass for a Spaniard, or a Portuguese, or an Indian princess, or any of the other things that people pretend to be when they wish to be something other than what they are. Look at me, Edward. My mother was a black woman, and my father was very little lighter, and I have their color, and I am not ashamed of it. If I came to Philadelphia, I should come as I am, and the first time I was seen upon the street with you, your fine position would go the way of every other thing that has been built upon a lie."

Langley came back to the table and sat down. His face was pale, and there were lines about his mouth which his wife had not seen there before.

"Do you think I have not thought of all that?" he asked. "Do you suppose I would leave you here, and go away, and forget you? I am not that kind of man, Lucinda, and you know it. But consider, for one moment, what our life is here, and what it is likely to be. I have worked in that school for eight years. I have taught children to read who will never be permitted to vote, and to cipher who will never be permitted to keep any accounts but those of the white men they work for. I have stood with my hat in my hand before a committee of men, not one of whom could pass the examination which the state requires of me, and been told that the colored people ought to be grateful for what is done for them. I have seen my salary cut twice in three years, while that of the white principal across the river was raised. And you know what is going on now in this state. You have read the papers. You know what they are saying in the Clarion every morning, and what they mean to do at the next election."

"I know," she said quietly.

"Then you know that it is going to be worse, not better. They mean to take away the ballot, and after that the schools, and after that whatever else they choose. A man might wear himself out in this place, and die, and leave nothing behind him but a headstone in the colored cemetery, and a name that his children would be ashamed to bear in any decent community. I do not wish that for myself, Lucinda, and I do not wish it for you, and I do not wish it for"—he glanced, involuntarily, at the little apron in her lap—"for any one who may come after us."

It is one of the curious features of the race question, as it is discussed in the South, that those who are most concerned in it are least often consulted. Statesmen debate it in the halls of Congress, editors expound it in leading articles, clergymen preach upon it, and learned professors write books to prove, by the measurement of skulls and the comparison of statistics, that the problem is insoluble, or that it has already been solved, or that it never existed at all. But the real problem, in its most acute and painful form, is worked out in obscure houses like that on Mulberry Street, by men and women whose names are never printed, around kitchen tables lit by kerosene lamps; and it is there decided, not by any principle of statesmanship or science, but by the simple and terrible question of what a man will give up, and what he will keep.

Mrs. Langley had followed her husband's glance, and a slight color rose in her cheeks; but she did not lose the thread of her argument.

"You speak of the children who will come after us," she said. "Have you thought what they would be, in Philadelphia? If they took after you, they might grow up white, and go to white schools, and marry white people, and never know that their mother was a colored woman, unless you or I should be so unkind as to tell them. And if they took after me—as they might, Edward; you know they might—then they would be colored children, with a white father who could not acknowledge them. Which would you prefer? Or would you leave that to chance, as a man leaves the weather?"

"Lucinda!"

"No, let me speak. You have had all day to think, and I have had a quarter of an hour. I must say what is in my mind, or I shall never say it." She drew a long breath. "You say that our life here is hard, and so it is. But it is our life, and it is honest. When I walk down Front Street, and some white woman draws her skirts aside, I know that she is the one who should be ashamed, and not I. When the committee insults you, you go away with your hat in your hand, but your conscience is clear. There is nothing they can find out about us, because there is nothing hidden. But if you go to Philadelphia and take this place, you will be a man with a secret all the rest of your life. Every time a stranger looks at you twice, you will wonder whether he has seen through you. Every time a letter comes from the South, you will open it with your heart in your mouth. You will be afraid to visit your mother's grave. You will be afraid of me."

"I could never be afraid of you."

"You would be afraid of what I am. It is the same thing."

Langley rose again and paced the length of the little room. From the kitchen behind them came the sound of old Aunt Patsy, who did the heavy work of the household for a dollar a week and her dinner, singing to herself as she scoured the pots,—a long, wavering hymn about the river of Jordan, which she had learned in slavery days and had never seen any reason to give up.

"Dat ribber am chilly an' de ribber am wide," came the quavering voice, "but I got a home on de udder side,—"

"You talk," said Langley, stopping before his wife, "as though there were something wrong in what I propose. But where is the wrong? The white man has made this line, not I. He has drawn it with his laws, and enforced it with his shotguns, and he has said to me, upon one side of it you shall be a man, and upon the other you shall be something less. He has never asked my consent. If I choose to step across, I take nothing from him that he has any right to keep from me. I am not ashamed of my mother; God knows I am not. But I do not see why I should be punished all my life because her skin was dark and my father's was white, and the law of this state saw fit to give me her condition instead of his."

"I do not say that the line is just," replied his wife. "I say that it is there, and that you cannot cross it alone. You talk of stepping across as though you were stepping over a ditch. But you would leave behind you everything you have ever known—your mother's people, your friends, your school, the church where we were married,—and you would leave me behind you, too, whatever you may say now. I do not blame you for wishing to go. I have wished it myself, a hundred times. But I could not go with you, and live as you would have to live, and you could not take me, and keep what you went to get. And so it comes to this, Edward, and you might as well say it plainly, as I have said everything else plainly: you must choose between Mr. Whitcomb's eighteen hundred dollars and your wife."

There was a long silence. The hymn in the kitchen had come to an end, and the only sound in the room was the faint ticking of the clock upon the mantel, which had been a wedding present from the members of the Zion Methodist Church, and which bore upon a small brass plate the inscription, "To Mr. and Mrs. E. Langley, from their friends."

Langley stood looking down at his wife. She had not wept, and he knew that she would not weep, at least not in his presence; but he saw that her hands, lying upon the half-mended apron, were trembling, and the sight moved him more than any tears could have done.

"You think very meanly of me," he said at last, in a low voice.

"No," she answered. "I think very highly of you. That is why I am afraid. If you were a worse man, I should not care so much what became of you."

He sat down beside her and took one of the trembling hands in his. For a moment neither of them spoke.

"Do you know," he said presently, "what Mr. Whitcomb said to me that afternoon, as we stood in the schoolhouse door? He said that he had never seen a man give up so much for so little. He meant it as a compliment. I have thought of it a great many times since, and I think I have only today understood what he meant. He thought that I had given up the whole world, which belonged to me by right, to come and labor among a people who were not mine. He did not know that I had given up nothing, because I never had anything to give up; and that the people were mine, whether I would or no."

"And now," said Mrs. Langley, "you have the chance to make his compliment true."

He looked at her quickly. There was no bitterness in her face, but a certain sad clearness, as of one who has seen to the bottom of a thing and has no more illusions about it.

"If you go," she went on, "you will be giving up very much indeed, Edward, for what may turn out to be very little. And if you stay, you will be giving up a great deal also. I shall not pretend that you will not. Whichever way you choose, you will pay for it. That is the way they have arranged things in this country, for people like us. There is no road that does not have a toll-gate upon it."

Langley took up the letter once more and read it through, slowly, from the date to the signature. It was a kind letter, written by a kind man, who had no suspicion that it would cause any one a moment's pain. It spoke of the writer's admiration for the work being done in the South by men of Langley's stamp; of the need, in a great commercial enterprise, of men of character and education; of the pleasant society of Philadelphia, and the opportunities it offered to a young man of parts. It closed with the hope that Mr. Langley would find it possible to accept, and that his good wife—of whom Mr. Whitcomb had, of course, heard nothing, but whose existence he courteously assumed—would not object too strongly to the change.

"He hopes," said Langley, with a short laugh that had no mirth in it, "that you will not object too strongly to the change."

"You may tell him," said his wife, "that I do not object at all. You may tell him that I should be very glad to come to Philadelphia, if Philadelphia would be glad to have me."

Langley folded the letter and held it for a moment above the chimney of the lamp. Then he lowered it again and put it back in his pocket.

"I shall not answer it tonight," he said. "A man ought not to answer such a letter in a hurry."

His wife looked at him for a long moment, and then, without a word, took up her needle and resumed her work. But the stitches she set that evening, as she afterwards confessed, were so crooked that they had all to be picked out the next morning and done over again.

In the kitchen, Aunt Patsy, who had heard every word of the conversation through the thin partition, and had understood perhaps half of it, shook her head slowly over the dishpan.

"Dem Langleys," she muttered, "is good folks, but dey sho' does make trouble fer deyse'ves. Ef I wuz dat young man, an' could pass fer w'ite, I'd 'a' be'n gone 'fo' sundown, an' sont fer my wife w'en I got good an' ready. But den agin," she added, after a reflective pause, "ef I wuz Miss Lucindy, I'd 'a' tol' him de same as she did. Dey ain' no road in dis worl', chile, dat ain' got a toll-gate on it. Dat's de Lawd's truf, an' de w'ite folks' too."

And having thus summed up, with the brevity of a philosopher, a problem which had baffled wiser heads than hers, she wiped her hands upon her apron, banked the kitchen fire, and went home to her cabin by the railroad track, leaving the young couple in the front room to settle it as best they might.

Here is an excerpt of Charles W. Chesnutt's writing, to show you their style:

Carteret fished from the depths of the waste-basket and handed to the general an eighteen by twenty-four sheet, poorly printed on cheap paper, with a "patent" inside, a number of advertisements of proprietary medicines, quack doctors, and fortune-tellers, and two or three columns of editorial and local news. Candor compels the admission that it was not an impressive sheet in any respect, except when regarded as the first local effort of a struggling people to make public expression of their life and aspirations. From this point of view it did not speak at all badly for a class to whom, a generation before, newspapers, books, and learning had been forbidden fruit.

"It's an elegant specimen of journalism, isn't it?" laughed the general, airily. "Listen to this 'ad':— "'Kinky, curly hair made straight by one application of our specific. Our face bleach will turn the skin of a black or brown person four or five shades lighter, and of a mulatto perfectly white. When you get the color you wish, stop using the preparation.' "Just look at those heads!—'Before using' and 'After using.' We'd better hurry, or there'll be no negroes to disfranchise! If they don't stop till they get the color they desire, and the stuff works according to contract, they'll all be white. Ah! what have we here? This looks as though it might be serious." Opening the sheet the general read aloud an editorial article, to which Carteret listened intently, his indignation increasing in strength from the first word to the last, while McBane's face grew darkly purple with anger. The article was a frank and somewhat bold discussion of lynching and its causes. It denied that most lynchings were for the offense most generally charged as their justification, and declared that, even of those seemingly traced to this cause, many were not for crimes at all, but for voluntary acts which might naturally be expected to follow from the miscegenation laws by which it was sought, in all the Southern States, to destroy liberty of contract, and, for the purpose of maintaining a fanciful purity of race, to make crimes of marriages to which neither nature nor religion nor the laws of other states interposed any insurmountable barrier. Such an article in a Northern newspaper would have attracted no special attention, and might merely have furnished food to an occasional reader for serious thought upon a subject not exactly agreeable; but coming from a colored man, in a Southern city, it was an indictment of the laws and social system of the South that could not fail of creating a profound sensation.

"Infamous—infamous!" exclaimed Carteret, his voice trembling with emotion. "The paper should be suppressed immediately."

"The impudent nigger ought to be horsewhipped and run out of town," growled McBane.

"Gentlemen," said the general soothingly, after the first burst of indignation had subsided, "I believe we can find a more effective use for this article, which, by the way, will not bear too close analysis,—there's some truth in it, at least there's an argument." "That is not the point," interrupted Carteret.

"No," interjected McBane with an oath, "that ain't at all the point. Truth or not, no damn nigger has any right to say it."

"This article," said Carteret, "violates an unwritten law of the South. If we are to tolerate this race of weaklings among us, until they are eliminated by the stress of competition, it must be upon terms which we lay down. One of our conditions is violated by this article, in which our wisdom is assailed, and our women made the subject of offensive comment. We must make known our disapproval."

"I say lynch the nigger, break up the press, and burn down the newspaper office," McBane responded promptly.

"Gentlemen," interposed the general, "would you mind suspending the discussion for a moment, while I mind Jerry across the street? I think I can then suggest a better plan." Carteret rang the bell for Jerry, who answered promptly. He had been expecting such a call ever since the gentlemen had gone in.

"Jerry," said the general, "step across to Brown's and tell him to send me three Calhoun cocktails. Wait for them,—here's the money."

"Yas, suh," replied Jerry, taking the proffered coin.

"And make has'e, charcoal," added McBane, "for we're gettin' damn dry." A momentary cloud of annoyance darkened Carteret's brow. McBane had always grated upon his aristocratic susceptibilities. The captain was an upstart, a product of the democratic idea operating upon the poor white man, the descendant of the indentured bondservant and the socially unfit. He had wealth and energy, however, and it was necessary to make use of him; but the example of such men was a strong incentive to Carteret in his campaign against the negro. It was distasteful enough to rub elbows with an illiterate and vulgar white man of no ancestry,—the risk of similar contact with negroes was to be avoided at any cost. He could hardly expect McBane to be a gentleman, but when among men of that class he might at least try to imitate their manners. A gentleman did not order his own servants around offensively, to say nothing of another's. The general had observed Carteret's annoyance, and remarked pleasantly while they waited for the servant's return:— "Jerry, now, is a very good negro. He's not one of your new negroes, who think themselves as good as white men, and want to run the government. Jerry knows his place,—he is respectful, humble, obedient, and content with the face and place assigned to him by nature."

"Yes, he's one of the best of 'em," sneered McBane. "He'll call any man 'master' for a quarter, or 'God' for half a dollar; for a dollar he'll grovel at your feet, and for a cast-off coat you can buy an option on his immortal soul,—if he has one! I've handled niggers for ten years, and I know 'em from the ground up. They're all alike,—they're a scrub race, an affliction to the country, and the quicker we're rid of 'em all the better." Carteret had nothing to say by way of dissent. McBane's sentiments, in their last analysis, were much the same as his, though he would have expressed them less brutally. "The negro," observed the general, daintily flicking the ash from his cigar, "is all right in his place and very useful to the community. We lived on his labor for quite a long time, and lived very well. Nevertheless we are better off without slavery, for we can get more out of the free negro, and with less responsibility. I really do not see how we could get along without the negroes. If they were all like Jerry, we'd have no trouble with them." Having procured the drinks, Jerry, the momentary subject of the race discussion which goes on eternally in the South, was making his way back across the street, somewhat disturbed in mind.

"O Lawd!" he groaned, "I never troubles trouble till trouble troubles me; but w'en I got dem drinks befo', Gin'l Belmont gimme half a dollar an' tol' me ter keep de change. Dis time he didn' say nothin' 'bout de change. I s'pose he jes' fergot erbout it, but w'at is a po' nigger gwine ter do w'en he has ter conten' wid w'ite folks's fergitfulniss? I don' see no way but ter do some fergittin' myse'f. I'll jes' stan' outside de do' here till dey gits so wrop' up in deir talk dat dey won' 'member nothin' e'se, an' den at de right minute I'll ban' de glasses 'roun, an' moa' lackly de gin'l 'll fergit all 'bout de change." While Jerry stood outside, the conversation within was plainly audible, and some inkling of its purport filtered through his mind.

"Now, gentlemen," the general was saying, "here's my plan. That editorial in the negro newspaper is good campaign matter, but we should reserve it until it will be most effective. Suppose we just stick it in a pigeon-hole, and let the editor,—what's his name?"

"The nigger's name is Barber," replied McBane. "I'd like to have him under me for a month or two; he'd write no more editorials."

"Let Barber have all the rope he wants," resumed the general, "and he'll be sure to hang himself. In the mean time we will continue to work up public opinion,—we can use this letter privately for that purpose,—and when the state campaign opens we'll print the editorial, with suitable comment, scatter it broadcast throughout the state, fire the Southern heart, organize the white people on the color line, have a little demonstration with red shirts and shotguns, scare the negroes into fits, win the state for white supremacy, and teach our colored fellow citizens that we are tired of negro domination and have put an end to it forever. The Afro-American Banner will doubtless die about the same time."

"And so will the editor!" exclaimed McBane ferociously; "I'll see to that. But I wonder where that nigger is with them cocktails? I'm so thirsty I could swallow blue blazes."

"Here's yo' drinks, gin'l," announced Jerry, entering with the glasses on a tray. The gentlemen exchanged compliments and imbibed—McBane at a gulp, Carteret with more deliberation, leaving about half the contents of his glass. The general drank slowly, with every sign of appreciation. "If the illustrious statesman," he observed, "whose name this mixture bears, had done nothing more than invent it, his fame would still deserve to go thundering down the endless ages."

"It ain't bad liquor," assented McBane, smacking his lips. Jerry received the empty glasses on the tray and left the room. He had scarcely gained the hall when the general called him back.

"O Lawd!" groaned Jerry, "he's gwine ter ax me fer de change. Yas, suh, yas, suh; comin', gin'l, comin', suh!"

"You may keep the change, Jerry," said the general. Jerry's face grew radiant at this announcement. "Yas, suh, gin'l; thank y', suh; much obleedzed, suh. I wuz jus' gwine ter fetch it in, suh, w'en I had put de tray down. Thank y', suh, truly, suh!" Jerry backed and bowed himself out into the hall.

"Dat wuz a close shave," he muttered, as he swallowed the remaining contents of Major Carteret's glass. "I 'lowed dem twenty cents wuz gone dat time,—an' whar I wuz gwine ter git de money ter take my gal ter de chu'ch festibal ter-night, de Lawd only knows!—'less'n I borried it offn Mr. Ellis, an' I owes him sixty cents a'ready. But I wonduh w'at dem w'ite folks in dere is up ter? Dere's one thing sho',—dey're gwine ter git after de niggers some way er 'nuther, an' w'en dey does, whar is Jerry gwine ter be? Dat's de mos' impo'tantes' question. I'm gwine ter look at dat newspaper dey be'n talkin' 'bout, an' 'less'n my min' changes might'ly, I'm gwine ter keep my mouf shet an' stan' in wid de Angry-Saxon race,—ez dey calls deyse'ves nowadays,—an' keep on de right side er my bread an' meat. Wat nigger ever give me twenty cents in all my bawn days?"

"By the way, major," said the general, who lingered behind McBane as they were leaving, "is Miss Clara's marriage definitely settled upon?"

"Well, general, not exactly; but it's the understanding that they will marry when they are old enough."

"I was merely thinking," the general went on, "that if I were you I'd speak to Tom about cards and liquor. He gives more time to both than a young man can afford. I'm speaking in his interest and in Miss Clara's,—we of the old families ought to stand together."

"Thank you, general, for the hint. I'll act upon it." This political conference was fruitful in results. Acting upon the plans there laid out, McBane traveled extensively through the state, working up sentiment in favor of the new movement. He possessed a certain forceful eloquence; and white supremacy was so obviously the divine intention that he had merely to affirm the doctrine in order to secure adherents. General Belmont, whose business required him to spend much of the winter in Washington and New York, lost no opportunity to get the ear of lawmakers, editors, and other leaders of national opinion, and to impress upon them, with persuasive eloquence, the impossibility of maintaining existing conditions, and the tremendous blunder which had been made in conferring the franchise upon the emancipated race. Carteret conducted the press campaign, and held out to the Republicans of the North the glittering hope that, with the elimination of the negro vote, and a proper deference to Southern feeling, a strong white Republican party might be built up in the New South. How well the bait took is a matter of history,—but the promised result is still in the future. The disfranchisement of the negro has merely changed the form of the same old problem. The negro had no vote before the rebellion, and few other rights, and yet the negro question was, for a century, the pivot of American politics. It plunged the nation into a bloody war, and it will trouble the American government and the American conscience until a sustained attempt is made to settle it upon principles of justice and equity. The personal ambitions entertained by the leaders of this movement are but slightly involved in this story. McBane's aims have been touched upon elsewhere. The general would have accepted the nomination for governor of the state, with a vision of a senatorship in the future. Carteret hoped to vindicate the supremacy of his race, and make the state fit for his son to live in, and, incidentally, he would not refuse any office, worthy of his dignity, which a grateful people might thrust upon him. So powerful a combination of bigot, self-seeking demagogue, and astute politician was fraught with grave menace to the peace of the state and the liberties of the people,—by which is meant the whole people, and not any one class, sought to be built up at the expense of another.

Carteret did not forget what General Belmont had said in regard to Tom. The major himself had been young, not so very long ago, and was inclined toward indulgence for the foibles of youth. A young gentleman should have a certain knowledge of life,—but there were limits. Clara's future happiness must not be imperiled. The opportunity to carry out this purpose was not long delayed. Old Mr. Delamere wished to sell some timber which had been cut at Belleview, and sent Tom down to the Chronicle office to leave an advertisement. The major saw him at the desk, invited him into his sanctum, and delivered him a mild lecture. The major was kind, and talked in a fatherly way about the danger of extremes, the beauty of moderation, and the value of discretion as a rule of conduct. He mentioned collaterally the unblemished honor of a fine old family, its contemplated alliance with his own, and dwelt upon the sweet simplicity of Clara's character. The major was a man of feeling and of tact, and could not have put the subject in a way less calculated to wound the amour propre of a very young man.

"He'll call any man 'master' for a quarter, or 'God' for half a dollar; for a dollar he'll grovel at your feet, and for a cast-off coat you can buy an option on his immortal soul,—if he has one! I've handled niggers for ten years, and I know 'em from the ground up. They're all alike,—they're a scrub race, an affliction to the country, and the quicker we're rid of 'em all the better." Carteret had nothing to say by way of dissent. McBane's sentiments, in their last analysis, were much the same as his, though he would have expressed them less brutally. "The negro," observed the general, daintily flicking the ash from his cigar, "is all right in his place and very useful to the community. We lived on his labor for quite a long time, and lived very well. Nevertheless we are better off without slavery, for we can get more out of the free negro, and with less responsibility. I really do not see how we could get along without the negroes. If they were all like Jerry, we'd have no trouble with them." Having procured the drinks, Jerry, the momentary subject of the race discussion which goes on eternally in the South, was making his way back across the street, somewhat disturbed in mind.

"O Lawd!" he groaned, "I never troubles trouble till trouble troubles me; but w'en I got dem drinks befo', Gin'l Belmont gimme half a dollar an' tol' me ter keep de change. Dis time he didn' say nothin' 'bout de change. I s'pose he jes' fergot erbout it, but w'at is a po' nigger gwine ter do w'en he has ter conten' wid w'ite folks's fergitfulniss? I don' see no way but ter do some fergittin' myse'f. I'll jes' stan' outside de do' here till dey gits so wrop' up in deir talk dat dey won' 'member nothin' e'se, an' den at de right minute I'll ban' de glasses 'roun, an' moa' lackly de gin'l 'll fergit all 'bout de change." While Jerry stood outside, the conversation within was plainly audible, and some inkling of its purport filtered through his mind.

"Now, gentlemen," the general was saying, "here's my plan. That editorial in the negro newspaper is good campaign matter, but we should reserve it until it will be most effective. Suppose we just stick it in a pigeon-hole, and let the editor,—what's his name?"

"The nigger's name is Barber," replied McBane. "I'd like to have him under me for a month or two; he'd write no more editorials."

"Let Barber have all the rope he wants," resumed the general, "and he'll be sure to hang himself. In the mean time we will continue to work up public opinion,—we can use this letter privately for that purpose,—and when the state campaign opens we'll print the editorial, with suitable comment, scatter it broadcast throughout the state, fire the Southern heart, organize the white people on the color line, have a little demonstration with red shirts and shotguns, scare the negroes into fits, win the state for white supremacy, and teach our colored fellow citizens that we are tired of negro domination and have put an end to it forever. The Afro-American Banner will doubtless die about the same time."

"And so will the editor!" exclaimed McBane ferociously; "I'll see to that. But I wonder where that nigger is with them cocktails? I'm so thirsty I could swallow blue blazes."

"Here's yo' drinks, gin'l," announced Jerry, entering with the glasses on a tray. The gentlemen exchanged compliments and imbibed—McBane at a gulp, Carteret with more deliberation, leaving about half the contents of his glass. The general drank slowly, with every sign of appreciation. "If the illustrious statesman," he observed, "whose name this mixture bears, had done nothing more than invent it, his fame would still deserve to go thundering down the endless ages."

"It ain't bad liquor," assented McBane, smacking his lips. Jerry received the empty glasses on the tray and left the room. He had scarcely gained the hall when the general called him back.

"O Lawd!" groaned Jerry, "he's gwine ter ax me fer de change. Yas, suh, yas, suh; comin', gin'l, comin', suh!"

"You may keep the change, Jerry," said the general. Jerry's face grew radiant at this announcement. "Yas, suh, gin'l; thank y', suh; much obleedzed, suh. I wuz jus' gwine ter fetch it in, suh, w'en I had put de tray down. Thank y', suh, truly, suh!" Jerry backed and bowed himself out into the hall.

"Dat wuz a close shave," he muttered, as he swallowed the remaining contents of Major Carteret's glass. "I 'lowed dem twenty cents wuz gone dat time,—an' whar I wuz gwine ter git de money ter take my gal ter de chu'ch festibal ter-night, de Lawd only knows!—'less'n I borried it offn Mr. Ellis, an' I owes him sixty cents a'ready. But I wonduh w'at dem w'ite folks in dere is up ter? Dere's one thing sho',—dey're gwine ter git after de niggers some way er 'nuther, an' w'en dey does, whar is Jerry gwine ter be? Dat's de mos' impo'tantes' question. I'm gwine ter look at dat newspaper dey be'n talkin' 'bout, an' 'less'n my min' changes might'ly, I'm gwine ter keep my mouf shet an' stan' in wid de Angry-Saxon race,—ez dey calls deyse'ves nowadays,—an' keep on de right side er my bread an' meat. Wat nigger ever give me twenty cents in all my bawn days?"

"By the way, major," said the general, who lingered behind McBane as they were leaving, "is Miss Clara's marriage definitely settled upon?"

"Well, general, not exactly; but it's the understanding that they will marry when they are old enough."

"I was merely thinking," the general went on, "that if I were you I'd speak to Tom about cards and liquor. He gives more time to both than a young man can afford. I'm speaking in his interest and in Miss Clara's,—we of the old families ought to stand together."

"Thank you, general, for the hint. I'll act upon it." This political conference was fruitful in results. Acting upon the plans there laid out, McBane traveled extensively through the state, working up sentiment in favor of the new movement. He possessed a certain forceful eloquence; and white supremacy was so obviously the divine intention that he had merely to affirm the doctrine in order to secure adherents. General Belmont, whose business required him to spend much of the winter in Washington and New York, lost no opportunity to get the ear of lawmakers, editors, and other leaders of national opinion, and to impress upon them, with persuasive eloquence, the impossibility of maintaining existing conditions, and the tremendous blunder which had been made in conferring the franchise upon the emancipated race. Carteret conducted the press campaign, and held out to the Republicans of the North the glittering hope that, with the elimination of the negro vote, and a proper deference to Southern feeling, a strong white Republican party might be built up in the New South. How well the bait took is a matter of history,—but the promised result is still in the future. The disfranchisement of the negro has merely changed the form of the same old problem. The negro had no vote before the rebellion, and few other rights, and yet the negro question was, for a century, the pivot of American politics. It plunged the nation into a bloody war, and it will trouble the American government and the American conscience until a sustained attempt is made to settle it upon principles of justice and equity. The personal ambitions entertained by the leaders of this movement are but slightly involved in this story. McBane's aims have been touched upon elsewhere. The general would have accepted the nomination for governor of the state, with a vision of a senatorship in the future. Carteret hoped to vindicate the supremacy of his race, and make the state fit for his son to live in, and, incidentally, he would not refuse any office, worthy of his dignity, which a grateful people might thrust upon him. So powerful a combination of bigot, self-seeking demagogue, and astute politician was fraught with grave menace to the peace of the state and the liberties of the people,—by which is meant the whole people, and not any one class, sought to be built up at the expense of another.

Carteret did not forget what General Belmont had said in regard to Tom. The major himself had been young, not so very long ago, and was inclined toward indulgence for the foibles of youth. A young gentleman should have a certain knowledge of life,—but there were limits. Clara's future happiness must not be imperiled. The opportunity to carry out this purpose was not long delayed. Old Mr. Delamere wished to sell some timber which had been cut at Belleview, and sent Tom down to the Chronicle office to leave an advertisement. The major saw him at the desk, invited him into his sanctum, and delivered him a mild lecture. The major was kind, and talked in a fatherly way about the danger of extremes, the beauty of moderation, and the value of discretion as a rule of conduct. He mentioned collaterally the unblemished honor of a fine old family, its contemplated alliance with his own, and dwelt upon the sweet simplicity of Clara's character. The major was a man of feeling and of tact, and could not have put the subject in a way less calculated to wound the amour propre of a very young man.

The train from the North, which was due at Clarendon at four o'clock in the afternoon, arrived, as was its custom, somewhat after five, and discharged upon the platform a small company of passengers. Among them was a well-dressed brown man of perhaps five and thirty, with a neatly trimmed beard, a valise of good leather, and that indefinable air of having been somewhere else which a Southern town detects in a stranger as readily as a dog detects a cat. He descended from the forward coach, the one placed next behind the baggage car, where the smoke and cinders were thickest, and which bore over its door, in letters freshly painted, the legend "For Colored Passengers." The law that put it there had been enacted during his absence. He had read of it in the newspapers, and had expressed his opinion of it, with some warmth, to a circle of friends in a city where such laws were matters of theory. But it is one thing to read of a wall and quite another to be put behind it, and Henry Pryor had ridden the last two hundred miles of his journey in a frame of mind which he would have found it difficult to describe to his Northern acquaintances, and which he did not at all intend to describe to his cousin.

That cousin, Isaac Merritt, stood at the end of the platform with a buggy and a sorrel horse. Fifteen years had passed since the two young men, then scarcely more than boys, had parted at this same station, one to seek his fortune in the North and the other to stay at home and make his fortune where he was. If either had been asked which of them had chosen the better part, he would have answered promptly and in his own favor. That is the fortunate disposition of most men, and it is perhaps as well. If every man thought his neighbor's lot the better, there would be a great deal of moving about and very little settling down.

Isaac had grown stout. The slender youth who had once outrun every boy on the Cape Fear road now carried before him a comfortable expanse of waistcoat, across which hung a watch chain of considerable weight, though its precise metallic composition was perhaps open to question. His face, of a deep and even brown, was as round and good-humored as a harvest moon, and his small eyes twinkled with a shrewdness that had been sharpened by long practice in the art, so necessary to a man of his complexion in that community, of seeing a great deal while appearing to see nothing at all.

"Well, well, well!" he exclaimed, advancing with both hands outstretched. "If it ain't Henry! I'd have knowed you anywhere,—leastways I'd have knowed you was somebody's cousin. You've got so mighty fine I was 'most afraid to come up and speak to you."

"Nonsense, Isaac," returned the traveler, grasping the proffered hands warmly. "It's you who've grown prosperous. I should hardly have known you, except for your voice. You haven't changed that."

"No," laughed Isaac, "I've kep' my voice. A man in my business needs it. I've got to talk one way to one set of customers and another way to another, but it's the same voice, I reckon, all the time. Get right in, Henry. Granny's been lookin' for you since daybreak, and Lucinda's killed a chicken, and there's no tellin' what else."

The buggy rolled up Front Street and turned into the main thoroughfare of the town. Henry looked about him with the curious double vision of a man who returns to the scenes of his youth: seeing at once the town as it was and the town as he remembered it, and finding the two not always in agreement. The market house still stood in the middle of the square, with the old bell in its cupola. Beneath that bell, within the memory of men still living, human beings had been sold at auction. Some of these men, it may be added, had prospered by the sales, and now sat on the bench before the court house and discussed the decay of the times. A new bank building of red brick rose where an old tavern had been. The streets were no better paved than formerly, but there were more of them, and the town had crept out in several directions, as towns will, with a certain indifference to the plans of the founders.

"You've got a new court house, I see," remarked Henry.

"Yes," said Isaac, "and a new jail. The jail come first. Folks said it was needed more."

Henry glanced at his cousin, but Isaac's face was a study in placid innocence, and his eyes were fixed upon the sorrel's ears.

"And how is business with you, Isaac?" he asked.

"Tol'able, Henry, tol'able. I've got the grocery on Mulberry Street, the one ole Mr. Hargrove used to have, and I own the buildin', and two little houses back of it that I rent out, and a piece of land out on the Wilmington road that I'm holdin' for the town to grow up to. I ain't rich, but I ain't beholden to nobody, and the bank lets me have money when I want it, which is more'n it does for some white folks I could name, if I was a namin' man, which I ain't."

There was in this recital a pride which Isaac made no effort to conceal, and which, it must be admitted, was not without justification. To have accumulated property in a community where the laws, the customs, and the sentiment of the dominant class were alike arrayed against such accumulation by men of his race was an achievement of no mean order. It is easy enough for a man to grow rich when the current sets in his direction. To row against the tide and still make headway requires a stout arm and a steady eye.

The house to which Isaac drove his guest stood in a quiet street on the edge of that quarter of the town which had come, by a process of gradual and unlegislated separation, to be inhabited chiefly by colored people. It was a story and a half in height, painted white, with green blinds, a deep piazza across the front, and a yard in which zinnias and marigolds bloomed in a profusion that bespoke a careful hand. On the piazza, in a split-bottomed rocking-chair, sat a very old woman. She wore a white head-handkerchief and a spotless apron, and her face, black and wrinkled as a walnut, lit up at the sight of the buggy with a radiance that years could not dim.

"Is dat him?" she cried, rising with the aid of a stick. "Is dat my Henry? Come heah, chile, come heah, an' lemme look at you! Lawd, Lawd, de Lawd done let me live ter see dis day!"

Henry sprang from the buggy and ran up the steps, and for a moment the old woman held him in an embrace from which he, a grown man and the father of children, felt no inclination to escape.

"You done got so tall," she said at length, holding him off and surveying him with an affectionate scrutiny. "An' you done growed a beard. Yo' mammy would 'a' be'n proud ter see you. She allus said you wuz gwine ter be somebody. I 'members de time you an' Isaac stole Mars Jim McRae's watermillions an' ate 'em down in de branch, an' got so sick yo' mammy had ter dose you bofe wid castor-ile. An' Isaac he lied 'bout it, an' you tol' de truf, an' de one dat lied didn' git whipped, an' de one dat tol' de truf did. I ain' nevuh fergot dat."

"Nor I, granny," laughed Henry. "It was my first lesson in Southern ethics."

"I don' know nothin' 'bout no ethics," returned the old woman, "but I knows you bofe got sick."

Lucinda Merritt, a comely, brisk woman with a manner at once hospitable and commanding, now appeared in the doorway and welcomed the guest. Behind her, peeping round her skirts with the frank curiosity of childhood, were three children of assorted sizes. The eldest was a slender boy of fourteen, with a high forehead and grave eyes, whom his father presented, with evident pride, as Frederick.

"Named him after Fred'rick Douglass," said Isaac, in a lower tone. "Course I don't tell everybody that. Down at the store folks thinks he's named for Fred'rick the Great, if they think about it at all, which mostly they don't."

The supper which followed was of a character to justify Isaac's prediction. There was fried chicken and hot biscuit, sweet potatoes baked in their jackets, collards cooked with a piece of side meat, a dish of rice and gravy, preserved figs, and a pound cake of such golden richness that Henry, whose wife was a Northern woman and an excellent housekeeper, felt a pang of something very like disloyalty in praising it. The meal was seasoned with reminiscence. Old names were spoken that Henry had not heard in years. Some belonged to people who were dead, some to people who had gone away, and some to people who had stayed and come to good or ill fortune according to their deserts, or, as more frequently happens, in total disregard of them.

"And what became of Sam Boney?" asked Henry. "He was the smartest boy in the colored school."

"Sam?" said Isaac. "Sam went to teachin', and then he went to preachin', and then he went to politics. He was in the legislature two terms, back in the time when we had some votes. Then things changed, and Sam couldn't change with 'em, and now he's a porter on the Pullman cars, runnin' between New York and Florida. He makes more money than he did in the legislature, and he says the company is mo' particular 'bout his manners than the State ever was."

"It seems a waste," said Henry.

"Lots of things seems a waste," observed Isaac philosophically, helping himself to another biscuit, "till you get used to 'em."

After supper, when the dishes had been cleared away and the children sent, with some protest, to bed, the two men sat upon the piazza in the cool of the evening. The old grandmother dozed in her rocking-chair between them. A mockingbird sang in the chinaberry tree, and somewhere down the street a woman was singing a hymn as she worked, in a voice that rose and fell like the wind in the pines. The moon came up over the roofs, full and yellow, and the shadows of the cedars lay black upon the white sand of the yard.

"Now, Henry," said Isaac, lighting a cigar and offering one to his cousin, "tell me 'bout yo'self. Yo' letters was mighty short. You always was a better hand at talkin' than writin', in spite of all yo' schoolin'."

Henry told his story. It was not, in its outlines, a remarkable one; but it had cost him something to live, and he told it with a certain quiet satisfaction. He had gone to Cleveland with eleven dollars in his pocket and a letter of introduction to a minister. He had worked as a hotel waiter and studied stenography at night. He had become, by dint of patience and of a skill which presently made his services sought after, a reporter in the courts, where he had taken down, with impartial accuracy, the testimony of murderers and millionaires. He had married a young woman whom he had met at a church social, a school teacher, the daughter of a colored barber who had been a station master on the Underground Railroad. He owned a house on a street where his neighbors were Germans and Irishmen and Bohemians, who borrowed his lawn mower and returned it, or failed to return it, quite without regard to the complexion of its owner. His two children went to the public school with the children of these neighbors, and had once been beaten in a spelling match by the son of a Polish shoemaker, a defeat which they had taken much to heart.

"And they let you vote?" asked Isaac.

"Of course they let me vote."

"And there ain't no separate cars?"

"None."

"And you can go in any restaurant?"

Henry hesitated. Candor compelled him to admit that there were restaurants in Cleveland where a colored man would not be welcome, and that the law, which was quite clear upon the subject, was not always so clear in its application. There were hotels where the clerk would discover that every room was taken. There were trades in which a colored man, however skillful, would find the door politely but firmly closed. The North, he confessed, was not the Promised Land. It was merely a country in which the promise had been written down, and where a man might, with sufficient persistence, sometimes collect upon it.

"I thought so," said Isaac, with something like satisfaction. "Folks that come back from up yonder always talks big at first, but when you get 'em settled down on the piazza after supper, it's 'most always the same story. White folks is white folks, Henry, wherever you find 'em."

"There is a difference, Isaac," returned Henry, with some warmth, "between a man who wrongs you in spite of the law, and a law that is made for the purpose of wronging you. In the one case you have a grievance. In the other you have a government."

Isaac smoked for a while in silence. The mockingbird had ceased its song, and the hymn down the street had died away. The old woman stirred in her chair and murmured something in her sleep.

"I ain't sayin' you're wrong," said Isaac at length. "I ain't never said nothin' was right that wasn't. But I'll tell you how it is with me, Henry, and then you can judge. When you left here, I had nothin'. Now I've got somethin'. Every dollar I've got, I made out of the folks in this town, white and colored. The white folks trades with me 'cause I give 'em good goods and fair weight, and 'cause they know I'm what they call a safe man. Do you know what a safe man is, Henry?"

"I can guess."

"A safe man," continued Isaac, "is a colored man that keeps his mouth shut and his books straight. I keeps both. When the election come round, two years ago, and they had the red shirts ridin' up and down the roads at night, I stayed in my store and sold groceries. Some of the colored folks called me a coward. Maybe I was. But when the trouble was over, there was three colored men's stores burnt in this county, and mine wasn't one of 'em. And Lawyer Haywood, that was one of the leaders, come in next mornin' and bought a sack of flour and called me 'Ike' and asked after my family, just like nothin' had happened. And I sold him the flour, and asked after his family, just like nothin' had happened."

"And you call that living, Isaac?"

"I call it stayin' alive," replied Isaac simply, "which comes first."

Henry made no answer. He was a just man, and he was aware that his own courage had never been put to so sore a test. It is a comparatively easy matter to be brave at a distance of seven hundred miles. Many a man who has stood up valiantly for the rights of his race in a Northern church convention would have found his eloquence strangely abated in the presence of a mob with torches. Nor was Henry blind to the fact that his cousin's prudence, however humiliating in its manifestations, had built a house and fed a family and laid aside a modest competence, in a land where every circumstance had conspired to prevent it. There is a heroism of endurance as well as of resistance. The world, which loves a spectacle, seldom gives it its due.

"I don't blame you, Isaac," he said at length. "I'm not sure I'd have done differently. I only wonder sometimes how long it can go on."

"So does I," said Isaac. "That's what I wanted to talk to you about."

He removed his cigar from his lips and examined the glowing end of it with great attention, as though it contained some secret he was anxious to discover.

"It's Fred'rick," he said. "He's a smart boy, Henry,—smarter'n I ever was, smarter'n you, maybe, though I wouldn't say that before company. He's got his head in a book all the time. The teacher at the colored school says she can't learn him nothin' more, 'cause she don't know nothin' more to learn him. He wants to be a doctor. A doctor! Down here a colored doctor can doctor colored folks, if they'll let him, which mostly they'd ruther have a white one, thinkin' he must know more. And he can't go in the hospital, and he can't go in the medical society, and if one of his patients dies he's a murderer, and if one of 'em gets well it's the will of God."

"Send him to me," said Henry quickly. "He can go to the high school in Cleveland, and then to the university. There'll be a place for him in my house, and a welcome."

Isaac looked at his cousin. In the moonlight Henry saw that the round brown face, so habitually composed into an expression of cheerful vacancy, was working with an emotion that it seemed unaccustomed to express.

"That's what I hoped you'd say," said Isaac huskily. "I've been savin' for it. I've got the money laid by. Lucinda don't want him to go, and granny don't know nothin' about it yet. But I've thought it all out, nights, when I couldn't sleep. I've bowed and scraped for twenty years, Henry. I reckon I'll bow and scrape the rest of my days, and I don't complain. But I ain't goin' to raise a son to do it after me. One safe man in the family is enough."

The old woman in the rocking-chair opened her eyes.

"W'at dat you all talkin' 'bout?" she demanded. "I heerd my name."

"We was talkin' 'bout watermelons, granny," said Isaac promptly.

"Watermillions!" she exclaimed, with a scornful toss of the white head-handkerchief. "You allus wuz talkin' 'bout watermillions. Henry, did Isaac evuh tell you de truf 'bout dem watermillions in yo' life?"

"Never, granny," said Henry gravely.

"Den he ain' changed none," declared the old woman, with a chuckle, and composed herself once more to slumber.

The two men sat on in silence. The moon climbed higher and grew smaller and whiter as it climbed. The shadows of the cedars shortened upon the sand. In the room above, a boy lay awake by an open window, with a book beneath his pillow, and listened to the murmur of voices below. He did not know that his future was being disposed of, nor that the price of it was a part of his father's pride. Had he known, he would scarcely have understood. The young seldom understand what they cost their elders, and it is perhaps a merciful provision of nature that they should not.

It was late when the cousins rose to go indoors. At the threshold Isaac paused and laid his hand upon Henry's arm.

"You 'member the mill pond, Henry?" he said. "Out on the Raleigh road, where we used to go swimmin'?"

"I remember it."

"They've drained it," said Isaac. "Built a cotton mill there. White folks works in it,—po' white folks, women and children mostly, twelve hours a day. They don't let no colored folks work in it at all. Sometimes when I drive by of a mornin', and see them little white children goin' in at the gate, with their faces all pale and pinched, I think maybe the Lord ain't got through with this country yet, and maybe He ain't goin' to settle it the way any of us expects."

He opened the door, and the two men went in. The sorrel horse stamped in his stall, the mockingbird took up its song again in the chinaberry tree, and the town of Clarendon slept, white and black, beneath the same impartial moon, quite as though nothing had happened.

Here is an excerpt of Charles W. Chesnutt's writing, to show you their style:

Carteret fished from the depths of the waste-basket and handed to the general an eighteen by twenty-four sheet, poorly printed on cheap paper, with a "patent" inside, a number of advertisements of proprietary medicines, quack doctors, and fortune-tellers, and two or three columns of editorial and local news. Candor compels the admission that it was not an impressive sheet in any respect, except when regarded as the first local effort of a struggling people to make public expression of their life and aspirations. From this point of view it did not speak at all badly for a class to whom, a generation before, newspapers, books, and learning had been forbidden fruit.

"It's an elegant specimen of journalism, isn't it?" laughed the general, airily. "Listen to this 'ad':— "'Kinky, curly hair made straight by one application of our specific. Our face bleach will turn the skin of a black or brown person four or five shades lighter, and of a mulatto perfectly white. When you get the color you wish, stop using the preparation.' "Just look at those heads!—'Before using' and 'After using.' We'd better hurry, or there'll be no negroes to disfranchise! If they don't stop till they get the color they desire, and the stuff works according to contract, they'll all be white. Ah! what have we here? This looks as though it might be serious." Opening the sheet the general read aloud an editorial article, to which Carteret listened intently, his indignation increasing in strength from the first word to the last, while McBane's face grew darkly purple with anger. The article was a frank and somewhat bold discussion of lynching and its causes. It denied that most lynchings were for the offense most generally charged as their justification, and declared that, even of those seemingly traced to this cause, many were not for crimes at all, but for voluntary acts which might naturally be expected to follow from the miscegenation laws by which it was sought, in all the Southern States, to destroy liberty of contract, and, for the purpose of maintaining a fanciful purity of race, to make crimes of marriages to which neither nature nor religion nor the laws of other states interposed any insurmountable barrier. Such an article in a Northern newspaper would have attracted no special attention, and might merely have furnished food to an occasional reader for serious thought upon a subject not exactly agreeable; but coming from a colored man, in a Southern city, it was an indictment of the laws and social system of the South that could not fail of creating a profound sensation.

"Infamous—infamous!" exclaimed Carteret, his voice trembling with emotion. "The paper should be suppressed immediately."

"The impudent nigger ought to be horsewhipped and run out of town," growled McBane.

"Gentlemen," said the general soothingly, after the first burst of indignation had subsided, "I believe we can find a more effective use for this article, which, by the way, will not bear too close analysis,—there's some truth in it, at least there's an argument." "That is not the point," interrupted Carteret.

"No," interjected McBane with an oath, "that ain't at all the point. Truth or not, no damn nigger has any right to say it."

"This article," said Carteret, "violates an unwritten law of the South. If we are to tolerate this race of weaklings among us, until they are eliminated by the stress of competition, it must be upon terms which we lay down. One of our conditions is violated by this article, in which our wisdom is assailed, and our women made the subject of offensive comment. We must make known our disapproval."

"I say lynch the nigger, break up the press, and burn down the newspaper office," McBane responded promptly.
