The lamp upon the table burned with a small and resentful flame. It seemed to have been lit against its will and to be awaiting an opportunity to go out. Its light fell in a yellow circle upon the oilcloth, upon a heap of mending, upon two hands that moved with the regularity of a machine. Beyond the circle the room retreated into a brown gloom, and in this gloom the furniture crouched like animals that had been beaten.

The woman sewed. From time to time she raised her head and looked at the door. Then she looked at the clock upon the shelf. The clock was a cheap thing with a painted face, and it ticked with a kind of insolence, as if it knew the hour and declined to share the knowledge in any manner that would be of comfort. She bent again to the shirt in her lap. It was his shirt. The cuff had been frayed by many days of labor at the yards, and she drew the thread through it with small vicious jerks.

Outside, the wind came up from the river and went about the house, trying the windows. It found a loose pane in the kitchen and rattled it with a persistent finger. Below, in the cooper's shop, there was no sound. The cooper had gone home at six. The street was empty save for a dog that went along close to the fences, and occasionally a wagon that passed with a grinding of wheels upon the frozen ruts, and then the silence came down again like a lid.

At a quarter to eleven there was a step upon the stair. The woman's hands stopped. She sat rigid, listening. The step was slow and heavy, and it paused upon the landing as if it were considering whether to go on. Then it came on. The door opened, and the young man entered, bringing with him a gust of cold air that made the lamp flame bow and shiver.

He closed the door behind him with elaborate care. He did not look at her. He went to the stove and held out his hands to it, and his back was toward her, a broad back in a coat that was too thin for the season.

"Well," she said.

"Well," he said.

The stove ticked as it cooled. The clock ticked. Between the two of them there was a contest of small noises, and the man and the woman listened to it as if it were of the most profound importance.

"Yer supper's in the oven," she said at last. "It's been in there since six. I guess it ain't much good now."

"I ain't hungry."

"No," she said. "I s'pose not."

He turned then and faced her. His face was red from the wind, and there was in his eyes a peculiar light, a kind of shining that she had seen before upon the faces of men coming out of saloons and of boys coming home from a fire. She looked at this light and her mouth became thin.

"Yeh been drinkin'," she said.

"I ain't," he said. "I had one glass with Hennessy. One glass. That ain't drinkin'."

"Where yeh been, then, till eleven o'clock at night?"

He did not answer at once. He took off his hat and turned it about in his hands, examining the brim as if he had never seen it before and found it full of curious interest. Then he put it upon the table, beside the lamp, where it sat like a black and shapeless thing that had crawled there.

"I been down t' the armory," he said.

The woman's needle had been halted in the cloth. Now it remained there. She looked at him and he looked at the hat.

"What fer?" she said.

"They was signin' men," he said. He spoke rapidly now, as if the words had been piled up behind his teeth all the way home and were glad to be let out. "The Sixty-ninth is fillin' up. Captain Rourke was there. He made a speech. He says there's goin' t' be a war with Spain sure as anything, an' every man that's a man ought t' be in it. He says the country needs—"

"Did yeh sign?"

The young man stopped. His mouth stayed open a little upon the next word, and then he closed it.

"Did yeh sign?" she said again.

"Yes," he said.

The wind found the loose pane in the kitchen and shook it. The lamp flame drew down into itself and then rose again, and the shadows in the corners of the room leaped forward and fell back like men who have been startled.

The woman put the shirt upon the table. She folded it with great precision, smoothing the sleeves, laying the frayed cuff over the other. Her hands were not steady, and she observed them with a kind of detached surprise, as if they belonged to another person who had come in and sat down in her chair.

"Yeh signed," she said.

"I did."

"Without sayin' a word t' me."

"Well, I'm sayin' it now, ain't I?" he said. His voice had grown loud, and the loudness seemed to encourage him. "A man can't go runnin' home t' ask his wife every time he wants t' do somethin'. There was fellers there signin' that's got wives an' kids both. Mulcahy signed. He's got four kids. An' Dutch Hoffman. They didn't run home."

"Mulcahy," she said, "is a fool. Everybody knows Mulcahy's a fool."

"Well, he ain't no coward, anyhow."

He had not meant to say this word, and when it was out he regarded it with a certain alarm. But the woman did not seem to have heard it. She was looking at the lamp.

"What about the rent?" she said.

"What about it?"

"It's due the first. Eleven dollars. What about it?"

The young man made a gesture of large contempt. It was the gesture of one who has lately been in the presence of great affairs and finds the conversation of common life to be beneath him.

"They pay," he said. "The government pays. Thirteen dollars a month an' everything found. Yeh'll get it. There's an allotment. Captain Rourke says—"

"Captain Rourke," she said. "Captain Rourke. Does Captain Rourke know the landlord? Does he know Mister Strauss, that comes up them stairs the first o' every month with his little book an' stands there in the door with his hat on? Does Captain Rourke know about him?"

"Yeh don't understand," he said.

"No," she said. "I guess I don't."

He walked across the room. It was a small room and he arrived at the wall almost at once, and then he was obliged to turn and walk back again. He did this several times. Each time he reached the wall he appeared to be surprised by it.

The truth was that he had walked home through the cold streets in a condition of glory. The speech of Captain Rourke had gone into him like hot liquor. He had seen himself in a blue coat with brass buttons upon it, charging up some hill under a foreign sun, while the Spaniards fled before him like sheep. He had seen himself returning, thin and brown and decorated, with the band of the Sixty-ninth playing before him and the whole street out upon the stoops to cheer. He had seen the face of Hennessy, who had not signed, and the face of the foreman at the yards, who had once called him a lummox before three other men. In all these visions the woman had stood somewhere at the edge of the crowd, weeping with pride, a vague and pleasant figure in a clean apron.

Now she sat at the table with the lamp, and her face was neither vague nor pleasant. It was a narrow face, sharpened by eight months in these rooms, and the light threw hollows under her eyes and at the corners of her mouth. She did not look like a woman who would weep with pride. She looked like a woman counting coins.

He felt that he had been robbed. The glory had leaked out of him somewhere upon the stairs, and he could not tell where.

"A man's got a duty," he said.

"Yeh got a duty here."

"T' the country, I mean. T' the flag."

She laughed. It was not a long laugh, nor a loud one. It was a single small sound, dry as a stick breaking, and it went into him deeper than anything she had yet said.

"The flag," she said. "Did the flag get yeh the job at the yards? Did the flag put coal in that stove? I'll tell yeh what the flag done, Tom Delaney. The flag stood up there on the armory an' flapped. That's all the flag ever done."

"Yeh got no right t' talk like that."

"I got every right."

"It's—it's near treason, talkin' like that."

"Then let 'em come take me," she said. "Let 'em come up the stairs. They'll have t' wait behind Mister Strauss."

The young man stood still in the middle of the room. His hands hung at his sides and the fingers moved a little, opening and closing, as if they were trying to grasp some argument that floated just beyond them. He was conscious that he was being beaten, and that he was being beaten by something small and mean and unanswerable, as a large dog is sometimes beaten by a cat. The knowledge filled him with a slow red anger.

"Yeh want me t' stay at the yards all my life," he said. "That's what yeh want. Yeh want me t' haul hides fer Kessler till I'm sixty an' my back's broke. Yeh want me t' come home every night stinkin' of 'em, an' set there, an' eat, an' go t' bed, an' get up, an' go back. That's all. That's what yeh want."

"I want yeh alive," she said.

He had raised his hand in some gesture, and it remained in the air. Then he let it fall.

"Huh," he said. "Alive. There ain't one in a hundred gets hit. Captain Rourke says the Spaniards can't shoot. He says they're all little fellers an' sick with the fever an' they'll run the minute they see us comin'. He says it'll be over in a month."

"An' if it ain't?"

"It will be."

"An' if it ain't?"

"Then I'll come back anyway," he said, with a magnificent carelessness. "I ain't goin' t' get hit."

The woman looked at him for a long moment. In her look there was something that he could not read, a kind of weariness that was older than she was, as if she had borrowed it from her mother and her mother's mother, from a long line of women who had sat at tables under lamps and listened to men explain that they would not be hit.

"No," she said. "Nobody ever does. That's the funny thing. My Uncle Pat, he went with the Irish Brigade in sixty-two. He wasn't goin' t' get hit neither. My mother used t' tell it. He wrote a letter from Virginia sayin' the Rebs couldn't shoot an' it'd all be over by the summer. They had the letter on the shelf fer years. It come the same week as the other one."

"That was a different war."

"Was it?"

"Sure it was. It was—" He searched for the difference and could not find it. "It was different," he said.

The clock upon the shelf struck the hour. It was eleven, and it said so eleven times in a thin, cracked voice, and the man and the woman were obliged to wait until it had finished. It seemed to them both that it went on for an unconscionable time. When it had done, the room was very still.

The young man went to the stove and opened the oven door. A plate sat inside, with a cover over it. He took the cover off and looked at the supper. It was boiled potatoes and a piece of salt pork, and the potatoes had shriveled and the pork had curled at the edges. He looked at it for a while. Then he took the plate out, and burned his fingers, and swore, and set it upon the table.

He sat down and began to eat. He was not hungry, but the eating gave him something to do with his hands and his face. The woman watched him. The pork was tough and he sawed at it with the knife, and the knife squeaked upon the plate.

"It's real tough," he said, by way of saying something.

"It's been in since six."

"I know it."

He ate a potato. Then he ate another. The woman took up the shirt again and unfolded it and began to sew the cuff, and for a time there was no sound but the knife and the needle and the clock.

"When do yeh go?" she said presently. She did not look up.

"I dunno. Two weeks, maybe. Maybe sooner. They're sendin' us t' camp first. Down t' Hempstead or someplace. Fer drillin'."

"Two weeks."

"Maybe."

She drew the thread through. "Kessler know?"

"No."

"Yeh'll tell him?"

"I'll tell him," the young man said. A small satisfaction came into his face. "I'll tell him t'morrow. I'll tell him in front o' the whole gang. I'll tell him he can haul his own hides." He considered this scene for a while with pleasure. Then the pleasure faded, and he put down his fork. "I'll tell him," he said again, more quietly.

The wind had dropped. In the street below, a man went by singing. He was singing a song about a girl in a blue dress, and he sang it badly and with great feeling, and his voice came up through the window and wandered about the room like a stray. Then it went off down the street and was gone.

"Nell," said the young man.

She did not answer.

"Nell. Look a-here." He leaned forward with his elbows upon the table. The lamplight fell full upon him now, and she could see that the shining had gone out of his eyes and that what remained was the face of a boy who has broken something in the parlor and is waiting to learn the price. "It ain't like I done it t' get away from yeh. It ain't that. It's—I dunno what it is. They was all standin' there, an' the captain was talkin', an' the band played a piece, an' I got all kind o' queer an' hot. An' Mulcahy says, 'Come on, Tom,' an' I went. An' I signed. It was like somebody else done it, kind of. An' then I was walkin' home, an' I felt fine. I felt like I was a big man. Yeh know?"

The woman looked at the shirt.

"An' now I come in here," he said, "an' I don't feel like nothin'."

"No," she said. "I guess yeh don't."

"Yeh could say somethin'."

"What d'yeh want me t' say?"

He did not know. He looked about the room as if the thing he wanted might be lying somewhere among the beaten furniture, but there was only the stove, and the broken chair, and the calendar from the grocer's with its picture of a smiling woman holding a sheaf of wheat. The smiling woman looked down upon them with great serenity. She had nothing to say either.

"I can't take it back," he said. "Once yeh sign, yeh can't take it back."

"I know."

"It'd be desertin'. They shoot yeh fer that."

"I know, Tom."

"Well, then."

"Well, then," she said.

She finished the cuff and bit off the thread. She held the shirt up to the lamp and examined the work, turning it this way and that, and the light came through the thin places in the cloth so that the shirt looked like something made of fog. Then she folded it again and laid it on the pile.

"Yeh'll want this one," she said. "Fer the camp. It's the best one."

The young man stared at her. He had prepared himself for tears, for shouting, perhaps for a plate thrown against the wall. Mrs. Mulcahy, it was said, had once thrown a flatiron. He had not prepared himself for the shirt. It lay upon the table between them, mended and folded, and it seemed to him a more terrible thing than any flatiron.

"Nell," he said.

"It's late," she said. "Yeh got t' be at the yards at six. Yeh still got t' go t' the yards till they send fer yeh. We still got t' pay Strauss."

She rose and took the plate away and set it in the basin. She stood with her back to him, and her shoulders were very straight, and he could not see her face. He thought that perhaps she was crying, and he sat waiting for the sound of it, half in dread and half in a kind of shameful hope, for if she cried then he would be obliged to comfort her, and in comforting her he might yet become the man of his visions upon the stairs. But she did not cry. She worked the pump handle, and the water came out of the spout with a cough and a gurgle, and she washed the plate.

He went into the other room and took off his boots. He sat on the edge of the bed in the dark with one boot in his hand. Through the doorway he could see the yellow circle of the lamp and her shadow moving across it, back and forth, back and forth, and the shadow was enormous and crooked and did not look like her at all.

Presently she came to the doorway and stood there with the lamp.

"Tom," she said.

"What?"

She did not say anything for a while. The lamp flame trembled in the draft from the stair, and the shadows fled up the walls and huddled upon the ceiling.

"Nothin'," she said. "Go t' sleep."

She blew out the lamp. He heard her moving in the dark, and the rustle of her dress, and the creak of the board by the window, and then the bed sank beside him and she lay down with her back to him. He lay very still. He was waiting for her to say something more, but she did not, and after a time he understood that she was not going to.

He stared upward into the blackness. Out of it there began to come again, faintly, the pictures of the armory: the blue coats, the brass, the hill under the foreign sun. He tried to make them bright. They would not become bright. The Spaniards upon the hill had faces now, and they did not run. And at the bottom of the hill, where the crowd should have been, there was only a small room, and a lamp, and a woman holding up a shirt to the light so that it looked like fog.

The clock struck the half hour. Out on the river a tug blew, long and hoarse, a sound like some great beast lamenting in the dark. The woman's breathing was slow and even. The young man listened to it for a long time, wondering whether she was asleep.

She was not. She lay with her eyes open, looking at the gray square of the window. She was thinking of eleven dollars, and of thirteen, and of the difference between them, which was two. She was thinking that two dollars was a sum. She turned it over in her mind, and examined it, and set it aside, and took it up again. It was the only thing in the whole affair that she could hold.

Toward morning the wind rose once more and went about the house, trying the windows, and finding the loose pane, it shook it with a patient and indifferent hand, as it had shaken it the night before, and as it would doubtless shake it upon many nights to come, whether there was a war or not.

I

The train came down the valley like a great black insect that had lost its temper. It shrieked at the hills, and the hills, being old and accustomed to such outrage, did not answer. At the little station of Hagenville it halted with a series of convulsions, and the brakeman swung from the step with the air of one who confers a favor upon the earth.

A man in a grey suit descended. He wore a derby hat of a shape which had been much admired in certain quarters of New York during the previous spring, and he carried a valise of yellow leather. He stood upon the platform and looked about him with the expression of a general who surveys a field that he has once lost and now intends to retake.

The station agent, a youth with an enormous Adam's apple, regarded the derby hat. The two loafers upon the baggage truck regarded it. A dog of no particular opinions came out from beneath the platform and regarded it also. The man in the grey suit was conscious of these attentions, and he arranged his shoulders.

Presently a wagon came around the corner of the feed store. It was drawn by two brown horses whose heads nodded in unison, as if they were agreeing to some long and tedious proposition. On the seat sat a large man in a blue shirt. His beard was the color of wet straw, and his hands lay upon his knees like two tools that had been set down after work.

The large man pulled up his horses and looked at the platform. The man in the grey suit looked at the wagon. For a moment there was a silence in which each of them seemed to be searching for something that he had mislaid eleven years before.

"Is that you, Will?" said the man on the wagon.

"Jim!" cried the visitor. He came forward with his hand out. He had decided upon the train that he would be hearty. "Jim, old man! Well, well, well!"

The farmer climbed down. He did it slowly, as he did everything, and when he stood upon the ground he took the visitor's hand and shook it twice, as a man works a pump handle that he suspects of being dry.

"You've got fat," said the farmer.

The visitor laughed in a high manner. "Prosperity, Jim. That's what does it. City living." He patted his waistcoat. It was a waistcoat with a small figure in it, and it had been purchased upon an occasion when the visitor had felt that the world was about to recognize him.

"I guess so," said the farmer. He looked at the yellow valise. "That all you brung?"

"Oh, I travel light. A man in my line learns to travel light."

The farmer seized the valise and swung it into the back of the wagon, where it lay among some sacks of meal and a coil of rope, looking very foreign and somewhat ashamed. Then the two men climbed upon the seat, and the farmer spoke to the horses, and the horses, after a moment of reflection, consented to move.

The loafers upon the baggage truck watched them go. "That there's Jim Burritt's cousin," said one. "Him that went off to the city."

"Is it?" said the other. He spat. "Looks like he got there."

II

The road wound between fields that were yellow with stubble. Upon the distant ridges the woods had turned crimson and orange, and they burned silently in the clear air, as if some vast conflagration had been arrested at the moment of its fury and frozen into a picture. The sky was a pale and enormous blue. It had no interest in the wagon.

For some time the cousins did not speak. The visitor was engaged in looking at the country. He looked at it with his eyes partly closed, in the manner of a man at an exhibition of paintings who wishes it to be known that he has seen better.

"Things ain't changed much," said the farmer at last.

"No," said the visitor. "No, they don't, out here. That's the charm of it, I suppose." He waved his hand at a red barn. "Old Heffner's place, isn't it?"

"Heffner's dead. His boy's got it."

"Dead! Old Heffner!" The visitor was shocked. He had a feeling that old Heffner had no right to die without informing him. In his mind the whole valley had remained fixed during eleven years, like a clock that has been stopped at a particular hour, and he had expected to walk back into it and find the hands where he had left them. "When was that?"

"Four years back. Fell off his hay-mow."

"Well, well."

The farmer chirruped to the horses. A crow flew up from a fence-post and went away over the field, crying out in a hoarse and scandalized voice.

"How's things in New York?" asked the farmer.

The visitor had been waiting for this question since the train left Albany. He had rehearsed several answers to it. Now that it had come, he found that it was necessary to clear his throat.

"Oh, pretty fair, pretty fair. Business is business, you know. A man has to keep his eye on the main chance. I'm with a firm down on Worth Street. Hosiery. Wholesale." He let this last word fall with a certain weight, as a man drops a gold piece upon a counter. "Very big concern. Very big. We do business all over the country. Chicago. St. Louis. Everywhere."

"That so?" said the farmer.

"Oh, yes. I've got a good deal of responsibility. A good deal." He paused, and then added, with an air of carelessness that had cost him some labor, "They depend upon me considerably."

The farmer was silent. He was looking at the rumps of his horses. The visitor glanced at him sidewise and could make nothing of his face. It was a large brown face, and it seemed to have been constructed for weather rather than for expression.

The truth was that the visitor was a clerk in the shipping department of the firm upon Worth Street, and that his responsibility consisted chiefly in counting boxes of stockings and writing numbers in a book. He had held this position for six years. During that time he had been noticed twice by the head of the firm: once when he had been late, and once when he had tipped over a pot of mucilage. But these facts were not present in his mind at the moment. In his mind there was a vision of himself as he had appeared in the window of a car on the elevated railway, very correct in his derby hat, and this vision seemed to him more true than the shipping department.

"How's the farm?" he asked.

"Middlin'."

"You've got children, I believe. Aunt Martha wrote me."

"Four," said the farmer. "Another comin'."

"Four!" The visitor laughed. "Well, you've been busy, Jim. You've been busy."

The farmer did not laugh. A slight red came into his neck above the blue collar. The visitor perceived that his jest had fallen into a well, and he listened in vain for the splash.

III

The farmhouse stood upon a little rise of ground, and it was white, or had been white at some former time. Now it was the color of an old tooth. Around it lay a confusion of sheds and fences, and in the dooryard there were hens, which fled before the wagon with shrieks of outraged virtue.

Upon the porch there appeared, as the wagon drew up, a woman and four children. The woman was thin, and she held her hands beneath her apron. The children were arranged in a row, according to size, like a set of jugs upon a shelf, and they gazed at the visitor with eyes that were round and unwinking.

"This is Will," said the farmer. "My cousin Will, from New York."

"How do," said the woman.

"How do you do, Mrs. Burritt," said the visitor. He removed his derby hat with a flourish. "It's a great pleasure. A great pleasure, I assure you."

The woman looked at the hat and then at her husband. The children looked at the hat. The smallest child, who was a girl of perhaps three years, put her thumb into her mouth and retreated behind the skirts of her mother, from whence she peered forth as from a fortress.

"Supper's near ready," said the woman.

The visitor was given a room under the eaves. It contained an iron bed, a chair, a washstand with a cracked pitcher, and a picture of a ship in a storm. The ship was going down, and a number of small persons were waving their arms upon its deck. The visitor sat upon the bed and looked at this picture. He felt for the first time a little weary. The room smelled of dried apples and of old wood, and this smell went into him suddenly and found something there, some small and forgotten thing, so that he sat for a moment quite still, with his hands between his knees.

Then he arose and brushed his coat and went downstairs.

At supper there was ham and potatoes and a great quantity of bread, and the children ate in silence, watching the visitor over the rims of their cups. The visitor talked. He talked of the elevated railway and of the bridge to Brooklyn and of a fire he had seen in Grand Street, where the engines had come plunging through the crowd with their horses wild and their smoke-stacks raining sparks. He told of a restaurant where a man could eat oysters in seventeen different styles. He mentioned the names of several actresses as if they were persons of his acquaintance.

The children listened as to a tale of distant wars. The eldest boy, whose name was Henry, forgot to eat. His mouth hung open, and there was a crumb upon his lower lip that remained there throughout the account of the fire.

The farmer ate steadily. Once or twice he said, "That so?" and once he said, "Pass the butter, Mary." His wife moved about between the stove and the table, and she said nothing at all, but she looked at the visitor from time to time with an expression that was not easy to read, as one looks at a peddler who is showing very fine goods at a price that is not mentioned.

When the visitor had finished with the oysters, there was a pause. In this pause the clock upon the shelf ticked loudly, as if it wished to call attention to the passage of time and was annoyed that no one had noticed.

"Pa," said the boy Henry suddenly, "did you ever see a fire like that?"

"No," said the farmer.

"Pa saw the Simmons barn burn," said the second boy, loyally. "Didn't you, Pa? Pa carried out a calf."

"Shut up, Ed," said the farmer.

The visitor laughed. "Well, that's a good deal, Eddie. That's a good deal. Carrying out a calf." He laughed again. It was meant kindly; he had felt, in the first moment, a disposition to be generous. But the laugh came out of him in the wrong shape, and he heard it go across the table and strike the farmer upon the face.

The farmer pushed back his chair. "I got to see to the stock," he said, and went out.

IV

The night came down upon the valley like a great dark hand closing over a toy. The stars appeared one by one, and then all at once, in a vast and glittering multitude, and they hung above the barn with the cold indifference of creditors.

The visitor sat upon the porch steps and smoked a cigar. It was a good cigar; he had bought three of them at a shop near the ferry, with the express purpose of smoking them at Hagenville. He had pictured himself smoking them. In the picture he had been at ease, and his cousin had looked at him with a certain respect. But the cigar now seemed to him merely a cigar, and the end of it glowed in the darkness, a small red point, very lonely.

Presently the farmer came across the yard with a lantern. The light swung against his legs and threw great leaping shadows upon the side of the barn, so that it seemed as if some giant were walking there, wild and disordered. Then he set the lantern upon the step and sat down, and the giant vanished, and he was only a large man who was tired.

They sat for a time without speaking. In the marsh beyond the road the frogs were holding some sort of convention, and their voices rose and fell in a sustained and passionate debate.

"You remember the mill pond?" said the visitor at last.

The farmer stirred. "I remember it."

"You remember the time we fought? Over that knife?"

"Barlow knife," said the farmer. "Two blades."

"That's it. That's it!" The visitor leaned forward. "I'd forgotten it was two blades. You remember how we went at it? Right there on the dam. I had you down, and you got out from under somehow, and we both went in the water."

"You didn't have me down," said the farmer.

The visitor laughed. "Oh, I had you down, Jim."

"No," said the farmer, "you didn't."

There was a silence. The visitor drew upon his cigar. He was conscious of a curious heat rising in him, a heat that was out of all proportion to the matter. He was thirty-one years old and he wore a waistcoat with a figure in it, and he was quarreling about a fight upon a mill dam. He perceived this, and yet the heat did not go down. It seemed to him somehow that if he had not had his cousin down upon the dam eighteen years before, then a great many other things were also not true.

"Well," he said, "it don't matter."

"No," said the farmer, "it don't matter."

But they both sat very stiff, and each was thinking of the dam, and in each mind the dam was a different dam.

A dog came out of the darkness and sniffed at the visitor's shoes. They were city shoes, narrow and shining, and the dog seemed to find in them some evidence of a distant and suspicious civilization. It sniffed them thoroughly, and then it went and lay down beside the farmer, with a sigh.

"Who's got the knife?" said the visitor.

"Huh?"

"The knife. Who kept it? After."

The farmer considered. "I dunno," he said. "I guess it got lost."

"Yes," said the visitor. "I guess it did."

The frogs continued their debate. Far off, upon the railroad, a freight train went down the valley, and its whistle came across the dark fields, thin and mournful, like the voice of something that had been left behind.

"Will," said the farmer.

"What?"

The farmer seemed to be looking for words among the stars. He found none there. He looked at the lantern. "You doin' all right? Down there?"

The visitor opened his mouth. He was going to say that he was doing splendidly. The words were all ready; they had been ready for eleven years. But at that moment there came into his mind the shipping department, with its high dusty windows and its stacks of pasteboard boxes, and the voice of Mr. Kessler, the head clerk, saying, "Fanhall, you've counted these wrong again," and the furnished room on Twenty-third Street, where there was a gas jet that made a noise like a small animal in pain, and where he sat in the evenings and read the newspapers, and heard through the wall the man in the next room coughing.

These things came all together, and they stood before him, and he looked at them.

"Well," he said slowly, "it ain't—" He stopped. The cigar had gone out. He looked at it with surprise, as if it had betrayed him.

The farmer waited. The lantern made a little round world upon the porch, and in this world the two men sat, and outside it lay all the vast darkness of the valley, and the hills, and the indifferent stars.

"It ain't so bad," said the visitor.

He had meant to say something else. He had felt it there, upon the very edge of his tongue, a great and simple thing, and for a moment it had seemed to him that if he could only say it, then his cousin would understand, and they would sit together upon the step like boys again, and the dam would be the same dam for both of them. But the thing was very heavy. It was heavier than the yellow valise, heavier than the derby hat, heavier than eleven years. And when he reached for it, it was not there; there was only the phrase, "It ain't so bad," which was a small phrase and fell easily.

"That's good," said the farmer.

"How about you, Jim? You doing all right?"

The farmer looked out at the dark fields. Somewhere out there lay the mortgage, which was held by a man in Hagenville with very white hands, and the north meadow, which had flooded in May, and the cow that had died of the bloat, and a great many mornings that had begun before light and ended after dark. He thought also of the boy Henry, who had looked at the visitor across the supper table with his mouth hanging open, as he had never looked at his father in all his life.

"Middlin'," he said. "I get along."

"That's good," said the visitor.

They had now told each other everything, and they sat in silence.

V

In the morning the visitor came down to breakfast wearing the grey suit and carrying the derby hat in his hand. The children were in their places. The woman was at the stove. Through the window he could see the farmer in the barnyard, forking hay to the horses in the grey light.

The boy Henry sidled up to him after breakfast. He had evidently been preparing a speech, and he delivered it all at once, with his eyes upon the floor.

"Mister, could I go to New York sometime? When I'm growed?"

The visitor looked down at him. The boy had a small brown face that was very like the face of his father, and his hair stood up behind like the crest of a startled bird. In his eyes there was a light that the visitor knew. He had seen it once, long ago, in a piece of looking-glass that hung by the pump.

"Why, sure," said the visitor. "Sure you can, Henry."

The boy's face shone. He ran out of the kitchen and across the yard, shouting something to his brothers, and the hens fled before him in their customary despair.

The visitor stood by the window. He was conscious of having done something, but he could not tell whether it was a good thing or a bad thing, and the more he examined it, the less he could tell.

At noon the farmer drove him back to the station. They passed again the red barn of old Heffner, who was dead, and the woods upon the ridges, which were still burning in their frozen and silent way. The horses nodded their heads together. The sky was blue and enormous and unconcerned.

They did not speak of the mill pond.

At the station the train was late. They stood upon the platform, and the two loafers upon the baggage truck observed them with the patience of men to whom all spectacles are of equal value.

"Well, Jim," said the visitor. He held out his hand.

"Well, Will."

They shook hands. It was the same handshake as before, two motions of the pump handle, but this time the visitor fancied that there was something at the bottom of the well, a little, a very little water.

"Write sometime," said the farmer.

"I will. I'll write, Jim."

The train came down the valley, shrieking. It stopped with its convulsions, and the brakeman swung down with his air of conferring a favor. The visitor climbed aboard with the yellow valise, and he went to a window and sat down and put on his derby hat. He arranged it carefully. Then he looked out.

The farmer was already climbing upon the wagon. He did it slowly, as he did everything. He did not look back at the train. He spoke to the horses, and the horses, after a moment of reflection, consented to move, and the wagon went around the corner of the feed store and was gone.

The train jerked. The station slid backward. The visitor sat with his hands upon his knees and gazed at the crimson woods, which were going past very swiftly now, and which did not care whether he looked at them or not.

Upon the baggage truck one loafer turned to the other.

"That there was Jim Burritt's cousin," he said. "Him that's in business in New York."

"Is it?" said the other. He spat thoughtfully upon the rails. "He looked kind of peaked to me."

The window of Mrs. Gilfoyle's conservatory had gone down in a single magnificent crash, and for a moment afterward there was no sound in the world. The three boys who stood in the lane behind the Gilfoyle hedge looked at one another with faces from which all the blood had fled. The green apple that had done the deed lay somewhere among the geraniums, a small hard missile, innocent now, like a bullet that has found its man.

Then the silence broke. A door banged. A voice, high and terrible, began to cry out from the depths of the Gilfoyle house, and the boys, without a word, without a sign, became three separate streaks of motion. They fled as soldiers flee when the line has broken, each man for himself, and the lane behind them was empty in the time it takes to draw a breath.

Georgie Haskell ran until his lungs were two coals in his chest. He went over the Pickering fence and through the Pickering cabbages and under the Pickering clothesline, where a sheet slapped him wetly across the face like an accusing hand. He did not stop. He came at last to his own back yard and to the woodshed, and he plunged into its brown gloom and crouched behind the pile of split hickory with the dust settling upon him.

It was very quiet in the woodshed. A wasp hummed somewhere in the rafters. Through the cracks in the boards came thin blades of yellow sunlight, and in them the dust turned and glittered with an indifference that seemed to Georgie almost wicked. He listened. He could hear his own heart. It was going like a little drum, and he was ashamed of it, for it seemed to him that any person passing must hear it and know at once that here was a guilty man.

He was eight years old, and he had committed a crime.

At first he could think of nothing but the noise. It had been a vast noise, a noise of a size out of all proportion to the apple. He had not known that a window could make such a sound. It had seemed to fill the whole sky over Whitby Street, and he imagined that it had been heard in every house, in the grocery store, at the depot, perhaps even at the courthouse, where the men with grey beards sat and decided who was to go to jail.

He was not certain that it had been his apple. Willie Pratt had thrown, and Alfred Moss had thrown, and Georgie himself had thrown, all in the same moment, for it had been a grand assault upon the hedge, which they had been pretending was a fort held by Indians. But in his heart he believed that it had been his apple. There was no reason for this belief, and yet it sat upon him with the weight of a stone. Willie Pratt's apples always fell short. Alfred Moss threw like a girl. It was Georgie who had the arm. He had boasted of it many times. Now the arm hung at his side and he looked upon it as one looks upon an accomplice who has betrayed him.

Time passed in the woodshed. The blades of sunlight moved slowly across the floor and climbed the wall. The wasp went out through a knothole. Georgie began to construct, in his mind, the various courses that lay open to him.

He could run away. This was the first idea, and the most splendid. He saw himself going down the railroad track with a bundle on a stick, as he had seen tramps do, and he saw himself many years later returning in a long coat with a gold watch chain across his stomach. The town would come out to meet him. His mother would weep. Mrs. Gilfoyle would be dead by that time, probably, and he would pay for the window out of his own pocket, a great handful of silver dollars, flung carelessly down upon the counter of somebody's store.

But the railroad track went past the Gilfoyle house. He abandoned the plan.

He could deny everything. He rehearsed this. "No, ma'am. I never. I was down by the creek." But even as he framed the words he knew that they would not do. His mother had a way of looking at him. Her eyes went into him like a pair of gimlets and came out the other side, and he had never yet told her a lie that did not die upon his lips like a moth in a lamp.

He could confess. The thought made him sick.

He was still debating when he heard the screen door of the kitchen open and close, and then his mother's voice came across the yard. It was not loud. It was, in fact, rather quiet, and the quietness of it was more dreadful than any shout.

"Georgie."

He did not move. He made himself small behind the hickory. He closed his eyes, as if by this means he might render himself invisible.

"Georgie Haskell. I know you're in that shed."

There was no help for it. The universe had closed upon him. He rose, brushing the dust from his knees with a hand that trembled, and he went to the door of the woodshed and stood in it, blinking at the light.

His mother was on the back step. She wore her blue gingham apron and her sleeves were turned back over her forearms, which were red from the washtub. Her hair had come down a little on one side. She did not look like an avenging angel. She looked tired. But Georgie, crossing the yard toward her with his feet dragging in the grass, saw her as a tall and terrible figure, black against the white kitchen wall, and the step on which she stood seemed to him a kind of platform from which justice would presently be handed down.

"Come in the house," she said.

He went in. The kitchen was hot and smelled of soap and of the bread that was rising under a cloth on the table. The kettle muttered on the stove. Everything was as it always was, and this seemed to him strange, for he felt that the walls ought to have changed color, that the clock ought to have stopped. The clock had not stopped. It went on with its stolid ticking, a fat, complacent, brown clock, and he hated it.

His mother sat down in the chair by the window. She did not tell him to sit. He stood in the middle of the floor, on the worn place in the oilcloth, and looked at his shoes.

"Mrs. Gilfoyle was here," his mother said.

Georgie said nothing. There seemed nothing to say. The name fell into the kitchen like a stone into a well, and he listened to it go down and down.

"She says you broke her window."

"I never," said Georgie. The words came out of him by themselves, without his permission. They were very small words and they hung in the air for an instant, and then they seemed to shrivel and fall. His mother looked at him. He looked at his shoes.

"Georgie."

"It might've been Willie," he said. "Willie Pratt. He was throwin' too. An' Alfred. We was all throwin'. It might've been anybody."

"Were you throwing apples at Mrs. Gilfoyle's house?"

"We wasn't throwin' at the house. We was throwin' at the hedge. It was a fort. There was Injuns in it." He became aware, as he said this, that it was not a very good defense. The Indians, which had been so real an hour before, were gone now. They had melted away and left him alone with the consequences. He felt deserted by them.

"Indians," said his mother.

"Yes'm."

"In Mrs. Gilfoyle's hedge."

"Yes'm. We was only playin'."

His mother was silent for a time. Georgie heard the kettle. He heard a fly bumping its head stupidly against the window glass. Outside, in the street, a wagon went by, the wheels grinding in the dust, and the driver called out something to his horse. It seemed to Georgie that the world had gone very far off, that it was going on about its business somewhere beyond a great distance, and that he was left here in a small, hot room with his crime.

"Do you know," his mother said at last, "what a pane of glass like that costs?"

He did not. He had a vague idea that it was a great deal. He imagined it to be about the price of a horse.

"No'm."

"Your father works all day at the mill," she said. "All day, from before you're awake till near supper. Do you know that?"

"Yes'm."

"And now he'll have to take money he's worked for and give it to Mrs. Gilfoyle for a window. Money that was going for your new shoes, maybe. Or for something for your sister."

This was a new and unexpected blow. Georgie had not thought of his father. He had thought of Mrs. Gilfoyle, and of the police, and of the courthouse, and of running away; but he had not thought of his father, who came home in the evenings smelling of oil and sawdust and who sat on the porch with his boots off and said very little. A queer, tight feeling came into Georgie's throat. He swallowed at it, but it would not go down.

"An' what will he say," his mother went on, "when he comes home tonight and I have to tell him that his boy has been throwing apples at the neighbors' houses like a hoodlum? Like one of those Riley boys from down by the tracks?"

The Riley boys. Georgie felt the comparison go into him like a blade. The Riley boys were the lowest creatures of which he had knowledge. They swore. They chewed tobacco. One of them had been taken away in a buggy by a man with a star on his coat. To be likened to the Riley boys was to be cast out of decent society altogether, to be thrown down among the outlaws and the damned.

"I ain't like the Rileys," he said, and his voice cracked in the middle.

"You're acting like them."

He could bear no more. The tight feeling in his throat rose up and became a sob, and the sob burst from him in a kind of bark, absurd and humiliating. He was furious at it. He had not meant to cry. He had resolved, in the woodshed, that whatever happened he would not cry, that he would stand up like a man and take his punishment with a stony face, as the heroes did in the books his uncle had given him. And now his face was crumpling up of its own accord, and the tears were coming, hot and salt, and running down into the corners of his mouth.

He made a great effort. He set his jaw. But the jaw trembled, and another sob came, and then another, and presently he was weeping openly, with his fists jammed into his eyes and his shoulders going up and down.

His mother watched him. Her face did not change. But something went across it, very quickly, a shadow or a light, it would have been hard to say which, and then it was gone.

"Stop that, now," she said. "Crying won't mend Mrs. Gilfoyle's window."

"I d-don't care about her ol' window."

"Georgie!"

"I don't! She's a mean ol' thing. She hollers at everybody. She hollered at Alfred once just for walkin' on her sidewalk. Her ol' window—" He choked. He did not know what he was saying. The words came out in a hot stream, and he felt, even as he spoke them, that they were wrong, that he was making it worse, but he could not stop. There was a kind of savage pleasure in it, the pleasure of a cornered animal that turns and shows its teeth.

His mother rose from the chair.

She did not come at him. She did not raise her hand. She only stood up, and in standing she seemed to Georgie to grow, to fill the kitchen, to rise until her head was among the shadows near the ceiling. His words died. He stood with his mouth open and his eyes wet and he looked up at her, and he was afraid.

"That," she said, "will be enough."

It was enough. It was more than enough. Georgie closed his mouth.

"You will not speak of Mrs. Gilfoyle that way in this house. She is an old woman and she lives alone and she has had a great deal of trouble in her life, more than you know anything about. If she hollers, maybe she has reason to. Maybe she's tired of little boys running through her yard and trampling her flowers and throwing things at her house. Did you think of that?"

"No'm," Georgie whispered.

"No. You didn't think. That's the trouble with you, Georgie. You never think. You just go running off and doing whatever comes into your head, and you never once stop to think what it might cost somebody else."

He hung his head. The worn place in the oilcloth swam before his eyes. It had a pattern of little red and brown squares, and he stared at it as though it were the most important thing in the world, as though by studying it closely enough he might find some hole in it into which he could crawl and disappear.

The clock ticked. The fly had stopped bumping against the glass and was walking slowly up the pane, as if it, too, had been reprimanded and had resolved upon better conduct.

"Now," said his mother. "You are going to go over to Mrs. Gilfoyle's."

Georgie's head came up. His eyes were very wide.

"You are going to go over there and knock on her front door, and when she comes, you are going to tell her that you are sorry for breaking her window and that your father will pay for it."

It was the worst thing. It was worse than a whipping. It was worse than being sent to bed without supper, worse than the courthouse, worse than anything he had imagined in the woodshed. To go to the very door of the enemy, alone, unarmed, and to stand there on the step under the eye of that dreadful old woman and to say that he was sorry—it was not to be thought of. His whole soul revolted against it.

"I can't," he said.

"You can."

"Ma, I can't. She'll holler at me."

"Then she'll holler at you, and you'll stand there and take it, because you've earned it."

"Can't Pa go? When he comes home?"

"Your father will go too, to settle up. But you're going first, and you're going now."

"Ma—"

"Now, Georgie."

There was a finality in her voice that he had heard before, upon a few memorable occasions, and he knew that it was useless to argue further. The door of escape had been shut and bolted. He stood for a moment longer on the worn place in the oilcloth, and then he turned and went slowly toward the door. His feet were like two lumps of iron. The distance across the kitchen seemed to him as great as the distance across a prairie.

At the door he stopped. He looked back. His mother was standing by the table with her hand resting upon the cloth that covered the bread. The light from the window fell across her and made her apron very blue and her arms very red, and her face, which was in shadow, he could not see at all.

"Wash your face first," she said. "You can't go over there looking like that."

He went to the basin and washed his face. The water was cold and it stung his eyes. When he had finished he dried himself on the roller towel, and his mother came and looked at him and pushed his hair back off his forehead with her fingers. Her fingers were damp and smelled of soap. She did not say anything. She only pushed his hair back, once, and then she turned away to the stove.

Georgie went out.

The yard was full of the long, slanting light of late afternoon. The shadows of the maples lay across the grass like great purple pools. A robin was walking about on the lawn with an air of importance, and it stopped and cocked its head at him as he passed, and he felt that even the robin knew. He went around the side of the house and out to the street.

Whitby Street lay before him, golden and still. He could see, far down at the corner, the high green wall of the Gilfoyle hedge. It looked very large. It looked, he thought, like the wall of a prison. He began to walk toward it.

He walked very slowly. He looked at the cracks in the sidewalk and he was careful to step over each one, for it seemed to him that at a time like this it would be foolish to take any unnecessary chances with fate. He passed the Pickering house. He passed the Moss house, and he looked at its windows with a sort of dull resentment, for Alfred was somewhere inside, safe, unpunished, and Georgie suspected that Alfred's mother knew nothing at all. He passed the empty lot where they played ball. The bases were still there, four flat stones in the trodden grass, and they seemed to belong to another life, to a time long ago when he had been young and innocent and free.

And then he was at the Gilfoyle gate.

The house stood back from the street behind its lawn. It was a tall grey house with a great many windows and a porch that went around three sides. At the back, glimmering among the leaves, he could see the conservatory, and he could see the place where one pane was gone, a black square in the shining glass like a missing tooth.

He stood at the gate for a long time. His hand was on the latch. He could not make it lift.

A thousand thoughts went through his head. He thought that he might simply go home and say that he had done it. He thought that he might go down to the creek instead and stay there until dark. He thought that Mrs. Gilfoyle might not be at home, and the hope of this rose up in him so strongly that it was almost a prayer. He thought of his father coming up the street in the evening with his dinner pail, and of his mother telling him on the porch. He thought of the Riley boys.

He lifted the latch.

The gate swung open with a long, complaining cry, and the sound of it was like the voice of the house itself, protesting his approach. He went up the walk. The walk was very long. The porch steps were very high. He climbed them, one by one, and he stood before the front door, which was of dark wood with a pane of colored glass in it, red and yellow and green, and through the colored glass he could see, dimly, the shape of a hallway and a staircase going up into gloom.

He raised his hand to knock.

For an instant, with his knuckles an inch from the wood, he felt himself to be the bravest person who had ever lived. He felt that no soldier on any field, no sailor in any storm, had ever faced so terrible a moment as this. His heart swelled. He was a hero. He was a martyr. He was going into the very jaws of the dragon, and he was going alone.

Then he knocked, and the sound was small and timid, and nothing in the world took any notice of it.

He waited. The house was silent. A breeze moved in the hedge. Somewhere a dog barked, twice, and was still. He was beginning to believe, with a wild, swelling joy, that no one would come, when he heard a step in the hallway, slow and uneven, and saw a shape loom up behind the colored glass.

The door opened.

Mrs. Gilfoyle stood there. She was very small. Georgie had always thought of her as large, as tall and bony and fierce, but she was a little bent old woman in a black dress, and she had to tilt her head back to look at him. Her face was all wrinkles. Her eyes were pale and watery behind a pair of steel spectacles. She held to the edge of the door with a hand that was spotted and thin, and the hand shook a little.

"Well?" she said.

Georgie opened his mouth. Nothing came out. He had prepared a speech. He had prepared it all the way down Whitby Street, and it had been a fine speech, manly and dignified. It was gone now. It had flown away like a bird.

"Well?" said Mrs. Gilfoyle again. "What is it, boy?"

"I'm sorry," said Georgie. The words fell out of him all in a lump. "I'm sorry I busted your window, ma'am. It was me. I done it. My pa's goin' to pay for it."

Mrs. Gilfoyle looked at him for a long moment through her spectacles. Georgie stood and waited for the holler. He had braced himself for it. He stood stiffly, with his arms at his sides and his chin up, as he had seen a picture of a man standing before a firing squad.

The holler did not come.

"Hm," said Mrs. Gilfoyle.

That was all. She looked at him a while longer, and then she nodded her head once, a short, sharp nod, and she began to close the door. At the last moment she stopped, and peered out at him through the narrowing space.

"You've got a good arm," she said. "My husband had a good arm. Don't throw it at my house again."

The door closed. Georgie heard her step going away down the hall, slow and uneven, until it was gone.

He stood on the porch. He did not understand. He had come up these steps to his doom, and there had been no doom. He felt, obscurely, that he had been cheated. Then, all at once, a vast lightness came over him, a lightness so enormous that he seemed to float down the steps and down the walk and through the gate, which cried out again behind him, and he did not care.

He went home through the purple shadows. As he passed the Moss house, a window went up, and Alfred's head came out.

"Did you get licked?" Alfred whispered.

Georgie stopped. He looked up at Alfred with an air of great weariness and great experience, like a veteran regarding a recruit.

"I went an' faced her," he said. "Right at her front door. All by myself."

Alfred's mouth fell open. Georgie walked on. He walked with a kind of swagger now, and he kicked a stone along the sidewalk before him, and he did not trouble to step over the cracks.

In the Haskell kitchen, his mother stood at the window and watched him come up the street. She watched the swagger and the kicked stone, and her lips moved a little, as if she were going to laugh, or perhaps to say something. But there was no one there to hear, and after a moment she turned back to the bread, which had risen, and began to punch it down.

Here is an excerpt of Stephen Crane's writing, to show you their style:

The youth felt, however, that his problem was in no wise lifted from him. There was, on the contrary, an irritating prolongation. The tale had created in him a great concern for himself. Now, with the newborn question in his mind, he was compelled to sink back into his old place as part of a blue demonstration. For days he made ceaseless calculations, but they were all wondrously unsatisfactory. He found that he could establish nothing. He finally concluded that the only way to prove himself was to go into the blaze, and then figuratively to watch his legs to discover their merits and faults. He reluctantly admitted that he could not sit still and with a mental slate and pencil derive an answer. To gain it, he must have blaze, blood, and danger, even as a chemist requires this, that, and the other. So he fretted for an opportunity. Meanwhile, he continually tried to measure himself by his comrades. The tall soldier, for one, gave him some assurance. This man’s serene unconcern dealt him a measure of confidence, for he had known him since childhood, and from his intimate knowledge he did not see how he could be capable of anything that was beyond him, the youth. Still, he thought that his comrade might be mistaken about himself. Or, on the other hand, he might be a man heretofore doomed to peace and obscurity, but, in reality, made to shine in war. The youth would have liked to have discovered another who suspected himself. A sympathetic comparison of mental notes would have been a joy to him. He occasionally tried to fathom a comrade with seductive sentences. He looked about to find men in the proper mood. All attempts failed to bring forth any statement which looked in any way like a confession to those doubts which he privately acknowledged in himself. He was afraid to make an open declaration of his concern, because he dreaded to place some unscrupulous confidant upon the high plane of the unconfessed from which elevation he could be derided. In regard to his companions his mind wavered between two opinions, according to his mood. Sometimes he inclined to believing them all heroes. In fact, he usually admired in secret the superior development of the higher qualities in others. He could conceive of men going very insignificantly about the world bearing a load of courage unseen, and although he had known many of his comrades through boyhood, he began to fear that his judgment of them had been blind. Then, in other moments, he flouted these theories, and assured him that his fellows were all privately wondering and quaking. His emotions made him feel strange in the presence of men who talked excitedly of a prospective battle as of a drama they were about to witness, with nothing but eagerness and curiosity apparent in their faces. It was often that he suspected them to be liars. He did not pass such thoughts without severe condemnation of himself. He dinned reproaches at times. He was convicted by himself of many shameful crimes against the gods of traditions. In his great anxiety his heart was continually clamoring at what he considered the intolerable slowness of the generals. They seemed content to perch tranquilly on the river bank, and leave him bowed down by the weight of a great problem. He wanted it settled forthwith. He could not long bear such a load, he said. Sometimes his anger at the commanders reached an acute stage, and he grumbled about the camp like a veteran. One morning, however, he found himself in the ranks of his prepared regiment. The men were whispering speculations and recounting the old rumors. In the gloom before the break of the day their uniforms glowed a deep purple hue. From across the river the red eyes were still peering. In the eastern sky there was a yellow patch like a rug laid for the feet of the coming sun; and against it, black and patternlike, loomed the gigantic figure of the colonel on a gigantic horse. From off in the darkness came the trampling of feet. The youth could occasionally see dark shadows that moved like monsters. The regiment stood at rest for what seemed a long time. The youth grew impatient. It was unendurable the way these affairs were managed. He wondered how long they were to be kept waiting. As he looked all about him and pondered upon the mystic gloom, he began to believe that at any moment the ominous distance might be aflare, and the rolling crashes of an engagement come to his ears. Staring once at the red eyes across the river, he conceived them to be growing larger, as the orbs of a row of dragons advancing. He turned toward the colonel and saw him lift his gigantic arm and calmly stroke his mustache. At last he heard from along the road at the foot of the hill the clatter of a horse’s galloping hoofs. It must be the coming of orders. He bent forward, scarce breathing. The exciting clickety-click, as it grew louder and louder, seemed to be beating upon his soul. Presently a horseman with jangling equipment drew rein before the colonel of the regiment. The two held a short, sharp-worded conversation. The men in the foremost ranks craned their necks. As the horseman wheeled his animal and galloped away he turned to shout over his shoulder, “Don’t forget that box of cigars!” The colonel mumbled in reply. The youth wondered what a box of cigars had to do with war. A moment later the regiment went swinging off into the darkness. It was now like one of those moving monsters wending with many feet. The air was heavy, and cold with dew. A mass of wet grass, marched upon, rustled like silk. There was an occasional flash and glimmer of steel from the backs of all these huge crawling reptiles. From the road came creakings and grumblings as some surly guns were dragged away. The men stumbled along still muttering speculations. There was a subdued debate. Once a man fell down, and as he reached for his rifle a comrade, unseeing, trod upon his hand. He of the injured fingers swore bitterly, and aloud. A low, tittering laugh went among his fellows. Presently they passed into a roadway and marched forward with easy strides. A dark regiment moved before them, and from behind also came the tinkle of equipments on the bodies of marching men. The rushing yellow of the developing day went on behind their backs. When the sunrays at last struck full and mellowingly upon the earth, the youth saw that the landscape was streaked with two long, thin, black columns which disappeared on the brow of a hill in front and rearward vanished in a wood. They were like two serpents crawling from the cavern of the night. The river was not in view. The tall soldier burst into praises of what he thought to be his powers of perception. Some of the tall one’s companions cried with emphasis that they, too, had evolved the same thing, and they congratulated themselves upon it. But there were others who said that the tall one’s plan was not the true one at all. They persisted with other theories. There was a vigorous discussion. The youth took no part in them. As he walked along in careless line he was engaged with his own eternal debate. He could not hinder himself from dwelling upon it. He was despondent and sullen, and threw shifting glances about him. He looked ahead, often expecting to hear from the advance the rattle of firing. But the long serpents crawled slowly from hill to hill without bluster of smoke. A dun-colored cloud of dust floated away to the right. The sky overhead was of a fairy blue. The youth studied the faces of his companions, ever on the watch to detect kindred emotions. He suffered disappointment. Some ardor of the air which was causing the veteran commands to move with glee—almost with song—had infected the new regiment. The men began to speak of victory as of a thing they knew. Also, the tall soldier received his vindication. They were certainly going to come around in behind the enemy. They expressed commiseration for that part of the army which had been left upon the river bank, felicitating themselves upon being a part of a blasting host. The youth, considering himself as separated from the others, was saddened by the blithe and merry speeches that went from rank to rank. The company wags all made their best endeavors. The regiment tramped to the tune of laughter. The blatant soldier often convulsed whole files by his biting sarcasms aimed at the tall one. And it was not long before all the men seemed to forget their mission. Whole brigades grinned in unison, and regiments laughed. A rather fat soldier attempted to pilfer a horse from a dooryard. He planned to load his knapsack upon it. He was escaping with his prize when a young girl rushed from the house and grabbed the animal’s mane. There followed a wrangle. The young girl, with pink cheeks and shining eyes, stood like a dauntless statue. The observant regiment, standing at rest in the roadway, whooped at once, and entered whole-souled upon the side of the maiden. The men became so engrossed in this affair that they entirely ceased to remember their own large war. They jeered the piratical private, and called attention to various defects in his personal appearance; and they were wildly enthusiastic in support of the young girl. To her, from some distance, came bold advice. “Hit him with a stick.” There were crows and catcalls showered upon him when he retreated without the horse. The regiment rejoiced at his downfall. Loud and vociferous congratulations were showered upon the maiden, who stood panting and regarding the troops with defiance. At nightfall the column broke into regimental pieces, and the fragments went into the fields to camp. Tents sprang up like strange plants. Camp fires, like red, peculiar blossoms, dotted the night. The youth kept from intercourse with his companions as much as circumstances would allow him. In the evening he wandered a few paces into the gloom. From this little distance the many fires, with the black forms of men passing to and fro before the crimson rays, made weird and satanic effects. He lay down in the grass. The blades pressed tenderly against his cheek. The moon had been lighted and was hung in a treetop. The liquid stillness of the night enveloping him made him feel vast pity for himself. There was a caress in the soft winds; and the whole mood of the darkness, he thought, was one of sympathy for himself in his distress. He wished, without reserve, that he was at home again making the endless rounds from the house to the barn, from the barn to the fields, from the fields to the barn, from the barn to the house. He remembered he had so often cursed the brindle cow and her mates, and had sometimes flung milking stools. But, from his present point of view, there was a halo of happiness about each of their heads, and he would have sacrificed all the brass buttons on the continent to have been enabled to return to them. He told himself that he was not formed for a soldier. And he mused seriously upon the radical differences between himself and those men who were dodging implike around the fires. As he mused thus he heard the rustle of grass, and, upon turning his head, discovered the loud soldier. He called out, “Oh, Wilson!” The latter approached and looked down. “Why, hello, Henry; is it you? What are you doing here?”

“Oh, thinking,” said the youth. The other sat down and carefully lighted his pipe. “You’re getting blue my boy. You’re looking thundering peek-ed. What the dickens is wrong with you?”

“Oh, nothing,” said the youth. The loud soldier launched then into the subject of the anticipated fight. “Oh, we’ve got ’em now!” As he spoke his boyish face was wreathed in a gleeful smile, and his voice had an exultant ring. “We’ve got ’em now. At last, by the eternal thunders, we’ll lick ’em good!”

“If the truth was known,” he added, more soberly, “they’ve licked us about every clip up to now; but this time—this time—we’ll lick ’em good!”

“I thought you was objecting to this march a little while ago,” said the youth coldly.

“Oh, it wasn’t that,” explained the other. “I don’t mind marching, if there’s going to be fighting at the end of it. What I hate is this getting moved here and moved there, with no good coming of it, as far as I can see, excepting sore feet and damned short rations.”

“Well, Jim Conklin says we’ll get plenty of fighting this time.”

“He’s right for once, I guess, though I can’t see how it come. This time we’re in for a big battle, and we’ve got the best end of it, certain sure. Gee rod! how we will thump ’em!” He arose and began to pace to and fro excitedly. The thrill of his enthusiasm made him walk with an elastic step. He was sprightly, vigorous, fiery in his belief in success. He looked into the future with clear proud eye, and he swore with the air of an old soldier. The youth watched him for a moment in silence. When he finally spoke his voice was as bitter as dregs. “Oh, you’re going to do great things, I s’pose!” The loud soldier blew a thoughtful cloud of smoke from his pipe. “Oh, I don’t know,” he remarked with dignity; “I don’t know. I s’pose I’ll do as well as the rest. I’m going to try like thunder.” He evidently complimented himself upon the modesty of this statement.

“How do you know you won’t run when the time comes?” asked the youth.

“Run?” said the loud one; “run?—of course not!” He laughed.

“Well,” continued the youth, “lots of good-a-’nough men have thought they was going to do great things before the fight, but when the time come they skedaddled.”

“Oh, that’s all true, I s’pose,” replied the other; “but I’m not going to skedaddle. The man that bets on my running will lose his money, that’s all.” He nodded confidently.

“Oh, shucks!” said the youth. “You ain’t the bravest man in the world, are you?”

“No, I ain’t,” exclaimed the loud soldier indignantly; “and I didn’t say I was the bravest man in the world, neither. I said I was going to do my share of fighting—that’s what I said. And I am, too. Who are you, anyhow? You talk as if you thought you was Napoleon Bonaparte.” He glared at the youth for a moment, and then strode away. The youth called in a savage voice after his comrade: “Well, you needn’t git mad about it!” But the other continued on his way and made no reply. He felt alone in space when his injured comrade had disappeared. His failure to discover any mite of resemblance in their viewpoints made him more miserable than before. No one seemed to be wrestling with such a terrific personal problem. He was a mental outcast. He went slowly to his tent and stretched himself on a blanket by the side of the snoring tall soldier. In the darkness he saw visions of a thousand-tongued fear that would babble at his back and cause him to flee, while others were going coolly about their country’s business. He admitted that he would not be able to cope with this monster. He felt that every nerve in his body would be an ear to hear the voices, while other men would remain stolid and deaf. And as he sweated with the pain of these thoughts, he could hear low, serene sentences. “I’ll bid five.” “Make it six.” “Seven.” “Seven goes.” He stared at the red, shivering reflection of a fire on the white wall of his tent until, exhausted and ill from the monotony of his suffering, he fell asleep.
