To gain it, he must have blaze, blood, and danger, even as a chemist requires this, that, and the other. So he fretted for an opportunity. Meanwhile, he continually tried to measure himself by his comrades. The tall soldier, for one, gave him some assurance. This man’s serene unconcern dealt him a measure of confidence, for he had known him since childhood, and from his intimate knowledge he did not see how he could be capable of anything that was beyond him, the youth. Still, he thought that his comrade might be mistaken about himself. Or, on the other hand, he might be a man heretofore doomed to peace and obscurity, but, in reality, made to shine in war. The youth would have liked to have discovered another who suspected himself. A sympathetic comparison of mental notes would have been a joy to him. He occasionally tried to fathom a comrade with seductive sentences. He looked about to find men in the proper mood. All attempts failed to bring forth any statement which looked in any way like a confession to those doubts which he privately acknowledged in himself. He was afraid to make an open declaration of his concern, because he dreaded to place some unscrupulous confidant upon the high plane of the unconfessed from which elevation he could be derided. In regard to his companions his mind wavered between two opinions, according to his mood. Sometimes he inclined to believing them all heroes. In fact, he usually admired in secret the superior development of the higher qualities in others. He could conceive of men going very insignificantly about the world bearing a load of courage unseen, and although he had known many of his comrades through boyhood, he began to fear that his judgment of them had been blind. Then, in other moments, he flouted these theories, and assured him that his fellows were all privately wondering and quaking. His emotions made him feel strange in the presence of men who talked excitedly of a prospective battle as of a drama they were about to witness, with nothing but eagerness and curiosity apparent in their faces. It was often that he suspected them to be liars. He did not pass such thoughts without severe condemnation of himself. He dinned reproaches at times. He was convicted by himself of many shameful crimes against the gods of traditions. In his great anxiety his heart was continually clamoring at what he considered the intolerable slowness of the generals. They seemed content to perch tranquilly on the river bank, and leave him bowed down by the weight of a great problem. He wanted it settled forthwith. He could not long bear such a load, he said. Sometimes his anger at the commanders reached an acute stage, and he grumbled about the camp like a veteran. One morning, however, he found himself in the ranks of his prepared regiment. The men were whispering speculations and recounting the old rumors. In the gloom before the break of the day their uniforms glowed a deep purple hue. From across the river the red eyes were still peering. In the eastern sky there was a yellow patch like a rug laid for the feet of the coming sun; and against it, black and patternlike, loomed the gigantic figure of the colonel on a gigantic horse. From off in the darkness came the trampling of feet. The youth could occasionally see dark shadows that moved like monsters. The regiment stood at rest for what seemed a long time. The youth grew impatient. It was unendurable the way these affairs were managed. He wondered how long they were to be kept waiting. As he looked all about him and pondered upon the mystic gloom, he began to believe that at any moment the ominous distance might be aflare, and the rolling crashes of an engagement come to his ears. Staring once at the red eyes across the river, he conceived them to be growing larger, as the orbs of a row of dragons advancing. He turned toward the colonel and saw him lift his gigantic arm and calmly stroke his mustache. At last he heard from along the road at the foot of the hill the clatter of a horse’s galloping hoofs. It must be the coming of orders. He bent forward, scarce breathing. The exciting clickety-click, as it grew louder and louder, seemed to be beating upon his soul. Presently a horseman with jangling equipment drew rein before the colonel of the regiment. The two held a short, sharp-worded conversation. The men in the foremost ranks craned their necks. As the horseman wheeled his animal and galloped away he turned to shout over his shoulder, “Don’t forget that box of cigars!” The colonel mumbled in reply. The youth wondered what a box of cigars had to do with war. A moment later the regiment went swinging off into the darkness. It was now like one of those moving monsters wending with many feet. The air was heavy, and cold with dew. A mass of wet grass, marched upon, rustled like silk. There was an occasional flash and glimmer of steel from the backs of all these huge crawling reptiles. From the road came creakings and grumblings as some surly guns were dragged away. The men stumbled along still muttering speculations. There was a subdued debate. Once a man fell down, and as he reached for his rifle a comrade, unseeing, trod upon his hand. He of the injured fingers swore bitterly, and aloud. A low, tittering laugh went among his fellows. Presently they passed into a roadway and marched forward with easy strides. A dark regiment moved before them, and from behind also came the tinkle of equipments on the bodies of marching men. The rushing yellow of the developing day went on behind their backs. When the sunrays at last struck full and mellowingly upon the earth, the youth saw that the landscape was streaked with two long, thin, black columns which disappeared on the brow of a hill in front and rearward vanished in a wood. They were like two serpents crawling from the cavern of the night. The river was not in view. The tall soldier burst into praises of what he thought to be his powers of perception. Some of the tall one’s companions cried with emphasis that they, too, had evolved the same thing, and they congratulated themselves upon it. But there were others who said that the tall one’s plan was not the true one at all. They persisted with other theories. There was a vigorous discussion. The youth took no part in them. As he walked along in careless line he was engaged with his own eternal debate. He could not hinder himself from dwelling upon it. He was despondent and sullen, and threw shifting glances about him. He looked ahead, often expecting to hear from the advance the rattle of firing. But the long serpents crawled slowly from hill to hill without bluster of smoke. A dun-colored cloud of dust floated away to the right. The sky overhead was of a fairy blue. The youth studied the faces of his companions, ever on the watch to detect kindred emotions. He suffered disappointment. Some ardor of the air which was causing the veteran commands to move with glee—almost with song—had infected the new regiment. The men began to speak of victory as of a thing they knew. Also, the tall soldier received his vindication. They were certainly going to come around in behind the enemy. They expressed commiseration for that part of the army which had been left upon the river bank, felicitating themselves upon being a part of a blasting host. The youth, considering himself as separated from the others, was saddened by the blithe and merry speeches that went from rank to rank. The company wags all made their best endeavors. The regiment tramped to the tune of laughter. The blatant soldier often convulsed whole files by his biting sarcasms aimed at the tall one. And it was not long before all the men seemed to forget their mission. Whole brigades grinned in unison, and regiments laughed. A rather fat soldier attempted to pilfer a horse from a dooryard. He planned to load his knapsack upon it. He was escaping with his prize when a young girl rushed from the house and grabbed the animal’s mane. There followed a wrangle. The young girl, with pink cheeks and shining eyes, stood like a dauntless statue. The observant regiment, standing at rest in the roadway, whooped at once, and entered whole-souled upon the side of the maiden. The men became so engrossed in this affair that they entirely ceased to remember their own large war. They jeered the piratical private, and called attention to various defects in his personal appearance; and they were wildly enthusiastic in support of the young girl. To her, from some distance, came bold advice. “Hit him with a stick.” There were crows and catcalls showered upon him when he retreated without the horse. The regiment rejoiced at his downfall. Loud and vociferous congratulations were showered upon the maiden, who stood panting and regarding the troops with defiance. At nightfall the column broke into regimental pieces, and the fragments went into the fields to camp. Tents sprang up like strange plants. Camp fires, like red, peculiar blossoms, dotted the night. The youth kept from intercourse with his companions as much as circumstances would allow him. In the evening he wandered a few paces into the gloom. From this little distance the many fires, with the black forms of men passing to and fro before the crimson rays, made weird and satanic effects. He lay down in the grass. The blades pressed tenderly against his cheek. The moon had been lighted and was hung in a treetop. The liquid stillness of the night enveloping him made him feel vast pity for himself. There was a caress in the soft winds; and the whole mood of the darkness, he thought, was one of sympathy for himself in his distress. He wished, without reserve, that he was at home again making the endless rounds from the house to the barn, from the barn to the fields, from the fields to the barn, from the barn to the house. He remembered he had so often cursed the brindle cow and her mates, and had sometimes flung milking stools. But, from his present point of view, there was a halo of happiness about each of their heads, and he would have sacrificed all the brass buttons on the continent to have been enabled to return to them. He told himself that he was not formed for a soldier. And he mused seriously upon the radical differences between himself and those men who were dodging implike around the fires. As he mused thus he heard the rustle of grass, and, upon turning his head, discovered the loud soldier. He called out, “Oh, Wilson!” The latter approached and looked down. “Why, hello, Henry; is it you? What are you doing here?”

“Oh, thinking,” said the youth. The other sat down and carefully lighted his pipe. “You’re getting blue my boy. You’re looking thundering peek-ed. What the dickens is wrong with you?”

“Oh, nothing,” said the youth. The loud soldier launched then into the subject of the anticipated fight. “Oh, we’ve got ’em now!” As he spoke his boyish face was wreathed in a gleeful smile, and his voice had an exultant ring. “We’ve got ’em now. At last, by the eternal thunders, we’ll lick ’em good!”

“If the truth was known,” he added, more soberly, “they’ve licked us about every clip up to now; but this time—this time—we’ll lick ’em good!”

“I thought you was objecting to this march a little while ago,” said the youth coldly.

“Oh, it wasn’t that,” explained the other. “I don’t mind marching, if there’s going to be fighting at the end of it. What I hate is this getting moved here and moved there, with no good coming of it, as far as I can see, excepting sore feet and damned short rations.”

“Well, Jim Conklin says we’ll get plenty of fighting this time.”

“He’s right for once, I guess, though I can’t see how it come. This time we’re in for a big battle, and we’ve got the best end of it, certain sure. Gee rod! how we will thump ’em!” He arose and began to pace to and fro excitedly. The thrill of his enthusiasm made him walk with an elastic step. He was sprightly, vigorous, fiery in his belief in success. He looked into the future with clear proud eye, and he swore with the air of an old soldier. The youth watched him for a moment in silence. When he finally spoke his voice was as bitter as dregs. “Oh, you’re going to do great things, I s’pose!” The loud soldier blew a thoughtful cloud of smoke from his pipe. “Oh, I don’t know,” he remarked with dignity; “I don’t know. I s’pose I’ll do as well as the rest. I’m going to try like thunder.” He evidently complimented himself upon the modesty of this statement.

“How do you know you won’t run when the time comes?” asked the youth.

“Run?” said the loud one; “run?—of course not!” He laughed.

“Well,” continued the youth, “lots of good-a-’nough men have thought they was going to do great things before the fight, but when the time come they skedaddled.”

“Oh, that’s all true, I s’pose,” replied the other; “but I’m not going to skedaddle. The man that bets on my running will lose his money, that’s all.” He nodded confidently.

“Oh, shucks!” said the youth. “You ain’t the bravest man in the world, are you?”

“No, I ain’t,” exclaimed the loud soldier indignantly; “and I didn’t say I was the bravest man in the world, neither. I said I was going to do my share of fighting—that’s what I said. And I am, too. Who are you, anyhow? You talk as if you thought you was Napoleon Bonaparte.” He glared at the youth for a moment, and then strode away. The youth called in a savage voice after his comrade: “Well, you needn’t git mad about it!” But the other continued on his way and made no reply. He felt alone in space when his injured comrade had disappeared. His failure to discover any mite of resemblance in their viewpoints made him more miserable than before. No one seemed to be wrestling with such a terrific personal problem. He was a mental outcast. He went slowly to his tent and stretched himself on a blanket by the side of the snoring tall soldier. In the darkness he saw visions of a thousand-tongued fear that would babble at his back and cause him to flee, while others were going coolly about their country’s business. He admitted that he would not be able to cope with this monster. He felt that every nerve in his body would be an ear to hear the voices, while other men would remain stolid and deaf. And as he sweated with the pain of these thoughts, he could hear low, serene sentences. “I’ll bid five.” “Make it six.” “Seven.” “Seven goes.” He stared at the red, shivering reflection of a fire on the white wall of his tent until, exhausted and ill from the monotony of his suffering, he fell asleep.

The husband came up the stairs slowly. Each step complained beneath him, and he paused on the landing, where a gas jet burned low, a little blue tongue that wavered as if it were trying to speak and could not. He stood there for some moments. He was composing himself. He had spent the latter part of the afternoon in the composition, and he had found it, in the saloon at the corner, a wondrously easy labor. There, with his elbow upon the wet bar and the brass rail cool beneath his boot, he had made a number of speeches that were very fine. They had been calm and manly speeches, and in each of them the wife had listened with lowered eyes and had finally said that he was right. But now, upon the landing, with the smell of cabbage coming from beneath a neighbor's door, he found that these speeches had fled from him. He could not recall the beginning of any one of them. He felt like a man who has been robbed in his sleep.

He opened the door. The wife was at the stove. She did not turn her head. The kitchen was small, and the lamp upon the table burned with a yellow, sullen flame that made the shadows of the chairs lie long and black across the floor, like things that had died there. The stove glowed through its seams. It crouched in the corner with a red eye at its belly, and it ticked and muttered as the iron cooled.

"You're late," said the wife.

"I know it," he replied. He hung his hat upon the nail. He did this with great care, as though the position of the hat were a matter of importance. Then he sat down at the table and looked at the oilcloth. There was a pattern upon it of small brown squares, and some of the squares had been worn away to a dull gray. He began to count them.

The wife brought a plate and set it before him. Upon the plate were potatoes and a piece of meat that had been kept warm too long. The meat had curled at the edges. It looked defiant. She sat down opposite him, folded her hands in her lap, and regarded him.

She was a small woman, with hair the color of dry straw drawn back tightly from her forehead. Her face had a certain sharpness to it, as of a blade that has been honed often against grief and small economies. When she was a girl the young men of the town had called her pretty, and some of that prettiness remained, but it had retreated into her eyes, where it stood guard.

He ate a potato. He was aware that she was looking at him. He felt the look upon the top of his head like a hand. He did not raise his eyes. The clock upon the shelf ticked with the insolence of a creditor.

"Well?" said the wife.

"Well what?"

"Well, nothing, I s'pose," she said.

He ate another potato. He resolved that he would tell her presently, when he had eaten. A man could not be expected to explain grave matters upon an empty stomach. It was unreasonable of her. He began to feel that she was very unreasonable, and he cherished this feeling, for it made him stronger. He told himself that she was always pushing him, always at him, never giving a man a minute's peace. He recalled several instances. They came to him readily, and he arranged them in a little row, like soldiers, and reviewed them with satisfaction.

"Mrs. Kearney was up," said the wife.

He paused with the fork lifted. "Was she?"

"She was. She come up about four o'clock. She said her Jim come home early from the mill. She said he come home about half-past two."

The husband put the fork down. He looked at it lying upon the plate. It seemed to him a curious object, with its four prongs bent a little out of true. He wondered who had bent them. He thought perhaps he had bent them himself, some long time ago, in a fit of temper, and had forgotten.

"Well," he said, "what of it?"

"Nothing," said the wife. "Only she said her Jim said something happened at the mill. She said there was a row."

"There's always rows at that mill."

"She said it was you."

There was a silence. Through the wall came the sound of the neighbor's child, wailing in a long, thin, monotonous voice, as if it had been wound up to wail and must continue until it ran down. A wagon went by in the street below. The window rattled faintly in its frame.

The husband lifted his head. He discovered that his face had grown hot. He felt that the wife had taken an unfair advantage. She had gone behind his back. She had sat in this kitchen with Mrs. Kearney and the two of them had picked him over, like crows at a carcass. He perceived a vast injustice. It loomed before him, and he was glad of it, for it was large enough to stand behind.

"You and Mrs. Kearney," he said bitterly. "You and Mrs. Kearney got it all settled, I guess. You don't need me to tell you nothing."

"I'd rather have it from you," said the wife.

"Well, you can have it, then!" He struck the table with the flat of his hand, and the lamp chimney jumped and gave a small, glassy cry. "Ferguson called me a loafer. Right in front of the whole floor, he called me a loafer. And I told him what I thought of him. And he said I could get my time. And I got it. There! Now you know it all."

He leaned back in his chair. He had expected that this declaration would have a great effect. He had pictured the wife growing pale, putting her hand to her throat, perhaps weeping a little. He had prepared himself to be generous with her tears. But the wife merely sat as before, with her hands in her lap, and looked at him with her guarded eyes.

"What did you tell him?" she asked.

"I told him plenty."

"What did you tell him, Will?"

He moved his shoulders uneasily. In truth, the speech that he had made to Ferguson had not been a great speech. He had said, "You can't talk to me like that," and Ferguson had said, "Can't I?" and he had said, "No, you can't," and then he had said a word that he would not have said before the wife. Afterward he had stood with his hands hanging at his sides and the eyes of the floor upon him, and he had felt that the planing machines were all looking at him too, with their bright, whirling teeth. He had walked out through the yard, among the stacks of yellow lumber, and the smell of the fresh-cut pine had seemed to mock him with its cleanliness. All the way to the corner he had been improving upon the speech. By the time he had reached the saloon it had become a thing of eloquence and great dignity, and Ferguson had shrunk before it, and the men upon the floor had murmured approval. He had told it to the barkeeper in this form, and the barkeeper had said, "Good for you." The barkeeper's approval had cost him eleven cents.

"I told him he couldn't talk to me like that," said the husband.

"And then?"

"And then he give me my time, I told you."

"How much?"

He did not answer at once. He took up the fork again and pushed the meat about the plate. It slid in its gray grease. The wife waited. She had a capacity for waiting that seemed to him monstrous. She could wait like the stove, like the walls. He felt that if he did not speak she would sit there until morning, until the lamp burned dry and the windows went gray, and she would be waiting still.

"Four dollars and some," he said.

"Four dollars and how much?"

"Eighty cents."

"Where is it?"

He reached into his pocket and drew out the money and laid it upon the oilcloth. There were three bills and some silver. The wife looked at it. She did not touch it. She counted it with her eyes.

"That's three dollars and forty-five," she said.

"Well," said the husband, "I had to have something. A man's got a right to a glass of beer, ain't he? After a thing like that? A man's got a right."

"Yes," said the wife. "A man's got a right."

She said it quietly, but the words fell upon him like stones. He perceived that she had placed herself upon a high and serene plane from which she could look down upon him and his glass of beer and his four dollars and eighty cents. He resented this elevation. He had a wild desire to pull her down from it. He searched his mind for some weapon.

"You don't care nothing about what he called me," he cried. "You don't care. A man gets insulted in front of everybody, and all you care about is the money. That's all you ever care about. Money, money. I don't believe you'd care if Ferguson knocked me down, so long as he paid me my time first."

The wife's face did not change, but a faint color came into it, high up, near the eyes. She looked at the window. Beyond the glass the night was black, and the lamp made a second kitchen out there in the darkness, a pale, wavering kitchen where a pale woman sat across from a pale man, and the two of them seemed to be drowning.

"Somebody has to care about it," she said.

"Oh, I know," said he. "I know. I ain't good enough for you. I never was. Your mother told you, didn't she? She told you I wasn't nothing but a mill hand and I'd never be nothing but a mill hand. Well, I ain't even that now. I guess you and your mother are satisfied."

"Don't you talk about my mother."

"I'll talk about who I like."

"Not in this house, you won't."

"Whose house is it?" he demanded. "Whose house? Who pays the rent?"

The question hung in the air between them. Both of them heard how it sounded, and both of them understood, at the same instant, that he would not pay the rent upon the first of the month, nor perhaps upon the first of the month after. The husband felt the question turn around in the air and come back to him, like a thrown stone that has struck a wall. He looked down at the money upon the oilcloth. It seemed very small. The bills were creased and soft and dirty, and the silver lay in a little heap like the scales of some poor fish.

The neighbor's child had ceased to wail. In the silence the clock ticked. The stove muttered. Somewhere below, in the street, a man was singing in a loud, uncertain voice, and the song came up to them in fragments, as if it had been broken on the stairs.

The wife rose and went to the shelf above the stove. She reached behind the clock and took down a small tin box, of the kind in which tea is sold. It had once been painted red, with gold Chinese figures upon it, but the paint had worn away at the corners, and the figures had lost their faces. She brought it to the table and set it down beside the money. She opened it. Inside there were some bills, folded very small, and a number of coins.

The husband looked at the box. He had known that it was there. He had always known. But he had pretended not to know, and the wife had pretended that he did not know, and this pretense had stood between them for two years like a piece of furniture that neither of them would move. Now she had moved it. He felt suddenly naked.

"There's thirty-one dollars," she said. "That's two months, if we're careful. Maybe more."

"I don't want it," said the husband.

"It ain't for you to want."

"I said I don't want it." His voice rose. "I ain't going to live off what you've been scrimping and hiding. What do you take me for? You think I can't get another place? I can get a place tomorrow. I can get a place at Holloway's. Holloway's been after me for a year. I can go to the city, if it comes to that. There's work in the city for a man that ain't afraid of it."

He had not known, until he said it, that he was going to speak of the city. But as soon as the words were out of his mouth they seemed to him very fine. He saw himself in the city. He saw tall buildings, and crowds, and himself among them, walking briskly, with a new hat. He saw himself writing letters home, generous letters with money folded in them. He saw the wife reading these letters and weeping with gratitude and remorse. The vision was so bright that it dazzled him, and for a moment he forgot the kitchen and the lamp and the faceless Chinese figures upon the tin.

"Holloway's ain't hiring," said the wife. "Mrs. Kearney's brother tried there in March."

The vision went out like a blown match.

"And the city," she went on, in the same level voice. "What would you do in the city? You don't know nobody in the city. You'd come back. You'd come back in a month, and you'd come back with nothing, and you'd be ashamed. And you'd be meaner then than you are now."

"Mean!" he cried. "I'm mean, am I?"

"You're mean when you're ashamed," said the wife. "You always was."

He stood up. The chair scraped backward and struck the wall. He stood there, breathing heavily, and looked down at her. She was so small. Her shoulders were narrow under the faded calico, and he could see the part in her hair, a thin white line, very straight, as if it had been drawn with a ruler. He had a desire to strike something. He looked about the kitchen. Everything in it was familiar and poor and patient. The stove, the shelf, the clock, the box. There was nothing that deserved to be struck. He perceived that his rage had nowhere to go. It turned in him like a dog in a cage, and presently, finding no door, it lay down.

He sat again. He put his elbows upon the table and his face in his hands. Through his fingers he could see the money, and the tin box, and the wife's hands, which she had laid flat upon the oilcloth on either side of them, as if to keep them from blowing away.

"He called me a loafer," he said, in a low voice. "In front of everybody."

"I know it," said the wife.

"I wasn't loafing. I'd only stopped a minute. Peterson was telling about his boy that's sick, and I'd only stopped a minute."

"I know it."

"You don't know it. You wasn't there."

"I know you," said the wife.

He took his hands from his face and looked at her. Her eyes were wet. She had not wept, and she did not weep now, but the guard in her eyes had stood aside a little, and he could see behind it something that frightened him more than her anger. It was a great tiredness. It was the tiredness of one who has carried a load up a long hill and has looked up and seen that the hill goes on.

He felt that he ought to say something. He groped for words. In the saloon there had been a great many words, and they had come easily, one after another, like beads upon a string. But now the string had broken and the beads had rolled away into the corners, and he could not find them.

"I'll go down to Holloway's anyhow," he said at last. "In the morning. It don't hurt to ask."

"No," said the wife. "It don't hurt to ask."

"And there's the brickyard. They might want somebody at the brickyard."

"They might."

He looked at the plate before him. The meat lay upon it, cold now, with a white rim of fat congealing at its edge. He took up the fork and began to eat. He ate slowly, chewing with great care, as though this, too, were a duty he owed her. The wife watched him. After a time she gathered the money from the oilcloth, his three dollars and forty-five cents, and smoothed the bills one by one with the flat of her thumb, and put them in the tin box with the rest. She closed the lid. The faceless Chinese figures went once more about their faded business.

She put the box back behind the clock.

Then she stood for a moment at the shelf, with her back to him, and he saw her shoulders lift and fall once, as if she had drawn a long breath and let it go. He waited for her to turn. He did not know what he would say when she turned. He thought that perhaps she would not turn at all, that she would stand there with her back to him forever, and he felt a sudden childish terror, as of a boy who has been left alone in a dark field.

But she turned. She came back to the table and took up the coffee pot from the stove and poured him a cup. The coffee was black and bitter and had been boiling for two hours. He drank it without complaint.

"There's pie," she said.

"I don't want no pie."

"It's dried apple. I made it this morning."

He looked up at her. She was standing beside him with the pot in her hand, and the lamp put a yellow light along one side of her face and left the other side in shadow, so that she seemed to him half a stranger and half the girl he had walked with along the river road, years ago, when the willows were green and the world was a thing that would certainly come right.

"Well," he said, "I'll have a little piece."

She cut it and set it before him. He ate it. It was very good. He wished, with a sudden and humble fervor, that he could tell her that it was very good, but the words lodged somewhere in his throat and would not come out. He ate the whole of it, and pressed the last crumbs with his fork, and that was all that he could manage.

Below in the street the man was still singing. He had come to the end of his song and had begun it again, and he sang the first verse very loudly and with tremendous feeling, as if it were a hymn of victory. Then he forgot the second verse and stopped. There was a silence. Then a door slammed somewhere, and the singer swore, plaintively, as one who has been wronged by the universe and expects no redress.

The husband laughed, a short laugh. The wife looked at him, and after a moment the corner of her mouth moved a little.

"That's Mullins," she said.

"I know it."

"He'll be at it till morning."

"Let him," said the husband. "Let him sing."

The clock ticked. The stove, cooling, muttered in its corner, and its red eye grew dim. The wife sat down across from him and folded her hands again in her lap, and the two of them sat there under the sullen lamp, not speaking, while the pale kitchen beyond the window wavered in the black glass, and the pale man and the pale woman in it waited, as they did, for whatever the morning would bring.

Here is an excerpt of Stephen Crane's writing, to show you their style:

The youth felt, however, that his problem was in no wise lifted from him. There was, on the contrary, an irritating prolongation. The tale had created in him a great concern for himself. Now, with the newborn question in his mind, he was compelled to sink back into his old place as part of a blue demonstration. For days he made ceaseless calculations, but they were all wondrously unsatisfactory. He found that he could establish nothing. He finally concluded that the only way to prove himself was to go into the blaze, and then figuratively to watch his legs to discover their merits and faults. He reluctantly admitted that he could not sit still and with a mental slate and pencil derive an answer. To gain it, he must have blaze, blood, and danger, even as a chemist requires this, that, and the other. So he fretted for an opportunity. Meanwhile, he continually tried to measure himself by his comrades. The tall soldier, for one, gave him some assurance. This man’s serene unconcern dealt him a measure of confidence, for he had known him since childhood, and from his intimate knowledge he did not see how he could be capable of anything that was beyond him, the youth. Still, he thought that his comrade might be mistaken about himself. Or, on the other hand, he might be a man heretofore doomed to peace and obscurity, but, in reality, made to shine in war. The youth would have liked to have discovered another who suspected himself. A sympathetic comparison of mental notes would have been a joy to him. He occasionally tried to fathom a comrade with seductive sentences. He looked about to find men in the proper mood. All attempts failed to bring forth any statement which looked in any way like a confession to those doubts which he privately acknowledged in himself. He was afraid to make an open declaration of his concern, because he dreaded to place some unscrupulous confidant upon the high plane of the unconfessed from which elevation he could be derided. In regard to his companions his mind wavered between two opinions, according to his mood. Sometimes he inclined to believing them all heroes. In fact, he usually admired in secret the superior development of the higher qualities in others. He could conceive of men going very insignificantly about the world bearing a load of courage unseen, and although he had known many of his comrades through boyhood, he began to fear that his judgment of them had been blind. Then, in other moments, he flouted these theories, and assured him that his fellows were all privately wondering and quaking. His emotions made him feel strange in the presence of men who talked excitedly of a prospective battle as of a drama they were about to witness, with nothing but eagerness and curiosity apparent in their faces. It was often that he suspected them to be liars. He did not pass such thoughts without severe condemnation of himself. He dinned reproaches at times. He was convicted by himself of many shameful crimes against the gods of traditions. In his great anxiety his heart was continually clamoring at what he considered the intolerable slowness of the generals. They seemed content to perch tranquilly on the river bank, and leave him bowed down by the weight of a great problem. He wanted it settled forthwith. He could not long bear such a load, he said. Sometimes his anger at the commanders reached an acute stage, and he grumbled about the camp like a veteran. One morning, however, he found himself in the ranks of his prepared regiment. The men were whispering speculations and recounting the old rumors. In the gloom before the break of the day their uniforms glowed a deep purple hue. From across the river the red eyes were still peering. In the eastern sky there was a yellow patch like a rug laid for the feet of the coming sun; and against it, black and patternlike, loomed the gigantic figure of the colonel on a gigantic horse. From off in the darkness came the trampling of feet. The youth could occasionally see dark shadows that moved like monsters. The regiment stood at rest for what seemed a long time. The youth grew impatient. It was unendurable the way these affairs were managed. He wondered how long they were to be kept waiting. As he looked all about him and pondered upon the mystic gloom, he began to believe that at any moment the ominous distance might be aflare, and the rolling crashes of an engagement come to his ears. Staring once at the red eyes across the river, he conceived them to be growing larger, as the orbs of a row of dragons advancing. He turned toward the colonel and saw him lift his gigantic arm and calmly stroke his mustache. At last he heard from along the road at the foot of the hill the clatter of a horse’s galloping hoofs. It must be the coming of orders. He bent forward, scarce breathing. The exciting clickety-click, as it grew louder and louder, seemed to be beating upon his soul. Presently a horseman with jangling equipment drew rein before the colonel of the regiment. The two held a short, sharp-worded conversation. The men in the foremost ranks craned their necks. As the horseman wheeled his animal and galloped away he turned to shout over his shoulder, “Don’t forget that box of cigars!” The colonel mumbled in reply. The youth wondered what a box of cigars had to do with war. A moment later the regiment went swinging off into the darkness. It was now like one of those moving monsters wending with many feet. The air was heavy, and cold with dew. A mass of wet grass, marched upon, rustled like silk. There was an occasional flash and glimmer of steel from the backs of all these huge crawling reptiles. From the road came creakings and grumblings as some surly guns were dragged away. The men stumbled along still muttering speculations. There was a subdued debate. Once a man fell down, and as he reached for his rifle a comrade, unseeing, trod upon his hand. He of the injured fingers swore bitterly, and aloud. A low, tittering laugh went among his fellows. Presently they passed into a roadway and marched forward with easy strides. A dark regiment moved before them, and from behind also came the tinkle of equipments on the bodies of marching men. The rushing yellow of the developing day went on behind their backs. When the sunrays at last struck full and mellowingly upon the earth, the youth saw that the landscape was streaked with two long, thin, black columns which disappeared on the brow of a hill in front and rearward vanished in a wood. They were like two serpents crawling from the cavern of the night. The river was not in view. The tall soldier burst into praises of what he thought to be his powers of perception. Some of the tall one’s companions cried with emphasis that they, too, had evolved the same thing, and they congratulated themselves upon it. But there were others who said that the tall one’s plan was not the true one at all. They persisted with other theories. There was a vigorous discussion. The youth took no part in them. As he walked along in careless line he was engaged with his own eternal debate. He could not hinder himself from dwelling upon it. He was despondent and sullen, and threw shifting glances about him. He looked ahead, often expecting to hear from the advance the rattle of firing. But the long serpents crawled slowly from hill to hill without bluster of smoke. A dun-colored cloud of dust floated away to the right. The sky overhead was of a fairy blue. The youth studied the faces of his companions, ever on the watch to detect kindred emotions. He suffered disappointment. Some ardor of the air which was causing the veteran commands to move with glee—almost with song—had infected the new regiment. The men began to speak of victory as of a thing they knew. Also, the tall soldier received his vindication. They were certainly going to come around in behind the enemy. They expressed commiseration for that part of the army which had been left upon the river bank, felicitating themselves upon being a part of a blasting host. The youth, considering himself as separated from the others, was saddened by the blithe and merry speeches that went from rank to rank. The company wags all made their best endeavors. The regiment tramped to the tune of laughter. The blatant soldier often convulsed whole files by his biting sarcasms aimed at the tall one. And it was not long before all the men seemed to forget their mission. Whole brigades grinned in unison, and regiments laughed. A rather fat soldier attempted to pilfer a horse from a dooryard. He planned to load his knapsack upon it. He was escaping with his prize when a young girl rushed from the house and grabbed the animal’s mane. There followed a wrangle. The young girl, with pink cheeks and shining eyes, stood like a dauntless statue. The observant regiment, standing at rest in the roadway, whooped at once, and entered whole-souled upon the side of the maiden. The men became so engrossed in this affair that they entirely ceased to remember their own large war. They jeered the piratical private, and called attention to various defects in his personal appearance; and they were wildly enthusiastic in support of the young girl. To her, from some distance, came bold advice. “Hit him with a stick.” There were crows and catcalls showered upon him when he retreated without the horse. The regiment rejoiced at his downfall. Loud and vociferous congratulations were showered upon the maiden, who stood panting and regarding the troops with defiance. At nightfall the column broke into regimental pieces, and the fragments went into the fields to camp. Tents sprang up like strange plants. Camp fires, like red, peculiar blossoms, dotted the night. The youth kept from intercourse with his companions as much as circumstances would allow him. In the evening he wandered a few paces into the gloom. From this little distance the many fires, with the black forms of men passing to and fro before the crimson rays, made weird and satanic effects. He lay down in the grass. The blades pressed tenderly against his cheek. The moon had been lighted and was hung in a treetop. The liquid stillness of the night enveloping him made him feel vast pity for himself. There was a caress in the soft winds; and the whole mood of the darkness, he thought, was one of sympathy for himself in his distress. He wished, without reserve, that he was at home again making the endless rounds from the house to the barn, from the barn to the fields, from the fields to the barn, from the barn to the house. He remembered he had so often cursed the brindle cow and her mates, and had sometimes flung milking stools. But, from his present point of view, there was a halo of happiness about each of their heads, and he would have sacrificed all the brass buttons on the continent to have been enabled to return to them. He told himself that he was not formed for a soldier. And he mused seriously upon the radical differences between himself and those men who were dodging implike around the fires. As he mused thus he heard the rustle of grass, and, upon turning his head, discovered the loud soldier. He called out, “Oh, Wilson!” The latter approached and looked down. “Why, hello, Henry; is it you? What are you doing here?”

“Oh, thinking,” said the youth. The other sat down and carefully lighted his pipe. “You’re getting blue my boy. You’re looking thundering peek-ed. What the dickens is wrong with you?”

“Oh, nothing,” said the youth. The loud soldier launched then into the subject of the anticipated fight. “Oh, we’ve got ’em now!” As he spoke his boyish face was wreathed in a gleeful smile, and his voice had an exultant ring. “We’ve got ’em now. At last, by the eternal thunders, we’ll lick ’em good!”

“If the truth was known,” he added, more soberly, “they’ve licked us about every clip up to now; but this time—this time—we’ll lick ’em good!”

“I thought you was objecting to this march a little while ago,” said the youth coldly.

“Oh, it wasn’t that,” explained the other. “I don’t mind marching, if there’s going to be fighting at the end of it. What I hate is this getting moved here and moved there, with no good coming of it, as far as I can see, excepting sore feet and damned short rations.”

“Well, Jim Conklin says we’ll get plenty of fighting this time.”

“He’s right for once, I guess, though I can’t see how it come. This time we’re in for a big battle, and we’ve got the best end of it, certain sure. Gee rod! how we will thump ’em!” He arose and began to pace to and fro excitedly. The thrill of his enthusiasm made him walk with an elastic step. He was sprightly, vigorous, fiery in his belief in success. He looked into the future with clear proud eye, and he swore with the air of an old soldier. The youth watched him for a moment in silence. When he finally spoke his voice was as bitter as dregs. “Oh, you’re going to do great things, I s’pose!” The loud soldier blew a thoughtful cloud of smoke from his pipe. “Oh, I don’t know,” he remarked with dignity; “I don’t know. I s’pose I’ll do as well as the rest. I’m going to try like thunder.” He evidently complimented himself upon the modesty of this statement.

“How do you know you won’t run when the time comes?” asked the youth.

“Run?” said the loud one; “run?—of course not!” He laughed.

“Well,” continued the youth, “lots of good-a-’nough men have thought they was going to do great things before the fight, but when the time come they skedaddled.”

“Oh, that’s all true, I s’pose,” replied the other; “but I’m not going to skedaddle. The man that bets on my running will lose his money, that’s all.” He nodded confidently.

“Oh, shucks!” said the youth. “You ain’t the bravest man in the world, are you?”

“No, I ain’t,” exclaimed the loud soldier indignantly; “and I didn’t say I was the bravest man in the world, neither. I said I was going to do my share of fighting—that’s what I said. And I am, too. Who are you, anyhow? You talk as if you thought you was Napoleon Bonaparte.” He glared at the youth for a moment, and then strode away. The youth called in a savage voice after his comrade: “Well, you needn’t git mad about it!” But the other continued on his way and made no reply. He felt alone in space when his injured comrade had disappeared. His failure to discover any mite of resemblance in their viewpoints made him more miserable than before. No one seemed to be wrestling with such a terrific personal problem. He was a mental outcast. He went slowly to his tent and stretched himself on a blanket by the side of the snoring tall soldier. In the darkness he saw visions of a thousand-tongued fear that would babble at his back and cause him to flee, while others were going coolly about their country’s business. He admitted that he would not be able to cope with this monster. He felt that every nerve in his body would be an ear to hear the voices, while other men would remain stolid and deaf. And as he sweated with the pain of these thoughts, he could hear low, serene sentences. “I’ll bid five.” “Make it six.” “Seven.” “Seven goes.” He stared at the red, shivering reflection of a fire on the white wall of his tent until, exhausted and ill from the monotony of his suffering, he fell asleep.

The train went away from him with a great snort, as if it had been insulted. It dragged its long body around the bend of the hills, and its smoke hung for a time above the trees, a gray rag upon the sky, and then it too was gone. The young man stood alone upon the platform with his valise. The station agent regarded him from a window, and then withdrew his face, as a turtle withdraws.

The young man had rehearsed this arrival many times. In the dark of the sleeping car he had arranged his features into a fine city carelessness. He had resolved to stand with one hand in his pocket and to look upon the village as a man looks upon a toy he has outgrown. He had thought that he would say, "Well, the old place ain't changed any," in a voice of easy pity. Now, with the platform boards under his feet and the smell of the mud and the wet fields coming to him, he found that he could not remember the precise attitude. He put his hand in his pocket and then took it out again. He was afraid that he looked foolish.

The village sat upon its hill like an old woman who has been told bad news and has decided not to believe it. The church steeple was white and sharp. There was a yellow light in the store. Beyond, the road went away into the brown country and lost itself among the fences.

Presently he heard wheels. A wagon came grinding down the road, and upon the seat was a large figure in a coat the color of a dead leaf. The horse was a gaunt beast with a melancholy head that swung from side to side, as if it disapproved of everything it saw. The wagon stopped below the platform, and the large figure looked up.

"That you, Ned?"

"Hello, Tom," said the young man.

He had meant to say more. He had meant to cry out something hearty and condescending. But the sight of his cousin had dealt him a blow. He had left a gangling boy with wrists that came out of his sleeves. Here was a man. The shoulders were thick. A brown mustache hung upon the lip like a thing that had grown there through long patience. The face was red and seamed, and the eyes looked out of it with a calm that seemed to the young man almost insolent.

The cousin climbed down and took the valise. He weighed it in his hand.

"Ain't much to it," he said.

"I travel light," replied the young man. He had a sense that this was a sophisticated remark, and he was pleased with it. Then he reflected that it might also be taken to mean that he was poor, and his pleasure departed.

They mounted the wagon. The melancholy horse turned its head and gazed back at the young man with a long, dark, accusing eye. Then it moved.

For a while neither spoke. The wheels sucked at the mud. The young man sat stiffly, and held his hat upon his knee, for he feared the wind might take it, and it was the best hat he owned. He studied his cousin from the corner of his eye. The large man drove with the reins held loosely in one hand, and he looked out over the fields with an air of proprietorship, as if he had personally arranged the hills.

The young man began to feel the old misery stir within him. It was a thing he had carried away from this country five years before, folded up small, and he had believed it lost in the city. He had walked upon pavements. He had eaten in restaurants where the waiters wore white aprons and spoke with contempt. He had stood in a crowd and watched a building burn. He had told himself that these experiences had wrought a great change, that he was now a man of the world, and that the folk at home would recognize it upon his face as plainly as a scar. Now he looked at his cousin's thick wrists upon the reins, and he began to doubt that any of it showed.

"Well," said the cousin at last, "how's the city?"

The young man had waited for this question. He had prepared for it during four hundred miles. Yet when it came it seemed to strike him unawares, like a stone thrown from a hedge.

"Oh, it's big," he said. "It's mighty big."

"I s'pose it is," said the cousin.

The young man perceived that this was not enough. He searched his mind for some grand fact. "There's a building down there," he said, "that's twenty stories. They got elevators. You get in a little room and it goes right up."

"I heard of them," said the cousin.

This calm reception of the elevator wounded the young man. He had expected wonder. He had expected to be questioned. He felt that he had offered a gold piece and had seen it examined and handed back. He sat in a sullen silence and watched the fences go by. They were gray and crooked and some of them had fallen, and they lay in the grass like old men who have fainted.

The road came out upon a rise, and below them was the creek. It ran brown and swollen with the spring, and it made a low, steady noise, like a crowd heard from a distance. The cousin pointed with his whip.

"Remember that?"

The young man looked. There was the bend, and the sycamore that leaned out over the water with its pale limbs, and the flat rock. A sudden warmth went through him. He remembered the summer sun upon his naked back, and the cold shock of the water, and the shouts.

"The swimming hole," he said.

"Yes, sir," said the cousin. "Remember when you was going to jump off the top limb and you got up there and you wouldn't come down?"

The warmth fled. The young man felt his ears grow hot. He had not remembered this. It came back to him now with a dreadful clearness—the swaying limb, the brown water far below, the faces of the other boys turned up like white plates, and his own voice saying that he had hurt his ankle climbing.

"I hurt my ankle," he said.

The cousin laughed. It was a large, easy laugh that seemed to roll out over the fields. "That's what you said," he answered. "That's just what you said."

The young man was convicted. He sat in the wagon and felt that a judgment had been passed upon him, and that it had been passed many years ago, and that all the while he had been gone the judgment had been standing in this valley, waiting, like the sycamore. He considered that the cousin had perhaps told this tale often. He imagined it repeated at the store, in barns, at suppers, and the faces of the listeners breaking into grins. He felt that he had been a jest in his absence. A dull rage grew in him. He told himself that the cousin was a clod, a man who had never been anywhere, a creature of mud and cows, and that his opinion was a thing of no importance. Yet he found that he cared for it very much.

"You jumped," he said, with some bitterness. "I remember you jumped."

"Shucks," said the cousin, "I like to drowned. Pa had to pull me out by the hair."

The young man turned and looked at him. The cousin was grinning at the road ahead. There was no malice in his face. It seemed to the young man a strange thing that this large person should remember his own disgrace with such cheerfulness. He wondered if the cousin was a fool. Then he wondered if he himself was the fool. He could not determine it. He sat in perplexity while the melancholy horse drew them over the hill.

The farmhouse came into view. It stood back from the road among bare apple trees, and its windows caught the low sun and burned with a red and steady fire. The barn behind it was larger than the young man remembered, and freshly painted, and it seemed to stare at him with a great blank face. Smoke went up from the chimney in a thin blue thread.

"You've painted the barn," said the young man.

"Last fall," said the cousin. He spoke the words with a quiet pride that the young man felt to be a kind of boast. He had nothing to set against a painted barn. He had a room on the fourth floor of a house in a street where the ash barrels stood like sentinels. He had a clerk's stool and a ledger. He had seventeen dollars in his pocket and a return ticket. He had told no one at home of the stool or of the ledger. In his letters he had spoken of "the firm," and of "prospects," and these words had seemed to him at the time to glitter.

A woman came out upon the porch. She was small and wore a blue apron, and she held a child upon her hip. The child had a round face like a pudding and regarded the newcomer with deep suspicion.

"This is Mary," said the cousin. "And that there is Sam."

The young man got down from the wagon. He took off his hat to the woman with a flourish that he had observed in the city. It had seemed graceful there. Here, under the wide sky and before the plain face of the house, it seemed to him at once to be absurd, and he finished it hastily, and put the hat back on crooked.

"Pleased to meet you," he said.

"We've heard so much," said the woman, and smiled.

He wondered what they had heard. He suspected the swimming hole.

---

At supper the lamp stood in the middle of the table and threw a yellow circle upon the cloth. Beyond the circle the room was dim and full of shapes. A clock upon the shelf ticked loudly, as if it were counting the young man's mistakes. There were potatoes and ham and a great pale loaf, and the young man ate with a care for his manners that made his elbows ache.

The cousin ate with a vast and simple industry. Between mouthfuls he spoke of the farm. He spoke of the north field and the price of feed and a cow that had been sick. The young man listened and nodded. He found that these matters, which he had fled from with contempt, now came to him with a peculiar and painful interest. He wished to ask questions, but he feared that questions would betray him, that they would show that he had not, after all, risen above cows.

"And how's the firm?" said the woman. "Tom says you've done real well."

The young man felt the eyes upon him. The child's eyes were the worst. They were round and blue and had no mercy.

"Oh, pretty well," he said. "Pretty well. There's a chance of getting moved up, they say." He added, after a moment, "To the front office."

He did not know whether there was a front office. He had never been in it if there was. But the words seemed to swell up in the lamplight and take on substance. He saw the woman look at her husband, and he saw the husband nod slowly, and he felt a great, guilty glow of triumph. He had placed himself upon a high plane. From this elevation he looked down upon the painted barn.

"That's fine," said the cousin. "That's mighty fine. I always said you'd get on."

The young man's triumph turned sour in him. He had not expected generosity. It seemed to him that a man who tells lies should be met with suspicion, so that he may defend himself with more lies, and that there is something unfair in belief. He looked at his plate. The ham lay there pink and accusing.

"I always said it," the cousin repeated, and reached for the bread.

---

After supper the two men went out upon the porch. The woman remained within, and they could hear her singing to the child in a low voice, a song without words that rose and fell like the sound of the creek. The night had come down blue and enormous. The stars were very many. The young man had forgotten that there were so many stars. In the city they were few and dim, as if they were ashamed to be seen above such a place. Here they crowded the sky like a population.

The cousin lighted his pipe. The flame of the match showed his face for an instant, red and heavy and thoughtful, and then it was gone, and there was only the small coal glowing and fading in the dark.

"Grandma went quick," said the cousin, after a time. "At the end."

"I got the letter," said the young man.

"She asked about you."

The young man was silent. He remembered the letter. It had come on a day when he had been reprimanded by a man with gray whiskers for a blot upon the ledger. He had read it on the stairs of the boarding house, and he had felt sorrow, but he had also felt a certain relief that he would not need to go home and stand among the relatives in his old suit. He had sent flowers. He had sent them because it was cheaper than the train. Now this fact rose up in the dark and stood beside him like a person.

"I couldn't get away," he said. "The firm—"

"Sure," said the cousin. "Sure. We knew."

Again this terrible gentleness. The young man began to feel a strange anger at it. He felt that his cousin was standing upon some height of his own, a height built of barns and fields and a wife and a child and an old woman's deathbed, and that from there he was able to forgive, and that forgiveness was a kind of contempt. He wished that the cousin would accuse him. He could have borne an accusation. He could have risen against it.

A whippoorwill began somewhere in the darkness. It repeated its cry with a mad persistence, as if it had been charged with some message and was determined to deliver it though no one should listen.

"Ned," said the cousin.

"What?"

The cousin was silent for a while. The coal of his pipe brightened and faded. When he spoke again his voice had changed. It had lost some of its largeness.

"You ever think about going off? I mean—you done it. You just went."

The young man turned his head. He could see nothing of his cousin but a dark bulk and the small red eye of the pipe.

"I s'pose I did," he said.

"I thought about it," said the cousin. "Before Mary. I had it all fixed. I was going to go out West. Kansas, maybe. I had the money saved." He paused. "Then Pa got sick, and there was the place, and—well." The pipe glowed. "I ain't saying I'm sorry. I ain't saying that."

"No," said the young man.

"Only sometimes I'm out there in the north field, and I look up at the road, and I think, Ned Hollis went up that road. He just went." The cousin laughed, but it was not the large laugh of the afternoon. It was a small sound that died quickly. "Seems like you was the brave one, after all."

The young man sat very still. A great tumult arose within him. Here, of a sudden, was the thing he had desired all through the long journey. Here was his cousin, his large, calm, mustached, barn-painting cousin, confessing a doubt. Here was a mind that had wrestled. For one wild moment the young man felt his heart leap toward it. He wished to cry out that he too had doubts, that the city was a cold place, that he sat upon a stool and blotted ledgers and was reprimanded by men with gray whiskers, that there was no front office, that he had been lonely in a way he could not have described, that he had walked the streets at night and looked into lighted windows at families eating supper and had felt himself to be a ghost. He wished to say that he had not come home for the funeral because he was ashamed. He wished to say that he had never jumped from anything.

The words came up into his throat. They crowded there like men pressing at a door.

Then he thought of the swimming hole. He thought of the tale told at the store, at the barns, at the suppers. He imagined this new tale added to it—Ned Hollis, who went to the city and come back and owned he was nothing but a clerk. He saw the grins. He felt that his confession, once given, would pass out of his keeping forever, and that it would become a thing that other men owned and could take out and look at when they pleased. And his cousin, whom he had just now glimpsed in a moment of weakness, would rise up again upon his height, restored, and be generous to him.

He swallowed the words. They went down hard.

"Oh, it ain't so much," he said, and he heard with a kind of wonder that his voice was careless and easy, the voice he had practiced in the sleeping car. "A man just has to make up his mind, that's all."

"I s'pose," said the cousin.

The whippoorwill ceased. The silence that came after it seemed very large. The young man felt that he had been offered something and had refused it, and that the offer would not be made again. He told himself that he had done well. He told himself that he had preserved his dignity. He found that his hands were cold.

"Well," said the cousin, and knocked out his pipe upon the rail. The sparks fell into the dark yard and lived for a moment upon the ground like small red insects, and then died. "We get up early here. I guess you forgot."

"No," said the young man. "I didn't forget."

---

He lay in the small room under the eaves where he had slept as a boy when he came to visit. The ceiling sloped down over him. The quilt smelled of cedar and of some old summer. Through the window he could see a corner of the painted barn, gray now in the starlight, and above it the crowded sky.

He was very miserable. He reviewed the conversation upon the porch and found it full of dreadful errors. He composed new speeches, in which he confessed everything with a fine manly candor and his cousin clasped his hand in silence. He composed others, in which he described the front office in such detail that it came to seem real even to himself. Neither kind of speech gave him any peace. He turned upon the narrow bed, and the bed complained.

He considered that perhaps the cousin had been lying also. Perhaps the cousin had never thought of Kansas at all, and had invented the tale out of pity, to make him comfortable. This idea filled him with a sudden fury, and then with a sudden relief, and then with a sense of desolation, for he saw that he could never know. Every man, he thought, sat behind his own face as behind a wall, and called over it, and could not tell whether the voices that called back were true.

From below he could hear the cousin and the woman talking in the kitchen. The words did not reach him. There was only the low murmur of the man and the higher murmur of the woman, rising and falling, and once the woman laughed softly. He strained to hear his own name. He was certain they spoke of him. He imagined the cousin saying, "He ain't changed. He's just the same." He did not know whether this would be a kindness or a condemnation.

Presently the murmur ceased. A door closed. The house settled itself with small creakings, like an old animal lying down.

The young man lay staring at the sloped ceiling. A moth had come in through some crack and was beating itself against the dark pane, a small, persistent, foolish sound. He listened to it for a long time. It seemed to him that it was trying very hard to get out into the enormous night, and he could not decide whether it would be better off there.

At last he heard, from the barn, the low and patient lowing of a cow, who had evidently some trouble of her own. It went out over the dark fields and was not answered. And upon that sound, with the moth still beating at the glass, he fell asleep, and dreamed that he stood upon a high limb above brown water, and that a great many faces were turned up toward him, white as plates, waiting.
