Here is an excerpt of Stephen Crane's writing, to show you their style:

The youth felt, however, that his problem was in no wise lifted from him. There was, on the contrary, an irritating prolongation. The tale had created in him a great concern for himself. Now, with the newborn question in his mind, he was compelled to sink back into his old place as part of a blue demonstration. For days he made ceaseless calculations, but they were all wondrously unsatisfactory. He found that he could establish nothing. He finally concluded that the only way to prove himself was to go into the blaze, and then figuratively to watch his legs to discover their merits and faults. He reluctantly admitted that he could not sit still and with a mental slate and pencil derive an answer. To gain it, he must have blaze, blood, and danger, even as a chemist requires this, that, and the other. So he fretted for an opportunity. Meanwhile, he continually tried to measure himself by his comrades. The tall soldier, for one, gave him some assurance. This man’s serene unconcern dealt him a measure of confidence, for he had known him since childhood, and from his intimate knowledge he did not see how he could be capable of anything that was beyond him, the youth. Still, he thought that his comrade might be mistaken about himself. Or, on the other hand, he might be a man heretofore doomed to peace and obscurity, but, in reality, made to shine in war. The youth would have liked to have discovered another who suspected himself. A sympathetic comparison of mental notes would have been a joy to him. He occasionally tried to fathom a comrade with seductive sentences. He looked about to find men in the proper mood. All attempts failed to bring forth any statement which looked in any way like a confession to those doubts which he privately acknowledged in himself. He was afraid to make an open declaration of his concern, because he dreaded to place some unscrupulous confidant upon the high plane of the unconfessed from which elevation he could be derided. In regard to his companions his mind wavered between two opinions, according to his mood. Sometimes he inclined to believing them all heroes. In fact, he usually admired in secret the superior development of the higher qualities in others. He could conceive of men going very insignificantly about the world bearing a load of courage unseen, and although he had known many of his comrades through boyhood, he began to fear that his judgment of them had been blind. Then, in other moments, he flouted these theories, and assured him that his fellows were all privately wondering and quaking. His emotions made him feel strange in the presence of men who talked excitedly of a prospective battle as of a drama they were about to witness, with nothing but eagerness and curiosity apparent in their faces. It was often that he suspected them to be liars. He did not pass such thoughts without severe condemnation of himself. He dinned reproaches at times. He was convicted by himself of many shameful crimes against the gods of traditions. In his great anxiety his heart was continually clamoring at what he considered the intolerable slowness of the generals. They seemed content to perch tranquilly on the river bank, and leave him bowed down by the weight of a great problem. He wanted it settled forthwith. He could not long bear such a load, he said. Sometimes his anger at the commanders reached an acute stage, and he grumbled about the camp like a veteran. One morning, however, he found himself in the ranks of his prepared regiment. The men were whispering speculations and recounting the old rumors. In the gloom before the break of the day their uniforms glowed a deep purple hue. From across the river the red eyes were still peering. In the eastern sky there was a yellow patch like a rug laid for the feet of the coming sun; and against it, black and patternlike, loomed the gigantic figure of the colonel on a gigantic horse. From off in the darkness came the trampling of feet. The youth could occasionally see dark shadows that moved like monsters. The regiment stood at rest for what seemed a long time. The youth grew impatient. It was unendurable the way these affairs were managed. He wondered how long they were to be kept waiting. As he looked all about him and pondered upon the mystic gloom, he began to believe that at any moment the ominous distance might be aflare, and the rolling crashes of an engagement come to his ears. Staring once at the red eyes across the river, he conceived them to be growing larger, as the orbs of a row of dragons advancing. He turned toward the colonel and saw him lift his gigantic arm and calmly stroke his mustache. At last he heard from along the road at the foot of the hill the clatter of a horse’s galloping hoofs. It must be the coming of orders. He bent forward, scarce breathing. The exciting clickety-click, as it grew louder and louder, seemed to be beating upon his soul. Presently a horseman with jangling equipment drew rein before the colonel of the regiment. The two held a short, sharp-worded conversation. The men in the foremost ranks craned their necks. As the horseman wheeled his animal and galloped away he turned to shout over his shoulder, “Don’t forget that box of cigars!” The colonel mumbled in reply. The youth wondered what a box of cigars had to do with war. A moment later the regiment went swinging off into the darkness. It was now like one of those moving monsters wending with many feet. The air was heavy, and cold with dew. A mass of wet grass, marched upon, rustled like silk. There was an occasional flash and glimmer of steel from the backs of all these huge crawling reptiles. From the road came creakings and grumblings as some surly guns were dragged away. The men stumbled along still muttering speculations. There was a subdued debate. Once a man fell down, and as he reached for his rifle a comrade, unseeing, trod upon his hand. He of the injured fingers swore bitterly, and aloud. A low, tittering laugh went among his fellows. Presently they passed into a roadway and marched forward with easy strides. A dark regiment moved before them, and from behind also came the tinkle of equipments on the bodies of marching men. The rushing yellow of the developing day went on behind their backs. When the sunrays at last struck full and mellowingly upon the earth, the youth saw that the landscape was streaked with two long, thin, black columns which disappeared on the brow of a hill in front and rearward vanished in a wood. They were like two serpents crawling from the cavern of the night. The river was not in view. The tall soldier burst into praises of what he thought to be his powers of perception. Some of the tall one’s companions cried with emphasis that they, too, had evolved the same thing, and they congratulated themselves upon it. But there were others who said that the tall one’s plan was not the true one at all. They persisted with other theories. There was a vigorous discussion. The youth took no part in them. As he walked along in careless line he was engaged with his own eternal debate. He could not hinder himself from dwelling upon it. He was despondent and sullen, and threw shifting glances about him. He looked ahead, often expecting to hear from the advance the rattle of firing. But the long serpents crawled slowly from hill to hill without bluster of smoke. A dun-colored cloud of dust floated away to the right. The sky overhead was of a fairy blue. The youth studied the faces of his companions, ever on the watch to detect kindred emotions. He suffered disappointment. Some ardor of the air which was causing the veteran commands to move with glee—almost with song—had infected the new regiment. The men began to speak of victory as of a thing they knew. Also, the tall soldier received his vindication. They were certainly going to come around in behind the enemy. They expressed commiseration for that part of the army which had been left upon the river bank, felicitating themselves upon being a part of a blasting host. The youth, considering himself as separated from the others, was saddened by the blithe and merry speeches that went from rank to rank. The company wags all made their best endeavors. The regiment tramped to the tune of laughter. The blatant soldier often convulsed whole files by his biting sarcasms aimed at the tall one. And it was not long before all the men seemed to forget their mission. Whole brigades grinned in unison, and regiments laughed. A rather fat soldier attempted to pilfer a horse from a dooryard. He planned to load his knapsack upon it. He was escaping with his prize when a young girl rushed from the house and grabbed the animal’s mane. There followed a wrangle. The young girl, with pink cheeks and shining eyes, stood like a dauntless statue. The observant regiment, standing at rest in the roadway, whooped at once, and entered whole-souled upon the side of the maiden. The men became so engrossed in this affair that they entirely ceased to remember their own large war. They jeered the piratical private, and called attention to various defects in his personal appearance; and they were wildly enthusiastic in support of the young girl. To her, from some distance, came bold advice. “Hit him with a stick.” There were crows and catcalls showered upon him when he retreated without the horse. The regiment rejoiced at his downfall. Loud and vociferous congratulations were showered upon the maiden, who stood panting and regarding the troops with defiance. At nightfall the column broke into regimental pieces, and the fragments went into the fields to camp. Tents sprang up like strange plants. Camp fires, like red, peculiar blossoms, dotted the night. The youth kept from intercourse with his companions as much as circumstances would allow him. In the evening he wandered a few paces into the gloom. From this little distance the many fires, with the black forms of men passing to and fro before the crimson rays, made weird and satanic effects. He lay down in the grass. The blades pressed tenderly against his cheek. The moon had been lighted and was hung in a treetop. The liquid stillness of the night enveloping him made him feel vast pity for himself. There was a caress in the soft winds; and the whole mood of the darkness, he thought, was one of sympathy for himself in his distress. He wished, without reserve, that he was at home again making the endless rounds from the house to the barn, from the barn to the fields, from the fields to the barn, from the barn to the house. He remembered he had so often cursed the brindle cow and her mates, and had sometimes flung milking stools. But, from his present point of view, there was a halo of happiness about each of their heads, and he would have sacrificed all the brass buttons on the continent to have been enabled to return to them. He told himself that he was not formed for a soldier. And he mused seriously upon the radical differences between himself and those men who were dodging implike around the fires. As he mused thus he heard the rustle of grass, and, upon turning his head, discovered the loud soldier. He called out, “Oh, Wilson!” The latter approached and looked down. “Why, hello, Henry; is it you? What are you doing here?”

“Oh, thinking,” said the youth. The other sat down and carefully lighted his pipe. “You’re getting blue my boy. You’re looking thundering peek-ed. What the dickens is wrong with you?”

“Oh, nothing,” said the youth. The loud soldier launched then into the subject of the anticipated fight. “Oh, we’ve got ’em now!” As he spoke his boyish face was wreathed in a gleeful smile, and his voice had an exultant ring. “We’ve got ’em now. At last, by the eternal thunders, we’ll lick ’em good!”

“If the truth was known,” he added, more soberly, “they’ve licked us about every clip up to now; but this time—this time—we’ll lick ’em good!”

“I thought you was objecting to this march a little while ago,” said the youth coldly.

“Oh, it wasn’t that,” explained the other. “I don’t mind marching, if there’s going to be fighting at the end of it. What I hate is this getting moved here and moved there, with no good coming of it, as far as I can see, excepting sore feet and damned short rations.”

“Well, Jim Conklin says we’ll get plenty of fighting this time.”

“He’s right for once, I guess, though I can’t see how it come. This time we’re in for a big battle, and we’ve got the best end of it, certain sure. Gee rod! how we will thump ’em!” He arose and began to pace to and fro excitedly. The thrill of his enthusiasm made him walk with an elastic step. He was sprightly, vigorous, fiery in his belief in success. He looked into the future with clear proud eye, and he swore with the air of an old soldier. The youth watched him for a moment in silence. When he finally spoke his voice was as bitter as dregs. “Oh, you’re going to do great things, I s’pose!” The loud soldier blew a thoughtful cloud of smoke from his pipe. “Oh, I don’t know,” he remarked with dignity; “I don’t know. I s’pose I’ll do as well as the rest. I’m going to try like thunder.” He evidently complimented himself upon the modesty of this statement.

“How do you know you won’t run when the time comes?” asked the youth.

“Run?” said the loud one; “run?—of course not!” He laughed.

“Well,” continued the youth, “lots of good-a-’nough men have thought they was going to do great things before the fight, but when the time come they skedaddled.”

“Oh, that’s all true, I s’pose,” replied the other; “but I’m not going to skedaddle. The man that bets on my running will lose his money, that’s all.” He nodded confidently.

“Oh, shucks!” said the youth. “You ain’t the bravest man in the world, are you?”

“No, I ain’t,” exclaimed the loud soldier indignantly; “and I didn’t say I was the bravest man in the world, neither. I said I was going to do my share of fighting—that’s what I said. And I am, too. Who are you, anyhow? You talk as if you thought you was Napoleon Bonaparte.” He glared at the youth for a moment, and then strode away. The youth called in a savage voice after his comrade: “Well, you needn’t git mad about it!” But the other continued on his way and made no reply. He felt alone in space when his injured comrade had disappeared. His failure to discover any mite of resemblance in their viewpoints made him more miserable than before. No one seemed to be wrestling with such a terrific personal problem. He was a mental outcast. He went slowly to his tent and stretched himself on a blanket by the side of the snoring tall soldier. In the darkness he saw visions of a thousand-tongued fear that would babble at his back and cause him to flee, while others were going coolly about their country’s business. He admitted that he would not be able to cope with this monster. He felt that every nerve in his body would be an ear to hear the voices, while other men would remain stolid and deaf. And as he sweated with the pain of these thoughts, he could hear low, serene sentences. “I’ll bid five.” “Make it six.” “Seven.” “Seven goes.” He stared at the red, shivering reflection of a fire on the white wall of his tent until, exhausted and ill from the monotony of his suffering, he fell asleep.

He finally concluded that the only way to prove himself was to go into the blaze, and then figuratively to watch his legs to discover their merits and faults. He reluctantly admitted that he could not sit still and with a mental slate and pencil derive an answer. To gain it, he must have blaze, blood, and danger, even as a chemist requires this, that, and the other. So he fretted for an opportunity. Meanwhile, he continually tried to measure himself by his comrades. The tall soldier, for one, gave him some assurance. This man’s serene unconcern dealt him a measure of confidence, for he had known him since childhood, and from his intimate knowledge he did not see how he could be capable of anything that was beyond him, the youth. Still, he thought that his comrade might be mistaken about himself. Or, on the other hand, he might be a man heretofore doomed to peace and obscurity, but, in reality, made to shine in war. The youth would have liked to have discovered another who suspected himself. A sympathetic comparison of mental notes would have been a joy to him. He occasionally tried to fathom a comrade with seductive sentences. He looked about to find men in the proper mood. All attempts failed to bring forth any statement which looked in any way like a confession to those doubts which he privately acknowledged in himself. He was afraid to make an open declaration of his concern, because he dreaded to place some unscrupulous confidant upon the high plane of the unconfessed from which elevation he could be derided. In regard to his companions his mind wavered between two opinions, according to his mood. Sometimes he inclined to believing them all heroes. In fact, he usually admired in secret the superior development of the higher qualities in others. He could conceive of men going very insignificantly about the world bearing a load of courage unseen, and although he had known many of his comrades through boyhood, he began to fear that his judgment of them had been blind. Then, in other moments, he flouted these theories, and assured him that his fellows were all privately wondering and quaking. His emotions made him feel strange in the presence of men who talked excitedly of a prospective battle as of a drama they were about to witness, with nothing but eagerness and curiosity apparent in their faces. It was often that he suspected them to be liars. He did not pass such thoughts without severe condemnation of himself. He dinned reproaches at times. He was convicted by himself of many shameful crimes against the gods of traditions. In his great anxiety his heart was continually clamoring at what he considered the intolerable slowness of the generals. They seemed content to perch tranquilly on the river bank, and leave him bowed down by the weight of a great problem. He wanted it settled forthwith. He could not long bear such a load, he said. Sometimes his anger at the commanders reached an acute stage, and he grumbled about the camp like a veteran. One morning, however, he found himself in the ranks of his prepared regiment. The men were whispering speculations and recounting the old rumors. In the gloom before the break of the day their uniforms glowed a deep purple hue. From across the river the red eyes were still peering. In the eastern sky there was a yellow patch like a rug laid for the feet of the coming sun; and against it, black and patternlike, loomed the gigantic figure of the colonel on a gigantic horse. From off in the darkness came the trampling of feet. The youth could occasionally see dark shadows that moved like monsters. The regiment stood at rest for what seemed a long time. The youth grew impatient. It was unendurable the way these affairs were managed. He wondered how long they were to be kept waiting. As he looked all about him and pondered upon the mystic gloom, he began to believe that at any moment the ominous distance might be aflare, and the rolling crashes of an engagement come to his ears. Staring once at the red eyes across the river, he conceived them to be growing larger, as the orbs of a row of dragons advancing. He turned toward the colonel and saw him lift his gigantic arm and calmly stroke his mustache. At last he heard from along the road at the foot of the hill the clatter of a horse’s galloping hoofs. It must be the coming of orders. He bent forward, scarce breathing. The exciting clickety-click, as it grew louder and louder, seemed to be beating upon his soul. Presently a horseman with jangling equipment drew rein before the colonel of the regiment. The two held a short, sharp-worded conversation. The men in the foremost ranks craned their necks. As the horseman wheeled his animal and galloped away he turned to shout over his shoulder, “Don’t forget that box of cigars!” The colonel mumbled in reply. The youth wondered what a box of cigars had to do with war. A moment later the regiment went swinging off into the darkness. It was now like one of those moving monsters wending with many feet. The air was heavy, and cold with dew. A mass of wet grass, marched upon, rustled like silk. There was an occasional flash and glimmer of steel from the backs of all these huge crawling reptiles. From the road came creakings and grumblings as some surly guns were dragged away. The men stumbled along still muttering speculations. There was a subdued debate. Once a man fell down, and as he reached for his rifle a comrade, unseeing, trod upon his hand. He of the injured fingers swore bitterly, and aloud. A low, tittering laugh went among his fellows. Presently they passed into a roadway and marched forward with easy strides. A dark regiment moved before them, and from behind also came the tinkle of equipments on the bodies of marching men. The rushing yellow of the developing day went on behind their backs. When the sunrays at last struck full and mellowingly upon the earth, the youth saw that the landscape was streaked with two long, thin, black columns which disappeared on the brow of a hill in front and rearward vanished in a wood. They were like two serpents crawling from the cavern of the night. The river was not in view. The tall soldier burst into praises of what he thought to be his powers of perception. Some of the tall one’s companions cried with emphasis that they, too, had evolved the same thing, and they congratulated themselves upon it. But there were others who said that the tall one’s plan was not the true one at all. They persisted with other theories. There was a vigorous discussion. The youth took no part in them. As he walked along in careless line he was engaged with his own eternal debate. He could not hinder himself from dwelling upon it. He was despondent and sullen, and threw shifting glances about him. He looked ahead, often expecting to hear from the advance the rattle of firing. But the long serpents crawled slowly from hill to hill without bluster of smoke. A dun-colored cloud of dust floated away to the right. The sky overhead was of a fairy blue. The youth studied the faces of his companions, ever on the watch to detect kindred emotions. He suffered disappointment. Some ardor of the air which was causing the veteran commands to move with glee—almost with song—had infected the new regiment. The men began to speak of victory as of a thing they knew. Also, the tall soldier received his vindication. They were certainly going to come around in behind the enemy. They expressed commiseration for that part of the army which had been left upon the river bank, felicitating themselves upon being a part of a blasting host. The youth, considering himself as separated from the others, was saddened by the blithe and merry speeches that went from rank to rank. The company wags all made their best endeavors. The regiment tramped to the tune of laughter. The blatant soldier often convulsed whole files by his biting sarcasms aimed at the tall one. And it was not long before all the men seemed to forget their mission. Whole brigades grinned in unison, and regiments laughed. A rather fat soldier attempted to pilfer a horse from a dooryard. He planned to load his knapsack upon it. He was escaping with his prize when a young girl rushed from the house and grabbed the animal’s mane. There followed a wrangle. The young girl, with pink cheeks and shining eyes, stood like a dauntless statue. The observant regiment, standing at rest in the roadway, whooped at once, and entered whole-souled upon the side of the maiden. The men became so engrossed in this affair that they entirely ceased to remember their own large war. They jeered the piratical private, and called attention to various defects in his personal appearance; and they were wildly enthusiastic in support of the young girl. To her, from some distance, came bold advice. “Hit him with a stick.” There were crows and catcalls showered upon him when he retreated without the horse. The regiment rejoiced at his downfall. Loud and vociferous congratulations were showered upon the maiden, who stood panting and regarding the troops with defiance. At nightfall the column broke into regimental pieces, and the fragments went into the fields to camp. Tents sprang up like strange plants. Camp fires, like red, peculiar blossoms, dotted the night. The youth kept from intercourse with his companions as much as circumstances would allow him. In the evening he wandered a few paces into the gloom. From this little distance the many fires, with the black forms of men passing to and fro before the crimson rays, made weird and satanic effects. He lay down in the grass. The blades pressed tenderly against his cheek. The moon had been lighted and was hung in a treetop. The liquid stillness of the night enveloping him made him feel vast pity for himself. There was a caress in the soft winds; and the whole mood of the darkness, he thought, was one of sympathy for himself in his distress. He wished, without reserve, that he was at home again making the endless rounds from the house to the barn, from the barn to the fields, from the fields to the barn, from the barn to the house. He remembered he had so often cursed the brindle cow and her mates, and had sometimes flung milking stools. But, from his present point of view, there was a halo of happiness about each of their heads, and he would have sacrificed all the brass buttons on the continent to have been enabled to return to them. He told himself that he was not formed for a soldier. And he mused seriously upon the radical differences between himself and those men who were dodging implike around the fires. As he mused thus he heard the rustle of grass, and, upon turning his head, discovered the loud soldier. He called out, “Oh, Wilson!” The latter approached and looked down. “Why, hello, Henry; is it you? What are you doing here?”

“Oh, thinking,” said the youth. The other sat down and carefully lighted his pipe. “You’re getting blue my boy. You’re looking thundering peek-ed. What the dickens is wrong with you?”

“Oh, nothing,” said the youth. The loud soldier launched then into the subject of the anticipated fight. “Oh, we’ve got ’em now!” As he spoke his boyish face was wreathed in a gleeful smile, and his voice had an exultant ring. “We’ve got ’em now. At last, by the eternal thunders, we’ll lick ’em good!”

“If the truth was known,” he added, more soberly, “they’ve licked us about every clip up to now; but this time—this time—we’ll lick ’em good!”

“I thought you was objecting to this march a little while ago,” said the youth coldly.

“Oh, it wasn’t that,” explained the other. “I don’t mind marching, if there’s going to be fighting at the end of it. What I hate is this getting moved here and moved there, with no good coming of it, as far as I can see, excepting sore feet and damned short rations.”

“Well, Jim Conklin says we’ll get plenty of fighting this time.”

“He’s right for once, I guess, though I can’t see how it come. This time we’re in for a big battle, and we’ve got the best end of it, certain sure. Gee rod! how we will thump ’em!” He arose and began to pace to and fro excitedly. The thrill of his enthusiasm made him walk with an elastic step. He was sprightly, vigorous, fiery in his belief in success. He looked into the future with clear proud eye, and he swore with the air of an old soldier. The youth watched him for a moment in silence. When he finally spoke his voice was as bitter as dregs. “Oh, you’re going to do great things, I s’pose!” The loud soldier blew a thoughtful cloud of smoke from his pipe. “Oh, I don’t know,” he remarked with dignity; “I don’t know. I s’pose I’ll do as well as the rest. I’m going to try like thunder.” He evidently complimented himself upon the modesty of this statement.

“How do you know you won’t run when the time comes?” asked the youth.

“Run?” said the loud one; “run?—of course not!” He laughed.

“Well,” continued the youth, “lots of good-a-’nough men have thought they was going to do great things before the fight, but when the time come they skedaddled.”

“Oh, that’s all true, I s’pose,” replied the other; “but I’m not going to skedaddle. The man that bets on my running will lose his money, that’s all.” He nodded confidently.

“Oh, shucks!” said the youth. “You ain’t the bravest man in the world, are you?”

“No, I ain’t,” exclaimed the loud soldier indignantly; “and I didn’t say I was the bravest man in the world, neither. I said I was going to do my share of fighting—that’s what I said. And I am, too. Who are you, anyhow? You talk as if you thought you was Napoleon Bonaparte.” He glared at the youth for a moment, and then strode away. The youth called in a savage voice after his comrade: “Well, you needn’t git mad about it!” But the other continued on his way and made no reply. He felt alone in space when his injured comrade had disappeared. His failure to discover any mite of resemblance in their viewpoints made him more miserable than before. No one seemed to be wrestling with such a terrific personal problem. He was a mental outcast. He went slowly to his tent and stretched himself on a blanket by the side of the snoring tall soldier. In the darkness he saw visions of a thousand-tongued fear that would babble at his back and cause him to flee, while others were going coolly about their country’s business. He admitted that he would not be able to cope with this monster. He felt that every nerve in his body would be an ear to hear the voices, while other men would remain stolid and deaf. And as he sweated with the pain of these thoughts, he could hear low, serene sentences. “I’ll bid five.” “Make it six.” “Seven.” “Seven goes.” He stared at the red, shivering reflection of a fire on the white wall of his tent until, exhausted and ill from the monotony of his suffering, he fell asleep.

The boy stood in the lane and regarded the window. It had a large and ragged hole in it, and from the edges of this hole long splinters of glass pointed inward like the teeth of a fish. Behind it, in the gloom of the parlor, he could see the dim white of the lace curtain, which stirred a little, as if something within had drawn a breath. He did not move. The stone was no longer in his hand. He was not certain at what instant it had left him, but he was certain of where it had gone, and the knowledge sat upon his chest like a flatiron.

A moment before, the lane had been a field of glory. Willie Sanders had stood at the far end of it, by the Grangers' fence, and had made a face of the most insulting kind, pulling down the lower lids of his eyes with his two forefingers and protruding his tongue. He had further declared that the boy threw like a girl. This was a statement which no man could permit to go unanswered. The boy had stooped, found a stone of noble proportions, and hurled it with all the righteous fury of his seven years. But the stone, being a stone, had not shared his purpose. It had veered from the path of justice in a long and treacherous curve, and had gone with a sound like a gun into the front window of his mother's parlor.

Willie Sanders had vanished instantly. He was simply gone. The fence by the Grangers' stood empty in the sunlight, and the place where he had been seemed to the boy to wear an expression of malicious innocence. A hen walked across it, pecking.

The boy was alone with his crime.

He looked about him. The afternoon was very bright and indifferent. Over in the Grangers' yard a dog lay on its side in the dust, and it did not so much as lift its head. The maples along the lane rustled their leaves together in a way that the boy conceived to be whispering. A wagon went by on the main street, at the end of the lane, and the driver did not look in his direction. It was evident that the world had not yet learned of the thing. There was still time. He might go away somewhere. He might go down to the creek and remain there until the affair was mysteriously settled by other people. Windows were broken by many agencies. There were tramps. There were birds. He had once heard of a bird that flew into a window in Port Jervis and broke it entirely.

He was considering the bird with a great deal of hope when the front door of the house opened.

His mother came out upon the porch. She held a dish towel in one hand, and her face was white with the white of a woman who has been in a quiet kitchen and has heard the house explode. She looked first at the window, from the outside, and the boy saw her mouth make a small round shape. Then she looked down the lane. Her eyes traveled over the hen, over the Grangers' dog, over the empty place by the fence, and arrived upon him.

He had not known until that moment that he was standing so plainly in the open. It seemed to him that the lane had grown suddenly very wide and very bare, and that he stood in the exact center of it like a post. There was no tree near him. There was no bush. The sun shone directly upon the top of his head and illuminated him for the inspection of the universe.

"Edward," said his mother.

She did not shout. This was a bad sign. The boy knew the many voices of his mother as a sailor knows weather. There was the high, quick voice, which fell upon him for mud on the stairs and was gone again in a moment like a summer squall. There was the long, plaintive voice, which inquired of heaven what she had ever done to deserve such children. But this voice was neither of these. It was low and level, and had in it a curious quality of stillness, and he had heard it only twice before in his life. Once was when he had set fire to the woodshed. The other time he did not care to remember.

"Edward, you come here to me."

He went. He did not go quickly, for his legs had become heavy and reluctant, and they seemed to consult with each other before each step. But he went. He passed the hen, which regarded him with one round eye and then turned away as if it wished to have nothing to do with him. He came to the foot of the porch steps and stopped there. He looked at the bottom step. There was a knot in the wood of it, shaped somewhat like a frog, and he examined this knot with profound attention.

"Look at me."

He looked at her for a fraction of a second and then returned to the knot. In that instant she had appeared to him enormous. She stood at the top of the steps, and the light was behind her, so that her figure was black and edged with fire, and the dish towel hung from her hand like a flag of dreadful significance.

"Did you throw a stone at this house?"

The boy's mind became at once a scene of tremendous activity. A dozen answers rose up in it and jostled one another for precedence. He reviewed them rapidly, as a general reviews his troops before a hopeless engagement. There was the bird. There was the tramp. There was Willie Sanders, who had indisputably been present and who had, moreover, made a face. There was the plain truth, which stood at the rear of the column, small and gray and unattractive, and which he passed over with some disdain.

"Willie Sanders," he began.

"I didn't ask you about Willie Sanders. Did you throw a stone at this house?"

"I didn't throw it at the house," said the boy. This seemed to him at once an inspired reply. It was, in its fashion, entirely true. He had not thrown it at the house. He had thrown it at Willie Sanders. The house had merely intervened. He felt that if this distinction could be properly explained, the whole matter would appear in a different light, and that his mother, who was a reasonable woman in many respects, would perceive that he was blameless, and indeed somewhat to be pitied.

"Then what did you throw it at?"

"At Willie Sanders. He was a-making faces. He said I throwed like a girl."

"And so you threw a stone at him."

"Yes'm."

"A stone. At a boy's head."

The boy had not considered the matter in this way. In the lane, with the insult still ringing, it had seemed only a stone, an ordinary stone of the kind which is everywhere about, and Willie Sanders had seemed only a target, a thing that wanted hitting. Now, as his mother pronounced the words, they assumed a sudden and appalling shape. He saw, quite vividly, Willie Sanders lying in the lane with his face in the dust, and Mrs. Sanders running with her apron over her head, and men coming with a door to carry him, and the minister in the parlor speaking in a low voice. He saw himself in this picture also, standing apart, a figure of shame and solitude, with all the town looking upon him. The vision was so complete that his throat began to ache.

"I didn't hit him," he said hoarsely.

"No. You hit my window. You might have hit Mrs. Granger. You might have hit the baby, if I had had her in there. Did you think of that?"

He had not thought of that. He had not, in fact, thought of anything. It came to him with a kind of dismay that the space between the picking up of the stone and the throwing of it had been entirely empty of thought, a little blank place in his life, like a page left out of a book. He was unable to account for it. He felt that he had been betrayed by his own arm.

"Come in the house."

He climbed the steps. Each step was a separate and laborious ascent. His mother stood aside to let him pass, and he went by her very close, and he could smell the starch of her apron and the onions she had been cutting, and these familiar smells, which he had known all his life, seemed now to belong to a stranger.

The parlor was cold and dim, as it always was, for it was used only on Sundays and when the minister came. The boy had a deep respect for it. It was a place of horsehair and of wax flowers under a glass bell, and of a large and solemn picture of his grandfather, who had a white beard and looked out of his frame with the expression of a man who has been told something disagreeable about his descendants. Upon the carpet beneath the window lay the glass. It was scattered widely, in a great glittering fan, and the stone sat in the midst of it, gray and squat and complacent, as if it had arrived at its destination after a long journey and were well satisfied.

The boy regarded the stone with hatred. It was the author of all his misfortunes. If he could have done so without attracting notice, he would have kicked it.

His mother did not speak for a time. She stood looking at the window, and at the glass, and at the curtain, which was torn in one place where the stone had passed through it. The boy saw her put out her hand and touch the torn place, and he understood dimly that the curtain was a thing of value to her, a thing which had a history he did not know. This troubled him more than the window. He had never before considered that his mother possessed any history. She had always been simply his mother, as the sky was the sky, and the barn was the barn.

"Your father put in that glass himself," she said at last. "The spring before you were born."

The boy was silent. He perceived that he had struck not only a window but a large and mysterious region of the past, peopled with events of which he had no knowledge, and he felt that he had blundered into it with muddy boots.

"Do you know what a pane of glass that size costs, Edward?"

"No'm."

"Neither do I. But I know it costs more than we have to spare this month. I know that much." She folded the dish towel slowly, in halves, and then in halves again. "I want you to look at me now, and not at the floor."

He lifted his eyes. It was one of the hardest things he had ever done. His mother's face was nearer now, and it was no longer black and edged with fire, but merely her own face, with a smudge of flour upon the cheekbone and a small line between the brows. She did not look angry, precisely. She looked tired, and a little frightened still, and it was this, more than any anger, which went into him like a nail.

"When you tell me 'I didn't throw it at the house,'" she said, "what are you trying to make me think?"

The boy opened his mouth and closed it again.

"You're trying to make me think it wasn't your fault. Isn't that so?"

"Willie Sanders—"

"Willie Sanders didn't pick up that stone. Willie Sanders didn't throw it. Willie Sanders is home eating his supper, I expect, and you're standing in my parlor with glass all over the floor. Isn't that so?"

"Yes'm," whispered the boy.

"Then whose fault is it?"

There was a long pause. The clock on the mantel ticked with a slow and deliberate cruelty. The grandfather in his frame waited. Somewhere outside, very far away, a cowbell clanked twice and was still. The boy felt that the whole house was leaning toward him to hear his answer.

He searched once more among his reserves. The bird was gone. The tramp was gone. Willie Sanders had been routed from the field. Only the small gray truth remained, standing patiently where he had left it, and he went to it at last as a beaten man goes to his last redoubt.

"Mine," he said.

The word came out of him very small, and he was surprised that it should have cost so much. He had expected that saying it would be like falling off the barn roof, which he had done once, and which had been all terror in the falling and all pain in the landing. But it was not like that. When the word was out, there was, oddly, a kind of loosening in him, as when a shoe that has pinched all day is at length unlaced. He did not feel better, precisely. But he felt that the thing had been set down somewhere outside of him, where it could be looked at.

Then, to his great shame and astonishment, he began to cry.

He had not intended to cry. He considered crying to be a womanish performance, and beneath the dignity of a person who could whistle through his fingers. He had fought Fatty Burke behind the schoolhouse without crying, though Fatty Burke had sat upon his head. But now the tears came up out of some deep and unguarded place, and he could not stop them, and they ran down his face and into the corners of his mouth and tasted of salt. He made a hideous noise in his throat. He put his fists into his eyes and ground them there. He felt that he was disgraced forever, and that the grandfather in the frame was regarding him with contempt.

His mother did not come to him at once. She let him cry for some little time, standing quite still with the folded towel in her hands, and the boy, through his fists, felt the weight of her waiting. It seemed to him a terrible and pitiless thing that she should stand there so. He wished that she would strike him. A blow would have been a definite and comprehensible event, and when it was over it would have been over. But this waiting was without bottom.

"Edward," she said presently, and her voice was changed. It was lower still, but the stillness had gone out of it. "Edward, take your hands down."

He took them down. His face was wet and hot and crooked.

"I'm not going to whip you," said his mother.

The boy received this news with a confused emotion. There was relief in it, a great deal of relief. But there was also, strangely, a small disappointment, as if he had been denied something that was owing to him. He had already, in a dim way, been composing the account of his whipping which he would give to the other boys, and in which he would figure as a stoic.

"I'm not going to whip you, because I don't think it would teach you a thing you don't already know. You know it was wrong. I could see you knowing it from clear across the yard." She paused. "But you're going to sweep up every bit of this glass. Every bit. You're going to get down on your knees and look under the sofa and under the whatnot, and if I find so much as one piece tomorrow with my bare foot, you'll hear about it. And you're going to give your father the half-dollar you have in the cocoa tin toward a new pane. And when he comes home tonight, you're going to tell him yourself what you did. Not me. You."

The boy received each of these sentences as a separate blow. The glass he could bear. The half-dollar was a severe wound, for it represented the labor of many weeks, and he had intended to buy with it a jackknife of surpassing beauty which lay in the window of Hagan's store, and which had two blades and a corkscrew. He saw the jackknife recede into an infinite distance, growing smaller and dimmer, until it was a mere point of light in a dark and hopeless future.

But the last sentence was the worst. He would have to tell his father. He would have to stand in the kitchen when his father came in from the mill, smelling of sawdust and tired, and he would have to say it, in his own voice, with his own mouth. He would have to watch his father's face as he said it. The prospect seemed to him altogether beyond the reach of human endurance.

"Do you understand me?"

"Yes'm."

"Then go get the broom."

He went to get the broom. In the kitchen his little sister sat upon the floor with a wooden spoon, and she looked up at him as he passed with an expression of serene and absolute knowledge. She was not quite three, and could say only a few words, but it was apparent to the boy that she knew everything, and that she would, at the first opportunity, tell it to the world. He scowled at her horribly. She regarded his scowl with interest and resumed beating upon the floor.

He swept the parlor for what seemed a great many hours. The glass was everywhere. It had gone into places where it could not possibly have gone, under the sofa and behind the coal scuttle and into the very fringe of the carpet, and each piece flashed at him with a small, malicious wink as he discovered it. He went down on his knees as he had been told. He looked under the whatnot and found there, in addition to glass, a button, a dead fly, and a marble which he had lost in the winter and had mourned. He put the marble in his pocket. He considered that he had earned it.

When the glass was gathered, his mother came and tacked a piece of brown paper over the hole, and the parlor became darker, and the brown paper glowed faintly with the light behind it, like the window of a church. The stone she took up and put upon the mantel, beside the clock.

"So we'll remember," she said.

The boy looked at the stone. It seemed to him an object of enormous and permanent reproach. He foresaw that it would remain upon the mantel for the rest of his life, and that visitors would ask about it, and that his mother would tell them.

At supper he ate very little. The potatoes had no taste. He was continually listening for the sound of the gate. Every creak of the house was his father's foot upon the walk. Every wind in the maples was his father's hand upon the latch. His mother said nothing to him about the window, and spoke of other things, of the Grangers' new calf and of a letter from Aunt Lizzie in Binghamton, and the boy thought this the most dreadful thing of all, for he felt that she was saving it, as one saves the last and largest gun for the final moment of a battle.

And then the gate creaked in earnest, and his father's step came up the walk, slow and heavy, and the door opened, and his father stood in the kitchen with sawdust upon his sleeves, and hung his hat upon the peg.

The boy rose from his chair. His legs again consulted with each other. His mother looked at him across the table and did not speak, and in her look there was neither help nor hindrance, but only a sort of waiting.

"Pa," said the boy.

His father turned. He was a large man, and the lamp had been lit, and his shadow went up the wall and across the ceiling, so that he seemed to fill the whole kitchen. The boy looked at the shadow and then at the man, and swallowed, and found that his voice had gone somewhere and would not come back.

"Well?" said his father.

The boy took a breath. It went down into him and seemed to go a long way. Then he told it. He told it badly and out of order, and Willie Sanders came into it more than he should have, and the face which Willie Sanders had made was described with greater elaboration than was perhaps necessary. But he told it. He told about the stone and the window and the curtain and the half-dollar in the cocoa tin. He did not tell about the marble.

When he had finished, his father stood for a time without speaking. Then he went into the parlor, and the boy heard him stop before the brown paper. There was a long silence. Then he came back, and sat down heavily at the table, and drew his plate toward him.

"Well," he said, "I guess that's two of us has broke a window in this house."

The boy did not understand this. He looked at his mother. She had turned to the stove, and her shoulders were shaking a little, though whether with laughter or with something else he could not tell.

That night he lay in his bed under the eaves and looked at the square of the window, where a single star hung over the Grangers' barn. He felt very old. He reflected upon the day as upon a long campaign, full of reverses, in which he had nevertheless come off with his life. He thought of the jackknife, and grieved for it. He thought of Willie Sanders, and resolved upon a vengeance of such magnitude that it would be spoken of in the town for generations. Then he thought of his mother touching the torn place in the curtain, and the vengeance grew small and uninteresting and went away.

The star winked at him. He regarded it with suspicion for a time, as one who has learned that even small, bright things may wink with malice. But it continued very mild and steady, and after a while he forgave it, and fell asleep.
