It rained in the night and in the morning it was still raining and the fishing boats did not go out until nearly noon. From the window of the hotel you could see them lying against the stone of the harbor wall with their masts moving a little and the men sitting under the awning of the café across the square, drinking coffee and looking at the sky. Then the wind went around to the south and the rain thinned and the men got up all at once and went down to the boats, and he went with them.

She stayed in the room until the afternoon. Then she went down to the café of the hotel and sat by the glass and ordered a vermouth. The café was empty. It was the end of November and the summer people had gone back to Madrid and Bilbao long ago and the hotel was closing all the rooms but theirs and one on the second floor where a commercial traveler slept on Tuesdays. The waiter brought the vermouth with a slice of lemon in it and a dish of olives and a dish of small salted almonds and stood by the bar wiping a glass that was already dry.

Outside the light was going gray over the water. The tide was out and the boats that had not gone out sat on the mud in the inner harbor, leaning over on their sides. Gulls walked on the mud. Beyond the harbor wall the sea was green and then gray and then there was no color at all where it met the sky. She ate an olive and put the pit in the dish and drank some of the vermouth. It was cold and good and she drank it slowly. There was a letter in her handbag and she did not take it out.

The boats came in at dark. She saw their lights first, low on the water, and then she heard the engines, and then the boats came around the end of the mole one after another and the women who had been waiting under the arcade went down the steps to the quay. She watched the men throw the baskets up onto the stones. The lights were on now along the quay and the fish shone in the baskets. After a while she saw him coming across the square. He walked with his head down against the wind and his hands in the pockets of the oilskin coat he had bought from the ship chandler and he did not look up at the window.

He came in and the waiter said, "Good evening," and he said, "Good evening, Manolo," and stood dripping by the door, taking off the coat.

"How was it?" she said.

"It was fine. It was really fine. You should have come."

"I didn't want to be wet."

"You don't get wet. You get wet at first and then you don't notice." He hung the coat on the hook and came over and sat down across from her. His face was red from the wind and his hair was wet and stuck to his forehead and he smelled of fish and diesel oil and the sea. "Manolo," he said. "A brandy. A big one."

"Did they catch anything?"

"They caught plenty. Besugo. We went way out past the point where you can see the lighthouse at Castro and old Ramón put the lines down and they were there. They were right there. He knew exactly where." He put his hands flat on the marble of the table. "Look at my hands."

She looked at them. They were cut across the palms in fine lines from the fishing line.

"You should put something on them."

"They're all right. I brought one back. Ramón gave me one. I gave it to the woman in the kitchen and she's going to do it for supper."

"That's nice."

The waiter brought the brandy and he drank half of it and set the glass down and breathed out.

"That's good," he said. "You don't know how good that is."

"I'm sure it's good."

"Have one."

"I have this."

"Have a brandy too."

"I don't want one."

He looked at her then. He looked at her and then he looked at the window and the lights on the quay and the women carrying the baskets on their heads up the steps to the market.

"I'll do the boats tomorrow," he said. "If the light is any good. I want to do them coming around the mole. I want to get the way they look against the wall."

"That would be nice."

"You keep saying that."

"I'm sorry. It would be. I mean it."

"All right."

He finished the brandy and held the glass up and the waiter came with the bottle. They sat there. The wind blew rain against the glass in gusts and then stopped and then blew again. Across the square a man in a beret came out of the café with a sack over his head and ran to the arcade.

"What did you do all day?" he said.

"Nothing. I read."

"What did you read?"

"The English book. The one you didn't like."

"Is it any good?"

"No."

"I told you it wasn't."

"You told me."

"Did you go out at all?"

"I went to the post office."

He was quiet. He turned the brandy glass on the marble.

"Was there anything?"

"There was a letter from Margaret."

"How is Margaret?"

"She's fine. They're in Paris. They have an apartment on the rue Jacob. They have it until March."

"That's nice for them."

"Now you're saying it."

"I suppose I am."

He drank some of the brandy. She ate an almond. Neither of them looked at the other.

"She says there's a room," she said. "In the apartment. She says there's a room nobody is using."

"Is there."

"She says it gets the sun in the morning."

"There isn't any sun in Paris in the winter."

"She says there is."

"Margaret would say that." He put the glass down. "Go on."

"There isn't any more. That's all she says."

"That isn't all she says."

"No," she said. "It isn't."

The waiter had gone into the kitchen. They could hear him talking to the woman who cooked and the woman laughing and then the sound of something frying in oil.

"When?" he said.

"There's a bus to Santander at seven. The train goes at eleven."

"Tomorrow."

"I thought tomorrow."

"I'm going to do the boats tomorrow."

"I know. You don't need me to do the boats."

"I didn't say I needed you."

"I know you didn't."

He looked at the window again. In the glass he could see the room behind them, the bar and the bottles and the clock with the brass pendulum that did not move, and the two of them sitting at the table, small, by the dark window.

"How long?" he said.

"I don't know. Not long. A while."

"How long is a while?"

"Please," she said. "I don't know. I just don't know."

"All right."

"Don't say all right like that."

"How do you want me to say it?"

"I don't want you to say it at all."

"All right," he said, and then he laughed a little, and she did not laugh.

The waiter came out of the kitchen and stood behind the bar and looked at them and then went back into the kitchen. The lights on the quay were going off one by one. The boats were dark now and you could not see them, only the masts against the lighter dark where the sky was.

"Is it the room?" he said. "Because I can get the woman to bring up a brazier. I asked her before. She said she had one. She said nobody asked for it so she didn't bring it."

"It isn't the room."

"It's cold in the room."

"It's cold everywhere. It isn't the room."

"Is it the town?"

"No."

"We could go to Madrid. We could go down to Madrid and stay at the place on the Calle de la Victoria. It would be dry in Madrid. It would be cold but it would be dry."

"I don't want to go to Madrid."

"We could go to Sevilla."

"No."

"You liked Sevilla."

"I liked Sevilla. That was two years ago."

"It's still there."

"Please," she said.

"I'm only telling you it's still there."

"I know it's still there."

He finished the brandy and did not ask for another. He sat with his cut hands on the table and looked at them.

"Is it the money?" he said.

"It isn't anything. It isn't any one thing."

"Because if it's the money I'll sell something. Klein said he could sell the two harbors. He said they would go easily."

"It isn't the money. I have money."

"You have money," he said. "That's right. I forgot about that."

"That wasn't fair."

"No," he said. "It wasn't. I'm sorry."

"It's all right."

"No. I'm sorry."

The woman from the kitchen came out wiping her hands on her apron and said the fish was ready, did they want it now or later, and he said now would be fine, and she smiled at them both and went back. Manolo came and laid the table near the stove where it was warmer, with a white cloth and the heavy plates and a bottle of the red wine from Rioja without a label, and they got up and moved to the table by the stove. He held her chair and she sat down. Manolo brought bread and a dish of the small green peppers fried in oil with coarse salt on them, and then he brought the fish on a long platter with the head on and the eyes gone white and the skin crisped brown and split along the side, with garlic and oil and slices of lemon around it.

"There's your fish," she said.

"There it is."

"It's a beautiful fish."

"It was a lot bigger in the water."

"They always are."

He filled her glass and then his own. He took the knife and lifted the skin back and the meat came away white from the bone in big flakes and he put the best of it on her plate and then took some for himself.

"Eat it while it's hot," he said.

She ate some of it. "It's very good."

"Ramón says they come in close in December. He says in December you can catch them right off the point and you don't have to go out at all."

"That would be nice for you."

He put his fork down.

"Look," he said.

"Don't," she said. "Please. Let's eat the fish. It's your fish and it's very good. Let's just eat it."

"All right."

They ate. The stove made a ticking sound as the iron got hot. The rain had stopped and they could hear the sea now, not loud, coming in against the mole and falling back. It was a sound you stopped hearing after the first week and then you heard it again at night when you could not sleep. He had stopped hearing it. She had not.

"Do you remember the first night," she said. "When we came here."

"I remember."

"We came in on the bus from Laredo and it was hot and the bus smelled of goats."

"It was chickens."

"It was goats. There was a man with a goat at the back. You don't remember."

"I remember the man. I thought it was chickens."

"And we came up to the room and you opened the shutters and there was the whole harbor and all the boats were in. Every boat was in and the sun was going down and the boats were all painted blue and red and white and you stood there and you didn't say anything. You stood there for maybe five minutes. And I thought, he's happy. I thought, now he's happy and he'll be happy here."

"I was happy."

"I know you were. And I was happy because you were."

"Weren't you happy?"

"I was. I said I was."

"You said you were happy because I was."

"That's what I meant. That's what I said."

He drank some of the wine. It was rough and cold from the cellar and it went well with the fish.

"And now you aren't," he said.

"I didn't say that."

"You don't have to say it."

"I'm tired," she said. "I'm only tired. I'm tired of hearing the sea at night. I'm tired of the commercial traveler on Tuesdays and the way he looks at me on the stairs. I'm tired of reading English books that aren't any good. I'm tired of waiting at the window for the boats to come in so I'll know you're not drowned."

"I'm not going to get drowned."

"I know you're not. I know that. But I wait anyway. And I don't want to wait anymore. That's all. That's the whole of it."

"That isn't the whole of it."

"It's enough of it."

He picked up a pepper by the stem and ate it and put the stem on the side of his plate. Then he did it again. They were small and hot and every so often there was one that was very hot and you could not tell which one it would be.

"I could stop going out," he said.

"You can't do the boats if you don't go out."

"I could do them from the wall."

"You'd hate it."

"I wouldn't hate it."

"You would. You'd hate it and you'd hate me a little for it and you wouldn't say anything and I'd know."

"You'd know," he said.

"I'd know."

"You know everything."

"No," she said. "I don't know anything. I don't know a single thing. I only know I want to go to Paris for a while and see Margaret and sit in a café where it's warm and people talk and nobody smells of fish."

He did not say anything to that. He poured more wine for both of them. She had not drunk much of hers and it came almost to the top of the glass.

"I'm sorry," she said. "I didn't mean that about the fish."

"It's true. I smell of fish."

"I like the way you smell. I didn't mean it."

"It's all right."

"It isn't all right. Nothing I say is right tonight. I've been thinking about it all day and I knew how I would say it and none of it came out the way I thought."

"How did you think it would come out?"

"I don't know. Better. Kinder."

"It was kind enough."

"It wasn't."

"It was all right," he said.

Manolo came and took the platter. There was nothing left on it but the bones and the head. He asked if they wanted cheese and he said yes and Manolo brought the hard cheese from La Mancha and a dish of quince paste and two small glasses and the bottle of anís, and set them on the table and went away and turned the lights off over the bar so there was only the light by the stove where they sat.

"He wants to go home," she said.

"He can go home. We'll go up."

"Not yet."

"No. Not yet."

He cut the cheese and put a slice of it on her plate with a piece of the quince. She ate it. He did not eat any.

"Do you want me to come with you?" he said.

She looked at him. It was the first time she had looked straight at him since he came in.

"Do you want to come?"

"I asked you."

"I know you asked me. I'm asking you."

"I've got the boats," he said.

"Yes."

"I've got the boats and the light is good here in the winter. Everybody says it's good in the winter. Ramón says the light in January is the best light there is."

"Then you should stay."

"I didn't say I would stay."

"You didn't have to."

He poured the anís into the two small glasses. It was clear and when he put a little water from the carafe into hers it went cloudy, and she watched it go cloudy and did not drink it.

"Do you want me to ask you to stay?" he said.

She was quiet for a long time. The sea came in against the mole and went out.

"I don't know," she said. "I thought I did. I thought all day that if you asked me I'd stay. I thought that's what I was waiting for. That's the stupid part."

"It isn't stupid."

"It's very stupid. Because now you could ask me and I'd stay and I'd still go. Do you understand that? I'd stay here and I'd still be gone."

"I understand it."

"I don't think you do."

"I understand it," he said. "I don't like it. But I understand it."

"I'm sorry."

"Stop saying you're sorry."

"I am, though."

"I know you are. Drink your anís."

She drank a little of it. It was sweet and it burned going down and then it was warm.

"It's only for a while," she said.

"Sure."

"Just until I'm not tired."

"Sure. That's fine."

"And you'll do the boats. And you'll write to me and tell me how they're going."

"I'll write you."

"And in the spring you'll come up and we'll go somewhere. We'll go to the Midi or somewhere and it'll be warm and you can paint the olive trees."

"I don't want to paint any olive trees."

"Then you can paint something else."

"All right," he said. "I'll paint something else."

She put her hand across the table and put it on top of his hand. Her hand was warm from the stove and his was cold still and rough and she could feel the cuts.

"You should put something on them," she said.

"I'll ask the woman. She'll have something."

"Ask her tonight."

"I'll ask her."

They sat with her hand on his. Then Manolo came out of the kitchen with his coat on and his cap in his hand and stood by the door, and she took her hand away.

"We're going up," he said to Manolo. "Leave the light. I'll turn it off."

"There is no hurry," Manolo said.

"No. Go on home. Good night, Manolo."

"Good night. Good night, señora."

"Good night," she said.

Manolo went out and they heard the door shut and the wind come against it after.

"I'm going up," she said. "I have to pack."

"Do you want help?"

"No. There isn't much."

"I'll come up in a while."

"Don't be long."

"I won't be long."

She stood and he stood and she came around the table and kissed him on the side of the face where it was still red from the wind, and then she went up the stairs. He heard her on the stairs and then he heard the door of the room and then he did not hear anything but the stove and the sea.

He sat down again. He poured another anís and did not put any water in it and drank it. Then he got up and put on the oilskin coat and turned off the light by the stove and went out.

It was not raining. The wind was still from the south and it was warm for November and there were breaks in the clouds and stars in the breaks. He crossed the square. The café was shut and the arcade was dark and smelled of fish and wet stone. He went down the steps to the quay and walked out along the mole. The tide was coming in and the water was black and slapped against the stones. At the end of the mole there was the small light on its iron post, green, and he stood under it and looked back at the town.

All the boats were in. He could see them now that his eyes were used to the dark, lying close together in the inner harbor with the tide lifting them, the masts moving against the hills behind the town. He could see Ramón's boat by its high bow. Ramón had said they would go out early if the wind held. He had said it would be good tomorrow. He had said that out past the point the fish were there and they had only to go to them.

He looked up at the hotel. There was a light in the window of their room. He could see the shutters standing open, and the light, and once her shadow passing across it and then passing back. He watched the window for a while. Then he looked at the boats again. He thought that in the morning if the light was good he would set up on the wall where the mole turned and do them coming around the end, one after another, with the lighthouse behind. He thought about how the light would come on the water early and how he would have to work fast to get it. He thought about the colors he would need. He thought about that for a long time, standing at the end of the mole, and he did not think about the bus at seven or the train at eleven or the apartment on the rue Jacob with the room that got the sun.

When he went back the light in the window was out. He went up the stairs quietly and opened the door. The room was cold. Her bag was packed and standing by the door, and her coat was laid over it, and she was in the bed with her back to him and he could not tell if she was asleep. He undressed in the dark and got in beside her. She did not move. He lay on his back and listened to the sea coming in against the mole and going out, and coming in again, and he heard it now the way he had heard it the first night, and he lay there and listened to it for a long time.

column308:
The train came in late in the afternoon and Tom got down with his bag and stood on the platform in the wind. The wind came down off the mountains and across the flat country and there was no snow on the ground yet but you could smell that it would come. There was a truck parked beside the station house and a man was leaning against the fender with his arms folded. The man straightened up when he saw Tom and came across the cinders.

"Hello, Ed," Tom said.

"Hello, Tommy."

They shook hands. Ed's hand was hard and dry and he held on a moment longer than he needed to and then he let go and took the bag.

"I can carry that."

"I know you can," Ed said. "Get in the truck."

They drove out of town on the gravel road. The town was not much. There was the station and the grain elevator and a street with a bank and a hardware store and a café and two bars and then there was nothing but the road and the fences and the country going away brown and yellow to the foot of the hills. The hills were dark with pine and above them the mountains were white at the tops.

"It hasn't changed," Tom said.

"Some."

"It looks the same."

"They paved the road to Lander. And the Swede sold the hardware store."

"Who bought it?"

"A fellow from Casper. Nobody likes him."

"Why not?"

"He's from Casper," Ed said.

Tom laughed. Ed did not laugh but Tom could see he was pleased. Ed drove with one hand on the bottom of the wheel and his hat pushed back. He was bigger than Tom remembered and his face was dark from the sun and there were lines at the corners of his eyes that had not been there before. They had been boys together on this road. They had ridden it in the back of Ed's father's truck with the dogs, and in winter they had ridden it on the hay sled behind the team, and Tom had thought then that it was the longest road in the world.

"How long has it been?" Ed said.

"Eleven years."

"That's right. Eleven years."

"It doesn't seem like it."

"It seems like it to me," Ed said.

They did not talk any more until they came to the gate. Tom got down and opened the gate and Ed drove the truck through and Tom closed the gate and fastened the chain and got back in. He had done it without thinking and when he got back in the truck he felt good about it.

"You haven't forgotten how," Ed said.

"No."

"Some fellows forget."

The house was where it had always been, in the cottonwoods by the creek, and the barn was behind it and the corrals were behind the barn. The house had been painted. It had been white and now it was white again but it was a cleaner white. There were two dogs in the yard and they came out barking and then they stopped barking and came and smelled Tom's legs and his hands.

"Those aren't the same dogs."

"No. Those are Buck's pups. Buck's been dead six years."

"I'm sorry."

"He was an old dog," Ed said. "He was a good old dog."

---

Inside the house it was warm and there was a fire in the stove. The kitchen was the same. The table was the same table with the oilcloth on it and there were the same chairs. Ed put the bag down and went to the cupboard and took down a bottle of whiskey and two glasses.

"You still drink?"

"I still drink."

"Good." He poured the whiskey and went to the pump at the sink and ran some water into a pitcher. "You want water?"

"A little."

Ed put a little water in Tom's glass and none in his own and they sat down at the table. The whiskey was good. It was not very good whiskey but it was cold out and the kitchen was warm and it tasted good. Tom held it in his mouth a moment and then swallowed it and felt it go down warm.

"Where's Margaret?" he said.

"She took the kids to her mother's in Riverton. She'll be back Sunday."

"I wanted to see them."

"You'll see them Sunday."

"I've never seen the kids."

"I know it," Ed said. "They've heard about you. The boy wants to know if you were in the war."

"What did you tell him?"

"I told him you were."

"What did he say?"

"He wanted to know if you killed anybody."

Tom drank some of the whiskey. "What did you tell him?"

"I told him to ask you."

"That's fine."

"I thought you'd want it that way."

"That's fine," Tom said. "I'll tell him something."

Ed poured more whiskey in his own glass and held the bottle over Tom's and Tom nodded and Ed poured. Outside it was getting dark. The window over the sink was blue and then it was grey and Ed got up and lit the lamp. He had electricity now, there was a bulb in a fixture in the ceiling, but he lit the lamp anyway and set it on the table.

"You've got the electric."

"Two years ago. I don't like it at night. It's too bright."

"It's a good lamp."

"It was Dad's," Ed said.

They looked at the lamp. Tom turned his glass on the oilcloth. He had known that it would come up and he had thought about how it would be and on the train he had thought of things to say. Now he did not say any of them.

"Are you hungry?" Ed said.

"Yes."

"There's a stew. Margaret made it before she left. It's better the second day."

"Everything is."

"Not everything," Ed said.

---

They ate the stew with bread and butter and drank coffee with it and afterward they sat by the stove. Ed had a pipe now and he filled it and lit it and Tom smoked a cigarette. The dogs had come in and they lay by the door with their heads on their paws and their eyes open.

"How's Chicago?" Ed said.

"It's all right."

"You still at the paper?"

"No. I quit the paper."

"When?"

"In the spring."

"What do you do now?"

"Nothing much. I'm writing some."

"Writing what?"

"Stories."

"Do they sell?"

"Some of them."

Ed nodded. He drew on the pipe and the bowl glowed and then went dark. "That's good," he said. "I didn't know you could do that."

"I don't know if I can."

"If they sell, you can."

"It isn't that simple."

"It seems pretty simple to me," Ed said. "If a man buys a steer from you it's because it's a good steer."

"Sometimes it's because he's a fool."

"Not twice," Ed said. "A man doesn't buy from you twice if he's a fool the first time."

Tom laughed. "No," he said. "Maybe not."

"How's Helen?"

"Helen's fine."

"You still married?"

"No."

Ed took the pipe out of his mouth and looked at it. "I'm sorry," he said.

"It's all right. It was a long time coming."

"Was it you or her?"

"It was both of us. It was mostly me."

"Well," Ed said. "That's honest anyhow."

"There's no point in it being any other way."

"There's a lot of fellows would make it the other way."

"I know it. I was one of them for a while."

"What changed?"

"I don't know," Tom said. "I got tired, I guess."

Ed put the pipe back in his mouth and they sat. The stove ticked. One of the dogs got up and turned around and lay down again. The wind had come up outside and you could hear it in the cottonwoods and against the side of the house.

"Do you want to go up to the lake tomorrow?" Ed said.

"Is it still good?"

"It's good this time of year. The big ones come up out of the deep water. It'll be cold."

"I'd like that."

"We'll go early."

"How early?"

"Early," Ed said. "Like we used to."

"I'd like that very much."

"I've got your rod."

"My rod?"

"The one you left. The split bamboo. Dad kept it."

"I didn't know that."

"He kept it in the closet in his room. He oiled the case every fall. I'd see him doing it."

Tom did not say anything. He finished his cigarette and put it out in the saucer Ed had given him and then he sat with his hands between his knees and looked at the stove.

"He thought you'd come back for it," Ed said.

"I should have."

"Well. You're here now."

"It isn't the same."

"No," Ed said. "It isn't the same. But you're here."

---

In the morning it was dark and cold when they went out to the truck. There was frost on the windshield and Ed scraped it off with the edge of his hand and they got in and he ran the motor a while before they started. Tom held the coffee. Ed had made it on the stove and put it in a jar with a lid and wrapped the jar in a towel and Tom held it on his knees and it was warm through the towel.

They drove up out of the valley on the old road. The road went up through the sagebrush and then into the aspens and the aspens had lost their leaves and were white and bare in the headlights. Then the road went into the pines and it was darker. The truck labored on the grade and Ed shifted down. When they came out on top the sky was getting light in the east, grey and then yellow along the edge of the hills behind them, and below them on the other side was the lake.

The lake was long and dark and there was mist on it. The mist lay on the water close and white and above the mist the far shore was black with trees. Beyond the trees the mountains went up and the snow on them was pink where the light was beginning to touch it.

"There it is," Ed said.

"Yes."

"You remember it?"

"I remember it."

"It's the same."

"Yes," Tom said. "This is the same."

They left the truck at the end of the road and walked down through the trees with the rods and the creel and the jar of coffee. The ground was soft with needles and it was quiet. Tom could hear the creek coming in at the head of the lake and somewhere a jay. At the shore there was a log where they had always sat and Tom saw it and stopped.

"That's the log."

"It's the same log," Ed said. "It'll be there after we're gone."

They sat on the log and drank the coffee out of the jar, passing it back and forth. It was still hot. Then Ed opened the long case and took out the sections of the bamboo rod and handed them to Tom one at a time. Tom fitted them together. The ferrules were tight and clean and the varnish was good. He sighted down the rod and it was straight. He waved it a little in the air and felt it come alive in his hand.

"It's a good rod," he said.

"Dad said it was the best rod in the county."

"It was. It cost me forty dollars. I worked all summer for it."

"I remember. You worked for the Swede."

"I hauled nails."

"You hauled a lot of nails," Ed said.

Tom put the reel on and ran the line through the guides and tied on the leader and a fly. His fingers were cold and stiff and it took him a long time to tie the knot and he did it twice before it was right. Ed waited and did not say anything. When it was right Tom stood up and walked out on the rocks at the edge of the water and stripped out line and began to cast.

He was bad at first. The line came back wrong and slapped the water and he had to stop and start over. Then he began to remember. He brought the rod back and waited and felt the line straighten behind him and brought it forward, and the line went out over the water in a long loop and the fly dropped onto the dark water at the edge of the mist and sat there.

"That's it," Ed said behind him.

Tom stripped in the line slowly. Nothing came. He cast again. Ed had gone down the shore a little way and was casting too and Tom could hear the line hiss in the air and then the small sound of it on the water. The mist was lifting now. It came up off the lake in pieces and went away into the trees and the sun had come over the hills behind them and the water in the open places was gold.

On the fifth cast a fish hit. Tom felt it before he saw it, a hard jolt that went up the line and down the rod into his wrist, and then the fish came up out of the water a long way out, silver and thrashing, and went down again. The rod bent nearly double. Tom held it up and let the reel go and the fish ran and he let it run.

"He's a good one," Ed called.

"He's a very good one."

"Don't horse him."

"I'm not horsing him."

"Let him tire."

"I know," Tom said. "I know how."

He brought the fish in slowly. It ran twice more and each time he let it go and each time it came back a little easier. When it was close he could see it in the clear water by the rocks, long and dark on the back and spotted, turning on its side. Ed came with the net and waded in up to his knees in the cold water and slid the net under the fish and lifted it out.

They looked at it in the net. It was a cutthroat and it was nearly as long as Tom's arm from the elbow and there was the red slash under its jaw and the colors on its side were very bright.

"That's the best fish I've seen out of here in two years," Ed said.

"He's beautiful."

"Do you want to keep him?"

Tom looked at the fish. Its gills moved slowly in and out.

"No," he said. "Let him go."

Ed knelt and held the fish in the water facing upstream into the little current from the creek, and moved it gently back and forth, and after a while the fish moved its tail and slid out of his hands and was gone into the dark water.

Ed stood up and wiped his hands on his trousers. His trousers were wet to the knee.

"You're going to freeze," Tom said.

"I've been colder."

---

They fished until the sun was high and kept four smaller fish and then they sat on the log and Ed built a fire out of dead pine on the rocks and cleaned the fish. He had brought bacon and a pan in the creel and he fried the bacon and then fried the fish in the grease. They ate the fish with their fingers and it was very good. The meat came away from the bones white and sweet and hot and they burned their fingers and did not care.

"You should have been here," Ed said.

Tom had a piece of fish in his fingers and he put it down on the rock.

"I know it."

"I'm not saying it to make you feel bad."

"I know you're not."

"I just wanted to say it. I've been wanting to say it for two years and now I've said it."

"I couldn't come," Tom said. "I got the wire and I couldn't come."

"Why not?"

"I don't know. I could have come. I didn't."

Ed fed a stick into the fire. "He asked for you," he said. "Near the end. He thought you were coming. He asked was Tommy here yet. I said you were on the train."

Tom looked at the lake. The wind had come up a little and the water was moving and there were small white edges on it far out.

"I told him you were on the train," Ed said again. "I didn't know what else to tell him."

"That was all right."

"I don't know if it was. I've thought about it. I don't know if it was right to tell him that."

"It was right," Tom said. "It was the right thing."

"He was more of a father to you than your own."

"I know that."

"He used to say you were the only one of us with any sense."

"He was wrong."

"Maybe," Ed said. "He wasn't wrong about much."

Tom picked up the piece of fish and ate it. It had gone cold on the rock. He ate it anyway and then he wiped his fingers on the grass and took out his cigarettes and offered one to Ed and Ed shook his head and filled his pipe instead. They smoked.

"Helen was leaving," Tom said. "That week. When the wire came. She was packing her things."

Ed looked at him.

"I'm not saying that's why. I'm not making it an excuse. I'm only telling you."

"All right."

"I sat in the kitchen with the wire on the table and she was in the other room packing and I couldn't get up out of the chair. I sat there all night. In the morning she was gone and I still had the wire and I thought, I'll go today. And then I didn't go."

"You could have wired back."

"I know it."

"We didn't know anything. We didn't know if you were dead."

"I know," Tom said. "I'm sorry, Ed."

Ed sat with the pipe in his mouth and looked at the fire. Then he took the pipe out.

"Well," he said. "That's done now."

"Is it?"

"It's done. You said it and I said it. There isn't anything else to say about it."

"There's a lot more."

"No there isn't," Ed said. "There's always a lot more if you want there to be. I don't want there to be."

Tom put out the cigarette on the rock. He felt something loosen in his chest and he did not trust it and he sat still and waited and it stayed loose.

"All right," he said.

"You can stay as long as you want. You know that."

"I don't know how long."

"It doesn't matter how long. There's the room. Margaret's fixed it up."

"Dad's room?"

"It's just a room now. It's a good room. It gets the morning sun."

"I'd like that."

"You can write in there. There's a table."

"I don't know if I'll write."

"Well," Ed said. "You can fish, then."

---

They put out the fire and kicked the ashes into the lake and walked back up through the trees to the truck. The sun was warm now on the open slope and the needles smelled of resin. Tom carried the rod in its case. At the truck he stopped and looked back down at the lake. It was blue now and the wind was moving on it and there was no mist anywhere.

"We'll come back," Ed said.

"Tomorrow?"

"Tomorrow if you want. Sunday the boy can come. He's been after me to bring him."

"Can he cast?"

"Not worth a damn," Ed said. "You can teach him."

"I'm not sure I'm the one to teach him."

"You're the one," Ed said. "Dad taught you. You can teach him."

They got in the truck. Ed started it and turned it around in the clearing and they started down. Tom held the rod case across his knees. The road went down into the pines and through the pines to the aspens and the aspens were white in the sun and below them the valley lay open and brown and far down in it, small in the cottonwoods by the creek, was the house.

"It's a good country," Tom said.

"It's the only one I know."

"It's a good one to know."

"Yes," Ed said. "I think it is."

He drove with one hand on the bottom of the wheel. The truck rattled on the washboard and the dust went up behind them and hung in the still air and settled slowly on the sage. Tom rolled the window down and the air came in cold and clean and smelling of sage, and he leaned his head back against the seat and closed his eyes and did not open them until they came to the gate.

The cabin stood on a rise above the lake and from the porch you could see the dock and the shallow water over the sand and beyond it the point with the dark hemlocks on it and beyond the point the open lake. In the mornings the lake was flat and grey and there was mist on it, and then the sun came up over the hills on the far shore and burned off the mist and the water was blue and clear and you could see the stones on the bottom a long way out. In the afternoons the wind came up from the southwest. It came up every afternoon that summer and the lake was rough then and there were whitecaps out past the point.

The man had been up before light to fish. He had gone down to the rocks below the cabin with the short rod and he had caught three bass on a frog and he had cleaned them on the flat rock by the water and washed them and put them in the spring box where it was cold. Then he had cooked eggs and bacon for himself and the boy and they had eaten on the porch, and afterward the boy had gone down to the dock with his can of worms and his line, and the man had sat in the canvas chair with a book. The sun was warm on his legs. He read for a while and then he put the book face down on his chest and closed his eyes. He had not slept well in a long time and it was good to sleep in the sun with the sound of the water.

When he woke the shade had come across the porch and the wind was up. He could hear it in the tops of the hemlocks and he could hear the waves on the rocks below. He sat up and the book fell on the boards. He looked down at the dock.

The boy was not on the dock. The can of worms was there and the line was there wound on its stick, but the boy was not there and the canoe was not there.

"Billy," the man called.

There was no answer. The wind took his voice and he called again louder. Then he went down the path to the dock. He did not run on the path. He walked fast and his heart was going and he did not let himself run. At the dock he stood and looked out at the lake. The water was dark now with the wind on it and the sun was in his eyes off the water and he could not see anything. He put his hand up against the sun. Then he saw the canoe. It was far out, past the end of the point, very small on the rough water, and it was turned the wrong way, broadside to the waves. He could see the boy in it. He could see the boy's red shirt.

The rowboat was pulled up on the sand beside the dock. He pushed it into the water and got in and fitted the oars in the locks and began to row. He rowed hard and steadily and did not look around. He had rowed a great deal as a young man and he knew how to do it and he did not hurry his stroke. When he hurried it the oars came out of the water and he lost time. He made himself row properly. Every twenty strokes he turned his head and looked over his shoulder at the canoe to get his line, and then he rowed again.

Past the point the waves were bigger. They came at him on the quarter and the rowboat climbed up them and slid down and spray came over the bow and wet his back. He kept rowing. The next time he turned his head the canoe was closer and he could see the boy holding the paddle across the gunwales and not paddling. The canoe was low in the water. It was drifting out toward the middle of the lake where the wind would take it all the way across, three miles, to the rocks on the far side.

"Sit down," the man shouted. "Sit down in the bottom."

The boy was already sitting down. He was sitting on the seat in the stern and the bow was high out of the water and that was why the wind had turned him. The man shouted again and the boy looked at him and did not move. The man rowed until the rowboat was alongside and then he shipped one oar and reached and took hold of the gunwale of the canoe. The two boats knocked together in the waves.

"Get down in the bottom," the man said. "In the middle. Get down low."

The boy got down off the seat into the bottom of the canoe. There was water in the bottom and it came up over his legs. His face was white and his lips were blue and he did not say anything.

"Give me the painter," the man said. "The rope. In front of you. Hand it to me."

The boy crawled forward and found the rope and handed it to him. The man made it fast to the stern ring of the rowboat. He tied it twice. Then he took up the oar again.

"Stay down," he said. "Stay down like that and hold on to the sides and don't move. Don't stand up whatever happens."

"All right," the boy said.

It was hard rowing back. The wind was against him now and the canoe pulled at the rope and swung behind him and he had to row a long time before the point was beside him. Then they were in the lee of the point and the water was calmer and he could see the dock. He rowed in to the dock and got out in the shallow water and pulled the canoe in by the rope and lifted the boy out of it. The boy was shaking. The man carried him up onto the dock and set him down on the boards and stood there and the water ran off him. He did not say anything for a while. He could not say anything. He stood with his hands at his sides and looked at the boy and the boy looked at the boards of the dock.

"Go up to the cabin," the man said finally. "Take off those wet things and put on dry ones. Put on your wool shirt. Then come out on the porch."

"I'm sorry, Papa."

"Go on up."

The boy went up the path. The man watched him go. Then he went back down into the water and turned the canoe over and emptied it and carried it up onto the dock and set it upside down on the rack. He pulled the rowboat up on the sand. The paddle was still in the canoe and he took it out and stood holding it. It was the short paddle he had cut down for the boy at the beginning of the summer. He had shaped the grip with his knife on the porch in the evenings and the boy had watched him do it. He put the paddle on the rack under the canoe. He found that his hands were shaking and he put them in his pockets and stood there until they stopped. Then he went up to the cabin.

He changed his own clothes in the bedroom. He could hear the boy in the other room. When he came out on the porch the boy was sitting on the top step in his wool shirt with his arms around his knees. The man sat down in the canvas chair. He picked up the book from the boards and closed it and put it on the table. Then he looked at the boy.

"Come here," he said.

The boy got up and came and stood in front of the chair.

"Did I tell you about the canoe?"

"Yes."

"What did I tell you?"

"Not to take it out."

"Not to take it out when?"

"Not to take it out alone."

"Not ever," the man said. "Not alone. Not ever. Isn't that what I told you?"

"Yes."

"And you took it out."

"Yes," the boy said. "I'm sorry."

"Why did you take it out?"

The boy did not answer. He looked at the man's boots.

"Look at me," the man said. "Why did you take it out?"

"I wanted to fish off the point. Where you fish. I didn't catch anything off the dock. The fish are all off the point."

"And then what?"

"Then the wind came. I was paddling and the wind came and it turned me around. I paddled and paddled and it kept turning me around. I couldn't make it go."

"No," the man said. "You couldn't make it go. You were sitting in the stern with nobody in the bow and the bow was up in the air like a sail. You couldn't have made it go if you were a grown man. Do you know where you were going?"

"No."

"You were going across the lake. Do you know what's across the lake?"

"Rocks," the boy said.

"Rocks. And three miles of water before the rocks. And the water's cold. It's cold even now in August. You were in it up to your knees. Was it cold?"

"Yes."

"If you'd turned over out there do you know how long you'd have lasted?"

The boy did not say anything.

"Not long," the man said. "Not long at all. Not as long as it would have taken me to wake up."

He stopped. He had not meant to say that last thing. He sat in the chair and looked past the boy at the lake. The whitecaps were still out there past the point. The sun was getting low and the water was bright and hard to look at.

"I was all right," the boy said. "I didn't turn over. I sat still. I knew to sit still."

"You were not all right."

"I was. I didn't tip."

"Listen to me," the man said. He did not raise his voice. He had raised his voice on the dock and he did not want to do that again. "You were not all right. You were lucky. That is a different thing. You think it is the same thing but it is not. I want you to understand the difference. Do you understand?"

"I think so."

"Being all right is when you know what you're doing and you do it right. Being lucky is when you don't know and nothing happens to you anyway. It's not the same. The lake doesn't care if you're lucky. The lake doesn't care about anything. You can be lucky every day and then one day you aren't and that's all."

The boy's chin was shaking now. He held it still and then it shook again.

"Don't cry," the man said. "There's nothing to cry about now. You're all right now. I just want you to understand."

"I'm not crying."

"Good."

They were quiet. Down below on the rocks the waves were coming in and going out. A kingfisher went along the shore low over the water and its rattle came up to them on the wind and then it was gone around the point.

"Am I going to be punished?" the boy asked.

"Yes."

"What is it?"

The man thought about it. He had not thought about it before. He had only thought about the canoe going out past the point.

"You won't fish tomorrow," he said. "I'll go out early and you'll stay at the cabin. And you won't go down to the dock alone. Not tomorrow and not the next day. You'll go down to the dock when I go down."

"For how long?"

"Until I say."

"That isn't fair," the boy said. "I said I was sorry."

"It isn't about fair. It's about the lake."

"I said I was sorry."

"I know you're sorry. Being sorry is fine. You should be sorry. But being sorry doesn't change what you did. You did it and now there's this. That's how it is."

"Would you have taken the canoe?" the boy said. "When you were little?"

The man looked at him.

"Yes," he said. "I would have taken it."

"Then why can't I?"

"Because I would have been wrong to take it. And somebody would have had to come out after me in a boat."

"Did somebody come after you?"

"Once."

"Who?"

"My father."

"Did he punish you?"

"Yes."

"What did he do?"

"It doesn't matter what he did," the man said. "That was a long time ago. That was a different lake."

The boy stood there in front of the chair. The wool shirt was too big for him and the sleeves came down over his hands. His hair was still wet and it stuck up on one side.

"Are you angry?" he said.

"Yes."

"Very angry?"

"I was very angry. Now I'm less angry. I'll be all right."

"Will you tell Mama?"

The man did not answer right away. He took his pipe out of his shirt pocket and looked at it and put it back.

"I'll write her about it," he said. "I write her every Sunday. I'll tell her."

"Do you have to?"

"I tell her everything that happens. That's the agreement. I'll tell her you made a mistake and you were sorry about it. I'll tell her you sat still in the canoe the way you were supposed to. I'll tell her that too."

"Will she come up?"

"No. She can't come up this summer. You know that."

"I know," the boy said.

The man reached out and put his hand on the boy's head. The hair was wet and cold. He left his hand there a moment and then he took it away.

"Go and get the fish out of the spring box," he said. "The three bass. Bring them in the pan. We'll eat early."

"Can I clean them?"

"They're already cleaned. You can roll them in the meal."

"All right."

The boy went off around the side of the cabin to the spring. The man sat in the chair. He took the pipe out again and filled it from the pouch and tamped it with his thumb and lit it and the smoke went away fast in the wind. He smoked and looked at the lake. He thought about the canoe out there broadside to the waves with the bow up and the red shirt in it. He did not want to think about it but he thought about it. He thought about what it would have been like to wake in the shade and look down at the dock and see the canoe gone and then look out at the lake and not see anything. Just the whitecaps and the sun on the water. He thought about that and then he stopped thinking about it. He made himself stop. He was good at stopping. He had learned to be good at it and he did it now. He smoked the pipe and watched the kingfisher come back along the shore.

The boy came back carrying the pan with both hands. The three bass lay in it on their sides, cold and wet from the spring.

"They're big," the boy said.

"They're good fish."

"Where did you catch them?"

"Off the rocks. Right down there."

"Not off the point?"

"No. Off the rocks below the cabin. You don't have to go to the point. There are fish everywhere if you're patient."

"I wasn't patient."

"No," the man said. "You weren't."

They went inside. The man built up the fire in the stove with split birch and the birch caught and roared and he shut the damper partway. The boy poured cornmeal onto a plate and salted it and rolled the fish in it, turning them carefully with his fingers. The man put lard in the big iron pan and when it was smoking he laid the fish in it and they spat and hissed. He cut bread and the boy set out the plates and the forks and the jar of pickles. The cabin was warm with the stove and it smelled of the birch smoke and the frying fish. Outside the wind was still blowing but the sound of it was smaller in the cabin.

They ate at the table by the window. The fish were good, the meal crisp and brown on the outside and the meat white and sweet and coming away easily from the bones. The boy picked the bones out carefully. He was careful about bones. He had choked on one once at the beginning of the summer and he had been careful ever since.

"These are good," he said.

"They're very good."

"Better than perch."

"Bass are better than perch. Perch are good too."

"Can I catch bass?"

"You can catch bass. Not tomorrow. But you can catch them."

"Off the rocks?"

"Off the rocks. With a frog. I'll show you how to hook the frog."

"When?"

"When I say."

The boy ate. Then he stopped eating and looked out the window at the lake.

"It was scary," he said. "Out there."

"Yes."

"I didn't think it would be scary. From the dock it didn't look like anything."

"It never looks like anything from the dock."

"The waves were big."

"They were big enough."

"Were you scared?"

The man put his fork down on the plate. He looked at the boy and then he looked out the window at the point and the hemlocks dark against the water. The sun was almost down behind the hills and the lake was turning from blue to grey.

"Yes," he said. "I was scared."

"You didn't look scared."

"No. You don't look scared when you're rowing. You think about rowing."

"I'll think about rowing too," the boy said. "Next time."

"There won't be a next time. Not alone."

"I mean when I'm big."

"When you're big," the man said. "All right. When you're big, think about rowing."

They finished the fish. The boy washed the plates in the basin and the man dried them and put them on the shelf. Then the boy went to bed in the small room under the eaves. The man stood in the door of the room and the boy lay in the bunk with the blanket up to his chin.

"Papa."

"Yes."

"I'm sorry I took the canoe."

"I know you are."

"Are you still angry?"

"No," the man said. "I'm not angry anymore. Go to sleep."

"Will you be on the porch?"

"I'll be on the porch."

"All right," the boy said.

The man went out onto the porch and sat in the canvas chair. It was dark now and the wind had dropped. It always dropped at night. The lake was flat and the stars were on it and he could hear a loon somewhere out past the point. He sat and listened to the loon and he did not light his pipe. After a while he got up and went down the path to the dock in the dark. He felt along the rack until he found the canoe and he checked that it was turned over and tied, and then he felt underneath for the short paddle and took it out. He carried it back up to the cabin and stood it in the corner by his bed. Then he went back out to the porch and sat down again. The loon called. It was a good sound and he sat a long time in the dark and listened to it and he did not think about anything at all.

Here is an excerpt of Ernest Hemingway's writing, to show you their style:

I was away for two days at the posts. When I got home it was too late and I did not see Miss Barkley until the next evening. She was not in the garden and I had to wait in the office of the hospital until she came down. There were many marble busts on painted wooden pillars along the walls of the room they used for an office. The hall too, that the office opened on, was lined with them. They had the complete marble quality of all looking alike. Sculpture had always seemed a dull business—still, bronzes looked like something. But marble busts all looked like a cemetery. There was one fine cemetery though—the one at Pisa. Genoa was the place to see the bad marbles. This had been the villa of a very wealthy German and the busts must have cost him plenty. I wondered who had done them and how much he got. I tried to make out whether they were members of the family or what; but they were all uniformly classical. You could not tell anything about them. I sat on a chair and held my cap. We were supposed to wear steel helmets even in Gorizia but they were uncomfortable and too bloody theatrical in a town where the civilian inhabitants had not been evacuated. I wore one when we went up to the posts and carried an English gas mask. We were just beginning to get some of them. They were a real mask. Also we were required to wear an automatic pistol; even doctors and sanitary officers. I felt it against the back of the chair. You were liable to arrest if you did not have one worn in plain sight. Rinaldi carried a holster stuffed with toilet paper. I wore a real one and felt like a gunman until I practised firing it. It was an Astra 7.65 caliber with a short barrel and it jumped so sharply when you let it off that there was no question of hitting anything. I practised with it, holding below the target and trying to master the jerk of the ridiculous short barrel until I could hit within a yard of where I aimed at twenty paces and then the ridiculousness of carrying a pistol at all came over me and I soon forgot it and carried it flopping against the small of my back with no feeling at all except a vague sort of shame when I met English-speaking people. I sat now in the chair and an orderly of some sort looked at me disapprovingly from behind a desk while I looked at the marble floor, the pillars with the marble busts, and the frescoes on the wall and waited for Miss Barkley. The frescoes were not bad. Any frescoes were good when they started to peel and flake off. I saw Catherine Barkley coming down the hall, and stood up. She did not seem tall walking toward me but she looked very lovely.

“Good-evening, Mr. Henry,” she said.

“How do you do?” I said. The orderly was listening behind the desk.

“Shall we sit here or go out in the garden?”

“Let’s go out. It’s much cooler.” I walked behind her out into the garden, the orderly looking after us. When we were out on the gravel drive she said, “Where have you been?”

“I’ve been out on post.”

“You couldn’t have sent me a note?”

“No,” I said. “Not very well. I thought I was coming back.”

“You ought to have let me know, darling.” We were off the driveway, walking under the trees. I took her hands, then stopped and kissed her.

“Isn’t there anywhere we can go?”

“No,” she said. “We have to just walk here. You’ve been away a long time.”

“This is the third day. But I’m back now.” She looked at me, “And you do love me?”

“Yes.”

“You did say you loved me, didn’t you?”

“Yes,” I lied. “I love you.” I had not said it before.

“And you call me Catherine?”

“Catherine.” We walked on a way and were stopped under a tree.

“Say, ‘I’ve come back to Catherine in the night.’ ” “I’ve come back to Catherine in the night.”

“Oh, darling, you have come back, haven’t you?”

“Yes.”

“I love you so and it’s been awful. You won’t go away?”

“No. I’ll always come back.”

“Oh, I love you so. Please put your hand there again.”

“It’s not been away.” I turned her so I could see her face when I kissed her and I saw that her eyes were shut. I kissed both her shut eyes. I thought she was probably a little crazy. It was all right if she was. I did not care what I was getting into. This was better than going every evening to the house for officers where the girls climbed all over you and put your cap on backward as a sign of affection between their trips upstairs with brother officers. I knew I did not love Catherine Barkley nor had any idea of loving her. This was a game, like bridge, in which you said things instead of playing cards. Like bridge you had to pretend you were playing for money or playing for some stakes. Nobody had mentioned what the stakes were. It was all right with me.

“I wish there was some place we could go,” I said. I was experiencing the masculine difficulty of making love very long standing up.

“There isn’t any place,” she said. She came back from wherever she had been.

“We might sit there just for a little while.” We sat on the flat stone bench and I held Catherine Barkley’s hand. She would not let me put my arm around her.

“Are you very tired?” she asked.

“No.” She looked down at the grass.

“This is a rotten game we play, isn’t it?”

“What game?”

“Don’t be dull.”

“I’m not, on purpose.”

“You’re a nice boy,” she said. “And you play it as well as you know how. But it’s a rotten game.”

“Do you always know what people think?”

“Not always. But I do with you. You don’t have to pretend you love me. That’s over for the evening. Is there anything you’d like to talk about?”

“But I do love you.”

“Please let’s not lie when we don’t have to. I had a very fine little show and I’m all right now. You see I’m not mad and I’m not gone off. It’s only a little sometimes.” I pressed her hand, “Dear Catherine.”

“It sounds very funny now—Catherine. You don’t pronounce it very much alike. But you’re very nice. You’re a very good boy.”

“That’s what the priest said.”

“Yes, you’re very good. And you will come and see me?”

“Of course.”

“And you don’t have to say you love me. That’s all over for a while.” She stood up and put out her hand. “Good-night.” I wanted to kiss her.

“No,” she said. “I’m awfully tired.”

“Kiss me, though,” I said.

“I’m awfully tired, darling.”

“Kiss me.”

“Do you want to very much?”

“Yes.” We kissed and she broke away suddenly. “No. Good-night, please, darling.” We walked to the door and I saw her go in and down the hall. I liked to watch her move. She went on down the hall. I went on home. It was a hot night and there was a good deal going on up in the mountains. I watched the flashes on San Gabriele. I stopped in front of the Villa Rossa. The shutters were up but it was still going on inside. Somebody was singing. I went on home. Rinaldi came in while I was undressing.

The fog was on the lake when he went down to the dock in the morning and he could not see the point. He could see the water close to the boat and it was black and very still and there were leaves on it. The leaves were yellow from the birches and some of them were red from the maples back on the hill. He put the rods and the minnow pail in the boat and pushed off and rowed out into the fog. It was cold and his hands were stiff on the oars. He rowed out past where he could see the dock and then he could not see anything but the water and the fog and the oars going into the water and coming out.

He anchored off the weed bed below the point. He knew it was the weed bed because he could see the tops of the weeds just under the water, brown now and lying over the way they did in the fall. He baited the hook with a minnow and let it down and sat holding the rod. It was very quiet. Somewhere across the lake a man was chopping wood and the sound came over the water a long time after he must have struck. He could not see the man or the shore. He sat and held the rod and did not think about anything.

He caught two perch and a small pike and put the pike back. Then he caught a good pike, a heavy one that went down hard into the weeds and he had to work it up slowly and get it to the side of the boat and get his fingers in under the gills. He hit it on the head with the handle of the knife and it straightened out and was still. It was a fine fish, green and gold along the sides with the spots on it, and the eye was clear. He put it in the bottom of the boat and the fog was lifting now and he could see the shore and the cabin up on the hill with the smoke going straight up from the chimney. She was up then. He pulled up the anchor and rowed in.

She was standing on the porch with a cup of coffee when he came up the path. She had on his old mackinaw over her nightgown and her legs were bare and her feet were in the moccasins.

"You'll catch cold," he said.

"I'm all right. Did you get anything?"

He held up the pike.

"That's a nice one," she said.

"He's a good one. He went into the weeds."

"There's coffee."

"Good."

He cleaned the fish on the board by the pump and threw the insides off into the brush for the raccoons and washed the board and pumped water over his hands. The water was very cold and his hands ached. He went in. The cabin was warm from the stove and she had the bacon on. Her suitcase was open on the bed in the other room. He could see it through the door. He sat down at the table and she poured him coffee.

"I'll fry the perch," she said. "The pike we can have tonight."

"Fine."

She put the bacon on a plate with a paper under it and broke the eggs into the grease. She did not look at him. He drank the coffee. It was hot and good and he held the cup in both hands to get them warm.

"I wrote to Mother," she said.

"When?"

"Yesterday. When you were up at the store. I gave it to the mail boat."

"That's fine."

"I told her I'd be on the Thursday train."

"That's what we said."

"I know it's what we said." She turned the eggs. "I just wanted you to know I wrote it."

"All right."

She put the eggs on the plate and brought it to him and sat down across from him. She had not taken anything for herself. She held her cup and looked out the window at the lake. The fog was all gone now and the sun was on the water and the far shore was very clear with the dark trees and the yellow ones.

"Aren't you going to eat?" he said.

"I had some toast."

"You ought to eat."

"Don't tell me what I ought to do."

He ate the eggs. They were good eggs, the yolks not broken. He ate the bacon. She sat and drank her coffee.

"I'm sorry," she said.

"It's all right."

"No. I'm sorry. I don't know why I said that."

"It doesn't matter."

"It does matter. Everything I say matters. That's the trouble." She put the cup down. "Are you going to come on Thursday?"

"I thought I'd stay and close up."

"You can close up in a day."

"There's the boat to get up. And the dock. I want to get the dock sections out before the ice."

"The ice won't be for two months."

"I know it."

"Then you can come Thursday and come back up."

"It's a long way to come back up."

She looked at him then. She had gray eyes and in the morning they were very clear and there was nothing in them that he could read.

"You don't want to come," she said.

"I didn't say that."

"You didn't have to say it."

"I said I wanted to close up."

"All right," she said. "All right. Close up."

He finished the coffee and got up and poured more from the pot on the stove. He stood by the stove and drank it. She sat at the table with her back to him and he could see her neck where her hair was pinned up and the little short hairs that did not go into the pins. He had always liked her neck.

"I'll get the boat up this morning," he said. "You could help me with the canvas."

"I'll help you."

"Good."

"I'll get dressed."

She went into the other room and he heard her moving around in there. He heard her close the suitcase. Then he heard her open it again. He finished the coffee and went outside.

---

The boat was heavy and they had to put the rollers under it, the old cedar posts he had cut two summers ago, and he pushed and she moved the rollers from the back to the front as the boat came up. It came up slowly. It was hard work and he was sweating in the sun though the air was cold. When they had it up on the grass under the big hemlock he turned it over and she held the end while he got under and lifted. Then it was over and lying on the grass and the bottom was green with the slime from the summer. He would scrape it in the spring. They got the canvas over it and he tied the ropes to the stakes and pulled them tight.

"That's that," he said.

"Yes."

She was standing with her hands in the pockets of the mackinaw looking at the lake. There was a wind coming now from the northwest and the water was dark and there were small whitecaps out past the point.

"It's going to blow," he said.

"It's pretty when it blows."

"It's pretty."

"I won't see it blow anymore," she said.

"You'll see it next summer."

She did not say anything. He coiled the extra rope and hung it on the nail on the tree.

"I don't think I'll come next summer," she said.

He finished hanging the rope. He looked at it hanging there.

"Why not?"

"I don't think I want to."

"All right."

"Is that all you're going to say? All right?"

"What do you want me to say?"

"I don't know. I want you to say something. I want you to ask me."

"I asked you why not."

"And I said I didn't want to and you said all right." She took her hands out of her pockets and then she put them back in again. "You always say all right. You say it as though it was all the same to you."

"It isn't all the same to me."

"Then why do you say it?"

"I don't know," he said. "It's what I say."

The wind was coming harder now and it moved the tops of the hemlocks and the needles came down. One of them caught in her hair. He wanted to take it out but he did not.

"I'm going to walk up the road," she said. "I want to walk."

"Do you want me to come?"

"No," she said. "Thank you. No."

He watched her go up the path to the road. She walked well. She had always walked well, with her shoulders back and her head up, and he watched her until the path turned in the birches and he could not see her. Then he went down to the dock and began taking the planks off the first section. The bolts were rusted and he had to get the wrench from the shed and he worked a long time on the bolts and it was good to have something to work at.

---

She came back after noon. He had two sections of the dock out and stacked on the shore and he was standing in the water in his boots working on the third. She came down and stood on the bank.

"Do you want lunch?"

"I'm not hungry."

"I made sandwiches."

"Thanks. I'll come up in a while."

She stood there. He worked at the bolt and it came loose finally and he lifted the plank off and carried it up and put it on the stack.

"I walked to the Hendersons'," she said. "They've gone already. The house was shut up."

"They go early."

"There's nobody on this whole side of the lake now. Just us."

"There's Olsen."

"Olsen doesn't count."

"No," he said. "I suppose not."

He went back into the water. It was very cold through the boots. She came down onto the part of the dock that was still in and sat on the end of it with her feet hanging over. Her shoes were just above the water.

"What will you do up here alone?"

"Work."

"You can work in the city."

"I don't work in the city."

"You did once."

"Once," he said.

"We were happy in the city once."

He did not say anything. He put the wrench on the next bolt and pulled and it would not come.

"Weren't we?" she said.

"Sure."

"Don't say sure like that."

"How do you want me to say it?"

"I want you to mean it."

He let go of the wrench and stood up straight. The water was up over his knees and he could not feel his feet very well.

"We were happy," he said. "We were happy in the city and we were happy up here. We were happy a lot of places."

"And now?"

"I don't know about now."

"No," she said. "Neither do I."

The wind blew on the water and the small waves came in and slapped against the posts of the dock. She looked down at the water.

"It's very clear," she said. "You can see all the way to the bottom."

"It gets clear in the fall."

"Why is that?"

"I don't know. The cold, I think."

"Everything gets clear in the fall," she said. "Isn't that what you'd say? If you were writing it."

"I wouldn't write that."

"No. You'd write it better."

"I wouldn't write it at all."

She laughed then, not very much. "No," she said. "You'd leave it out. You'd leave everything out." She stood up on the dock. "Come and eat your sandwich."

"I'll come when I get this bolt."

"Come now. Please. It's cold and you're standing in the lake."

"All right," he said, and then he heard himself say it and he looked at her and she was looking at him and for a moment they were both almost smiling and then it was gone.

---

In the evening he fried the pike in the iron pan with butter and they ate it with the potatoes and the last of the tomatoes from the garden behind the shed. The tomatoes had been green when the frost came and she had put them on the windowsill and they had ripened there but they did not taste like the ones from August. The pike was very good. It was white and firm and it came off the bones well. They ate and did not talk much. The wind was blowing hard now and the cabin creaked with it and the stove pipe ticked as it got hot.

After supper he got the bottle and two glasses and went out to the pump for the water and came back. They sat by the stove. She had her feet up on the wood box. He poured the whiskey and the cold water into it and gave her the glass.

"That's too much," she said.

"Drink what you want of it."

"I'll drink all of it."

"Good."

She drank. "It's good."

"It's the water. The lake water makes it."

"You always say that."

"It's true."

"I know it's true." She held the glass and looked at it. "I'll miss the water. I won't miss anything else but I'll miss the water."

"You'll miss the lake."

"No," she said. "Only the water in the whiskey. That's all I'll miss."

He drank and did not say anything. The wind blew and the fire made a sound in the stove.

"I didn't mean that," she said.

"I know it."

"I don't know why I say things. I want to say one thing and I say another. Do you do that?"

"Sometimes."

"You don't say anything. That's what you do."

"That's better than saying the wrong thing."

"Is it?" She put her feet down and turned in the chair and looked at him. "Is it better? I'd rather you said the wrong thing. I'd rather you said something terrible. I'd rather you threw the glass at the wall."

"It's a good glass."

"Oh, damn the glass."

"All right. Damn the glass."

"Don't," she said. "Please don't make jokes. I can't stand it tonight."

"I'm sorry."

"You're not sorry."

"I am sorry," he said. "I'm sorry about a lot of things."

"Tell me one."

He looked at the stove. Through the crack in the door he could see the fire, very red now, the birch going fast the way birch did.

"I'm sorry about the summer," he said.

"What about the summer?"

"That it wasn't a better summer."

"It was a lovely summer," she said. "It was the loveliest summer. The weather was lovely every day. We swam every day. You caught fish every day. We had the tomatoes. It was the loveliest summer there ever was." She was crying now but her voice was not crying and she did not wipe her eyes. "There was nothing wrong with the summer."

"No."

"There was nothing wrong with anything. That's what's so awful. Nothing happened. Nobody did anything. There isn't anything to be sorry about."

"No," he said. "There isn't."

"Then why is it like this?"

"I don't know."

"You must know. You know about everything. You know why the water gets clear. You know where the pike are. You know about the bolts and the ice and the boat." She put the glass down on the floor. "You must know about this."

"I don't," he said. "I don't know about it at all."

She sat there and the tears went down her face and she let them go. He wanted to get up and go to her. He thought about getting up. He sat in the chair and held the glass.

"Do you want me to go Thursday?" she said.

"I want you to do what you want."

"That isn't what I asked you."

"I know it isn't."

"Then answer me."

He drank the rest of the whiskey. He set the glass down on the wood box.

"I think you'd better go Thursday," he said.

She did not say anything for a while. Then she wiped her face with the heel of her hand, one side and then the other, the way a child does.

"Thank you," she said.

"For what?"

"For saying something. For saying anything." She got up. "I'm going to bed."

"All right."

She stood there by the chair. She looked down at him and he looked up at her.

"Say it once more," she said. "Say all right once more and I'll never hear you say it again."

"All right," he said.

She went into the other room. He heard her sit down on the bed and he heard the springs, and then nothing.

---

He went out onto the porch. The wind had gone around into the north and it was very cold and the sky was clear and there were a great many stars. He went down the path to the shore. The dock was gone now except the one section by the land and he walked out on it to the end. The lake was black and moving and the waves came in and he could hear them on the stones all along the shore. Across the lake there was one light. That would be Olsen. Olsen did not count.

He stood at the end of the dock with his hands in his pockets. He thought that in the morning he would get the last section out. Then there was the water to drain from the pipes and the shutters to put up and the canoe to get into the shed. He would carry her bag up to the road on Thursday and they would wait for the mail car and the man would put the bag in the back. He would stand in the road and she would wave from the car or she would not wave. Then he would come back down the path and there would be the shutters to do.

He thought about the summer. They had swum every day. That was true. The water had been very warm in August and they had swum out to the raft and lain on the raft in the sun. He thought about her on the raft with her hair wet and her eyes shut. Then he stopped thinking about it.

It was cold on the dock. The wind came across the water and he could feel it through his coat. He stood there a while longer and then he went back up the path to the cabin. The light was out in the other room. He put more wood in the stove and shut the damper down and sat in the chair. He could hear her breathing through the door, slowly and evenly, and he did not know if she was asleep. He sat and listened to it and to the wind. After a while he poured another drink, with the water from the lake in it, and it was good. It was the water that made it.
