Here is an excerpt of Ernest Hemingway's writing, to show you their style:

I was away for two days at the posts. When I got home it was too late and I did not see Miss Barkley until the next evening. She was not in the garden and I had to wait in the office of the hospital until she came down. There were many marble busts on painted wooden pillars along the walls of the room they used for an office. The hall too, that the office opened on, was lined with them. They had the complete marble quality of all looking alike. Sculpture had always seemed a dull business—still, bronzes looked like something. But marble busts all looked like a cemetery. There was one fine cemetery though—the one at Pisa. Genoa was the place to see the bad marbles. This had been the villa of a very wealthy German and the busts must have cost him plenty. I wondered who had done them and how much he got. I tried to make out whether they were members of the family or what; but they were all uniformly classical. You could not tell anything about them. I sat on a chair and held my cap. We were supposed to wear steel helmets even in Gorizia but they were uncomfortable and too bloody theatrical in a town where the civilian inhabitants had not been evacuated. I wore one when we went up to the posts and carried an English gas mask. We were just beginning to get some of them. They were a real mask. Also we were required to wear an automatic pistol; even doctors and sanitary officers. I felt it against the back of the chair. You were liable to arrest if you did not have one worn in plain sight. Rinaldi carried a holster stuffed with toilet paper. I wore a real one and felt like a gunman until I practised firing it. It was an Astra 7.65 caliber with a short barrel and it jumped so sharply when you let it off that there was no question of hitting anything. I practised with it, holding below the target and trying to master the jerk of the ridiculous short barrel until I could hit within a yard of where I aimed at twenty paces and then the ridiculousness of carrying a pistol at all came over me and I soon forgot it and carried it flopping against the small of my back with no feeling at all except a vague sort of shame when I met English-speaking people. I sat now in the chair and an orderly of some sort looked at me disapprovingly from behind a desk while I looked at the marble floor, the pillars with the marble busts, and the frescoes on the wall and waited for Miss Barkley. The frescoes were not bad. Any frescoes were good when they started to peel and flake off. I saw Catherine Barkley coming down the hall, and stood up. She did not seem tall walking toward me but she looked very lovely.

“Good-evening, Mr. Henry,” she said.

“How do you do?” I said. The orderly was listening behind the desk.

“Shall we sit here or go out in the garden?”

“Let’s go out. It’s much cooler.” I walked behind her out into the garden, the orderly looking after us. When we were out on the gravel drive she said, “Where have you been?”

“I’ve been out on post.”

“You couldn’t have sent me a note?”

“No,” I said. “Not very well. I thought I was coming back.”

“You ought to have let me know, darling.” We were off the driveway, walking under the trees. I took her hands, then stopped and kissed her.

“Isn’t there anywhere we can go?”

“No,” she said. “We have to just walk here. You’ve been away a long time.”

“This is the third day. But I’m back now.” She looked at me, “And you do love me?”

“Yes.”

“You did say you loved me, didn’t you?”

“Yes,” I lied. “I love you.” I had not said it before.

“And you call me Catherine?”

“Catherine.” We walked on a way and were stopped under a tree.

“Say, ‘I’ve come back to Catherine in the night.’ ” “I’ve come back to Catherine in the night.”

“Oh, darling, you have come back, haven’t you?”

“Yes.”

“I love you so and it’s been awful. You won’t go away?”

“No. I’ll always come back.”

“Oh, I love you so. Please put your hand there again.”

“It’s not been away.” I turned her so I could see her face when I kissed her and I saw that her eyes were shut. I kissed both her shut eyes. I thought she was probably a little crazy. It was all right if she was. I did not care what I was getting into. This was better than going every evening to the house for officers where the girls climbed all over you and put your cap on backward as a sign of affection between their trips upstairs with brother officers. I knew I did not love Catherine Barkley nor had any idea of loving her. This was a game, like bridge, in which you said things instead of playing cards. Like bridge you had to pretend you were playing for money or playing for some stakes. Nobody had mentioned what the stakes were. It was all right with me.

“I wish there was some place we could go,” I said. I was experiencing the masculine difficulty of making love very long standing up.

“There isn’t any place,” she said. She came back from wherever she had been.

“We might sit there just for a little while.” We sat on the flat stone bench and I held Catherine Barkley’s hand. She would not let me put my arm around her.

“Are you very tired?” she asked.

“No.” She looked down at the grass.

“This is a rotten game we play, isn’t it?”

“What game?”

“Don’t be dull.”

“I’m not, on purpose.”

“You’re a nice boy,” she said. “And you play it as well as you know how. But it’s a rotten game.”

“Do you always know what people think?”

“Not always. But I do with you. You don’t have to pretend you love me. That’s over for the evening. Is there anything you’d like to talk about?”

“But I do love you.”

“Please let’s not lie when we don’t have to. I had a very fine little show and I’m all right now. You see I’m not mad and I’m not gone off. It’s only a little sometimes.” I pressed her hand, “Dear Catherine.”

“It sounds very funny now—Catherine. You don’t pronounce it very much alike. But you’re very nice. You’re a very good boy.”

“That’s what the priest said.”

“Yes, you’re very good. And you will come and see me?”

“Of course.”

“And you don’t have to say you love me. That’s all over for a while.” She stood up and put out her hand. “Good-night.” I wanted to kiss her.

“No,” she said. “I’m awfully tired.”

“Kiss me, though,” I said.

“I’m awfully tired, darling.”

“Kiss me.”

“Do you want to very much?”

“Yes.” We kissed and she broke away suddenly. “No. Good-night, please, darling.” We walked to the door and I saw her go in and down the hall. I liked to watch her move. She went on down the hall. I went on home. It was a hot night and there was a good deal going on up in the mountains. I watched the flashes on San Gabriele. I stopped in front of the Villa Rossa. The shutters were up but it was still going on inside. Somebody was singing. I went on home. Rinaldi came in while I was undressing.

“Ah, ha!” he said. “It does not go so well. Baby is puzzled.”

“Where have you been?”

“At the Villa Rossa. It was very edifying, baby. We all sang. Where have you been?”

“Calling on the British.”

“Thank God I did not become involved with the British.” I came back the next afternoon from our first mountain post and stopped the car at the smistimento where the wounded and sick were sorted by their papers and the papers marked for the different hospitals. I had been driving and I sat in the car and the driver took the papers in. It was a hot day and the sky was very bright and blue and the road was white and dusty. I sat in the high seat of the Fiat and thought about nothing. A regiment went by in the road and I watched them pass. The men were hot and sweating. Some wore their steel helmets but most of them carried them slung from their packs. Most of the helmets were too big and came down almost over the ears of the men who wore them. The officers all wore helmets; better-fitting helmets. It was half of the brigata Basilicata. I identified them by their red and white striped collar mark. There were stragglers going by long after the regiment had passed—men who could not keep up with their platoons. They were sweaty, dusty and tired. Some looked pretty bad. A soldier came along after the last of the stragglers. He was walking with a limp. He stopped and sat down beside the road. I got down and went over.

“What’s the matter?” He looked at me, then stood up.

“I’m going on.”

“What’s the trouble?”

“—— the war.”

“What’s wrong with your leg?”

“It’s not my leg. I got a rupture.”

“Why don’t you ride with the transport?” I asked. “Why don’t you go to the hospital?”

“They won’t let me. The lieutenant said I slipped the truss on purpose.”

“Let me feel it.”

“It’s way out.”

“Which side is it on?”

“Here.” I felt it.

“Cough,” I said.

“I’m afraid it will make it bigger. It’s twice as big as it was this morning.”

“Sit down,” I said. “As soon as I get the papers on these wounded I’ll take you along the road and drop you with your medical officers.”

“He’ll say I did it on purpose.”

“They can’t do anything,” I said. “It’s not a wound. You’ve had it before, haven’t you?”

“But I lost the truss.”

“They’ll send you to a hospital.”

“Can’t I stay here, Tenente?”

“No, I haven’t any papers for you.” The driver came out of the door with the papers for the wounded in the car.

“Four for 105. Two for 132,” he said. They were hospitals beyond the river.

“You drive,” I said. I helped the soldier with the rupture up on the seat with us.

“You speak English?” he asked.

“Sure.”

“How you like this goddam war?”

“Rotten.”

“I say it’s rotten. Jesus Christ, I say it’s rotten.”

“Were you in the States?”

“Sure. In Pittsburg. I knew you was an American.”

“Don’t I talk Italian good enough?”

“I knew you was an American all right.”

“Another American,” said the driver in Italian looking at the hernia man.

“Listen, lootenant. Do you have to take me to that regiment?”

“Yes.”

“Because the captain doctor knew I had this rupture. I threw away the goddam truss so it would get bad and I wouldn’t have to go to the line again.”

“I see.”

“Couldn’t you take me no place else?”

“If it was closer to the front I could take you to a first medical post. But back here you’ve got to have papers.”

“If I go back they’ll make me get operated on and then they’ll put me in the line all the time.” I thought it over.

“You wouldn’t want to go in the line all the time, would you?” he asked.

“No.”

“Jesus Christ, ain’t this a goddam war?”

“Listen,” I said. “You get out and fall down by the road and get a bump on your head and I’ll pick you up on our way back and take you to a hospital. We’ll stop by the road here, Aldo.” We stopped at the side of the road. I helped him down.

“I’ll be right here, lieutenant,” he said.

“So long,” I said. We went on and passed the regiment about a mile ahead, then crossed the river, cloudy with snow-water and running fast through the spiles of the bridge, to ride along the road across the plain and deliver the wounded at the two hospitals. I drove coming back and went fast with the empty car to find the man from Pittsburg. First we passed the regiment, hotter and slower than ever: then the stragglers. Then we saw a horse ambulance stopped by the road. Two men were lifting the hernia man to put him in. They had come back for him. He shook his head at me. His helmet was off and his forehead was bleeding below the hair line. His nose was skinned and there was dust on the bloody patch and dust in his hair.

“Look at the bump, lieutenant!” he shouted. “Nothing to do. They come back for me.” When I got back to the villa it was five o’clock and I went out where we washed the cars, to take a shower. Then I made out my report in my room, sitting in my trousers and an undershirt in front of the open window. In two days the offensive was to start and I would go with the cars to Plava. It was a long time since I had written to the States and I knew I should write but I had let it go so long that it was almost impossible to write now. There was nothing to write about. I sent a couple of army Zona di Guerra post-cards, crossing out everything except, I am well. That should handle them. Those post-cards would be very fine in America; strange and mysterious. This was a strange and mysterious war zone but I supposed it was quite well run and grim compared to other wars with the Austrians. The Austrian army was created to give Napoleon victories; any Napoleon. I wished we had a Napoleon, but instead we had Il Generale Cadorna, fat and prosperous, and Vittorio Emmanuele, the tiny man with the long thin neck and the goat beard. Over on the right they had the Duke of Aosta. Maybe he was too good-looking to be a great general but he looked like a man. Lots of them would have liked him to be king. He looked like a king. He was the King’s uncle and commanded the third army. We were in the second army. There were some British batteries up with the third army. I had met two gunners from that lot, in Milan. They were very nice and we had a big evening. They were big and shy and embarrassed and very appreciative together of anything that happened. I wish that I was with the British. It would have been much simpler. Still I would probably have been killed. Not in this ambulance business. Yes, even in the ambulance business. British ambulance drivers were killed sometimes. Well, I knew I would not be killed. Not in this war. It did not have anything to do with me. It seemed no more dangerous to me myself than war in the movies. I wished to God it was over though. Maybe it would finish this summer. Maybe the Austrians would crack. They had always cracked in other wars. What was the matter with this war? Everybody said the French were through. Rinaldi said that the French had mutinied and troops marched on Paris. I asked him what happened and he said, “Oh, they stopped them.” I wanted to go to Austria without war. I wanted to go to the Black Forest. I wanted to go to the Hartz Mountains. Where were the Hartz Mountains anyway? They were fighting in the Carpathians. I did not want to go there anyway. It might be good though. I could go to Spain if there was no war. The sun was going down and the day was cooling off. After supper I would go and see Catherine Barkley. I wished she were here now.

“Kiss me.”

“Do you want to very much?”

“Yes.” We kissed and she broke away suddenly. “No. Good-night, please, darling.” We walked to the door and I saw her go in and down the hall. I liked to watch her move. She went on down the hall. I went on home. It was a hot night and there was a good deal going on up in the mountains. I watched the flashes on San Gabriele. I stopped in front of the Villa Rossa. The shutters were up but it was still going on inside. Somebody was singing. I went on home. Rinaldi came in while I was undressing.

“Ah, ha!” he said. “It does not go so well. Baby is puzzled.”

“Where have you been?”

“At the Villa Rossa. It was very edifying, baby. We all sang. Where have you been?”

“Calling on the British.”

“Thank God I did not become involved with the British.” I came back the next afternoon from our first mountain post and stopped the car at the smistimento where the wounded and sick were sorted by their papers and the papers marked for the different hospitals. I had been driving and I sat in the car and the driver took the papers in. It was a hot day and the sky was very bright and blue and the road was white and dusty. I sat in the high seat of the Fiat and thought about nothing. A regiment went by in the road and I watched them pass. The men were hot and sweating. Some wore their steel helmets but most of them carried them slung from their packs. Most of the helmets were too big and came down almost over the ears of the men who wore them. The officers all wore helmets; better-fitting helmets. It was half of the brigata Basilicata. I identified them by their red and white striped collar mark. There were stragglers going by long after the regiment had passed—men who could not keep up with their platoons. They were sweaty, dusty and tired. Some looked pretty bad. A soldier came along after the last of the stragglers. He was walking with a limp. He stopped and sat down beside the road. I got down and went over.

“What’s the matter?” He looked at me, then stood up.

“I’m going on.”

“What’s the trouble?”

“—— the war.”

“What’s wrong with your leg?”

“It’s not my leg. I got a rupture.”

“Why don’t you ride with the transport?” I asked. “Why don’t you go to the hospital?”

“They won’t let me. The lieutenant said I slipped the truss on purpose.”

“Let me feel it.”

“It’s way out.”

“Which side is it on?”

“Here.” I felt it.

“Cough,” I said.

“I’m afraid it will make it bigger. It’s twice as big as it was this morning.”

“Sit down,” I said. “As soon as I get the papers on these wounded I’ll take you along the road and drop you with your medical officers.”

“He’ll say I did it on purpose.”

“They can’t do anything,” I said. “It’s not a wound. You’ve had it before, haven’t you?”

“But I lost the truss.”

“They’ll send you to a hospital.”

“Can’t I stay here, Tenente?”

“No, I haven’t any papers for you.” The driver came out of the door with the papers for the wounded in the car.

“Four for 105. Two for 132,” he said. They were hospitals beyond the river.

“You drive,” I said. I helped the soldier with the rupture up on the seat with us.

“You speak English?” he asked.

“Sure.”

“How you like this goddam war?”

“Rotten.”

“I say it’s rotten. Jesus Christ, I say it’s rotten.”

“Were you in the States?”

“Sure. In Pittsburg. I knew you was an American.”

“Don’t I talk Italian good enough?”

“I knew you was an American all right.”

“Another American,” said the driver in Italian looking at the hernia man.

“Listen, lootenant. Do you have to take me to that regiment?”

“Yes.”

“Because the captain doctor knew I had this rupture. I threw away the goddam truss so it would get bad and I wouldn’t have to go to the line again.”

“I see.”

“Couldn’t you take me no place else?”

“If it was closer to the front I could take you to a first medical post. But back here you’ve got to have papers.”

“If I go back they’ll make me get operated on and then they’ll put me in the line all the time.” I thought it over.

“You wouldn’t want to go in the line all the time, would you?” he asked.

“No.”

“Jesus Christ, ain’t this a goddam war?”

“Listen,” I said. “You get out and fall down by the road and get a bump on your head and I’ll pick you up on our way back and take you to a hospital. We’ll stop by the road here, Aldo.” We stopped at the side of the road. I helped him down.

“I’ll be right here, lieutenant,” he said.

“So long,” I said. We went on and passed the regiment about a mile ahead, then crossed the river, cloudy with snow-water and running fast through the spiles of the bridge, to ride along the road across the plain and deliver the wounded at the two hospitals. I drove coming back and went fast with the empty car to find the man from Pittsburg. First we passed the regiment, hotter and slower than ever: then the stragglers. Then we saw a horse ambulance stopped by the road. Two men were lifting the hernia man to put him in. They had come back for him. He shook his head at me. His helmet was off and his forehead was bleeding below the hair line. His nose was skinned and there was dust on the bloody patch and dust in his hair.

“Look at the bump, lieutenant!” he shouted. “Nothing to do. They come back for me.” When I got back to the villa it was five o’clock and I went out where we washed the cars, to take a shower. Then I made out my report in my room, sitting in my trousers and an undershirt in front of the open window. In two days the offensive was to start and I would go with the cars to Plava. It was a long time since I had written to the States and I knew I should write but I had let it go so long that it was almost impossible to write now. There was nothing to write about. I sent a couple of army Zona di Guerra post-cards, crossing out everything except, I am well. That should handle them. Those post-cards would be very fine in America; strange and mysterious. This was a strange and mysterious war zone but I supposed it was quite well run and grim compared to other wars with the Austrians. The Austrian army was created to give Napoleon victories; any Napoleon. I wished we had a Napoleon, but instead we had Il Generale Cadorna, fat and prosperous, and Vittorio Emmanuele, the tiny man with the long thin neck and the goat beard. Over on the right they had the Duke of Aosta. Maybe he was too good-looking to be a great general but he looked like a man. Lots of them would have liked him to be king. He looked like a king. He was the King’s uncle and commanded the third army. We were in the second army. There were some British batteries up with the third army. I had met two gunners from that lot, in Milan. They were very nice and we had a big evening. They were big and shy and embarrassed and very appreciative together of anything that happened. I wish that I was with the British. It would have been much simpler. Still I would probably have been killed. Not in this ambulance business. Yes, even in the ambulance business. British ambulance drivers were killed sometimes. Well, I knew I would not be killed. Not in this war. It did not have anything to do with me. It seemed no more dangerous to me myself than war in the movies. I wished to God it was over though. Maybe it would finish this summer. Maybe the Austrians would crack. They had always cracked in other wars. What was the matter with this war? Everybody said the French were through. Rinaldi said that the French had mutinied and troops marched on Paris. I asked him what happened and he said, “Oh, they stopped them.” I wanted to go to Austria without war. I wanted to go to the Black Forest. I wanted to go to the Hartz Mountains. Where were the Hartz Mountains anyway? They were fighting in the Carpathians. I did not want to go there anyway. It might be good though. I could go to Spain if there was no war. The sun was going down and the day was cooling off. After supper I would go and see Catherine Barkley. I wished she were here now.

The train was late and Jim stood on the platform with his hands in his pockets and watched the tracks where they went off into the cedars. It was hot and there was no wind. The station agent had come out twice to look down the line and had gone back inside. There were two milk cans by the freight door and a dog asleep in the shade of them. Jim walked to the end of the platform and back. Then he sat down on the bench and waited.

He heard the train before he saw it. It came around the bend slowly, the engine black and hot-looking, and stopped with the cars banging together all down the line. A woman got off with a basket and then a man in a straw hat and then nobody. Jim stood up. Then his cousin came down the steps of the last car carrying a leather bag and a coat over his arm. He stood on the platform and looked around at the station and the water tower and the road going up the hill into town. He did not see Jim at first.

"Will," Jim said.

His cousin turned. "Hello, Jim."

"Hello."

They shook hands. Will's hand was dry and thin. He was thinner all over than Jim remembered and his face was brown and there were lines at the corners of his eyes. He wore a gray suit that had been a good suit once.

"You look fine," Jim said.

"I'm all right. You look fine too."

"I'm fat."

"No. You look fine."

"Give me the bag."

"I can carry it."

"Give it here."

Will gave him the bag and they walked around the side of the station to where the car was. The dog woke up and watched them and then put his head down again.

"Is this the same car?"

"No. That one's gone. This is a Ford."

"It looks like the same car."

"They all look like the same car."

Jim put the bag in the back and they got in. The seat was hot from the sun. Jim started the motor and they went up the hill and through the town. Will looked at everything. They passed the bank and the hardware store and the place where the hotel had been.

"What happened to the hotel?"

"It burned. Three winters ago."

"Was anybody hurt?"

"No. It was empty. Nobody stays there in the winter."

"Nobody stayed there in the summer either."

"Some people did."

"I remember it was full of old women in rocking chairs."

"They're all dead now," Jim said. "Or they go some place else."

They went out of town on the lake road. It was gravel and the car made a dust behind them that hung in the air because there was no wind. The fields were brown on one side and on the other side there were the woods and through the trees you could see the lake, very blue and flat. Will rolled down his window and put his arm out.

"It smells the same," he said.

"What does?"

"All of it. The road. The trees. It smells exactly the same."

"It ought to. Nothing's changed much."

"The hotel burned."

"That's about all."

They drove along the road and did not talk. Jim thought about how long it had been. It had been eleven years. Will had gone to Chicago and then to the war and after the war he had stayed in France. He had written letters at first, mostly to his father, and then not so many. Then he had written from Spain. Then nothing for a long time. Then the letter last month that said he was coming home to see about the cottage.

"How was the boat?" Jim asked.

"Long. It was all right."

"Were you sick?"

"The second day. Everybody was sick the second day."

"I've never been on a boat."

"You've been on a boat. We were on boats all the time."

"I mean a real boat. On the ocean."

"It's just bigger," Will said. "It's not much different."

They turned off the road onto the two ruts that went down through the woods to the point. The branches scraped on the sides of the car. Then they came out of the trees and there was the cottage with the lake behind it and the dock going out into the water. The cottage was gray and the screens on the porch were rusted. The grass had grown long around it.

Jim stopped the car and they sat there.

"It's smaller," Will said.

"Everybody says that."

"It is, though."

"You were smaller then too."

"I know it." Will opened the door and got out. He stood looking at the cottage. Then he walked down to the edge of the water and stood there with his hands in his pockets. Jim got the bag out of the back and carried it up on the porch. The door stuck and he had to push it with his shoulder. Inside it was hot and close and smelled of mice and old wood and the lake. He opened the windows. Then he went out again. Will was still standing by the water.

"You want to swim?" Jim called.

"Sure."

"There are suits inside. I don't know if they fit."

"I don't need a suit."

"Nobody's going to see. There's nobody on this side now."

They undressed on the dock and dove in. The water was very cold at first and then it was fine. Jim came up and shook the water out of his eyes and saw Will swimming out with a long slow stroke, his head going down into the water and coming up. He swam well. He had always swum well. Jim swam out after him and they lay on their backs in the deep water and looked up at the sky. It was very high and blue with no clouds in it.

"This is the best water in the world," Will said.

"You've been everywhere. You ought to know."

"I haven't been everywhere. But it's the best water."

"What about the ocean?"

"The ocean's no good. It's salt and it makes your eyes sting. This is good water."

They swam back in and climbed up on the dock and lay on the hot boards in the sun. Jim could feel the sun drying the water on his back. He lay with his face on his arm and smelled the wet wood. After a while Will sat up.

"Are there still perch off the end?"

"There were last week."

"Have you got rods?"

"They're in the shed. Your father's rods are in there too."

Will did not say anything. Then he said, "Let's catch some for supper."

"All right."

They put their clothes on and Jim went up to the shed behind the cottage and got the rods and the minnow pail. Will's father's rods were on the wall where they had always been. They were split bamboo and there were three of them. Jim took down the short steel rod he used himself and one of the bamboo rods and carried them down. Will looked at the bamboo rod but did not say anything about it. He took it and looked at the guides and the reel and worked the reel with his thumb.

"It needs oil," he said.

"There's oil in the shed."

"It's all right. It'll work."

Jim took the pail and went in to the shallows by the reeds and seined some minnows with the little net. They were very small and silver and they went around and around in the pail. Then they went out on the end of the dock and baited up and dropped the lines down along the piling where the weeds were. The sun was getting lower now and the water was very still. You could see down a long way. The minnows went down kicking and then you could not see them.

"Your mother wrote me," Will said. "When it happened."

"I know. She said she did."

"I got it in Madrid. It was two months old when I got it."

"That's what she thought would happen."

"I wired. I don't know if the wire came."

"It came."

"I couldn't have got here anyway. Not in time."

"No," Jim said. "Nobody thought you could."

Jim's line tightened and he struck and felt the fish. He brought it up. It was a good perch, yellow and green with the dark bars down the sides, and he took it off the hook and put it on the stringer and dropped the stringer over the side. He baited up again.

"Who was there?" Will asked.

"Everybody. Your father had a lot of friends."

"I know he did."

"The whole town came. Old Mr. Pruitt from the mill gave a talk."

"Was it a good talk?"

"It was long."

Will laughed. Then he stopped laughing. "He always gave long talks."

"He talked about the time your father went through the ice. Out by the island."

"I remember that."

"He told it different than your father used to."

"Everybody told it different."

"He made it sound like your father was a hero."

"He wasn't, though. He was just cold."

"That's what I thought," Jim said. "But it was a good talk anyway."

Will got a strike and missed it. He reeled in and the minnow was gone. He put on another minnow and dropped it down again. He watched the line where it went into the water.

"Where is he?" he said.

"Up on the hill. By your mother."

"Is there a stone?"

"Yes. My father saw to it."

"I'll pay him for it."

"You don't have to."

"I'll pay him."

"All right," Jim said. "You can talk to him about it."

They fished until the sun was down behind the trees on the far shore and the lake was red and then gray. They caught eleven perch. Will caught four of them on his father's rod and he caught them well, not hurrying, letting them take it and then striking hard. When the light was gone they pulled up the stringer and carried the fish up to the cottage and Jim cleaned them on the board by the pump while Will lit the lamps and started a fire in the stove. Jim could hear him in the kitchen opening the cupboards and shutting them.

"There's nothing in here," Will called.

"I brought things. They're in the box by the door."

Will found the box. There was bread and butter and potatoes and a can of coffee and a bottle of whiskey that Jim had got in town from a man he knew.

"Where'd you get this?"

"From a man."

"Is it any good?"

"It's not bad. It's Canadian. It comes across the lake."

"I'll bet it does."

Will cut up the potatoes and fried them in the big iron pan and Jim rolled the fish in meal and fried them in another pan. The kitchen got very hot and full of smoke and the smell of the fish. They ate at the table on the porch with the lamp between them and the moths beating against the screen. The fish were very good. The meat was white and sweet and came off the bones in long flakes. They ate all of them and all the potatoes and most of the bread. Then Jim got two glasses and poured the whiskey and they put water in it from the pump and sat back.

"That was a good supper," Will said.

"It was all right."

"It was a hell of a good supper."

"The fish were good."

"I haven't had a perch in eleven years."

"They have fish over there."

"They have fish. They don't have perch." Will drank some of the whiskey. "They have good fish, though. In Spain they have a fish they cook with garlic in a clay dish. It comes to the table still bubbling."

"Is it good?"

"It's very good. You'd like it."

"I don't know if I would."

"You'd like it."

The lake was black now and there was no moon yet. You could hear the water moving very softly against the stones on the shore. Far off across the lake there was a light, and then it went out.

"Is that the Henshaw place?" Will asked.

"No. The Henshaws sold. That's somebody from Detroit."

"Everybody's from Detroit now."

"Pretty near."

"Is that who's going to buy this?"

Jim did not answer for a while. He turned his glass around on the table. "There's a man who wants it. He's from Grand Rapids. He came out in June and looked at it."

"What did he say?"

"He said it was a nice point. He said he'd tear the cottage down and build a new one."

"He'd tear it down?"

"He said it was too old to fix."

"It's not too old."

"The sills are rotten on the lake side. And the roof's bad."

Will looked at the screen where the moths were. "It's not too old," he said.

"It's pretty old."

"We could fix the sills."

"We could," Jim said. "Who'd live in it?"

Will did not say anything. He finished his drink and Jim poured him another one and poured one for himself.

"How's Ruth?" Jim asked. He had been waiting to ask it all day.

"She's fine. I guess she's fine."

"You guess?"

"She's in Paris. I haven't seen her since spring."

"Your letter didn't say."

"There wasn't any reason to put it in a letter."

"No," Jim said. "I suppose there wasn't."

"It didn't work out, that's all. Nobody did anything. It just didn't work out."

"That happens."

"It happens all the time over there. It's nothing over there. Everybody's divorced."

"Are you divorced?"

"Not yet. We will be."

Jim drank his whiskey. He thought about Ruth. He had never seen her. There had been a photograph once that Will's father had kept on the bureau, of a dark girl in a white dress standing in front of a fountain. She had looked very pretty in the photograph. She had looked like a girl who would laugh a lot.

"Your father liked her picture," Jim said.

"Did he?"

"He kept it on the bureau. He showed it to people."

"I didn't know that."

"He showed it to everybody. He'd say, that's my son's wife, she's French."

"She's not French. She's from Baltimore."

"He said she was French."

Will laughed and then he put his hand over his eyes and sat that way for a while. Jim looked out at the lake. He did not look at his cousin. He sat and drank his whiskey and listened to the water on the stones and after a while Will took his hand down and picked up his glass.

"This is good whiskey," he said.

"It's not bad."

"It's good. You can tell them that in Canada."

"I'll tell them."

The moon came up then over the trees behind the cottage and they could see it on the water, a long yellow road going out across the lake. It was very bright. They could see the dock and the end of the point and the island far out, black against the water.

"Do you remember when we swam to the island?" Will said.

"Sure."

"How old were we?"

"I was twelve. You were thirteen."

"Your mother was crazy."

"She whipped me."

"My father didn't whip me. He wanted to know how long it took."

"Did you tell him?"

"I told him an hour. It wasn't an hour. It was more."

"It was a lot more," Jim said. "I thought I was going to drown."

"You didn't, though."

"No. I didn't."

"I could still do it," Will said.

"I don't think I could."

"Sure you could. We'll do it tomorrow."

"You're crazy."

"Tomorrow morning. Early, when it's flat. We'll take the boat out alongside to be safe."

"Who'll row the boat?"

"We'll get somebody."

"There's nobody out here."

"Then we'll go without the boat."

Jim looked at him. Will was looking out at the island and the moon was on his face. He looked young in the moonlight. He looked about thirteen.

"All right," Jim said. "If it's flat."

"It'll be flat. It's always flat in the morning."

"Not always."

"It'll be flat tomorrow," Will said.

They finished the whiskey that was in their glasses and did not pour any more. Then Jim got up and went in and made up the two beds in the back room where they had slept when they were boys. The blankets smelled of camphor and he shook them out the window. When he came back out on the porch Will was standing at the screen door looking at the lake.

"I'll have to tell him about Grand Rapids," Will said. "The man."

"You don't have to tell him anything tonight."

"No. I know. I'll write him next week."

"There's no hurry."

"I know there isn't."

"He can wait. He's not going anywhere."

"No," Will said. "I guess he's not." He opened the screen door and went out and stood on the steps. Jim went out and stood beside him. The air was cool now and smelled of the pines and the water. There were a great many stars. They stood there a while and did not say anything. Then Will said he was going to bed and went in, and Jim heard him in the back room taking off his shoes and dropping them one at a time on the floor. Jim stayed on the steps. He was not sleepy. He sat down and looked at the island. It did not seem very far. In the morning, if it was flat, they would swim to it, and it would be cold at first and then it would be fine, and then they would have to see about the sills.

Here is an excerpt of Ernest Hemingway's writing, to show you their style:

I was away for two days at the posts. When I got home it was too late and I did not see Miss Barkley until the next evening. She was not in the garden and I had to wait in the office of the hospital until she came down. There were many marble busts on painted wooden pillars along the walls of the room they used for an office. The hall too, that the office opened on, was lined with them. They had the complete marble quality of all looking alike. Sculpture had always seemed a dull business—still, bronzes looked like something. But marble busts all looked like a cemetery. There was one fine cemetery though—the one at Pisa. Genoa was the place to see the bad marbles. This had been the villa of a very wealthy German and the busts must have cost him plenty. I wondered who had done them and how much he got. I tried to make out whether they were members of the family or what; but they were all uniformly classical. You could not tell anything about them. I sat on a chair and held my cap. We were supposed to wear steel helmets even in Gorizia but they were uncomfortable and too bloody theatrical in a town where the civilian inhabitants had not been evacuated. I wore one when we went up to the posts and carried an English gas mask. We were just beginning to get some of them. They were a real mask. Also we were required to wear an automatic pistol; even doctors and sanitary officers. I felt it against the back of the chair. You were liable to arrest if you did not have one worn in plain sight. Rinaldi carried a holster stuffed with toilet paper. I wore a real one and felt like a gunman until I practised firing it. It was an Astra 7.65 caliber with a short barrel and it jumped so sharply when you let it off that there was no question of hitting anything. I practised with it, holding below the target and trying to master the jerk of the ridiculous short barrel until I could hit within a yard of where I aimed at twenty paces and then the ridiculousness of carrying a pistol at all came over me and I soon forgot it and carried it flopping against the small of my back with no feeling at all except a vague sort of shame when I met English-speaking people. I sat now in the chair and an orderly of some sort looked at me disapprovingly from behind a desk while I looked at the marble floor, the pillars with the marble busts, and the frescoes on the wall and waited for Miss Barkley. The frescoes were not bad. Any frescoes were good when they started to peel and flake off. I saw Catherine Barkley coming down the hall, and stood up. She did not seem tall walking toward me but she looked very lovely.

“Good-evening, Mr. Henry,” she said.

“How do you do?” I said. The orderly was listening behind the desk.

“Shall we sit here or go out in the garden?”

“Let’s go out. It’s much cooler.” I walked behind her out into the garden, the orderly looking after us. When we were out on the gravel drive she said, “Where have you been?”

“I’ve been out on post.”

“You couldn’t have sent me a note?”

“No,” I said. “Not very well. I thought I was coming back.”

“You ought to have let me know, darling.” We were off the driveway, walking under the trees. I took her hands, then stopped and kissed her.

“Isn’t there anywhere we can go?”

“No,” she said. “We have to just walk here. You’ve been away a long time.”

“This is the third day. But I’m back now.” She looked at me, “And you do love me?”

“Yes.”

“You did say you loved me, didn’t you?”

“Yes,” I lied. “I love you.” I had not said it before.

“And you call me Catherine?”

“Catherine.” We walked on a way and were stopped under a tree.

“Say, ‘I’ve come back to Catherine in the night.’ ” “I’ve come back to Catherine in the night.”

“Oh, darling, you have come back, haven’t you?”

“Yes.”

“I love you so and it’s been awful. You won’t go away?”

“No. I’ll always come back.”

“Oh, I love you so. Please put your hand there again.”

“It’s not been away.” I turned her so I could see her face when I kissed her and I saw that her eyes were shut. I kissed both her shut eyes. I thought she was probably a little crazy. It was all right if she was. I did not care what I was getting into. This was better than going every evening to the house for officers where the girls climbed all over you and put your cap on backward as a sign of affection between their trips upstairs with brother officers. I knew I did not love Catherine Barkley nor had any idea of loving her. This was a game, like bridge, in which you said things instead of playing cards. Like bridge you had to pretend you were playing for money or playing for some stakes. Nobody had mentioned what the stakes were. It was all right with me.

“I wish there was some place we could go,” I said. I was experiencing the masculine difficulty of making love very long standing up.

“There isn’t any place,” she said. She came back from wherever she had been.

“We might sit there just for a little while.” We sat on the flat stone bench and I held Catherine Barkley’s hand. She would not let me put my arm around her.

“Are you very tired?” she asked.

“No.” She looked down at the grass.

“This is a rotten game we play, isn’t it?”

“What game?”

“Don’t be dull.”

“I’m not, on purpose.”

“You’re a nice boy,” she said. “And you play it as well as you know how. But it’s a rotten game.”

“Do you always know what people think?”

“Not always. But I do with you. You don’t have to pretend you love me. That’s over for the evening. Is there anything you’d like to talk about?”

“But I do love you.”

“Please let’s not lie when we don’t have to. I had a very fine little show and I’m all right now. You see I’m not mad and I’m not gone off. It’s only a little sometimes.” I pressed her hand, “Dear Catherine.”

“It sounds very funny now—Catherine. You don’t pronounce it very much alike. But you’re very nice. You’re a very good boy.”

“That’s what the priest said.”

“Yes, you’re very good. And you will come and see me?”

“Of course.”

The father came up from the dock in the late afternoon. He had been working on the boat all day, scraping the old paint off the bottom where it had blistered, and his hands were stiff and smelled of turpentine. He washed them in the basin on the bench by the door and dried them on the towel that hung on the nail. Then he went inside to get the rod.

The cabin was cool and dark after the sun on the water. It was one room with two cots and the stove and a table under the window, and the rods were kept on the pegs over the door to the back. There were three rods. Two were steel rods that he used for trolling. The third was a split-bamboo rod he had bought in Chicago the year before the war. It was eight and a half feet long and it was in a cloth case and the cloth case was in an aluminum tube with a cap that screwed on. He had fished it in Michigan and in Wyoming and once in Spain, on the Irati, and it was the only thing he owned that he cared about very much. He took the tube down and unscrewed the cap and slid the cloth case out and untied the strings.

The tip section was broken. It had been broken about four inches from the top and someone had wound it with black thread, around and around, very tight, so that the two pieces held together at an angle. The thread was knotted many times at the end. He held it up to the window and looked at it. The bamboo had split along the grain below the break and the thread did not reach the split. He turned it in the light. Then he put it back in the cloth case and tied the strings and put the case back in the tube and screwed the cap on. He hung the tube on the pegs. He went out and sat on the step.

The sun was low over the far side of the lake and the water was flat and there was no wind. Out past the point the fish were starting to rise. He could see the rings spreading on the smooth water where they came up. It would be a good evening. It was the first good evening in a week. He sat on the step and watched the rings and did not get up.

The boy came along the shore from the point. He was carrying a lard pail and walking carefully so the water would not slop out of it. He was seven and he was brown from the summer and his hair was almost white from it. He wore an old pair of his father's khaki shorts that his mother had cut down and pinned at the waist. He came up the path from the beach and stopped in front of the step and held up the pail.

"Look," he said. "I got eleven."

The father looked into the pail. There were crayfish in it, backing into each other in the brown water, their claws up.

"That's a lot," he said.

"I got them under the rocks off the point. You have to come up behind them. If you come up in front they go backward and you can't ever get them."

"That's right."

"Can we use them for bait?"

"Maybe. Put them in the shade."

The boy set the pail down in the shade of the cabin, by the woodpile. He crouched and looked into it. Then he came back and stood by the step.

"Aren't you going fishing?" he asked. "They're rising out there. I saw them from the point."

"I know."

"Aren't you going?"

"Sit down a minute," the father said.

The boy sat down on the step. He sat on the far end of it, near the post. He looked out at the water.

"Somebody broke my rod," the father said.

The boy did not say anything. He watched the water.

"The bamboo rod. The one in the tube. Somebody broke the tip and wrapped it up with thread and put it back."

"Maybe it was broken before."

"No. It wasn't broken before."

"Maybe it broke in the tube."

"Rods don't break in the tube. That's what the tube is for."

The boy picked at a scab on his knee. He did not look at his father.

"Maybe a porcupine got in," he said. "Mr. Garner said a porcupine got in his shed and ate the handle off his axe. They like the salt from your hands."

"Did a porcupine wind it up with thread?"

The boy did not answer. Out on the lake a fish came up, a big one, and the sound of it carried across the flat water. They both heard it. Neither of them looked.

"Where did you get the thread?" the father asked.

"I don't know."

"It's your mother's thread. It's out of her sewing box. The black spool."

"I don't know."

The father sat and looked at the lake. He did not want to look at the boy. He knew that if he looked at the boy now it would go badly. He waited. It was very quiet. A kingfisher went along the shore low over the water, rattling, and lit on the dead branch of the cedar that leaned out past the dock, and sat there.

"I'm going to ask you one more time," the father said. "Then I'm not going to ask you anymore."

The boy pulled the scab off. A small bead of blood came up on his knee. He looked at it.

"I only wanted to try it," he said.

"All right."

"I only wanted to try it once. You never let me try it. I was just going to try it off the dock and put it back. I wasn't going to take it anywhere."

"When?"

"Tuesday. When you went to town with Mr. Garner."

"What happened?"

"I put it together like you do. And I put the reel on. And I went out on the dock and I tried to cast like you do and it went back and hit the post." He was talking fast now. "It hit the post when it went back. I didn't see the post. And it made a noise and the top was hanging down."

"So you fixed it."

"I tried to fix it."

"And then you put it back."

"Yes."

"And you didn't tell me."

"No."

"And then when I asked you, you told me it was broken before. And then you told me it broke in the tube. And then you told me about the porcupine."

The boy began to cry. He did not cry loudly. He put his head down on his knees and his shoulders moved and he made no sound at all for a while and then he made a small sound. The father sat and let him cry. He thought about putting his hand on the boy's back and he did not do it. He did not want to do it yet. He sat and looked at the water where the fish were rising, more of them now, all along the edge of the weeds past the point, and the light was going yellow and then orange on the water, and it was the best part of the evening, and he sat on the step.

When the boy stopped crying the father said, "Look at me."

The boy lifted his head. His face was wet and dirty where he had wiped it with his hands.

"I'm not angry about the rod," the father said.

The boy looked at him. He did not believe it.

"I'm angry about the rod some," the father said. "It was a good rod. It was the best rod I ever had. It came from a long way off and I can't get another one like it. But that's not what I'm talking about. A rod is only a rod. Things break. You broke it and that's bad but it's not the worst."

"I'm sorry."

"I know you're sorry. Listen to me. You lied to me three times. You lied to me about it being broken before, and about the tube, and about the porcupine. And before that you lied when you put it back and didn't say anything. That's four times."

"I didn't say anything when I put it back."

"That's a lie too. Not saying is a lie when you know a thing and the other person doesn't. You knew it and I didn't. That's a lie."

The boy wiped his nose on his arm.

"If you had come and told me on Tuesday," the father said, "I'd have been sore. I'd have been sore all right. But it would be over. It would be all over by now. We'd have fixed it or not fixed it and it would be done. Now it isn't done."

"Are you going to whip me?"

The father did not answer right away. When he was a boy his own father had kept a razor strop on a hook behind the bathroom door. It was a heavy strop of brown leather, polished on one side and rough on the other, and it had a ring at the top, and his father had used the rough side. His father had used it for lying more than for anything else. He had used it for other things too. The father remembered standing in the bathroom with his trousers down and his hands on the edge of the tub, and the smell of his father's shaving soap, and how the porcelain was cold under his hands, and how afterward his father would always go out on the back porch alone and stand there for a long time. He had not understood that then. He had not understood it until he was older. He had not liked his father very much for a long time and then later he had liked him better, and then his father was dead.

"No," he said. "I'm not going to whip you."

The boy looked at him.

"You're going to go inside," the father said. "You're going to go inside and lie on your cot. You're not going to have any supper. You're going to stay there until I come in. You can think about it or you can go to sleep. I don't care which."

"It's not even dark."

"I know it's not dark."

"Can I take the crayfish in?"

"No. Leave them."

"They'll die."

"They won't die. They're in the shade. Go on."

The boy stood up. He stood a moment on the step as if he would say something more, and then he did not say it, and he went in. The screen door banged behind him on its spring. The father heard the cot creak inside. Then there was nothing.

He sat on the step. The sun was down now behind the hemlocks on the far shore and the sky over the trees was very clear and the water had gone from orange to a kind of gray that still held the light. The fish were feeding everywhere. They were feeding along the weed beds and out in the open water and right off the end of the dock, and you could hear them come up, the soft sound and sometimes the hard slap of a big one. He could have taken one of the steel rods and gone out in the boat with a fly on it. It would have worked well enough. The fish were not particular tonight. He sat and did not do it.

He thought about the boy on the dock with the rod. He could see it very well. He could see the boy putting the sections together the way he had watched it done, lining up the guides, squinting down them, and fitting the reel into the seat, and threading the line through. He had probably missed one of the guides. He would have stood on the end of the dock with his feet apart and brought the rod back hard, the way a boy would, all arm and no wrist, and the post was right there. The father could hear the sound it made. It was a small sound. Bamboo did not make much of a sound.

Then the boy would have stood there holding it with the tip hanging. He would have looked around to see if anyone saw. There was no one. Then he would have gone in and gotten the thread out of his mother's box and sat on the floor and wound it. He would have worked a long time on that. He would have done it very carefully and tied all those knots, one on top of the other, and then he would have looked at it and known it was no good. And then he had put it back in the case and tied the strings and put it in the tube and screwed the cap on and hung it on the pegs exactly where it went. And then for four days he had gone around knowing it was there.

The father thought about the four days. He thought about the boy at supper on Tuesday and Wednesday and last night, eating his supper and talking about the crayfish and the loon that had come into the bay, and all the while the rod up there on the pegs over the door. He thought about the boy looking at it in the morning when he woke. The boy slept on the cot nearest the door. He would have seen it every morning when he opened his eyes.

It was dark now. The fish were still rising but he could not see them anymore. He could only hear them. A loon called from down the lake, the long call, and then another answered from farther off. The mosquitoes had come out and he slapped at them and then he got up and went down to the shore and stood there. The water was black and very still and the stars were coming out in it. He stood there a while and smoked a cigarette. Then he threw it in the water and went back up the path.

He picked up the lard pail and carried it down and set it in the shallows at the edge of the beach so the water would come up over the rim and keep it fresh. Then he went into the cabin.

He lit the lamp on the table. The boy was lying on his cot with his face to the wall. He had not taken his shorts off and he was lying on top of the blanket. The father could tell from his breathing that he was not asleep.

The father took the tube down from the pegs and unscrewed the cap and took the cloth case out and untied it. He laid the tip section on the table under the lamp. He got his knife out of his pocket and opened the small blade and began to cut the thread away. It took a long time. The boy had wound it very tight and there were many knots. He cut it carefully so as not to cut into the bamboo. When he had it all off he laid the two pieces side by side on the table and looked at them.

The cot creaked. He did not look around.

"Is it ruined?" the boy said.

"I don't know yet."

"Can you fix it?"

"Come here and look."

The boy got up off the cot and came over to the table. He stood beside his father's chair. He stood a little way off.

"Come closer. You can't see from there."

The boy came closer. The father showed him with the point of the knife.

"It broke here," he said. "That's a clean break. If that was all it would be all right. You can put a ferrule on that, or you can splice it and wrap it and varnish it, and it'll fish. It won't be the same but it'll fish. But see here? It split up here along the grain. That's the bad part."

"Is that from when I wound it?"

"No. That's from when it hit the post."

"Oh."

"Your winding was all right. You wound it pretty tight. You just didn't go far enough."

The boy looked at the two pieces of bamboo under the lamp.

"Can you still fix it?"

"I think so. I'll have to cut it back below the split. It'll be shorter. It'll be shorter and stiffer at the top and it won't cast the same. But I think it'll fish."

"I'm sorry I broke it."

"I know."

"I'm sorry I said about the porcupine."

"I know you are."

The boy stood there. He was close enough now that the father could feel the warmth of him through his shirt. The lamp hissed a little. Outside the loons were still calling.

"Are you still angry?"

"Some."

"How long will you be angry?"

"Not very long."

"Tomorrow?"

"No. Not tomorrow."

The boy put his hand on the edge of the table near the bamboo. He did not touch it.

"Are you hungry?" the father asked.

"Yes."

"There's bread in the box. You can have some bread and some of the milk. Then you go to bed."

The boy went to the bread box and got the end of the loaf out and tore a piece off. He poured milk from the jar into a cup and sat down on the other chair at the table and ate the bread and drank the milk and watched his father. The father had gotten the little bottle of varnish and the spool of silk winding thread out of the tackle box. He laid them on the table. He did not start yet. He sat and looked at the broken tip under the lamp and turned it in his fingers.

"Can I watch you fix it?" the boy said.

"Not tonight. I'm not going to fix it tonight. I have to think about where to cut it."

"Tomorrow?"

"Maybe tomorrow."

"Can I watch tomorrow?"

"Yes. You can watch tomorrow."

The boy finished the milk and put the cup down. He sat there.

"Go on to bed," the father said. "Take your shorts off this time."

The boy went to the cot and took off his shorts and got under the blanket. The father heard him turn over twice and then lie still.

"The crayfish," the boy said in the dark.

"I put them in the lake. In the pail. They'll be all right."

"They won't get out?"

"No. They won't get out."

"We can use them tomorrow."

"Yes."

After a while the boy's breathing changed and the father knew he was asleep. He sat at the table with the bamboo in front of him. He sat there a long time. Then he put the tip back in the cloth case with the other sections and tied the strings and slid it into the tube, and did not screw the cap on, and laid the tube on the table where he would see it in the morning. He turned down the lamp. He went out and sat on the step in the dark. The fish had stopped rising. The lake was quiet and the stars were all out in it and it was cool now. He sat there for a long time before he went in.
