The train came down out of the low hills a little after four o'clock, and for the last hour Ruth Thorne had not opened her book. She sat with her gloves in her lap and watched the country slide past the window, flat and tawny and shining, with the stubble fields running off on either side until they met the sky in a long, unbroken line. The wheat had been cut and stacked a month since. Here and there a threshing outfit stood idle at the edge of a field, the separator throwing a long blue shadow across the ground, and the men who had worked it lay asleep in the shade of the straw-pile, their hats over their faces. The corn was tall and dark and very still. Nothing moved in all that wide land but the train, and a hawk, and once a boy on a gray horse who rode along the section line for a quarter of a mile, keeping even with the engine, and then fell behind and waved his hat.

It had been twenty-two years. She had counted them over at Omaha, the night before, sitting on the edge of a hotel bed with her hair down, and the number had seemed to her both too large and too small. She had been eighteen when she left, a tall, thin girl with a braid down her back and a trunk full of drawings that her grandmother had tied up with binding twine. She was forty now, and her hair was put up in the fashion of women who live in cities and have no one to please but themselves, and her drawings had been printed in magazines that people read on trains like this one. She had not been unhappy in those years. She had worked very hard, and work, when one is young and has some talent, is a kind of happiness that leaves no room for asking whether it is happiness at all.

The town of Wayland rose up out of the plain all at once, as such towns do: first the grain elevator, red and narrow against the sky, then the water tower, then the cottonwoods along the creek, and then the low roofs huddled about the depot as if for company. The engine slowed, and the bell rang, and Ruth stood up and took down her bag before the porter could come for it. She was afraid, suddenly, that she would not know anyone; and then she was afraid that she would.

There was only one person on the platform who was not a railroad man or a loafer, and Ruth knew her at once, though she had been fifteen when they last saw each other. Signe Halvorsen—Signe Lund, she was now—stood at the end of the platform with her hands folded over the handle of a black umbrella, which she carried against the sun. She was a large woman, broad through the shoulders and deep in the bosom, and her face was brown and creased about the eyes. She wore a gray print dress and a straw hat with a band of black ribbon, and she did not wave or call out, but stood quite still and watched the cars until Ruth stepped down. Then she came forward with her slow, heavy walk, and for a moment the two women stood and looked at each other without speaking.

"Well," said Signe at last. "You've got thin, Ruthie."

"I was always thin."

"Not so thin as this." Signe took her hand and held it, turning it a little, as if she were looking at a piece of goods in a store. Her own hand was hard and warm and very strong. "You don't eat right. I knew you wouldn't. I said to Emil, she won't have eaten right in all them years, living in rooms."

Ruth laughed, and found that her eyes had filled. It was the voice that undid her. Signe's voice had not changed at all; it was the same low, unhurried voice, with the Norwegian lift at the ends of the sentences that their grandmother had given to all her grandchildren, and that Ruth had lost long ago in classrooms and offices in the East. She had not known until this moment that she had missed it.

"You look exactly the same," she said, which was not true.

"I look like an old woman," said Signe placidly. "I've had seven children and buried one. Come, the team don't like the engine."

The spring wagon stood behind the depot, and two bay horses were tied to the hitch-rail, stamping and switching at the flies. Signe untied them herself and climbed up over the wheel with a briskness that surprised Ruth, and took the lines in her brown hands. When they had turned out of the town and were going north along the section road, with the dust rising up behind them in a long, pale plume, she let the horses walk and sat back on the seat.

"Emil wanted to come," she said, "but he's got the hay down in the bottom field and it looked like rain this morning. He said you'd understand."

"Of course I understand."

"I told him you would. I told him Ruthie was raised on a farm, the same as me, she knows hay won't wait for company."

The road ran straight before them for miles, between fields of corn so high that the wagon moved along it as through a green corridor. Overhead the sky was enormous and cloudless, and the light had begun to turn from white to gold. Ruth had forgotten that light. She had tried, in the first years in Chicago, to put it into her pictures, and had never succeeded; and after a while she had stopped trying, and had drawn what was in front of her—streets and rooftops and women in the park—and had done well enough. But she had never forgotten that there was something she could not do.

"Is the old place still standing?" she asked.

Signe shook her head. "Peterson bought it after Grandmother died. He tore down the house and put up a new one, frame, with a porch all round. The sod barn fell in by itself. You can still see where it was, though. The grass grows different."

"And the plum thicket? Down by the draw?"

"That's there. Nobody ever cleared the draw. The plums are getting ripe now. I'll take you if you want to go."

They talked of the family then, as the horses walked on—of Uncle Knut, who had gone to Oregon and done well in timber, and of Aunt Bertha, who had died of the influenza the winter before last, and of all the cousins, scattered now from Minnesota to California, whose children Ruth had never seen. Signe knew everything about everyone. She had kept up a correspondence with the whole family for twenty years, writing her letters at the kitchen table on Sunday afternoons in a round, careful hand, and in her mind all of them were still gathered in one place, as they had been once at Grandmother's at Christmas. Ruth listened, and asked questions, and was ashamed to find how much she had let go.

"You never wrote to anybody but me," Signe said, not reproachfully. "And not so often to me, after the first."

"I know. I meant to. There was always so much to do."

"I expect there was." Signe looked out over the corn. "I used to read your letters to Mother. She'd say, that girl will be somebody. She was proud of you. She used to cut your pictures out of the magazines when Mrs. Fenton was done with them, and paste them in a book. I've got the book yet."

Ruth could not answer. She had not known this. Her Aunt Inga had been a silent, heavy woman who spoke very little English and seemed to Ruth, as a girl, to disapprove of her; she had thought of her, when she thought of her at all, as one of the forces she had been obliged to escape.

The Lund farm lay on a rise of ground above a little creek, with a windbreak of box-elders and ash on the north and west, and a white house with green shutters set well back from the road. As they turned in at the gate, a crowd of children came running down the lane to meet them, barefoot and brown and tow-headed, the smallest ones holding on to the hands of the larger. They stopped a little way off and stared at Ruth with frank, serious eyes, and when their mother told them to say good evening to their cousin, they said it all together, like a school recitation, and then ran away laughing toward the barn.

"They're shy," Signe said. "They never saw a lady from the city before. They'll be all over you by tomorrow."

Emil Lund came up from the hayfield at sundown. He was a tall, spare man, a good deal older than his wife, with pale blue eyes and a long mustache faded almost white by the sun, and he shook Ruth's hand gravely and said he was glad she had come at last, Signe had talked of nothing else since spring. Then he went out to wash at the pump, and did not say much more through supper, but sat at the head of the table and ate steadily and watched his wife and her cousin with an expression of quiet satisfaction, as if he had arranged their meeting himself.

It was a long supper. There was fried chicken and new potatoes and green beans cooked with bacon, and sliced tomatoes, and cucumbers in vinegar, and bread that Signe had baked that morning, and three kinds of preserves, and a custard pie. The children ate with silent concentration, and the older girls got up and down to fill the plates and the coffee cups without being told. The lamp was lit before they had finished, and the moths came in through the screen door and beat themselves against the chimney, and outside the frogs had begun to sing down along the creek. Ruth ate more than she had eaten at one sitting in years, and Signe watched her with approval and pressed her to take more.

When the dishes were done and the younger children had been put to bed, Signe took off her apron and hung it on the nail behind the door. "Now," she said, "we'll go and see about them plums."

They went out together through the yard and past the barn, where the horses moved and breathed in the darkness, and down across the pasture toward the draw. The moon had come up, very large and yellow, out of the cornfields to the east, and it laid a soft light over everything, so that the pasture grass looked silver and the cattle lying in it were like gray stones. The air was warm and smelled of hay and of the earth cooling after the heat of the day. Signe walked ahead, holding up her skirt a little in one hand, and Ruth followed in the path she made.

The draw lay along the north boundary of the farm and ran on across Peterson's land and the land beyond it, a shallow, winding ravine where the water ran in spring and dried away to nothing by midsummer. The plum thicket grew along its sides in a dark, tangled mass, and as they came near, Ruth could smell the fruit, a sweet, heavy, almost winy smell that she had not smelled since she was a child. She stopped, and stood quite still, and Signe came back and stood beside her.

"It's the same," Ruth said. "It's exactly the same."

"Things don't change so much out here. Only people."

They went down among the bushes and picked the plums by moonlight, feeling for them among the leaves; they were small and red and very ripe, and some of them burst in the fingers. Signe had brought a tin pail, and she filled it while Ruth ate the plums one after another, spitting the stones into the grass as she had done at ten years old. Then they sat down together on the bank of the draw, where the grass was short and dry, and looked out over the long, shining country under the moon.

"Do you remember," said Signe, after a while, "the day we got lost?"

Ruth remembered. They had been eleven and eight, and they had followed the draw to see where it went, and had walked all one hot afternoon, eating plums and wild grapes and talking, until the sun went down and they did not know where they were. There had been no houses anywhere, only the grass and the sky, and the coyotes had begun to call. Signe had cried, and Ruth had not, because she was the elder and had to be brave; and they had sat down in the grass and held each other's hands, and Ruth had told her stories until Uncle Nils found them a little before midnight, riding along the draw with a lantern and calling their names.

"You told me about the princess who lived in the glass mountain," Signe said. "I never forgot it. I tell it to my children yet. They think I made it up."

"I think I made it up."

"Well, then. It's yours. They like it better than anything."

They were quiet for a time. The frogs sang, and somewhere far off a dog barked and was answered by another, and the sound came to them very thin and clear across the miles. Ruth drew her knees up and clasped them in her arms, as she used to do when she was a girl.

"Are you happy, Signe?" she asked, and was surprised at herself, for it was not a question she had meant to ask.

Signe did not answer at once. She sat looking out over the pasture, her large hands folded in her lap, her face calm and grave in the moonlight. When she spoke, it was slowly, as if she were thinking it over for the first time.

"I don't know as I ever thought about it," she said. "There's always been so much to do. When I married Emil, I didn't know him very well. Mother wanted it; he had the land, and he was a good man, everybody said so. And he is a good man. He's never said a hard word to me in twenty years. We've had bad times—the dry years, and when we lost little Karl—but we've got through them. The children are healthy. The land is paid for." She stopped. "I used to think about you, though. When I was young. I used to think about you in the city, going to the theater, and wearing nice clothes, and drawing your pictures. I used to wish I'd gone too."

"I wish you had," Ruth said. "I wish you'd come with me."

"No." Signe shook her head. "I wouldn't have been any good there. I can't draw, nor do anything. I'd have been a hired girl in somebody's kitchen. I'm better off here. It's only sometimes, in the evening, when the work's done—" She did not finish.

Ruth knew what she meant. There is an hour at the end of the day, in every life, when the work is done and the hands are idle, and the heart goes out of its own accord toward the things it did not choose. Ruth had known that hour in rented rooms, with the noise of the street coming up through the window and the lamps lighting one by one in the windows across the way; she had known it in galleries and concert halls, sitting among strangers; and she knew now, sitting on the bank of the draw with her cousin beside her, that it was the same hour everywhere, and that no choice anyone could make would spare them from it.

"And you?" said Signe. "You've done what you wanted. Are you happy?"

Ruth laughed a little. "I've done what I wanted," she said. "I don't know that it's the same thing. I've been lonely, sometimes. More than you'd think. I have friends, and I have my work, and I'm grateful for both. But there's nobody who remembers me when I was little. Nobody who knew Grandmother, or the old sod house, or this." She put out her hand and touched the grass. "When I'm gone, there'll be nobody to tell my stories to their children."

Signe turned and looked at her. "There's me," she said simply. "There's always been me."

They sat a long while after that, not talking. The moon climbed higher and grew smaller and whiter, and the shadows of the plum bushes drew in close about their roots. A little wind came up out of the south and moved over the corn with a long, dry, whispering sound, like breathing; and Ruth thought that she had never heard anything so old, or so patient. The land had been here before her grandmother came across the sea in a crowded ship, before the sod house was built, before any of them were born; it would be here when they were all forgotten. It asked nothing of them. It had given them what it could—bread and plums and hard work and the sky—and it would take them back when they were done, without grief and without remembrance. And yet it seemed to Ruth that something of them would remain in it: in the draw where two little girls had once been lost, in the grass that grew differently where the barn had stood, in the story of the glass mountain that would go on being told on winter nights in a white farmhouse long after the woman who had first told it was dead.

At last Signe stirred, and got heavily to her feet, and picked up the pail of plums.

"Come," she said. "It's getting late, and you've had a long day. And Emil will be wanting his sleep."

Ruth rose and shook out her skirt, and they went back together across the pasture, the moon lighting their way, the cattle lifting their heads to watch them pass. At the gate of the barnyard Signe stopped and took her cousin's hand again, holding it in her own hard, warm one, as she had done on the station platform.

"I'm glad you came, Ruthie," she said. "I was afraid you never would."

"So was I," said Ruth.

The lamp was still burning in the kitchen window, and its light lay across the dark yard in a long, yellow bar. They walked into it side by side, and up the steps, and went in.

The Halvorsen farm lay on the high land north of the river, where the country began to roll in long, slow swells like the sea, and where in summer the wind never quite stopped blowing. The house was a frame one, painted white the year before, and it stood a little apart from the sod barn and the windmill, as if it were not yet sure it belonged there. Behind it the cornfields ran up over the rise and out of sight. In front, the pasture sloped down to a dry draw where a few box-elders grew, and beyond the draw was the Pavelka place, a dugout in a clay bank, with a stovepipe sticking up out of the ground and a great many children who were forever running in and out of the door.

It was the middle of August, and the whole country had turned the color of a lion. The wheat was in the stack, and the corn had tasseled and stood very still in the heat of the afternoons, rustling only when the wind came up toward evening. The sunflowers along the section lines were taller than a man, and their heavy faces all turned the same way, following the sun across the sky with a kind of patient devotion. There was something solemn about the land at that season. It seemed to be waiting for something, though nobody could have said what.

Mrs. Halvorsen was a tall woman with smooth fair hair which she wore braided and pinned close about her head, and grey eyes that were very steady. She had come out from Norway as a girl of nineteen to marry a man she had known only as a boy in her father's parish, and she had been eleven years on the Divide. In that time she had buried one child in the little graveyard by the Lutheran church and raised three others. She was not a woman who talked much, and the neighbors thought her proud. She kept her kitchen as clean as a ship's deck, and on Sundays she read aloud from a Norwegian Bible with a cracked leather cover, and her voice when she read was different from her everyday voice, lower and more musical, so that her children, who did not always follow the words, liked to listen to it as they liked to listen to the wind in the cottonwoods.

The youngest of the children was a girl of seven, named Kristine, though no one called her anything but Tina. She was a sturdy little thing, brown as a hazelnut from running about bareheaded, with her mother's grey eyes and a stubborn, square chin that came from her father's side. She had two older brothers, Nils and Peder, who worked in the fields with their father now and had no time for her, and so she had made her own life that summer, and most of it was spent across the draw with the Pavelka children, who were Bohemians and spoke a language she did not understand at first, though by August she could swear in it very creditably.

On the morning of which I am speaking, Mrs. Halvorsen had driven to town with her husband to sell butter and eggs, and Tina had been left at home in the care of her brothers, who were cutting hay in the bottom and did not come up to the house until noon. She had the whole morning to herself. She swept the kitchen, as she had been told, and fed the chickens, and then she went into her mother's room, where she was not supposed to go.

There was a tin box on the shelf above the bed, painted black with red roses on the lid. In it Mrs. Halvorsen kept her marriage lines, and some letters from Norway tied with a blue ribbon, and a lock of hair from the child who had died, and a brooch. The brooch was of old silver, wrought in a pattern of twisted leaves, with little silver discs hanging from it that trembled and chimed when it was moved. It had belonged to Mrs. Halvorsen's grandmother, and to her grandmother before that, and it had been worn by every bride in the family for more than a hundred years. Mrs. Halvorsen had worn it on her wedding day, in the church at home, and she had not worn it since. Once a year, on Christmas Eve, she took it out of the box and let the children look at it in the lamplight, and told them where it came from, and then put it away again.

Tina had been thinking about that brooch for a long while. The Pavelka girls had a string of red glass beads which their aunt had sent them from Chicago, and they wore it by turns and were very vain of it, and Tina had nothing at all to set against it. She stood on the bed and took down the box and opened it. The brooch lay on its bed of faded velvet, and when she lifted it the little discs rang together like far-off bells. She pinned it to the front of her calico dress, where it looked very grand indeed, and she ran out of the house and down through the pasture, holding it steady with one hand so that it would not bounce.

The Pavelka girls were properly impressed. They turned it over and over and held it up to the light and made Tina tell them three times where it had come from. Then they all went down to the draw to play, and climbed in the box-elders, and chased a jack rabbit, and rolled down the clay bank, and waded in the one green pool that was left in the creek bed, and when the sun was already low and red over the cornfields, Tina looked down at the front of her dress and saw that the brooch was gone.

They hunted for it until the light failed. They went back over every foot of ground they could remember having crossed. The Pavelka children, who were good-hearted, crawled through the tall grass on their hands and knees, calling out to one another in Bohemian, and the smallest one cried because Tina was crying. But the grass on the slopes of the draw was as high as their shoulders and as thick as fur, and the brooch was no larger than a silver dollar, and at last old Mrs. Pavelka came out of the dugout and shouted for her children to come to supper, and Tina went home alone across the darkening pasture.

The lamp was lit in the kitchen when she came up to the house. Her mother was standing at the stove with her back to the door, and her father and the boys were already at the table. Nobody said anything when she came in. Tina knew at once, from the quiet, that her mother had been to the tin box.

Mrs. Halvorsen did not turn around. She dished up the potatoes and set them on the table, and poured the coffee, and then she said, without raising her voice, "Sit down and eat your supper, Kristine."

It was the use of her whole name that frightened Tina more than anything. She sat down and tried to eat, but the food stuck in her throat. Her father looked at her once from under his heavy eyebrows and then looked at his plate. Her brothers ate fast and kept their eyes down, and as soon as they had finished they went out to see to the horses, and their father went with them. The screen door banged behind them, and Tina was left alone with her mother.

Mrs. Halvorsen cleared the table and put the dishes in the pan. Then she dried her hands carefully on the roller towel and came and sat down across the table from her daughter, folding her hands in front of her. The lamp stood between them, and Tina could see her mother's face very plainly in its light. It was not an angry face. That was the worst of it. It was quiet and grave and a little pale, and there was something in the set of the mouth that Tina had never seen there before and did not understand.

"Where is it?" Mrs. Halvorsen asked.

Tina opened her mouth, and nothing came out of it. She looked down at the oilcloth, which had a pattern of blue squares, and began to count them.

"Look at me, Kristine."

Tina looked up.

"I asked you where it is."

"I lost it," said Tina, in a voice so small she hardly heard it herself. "Down in the draw. We looked and looked. We looked till it was dark."

Her mother was silent for a long moment. Outside, the windmill creaked as the evening wind turned it, and somewhere far off a coyote began to yelp, and then another answered it, and then they were still.

"Did I ever tell you that you might go to that box?"

"No, Mother."

"Did I ever tell you that you might not?"

Tina hung her head. "Yes, Mother."

"Then you knew. You knew, and you went to it anyway, and you took the one thing in it that was not yours nor mine nor anybody's to take." Mrs. Halvorsen spoke slowly, choosing her English words with care, as she always did when she was moved. "That was my grandmother's. She wore it in the church at Opdal when she was married, and her mother before her, and I wore it, and some day you would have worn it. It was not a thing for playing. It was not a thing to show off to the Bohemian children so they would think you were somebody. It was like the church bell at home, or the names in the Bible. It was a thing that belonged to all of us together, the ones that are living and the ones that are dead. Do you understand what I am telling you?"

Tina did not altogether understand, but she nodded, because she understood enough to be ashamed. The tears had begun to run down her face again, and she let them run, not daring to wipe them away.

"You think I am angry because it was silver," her mother went on, "because it was worth money. It is not that. If you had lost a silver dollar I would be angry, yes, but I would get over it. This is another thing." She stopped, and looked away from Tina toward the black window, where the lamp was reflected, and her own face with it. "When I came to this country I brought very little with me. One trunk. My mother packed it. She put in my wedding dress and my good shoes and some linen she had woven herself, and she put in that brooch, wrapped in a handkerchief, and she said to me, 'Now you will be a long way off, and you will not see any of us again, but you will have this, and when you look at it you will know where you come from.' And that was true. I did not see her again. She died the second winter I was out here, and I did not hear of it till spring."

Tina had never heard her mother speak of these things. She had never thought of her mother as having had a mother of her own, or as ever having been young, or as having come from anywhere at all. Her mother was simply there, like the house and the windmill and the sky. She stared at her now through her tears as though she were looking at a stranger.

"There are not many things out here," Mrs. Halvorsen said, "that are old. Everything is new. The house is new, and the fences, and the roads, and the churches. Even the people are new. Nobody has been here long enough to have a grandmother buried in the ground. So when you have something that is old, something that has come down a long way to you, you must hold on to it. You must hold on to it with both hands. Because if you do not, there will be nothing to show that you ever came from anywhere, and you will be like the tumbleweeds that blow across the fields in the fall and fetch up against the fences and do not belong to any place."

She was silent again. Then she said, in a different voice, harder and more ordinary, "You have done a very wrong thing, Kristine. You have done a thing that cannot be undone, maybe. You have disobeyed me, and you have taken what was not yours, and you have been careless with it because you were thinking only of yourself. I am not going to whip you. You are too old for that to do any good, and besides, I think you are sorry. But I want you to remember this night. I want you to remember it all your life."

Tina put her head down on her arms on the oilcloth and sobbed as though her heart would break. Her mother let her cry. She sat without moving, her hands still folded on the table, and waited until the sobbing had worn itself out into hiccups and sniffles. Then she got up and took the lantern down from its nail beside the door and lit it.

"Get your shawl," she said. "We will go and look."

They went out together into the night. The wind had fallen, as it often did after sundown, and the air was soft and warm and smelled of dust and ripe grass and the faint sweetness of the sunflowers. The moon was not yet up, but the sky was thick with stars, more stars than Tina had ever noticed before, crowding down to the very edge of the land on every side. The lantern made a small yellow world around their feet, and beyond it the pasture stretched away into darkness, grey and silver where the starlight caught the tops of the grass.

They went down to the draw by the path Tina had taken that morning. Her mother walked ahead, holding the lantern low and moving it slowly from side to side, and Tina followed close behind her, holding onto a fold of her mother's skirt as she had not done since she was very small. Neither of them spoke. Now and then Mrs. Halvorsen stopped and bent down and parted the grass with her free hand, and Tina's heart leaped up each time, and each time it was nothing, a pebble or a bit of bleached bone or a beetle's shell.

When they reached the bottom of the draw, Mrs. Halvorsen set the lantern on a flat stone and stood looking about her. The box-elders made a black shape against the stars, and the pool in the creek bed gave back a little gleam of light. Tina pointed out the places where they had played: the tree they had climbed, the clay bank they had rolled down, the place in the grass where they had flushed the rabbit. Her mother went to each place in turn and searched it carefully, on her knees, moving her hands over the ground as if she were smoothing a sheet. Tina knelt beside her and searched too, though she could see almost nothing, and the dry grass scratched her arms and the dew was beginning to come down and soak through her dress.

They searched for a long time. The moon came up, very large and red, over the eastern edge of the world, and then grew smaller and whiter as it climbed, and the whole draw was flooded with a pale, unearthly light in which every blade of grass threw its own thin shadow. In that light the country looked older than it did by day, and lonelier, as if no one had ever lived there or ever would. Tina had never been out so late. She was cold, and her knees ached, and she was very tired, but she did not dare to say so.

At last Mrs. Halvorsen sat back on her heels and was still. Tina looked up at her. Her mother's face, in the moonlight, was turned toward the west, where the last of the afterglow had long since faded, and it was a face Tina did not know, very young and very sad and very far away. She was looking, Tina thought, at something a great distance off, farther than the cornfields and the Pavelka place and the river, farther than anything you could see from the Divide.

"It is no use," Mrs. Halvorsen said at last, quietly. "Not tonight. Maybe in the daylight. Maybe never."

Tina began to cry again, but softly this time, because she was too tired to cry hard. Her mother turned and looked at her, and something in her face changed and softened, and she put out her arm and drew the child against her side and held her there. They sat together on the damp grass with the lantern burning beside them, and the moon climbed higher, and the stars wheeled slowly over their heads.

"Well," said Mrs. Halvorsen, after a while, "the grass has it now. Maybe it is not so bad. My grandmother is in the ground at Opdal, and my mother is in the ground at Opdal, and now a little piece of them is in the ground here. Maybe that is how it is meant to be. Maybe that is how a place begins to be home."

She did not say anything more. She got up, and lifted Tina to her feet, and took up the lantern, and they went home together through the pasture, slowly, because the child was stumbling with sleep. When they reached the house, Mrs. Halvorsen undressed her and washed her scratched arms and put her to bed, and stood for a moment in the doorway looking down at her, with the lamp in her hand. Then she went out, and Tina heard her moving about in the kitchen, and then heard the creak of the bedroom door, and the scrape of the tin box being set back on its shelf, and then nothing more.

The brooch was never found. Peder searched for it with a rake the next day, and the Pavelka children searched for it for a week, and in the fall, when the grass was burned off the draw, Mr. Halvorsen walked over every inch of the blackened ground. But whether a crow had carried it off, or a gopher had dragged it down into its burrow, or it had simply sunk into the soft earth by the creek and been covered over, nobody ever knew. Mrs. Halvorsen did not speak of it again, and after a time the children forgot to wonder.

Tina did not forget. She grew up and went away, as the children of that country nearly all did. She went to the university at Lincoln, and afterward to teach school in Omaha, and afterward farther east still, and she married and had children of her own, and lived for many years in a city where the only sky she saw was a narrow strip of grey between tall buildings. Her mother lived to be very old, and died on the farm, and was buried in the graveyard by the Lutheran church, beside the child who had died so long ago.

When Tina went home for the funeral, it was August again. After the service, while the neighbors were gathered in the house, she slipped away by herself and walked down through the pasture to the draw. The Pavelka dugout had long since fallen in, and there was a frame house on the place now, and a grove of trees, and a red barn. But the draw itself was hardly changed. The box-elders were taller, and the creek was dry, and the grass was as high and thick and tawny as it had been fifty years before.

She stood there a long while, with the hot wind blowing in her face. She understood now, as she had not understood that night, what her mother had been trying to tell her. It was not only the brooch that had been lost in the grass. It was the whole old world her mother had come from: the church at Opdal, and the mountains, and the fjords, and the dead grandmothers, and the language of the cracked Bible. All of it had gone down into this ground, little by little, and had been covered over, and the ground had kept it. And out of it, without anybody quite meaning it to, something new had grown, something that belonged to this country and to no other, and that she herself, standing there with the tears drying on her face, was a part of.

It seemed to her then that her mother had been right about everything, and that she had known it all along. When at last she turned and went back up the slope toward the house, she did not look back. She did not need to. She knew where the brooch was. It was where it had always been meant to be.

Here is an excerpt of Willa Cather's writing, to show you their style:

Bergson had spent his first five years on the Divide getting into debt, and the last six getting out. He had paid off his mortgages and had ended pretty much where he began, with the land. He owned exactly six hundred and forty acres of what stretched outside his door; his own original homestead and timber claim, making three hundred and twenty acres, and the half-section adjoining, the homestead of a younger brother who had given up the fight, gone back to Chicago to work in a fancy bakery and distinguish himself in a Swedish athletic club. So far John had not attempted to cultivate the second half-section, but used it for pasture land, and one of his sons rode herd there in open weather. John Bergson had the Old-World belief that land, in itself, is desirable. But this land was an enigma. It was like a horse that no one knows how to break to harness, that runs wild and kicks things to pieces. He had an idea that no one understood how to farm it properly, and this he often discussed with Alexandra. Their neighbors, certainly, knew even less about farming than he did. Many of them had never worked on a farm until they took up their homesteads. They had been handwerkers at home; tailors, locksmiths, joiners, cigar-makers, etc. Bergson himself had worked in a shipyard. For weeks, John Bergson had been thinking about these things. His bed stood in the sitting-room, next to the kitchen. Through the day, while the baking and washing and ironing were going on, the father lay and looked up at the roof beams that he himself had hewn, or out at the cattle in the corral. He counted the cattle over and over. It diverted him to speculate as to how much weight each of the steers would probably put on by spring. He often called his daughter in to talk to her about this. Before Alexandra was twelve years old she had begun to be a help to him, and as she grew older he had come to depend more and more upon her resourcefulness and good judgment. His boys were willing enough to work, but when he talked with them they usually irritated him. It was Alexandra who read the papers and followed the markets, and who learned by the mistakes of their neighbors. It was Alexandra who could always tell about what it had cost to fatten each steer, and who could guess the weight of a hog before it went on the scales closer than John Bergson himself. Lou and Oscar were industrious, but he could never teach them to use their heads about their work. Alexandra, her father often said to himself, was like her grandfather; which was his way of saying that she was intelligent. John Bergson’s father had been a shipbuilder, a man of considerable force and of some fortune. Late in life he married a second time, a Stockholm woman of questionable character, much younger than he, who goaded him into every sort of extravagance. On the shipbuilder’s part, this marriage was an infatuation, the despairing folly of a powerful man who cannot bear to grow old. In a few years his unprincipled wife warped the probity of a lifetime. He speculated, lost his own fortune and funds entrusted to him by poor seafaring men, and died disgraced, leaving his children nothing. But when all was said, he had come up from the sea himself, had built up a proud little business with no capital but his own skill and foresight, and had proved himself a man. In his daughter, John Bergson recognized the strength of will, and the simple direct way of thinking things out, that had characterized his father in his better days. He would much rather, of course, have seen this likeness in one of his sons, but it was not a question of choice. As he lay there day after day he had to accept the situation as it was, and to be thankful that there was one among his children to whom he could entrust the future of his family and the possibilities of his hard-won land. The winter twilight was fading. The sick man heard his wife strike a match in the kitchen, and the light of a lamp glimmered through the cracks of the door. It seemed like a light shining far away. He turned painfully in his bed and looked at his white hands, with all the work gone out of them. He was ready to give up, he felt. He did not know how it had come about, but he was quite willing to go deep under his fields and rest, where the plow could not find him. He was tired of making mistakes. He was content to leave the tangle to other hands; he thought of his Alexandra’s strong ones.

“Dotter,” he called feebly, “dotter!” He heard her quick step and saw her tall figure appear in the doorway, with the light of the lamp behind her. He felt her youth and strength, how easily she moved and stooped and lifted. But he would not have had it again if he could, not he! He knew the end too well to wish to begin again. He knew where it all went to, what it all became. His daughter came and lifted him up on his pillows. She called him by an old Swedish name that she used to call him when she was little and took his dinner to him in the shipyard.

“Tell the boys to come here, daughter. I want to speak to them.”

“They are feeding the horses, father. They have just come back from the Blue. Shall I call them?” He sighed. “No, no. Wait until they come in. Alexandra, you will have to do the best you can for your brothers. Everything will come on you.”

“I will do all I can, father.”

“Don’t let them get discouraged and go off like Uncle Otto. I want them to keep the land.”

“We will, father. We will never lose the land.” There was a sound of heavy feet in the kitchen. Alexandra went to the door and beckoned to her brothers, two strapping boys of seventeen and nineteen. They came in and stood at the foot of the bed. Their father looked at them searchingly, though it was too dark to see their faces; they were just the same boys, he told himself, he had not been mistaken in them. The square head and heavy shoulders belonged to Oscar, the elder. The younger boy was quicker, but vacillating.

“Boys,” said the father wearily, “I want you to keep the land together and to be guided by your sister. I have talked to her since I have been sick, and she knows all my wishes. I want no quarrels among my children, and so long as there is one house there must be one head. Alexandra is the oldest, and she knows my wishes. She will do the best she can. If she makes mistakes, she will not make so many as I have made. When you marry, and want a house of your own, the land will be divided fairly, according to the courts. But for the next few years you will have it hard, and you must all keep together. Alexandra will manage the best she can.” Oscar, who was usually the last to speak, replied because he was the older, “Yes, father. It would be so anyway, without your speaking. We will all work the place together.”

“And you will be guided by your sister, boys, and be good brothers to her, and good sons to your mother? That is good. And Alexandra must not work in the fields any more. There is no necessity now. Hire a man when you need help. She can make much more with her eggs and butter than the wages of a man. It was one of my mistakes that I did not find that out sooner. Try to break a little more land every year; sod corn is good for fodder. Keep turning the land, and always put up more hay than you need. Don’t grudge your mother a little time for plowing her garden and setting out fruit trees, even if it comes in a busy season. She has been a good mother to you, and she has always missed the old country.” When they went back to the kitchen the boys sat down silently at the table. Throughout the meal they looked down at their plates and did not lift their red eyes. They did not eat much, although they had been working in the cold all day, and there was a rabbit stewed in gravy for supper, and prune pies. John Bergson had married beneath him, but he had married a good housewife. Mrs. Bergson was a fair-skinned, corpulent woman, heavy and placid like her son, Oscar, but there was something comfortable about her; perhaps it was her own love of comfort. For eleven years she had worthily striven to maintain some semblance of household order amid conditions that made order very difficult. Habit was very strong with Mrs. Bergson, and her unremitting efforts to repeat the routine of her old life among new surroundings had done a great deal to keep the family from disintegrating morally and getting careless in their ways. The Bergsons had a log house, for instance, only because Mrs. Bergson would not live in a sod house. She missed the fish diet of her own country, and twice every summer she sent the boys to the river, twenty miles to the southward, to fish for channel cat. When the children were little she used to load them all into the wagon, the baby in its crib, and go fishing herself. Alexandra often said that if her mother were cast upon a desert island, she would thank God for her deliverance, make a garden, and find something to preserve. Preserving was almost a mania with Mrs. Bergson. Stout as she was, she roamed the scrubby banks of Norway Creek looking for fox grapes and goose plums, like a wild creature in search of prey. She made a yellow jam of the insipid ground-cherries that grew on the prairie, flavoring it with lemon peel; and she made a sticky dark conserve of garden tomatoes. She had experimented even with the rank buffalo-pea, and she could not see a fine bronze cluster of them without shaking her head and murmuring, “What a pity!” When there was nothing more to preserve, she began to pickle. The amount of sugar she used in these processes was sometimes a serious drain upon the family resources. She was a good mother, but she was glad when her children were old enough not to be in her way in the kitchen. She had never quite forgiven John Bergson for bringing her to the end of the earth; but, now that she was there, she wanted to be let alone to reconstruct her old life in so far as that was possible. She could still take some comfort in the world if she had bacon in the cave, glass jars on the shelves, and sheets in the press. She disapproved of all her neighbors because of their slovenly housekeeping, and the women thought her very proud. Once when Mrs. Bergson, on her way to Norway Creek, stopped to see old Mrs. Lee, the old woman hid in the haymow “for fear Mis’ Bergson would catch her barefoot.”

One Sunday afternoon in July, six months after John Bergson’s death, Carl was sitting in the doorway of the Linstrum kitchen, dreaming over an illustrated paper, when he heard the rattle of a wagon along the hill road. Looking up he recognized the Bergsons’ team, with two seats in the wagon, which meant they were off for a pleasure excursion. Oscar and Lou, on the front seat, wore their cloth hats and coats, never worn except on Sundays, and Emil, on the second seat with Alexandra, sat proudly in his new trousers, made from a pair of his father’s, and a pink-striped shirt, with a wide ruffled collar. Oscar stopped the horses and waved to Carl, who caught up his hat and ran through the melon patch to join them.

“Want to go with us?” Lou called. “We’re going to Crazy Ivar’s to buy a hammock.”

“Sure.” Carl ran up panting, and clambering over the wheel sat down beside Emil. “I’ve always wanted to see Ivar’s pond. They say it’s the biggest in all the country. Aren’t you afraid to go to Ivar’s in that new shirt, Emil? He might want it and take it right off your back.” Emil grinned. “I’d be awful scared to go,” he admitted, “if you big boys weren’t along to take care of me. Did you ever hear him howl, Carl? People say sometimes he runs about the country howling at night because he is afraid the Lord will destroy him. Mother thinks he must have done something awful wicked.” Lou looked back and winked at Carl. “What would you do, Emil, if you was out on the prairie by yourself and seen him coming?” Emil stared. “Maybe I could hide in a badger-hole,” he suggested doubtfully.

“But suppose there wasn’t any badger-hole,” Lou persisted. “Would you run?”

“No, I’d be too scared to run,” Emil admitted mournfully, twisting his fingers. “I guess I’d sit right down on the ground and say my prayers.” The big boys laughed, and Oscar brandished his whip over the broad backs of the horses.

“He wouldn’t hurt you, Emil,” said Carl persuasively. “He came to doctor our mare when she ate green corn and swelled up most as big as the water-tank. He petted her just like you do your cats. I couldn’t understand much he said, for he don’t talk any English, but he kept patting her and groaning as if he had the pain himself, and saying, ‘There now, sister, that’s easier, that’s better!’” Lou and Oscar laughed, and Emil giggled delightedly and looked up at his sister.

“I don’t think he knows anything at all about doctoring,” said Oscar scornfully. “They say when horses have distemper he takes the medicine himself, and then prays over the horses.” Alexandra spoke up. “That’s what the Crows said, but he cured their horses, all the same. Some days his mind is cloudy, like. But if you can get him on a clear day, you can learn a great deal from him. He understands animals. Didn’t I see him take the horn off the Berquist’s cow when she had torn it loose and went crazy? She was tearing all over the place, knocking herself against things. And at last she ran out on the roof of the old dugout and her legs went through and there she stuck, bellowing. Ivar came running with his white bag, and the moment he got to her she was quiet and let him saw her horn off and daub the place with tar.”

Throughout the meal they looked down at their plates and did not lift their red eyes. They did not eat much, although they had been working in the cold all day, and there was a rabbit stewed in gravy for supper, and prune pies. John Bergson had married beneath him, but he had married a good housewife. Mrs. Bergson was a fair-skinned, corpulent woman, heavy and placid like her son, Oscar, but there was something comfortable about her; perhaps it was her own love of comfort. For eleven years she had worthily striven to maintain some semblance of household order amid conditions that made order very difficult. Habit was very strong with Mrs. Bergson, and her unremitting efforts to repeat the routine of her old life among new surroundings had done a great deal to keep the family from disintegrating morally and getting careless in their ways. The Bergsons had a log house, for instance, only because Mrs. Bergson would not live in a sod house. She missed the fish diet of her own country, and twice every summer she sent the boys to the river, twenty miles to the southward, to fish for channel cat. When the children were little she used to load them all into the wagon, the baby in its crib, and go fishing herself. Alexandra often said that if her mother were cast upon a desert island, she would thank God for her deliverance, make a garden, and find something to preserve. Preserving was almost a mania with Mrs. Bergson. Stout as she was, she roamed the scrubby banks of Norway Creek looking for fox grapes and goose plums, like a wild creature in search of prey. She made a yellow jam of the insipid ground-cherries that grew on the prairie, flavoring it with lemon peel; and she made a sticky dark conserve of garden tomatoes. She had experimented even with the rank buffalo-pea, and she could not see a fine bronze cluster of them without shaking her head and murmuring, “What a pity!” When there was nothing more to preserve, she began to pickle. The amount of sugar she used in these processes was sometimes a serious drain upon the family resources. She was a good mother, but she was glad when her children were old enough not to be in her way in the kitchen. She had never quite forgiven John Bergson for bringing her to the end of the earth; but, now that she was there, she wanted to be let alone to reconstruct her old life in so far as that was possible. She could still take some comfort in the world if she had bacon in the cave, glass jars on the shelves, and sheets in the press. She disapproved of all her neighbors because of their slovenly housekeeping, and the women thought her very proud. Once when Mrs. Bergson, on her way to Norway Creek, stopped to see old Mrs. Lee, the old woman hid in the haymow “for fear Mis’ Bergson would catch her barefoot.”

One Sunday afternoon in July, six months after John Bergson’s death, Carl was sitting in the doorway of the Linstrum kitchen, dreaming over an illustrated paper, when he heard the rattle of a wagon along the hill road. Looking up he recognized the Bergsons’ team, with two seats in the wagon, which meant they were off for a pleasure excursion. Oscar and Lou, on the front seat, wore their cloth hats and coats, never worn except on Sundays, and Emil, on the second seat with Alexandra, sat proudly in his new trousers, made from a pair of his father’s, and a pink-striped shirt, with a wide ruffled collar. Oscar stopped the horses and waved to Carl, who caught up his hat and ran through the melon patch to join them.

“Want to go with us?” Lou called. “We’re going to Crazy Ivar’s to buy a hammock.”

“Sure.” Carl ran up panting, and clambering over the wheel sat down beside Emil. “I’ve always wanted to see Ivar’s pond. They say it’s the biggest in all the country. Aren’t you afraid to go to Ivar’s in that new shirt, Emil? He might want it and take it right off your back.” Emil grinned. “I’d be awful scared to go,” he admitted, “if you big boys weren’t along to take care of me. Did you ever hear him howl, Carl? People say sometimes he runs about the country howling at night because he is afraid the Lord will destroy him. Mother thinks he must have done something awful wicked.” Lou looked back and winked at Carl. “What would you do, Emil, if you was out on the prairie by yourself and seen him coming?” Emil stared. “Maybe I could hide in a badger-hole,” he suggested doubtfully.

“But suppose there wasn’t any badger-hole,” Lou persisted. “Would you run?”

“No, I’d be too scared to run,” Emil admitted mournfully, twisting his fingers. “I guess I’d sit right down on the ground and say my prayers.” The big boys laughed, and Oscar brandished his whip over the broad backs of the horses.

“He wouldn’t hurt you, Emil,” said Carl persuasively. “He came to doctor our mare when she ate green corn and swelled up most as big as the water-tank. He petted her just like you do your cats. I couldn’t understand much he said, for he don’t talk any English, but he kept patting her and groaning as if he had the pain himself, and saying, ‘There now, sister, that’s easier, that’s better!’” Lou and Oscar laughed, and Emil giggled delightedly and looked up at his sister.

“I don’t think he knows anything at all about doctoring,” said Oscar scornfully. “They say when horses have distemper he takes the medicine himself, and then prays over the horses.” Alexandra spoke up. “That’s what the Crows said, but he cured their horses, all the same. Some days his mind is cloudy, like. But if you can get him on a clear day, you can learn a great deal from him. He understands animals. Didn’t I see him take the horn off the Berquist’s cow when she had torn it loose and went crazy? She was tearing all over the place, knocking herself against things. And at last she ran out on the roof of the old dugout and her legs went through and there she stuck, bellowing. Ivar came running with his white bag, and the moment he got to her she was quiet and let him saw her horn off and daub the place with tar.”

The harvest that year had been a poor one all along the creek, and by the middle of October there was nothing left in the Vrana fields but the stubble and the dry stalks of the late corn, which rattled when the wind went through them. Joseph Vrana had cut the corn himself and shocked it in the old way, because he did not trust the new binders and did not like to be beholden to the Lindgren boys, who owned one and hired it out. He was a careful man, and slow, and he liked to have his hands on a thing before he would believe in it. He had come to Pennock County from a village in Moravia when he was twenty-two, with a featherbed, a set of carpenter's tools, and eleven dollars sewn into the lining of his coat. In the twenty years since, he had put up a frame house with a porch on two sides, a barn larger than the house, and a windmill that pumped water into a tank so clear that his wife's ducks would swim in nothing else. He had never borrowed money but once, and he had paid that back before it was due, walking eighteen miles to the bank at Pennock to do it because his team was lame.

Clara Vrana was not from the old country. She had been born in Iowa, of a family that had come out from Ohio and kept a store, and she had been a schoolteacher for three years before she married. She had taught in a sod schoolhouse four miles north of the Vrana place, and Joseph had first seen her when he went to mend the stove there one January. She was tall then, and very straight, with grey eyes and a quick way of turning her head when she was spoken to, as if she meant to take hold of whatever was said and examine it. She was still straight. Her hair had gone grey early, at the temples, and she wore it drawn back plainly, but her eyes had not changed. The neighbors' wives, who were mostly Bohemian and Swedish women, respected her and were a little afraid of her. She could write a letter to the county commissioners, or read a mortgage, or tell a woman what to do for a child with the croup; and she did these things without being asked twice, and without seeming to think much of them afterward.

They had two children. Lottie, the younger, was a fat, contented girl of nine who followed her father about the barn and talked to the calves. Rudolph was seventeen. He had his mother's eyes and his father's heavy shoulders, and he had finished the district school three years before, and since then had read every book in the county that he could borrow or beg. He kept them in a box under his bed and read them by a lantern in the hayloft, where his father had once found him at two o'clock in the morning, asleep with his cheek on an open page and the lantern still burning beside him in the dry hay. Joseph had said nothing about it at the time. He had carried the lantern down the ladder and blown it out and stood for a long while in the barn door, looking at the stars, and had gone back to bed without waking his wife.

It was Rudolph they were talking about on that October night, though neither of them had said his name yet.

The boy had gone over to the Lindgrens' to help them with a sick horse, and Lottie was asleep in the little room off the kitchen. The supper dishes were washed and put away. Clara sat at the end of the table nearest the lamp, with the account book open before her and a letter laid flat beside it. Joseph sat across from her, in his stocking feet, with his boots drying on the oven door. He had taken out his pipe, but he had not lit it. He kept turning it over in his thick fingers and looking at the bowl, as if there were something written there.

"The letter came Thursday," Clara said. "I have read it over four times. They will take him at the university in January, if he passes the examination in Latin. Professor Hale says he can tutor him through the winter by post. The board in Lincoln is three dollars and a half a week, and there is work in the library for students who need it."

Joseph nodded slowly. "I know what it says. You told me Thursday."

"You didn't say anything on Thursday."

"No." He set the pipe down on the oilcloth. "I was thinking."

"Well, you have had four days to think." She did not say it unkindly. She said it in the same voice she used to tell the children it was time to come in from the yard. But Joseph heard something under it, and he looked up at her quickly and then down again.

Outside the wind had risen. It came across the open country from the northwest, as it always did at that season, and pressed against the north wall of the house until the boards creaked. It was a lonely sound, and it had frightened Clara when she first came to live in that house; she used to lie awake and listen to it and think of all the empty miles it had come over, with nothing to stop it. She did not mind it any longer. She had come to feel that the house was strong, and that it would stand.

"Three dollars and a half a week," Joseph said at last. "And books. And clothes. He cannot go to the city in the clothes he wears to the hogs. And the railroad fare. And when he comes home summers he will not want to come home."

"That isn't the money talking."

"No," he said. "That is not the money."

She closed the account book, keeping her finger in the page. "We have the money, Joseph. You know we have it. There is four hundred dollars in the bank at Pennock, and the hogs will bring something in December, even with the price where it is. I have figured it every way. We can keep him there two years without touching the land."

"Two years. And then?"

"Then he can earn his own way. Professor Hale says there are scholarships. A boy like Rudolph will get one."

Joseph got up and went to the window. There was nothing to see there; the night was black, and the glass only gave him back the lamp and his own heavy figure and, behind it, the white of his wife's face. He stood looking at these things for some time. He was a man who could not say what he felt until he had found the plainest possible words for it, and he did not often find them. He envied his wife her readiness. When they quarreled, which was seldom, she always had her reasons laid out in order before he had got hold of the first of his, and he would end by giving way to her, not because he was persuaded, but because he could not make his own thoughts stand up and be counted.

"When I came here," he said, still looking at the window, "there was nothing on this place. Not a tree. Not a fence post. Old Svoboda had the quarter east, and he lived in a dugout in the bank of the creek with his goats, and he told me I was a fool. He said the land would break me like it broke him. He said, 'You will see, Vrana, this country is not for people. It is for the wind and the grasshoppers.' The second year the grasshoppers came, and I thought he was right. I sat on the step of my shanty and watched them eat the handles of my hoe. I thought then I would go back. I had the money for the fare. I had it counted out."

Clara had heard this story before, many times, but she did not stop him. She waited.

"I did not go back," he said. "I do not know why. Maybe I was too proud. Maybe I was only too tired to pack up my tools. But I stayed, and the next year was good, and the year after that was better, and I began to see that the land would do what you wanted if you kept at it long enough and did not ask it to hurry. Twenty years now. Every tree on this place I planted. The cottonwoods along the draw, the box elders by the house, the plum thicket. Every one." He turned around. "I thought I was doing it for him."

"You were doing it for all of us."

"For him," Joseph said stubbornly. "A man does not plant trees for himself. He will not sit in the shade of them. I thought, when I am old, the boy will have this place, and it will be a good place, the best on the creek, and he will not have to sit on the step and watch the grasshoppers eat his hoe."

Clara laid the account book down on the table and folded her hands on top of it. Her hands were large and work-roughened, with a scar across the back of the left one where she had burned it on the boiler the first winter of their marriage. She looked at them for a moment before she spoke.

"He doesn't want it, Joseph."

He made a sound in his throat, not quite a word.

"I know you know that," she went on. "You have known it longer than I have. You found him in the haymow with his books. You never told me, but Lottie did. You have seen him at the plow, how he goes along with his eyes on the sky and lets the furrow wander off every which way. He is a good boy and he works hard because you ask him to, and because he loves you. But his heart is not in it. It never will be."

"A heart is not everything. I did not have my heart in it, that second year."

"You had something. You had whatever it was that made you put the fare money back in your coat. Rudolph doesn't have that, not for this. He has it for something else." She leaned forward a little. "Do you know what he said to me last week? We were out by the windmill and the sun was going down, and he stood there looking at it for so long I thought he was sick. And then he said, 'Mother, do you suppose anybody has ever written down exactly what that looks like? So that a person in a city who had never seen it would know?' And I said I didn't know, maybe somebody had. And he said, 'I would like to try.'"

Joseph was silent. He came back to the table and sat down heavily and picked up his pipe again.

"Writing things down," he said. "Does that feed a man?"

"Sometimes it does. Not often, maybe. But that is not the question." She hesitated, and her voice changed; it became lower, and Joseph, who knew her well, looked up at her with a kind of alarm. "I was going to be something once, too. Did you ever think of that? My father had promised to send me to the normal school at Iowa City. I had my trunk packed. And then the store failed, and there was no more money, and I came out here to teach in a sod schoolhouse instead, because they would take a girl without a certificate. I don't regret it. I want you to understand me, Joseph. I don't regret one day of it. I have had a good life with you. But I know what it is to stand at a door and see it shut. I won't stand by and see it shut on him, not if I can hold it open with my two hands."

The lamp had begun to smoke a little, and she reached over and turned down the wick. In the dimmer light the kitchen seemed to grow larger and to draw away from them; the stove, the cupboard, the row of blue crocks on the shelf, all receded into shadow, and the two of them sat as if they were alone on an island of yellow light.

Joseph did not answer for a long while. He was thinking of things he had never told her, and did not know how to tell her now. He was thinking of his own father, a cooper in the village at home, who had wanted him to be a priest, and how he had run away instead and walked to Bremen to take ship. He had never written to his father after that. The old man had died the winter Lottie was born, and the letter telling of it had come six months late, and Joseph had read it standing in the barn and then put it in the stove. He had not understood until that moment that he had always meant to write, someday, when the farm was good enough that he could say to his father, "See what I have made." He had waited too long. A man always thinks there will be time.

"If he goes to the city," he said finally, "he will not come back. I know how it is. Ondrej Mares's boy went to Omaha to work in the packing houses, and he has not been home in six years. They get used to the streetcars and the electric lights and the shows. They forget how to be quiet. When they come home they look at their fathers like they were strangers, and they laugh at the way the old people talk."

"Rudolph will never laugh at you."

"Not to my face, maybe. But in his heart he will be ashamed." He said this with great difficulty, and his face, which was broad and brown and not used to showing much, worked for a moment as if he were in pain. "I am not an educated man, Clara. I do not know Latin. I write my name in the bank book, and that is all the writing I do. When he has been two years in Lincoln with the professors, what will he have to say to me?"

So that was it. Clara had known it must be something of the kind, but she had not been sure, and she felt a sudden great tenderness for her husband, sitting there across the table from her with his heavy shoulders bent and his big hands turning the cold pipe over and over. She wanted to go around the table to him, but she did not. They had never been demonstrative people. It was not the custom of the country, and it was not their custom with each other. She stayed where she was, but she spoke more gently.

"Joseph. Do you remember the night Lottie had the diphtheria?"

He nodded without looking up.

"You sat up with her three nights. I was so worn out I couldn't hold my head up, and you sent me to bed and sat by her yourself and kept the steam going. And Rudolph sat with you. He was only eight. He wouldn't go to bed. And when it was over, and she could breathe, you picked him up and carried him in to his cot, and he said to you, half asleep, 'Papa, you are the best man in the world.' I heard him. I was lying awake in the next room." She paused. "He has never stopped thinking that. Do you suppose a few books will change it? He is your son, Joseph. He has your stubbornness, and your patience, and your way of looking at a thing until he understands it. He only wants to look at different things."

The wind had let up somewhat. In the quiet they could hear the windmill turning slowly in the yard, with a long, dry creak at the top of every revolution where the bearing needed grease. Joseph had meant to see to it for a week. He listened to it now as if it were telling him something.

"The land is good now," he said, half to himself. "It is the best on the creek. It would have been easy for him. Everything I did the hard way, he could do easy."

"Maybe that is why he doesn't want it," Clara said. "Maybe a man has to do something the hard way, or it's never really his."

He looked at her then, a long, searching look, and she met it steadily. She saw in his face the struggle he was making, and she knew better than to say anything more. She had said what she had to say. The rest was his to do. She had learned, in eighteen years of marriage, that Joseph could be led a certain distance and no farther; past that point he must go on alone, at his own pace, or not at all. She took up the account book again and opened it, not because she meant to read it, but because she wanted to give him the privacy of her lowered eyes.

He sat for a long time without moving. Once he got up and put a stick of wood in the stove, though the kitchen was warm enough, and stood with his back to her, warming his hands. Once he went to the door and opened it and looked out into the dark, and a cold breath of air came in and stirred the pages of the letter on the table, and Clara put her hand on it to keep it from blowing away. Far off, across the fields, there was a light moving; it was Rudolph coming home with the Lindgrens' lantern. They both watched it, Joseph from the door and Clara from her chair, as it bobbed and swung along the section line, now hidden by a rise in the ground, now showing again, small and yellow and steady.

"He is walking fast," Joseph said. "The horse must be better."

"He'll be cold. I'll heat some milk."

She got up and went to the cupboard, and Joseph closed the door and came back to the table. He picked up the letter from the university and held it close to the lamp, moving his lips a little over the English words. He read slowly, but he read it all the way through, to the professor's name at the bottom. Then he laid it down very carefully, smoothing it flat with the side of his hand.

"In the spring," he said, "I will need help with the planting. He could come home for that? A few weeks?"

Clara stood with the milk pan in her hand. She did not turn around at once. When she did, her eyes were bright, but her voice was quite steady.

"I expect he could. I expect he would want to."

"And the summers. There is the haying."

"Yes."

Joseph nodded. He picked up his pipe, and this time he filled it from the tin on the shelf and lit it with a splinter from the stove, drawing on it slowly until it caught. The smoke went up blue in the lamplight. He sat down again in his chair and stretched his feet toward the stove, and for a moment he looked very tired, older than she had ever seen him look, and then the look passed and he was only Joseph again, heavy and patient and quiet, waiting for his son to come in out of the cold.

"You will have to write the letter," he said. "Tell the professor. I do not know how to say it right."

"I'll write it tomorrow."

"Tell him," Joseph said, and stopped, and frowned at the stove. "Tell him the boy is a good worker. Tell him he does not quit. Tell him that is from his father."

They heard Rudolph's step on the porch, and the scrape of his boots on the iron scraper by the door. Clara poured the milk into the pan and set it on the front of the stove, where the heat was greatest, and did not look at her husband again, because she knew he would not want her to.
