Here is an excerpt of Willa Cather's writing, to show you their style:

Bergson had spent his first five years on the Divide getting into debt, and the last six getting out. He had paid off his mortgages and had ended pretty much where he began, with the land. He owned exactly six hundred and forty acres of what stretched outside his door; his own original homestead and timber claim, making three hundred and twenty acres, and the half-section adjoining, the homestead of a younger brother who had given up the fight, gone back to Chicago to work in a fancy bakery and distinguish himself in a Swedish athletic club. So far John had not attempted to cultivate the second half-section, but used it for pasture land, and one of his sons rode herd there in open weather. John Bergson had the Old-World belief that land, in itself, is desirable. But this land was an enigma. It was like a horse that no one knows how to break to harness, that runs wild and kicks things to pieces. He had an idea that no one understood how to farm it properly, and this he often discussed with Alexandra. Their neighbors, certainly, knew even less about farming than he did. Many of them had never worked on a farm until they took up their homesteads. They had been handwerkers at home; tailors, locksmiths, joiners, cigar-makers, etc. Bergson himself had worked in a shipyard. For weeks, John Bergson had been thinking about these things. His bed stood in the sitting-room, next to the kitchen. Through the day, while the baking and washing and ironing were going on, the father lay and looked up at the roof beams that he himself had hewn, or out at the cattle in the corral. He counted the cattle over and over. It diverted him to speculate as to how much weight each of the steers would probably put on by spring. He often called his daughter in to talk to her about this. Before Alexandra was twelve years old she had begun to be a help to him, and as she grew older he had come to depend more and more upon her resourcefulness and good judgment. His boys were willing enough to work, but when he talked with them they usually irritated him. It was Alexandra who read the papers and followed the markets, and who learned by the mistakes of their neighbors. It was Alexandra who could always tell about what it had cost to fatten each steer, and who could guess the weight of a hog before it went on the scales closer than John Bergson himself. Lou and Oscar were industrious, but he could never teach them to use their heads about their work. Alexandra, her father often said to himself, was like her grandfather; which was his way of saying that she was intelligent. John Bergson’s father had been a shipbuilder, a man of considerable force and of some fortune. Late in life he married a second time, a Stockholm woman of questionable character, much younger than he, who goaded him into every sort of extravagance. On the shipbuilder’s part, this marriage was an infatuation, the despairing folly of a powerful man who cannot bear to grow old. In a few years his unprincipled wife warped the probity of a lifetime. He speculated, lost his own fortune and funds entrusted to him by poor seafaring men, and died disgraced, leaving his children nothing. But when all was said, he had come up from the sea himself, had built up a proud little business with no capital but his own skill and foresight, and had proved himself a man. In his daughter, John Bergson recognized the strength of will, and the simple direct way of thinking things out, that had characterized his father in his better days. He would much rather, of course, have seen this likeness in one of his sons, but it was not a question of choice. As he lay there day after day he had to accept the situation as it was, and to be thankful that there was one among his children to whom he could entrust the future of his family and the possibilities of his hard-won land. The winter twilight was fading. The sick man heard his wife strike a match in the kitchen, and the light of a lamp glimmered through the cracks of the door. It seemed like a light shining far away. He turned painfully in his bed and looked at his white hands, with all the work gone out of them. He was ready to give up, he felt. He did not know how it had come about, but he was quite willing to go deep under his fields and rest, where the plow could not find him. He was tired of making mistakes. He was content to leave the tangle to other hands; he thought of his Alexandra’s strong ones.

“Dotter,” he called feebly, “dotter!” He heard her quick step and saw her tall figure appear in the doorway, with the light of the lamp behind her. He felt her youth and strength, how easily she moved and stooped and lifted. But he would not have had it again if he could, not he! He knew the end too well to wish to begin again. He knew where it all went to, what it all became. His daughter came and lifted him up on his pillows. She called him by an old Swedish name that she used to call him when she was little and took his dinner to him in the shipyard.

“Tell the boys to come here, daughter. I want to speak to them.”

“They are feeding the horses, father. They have just come back from the Blue. Shall I call them?” He sighed. “No, no. Wait until they come in. Alexandra, you will have to do the best you can for your brothers. Everything will come on you.”

“I will do all I can, father.”

“Don’t let them get discouraged and go off like Uncle Otto. I want them to keep the land.”

“We will, father. We will never lose the land.” There was a sound of heavy feet in the kitchen. Alexandra went to the door and beckoned to her brothers, two strapping boys of seventeen and nineteen. They came in and stood at the foot of the bed. Their father looked at them searchingly, though it was too dark to see their faces; they were just the same boys, he told himself, he had not been mistaken in them. The square head and heavy shoulders belonged to Oscar, the elder. The younger boy was quicker, but vacillating.

“Boys,” said the father wearily, “I want you to keep the land together and to be guided by your sister. I have talked to her since I have been sick, and she knows all my wishes. I want no quarrels among my children, and so long as there is one house there must be one head. Alexandra is the oldest, and she knows my wishes. She will do the best she can. If she makes mistakes, she will not make so many as I have made. When you marry, and want a house of your own, the land will be divided fairly, according to the courts. But for the next few years you will have it hard, and you must all keep together. Alexandra will manage the best she can.” Oscar, who was usually the last to speak, replied because he was the older, “Yes, father. It would be so anyway, without your speaking. We will all work the place together.”

“And you will be guided by your sister, boys, and be good brothers to her, and good sons to your mother? That is good. And Alexandra must not work in the fields any more. There is no necessity now. Hire a man when you need help. She can make much more with her eggs and butter than the wages of a man. It was one of my mistakes that I did not find that out sooner. Try to break a little more land every year; sod corn is good for fodder. Keep turning the land, and always put up more hay than you need. Don’t grudge your mother a little time for plowing her garden and setting out fruit trees, even if it comes in a busy season. She has been a good mother to you, and she has always missed the old country.” When they went back to the kitchen the boys sat down silently at the table. Throughout the meal they looked down at their plates and did not lift their red eyes. They did not eat much, although they had been working in the cold all day, and there was a rabbit stewed in gravy for supper, and prune pies. John Bergson had married beneath him, but he had married a good housewife. Mrs. Bergson was a fair-skinned, corpulent woman, heavy and placid like her son, Oscar, but there was something comfortable about her; perhaps it was her own love of comfort. For eleven years she had worthily striven to maintain some semblance of household order amid conditions that made order very difficult. Habit was very strong with Mrs. Bergson, and her unremitting efforts to repeat the routine of her old life among new surroundings had done a great deal to keep the family from disintegrating morally and getting careless in their ways. The train from the east was an hour late, and Anna Hruby had been waiting on the platform at Brodie since four o'clock. She had driven in early because she did not trust the roads after the rain, and because she had not known what else to do with the afternoon. The station agent, a thin young man with sleeve-garters, had come out twice to tell her that Number Seven was held up at Fairmont, and twice she had thanked him and gone on sitting on the bench beside the baggage truck, her hands folded in her lap. Her team stood at the hitching-bar across the street, switching their tails at the late flies. Brodie was not much of a town: a grain elevator, two stores, a lumber yard, a bank with a stone front that the people were proud of, and a row of cottonwoods along the creek that ran behind the depot. In September the town always looked tired, as if it, too, had been working all summer and wanted to lie down.

Anna was a large woman, broad through the shoulders, with a brown, weathered face and very clear gray eyes. She wore her good black dress and a hat that her daughter-in-law had trimmed for her, and she was uncomfortable in both. She had not seen her cousin Josef in thirty-one years. When he left the country he had been sixteen, and she had been fourteen, and she remembered him as a slight, black-haired boy with a quick tongue, who could do anything with a fiddle and nothing at all with a plow. His father, her Uncle Vaclav, had beaten him for it more than once. One morning in March the boy was gone, and the fiddle with him, and a letter was found on the kitchen table saying that he had taken work with the railroad and would send money home. He did send money, for a while, and then the letters came less often, from Omaha, from Denver, from places in Montana whose names the family could not pronounce, and at last from Seattle, where it seemed he had settled. Uncle Vaclav died without seeing him again. Josef's mother died the winter after. Anna had written to him both times, and both times he had answered with a long letter, very carefully written, in which he said a great deal about the old people and very little about himself.

Then in August a letter had come saying that he was going east on business and would like to stop on the way, if she would have him. She had read it over three times standing in the road by the mailbox, and had carried it in her apron pocket for a week before she answered.

The whistle sounded at last, far down the line, and she saw the smoke before she saw the engine, a gray feather lying along the edge of the sky. The young agent came out with his cart. Anna stood up and smoothed her skirt. She felt, all at once, that she had made a mistake in coming alone; that she should have brought one of the boys, or her daughter-in-law, who talked easily to anybody. The train came in slowly, as if it were reluctant to stop at so small a place. Two drummers got off with their sample cases, and a farm woman with a basket, and after them a gentleman in a gray overcoat, who stood on the step a moment and looked up and down the platform before he came down.

She would not have known him. He was not tall, and he had grown stout in the middle, and his hair, what she could see of it under his hat, was quite white. He had a short beard, trimmed close, and he carried a leather bag in one hand and a long, narrow case in the other. It was the case she recognized. She went toward him, and he set down his bag and took off his hat.

"Anna," he said. "Is it Anna?"

"It is me, Josef. You would not know me, I guess."

"I would know you anywhere," he said, which was not true, and they both knew it was not true, and it did not matter. He took her hand in both of his and held it, and she saw that his eyes were wet. She had not expected that. She had expected him to be a city man, smooth and a little condescending, as the men who came back from Omaha often were. But he only stood there holding her rough hand and looking at her as if he were trying to find, somewhere in her face, the little girl who used to carry water to the men in the hayfield.

"You have still got the fiddle," she said, because she could think of nothing else.

He laughed. "Not the same one. That one I sold in Cheyenne, when I was hungry. But I have always had one."

She took him across the street to the wagon, and he stood back and admired the team, two big sorrels with white faces, and asked their names, and patted their noses as if he had been away from horses a long time and had missed them. She saw that he did not quite know how to climb into the spring wagon, and she pretended not to see. When he was settled beside her with his bag at his feet and the fiddle case across his knees, she spoke to the horses and they went off at a good trot up the north road.

The country north of Brodie is high, rolling land, and in those days it was nearly all under the plow. The wheat had been cut and stacked in July and threshed in August, and the stubble fields lay pale gold on either side of the road, with the long shadows of the stacks reaching across them. The corn was still standing, and it rustled dryly when the wind went over it. Along the fence lines the sunflowers had gone to seed, and the goldenrod was out, and here and there a hedge of Osage orange made a dark green wall against the sky. The sky itself was enormous, as it always is in that country in autumn; it seemed to come down all around them to the very edge of the fields, so that the wagon moved along at the bottom of a great clear bowl of light.

Josef did not say anything for a long while. He sat with his hands on the fiddle case and looked out over the land, turning his head slowly from one side to the other, the way a man looks over a room where he once lived.

"It was not like this," he said at last. "When we came it was all grass. I remember the grass higher than my head, and red in the fall. Where are the prairie chickens?"

"There are some yet, down toward the river. Not like before. Nothing is like before." She glanced at him sideways. "You would hardly know where our old places were. Your father's house is gone. Pavlik tore it down when he bought the land, and built a frame house farther up the hill. The dugout where we lived the first winter, that fell in long ago. My boys plowed over it."

"And the creek? The little creek where we used to watch the cattle?"

"That is there. A creek does not go away so easy."

He seemed pleased at that, and smiled to himself. She remembered the creek too: a shallow, winding stream with mud banks, where the cattle went down to drink in the heat of the day and stood switching their tails in the water. The two of them had herded there all one summer, the summer before he went away, sitting in the shade of the one big box-elder while the cattle grazed, and he had talked to her about the cities he was going to see. He had told her about Prague, where their grandmother had been in service as a girl, and about Vienna, where there were more fiddlers than there were farmers in all Nebraska. She had believed every word of it. She had thought him the cleverest boy in the world.

"Did you ever get to Vienna, Josef?" she asked.

He shook his head. "No. I never got anywhere I meant to go. I got to Seattle." He said it without bitterness, as a man states the price of wheat. "That is a fine town. Lots of water, lots of rain. Ships coming in from everywhere. I have a little store there now, for musical instruments. I sell pianos to the people who get rich in the lumber business, and I mend fiddles for the Swedes and the Norwegians who come to play at dances. It is a good enough living."

"You never married?"

"Once. She died the second year. That was a long time ago." He looked down at his hands. "I did not write about it. I did not know how to put it in a letter to your mother, and to mine. They would have wanted to know if she was Catholic, and she was not."

Anna nodded. She did not say anything. She thought it was probably true that the old people would have asked that first, and she felt a little ashamed for them, and a little ashamed for herself because she, too, had wondered.

The sun was low when they came over the last hill and saw the Hruby place below them: a white house with a green roof, a red barn larger than the house, a windmill turning slowly in the evening wind, and behind the house an orchard of apple and cherry trees, already shaking down yellow leaves. A row of tall cottonwoods ran along the west side of the yard, and Anna told him that her husband had set them out as switches the first spring they were married, and that now they were taller than the windmill. Frank Hruby had been dead six years. She said this plainly, and Josef said he had heard it from her letter and was sorry, and that was all.

Her eldest son, Rudolph, came out of the barn to take the team. He was a big, fair, slow-spoken man of twenty-eight, much like his father, and he shook hands with his uncle shyly and called him "sir." His wife, Marie, came to the kitchen door with the baby on her hip and two more children hanging to her skirts. The younger son, Tony, who was still unmarried and lived at home, was out in the far field and did not come in until supper was on the table. The children stared at the strange gentleman with the white beard and the leather bag, and the smallest one hid her face in her mother's apron. Josef knelt down on the porch boards, in his good gray trousers, and took a little paper sack of peppermints out of his pocket. In five minutes they were all three sitting on the step beside him.

Supper was a serious affair, for Anna had been cooking for two days. There was roast chicken and dumplings, and sauerkraut that she had put down the fall before, and new potatoes in butter, and cucumbers sliced thin in sour cream, and a great plate of kolache, some filled with apricot and some with poppy seed, which was the kind Josef's mother used to make. He ate one of the poppy-seed ones very slowly and did not say anything, and Anna, watching him from the stove, knew what he was thinking. The men talked about the threshing and the price of hogs and whether it would be a dry winter. Josef asked a great many questions about the farm, how many acres were in wheat and how many in corn, how deep the well went down, what they paid a hired man; and Rudolph, who had been afraid of the city uncle, warmed to him and answered at length. Tony said little. He was a dark, restless boy, and Anna saw that he kept looking at the fiddle case in the corner.

After supper, when the dishes were done and Marie had taken the children up to bed, Anna and her cousin went out and sat on the porch. The night had come down cool and very still. The windmill had stopped turning. Out in the dark the corn whispered now and then, and from the pasture came the occasional low, contented sound of the cattle. There was no moon yet, and the stars were so thick over the fields that they seemed to hang down among the cottonwoods. Josef lit a cigar, and the smell of it drifted out across the yard, a strange city smell in that country place.

"You have done well, Anna," he said. "This is a good farm. Your boys are good boys."

"Frank did it, mostly. And the boys. I only cooked and kept chickens."

"No," he said, "I can see. It is you." He was quiet a moment. "When I was in the cities, all those years, I used to think about this country. Not often. Sometimes, when I was sick, or when I had no work. I used to think I had got away from it, and that was the best thing I ever did. And then I would think about the grass, and the way the wind came over it in the morning, and Grandmother sitting in the door of the dugout with her rosary. I would think about you, carrying the water jug out to the field with both hands, the way you did, so careful not to spill it."

Anna laughed, a short, embarrassed laugh. "I was a fat little thing. I could never keep up with you."

"You kept up. You were always there." He drew on his cigar, and the end of it glowed and faded. "Do you remember the grasshopper year?"

"How should I not remember? We had nothing all that winter but cornmeal and what the church sent. Your father killed the old red cow in February. Mother cried over it like a person was dead."

"I remember the sound they made," he said. "Eating. Like fire in the dry grass. And the sky dark with them. I was so scared I hid under the bed, and your mother pulled me out and gave me a sack and made me go beat them off the cabbages. You were already out there, beating away. You were not scared at all."

"I was scared," Anna said. "I was too scared to stop."

They were silent for a while. Somewhere far off a dog barked, and another answered it, and then the stillness closed over again, deeper than before.

"Is it true," she asked presently, "that you play in a theater? Mother heard it from somebody. From the Kucera girl, who went out to Portland."

"I played in a theater orchestra for twelve years. Second violin. Light operas, mostly, and the music between the acts of plays. It was not much. But I liked it. You sit down there in the dark, under the stage, and nobody sees you, and you make the people happy or sad just as the music says. There is something to that." He laughed softly. "Father always said I would come to nothing with my fiddle. Well, I came to second violin. That is something better than nothing."

"Your father was proud of you, Josef. He would not say it. But he kept your letters in his Bible, every one. When he died, Mother found them there."

He did not answer, and she did not look at him. She knew that it had cost him something to come back to this country, and that this was part of the price, and that he would have to pay it in his own way. She folded her hands in her lap and looked out at the dark fields. The moon was coming up now behind the barn, very large and red, and as it climbed it grew paler, and the stubble fields began to show silver under it, as far as she could see.

"Anna," he said after a long time, "do you ever wish you had gone away? Seen something?"

She considered this honestly, as she considered everything. "When I was young I wished it. I used to think about those cities you told me. She paused. "I have seen a good deal, I guess, right here. I have seen this country come up out of the grass. I have seen my children grow. "You say that because you went away. If you had stayed, maybe you would say different."

He laughed, and she was glad to hear it. "Maybe. People always want the thing they did not take."

"Uncle," he said, "Mother says you play the fiddle. Would you play something? If you are not too tired."

Josef looked at Anna, and she nodded. "What was that last?" Tony asked in a low voice.

"I will go in now, Anna," he said. "I am an old man, and I have been on the train two days."

"Then we are both old," he said, and he put his hand on her shoulder a moment as he passed her, and went into the house.

The moon had climbed high and gone small and white. Down in the pasture one of the cows lowed once, softly, and was still. Then Anna rose, and went in, and barred the door behind her.

“I don’t think he knows anything at all about doctoring,” said Oscar scornfully. “They say when horses have distemper he takes the medicine himself, and then prays over the horses.” Alexandra spoke up. “That’s what the Crows said, but he cured their horses, all the same. Some days his mind is cloudy, like. But if you can get him on a clear day, you can learn a great deal from him. He understands animals. Didn’t I see him take the horn off the Berquist’s cow when she had torn it loose and went crazy? She was tearing all over the place, knocking herself against things. And at last she ran out on the roof of the old dugout and her legs went through and there she stuck, bellowing. Ivar came running with his white bag, and the moment he got to her she was quiet and let him saw her horn off and daub the place with tar.”

Using that only as a guide to voice, not content to copy, write a 2,500–3,000-word prose narrative in the exact literary style and voice of Willa Cather, depicting the following scene: A parent reprimanding a young child.
Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can. Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
column308:
Anton Kovar had come to the Little Blue country in the spring of the dry year, when the grass was short and the creeks were standing in pools. He brought with him a wife, two horses that were not well matched, a plow, a sewing-machine, and a feather bed which his wife's mother had made for her in Bohemia and which had crossed the ocean rolled up in a piece of oilcloth. Before he took up his claim he had worked four years in a packing-house in Omaha, and he used to say that he had learned more English there than he wanted, and none of it fit to say in front of a priest. He was a lean, dark man, quiet in his ways, with a long upper lip and grey eyes that were slow to change. The neighbors thought him close, and perhaps he was; but no one ever said that he had cheated a man or let a debt run past the day it was due.

His wife, Marie, was a small woman who had been pretty when she was a girl, and who was still pretty when she laughed, though she did not laugh often in the first years. She had been brought up in a town, in a house with a tiled stove and a garden behind it, and the open country frightened her. For a long while she would not go out of sight of the house alone. When the wind blew for three days together she sat by the stove with her hands in her lap and did not speak to anyone, and Anton let her alone; he knew that it was not the wind she was listening to. But she was a good manager, and she kept her children clean, and when the sod house gave way to a frame one she papered the front room with a pattern of little blue roses that she had chosen out of a book at the store in Red Cloud. She had four children living, and one buried on the rise behind the windbreak, under a wooden cross that Anton painted white every spring.

The youngest of the four was Rudolph, who was seven years old the summer the peddler came. He was a quick, light, brown little boy, with his mother's curly hair and her way of tilting her head when she was pleased with something. He was not a bad child, but he was a heedless one; he ran off after gophers when he had been told to watch the calves, and he could never remember to shut a gate. His sisters spoiled him, and his mother, who had lost the baby before him, could not bring herself to be hard with him. When he had done some mischief he would come and lean against her knee and look up at her, and she would smooth his hair and say that he was only a little one yet. Anton said nothing about it, but he saw it, and he thought about it more than his wife knew.

The peddler came along the river road one afternoon in July, when Anton and the two older girls were in the field shocking oats. He was a Syrian, a thin, yellow-faced man with a black moustache and a pack on his back nearly as big as himself, and he walked with a stoop, as if the pack were always going downhill ahead of him. Marie was lying down with a headache, and Rudolph was alone in the yard. The peddler set his pack down in the shade of the cottonwoods and opened it out on the grass. There were spools of thread in it, and papers of needles, and ribbons, and a card of pearl buttons, and a pair of spectacles, and, in a little box lined with red cloth, a mouth-organ with a picture of a steamboat stamped on the side of it.

Rudolph had never seen anything so beautiful as that mouth-organ. The peddler blew a few notes on it, and the sound went up thin and sweet into the cottonwood leaves; then he wiped it on his sleeve and put it into the boy's hands. Rudolph had no money; he had never had any money in his life, except a nickel at Christmas. The peddler did not seem to mind. He looked about the yard, and at the house, and he asked, in his strange English, whether the little man did not have something of silver, some small thing, a spoon, a ring, anything at all.

The thimble lay in Marie's work-basket on the window-sill, where it always lay. It had belonged to her grandmother, and it was the only thing of real silver in the house. It was worn very thin at the top, from the long sewing of two women before Marie, and there was a little band of flowers around the rim, so rubbed down that you had to hold it to the light to see them. Marie never let the girls use it. Rudolph knew that. He knew it, and he stood in the kitchen with the thimble in his hot hand for a long time, listening to his mother breathing in the next room; and then he went out and gave it to the peddler. The peddler turned it over, bit it, nodded, and put it away inside his shirt. In a few minutes he had tied up his pack and gone on down the road toward the Norwegian settlement, stooping as before, and Rudolph went behind the corn-crib and played on the mouth-organ until his lips were sore.

Marie did not miss the thimble until after supper, when she sat down by the lamp to mend. She looked in the basket, and then on the floor under the window, and then in the pockets of her aprons. The girls looked, too. It was Hulda, the eldest, who remembered that a peddler had gone by, and who turned and looked at her little brother. Rudolph was sitting on the bench by the door, and his face had gone quite white under the brown. He had the mouth-organ inside his blouse, and it seemed to him that it must be shining right through the cloth.

Anton was washing at the bench outside, and he heard his wife's voice rise and break. He came in with the towel in his hands. Marie was not scolding; she was crying, in the way she had cried in the first years, without any noise, and she kept saying in Bohemian that it did not matter, that it was only a thimble, that a thimble could be bought in any store for ten cents. Anton looked at her a moment, and then he looked at the boy.

"Rudo," he said, "come outside with me."

Marie half rose from her chair. "Anton, he is only little. He did not know."

"He knew," said Anton quietly. "Come, Rudo."

The boy got up and followed his father out into the yard. The sun had gone down, but the sky was still full of light, a clear, hard yellow along the west, and the windmill stood up black against it. The wind had fallen, as it did nearly every evening at that time of year, and the whole country seemed to be holding its breath. Somewhere down on the creek a killdeer was crying. Anton walked past the barn and past the corn-crib, without looking back, until he came to the fence at the edge of the pasture, and there he stopped and put his arms on the top wire. Rudolph stood a little way behind him. He had expected to be whipped in the barn, the way his cousin Joe had been whipped once in Wilber, and he did not know what to make of this.

For a while his father did not speak. He looked out over the pasture, where the cattle were moving slowly toward the water-hole, and beyond it to the wheat stubble, and beyond that to the long, low swell of the prairie, which was turning from gold to brown as the light went out of it. Rudolph waited. He could feel the mouth-organ against his ribs. At last he took it out and held it toward his father, and his hand shook.

Anton took it and looked at it. He turned it over and saw the steamboat on the side.

"That is a pretty thing," he said. "I never had one like that." He handed it back. "No, you keep it. It is yours now. You paid for it."

Rudolph began to cry. He had not cried in the house, but he cried now, standing in the grass with his bare feet wet from the dew, and his father let him cry for some time.

"Do you know why your mother has that thimble?" Anton asked presently.

The boy shook his head.

"I will tell you, then. When your mother was a girl, younger than Hulda, her grandmother lived with them, in the room over the bakeshop. She was a seamstress, a very good one. She made dresses for ladies in Pisek, for the doctor's wife and the wife of the man who owned the mill. She sewed with that thimble every day for forty years. When she got old and her eyes were bad, your mother used to thread her needles for her, and sit by her at the window, and the old woman taught her to sew. When your mother came away to this country, her grandmother was dead already, and her mother gave her that thimble at the station. That was the last thing. Her mother is dead now too. Your mother has never seen her grave."

Anton spoke slowly, as he always did when he spoke English, choosing each word as if he were picking up stones in a field. Rudolph listened with his head down.

"You think it is only a little thing," his father went on. "It is little, yes. You could put it on the end of your finger. But your mother has not got very much from the old country. She has the feather bed, and she has that, and she has a picture of the church where she was married. Everything else is here. Everything else is new. When she sits down at night to mend your stockings, and she puts that on her finger, I think she is not here any more, for a little while. I think she is back in that room over the bakeshop, with the old woman by the window. That is what you gave to the peddler for a mouth-organ."

The boy's shoulders shook. "I didn't—" he began, and stopped, because it was not true, and he could not finish it with his father looking at him.

"You knew it was hers," Anton said. "You knew she did not let anybody touch it. I am not angry because you wanted the mouth-organ. Everybody wants things. When I was a boy I wanted a pair of boots with red tops, like the forester's son had, so much that I could not sleep. That is nothing. But you waited until your mother was lying down. You waited until there was nobody in the yard. That is what I don't like, Rudo. That is the part that makes me ashamed."

He had not raised his voice once. Rudolph would have been less frightened if he had. He would have known what to do with shouting; he had heard men shout at horses and at each other in town, and it passed over like weather. But his father's voice was low and tired, and it went into him and stayed there.

"Your mother will tell you it doesn't matter," Anton said. "She will tell you because she loves you, and because she lost the little one before you and she is afraid to be hard. But it does matter. A man has to be able to trust what is in his own house. Out there"—he moved his hand toward the dark land beyond the fence—"out there nothing is sure. The hail comes, or the grasshoppers, or it doesn't rain. A man can work all year and have nothing. You saw that two years ago, when we burned the corn for fuel because it was not worth hauling. So in the house, at least, things have to be sure. If I cannot leave you alone in the yard for an afternoon, then I have got one more thing to watch, and I have got enough to watch already."

The light had nearly gone. The windmill was only a shape now, and the first stars had come out over the river. The cattle had reached the water-hole, and they could hear them drinking, a soft, sucking sound in the stillness. Rudolph wiped his nose on his sleeve.

"Can we get it back?" he whispered.

Anton considered. "The peddler went toward Ole Thorsen's. Thorsen will keep him for the night, I think; he likes company, and he will want to buy a razor. In the morning, maybe, he will still be there. Maybe he will be gone to Guide Rock. I don't know."

"I'll give him back the mouth-organ."

"He will not want it back. He made a good trade. He knows what silver is worth." Anton was silent a moment. Then he said, "I will give him money for it. But it is not my money I will be giving, Rudo. You understand? It is yours. You will work for it. Every evening this summer, when the girls do the milking, you will carry the water for the chickens, and you will keep the woodbox full, without anybody telling you. And when we sell the steers this fall, I will not buy you anything in town. That is how you will pay me. Is it fair?"

The boy nodded. He could not have spoken.

"Now go in and go to bed. Don't say anything to your mother tonight. Let her be. Tomorrow you will get up when I call you, before it is light."

Rudolph went back across the yard alone. He did not look at his mother when he passed through the kitchen, and she did not call to him. He climbed the ladder to the loft where he slept, and lay down in his clothes, and heard, a long time afterward, the murmur of his father's and mother's voices below, rising and falling, in Bohemian. He held the mouth-organ in his hand under the quilt, but he did not play it. He thought he would never want to play it again.

His father called him in the grey of the morning, when the roosters were just beginning and the air was cold and sweet. Anton had saddled the old mare, Kitty, and he lifted the boy up in front of him, and they rode out along the river road while the mist was still lying in the low places like milk in a pan. Neither of them said anything. The sun came up behind them, red and enormous, and laid their shadow out long on the road ahead, a man and a boy on one horse, and the meadowlarks began to sing from the fence-posts, one after another, as if they were passing something along.

The peddler was still at Thorsen's. He was sitting on the step of the bunkhouse, drinking coffee out of a tin cup, with his pack beside him, and he looked up without surprise when they rode into the yard, as if men often came after him in the morning on such business. Anton got down and set the boy on the ground.

"Go on," he said.

Rudolph walked across the yard by himself. It was the longest walk he had ever taken. The Thorsen dogs came out and smelled him, and Ole Thorsen's wife watched from the kitchen door with her hands rolled up in her apron. When he came to the step he held out the mouth-organ in its box, and he said, in a voice that did not sound like his own, that he wanted his mother's thimble back, please, and that it was not his to trade.

The peddler looked at him, and then over the boy's head at Anton, who stood by the mare with the reins in his hand. He set his cup down slowly. Then he reached inside his shirt and brought out the thimble and laid it on the step. He shook his head when Rudolph offered him the mouth-organ, and pushed it back toward him. Anton came forward then and put two silver dollars beside the cup, which was more than the thimble would have fetched in any store in the county, and the peddler took them without arguing, and said something in his own language, and touched his forehead.

They rode home in the full sun. The boy held the thimble shut in his fist the whole way, so tightly that when he opened it at last it had left a red ring in his palm. His mother was in the garden, pulling beets for dinner, and she straightened up when she saw them coming and shaded her eyes. Anton set the boy down at the gate and rode on to the barn, without stopping.

Rudolph went down between the rows to where she stood. He held out his hand and opened it. Marie looked at the thimble for a long moment, and then she knelt down in the dirt, in her clean apron, and put her arms around him, and he felt that she was trembling. She did not say that it did not matter. She did not say anything at all.

Many years afterward, when Rudolph Kovar was a man with a farm of his own on the Republican, and children of his own who left gates open and ran off after gophers, he used to tell that story to his wife; but he never told it as a story about the thimble. He told it as a story about the evening at the pasture fence, with the light going out of the sky and the cattle drinking in the dark, and his father's voice, so low and so tired, saying that in the house, at least, things had to be sure. He said that he did not understand it then. He said that he understood it only after his father was dead, and the land was his to hold against the weather, and he knew how little there is in this world that a man can be certain of, and how much depends upon that little.
