column308:
Kinship in the desert is a thinner and a tougher thing than it is in the towns. It does not go about in visits and Sunday dinners and the borrowing of a cradle; it lies by, like seed of the desert annuals that will wait out three dry years in the sand and still come up, with no great show of leaf, the first spring there is rain enough to wet them. People who are of one blood in that country may live for half their lives on opposite sides of a range, knowing of each other only what the freighters bring, or what is told at the store by a man who heard it at the stage station; and then some turn of the season brings them together, and they find that the thing between them has been keeping all that while, dry and close and alive, in the way of seeds.

It was so with Ellen Sayre and her cousin Lafe. They had been children together on the lower Toyabe ranch, where the creek comes down out of the hills in a crease of willows and gives out in the sand a mile below the house. That was when Lafe's father and Ellen's mother were still holding the place between them, before the drought that killed the stock and sent half the family over the Sierras to live on the coast. Ellen went with that half. She was eleven, and Lafe, who was thirteen, stayed on with his father, and the two of them did not see each other again for six and twenty years.

There was no quarrel in it. It is simply the way of that land to divide people as a ridge divides water, without malice, by the mere lie of it, so that one drop goes down to the sea and another to a sink in the sand that never reaches anywhere at all. Ellen went down to the sea. She married there, a man in the hardware business who was very decent to her and died of a fever in the ninth year, and afterward she kept house for her mother until the old woman died too. Lafe went to the sink. He ran cattle when there was grass and freighted for the mines when there was none, and he married a Shoshone woman out of the campoodie at Pine Nut, which the family on the coast did not speak of, and which Lafe, when the occasion came, did not explain.

What brought Ellen back was a letter from a lawyer in Bishop about a piece of the old water right, which had come to her by some crookedness of inheritance and was wanted by a man who was putting in alfalfa. She might have signed it away by post. Instead she put on her brown traveling dress and came up by the narrow-gauge and the stage, and if you had asked her why, she could not have told you, except that a woman who has buried two people and has no third to take care of begins to be restless in her hands.

She found Lafe at the lower crossing of the creek, where he had driven down with the buckboard to meet the stage, and the first thing she knew of him was his hat.

He was standing by the horses' heads with his back half to the road, and the hat was the old high-crowned gray kind that cattlemen wore in that country when Ellen was a child, gone soft and greenish with weather, with a bit of horsehair braided for a band. She knew before he turned that it was Lafe, not by his shape, which had thickened and gone a little stooped in the shoulders, but by the way he stood, with one hand lying flat on the near horse's neck as if he were listening to it. Her uncle had stood so. There are ways of standing that run in a family like the color of eyes.

"Well, Nellie," said Lafe, when he had lifted her trunk into the buckboard and her after it, "you've come back."

That was all the greeting there was. The desert does not teach people to say much at meetings, having so few of them; it is the partings that are long in that country, and the meetings are short, like the rain.

They drove up the creek in the late afternoon with the sun at their backs and the shadow of the buckboard going on before them long and thin over the sand, like a spider walking. The road kept to the willows as long as it could. It was April, and the willows were in that first gauzy yellow which is less a color than a kind of light hung in the branches, and under them the wild rose was in leaf and the creek ran brown and loud with snow water. Above the creek, on both sides, the land went up in long smooth fans of rubble to the foot of the hills, and on the fans the sage was gray and the rabbit brush a duller gray, and between the bushes there was a faint green fur of the little annual plants that come for a fortnight in a good year and are gone. Ellen looked at it all a long time without speaking. She had forgotten nothing, but she had forgotten that she knew it; and now each thing as it came up to her was like a word in a language she had stopped speaking, coming back on the tongue.

"There used to be a shrike," she said finally, "that nested in the big mesquite at the turn of the road. It hung lizards on the thorns."

"There's one yet," said Lafe. "Likely not the same one."

"No," she said, "likely not."

It is a curious thing that people meeting after a long while will begin almost always with the things that have not changed. It is a way of finding the floor before they go to walking on it. Ellen and Lafe talked of the shrike, and the mesquite, and the ford below the house where the bank had caved in the flood of the year she went away, and of a spring on the hill above the corrals which used to show only after a wet winter and which Lafe said had come again this year. They spoke as if these were persons they had both known. In a way they were.

The house when they came to it was the old house still, adobe at one end and board at the other, with the board end added on and weathered now to the same color as the adobe, so that it looked as though it had been grown rather than built. There was a ramada of willow poles over the door, and under it a woman sitting on her heels, shelling something into a basket. She got up when the buckboard came into the yard, and stood waiting, with her hands hanging and the basket against her knees.

"That's Tuhudda," said Lafe. "My wife."

Ellen had wondered, coming up on the stage, what she should do at this moment, and now that it was here she found there was nothing at all to do but get down from the buckboard and go and take the woman's hand. Tuhudda let it be taken. She was a broad, quiet woman with her hair cut square across her forehead in the fashion of her people, and a man's coat over her calico, and she looked at Ellen with no curiosity that could be seen, the way the Indian women look at anything they have not yet made up their minds about. Then she said something in her own tongue to Lafe, and went back under the ramada, and took up her basket again.

"She says you favor your mother," said Lafe.

"Did she know my mother?"

"She knew all of you. Her people were camped at the forks the year of the dry. She was a little thing, but she remembers. She says your mother gave her a red ribbon once."

Ellen did not remember any red ribbon. But she remembered the camp at the forks, the brush shelters gray against the gray hill, and the smoke going up straight in the windless mornings, and the children who used to come down to the ranch to stare at the white children through the fence; and it seemed to her, standing there with the dust of the road on her skirt, that one of them must have been this woman, and that it was a strange thing to have been looked at so long ago by someone and then to come back and find her keeping your cousin's house.

---

They ate supper inside, by lamplight, the three of them, and afterward Tuhudda took the dishes out to the bench by the spring box, and Lafe and Ellen sat on in the room with the door open and the night coming in.

It is in the dark that the desert people talk, if they talk at all. Something in the great quietness of the land after sundown, when the heat goes up off the sand like a hand lifted, loosens the tongue that has been held all day against the glare. Ellen had found it so as a child, lying awake to hear her uncle and her mother talking low over the dead fire about the water and the grass and the debts; and she found it so now. Lafe filled his pipe and did not light it. A cricket somewhere under the floor began, and stopped, and began again.

"You never wrote," Ellen said. "Not once in all that time."

"No," said Lafe. "I didn't."

"Mother used to wonder."

"I reckoned she would." He turned the pipe over in his fingers. "I'll tell you how it was, Nellie. The first years there was nothing to write. We were just hanging on. You don't put that in a letter; you'd as soon write that you were still breathing. And then after the old man died, and I took up with Tuhudda—well. I reckoned your mother knew about it by then from somebody. I reckoned if she wanted to hear from me she'd have written first."

"She did want to," said Ellen. "She didn't know how to begin."

Lafe was quiet a while.

"That's the trouble," he said at last. "There's no beginning to a thing like that. It's all middle."

Ellen thought that was very likely true, and that it was true of a good many things besides. She had not known that Lafe would have thought of it. When she went away he had been a boy with sun-blistered ears who could ride anything on the place and could not be made to read past the third reader, and she had carried him in her mind all these years as that boy, fixed, the way people fix the dead. It came to her now that he had been going on all that while, out here, thinking his own thoughts in the long silences of the range, and that some of them had been, perhaps, as good as any thought in Sacramento.

"Tell me about your husband," said Lafe.

So she told him. She told him about Will Sayre and the hardware store on J Street, and the house with the bay window and the lemon verbena by the step, and the way Will used to come home at noon on Saturdays and wind the clock. She told about the fever. She found she could tell it now without her voice going thin, which she had not been able to do two years ago, and that the telling of it to Lafe in this room, with the night outside and the cricket under the floor, made it into a kind of story, a thing that had a shape and was finished, the way the stories her uncle used to tell about the early days had shapes. Lafe listened without saying anything. When she was done he nodded, slowly, as if she had given him the price of something and he found it fair.

"He sounds like a good man," he said.

"He was a good man. He was a better man than I knew what to do with, I think, sometimes." She had not meant to say that. "I mean that I was always waiting for something, and I never knew what. He couldn't give it to me because I couldn't tell him what it was."

"Did you find out?"

"No," said Ellen. "Maybe I came up here to see."

---

There is a kind of knowledge that the desert gives which is neither learned nor taught, but grows in a person the way the shape of a juniper grows on a ridge where the wind blows always from one quarter. It is a knowledge of how much can be done without. A man who has lived long in that country knows to a cup how much water will carry him from one spring to the next, and to an hour how long he may lie up in the shade at noon, and he comes to know, if he is the right sort, how little of what people call necessary is necessary at all; and the knowledge leaves its mark on him, so that you can tell a desert man in a town by the way he looks at a table set for dinner, as if he were counting.

Ellen saw that mark on Lafe the next morning when they walked out together to look at the water right. They went up along the ditch, which was an old one, dug by her uncle and his brother with a Fresno scraper and a span of mules the year the place was taken up, and grown along its banks now with wire grass and yerba mansa. Lafe walked ahead, and every little while he stooped and pulled a weed out of the ditch, or kicked a stone back into the bank where the water had worried it loose, not as if he thought about it, but as a man brushes a fly. He never wasted a step. Ellen, coming behind in her town boots, felt herself all elbows.

"This is the piece," said Lafe, when they came to the head gate. "From here up to the forks. It's not much water. In a dry year you can step across it. But it comes in early, before the snow water gets down, and that's when you want it."

"And the man in Bishop wants it for his alfalfa."

"He wants it bad. He'll pay you more than it's worth."

"Do you want me to sell it?"

Lafe took a long time answering. He looked up the creek toward the forks, where the willows thinned out and the canyon walls came in red and broken, and beyond them the hills went up bare and tawny to the snow.

"It's yours," he said. "I'm not going to tell you what to do with it."

"That's not what I asked you."

He turned and looked at her then, full, for the first time since she came, and she saw that his eyes had the same pale, burnt look that her uncle's had, the look of a man who has stared a long time at far-off things in a hard light.

"No," he said. "I don't want you to sell it. I'd rather you'd let me use it, the way I been doing, and I'll pay you what's fair out of the beef money when there is any. But that's only what I want. It's not what you ought to do. A woman alone wants money in the bank."

"A woman alone," said Ellen, "wants something to come back to."

She had not known she was going to say that either. It seemed to her that the country was saying things through her, the way the wind says things through a pine on the ridge that the pine itself has no notion of. She stood by the head gate in her brown dress, with the water going by at her feet clear and quick and very cold, and she felt something give in her that had been held a long time, as the ice gives on the creek in spring, not all at once but in a long settling crack that you hear before you see.

"Then don't sell it," said Lafe.

---

They sat down on the bank by the head gate, in the sun, and for a long while said nothing at all. A pair of mourning doves came down to the water a little way above them and drank, tipping their heads back after each sip the way doves do, as if in thanks. Out on the fan a quail called, the three-note call that sounds like a question asked of no one in particular. The sun was warm on Ellen's back through the stuff of her dress. She took off her hat and laid it in her lap.

"Do you remember," she said, "the time we went up to the forks to see the Indian doctor?"

Lafe laughed. It was the first time she had heard him laugh, and it was not like the laugh she remembered, which had been a boy's laugh, all on top; this one came from down somewhere under his ribs and was short and dry.

"I remember you cried the whole way back."

"I did not."

"You cried. He showed you the rattlesnake rattles in his bag, and you cried."

"I was nine years old."

"You were ten," said Lafe. "It was the spring before the dry."

She thought about it, and he was right. It was strange to have a piece of your own life kept for you by somebody else, out of your sight, like a thing put away in another person's trunk. It made her feel that she had not altogether gone away, all those years; that some part of her had stayed on in Lafe's remembering and had been growing up there in its own fashion, in this country, along with him.

"What became of him? The doctor?"

"He died. A long time ago. They burned his wickiup and everything in it, the way they do." Lafe pulled a stem of wire grass and chewed it. "Tuhudda's uncle, he was."

"I didn't know that."

"There's a good deal you wouldn't know," said Lafe, not unkindly. "You can't expect to. You been gone."

That was the plainest thing that had been said between them, and they both let it lie. It is the custom of that country, when a true thing is said, to give it room, as you give room to a horse that has been ridden hard. Ellen looked at her hands in her lap, which were town hands, white and a little soft, with the mark on the third finger where Will's ring had been until she took it off last winter and put it in a box. She thought of all the things she did not know about Lafe: how it was the winter the old man died, and what it was like to go to the campoodie and ask for a wife, and whether there had been children, and what had become of them if there had. There had been no children spoken of. She did not ask. There would be time for that, or there would not; and either way the asking was not hers to begin.

"You're thinking," said Lafe, "that you'd like to stay a while."

"I was thinking that."

"Tuhudda said last night you would. She said it before you'd got down out of the buckboard. She said you had the look."

"What look?"

"She didn't say. She just said you had it." He threw away the grass stem. "She's mostly right about those things."

---

They went back down the ditch toward the house in the middle of the morning. The sun was well up now, and the light had that thin, high, burnished quality it gets in that country in spring, before the haze of summer comes, so that every bush on the fan stood out separate and round with its own small shadow pooled under it, and the hills looked near enough to touch. Lafe went ahead as before, pulling weeds. Ellen came behind. She had stopped noticing her boots.

Under the ramada Tuhudda was grinding something on a flat stone, rocking the hand stone back and forth with a sound like a slow breathing. She looked up when they came into the yard, and looked at Ellen, and looked at Lafe; and whatever she saw seemed to satisfy her, for she nodded once, the way a woman nods over bread that has risen, and went back to her grinding.

Ellen sat down on the bench by the door. In a little while, without anything being said, Tuhudda pushed a second hand stone across the ground toward her, and a heap of the seed beside it. Ellen did not know how it was done. She watched for a while and then began, badly, and Tuhudda let her go on badly, and did not show her, which Ellen understood after a time to be a kind of courtesy. Lafe went off to see about a horse. The doves came down to the spring box. The sound of the two stones went on under the ramada, the one sure and the one uncertain, and between them the meal came slowly out, gray and fine, on the flat stone.

It is not to be supposed that anything was settled that morning, or that Ellen knew then what she would do about the water right, or the house in Sacramento with the lemon verbena by the step, or the rest of her life. People do not settle things in that country so much as let them settle, the way silt settles out of the snow water in the ditch when it comes to a slack place, and the water goes on clear. All that can be said is that she stayed the week out, and then the month; and that the man in Bishop got his water somewhere else; and that the freighters, coming up the creek road that summer, used to see two women under the ramada at the old Toyabe place, one with her hair cut square and one with her hair in a knot, grinding seed together in the shade, and a man's gray hat hanging on a nail by the door.

The desert keeps what is given it. That is the hardest thing about it, and the kindest.

There is a law of the desert that is older than any statute, and it is this: that what the land gives it gives once, and grudgingly, and the giving is not to be squandered. Every creature that lives between the sink of the Amargosa and the long blue line of the Sierras has this law somewhere in the marrow of it. The coyote knows it, and the cactus wren, and the little gray lizards that sun themselves on the hot sides of boulders; even the creosote, which spaces itself across the mesa as nicely as if a surveyor had laid it out, knows it, for each bush takes no more of the ground's moisture than will keep it, and leaves its neighbor the rest. Only men come into the country not knowing it, and some of them never learn, and these the land puts away quietly under a little heap of stones with a board at the head of it, and the sand drifts over the board in time.

Mrs. Hallam had learned it. She had come into the country nine years before, a tall, fair, deliberate woman out of Iowa, with her husband and a wagon and a crate of hens, and she had learned it as one learns a hard language, word by word, and by being shamed in it. She kept the station at Coyote Wells, which is on the old freight road between the borax works and the railroad, at a place where a spring comes out of a fold of the hills and runs perhaps a quarter of a mile before the sand has the whole of it. Her husband freighted. He was away three weeks of every four, and in that time the station was hers: the adobe house with its ramada of willow poles, the corral, the stone tank where the teams were watered, the half acre of alfalfa that was the only green thing in a day's travel, and the ditch that fed them all. The ditch was the heart of the place. It ran from the spring along the foot of the slope, lined here and there with flat stones, and the whole of the station's living went up and down in it as blood goes in a vein.

She had one child, a boy called Davy, who was six that spring.

It is a thing worth noting about children born in that country, that they take on the color of it early. Davy was brown as a chuckwalla, with hair the bleached tan of galleta grass, and eyes that had the long, unfocused look of people who are used to seeing a great way. He played as desert children play, much alone and much with small live things, horned toads and tarantula hawks and the young of the ground squirrel, and he talked to them in a private language which his mother did not inquire into. She had not much time for inquiring. There was the cooking for whatever teamsters lay over, and the hens, and the mending, and the water to be watched; and in the long afternoons, when the heat stood up off the mesa like a wall, she would sit in the shade of the ramada and look out toward the Panamints and not think of anything at all. This is a habit the desert gives to women who live in it, and it is not idleness, though it may look so. It is the mind lying fallow, as the land lies.

It was in the third week of her husband's absence, at the time of year when the spring runs lowest, that Davy found the ditch.

He had known it always, of course, as one knows the floor of one's house. But on this day, the day after a freighter had gone through and left a bundle of illustrated papers for Mrs. Hallam, he had seen a picture of a river with boats on it, and steamboats with smoke going up out of them, and men on the bank with long poles; and the picture had worked in him all night as yeast works. In the morning he went down to the ditch where it bent around a shoulder of the hill, out of sight of the house, and he took a stick and his two hands and began to make a river.

There is no use in saying the child should have known better. He was six. The water came to him clear and quick, with little bright wrinkles on it where it ran over the stones, and it seemed to him that there was a great deal of it, as there seems to be a great deal of anything to which one has never had to be stingy. He cut the bank. He made a channel out into the sand of the wash, and a harbor at the end of it, and a fleet of boats out of the dry pods of the yucca, and he sailed them all the long hot morning and into the afternoon. The water followed his channel gladly, as water will follow any way that is opened to it, and the sand drank it, and drank it, and was not satisfied, as sand is never satisfied. He did not notice. When he came up to the house at supper time his knees were caked and his face was shining, and he said nothing about the river, because it was his and he did not want it spoiled with telling.

Mrs. Hallam found it out the next morning, when she went to the tank to water the hens and saw the stone sides of it standing bare a foot below where the scum line was.

She stood a moment looking. Then she went along the ditch, not hurrying, for she had learned that one does not hurry in that country except for fire or snakes, and at the bend of the hill she came upon what the boy had done. The channel had widened in the night. The water, finding its own way, had cut deeper than any child's stick could have cut, and gone out across the wash in a broad dark fan, and the fan was already drying at the edges, going pale and crusted in the early sun. Down at the end of it a dozen little birds, linnets and the gray sparrows that live in the brush, were drinking and flirting their wings in the last of the wet. A ground squirrel sat up on a stone and looked at her. Of the fleet of yucca pods there was nothing left but one, stranded on a hummock, with a little ant crawling over it.

She mended the bank first. That was the order of things. She went back to the house for a shovel and came again and filled in the cut, and laid stones along it and stamped them down, and stood watching until the water took up its old way along the foot of the hill and went on, thin and quick, toward the tank. It would be two days filling. The freighters from the borax works were due tomorrow night, sixteen mules to a team, and three teams; and mules drink as if they were paid by the gallon.

Then she went to find her son.

He was in the corral with the old burro, making it a necklace of devil's-claw pods, and he looked up when her shadow fell across him and knew at once, in the way children know, that the sky had changed. He did not ask what was the matter. He put down the devil's-claw and stood up.

"Come with me," said Mrs. Hallam.

She did not take his hand. She walked ahead of him along the path, and he came behind, and the sun was well up now and the shadows of the creosote bushes were short and black and sharply edged, and the whole mesa had that look of being held in the palm of something enormous and indifferent that it has in the mornings of late spring. A road runner went across in front of them with its tail up and its head flat, very busy about its own affairs. Davy watched it go. He would have liked to go with it.

At the bend of the ditch his mother stopped.

"Look," she said.

He looked. He saw the mended bank, raw with new earth, and the dark fan going pale on the sand, and the birds still at the end of it, fewer now, and his one boat stranded on the hummock. He did not see anything wrong with it, except that his river was spoiled; and his lip began to go out at the corner.

It is in such moments that one learns what manner of woman one is. Mrs. Hallam had been raised in a country of soft rains and plenty, where children were whipped for disobedience and the whipping was supposed to end it; and there was a moment, standing there with the shovel still in her hand, when her arm remembered Iowa. She had been very much afraid in the night, when she had lain awake hearing nothing. Fear goes easily into anger, and anger into the hand. But she had lived nine years in the desert, and the desert had worked on her as it works on stone, very slowly, wearing away what is soft and leaving the hard true shape that was underneath; and the thing that was underneath in her was patience. She set the shovel against a bush.

"Davy," she said, "where do you think the water went?"

He looked at the wet sand, and then at her, and said that it went into the ground.

"And what is it doing in the ground?"

He did not know. He supposed it was there yet, and he said so.

"It is not there," said Mrs. Hallam. "The sand has drunk it. It goes down and down until there is nothing to stop it, and then it is gone. You cannot dig for it. You cannot pray for it back. Whatever the land takes, it keeps." She was aware, saying it, that she spoke more slowly than her custom was, and with a kind of weight in her voice that she had heard sometimes in the voices of the old Paiute women who came down from the campoodie at the head of the canyon to trade baskets for flour. They talked to their children in that way, not loud, but as if every word had been carried a long distance and set down carefully. "That water," she said, "was the mules' water. Tomorrow night the Dutchman's teams come in from the borax, and the mules have come forty miles across the dry since the last well, and they will put their noses into the tank, and there will be half what there should be. Do you know what a mule does when it is thirsty and there is not enough?"

He shook his head.

"It fights. It kicks the one beside it, and bites, and screams. And the men have to beat them off the tank by turns, and the last ones get only the mud at the bottom. And the next day they go on forty miles more to the railroad, with their tongues swelled up in their mouths."

The boy's lip had stopped going out. He was looking at the sand.

"And the alfalfa," his mother said. "There will be no water for the alfalfa this week. It will go yellow at the tips. And the hens will lay less, and the Dutchman will not get his eggs, and he will not pay for them, and we will not have the money for the shoes I was going to send for. All that is in the sand, there. You put it there."

She stopped. The road runner had come back and was standing at a little distance, regarding them with its head on one side, the way a road runner will regard anything it has not settled the meaning of. A lizard ran up on a stone and did push-ups, as lizards do, and ran down again.

"I didn't know," said Davy. His voice was very small.

"No," said Mrs. Hallam. "But now you know."

That, if she had been a woman of another country, might have been the end of it. She had not struck him, and she had made him understand, and a woman in a town would have taken him by the hand and gone home and given him his breakfast and let the matter lie. But Mrs. Hallam had a deeper notion of the business than that. She had seen men come into the desert who had been told things, and had nodded, and had not known them; and she had seen what became of such men. The land did not tell a thing twice. It was not cruel; there is no cruelty in the desert, as there is no kindness; there is only the fact, and the fact keeps. And she understood, standing there with the light growing hot on her shoulders, that the thing she had to give her son was not her own anger, which would pass, but some small part of the long, patient implacability of the country itself, which would not.

So she sat down on a flat rock in the full sun, and she said to him: "Now you will sit here with me until the birds go."

He sat down beside her. He did not understand, and he did not ask. The rock was warm already, and the light came down on them out of a sky so wide and pale it seemed hardly to be color at all, and there was no sound but the small sound of the ditch running past behind them in its mended bed.

They sat a long while. The birds at the end of the wet fan grew fewer. The linnets went first, up into the mesquite on the slope, and then the sparrows by ones and twos, and the ground squirrel, which had been working cautiously nearer, came down to the very edge of the last damp and put its nose to it and found nothing and went away. The fan shrank. One could see it shrinking, if one watched, the pale crust creeping in from the edges as frost creeps in on a window, until there was only a dark spot about the size of a saddle blanket in the lowest place, and then about the size of a hat. The heat came up. Davy's face grew red and wet, and his mother's also; she did not move to shade him, nor herself. The lizard came back to its stone and lay flat. The boat of yucca pod on the hummock dried white, and split a little along one side, and the ant went away from it.

When the last dark spot was gone, and the sand of the wash lay as gray and clean as if no water had ever touched it, Mrs. Hallam stood up.

"That is how long," she said. "Half a morning. That is how long the land took to drink what you gave it, and what the spring took two days to make. It does not take any longer than that, Davy. Not for water, and not for a man, and not for a mule."

She took up her shovel and went back to the house, and he came after her, and she gave him his breakfast and said no more about it.

It is told in the country, by the people who knew them afterward, that Davy Hallam grew up to be one of the best water men between Owens Lake and the Colorado, a man who could find seepage in a dry wash by the color of the brush and who was sent for, at a good wage, by the mining companies when they wanted a well sunk where no well had been. He never wasted a cupful in his life. Men who traveled with him said it was a kind of foolishness in him; that he would sit with a canteen in his hand at the end of a long day's ride, and drink from it as slowly and deliberately as if he were at a sacrament. They did not know why, and he never told them. But there was an old Paiute woman at the campoodie, very old by that time, who had come down to the station the week after it happened, to trade a basket, and had seen the mended place in the ditch and asked about it, and had heard; and she said a thing about Mrs. Hallam that went the round of the wickiups and was remembered.

What she said was, that the white woman had punished her son the Indian way, which is to let the land do it.

It is not, perhaps, the whole truth, for the Paiutes are not more patient with their children than other people, and are sometimes less; but there is a kind of truth in it. The desert has its own way of correcting those who live in it, and it is a slow way, and a silent one, and it does not lift its hand. It shows. It sets the fact before you and waits, with that immense, unhurried, uninterested attention which is the chief quality of the country, until you see it. And those who have seen it once do not, as a rule, need to be shown again.

As for the mules, the Dutchman's teams came in the next night as was expected, forty miles from the last well, with the dust caked white on their flanks and their heads hanging; and the tank was low, and there was the kicking and screaming that Mrs. Hallam had foretold, and the Dutchman swore in two languages at the station and the spring and the country and his own mother that bore him. Davy stood at the corner of the corral in the dark and watched it all. He did not cry. He watched the last mules come down to the bottom of the tank and put their noses into the mud there and lift them dripping and bawl; and when it was over and the men had gone to their blankets under the ramada, his mother found him still standing there, with his small hands holding to the top rail and his face turned toward the tank, in which a little starlight now lay very thin and far down.

She did not say anything. She put her hand on his head a moment, and then she went in, and after a while he came in too and went to bed.

The spring ran on in the night, filling the tank slowly, as it had done since before there were any mules in the country, or any men, or any law but the one law; and out on the mesa the creosote stood each in its own measured space and took no more than its share, and the sand in the wash lay gray and level and gave no sign of what it had swallowed. In the morning the alfalfa was yellow at the tips. It greened again in a week, when the water came back to it; but the boy, who went down every day to look, remembered the yellow.

Here is an excerpt of Mary Austin's writing, to show you their style:

He had been sitting just so in his library with the lamp behind him and the hollow flare of the coals making an excellent starting place for the House which was now so near him that the mere exhibition in shop windows of the stuffs with which it was being modernly renewed, was enough to set him off for it. It was so near now, that since the announcement of their engagement in September, he had moved through all its obligations benumbed by the white, blinding flash thrown backward from its consummating moment, the moment of her cry to him, of their welding at the core of light and harmony, bounded inevitably by the approaching date of marriage. It had been, he recalled on some one of those occasions of social approval by which it appeared engagements in the Best Society proceeded, that he had sat thus, waiting until the clock ticked on the moment when he might properly join her, sat so full of the sense of her that for the instant he accepted her unannounced appearance at the darkened doorway as the mere extension of his white-heated fancy. The next moment as she charged into the circle of the lamp he saw that the umbra of some strange electrical excitement hung about her. It fairly crackled between them as he rose hurriedly to his feet.

"You have come, Eunice! You have come——" But he saw well enough what she had come for. She laid the case on the table, but as she tugged impatiently at her glove, the fringe of her wrap caught the clasp of it and scattered the jewels on the cloth. She tried then to put the ring beside them, but her hand shook so that it fell and rolled upon the floor behind them. Peter picked it up quietly, but he did not offer it to her hand again.

"I have come," said Eunice, "to say what in my mother's house I was afraid of being interrupted in saying; what you must see, what my mother won't see."

"I see you are greatly excited about something!"

"I'm not, I'm not.... That is ... I am, but not in the way you think," she was sharp with insistence; "that is what you and mother always say, that I'm nervous or excited, and all the time you don't see."

"What is it I don't see, Eunice?"

"That I can't stand it, that I can't go on with it, that it is dreadful to me,—dreadful!"

"What is dreadful?"

"Everything, being engaged—being married and giving up...." It was fairly racked out of her by some inward torture to which he had not the key.

"Of course, Eunice, if you don't wish to be married so soon——" Peter was all at sea. He brought a chair for her, and perceiving that he would go on standing as long as she did, she sat upon the edge of it but kept both the arms as a measure of defence. The slight act of doing something for her restored him for the moment to reality; he bent over her. "I've never wanted to hurry you, dearest—— It shall be when you say." She put up her hands suddenly with a shivering movement.

"Oh, never, never at all; never to you!" Peter could feel that working its track of desolation inward, but the first instinctive movement of his surface was to close over the wound. He took it as he knew he could only take it: as the explosive crisis of the virginal resistance which he remembered he had heard came to girls when marriage loomed upon them. He took a turn down the room to steady himself, praying dumbly for the right word.

"It isn't as if I didn't respect you"—she was eager in explanation, hurried and stumbling—"as if I didn't know how good you are ... it is only, because we are so different."

"How different, Eunice?"

"Oh ... older, I suppose." She grew quieter; it appeared on the whole they were getting on. "I care for so many things, you know—dancing—and bridge—young things—and you are always reading and reading. Oh! I couldn't stand it." So it was out now. She was jealous of his books, a little. Well, he had been self-absorbed. It occurred to him dimly that the thing to have done if he had known a little more about women, had practised with them, was to have provoked her at this point to the tears which should have sealed the renewal of his claim to her. What he said was, very quietly: "Of course I never meant, Eunice, that you shouldn't have everything you want."

"Oh," she seemed to have found a suffocating quality in his gentleness, against which she struck out with drowning gestures, "if you could only understand what it would mean to me never to have anybody I liked to talk to about things,—anybody I liked to be with all the time!" She was choked and aghast at the enormity of it.

"But I thought...." Peter was not able to go on with that. "Isn't there anybody you like to be with, Eunice?"

"Yes," said Eunice. "Burton Henderson." Mutinous and bright she looked at him out of the chair with a hand on either arm of it poised for flight or defence. After an interval Peter heard his own voice out of a fog rising to the conventional utterance.

"Of course, if you have learned to love him——" "I've loved him all the time." She was so bent on making this clear to him that she was careless what went down before her. "From the very beginning," she said, "but he had so little money, and mother ... I promised you, I know, but it's not as if I ever said I loved you." She should have spared him that! He had not put out a hand to hold her that he should be so pierced through with needless cruelty. But she was bent on clearing her skirts of him.

"Do you think," she expostulated to his stricken silence, "that if I'd cared in the least I'd have made it so easy for you? Can't you see that it was all arranged, that we jumped at you?" All the time she sat opposite him, thrusting swift and hard, there was no diminution of her appealing beauty, the flaming rose of her cheeks and the soft, dark flare of her hair. As if she felt how it belied at every turn the quality of her unyielding intention, her voice railed against him feverishly. "I suppose you think I'm mercenary, and I thought I was, too. You don't know how people like us need money sometimes. All the things we like cost so—all the real things. And poor mamma, she needed things; she'd never had them, and I thought that I could stand being married to you if I could get them that way.... Maybe I could, you know, if you'd been different, more like us I mean. But there was such a lot you didn't understand ... things you hadn't even heard about. I found that out as soon as we were engaged. There wasn't a thing between us; not a thing." It poured scalding hot on Peter's sensitive surfaces: made sensitive by the way in which even in this hour her beauty moved him. He felt tears starting in his heart and prayed they might not come to his face. "So you see as we hadn't anything in common it would be better for us not to go on with it even"—she broke a little at this—"even if there hadn't been anybody else. You see that, don't you?" She dared him to deny it rather than begged the concession of him as she gathered herself for departure.

"I see that."

"You never really belonged to our set, you know——" She rose now and he rose blindly with her; he hoped that she was done, but there was something still. "It hasn't been easy to go through with it.... Mother isn't going to make it any easier. It's natural for her to want me to have everything that money would mean, and I thought that if you would just keep away from her ... you owe something to Burton and me for what we've been through, I think ... just leave it to me to manage in my own way...."

"I shall never trouble you, Eunice." He came close to her then to open the door, seeing that she was to leave him, and he saw too that she had suffered, was at the very ebb and stony bottom of emotion as she hung for the moment in the doorway searching for some winged shaft of separation that should cut her off from the remotest implication of the situation. She found at last the barbedest. All the succeeding time after he closed the door on her was marked for Peter, not by the ticked moments but by successive waves of anguish as that poisoned arrow worked its way to his secret places.

"It isn't as if I had ever loved you; I owe it to Mr. Henderson to remind you that I never said I did.... You know I never liked to have you kiss me." He had in the months that succeeded to that last sight of Eunice Goodward, moments of unbearably wanting to go to her to try for a little to ease his torment in a more tender recognition of it—days when he would have taken from her, gratefully even if she had fooled him and he had seen her do it, whatever would have saved him from the certainty that never even in those first exquisite moments had she been his. The sharp edge of her young sufficiency had lopped off the right limb of his manhood. Never, even in his dreams, if life had allowed him to dream again, should he be able to see himself in any other guise than the meagre, austere front which his obligation to his mother and Ellen had obliged him to present to destiny. She had beggared him of all those aptitudes for passionate relations, by the faith in which he had kept himself inwardly alive. The capacity for loving died in him with the knowledge of not being able to be loved. Out of the anæsthesia of exhaustion from which Italy had revived him, it rolled back upon him that by just the walled imperviousness that shut Eunice Goodward from the appreciation of his passion, he was prevented now from Savilla Dassonville.

It was odd, then, having come to this conclusion in the middle of the night, that when he joined the ladies in the morning he should have experienced a sinking pang in not being able any longer to be sure what Miss Dassonville thought of him. There was in her manner, as she thanked him for the flowers, nothing to ruffle the surface of the bright, impersonal companionship which she had afforded him for weeks past. The occasion which brought them together was an agreement entered into some days earlier, to go and look at palaces, and as they turned past the Saluti to the Grand Canal, he found himself wondering if there had not been a touch of fatuity in his reading of the incident of the morning before. He had gone so far in the night as to think even of leaving Venice, and saw himself now forlornly wishing for some renewal of yesterday's mood to excuse him from the caddishness that such a flight implied. It came out a little later, perhaps, when after traversing many high and resounding marble halls, with a great many rooms opening into one another in a way that suggested rather the avoidance of privacy than its security, they found themselves in one of those gardens of shut delight of which the exteriors of Venetian houses give so little intimation. As she went about from bough to bough of the neglected roses, turned all inward as if they took their florescence from that still lighted human passion which had found its release and centre there, her face glowed for the moment with the colour of her quick sympathies. She turned it on him with an unconscious, tender confidence, which not to meet seemed to Peter, in that gentle enclosure full of warmth and fragrance, to assume the proportions of a betrayal. He did meet it there as she came back to him for the last look from the marble balustrade by which they had descended, covering her hand, there resting, lingeringly with his own. He was awakened only to the implication of this movement by the discovery that she had deeply and exquisitely blushed. It was a further singularity in view of the conviction with which Peter had come through the night, that the mood of protectingness which the girl provoked in him should have multiplied itself in pointing out to him how many ways, if he had not made up his mind not to marry her at all, such a marriage could be made to serve its primal uses. She had turned up her cuff to trail her hand overside as they slid through the lucent water, and the pretty feminine curve of it had brought to mind what the Princess had told him of the shirt-waists she made herself. He decided that she made them very well. But she was too thin for their severity—and if he married her he would have insisted on her wearing them now and then as a tender way to prevent her suspecting that it was on their account he had thought of not marrying her. He saw himself so intrigued by it that, by the time lunch was over, he felt himself in a position which to his own sensitiveness, demanded that he must immediately leave Venice or propose to Miss Dassonville. He caught himself in the act even of trying to fix Miss Dassonville's eye to include her by complicity in the beguilement of the captain, a business which she seemed to have undertaken on her own account on quite other grounds. He perceived with a kind of pride for her that she had the ways of elderly sea-going gentlemen by heart. It was something even if she had failed to charm Peter, that she shouldn't be found quite wanting in it by other men. When they had put him back aboard of the Merrythought they had come to such a pitch among them all, that as the captain leaned above the rail to launch an invitation, he addressed it to Miss Dassonville, as, if not quite the giver of the feast, the mistress of the situation.

"When are you coming to lunch with me?" demanded the captain.

He had been sitting just so in his library with the lamp behind him and the hollow flare of the coals making an excellent starting place for the House which was now so near him that the mere exhibition in shop windows of the stuffs with which it was being modernly renewed, was enough to set him off for it. It was so near now, that since the announcement of their engagement in September, he had moved through all its obligations benumbed by the white, blinding flash thrown backward from its consummating moment, the moment of her cry to him, of their welding at the core of light and harmony, bounded inevitably by the approaching date of marriage. It had been, he recalled on some one of those occasions of social approval by which it appeared engagements in the Best Society proceeded, that he had sat thus, waiting until the clock ticked on the moment when he might properly join her, sat so full of the sense of her that for the instant he accepted her unannounced appearance at the darkened doorway as the mere extension of his white-heated fancy. The next moment as she charged into the circle of the lamp he saw that the umbra of some strange electrical excitement hung about her. It fairly crackled between them as he rose hurriedly to his feet.

"You have come, Eunice! You have come——" But he saw well enough what she had come for. She laid the case on the table, but as she tugged impatiently at her glove, the fringe of her wrap caught the clasp of it and scattered the jewels on the cloth. She tried then to put the ring beside them, but her hand shook so that it fell and rolled upon the floor behind them. Peter picked it up quietly, but he did not offer it to her hand again.

"I have come," said Eunice, "to say what in my mother's house I was afraid of being interrupted in saying; what you must see, what my mother won't see."

"I see you are greatly excited about something!"

"I'm not, I'm not.... That is ... I am, but not in the way you think," she was sharp with insistence; "that is what you and mother always say, that I'm nervous or excited, and all the time you don't see."

"What is it I don't see, Eunice?"

"That I can't stand it, that I can't go on with it, that it is dreadful to me,—dreadful!"

"What is dreadful?"

"Everything, being engaged—being married and giving up...." It was fairly racked out of her by some inward torture to which he had not the key.

"Of course, Eunice, if you don't wish to be married so soon——" Peter was all at sea. He brought a chair for her, and perceiving that he would go on standing as long as she did, she sat upon the edge of it but kept both the arms as a measure of defence. The slight act of doing something for her restored him for the moment to reality; he bent over her. "I've never wanted to hurry you, dearest—— It shall be when you say." She put up her hands suddenly with a shivering movement.

"Oh, never, never at all; never to you!" Peter could feel that working its track of desolation inward, but the first instinctive movement of his surface was to close over the wound. He took it as he knew he could only take it: as the explosive crisis of the virginal resistance which he remembered he had heard came to girls when marriage loomed upon them. He took a turn down the room to steady himself, praying dumbly for the right word.

"It isn't as if I didn't respect you"—she was eager in explanation, hurried and stumbling—"as if I didn't know how good you are ... it is only, because we are so different."

"How different, Eunice?"

"Oh ... older, I suppose." She grew quieter; it appeared on the whole they were getting on. "I care for so many things, you know—dancing—and bridge—young things—and you are always reading and reading. Oh! I couldn't stand it." So it was out now. She was jealous of his books, a little. Well, he had been self-absorbed. It occurred to him dimly that the thing to have done if he had known a little more about women, had practised with them, was to have provoked her at this point to the tears which should have sealed the renewal of his claim to her. What he said was, very quietly: "Of course I never meant, Eunice, that you shouldn't have everything you want."

"Oh," she seemed to have found a suffocating quality in his gentleness, against which she struck out with drowning gestures, "if you could only understand what it would mean to me never to have anybody I liked to talk to about things,—anybody I liked to be with all the time!" She was choked and aghast at the enormity of it.

"But I thought...." Peter was not able to go on with that. "Isn't there anybody you like to be with, Eunice?"

"Yes," said Eunice. "Burton Henderson." Mutinous and bright she looked at him out of the chair with a hand on either arm of it poised for flight or defence. After an interval Peter heard his own voice out of a fog rising to the conventional utterance.

"Of course, if you have learned to love him——" "I've loved him all the time." She was so bent on making this clear to him that she was careless what went down before her. "From the very beginning," she said, "but he had so little money, and mother ... I promised you, I know, but it's not as if I ever said I loved you." She should have spared him that! He had not put out a hand to hold her that he should be so pierced through with needless cruelty. But she was bent on clearing her skirts of him.

"Do you think," she expostulated to his stricken silence, "that if I'd cared in the least I'd have made it so easy for you? Can't you see that it was all arranged, that we jumped at you?" All the time she sat opposite him, thrusting swift and hard, there was no diminution of her appealing beauty, the flaming rose of her cheeks and the soft, dark flare of her hair. As if she felt how it belied at every turn the quality of her unyielding intention, her voice railed against him feverishly. "I suppose you think I'm mercenary, and I thought I was, too. You don't know how people like us need money sometimes. All the things we like cost so—all the real things. And poor mamma, she needed things; she'd never had them, and I thought that I could stand being married to you if I could get them that way.... Maybe I could, you know, if you'd been different, more like us I mean. But there was such a lot you didn't understand ... things you hadn't even heard about. I found that out as soon as we were engaged. There wasn't a thing between us; not a thing." It poured scalding hot on Peter's sensitive surfaces: made sensitive by the way in which even in this hour her beauty moved him. He felt tears starting in his heart and prayed they might not come to his face. "So you see as we hadn't anything in common it would be better for us not to go on with it even"—she broke a little at this—"even if there hadn't been anybody else. You see that, don't you?" She dared him to deny it rather than begged the concession of him as she gathered herself for departure.

"I see that."

"You never really belonged to our set, you know——" She rose now and he rose blindly with her; he hoped that she was done, but there was something still. "It hasn't been easy to go through with it.... Mother isn't going to make it any easier. It's natural for her to want me to have everything that money would mean, and I thought that if you would just keep away from her ... you owe something to Burton and me for what we've been through, I think ... just leave it to me to manage in my own way...."

"I shall never trouble you, Eunice." He came close to her then to open the door, seeing that she was to leave him, and he saw too that she had suffered, was at the very ebb and stony bottom of emotion as she hung for the moment in the doorway searching for some winged shaft of separation that should cut her off from the remotest implication of the situation. She found at last the barbedest. All the succeeding time after he closed the door on her was marked for Peter, not by the ticked moments but by successive waves of anguish as that poisoned arrow worked its way to his secret places.

"It isn't as if I had ever loved you; I owe it to Mr. Henderson to remind you that I never said I did.... You know I never liked to have you kiss me." He had in the months that succeeded to that last sight of Eunice Goodward, moments of unbearably wanting to go to her to try for a little to ease his torment in a more tender recognition of it—days when he would have taken from her, gratefully even if she had fooled him and he had seen her do it, whatever would have saved him from the certainty that never even in those first exquisite moments had she been his. The sharp edge of her young sufficiency had lopped off the right limb of his manhood. Never, even in his dreams, if life had allowed him to dream again, should he be able to see himself in any other guise than the meagre, austere front which his obligation to his mother and Ellen had obliged him to present to destiny. She had beggared him of all those aptitudes for passionate relations, by the faith in which he had kept himself inwardly alive. The capacity for loving died in him with the knowledge of not being able to be loved. Out of the anæsthesia of exhaustion from which Italy had revived him, it rolled back upon him that by just the walled imperviousness that shut Eunice Goodward from the appreciation of his passion, he was prevented now from Savilla Dassonville.

It was odd, then, having come to this conclusion in the middle of the night, that when he joined the ladies in the morning he should have experienced a sinking pang in not being able any longer to be sure what Miss Dassonville thought of him. There was in her manner, as she thanked him for the flowers, nothing to ruffle the surface of the bright, impersonal companionship which she had afforded him for weeks past. The occasion which brought them together was an agreement entered into some days earlier, to go and look at palaces, and as they turned past the Saluti to the Grand Canal, he found himself wondering if there had not been a touch of fatuity in his reading of the incident of the morning before. He had gone so far in the night as to think even of leaving Venice, and saw himself now forlornly wishing for some renewal of yesterday's mood to excuse him from the caddishness that such a flight implied. It came out a little later, perhaps, when after traversing many high and resounding marble halls, with a great many rooms opening into one another in a way that suggested rather the avoidance of privacy than its security, they found themselves in one of those gardens of shut delight of which the exteriors of Venetian houses give so little intimation. As she went about from bough to bough of the neglected roses, turned all inward as if they took their florescence from that still lighted human passion which had found its release and centre there, her face glowed for the moment with the colour of her quick sympathies. She turned it on him with an unconscious, tender confidence, which not to meet seemed to Peter, in that gentle enclosure full of warmth and fragrance, to assume the proportions of a betrayal. He did meet it there as she came back to him for the last look from the marble balustrade by which they had descended, covering her hand, there resting, lingeringly with his own. He was awakened only to the implication of this movement by the discovery that she had deeply and exquisitely blushed. It was a further singularity in view of the conviction with which Peter had come through the night, that the mood of protectingness which the girl provoked in him should have multiplied itself in pointing out to him how many ways, if he had not made up his mind not to marry her at all, such a marriage could be made to serve its primal uses. She had turned up her cuff to trail her hand overside as they slid through the lucent water, and the pretty feminine curve of it had brought to mind what the Princess had told him of the shirt-waists she made herself. He decided that she made them very well. It was not until the lamp had been lit and the girl had gone off down the arroyo trail to her own people that Anne Rendell was able to bring herself to the point of it, though she had been carrying it about with her all day as one carries a letter that must be posted and yet keeps finding in the pocket. She had meant, indeed, to say it at noon, when Hollis had come in from the lower field with the dust of the ditch-cutting still on him and the look he wore at such times of being pleased with the land for having behaved so exactly as he had foretold. But there had been something in that look, some boyish confidence in the reasonableness of things which she could not bring herself to be the first to disturb, and she had let the meal go by in talk of the headgate and of whether the Morales boys could be had for the second cutting. Now, with the long blue dusk pressing against the windows and the smell of the greasewood coming in at the door, it appeared to her that if she did not say it to-night she would never say it, and that the not saying would harden about her like the adobe in which, for six years, she had been walled.

He was at the table with his accounts spread under the lamp, a pencil behind his ear and another between his teeth, and he did not look up when she came and stood across from him with her hands on the back of a chair, so that she had for a moment the advantage of seeing him as she was not often able to see him now, simply as a man she had married. He had grown heavier about the shoulders; there was a line between his brows which she could remember the coming of, the year the water failed; and the hair at his temples, which had been so fair when he came courting her in her aunt's parlour on Pine Street, had taken on the bleached and indeterminate colour of the country itself. It struck her, with a pang she had not reckoned on, that the land had been at him as patiently as it had been at the fence-posts, and that she had not noticed it happening.

"Hollis," she said, "I have had a letter from Mr. Kessler."

He took the pencil out of his mouth, but he finished the column before he answered her. "Kessler? That's your old music man, isn't it, in the city?"

"He isn't in the city now. He has gone East. He has a place, a very good place, with the conservatory in Boston, and he writes...." She found that she must stop there and begin again, not because her voice failed her, but because she perceived in the very mildness of his attention that he had not the least notion of what was coming, and the unfairness of springing it on him unarmed was more than she had allowed for. "He writes that there is a vacancy for an assistant in the vocal department. He has kept it open for me until the first of the month."

"For you?" He laid the pencil down now, quite gently, parallel with the edge of the ledger, as he had a way of doing with things when he wished to give them his full regard. "That's a fine compliment, Anne. I'm glad he remembers you."

"It isn't a compliment. It's an offer."

"Well——" He smiled at her across the lamp, the slow, considering smile which had once seemed to her the most restful thing in the world, and which she saw now to be the smile of a man who has never had to consider that the ground could shift under him. "You'll write him a nice letter, I expect. You always did write a nice letter."

It was this, more than anything, the assumption so complete that it did not even know itself for an assumption, which brought her round the chair and into it, sitting very straight with her hands folded on the oilcloth, as if she were a petitioner at some office where the hours were nearly over.

"I mean to take it, Hollis."

He did not answer at once. Outside, a little owl began its soft, interrogative note from the cottonwoods by the ditch, and she heard with an odd distinctness the tick of the cooling stove behind her. She had prepared herself for anger, for the dark flush that came up into his face on the rare occasions when he was crossed by a neighbour over the water; she had prepared herself even for the possibility that he would laugh. What she had not prepared herself for was the look which came instead, a kind of slow bewilderment, as if he had walked into a room of his own house and found the furniture all changed about.

"Take it," he said. "Go to Boston, you mean."

"Yes."

"For how long?"

"I don't know. For as long——" She looked down at her hands. "For as long as it takes, I suppose."

"As long as what takes, Anne?" He leaned towards her, and his voice was so reasonable, so patiently bent on understanding, that she felt it close over her like water. "I'm not following you. If you're tired of the place, if it's been too lonesome this winter, why, there's no reason you shouldn't go down to your aunt's for a month or two. I've said so before. We can manage that, now the crop's in."

"It isn't a month or two. And it isn't my aunt's." She was conscious of speaking too quickly, of the words tumbling out of her ahead of the order in which she had so often, lying awake beside him, arranged them. "It isn't that I'm lonely, though I am lonely, Hollis, I am lonely in a way you would never.... It's that I'm going out. Like a lamp. Like a lamp with the oil not put in. Every day a little lower, and nobody noticing, because there's always so much to do, and the light from the window is enough to work by."

"You've been reading," he said, and she saw that he was relieved to have found a handle for it. "Those books Mrs. Trask sends you. They put notions in a woman's head."

"They haven't put anything in. They've only made me see what was taken out."

She was sorry the moment she had said it; she saw it go into him and saw him, after the fashion of his kind, refuse to let it show. He got up and went to the door and stood looking out into the dark, where there was nothing at all to be seen but the low line of the mesa against the stars and the single far light of the Moraleses' cabin, and when he spoke again it was with his back to her.

"I didn't know I'd taken anything out of you, Anne."

"Oh, not you!" It was wrung from her. "Not you, Hollis. Not anything you did. You've been good to me. You've always been good. That's what makes it so——" She could not finish that. She pressed her hands together until the knuckles whitened. "It's the life. It's the being here, and the dust, and the days all alike, and the never hearing anything but the wind and the cows and the windmill. I used to sing. You remember I used to sing. Mr. Kessler said I had the best natural placement of any pupil he'd ever had west of Chicago. And I haven't sung, not really, not so as anybody heard, in six years."

"You sing to the Morales children," he said, still not turning.

"I sing to the Morales children," she repeated, and it was astonishing to her how bitter it sounded, coming back. "And to the hens, and to the dishpan. Hollis, you don't know what it is to have a thing in you that wants to come out, and to feel it every year shrinking back, getting smaller, getting more ashamed of itself, until some day you'll go to open your mouth and there'll be nothing there. Nothing at all. Only an old woman with good bread."

He came back from the door then and stood over her, and she saw that the bewilderment had gone out of his face and left it stern, almost grey, in the yellow lamplight. "And me?" he said. "Where do I come in, in all this? Have you thought about that?"

"I have thought of nothing else for three days."

"Three days." He took that in, and she could see him measure it, see him go back over the three days in his mind, the meals, the evenings, the night before last when she had let him put his arm about her in the dark and had lain so still under it. "Three days you've had this letter, and said nothing."

"I didn't know how."

"You might have tried. You might have given me the chance to——" He broke off, and she had the sense, which was to come back to her afterward with a particular sharpness, that he had been about to say something which would have altered everything, and had at the last moment shut his mouth upon it out of some masculine pride she could not reach. What he said instead was, "I suppose it's settled, then. I suppose you've written him already."

"No. I haven't written. I wanted ... I wanted you to understand first."

"Understand!" He sat down abruptly across from her, the ledger pushed aside so that the lamp stood alone between them like an arbiter. "What is it you want me to understand, Anne? That my wife is going three thousand miles away to teach singing in a city I never saw, among people I never heard of, for as long as it takes? I understand that well enough. I'm not a fool. What I don't understand is what you expect me to do about it. Sell out? Go with you? Stand behind a counter in Boston, maybe, and carry your music for you?"

"I never asked you to go."

The words were out, and lay there on the oilcloth between them, and neither of them could take them up. She had not meant them so; she had meant only that she would not drag him from the land, that she knew what it was to him, that she was not so selfish as to ask him to give for her what she could not give for him. But she saw by the way his hand closed slowly on the edge of the table that he had taken them in another sense, the only sense, perhaps, that a man in his position could have taken them, and that they had gone down past all his defences to some place where he had kept, unexamined, the simple faith that she was his as the water rights were his, by deed and use and the long patience of possession.

"No," he said, after a moment. "No, you didn't ask me that."

"Hollis, I didn't mean——"

"I think you did." He was quite quiet now. The owl had stopped, and in the silence she could hear the windmill turning over slowly in the night breeze, with the little catch and creak at the top of the stroke that he had been meaning all summer to oil. "I think you've been meaning it a long while, maybe without knowing. I've watched you, Anne. I'm not so thick as you take me for. I've seen you stand at that window evenings like you were waiting for a train. I thought it would pass. I thought, when we got the new ditch through and the alfalfa came on, and we could put a floor in the front room and get you that organ from Los Angeles——"

"An organ!" She laughed, and was horrified to hear herself, for it was not a kind laugh, and she saw him flinch from it. "Oh, Hollis, an organ in the front room, with a floor under it! As if that were the thing! As if I wanted something to play on, when what I want is somebody to play to. Somebody who would know, when I'd done it well, that I'd done it well. You'd sit and listen, and say it was very nice, and go out to look at the stock. I know you would. You can't help it. You haven't the ear. It isn't a fault. But it means that whatever I do here, I do it into the wind."

It appeared to her, even as she said it, that she had gone further than she had any right to go, and that the thing she was saying, though true, was true in a way that made it no better than a lie. For she remembered, with a vividness that turned her cold, the evening of their first spring here, before the drought, when she had sung for him on the step in the dusk, an old song of her mother's, and he had sat with his hat between his knees and not moved for a long while after, and then had got up and gone off quickly into the dark without a word; and she had known, without his telling her, that he had gone because he could not trust his face. She had forgotten that. She had let six years of dust bury it, and now it rose up between them like a ghost she had herself conjured, and she could not tell whether he remembered it too.

If he did, he gave no sign. He sat looking at the lamp, and when he spoke it was in the flat, even voice he used for bargaining over feed.

"How much does it pay, this place of Kessler's?"

She told him. It was more than the ranch had cleared in the best of the six years, and she saw him take that in, too, and lay it away with the rest.

"Well," he said, "it seems you'd do better without me than with me. On every count."

"That's not fair."

"Isn't it? I'm trying to see it the way you see it, Anne. You've got a gift, and I've been sitting on it. You've got a chance, and I'm the thing that's in the way of it. I don't know what's fair. I never was much for knowing that. I only know I took you out here believing you wanted to come, and I've worked every day of six years believing it was for both of us, and now you tell me it's been like being buried alive. What am I supposed to say to that? Thank you? Good luck? Write when you get there?"

She could not answer him. She sat with her hands pressed between her knees and the tears running down her face without any sound, and it was the more dreadful to her that she did not feel she had the right to them, that they were in some way an unfair advantage which she was taking of him, and that he knew it. For a long while he let her cry, and did not move to come to her, and she understood that he would not; that the thing in him which would once have crossed the room at the first sign of her distress had been turned back, not by anything she had done to-night, but by the long accumulation of things not done, of evenings when she had stood at the window and he had seen her there and had gone out quietly to the stock, believing it would pass.

"I'm not leaving you, Hollis," she said at last, when she could. "Not the way you mean. I'm only going where I can breathe. You could come, in the winters, when there's nothing to do here. Or I could come back summers. People do. People arrange these things."

"People," he said. "Your kind of people, maybe." He got up and began, with great deliberateness, to gather up the papers on the table, squaring their edges, laying the pencils on top. "I'll tell you what I think, Anne, and then I won't say any more about it. I think if you go, you'll go. I think you'll get there and find it's all you thought, and more, and you'll write me nice letters about it, because you always did write a nice letter, and every year the letters will come a little further apart, and every year it'll be a little harder to make the trip, and one day you'll look up and find you've been gone longer than you were here. And I'll be sitting at this table with the accounts. That's what I think."

"And if I don't go?"

He stopped, with the ledger in his hands, and for the first time that evening looked full at her, a long look in which she saw, with a sinking that she could not have explained, that he had already begun, in that half-hour, to do without her.

"If you don't go," he said, "you'll stand at that window. And I'll have to watch you stand there, knowing what you're thinking. I don't know which would be worse. I don't know that it's for me to say."

He went out then, not hurriedly, taking the lantern from its nail by the door, and she heard his steps go off across the yard towards the windmill, and after a while the clink of the oil can and the small protesting shriek of the iron as he climbed. The revealed whiteness of her wrist, the intimacy of her relaxed posture, for though her mind had played into his as freely as a child in a meadow, she had been always, as regards her person, a little prim with him, had lent to their errand of house visiting a personal note in which it was absurdly apt for them to have run across Captain Dunham of the Merrythought at the door of the Consulate. He told himself afterward that he would not have done it if he had recalled in time the friendly seaman's romantic appreciation of the situation between himself and Miss Dassonville. He saw himself so intrigued by it that, by the time lunch was over, he felt himself in a position which to his own sensitiveness, demanded that he must immediately leave Venice or propose to Miss Dassonville. He caught himself in the act even of trying to fix Miss Dassonville's eye to include her by complicity in the beguilement of the captain, a business which she seemed to have undertaken on her own account on quite other grounds. He perceived with a kind of pride for her that she had the ways of elderly sea-going gentlemen by heart. It was something even if she had failed to charm Peter, that she shouldn't be found quite wanting in it by other men. When they had put him back aboard of the Merrythought they had come to such a pitch among them all, that as the captain leaned above the rail to launch an invitation, he addressed it to Miss Dassonville, as, if not quite the giver of the feast, the mistress of the situation.

"When are you coming to lunch with me?" demanded the captain.
