It was not until the carriage had turned in at the gate, where the two stone urns which had always been too large for it stood up out of the early dusk with something of the air of elderly relatives who had been kept waiting, that Anstice Wellwood admitted to herself that she had been afraid of coming. She had been all the way from Inyo, and through the three days of the plains, where the land lay out on either hand in the flat, inexpressive monotony of a face that has given up expecting anything of you, so full of the business of returning that she had not once looked squarely at what she should find at the end of it. She looked now, as the wheels ground upon the gravel which nobody, it appeared, had raked since her grandmother died, and saw that the house had shrunk. It had shrunk in the way houses do in which one has been a child, not so much in its dimensions as in its capacity for keeping her out, and she felt, getting down at the steps with her bag in her hand because there was nobody to take it from her, a pang so sharp at being suffered to walk into it unchallenged that she very nearly turned round to the driver and asked to be taken back to the hotel.

It was Ludlow himself who prevented her. He came out upon the porch before she had got to the top of the steps, a little stooped, a little gray at the temples, with the lamp of the hall behind him throwing his shadow down at her feet like something he had cast in welcome before he could find the words for it. For the moment she did not know him. That is to say, she knew perfectly that it was Ludlow Carrington, her cousin, with whom she had shared every summer of her girlhood in this very house, and who had kissed her good-bye at the station twelve years ago with the tears quite frankly standing in his eyes; but she did not know this man who held out his hand to her with a kind of shy formality, as though he were not certain how much of that old intimacy he might still lay claim to.

"Anstice!" he said. "You have come—you have really come——" And then, as if the inadequacy of it struck him, "I meant to meet the train. I had the hour wrong. I have had everything wrong to-day."

"It doesn't matter in the least." She gave him her hand and he kept it, turning her a little so that the lamplight fell on her, and she bore his scrutiny as she would have borne the inspection of a doctor, knowing that the desert had written on her face whatever it chose to write and that she had not been at the pains to erase it. "You see, I've grown brown," she offered him by way of mitigation.

"You've grown——" He stopped, and she saw him put away whatever he had been going to say as one puts a letter back into a drawer unread. "You've grown like Grandmother," he finished. "About the eyes. I suppose I had forgotten she had any eyes but the ones she used to look at us with when we came in late from the river."

They went in together, and it was a piece of the strangeness of the evening that the hall should smell exactly as it had always smelled, of beeswax and old matting and the faint dry sweetness of rose leaves which her grandmother had kept in a blue jar on the newel post, and which, it seemed, Ludlow had never had the heart to throw away. She stood a moment breathing it with her eyes shut, and when she opened them she found him watching her with an expression she could not at once interpret; it was as though he had prepared himself for her coming as for some ordeal, and was now astonished, and a little disappointed, to find it so easy.

It came out a little later, at dinner, which they ate alone in the long dining-room at a table that might have seated twelve, with the old Irishwoman who had been cook in her grandmother's time moving about behind them in a silence charged with a kind of personal grievance at Anstice for having been so long away, that he had lived here by himself since the spring. He told it with a lightness that did not deceive her, as he might have mentioned that the roof wanted mending.

"Marian has gone to her people in Hartford," he said. "For the present. We thought it best." And then, before she could arrange her face for it, "You needn't look as though I had told you of a death, Anstice. Nobody has died. That is precisely the trouble with it."

"I didn't know," she said. "You never wrote."

"I never wrote about anything, did I? Not for years." He turned the stem of his glass slowly between his fingers, and she remembered, with a rush of tenderness which surprised her by its force, that he had always done that as a boy with whatever came to his hand when he had something to say and did not know how to begin it, a pebble or a dandelion stalk or the rim of his hat. "I used to begin letters to you," he went on. "Long ones. I would sit up half the night over them. And then in the morning I would read them over and see that there was nothing in them that would interest a woman who had gone to live among Indians and mountains and—what was it you wrote once?—the wind that comes down off the Sierras smelling of snow and sage. What had I to set beside that? The price of hides. The new pastor at St. John's. The Leffingwells' boy getting into trouble at Yale."

"You might have known I should have liked the price of hides from you better than the Sierras from anybody else."

He gave her a quick look at that, and then a slower one, and she saw that she had touched something which he had kept a long time in the dark and which flinched now at the light. "That is kind of you," he said, with a formality that shut it off; and she had the sense, which was to grow upon her all the evening, of moving about in him as she had moved about in the house, finding everything in its old place and yet nothing quite where she could put her hand upon it.

They had their coffee in the library, where a fire had been laid against the October chill, and she found that she was able to sit in her grandmother's chair without any of those pangs she had dreaded, because it had been so obviously sat in since by somebody else. There was a work-basket on the table at its elbow, with a piece of fine embroidery folded upon it and a needle still threaded, as if it had been laid down in the middle of a stitch and never taken up again. Anstice did not touch it. She saw Ludlow see that she did not touch it, and it seemed for the moment to establish between them a kind of compact, the first clear understanding they had arrived at, that there were things in this room they were not, just yet, to speak of.

"And you," he said, settling himself across the hearth in the low chair which had always been his, though his knees came up into it now in a way that made him look, she thought, rather like a heron folded for the night, "you haven't told me anything. You've let me run on about myself the whole of dinner. It's what you always did. You used to sit on the river wall and let me tell you what I was going to be, and never say a word about yourself, and then go and do something that made all my talk ridiculous."

"I never meant to make anything ridiculous."

"You didn't need to mean it." He laughed, but it was a laugh without much breath behind it. "Well, there's nothing ridiculous left to make. I am what you see. I am the president of the Thessaly Tanning Company and a vestryman and a director of the Second National Bank, and I am forty-one years old, and my wife is in Hartford. Now it is your turn. Tell me about Robert."

She had known that it would come, and she had thought she was ready for it; but she found, with his eyes upon her, that the thing she had made of Robert's death in the three years since, the smooth, worn surface she had shaped it to by handling, so that she could take it out and show it to people without cutting them or herself, was not the thing that wanted telling to Ludlow. He was the one person in the world, it struck her, to whom she could not give the shaped and polished version, because he had known her before there had been any Robert at all, and would know at once, by the very finish of it, how much had gone into the polishing.

"It was very quick," she said at last. "We were in the Panamints. He had gone up alone to look at a claim, and his horse came back without him, and the men found him two days later at the bottom of a wash. They said he could not have suffered. They always say that, I think, out there. It is a kind of courtesy of the country, like giving you water before they ask your name."

"Anstice——"

"No, let me tell it. I want to tell it to you." She leaned forward, and the fire leaped up between them, making a little wall of brightness on which she seemed to see the thing she meant to say before she said it. "I have never told anybody the true part. People write to you, and you write back, and it all goes into words that have been used so many times they have no edges left. But what I want you to know, Lud, is that I wasn't sorry in the way I should have been. Oh, I was sorry. I was desolate. But there was something underneath it that was not desolate at all, that was—I can't find the word for it—that was almost glad to be left alone with the country. As if I had married Robert to get there, and now that I was there I didn't need him. Isn't that dreadful? I have been ashamed of it every day for three years, and I can't stop being it."

She had not known she was going to say so much, and when she had said it she sat back, breathing quickly, appalled at the nakedness of it, and waited for him to be shocked. He was not shocked. He sat looking into the fire with his long hands hanging between his knees, and the expression on his face, when at length he turned it to her, was one she had seen there only once before, on the evening of her wedding, when he had stood a little apart from the others at the station and had seemed to be looking not at her at all but at something a long way off, down the track, beyond the bend where the train would carry her out of sight.

"I don't think it is dreadful," he said slowly. "I think it is the most natural thing I ever heard. I think if I had been in your place I should have felt exactly the same." He paused, and she saw his hand close upon the arm of his chair as if to steady himself against some current that set too strongly in one direction. "Do you know, I very nearly came out there? The year after you went. I had my trunk packed."

"Ludlow! You never told me."

"I never told anybody. Grandmother found the trunk. She came up to my room one night—you remember how she used to come, without knocking, with that candle she would carry long after the gas was in—and she stood looking at it, and then she looked at me, and she said, 'I suppose you know the Company can't go on without a Carrington in it.' That was all. She didn't argue. She never argued, did she? She just stood there with her candle, letting the hot wax run down on her fingers, until I said I supposed I knew it. Then she went away, and in the morning I unpacked."

The fire had burned down a little, and in the reduced light Anstice could see the shape of the room changing about them, the bookshelves receding, the portrait of their great-grandfather over the mantel withdrawing into its own darkness so that only the white of his stock and the sharp, unforgiving glint of his eye remained to oversee them. It was odd, then, that she should feel the old house closing in upon her with a protectingness which was very like that of her grandmother herself, who had kept them both, it now appeared, at a cost neither of them had suspected. She thought of the trunk standing packed in the little room under the eaves, and of the boy sitting on the edge of his bed in the candlelight with his hands hanging between his knees, just so, as he sat now, and something rose in her throat which she had to swallow twice before she could speak.

"And Marian," she said. "Did Marian know?"

"Marian?" He seemed to have to bring her back from a long way off. "No. How should she? It was before Marian. I married Marian two years after. She was the Delafield girl, you remember, from the house with the iron deer on the lawn. You used to say the deer looked as if it were waiting for someone to tell it it might go home." He smiled faintly. "I think Marian was a little like that. Waiting to be told she might go home. And I never told her, because I didn't know where home was for either of us. We were very civil to each other. We were civil for fourteen years. And then one day last spring she said she thought she would go and stay with her mother for a while, and I said I thought perhaps she had better, and we were both so relieved at being agreed about something that we nearly kissed each other good-bye." He broke off, and she saw that he had not meant to say so much either, and was as appalled at it as she had been. "You see," he said, with a kind of rueful lightness, "I have confessed as much as you. Now we are quits."

"We were always quits, Lud."

"No," he said. "No, we weren't. You always had the better of me. You had the courage for things. You went." He got up abruptly and went to the window, where the curtains had not been drawn, and stood looking out at the dark lawn, at the black shapes of the elms which had given the house its name and which tossed faintly now in a little wind that had come up with the night. "I have stood here a great many evenings," he said, without turning round, "trying to imagine what you were seeing. I bought books. I have a whole shelf of books about your desert, there behind you. I know the names of the plants. I know there is a thing called a creosote bush, and that it smells, when it rains, like—what do they say?—like the inside of an old church."

"It smells like rain," said Anstice. "Only like rain. There is nothing else in the world it smells like."

He turned at that, and she saw, by the little light that was left, that his eyes were wet; and she understood all at once, with a clearness that went through her like the cold of the high passes at dawn, that he had been envying her all these years, had been living a second life out there beside her in the country of her choosing, a life made up of names out of books and the few poor sentences she had sent him at Christmas; and that she, for her part, had never once in all that time thought of him as anything but safely and forever here, part of the house and the elms and the river wall, kept for her like the rose leaves in the blue jar, against her coming back. The injustice of it struck her so sharply that she half rose from her chair.

"Lud," she said, "come and sit down. Come and sit down by me, and let me tell you about the creosote."

He came and sat, not in his own chair, but on the low stool at her feet which had been his place in the old days when their grandmother read aloud to them on winter evenings, and he leaned his head back against the arm of her chair as he used to lean it then, so that she had only to put down her hand to touch his hair. She did not touch it. But she began, in a low voice, as one tells a story to a child who is not quite asleep, to tell him how the rain came down off the Coso range in the late summer, all in an hour, after weeks of a sky like hot brass; how the washes ran bank-full with water the color of chocolate and the whole floor of the valley gave up its smell at once, so that you could stand at your door and breathe it as you would breathe the breath of some great animal that had waked beside you in the night; how the Paiute women went out afterward to gather the seeds of the chia, and sang while they gathered, songs that had no beginning and no end but went round and round like the circling of a hawk; and how she had stood once at the edge of the Panamints, a month after Robert died, and looked across forty miles of light to the other range, and had known, with the certainty of something written in the blood, that she would never be able to live anywhere else.

"And yet you have come back," said Ludlow, when she had done.

"I have come back," she agreed. "Grandmother left me the house. Didn't you know? Half of it. She left you the other half. The lawyer wrote me in August."

He sat up at that and turned round to look at her, and she saw that he had not known, and that the knowledge was working in him some change which she could not at once follow, as a stone dropped in still water works its circles outward to the shore.

"Then she meant——" he began, and stopped.

"I think she meant us to be here together. For a little while, at least. I think she knew something about both of us that we didn't know ourselves." Anstice looked at the work-basket on the table beside her, with the needle still threaded in the fine embroidery, and this time she put out her hand and laid it there, lightly, upon the folded linen. "She always did know, didn't she? It was the most uncomfortable thing about her."

Ludlow laughed then, really laughed, for the first time that evening, with his head thrown back against her chair, and the sound of it went up through the dim room and set the old glass of the bookcases faintly ringing. It seemed to Anstice that the portrait over the mantel relaxed a little in its darkness, and that the house, which had been holding its breath ever since she came in at the gate, let it go at last in a long sigh that was only the wind in the elms.

"I shall have to write to Marian," he said presently, when he had done laughing. "I shall have to tell her you have come."

"Yes," said Anstice. "You must tell her. And you must tell her, Lud, that you have a shelf of books about the desert. I don't believe you ever told her that."

"No," he said, after a moment. "I don't believe I ever did."

They sat on together until the fire was quite out, and the old Irishwoman came to the door with a candle and stood there, as their grandmother used to stand, looking at them without a word until they rose and went up to bed. And Anstice, lying awake afterward in the room that had been hers as a girl, with the window open on the October night and the smell of wet leaves coming in from the lawn, found that she was not thinking of the Panamints at all, but of a trunk packed and unpacked in a little room under the eaves, twenty years ago, by the light of a candle that dripped hot wax on an old woman's fingers.

Here is an excerpt of Mary Austin's writing, to show you their style:

He had been sitting just so in his library with the lamp behind him and the hollow flare of the coals making an excellent starting place for the House which was now so near him that the mere exhibition in shop windows of the stuffs with which it was being modernly renewed, was enough to set him off for it. It was so near now, that since the announcement of their engagement in September, he had moved through all its obligations benumbed by the white, blinding flash thrown backward from its consummating moment, the moment of her cry to him, of their welding at the core of light and harmony, bounded inevitably by the approaching date of marriage. It had been, he recalled on some one of those occasions of social approval by which it appeared engagements in the Best Society proceeded, that he had sat thus, waiting until the clock ticked on the moment when he might properly join her, sat so full of the sense of her that for the instant he accepted her unannounced appearance at the darkened doorway as the mere extension of his white-heated fancy. The next moment as she charged into the circle of the lamp he saw that the umbra of some strange electrical excitement hung about her. It fairly crackled between them as he rose hurriedly to his feet.

"You have come, Eunice! You have come——" But he saw well enough what she had come for. She laid the case on the table, but as she tugged impatiently at her glove, the fringe of her wrap caught the clasp of it and scattered the jewels on the cloth. She tried then to put the ring beside them, but her hand shook so that it fell and rolled upon the floor behind them. Peter picked it up quietly, but he did not offer it to her hand again.

"I have come," said Eunice, "to say what in my mother's house I was afraid of being interrupted in saying; what you must see, what my mother won't see."

"I see you are greatly excited about something!"

"I'm not, I'm not.... That is ... I am, but not in the way you think," she was sharp with insistence; "that is what you and mother always say, that I'm nervous or excited, and all the time you don't see."

"What is it I don't see, Eunice?"

"That I can't stand it, that I can't go on with it, that it is dreadful to me,—dreadful!"

"What is dreadful?"

"Everything, being engaged—being married and giving up...." It was fairly racked out of her by some inward torture to which he had not the key.

"Of course, Eunice, if you don't wish to be married so soon——" Peter was all at sea. He brought a chair for her, and perceiving that he would go on standing as long as she did, she sat upon the edge of it but kept both the arms as a measure of defence. The slight act of doing something for her restored him for the moment to reality; he bent over her. "I've never wanted to hurry you, dearest—— It shall be when you say." She put up her hands suddenly with a shivering movement.

"Oh, never, never at all; never to you!" Peter could feel that working its track of desolation inward, but the first instinctive movement of his surface was to close over the wound. He took it as he knew he could only take it: as the explosive crisis of the virginal resistance which he remembered he had heard came to girls when marriage loomed upon them. He took a turn down the room to steady himself, praying dumbly for the right word.

"It isn't as if I didn't respect you"—she was eager in explanation, hurried and stumbling—"as if I didn't know how good you are ... it is only, because we are so different."

"How different, Eunice?"

"Oh ... older, I suppose." She grew quieter; it appeared on the whole they were getting on. "I care for so many things, you know—dancing—and bridge—young things—and you are always reading and reading. Oh! I couldn't stand it." So it was out now. She was jealous of his books, a little. Well, he had been self-absorbed. It occurred to him dimly that the thing to have done if he had known a little more about women, had practised with them, was to have provoked her at this point to the tears which should have sealed the renewal of his claim to her. What he said was, very quietly: "Of course I never meant, Eunice, that you shouldn't have everything you want."

"Oh," she seemed to have found a suffocating quality in his gentleness, against which she struck out with drowning gestures, "if you could only understand what it would mean to me never to have anybody I liked to talk to about things,—anybody I liked to be with all the time!" She was choked and aghast at the enormity of it.

"But I thought...." Peter was not able to go on with that. "Isn't there anybody you like to be with, Eunice?"

"Yes," said Eunice. "Burton Henderson." Mutinous and bright she looked at him out of the chair with a hand on either arm of it poised for flight or defence. After an interval Peter heard his own voice out of a fog rising to the conventional utterance.

"Of course, if you have learned to love him——" "I've loved him all the time." She was so bent on making this clear to him that she was careless what went down before her. "From the very beginning," she said, "but he had so little money, and mother ... I promised you, I know, but it's not as if I ever said I loved you." She should have spared him that! He had not put out a hand to hold her that he should be so pierced through with needless cruelty. But she was bent on clearing her skirts of him.

"Do you think," she expostulated to his stricken silence, "that if I'd cared in the least I'd have made it so easy for you? Can't you see that it was all arranged, that we jumped at you?" All the time she sat opposite him, thrusting swift and hard, there was no diminution of her appealing beauty, the flaming rose of her cheeks and the soft, dark flare of her hair. As if she felt how it belied at every turn the quality of her unyielding intention, her voice railed against him feverishly. "I suppose you think I'm mercenary, and I thought I was, too. You don't know how people like us need money sometimes. All the things we like cost so—all the real things. And poor mamma, she needed things; she'd never had them, and I thought that I could stand being married to you if I could get them that way.... Maybe I could, you know, if you'd been different, more like us I mean. But there was such a lot you didn't understand ... things you hadn't even heard about. I found that out as soon as we were engaged. There wasn't a thing between us; not a thing." It poured scalding hot on Peter's sensitive surfaces: made sensitive by the way in which even in this hour her beauty moved him. He felt tears starting in his heart and prayed they might not come to his face. "So you see as we hadn't anything in common it would be better for us not to go on with it even"—she broke a little at this—"even if there hadn't been anybody else. You see that, don't you?" She dared him to deny it rather than begged the concession of him as she gathered herself for departure.

"I see that."

"You never really belonged to our set, you know——" She rose now and he rose blindly with her; he hoped that she was done, but there was something still. "It hasn't been easy to go through with it.... Mother isn't going to make it any easier. It's natural for her to want me to have everything that money would mean, and I thought that if you would just keep away from her ... you owe something to Burton and me for what we've been through, I think ... just leave it to me to manage in my own way...."

"I shall never trouble you, Eunice." He came close to her then to open the door, seeing that she was to leave him, and he saw too that she had suffered, was at the very ebb and stony bottom of emotion as she hung for the moment in the doorway searching for some winged shaft of separation that should cut her off from the remotest implication of the situation. She found at last the barbedest. All the succeeding time after he closed the door on her was marked for Peter, not by the ticked moments but by successive waves of anguish as that poisoned arrow worked its way to his secret places.

"It isn't as if I had ever loved you; I owe it to Mr. Henderson to remind you that I never said I did.... You know I never liked to have you kiss me." He had in the months that succeeded to that last sight of Eunice Goodward, moments of unbearably wanting to go to her to try for a little to ease his torment in a more tender recognition of it—days when he would have taken from her, gratefully even if she had fooled him and he had seen her do it, whatever would have saved him from the certainty that never even in those first exquisite moments had she been his. The sharp edge of her young sufficiency had lopped off the right limb of his manhood. Never, even in his dreams, if life had allowed him to dream again, should he be able to see himself in any other guise than the meagre, austere front which his obligation to his mother and Ellen had obliged him to present to destiny. She had beggared him of all those aptitudes for passionate relations, by the faith in which he had kept himself inwardly alive. The capacity for loving died in him with the knowledge of not being able to be loved. Out of the anæsthesia of exhaustion from which Italy had revived him, it rolled back upon him that by just the walled imperviousness that shut Eunice Goodward from the appreciation of his passion, he was prevented now from Savilla Dassonville.

It was odd, then, having come to this conclusion in the middle of the night, that when he joined the ladies in the morning he should have experienced a sinking pang in not being able any longer to be sure what Miss Dassonville thought of him. There was in her manner, as she thanked him for the flowers, nothing to ruffle the surface of the bright, impersonal companionship which she had afforded him for weeks past. The occasion which brought them together was an agreement entered into some days earlier, to go and look at palaces, and as they turned past the Saluti to the Grand Canal, he found himself wondering if there had not been a touch of fatuity in his reading of the incident of the morning before. He had gone so far in the night as to think even of leaving Venice, and saw himself now forlornly wishing for some renewal of yesterday's mood to excuse him from the caddishness that such a flight implied. It came out a little later, perhaps, when after traversing many high and resounding marble halls, with a great many rooms opening into one another in a way that suggested rather the avoidance of privacy than its security, they found themselves in one of those gardens of shut delight of which the exteriors of Venetian houses give so little intimation. As she went about from bough to bough of the neglected roses, turned all inward as if they took their florescence from that still lighted human passion which had found its release and centre there, her face glowed for the moment with the colour of her quick sympathies. She turned it on him with an unconscious, tender confidence, which not to meet seemed to Peter, in that gentle enclosure full of warmth and fragrance, to assume the proportions of a betrayal. He did meet it there as she came back to him for the last look from the marble balustrade by which they had descended, covering her hand, there resting, lingeringly with his own. He was awakened only to the implication of this movement by the discovery that she had deeply and exquisitely blushed. It was a further singularity in view of the conviction with which Peter had come through the night, that the mood of protectingness which the girl provoked in him should have multiplied itself in pointing out to him how many ways, if he had not made up his mind not to marry her at all, such a marriage could be made to serve its primal uses. She had turned up her cuff to trail her hand overside as they slid through the lucent water, and the pretty feminine curve of it had brought to mind what the Princess had told him of the shirt-waists she made herself. He decided that she made them very well. But she was too thin for their severity—and if he married her he would have insisted on her wearing them now and then as a tender way to prevent her suspecting that it was on their account he had thought of not marrying her. The revealed whiteness of her wrist, the intimacy of her relaxed posture, for though her mind had played into his as freely as a child in a meadow, she had been always, as regards her person, a little prim with him, had lent to their errand of house visiting a personal note in which it was absurdly apt for them to have run across Captain Dunham of the Merrythought at the door of the Consulate. Mr. Weatheral had some papers which Lessing had sent him to acknowledge there, and it was a piece of the morning's performance, when he had come back from that business, to find that the meeting had taken on—from some mutual discovery of the captain's and Mrs. Merrithew's of a cousin's wife's sister who had married one of the Applegates who was a Dunham on the mother's side—quite the aspect of a family party. It came in the end to the four of them going off at Peter's invitation to have lunch together in a café overhanging the calle. He told himself afterward that he would not have done it if he had recalled in time the friendly seaman's romantic appreciation of the situation between himself and Miss Dassonville. He saw himself so intrigued by it that, by the time lunch was over, he felt himself in a position which to his own sensitiveness, demanded that he must immediately leave Venice or propose to Miss Dassonville. To see the way he was going and to go on in it, had for him the fascination of the abyss. He caught himself in the act even of trying to fix Miss Dassonville's eye to include her by complicity in the beguilement of the captain, a business which she seemed to have undertaken on her own account on quite other grounds. He perceived with a kind of pride for her that she had the ways of elderly sea-going gentlemen by heart. It was something even if she had failed to charm Peter, that she shouldn't be found quite wanting in it by other men. When they had put him back aboard of the Merrythought they had come to such a pitch among them all, that as the captain leaned above the rail to launch an invitation, he addressed it to Miss Dassonville, as, if not quite the giver of the feast, the mistress of the situation.

"When are you coming to lunch with me?" demanded the captain.

"That I can't stand it, that I can't go on with it, that it is dreadful to me,—dreadful!"

"What is dreadful?"

"Everything, being engaged—being married and giving up...." It was fairly racked out of her by some inward torture to which he had not the key.

"Of course, Eunice, if you don't wish to be married so soon——" Peter was all at sea. He brought a chair for her, and perceiving that he would go on standing as long as she did, she sat upon the edge of it but kept both the arms as a measure of defence. The slight act of doing something for her restored him for the moment to reality; he bent over her. "I've never wanted to hurry you, dearest—— It shall be when you say." She put up her hands suddenly with a shivering movement.

"Oh, never, never at all; never to you!" Peter could feel that working its track of desolation inward, but the first instinctive movement of his surface was to close over the wound. He took it as he knew he could only take it: as the explosive crisis of the virginal resistance which he remembered he had heard came to girls when marriage loomed upon them. He took a turn down the room to steady himself, praying dumbly for the right word.

"It isn't as if I didn't respect you"—she was eager in explanation, hurried and stumbling—"as if I didn't know how good you are ... it is only, because we are so different."

"How different, Eunice?"

"Oh ... older, I suppose." She grew quieter; it appeared on the whole they were getting on. "I care for so many things, you know—dancing—and bridge—young things—and you are always reading and reading. Oh! I couldn't stand it." So it was out now. She was jealous of his books, a little. Well, he had been self-absorbed. It occurred to him dimly that the thing to have done if he had known a little more about women, had practised with them, was to have provoked her at this point to the tears which should have sealed the renewal of his claim to her. What he said was, very quietly: "Of course I never meant, Eunice, that you shouldn't have everything you want."

"Oh," she seemed to have found a suffocating quality in his gentleness, against which she struck out with drowning gestures, "if you could only understand what it would mean to me never to have anybody I liked to talk to about things,—anybody I liked to be with all the time!" She was choked and aghast at the enormity of it.

"But I thought...." Peter was not able to go on with that. "Isn't there anybody you like to be with, Eunice?"

"Yes," said Eunice. "Burton Henderson." Mutinous and bright she looked at him out of the chair with a hand on either arm of it poised for flight or defence. After an interval Peter heard his own voice out of a fog rising to the conventional utterance.

"Of course, if you have learned to love him——" "I've loved him all the time." She was so bent on making this clear to him that she was careless what went down before her. "From the very beginning," she said, "but he had so little money, and mother ... I promised you, I know, but it's not as if I ever said I loved you." She should have spared him that! He had not put out a hand to hold her that he should be so pierced through with needless cruelty. But she was bent on clearing her skirts of him.

"Do you think," she expostulated to his stricken silence, "that if I'd cared in the least I'd have made it so easy for you? Can't you see that it was all arranged, that we jumped at you?" All the time she sat opposite him, thrusting swift and hard, there was no diminution of her appealing beauty, the flaming rose of her cheeks and the soft, dark flare of her hair. As if she felt how it belied at every turn the quality of her unyielding intention, her voice railed against him feverishly. "I suppose you think I'm mercenary, and I thought I was, too. You don't know how people like us need money sometimes. All the things we like cost so—all the real things. And poor mamma, she needed things; she'd never had them, and I thought that I could stand being married to you if I could get them that way.... Maybe I could, you know, if you'd been different, more like us I mean. But there was such a lot you didn't understand ... things you hadn't even heard about. I found that out as soon as we were engaged. There wasn't a thing between us; not a thing." It poured scalding hot on Peter's sensitive surfaces: made sensitive by the way in which even in this hour her beauty moved him. He felt tears starting in his heart and prayed they might not come to his face. "So you see as we hadn't anything in common it would be better for us not to go on with it even"—she broke a little at this—"even if there hadn't been anybody else. You see that, don't you?" She dared him to deny it rather than begged the concession of him as she gathered herself for departure.

"I see that."

"You never really belonged to our set, you know——" She rose now and he rose blindly with her; he hoped that she was done, but there was something still. "It hasn't been easy to go through with it.... Mother isn't going to make it any easier. It's natural for her to want me to have everything that money would mean, and I thought that if you would just keep away from her ... you owe something to Burton and me for what we've been through, I think ... just leave it to me to manage in my own way...."

"I shall never trouble you, Eunice." He came close to her then to open the door, seeing that she was to leave him, and he saw too that she had suffered, was at the very ebb and stony bottom of emotion as she hung for the moment in the doorway searching for some winged shaft of separation that should cut her off from the remotest implication of the situation. She found at last the barbedest. All the succeeding time after he closed the door on her was marked for Peter, not by the ticked moments but by successive waves of anguish as that poisoned arrow worked its way to his secret places.

"It isn't as if I had ever loved you; I owe it to Mr. Henderson to remind you that I never said I did.... You know I never liked to have you kiss me." He had in the months that succeeded to that last sight of Eunice Goodward, moments of unbearably wanting to go to her to try for a little to ease his torment in a more tender recognition of it—days when he would have taken from her, gratefully even if she had fooled him and he had seen her do it, whatever would have saved him from the certainty that never even in those first exquisite moments had she been his. The sharp edge of her young sufficiency had lopped off the right limb of his manhood. Never, even in his dreams, if life had allowed him to dream again, should he be able to see himself in any other guise than the meagre, austere front which his obligation to his mother and Ellen had obliged him to present to destiny. She had beggared him of all those aptitudes for passionate relations, by the faith in which he had kept himself inwardly alive. The capacity for loving died in him with the knowledge of not being able to be loved. Out of the anæsthesia of exhaustion from which Italy had revived him, it rolled back upon him that by just the walled imperviousness that shut Eunice Goodward from the appreciation of his passion, he was prevented now from Savilla Dassonville.

It was odd, then, having come to this conclusion in the middle of the night, that when he joined the ladies in the morning he should have experienced a sinking pang in not being able any longer to be sure what Miss Dassonville thought of him. There was in her manner, as she thanked him for the flowers, nothing to ruffle the surface of the bright, impersonal companionship which she had afforded him for weeks past. The occasion which brought them together was an agreement entered into some days earlier, to go and look at palaces, and as they turned past the Saluti to the Grand Canal, he found himself wondering if there had not been a touch of fatuity in his reading of the incident of the morning before. He had gone so far in the night as to think even of leaving Venice, and saw himself now forlornly wishing for some renewal of yesterday's mood to excuse him from the caddishness that such a flight implied. It came out a little later, perhaps, when after traversing many high and resounding marble halls, with a great many rooms opening into one another in a way that suggested rather the avoidance of privacy than its security, they found themselves in one of those gardens of shut delight of which the exteriors of Venetian houses give so little intimation. As she went about from bough to bough of the neglected roses, turned all inward as if they took their florescence from that still lighted human passion which had found its release and centre there, her face glowed for the moment with the colour of her quick sympathies. She turned it on him with an unconscious, tender confidence, which not to meet seemed to Peter, in that gentle enclosure full of warmth and fragrance, to assume the proportions of a betrayal. He did meet it there as she came back to him for the last look from the marble balustrade by which they had descended, covering her hand, there resting, lingeringly with his own. He was awakened only to the implication of this movement by the discovery that she had deeply and exquisitely blushed. It was a further singularity in view of the conviction with which Peter had come through the night, that the mood of protectingness which the girl provoked in him should have multiplied itself in pointing out to him how many ways, if he had not made up his mind not to marry her at all, such a marriage could be made to serve its primal uses. She had turned up her cuff to trail her hand overside as they slid through the lucent water, and the pretty feminine curve of it had brought to mind what the Princess had told him of the shirt-waists she made herself. He decided that she made them very well. But she was too thin for their severity—and if he married her he would have insisted on her wearing them now and then as a tender way to prevent her suspecting that it was on their account he had thought of not marrying her. The revealed whiteness of her wrist, the intimacy of her relaxed posture, for though her mind had played into his as freely as a child in a meadow, she had been always, as regards her person, a little prim with him, had lent to their errand of house visiting a personal note in which it was absurdly apt for them to have run across Captain Dunham of the Merrythought at the door of the Consulate. Mr. Weatheral had some papers which Lessing had sent him to acknowledge there, and it was a piece of the morning's performance, when he had come back from that business, to find that the meeting had taken on—from some mutual discovery of the captain's and Mrs. Merrithew's of a cousin's wife's sister who had married one of the Applegates who was a Dunham on the mother's side—quite the aspect of a family party. It came in the end to the four of them going off at Peter's invitation to have lunch together in a café overhanging the calle. He told himself afterward that he would not have done it if he had recalled in time the friendly seaman's romantic appreciation of the situation between himself and Miss Dassonville. He saw himself so intrigued by it that, by the time lunch was over, he felt himself in a position which to his own sensitiveness, demanded that he must immediately leave Venice or propose to Miss Dassonville. To see the way he was going and to go on in it, had for him the fascination of the abyss. He caught himself in the act even of trying to fix Miss Dassonville's eye to include her by complicity in the beguilement of the captain, a business which she seemed to have undertaken on her own account on quite other grounds. He perceived with a kind of pride for her that she had the ways of elderly sea-going gentlemen by heart. It was something even if she had failed to charm Peter, that she shouldn't be found quite wanting in it by other men. When they had put him back aboard of the Merrythought they had come to such a pitch among them all, that as the captain leaned above the rail to launch an invitation, he addressed it to Miss Dassonville, as, if not quite the giver of the feast, the mistress of the situation.

"When are you coming to lunch with me?" demanded the captain.

It was not until he had come the whole length of the orchard path, with the lamp already lit behind him in the window of the room he called his study, that Anson Wyeth understood what he had been sent for, and then only by the attitude of his sister-in-law, who stood at the head of the ditch in the posture of one who has done her part and means to see the rest of it done by somebody else. The child was not with her. That was the first thing he made out against the failing light, which lay along the edges of the poplars and drained down the irrigating ditch like the last of the water itself, and the second was that Miss Bassett held something in her hand, a little sodden and grey, which she did not offer him so much as exhibit, as if it were the evidence in a case which had already gone against him.

"She is in the tool-house," said Miss Bassett. "I told her she was to stay there until you came. I thought, Anson, that this time you had better see to it yourself."

He took the thing from her and saw that it was a boat, or had been a boat, folded in the way children fold them, with the peak still standing up a little from the wet, and across the inner fold of it, blurred but not past reading, a line of the old black-letter which he would have known in any light: *... and so we came to anker in the bay, where the people of the countrey ...* He turned it over, and the whole wet fleet of them, the others he could see now lodged along the weir where the ditch broke into the lower field, rose up between him and his sister-in-law like an accusation he had somehow always expected.

"How many?" he said.

"I didn't count. Hannah fished out what she could. There were more that went over into the Carsons' field before anybody saw." Miss Bassett had a way of letting the worst of a thing come last, not out of any cruelty but out of a kind of conscientious exactness, so that a man should have it all and not be able to say afterward he had been spared. "It is the big book, Anson, the one on the shelf by the window. She had the stool from the kitchen to reach it."

He was aware that she watched him, and that the watching was not unkindly. It was only that in the two years since his wife's death the household had settled into a balance which neither of them had ever named, by which Caroline Bassett kept the child and the child's clothes and the child's manners, and he kept the books and the orchard and the long, dim, unaccountable evenings; and it appeared now, from the way she stood, that the balance had tipped, that the child had come over into his side of it by the most direct of all possible routes, and that Caroline meant to let her stay there until he had found out what to do with her.

"I'll go to her," he said.

"You'll be firm with her, Anson?" It was not quite a question. "She has to understand. It isn't as if she were a baby any longer. She knew perfectly well what she was doing; she waited until I was at the Ladies' Aid and Hannah was in the cellar. It's that I mind—that she planned it."

"Yes," he said; "yes, of course." But he was not, as he went down the path toward the tool-house with the wet boat still in his fingers, thinking of the planning. He was thinking with a kind of dull astonishment of the book itself, which had been his father's, and his father's before that, in its brown calf with the corners rubbed to suede by three generations of hands, the one possession he would have said, if anybody had asked him, that he would carry out of a burning house; and he found, examining himself for the anger that ought by every rule of the situation to have been there, only a curious hollowness, like the hollowness of a room from which the furniture has been taken, where one hears one's own step too loudly.

The tool-house stood at the bottom of the orchard where the ditch turned, a lean-to of unpainted boards with a single square of window, and the door, which Hannah had latched from the outside, gave on its hinges with the protesting creak that he remembered all at once as the sound of his own childhood, of other tool-houses and other latched doors. It was very nearly dark inside. The child sat on an upturned box between the lawn-mower and the stack of smudge-pots, with her feet drawn up under her pinafore and her hands folded in the very attitude, he saw with a pang that was half amusement, of the little girls in the Sunday-school cards, the attitude of a patience that has been told to it and does not mean a word of it. She did not get up. She looked at him with her mother's eyes, which were grey and set wide, and with an expression which was not at all her mother's, of having already measured him and found him exactly what she had expected.

"Aunt Caroline sent you," said Tilly.

"I came," he corrected her; and then, because that was not quite true either and he had a scrupulousness about such things even with a child of six, "Aunt Caroline told me, and I came."

He did not know at once what to do with himself. The box was the only seat, and it seemed to him an indignity, which he could not have explained, to stand over her in the half-dark like a constable; so he let himself down at last on his heels, with his back against the door-post and his knees awkwardly drawn up, which brought his face very nearly to the level of hers. He laid the wet boat on the floor between them.

"Do you know what that is, Tilly?"

"It's a boat." She looked at it without remorse, rather with a professional disparagement, as if she found it had not held its shape so well as she had intended. "It's one of the little ones. The big ones went better. The big ones went all the way to the weir."

"I mean, do you know what it was made of?"

"Paper." But she saw that would not do, and her glance flickered from him to the boat and back again with a sudden wariness. "It was made of pages," she conceded. "Out of the book."

"Out of my book."

"It was a big book," said Tilly, as though that settled something; "there were *hundreds* of pages. I only took the ones with no pictures."

It was so exactly the defence he might have made himself at her age, it had so precisely that quality of a reasonableness grounded upon some inner economy of which the grown world takes no account, that Anson Wyeth found himself for the moment unable to go on. He was aware that he ought to be angry, that Caroline was waiting at the top of the orchard for the sound, or at least the aftermath, of his anger; and he searched in himself for it again as a man searches his pockets for a key he is sure he put there, and found instead, rising slow and cold out of the hollowness, a perception of how little in all their two years together he had ever been obliged to say to this child that mattered, how he had left it all to Caroline, the scoldings and the comfortings alike, and had come down to her from his study at the hour before supper as one comes down to a pleasant view.

"Tilly," he said, "you knew you mustn't touch that book."

"Nobody told me."

"You knew it, all the same." He could feel his voice taking on, without his willing it, the dry, measured edge which his own father had used, and he hated it a little and was glad of it a little, since it seemed to be the only instrument that came to hand. "You knew it, because you waited until Aunt Caroline had gone out. You took the stool from the kitchen so you could reach. If you had thought it was a thing you might do, you would have asked me for it."

She was silent at that, and he saw that it had gone home, though not in the way he meant. It was not the wrongness she was considering, but the fact of having been seen through; her small face set itself against him with the mutinous composure of a creature that will be caught, if it must, but will not be caught *out*.

"You'd have said no," said Tilly.

"Very likely."

"Then it wouldn't have been any use asking." She brought it out with a fine logic, as though it had cost her a good deal to work it through and she meant he should have the whole benefit of it. "If I'd asked and you'd said no, then I'd have been bad if I took it. But I didn't ask, so you never said, so...." She broke off, perceiving perhaps that the argument had a hole in it somewhere, though she could not have said where, and finished in a rush, "Anyway, they were *good* boats."

He did not answer that at once. Outside, the water was still running in the ditch, with the small, continuous, contented sound of irrigating water that has found its level, and the last of the light lay along the floor in a pale oblong from the window, just touching the edge of the sodden boat. He had a sudden vision, which he could not afterward account for, of the whole long procession of them going down the ditch in the late afternoon, white and brave and bobbing, carrying their fragments of old voyages, the anchorings and the soundings and the strange people of strange countries, down past the orchard and the poplars and over the weir into the Carsons' field; and of the child running beside them on the bank, with her pinafore flying, alone in all that wide, empty, golden afternoon, with nobody to see.

"Tilly," he said, "why did you want to make boats?"

It was not, he knew as soon as he had said it, the question Caroline would have asked; it was not, perhaps, a question that ought to have been asked at all until the other business was settled. But it was out, and he saw it strike against her guard and glance off, and then, after a moment, by some flaw he could not see, get in.

"I wanted to send them," said Tilly.

"Send them where?"

She looked at him then, for the first time, not as an adversary but as one who is uncertain whether a thing is safe to say; and he saw her small hands, which had been folded in that Sunday-school attitude, unclasp and take hold of the edges of the box.

"Hannah said," she began, and stopped, and began again with the curious formality with which children report the sayings of their elders, as if the words had a separate existence of their own that must be handed on exactly. "Hannah said all the water goes to the river, and the river goes to the sea. And Aunt Caroline said—that time—Mamma had gone a long way off, like over the sea. So I thought...." She was not crying; she was looking at him with an extraordinary intentness, as though she were reading his face for the answer to some problem in arithmetic. "I thought if I sent enough of them, *one* would get there. And I took the book pages because they had writing. So she'd know they were from here."

Anson Wyeth did not move. He was aware of the door-post hard against his back and of a numbness creeping into his knees, and of the sound of the water, and of nothing else for a long moment except the effort of keeping his face exactly as it had been, since he understood, with a clearness that was almost a physical light, that the child was watching it and would know. He had a sense, which he had had once or twice before in his life and never without dread, of standing at the edge of some place in himself where he had not been for a long time, and to which he had believed the way was closed. It was not only the child's grief, though that was there, laid bare in the small, matter-of-fact voice as a stone is laid bare when the water goes down; it was the discovery that she had been carrying it all this while, under Caroline's neat pinafores and her own wilful composure, as he had carried his, in silence, without any notion that there might be another in the house who carried the same.

"Did Aunt Caroline know?" he said at last. "Why you wanted to send them?"

"Nobody knew. It was a secret." And then, with a lift of something that was almost defiance and almost appeal, "It was *my* secret. You made me tell."

"Yes," he said. "Yes, I did." He reached out and took up the wet boat again from the floor, and turned it about in his fingers, and saw the line of old print running across the fold, *and so we came to anker in the bay*, and found that he could not for the moment see it very well. "Tilly, listen to me. You'll have to listen very carefully, because it's a hard thing, and I'm not sure I know how to say it."

She waited. He saw that she had braced herself, that she expected now the punishment she had been sent to the tool-house to receive, and that she would take it, very likely, with that fine, fierce stoicism of hers, and go to bed without supper and not cry until Caroline had put out the light; and he saw, too, with a sinking certainty, that if he let her off now, if he gathered her up as every instinct in him clamoured to do and told her it did not matter, she would know that it was only because of the secret, that the wrong she had done had been made right by the sorrow under it, and she would carry that lesson also, mixed in with the rest, all the days of her life. It was this which held him; that, and some dim feeling that the book, too, had its claim, that his father and his father's father had their part in the business, and were not to be thrown down the ditch even for the best of reasons.

"It was wrong to take the book," he said. "It doesn't make it right that you wanted to send the boats to Mamma. Do you understand that? The two things aren't the same thing at all. You wanted something very much, and it was a good thing to want; but you took what wasn't yours to get it, and you did it in secret because you knew I'd say no. That part was wrong. That part would be wrong no matter what you wanted it for."

"But——"

"No, wait." He was surprised at the steadiness of his own voice, which seemed to come from somewhere a little outside him, as though another and wiser man had taken the business in hand. "If you'd come to me and told me, I might have said no to the book. But I'd have found you something else. I'd have found you the best paper in the house. I'd have——" He stopped, because he did not know, in fact, what he would have done; because the truth was that she would not have come, that in two years he had never given her any reason to suppose he was a person to whom such things could be brought, and the knowledge of it sat in him like a stone. "That's my fault, Tilly. That part is my fault, that you didn't think you could tell me. But the book is yours."

She considered this for a long time, her eyes going from his face to the boat in his hand and back again; and he could see her working it over, testing the joints of it as she had tested the folds of her boats, to see whether it would hold.

"What are you going to do to me?" she said at last.

"You're going to help me," said Anson Wyeth, "every evening, until it's done, to dry the pages Hannah got out, and press them flat between blotters, and we'll paste them back where they belong as well as we can. Some of them won't go back. Some of them are in the Carsons' field. Those you'll have to write out for me, a line at a time, from my other copy, in your best hand, so there'll be something in the place where they were. It'll take a long time. It'll take you all summer, I expect."

He saw her face fall at that, and then, curiously, saw it lift again, as though some part of the sentence had reached her late.

"In the study?" said Tilly. "With you?"

"In the study. With me."

She did not say anything to that. She got down from the box, very carefully, as though she were afraid something might be spilled, and stood before him in the oblong of failing light with her pinafore crumpled and the mud of the ditch still drying on her shoes; and he saw her mouth begin to work, and saw her struggle with it and lose, and then she was against him, all at once, with her face in his coat and her small sharp fists knotted in the cloth of it, crying at last as she had not, he understood, been able to cry before Caroline or Hannah or anyone, crying for the boats and the book and her own wickedness and the long, empty afternoons, and for that other thing which had no name between them and needed none.

He held her. He found that it was not, after all, so hard a thing to do as he had supposed; that the arms knew it, if the man did not. Over her head, through the square of window, he could see the last pale gleam of the ditch where it ran down toward the weir, and he thought of the one boat, the fortunate one, if there had been one, gone on beyond the Carsons' field into the river, carrying its fragment of old print down toward the sea; and he could not have said whether the thing that rose in his throat was grief or something so near the opposite of it that the difference hardly mattered.

"Will one get there?" said Tilly against his coat, muffled and indistinct. "Do you think—even one?"

He was a scrupulous man; he had made it a rule never to tell her what he did not believe. He sat for a long moment with his cheek against her hair, weighing it, while the water ran on outside and the dark came up out of the orchard and filled the little house to the rafters.

"I think," said Anson Wyeth at last, "that it has already."

It was full night when they came up the path together, the child's hand gripped in his, and Caroline Bassett, who had waited at the head of the ditch until the dew drove her in, met them at the kitchen door with the lamp held high and her lips already parted on a question. She looked at the child's swollen face and at his own, and whatever she saw there, she did not ask it. She only stood aside to let them pass, and said, in a voice he had never heard her use, that she had kept their supper hot.
