When Mr. and Mrs. Ellery Tabor came home from the Kinnemans' dinner, they came home by the street car, which was not Mrs. Tabor's idea of the proper conclusion to such an evening. They had gone in a hired cab, an indulgence of seventy-five cents, and she had supposed, with the faith that sustains wives through the greater part of their lives, that they would return in one. But at the Kinnemans' iron gate, under the light of a new arc-lamp that hissed and sputtered like an indignant cat, Mr. Tabor had looked up the Boulevard and observed that the car would be along in a minute, and that it was a fine night for March. Mrs. Tabor had said nothing whatever. A woman who has been married twenty-two years learns the uses of saying nothing, and she had now brought this art to a pitch where her silence could be heard above the clanging of a gong.

It was not a fine night for March. It was a night like most March nights in that Midland city, damp, raw, and sooty. The smoke that by day was merely a nuisance had settled at dusk into a kind of brown flannel, so that the street lamps wore haloes, and every passer-by brought home on his collar the evidence of the town's prosperity. The city was growing; everybody said so, and everybody said it proudly, as though growth were a virtue rather than a symptom. It had grown out past the old brick houses with their cupolas and iron deer, past the fairgrounds, past the creek where boys had once caught sunfish, and now it was spreading northward in a fever of stone and stucco along the Boulevard, where the Kinnemans had built. The Tabors lived on Wilmot Street, which had once been the Boulevard of its own day, and which now, in the manner of streets that have been passed by, had taken to boarding-houses, and a dentist's sign, and a general look of having seen better company.

Mrs. Tabor sat very straight in the street car. She was a handsome woman still, with a good deal of fair hair arranged in a fashion that had cost her an hour that afternoon, and she wore a dove-colored silk that had been made over twice, so cleverly that only another woman could have told it, and every other woman at the Kinnemans' had told it, silently, within thirty seconds of her entrance. Mr. Tabor sat beside her, a mild, broad man of fifty with a gray mustache and the patient eyes of one who keeps the books of a wholesale hardware house and has kept them for a quarter of a century without discovering an error that was not somebody else's. He held his hat upon his knee and looked out of the window at nothing, for there was nothing to see but his own reflection, and that of his wife, who was not looking at him.

They got down at the corner of Wilmot Street, and Mr. Tabor offered his arm, and Mrs. Tabor took it, because one does, but she took it as though it were a banister in a house where she did not care for the owner. They walked the half block in the soft, sooty dark without a word. The house was dark too, except for the transom over the front door, where a gas jet burned low, as they had left it. Mr. Tabor fitted his key to the lock, and the door swung in upon the familiar smell of the place, a smell of furnace-heat and old carpet and the oranges that stood in a dish upon the hall table, and Mrs. Tabor went past him and up three steps of the stairway and then stopped, with her hand upon the newel post, and turned.

"Well?" she said.

Mr. Tabor closed the door carefully, and turned up the gas, and hung his hat upon the rack. He did these things deliberately, for he knew the tone, and a man who knows the tone will do almost anything rather than answer it at once.

"Well what, Mattie?"

"You know perfectly well 'what.'"

"I don't believe I do," he said, which was untrue, and both of them knew it was untrue, and the knowledge hung between them in the hall like a third person who had come in with them out of the fog.

"Ellery Tabor," said his wife, "Henry Kinneman took you into the library after dinner and kept you there forty minutes. I counted. I sat in that drawing room of Bessie Kinneman's, with those gold chairs that nobody can sit back in, and I listened to Bessie tell me what she paid for her rugs, and I counted every one of those forty minutes. And when you came out, Henry Kinneman's face was as red as a beet, and yours looked the way it looks when the furnace goes out in the night and you've decided not to get up and fix it. Now, what did he say to you, and what did you say to him?"

Mr. Tabor considered the oranges on the hall table. He selected one, examined it, and put it back.

"Henry had a proposition," he said.

"I know he had a proposition. Bessie told me he had a proposition. Bessie told me before the soup."

"Then I don't see why you need me to—"

"Because Bessie told me what it was, and she told me how much it would mean, and she told me Henry was doing it purely out of old friendship, and she told me—" Mrs. Tabor's voice wavered upon a high and dangerous note, recovered itself, and went on with a terrible steadiness, "she told me she was sure you'd jump at it. Those were her words. 'I'm sure Ellery'll jump at it, Mattie.' And then you came out of that library with your furnace face on, and Henry wouldn't look at you, and I had to sit through the ices knowing that whatever it was, you'd gone and refused it. Didn't you?"

Mr. Tabor did not answer immediately, and this, to a wife, is the most complete of all answers.

"Didn't you?" she said again.

"Come into the sitting room, Mattie. There's no sense standing in the hall."

"I prefer the hall."

"Well, I don't," he said, with a firmness that surprised them both, and he went into the sitting room and lit the gas there, and after a moment she followed him, not because he had told her to, but because she found it impossible to quarrel effectively with a man who was in another room.

The sitting room was the kind of room that had been the height of elegance in 1888 and had been allowed to remain so. There was a mantel of black marble, veined like a frightened countenance, and above it a steel engraving of Lord Byron in an attitude. There was a Morris chair, which was Mr. Tabor's, and a platform rocker, which was Mrs. Tabor's, and a horsehair sofa, which was nobody's, for no one had ever been able to stay on it. Mrs. Tabor did not take the rocker. She stood by the center table, in her made-over silk, and took off her gloves finger by finger, as though each finger had personally offended her.

"Now," she said.

Mr. Tabor stood upon the hearth rug with his hands behind him, in the posture of a man about to address a lodge meeting, though he had never in his life addressed one.

"Henry's got a piece of ground," he said. "Out north, past the Boulevard, past the end of the car line. Four hundred acres, or he's got an option on it. He's going to cut it up into lots. He's going to call it Kinneman Heights."

"There isn't any height out there," said Mrs. Tabor. "It's as flat as a griddle. I've seen it from the train."

"That's what I told Henry."

"Oh!" she cried. "You *told* him that?"

"Well, it is flat, Mattie."

"What on earth difference does it make whether it's flat? People don't buy lots to stand on top of them and look at the view. They buy them because they're going up in value, and everybody knows the town's going north, and Henry Kinneman has made more money out of land than any man in this city except old Mr. Sefton, and he's offered you—Bessie said—he's offered you a third interest. A third interest, Ellery! For nothing!"

"Not for nothing," said Mr. Tabor.

"Bessie said—"

"Bessie doesn't know. Henry didn't offer me a third interest for nothing. He offered me a third interest for eleven thousand dollars."

Mrs. Tabor's gloves, which had been describing small agitated arcs in her hands, became still.

"Eleven thousand dollars," she said.

"Yes."

"But we haven't—" She stopped. "Ellery, we haven't got eleven thousand dollars."

"We've got this house," said Mr. Tabor, "and we've got the building and loan shares, and we've got the money your Aunt Sophia left you, that's in the savings bank, that you said was for Lucy, for when she marries. Henry had it all figured out. He knew what this house would carry on a mortgage better than I did. I suppose that's his business, knowing such things. He figured it all out on a sheet of paper, very neat, and he passed it over to me, and he said, 'There you are, Ellery. In three years you'll be out of Wilmot Street, and you'll be out of Frick and Hammersley's back office, and you'll never have to add up another column for anybody but yourself.' That's what he said."

The gas jet hummed. Somewhere in the house a radiator knocked, twice, as though it wished to be admitted to the conversation.

"And you said no," said Mrs. Tabor.

"I said I'd think it over."

"Ellery, you said no. I saw your face. I've seen that face for twenty-two years. When you said you'd think it over, you'd already thought it over, and Henry knew it, and that's why he was red."

Mr. Tabor did not deny it. He looked at Lord Byron, who looked past him at something more interesting.

"Mattie," he said, "do you know what's out there past the end of the car line? There's mud. There's a slaughter-house a mile and a half to the west, and when the wind's right you can smell it clear to the Boulevard. There's no water main, and no sewer, and the gas company won't run a line out there for five years, because I know a man that works for the gas company, and he told me. Henry's going to sell lots to people that'll buy them on the strength of a picture in the Sunday paper with trees in it, and there aren't any trees, and if the town doesn't come out that way as fast as Henry thinks it will—"

"It will. Everybody says it will."

"Everybody said that about Ridgemont, too."

Mrs. Tabor's color rose. Ridgemont was a word that had a history in that city; it was the name of an addition that had been laid out, with great brass-band fanfare, in the year of the World's Fair, and that was now, after twenty years, a region of weeds and cracked sidewalks leading nowhere, with here and there a lonely cottage standing in the midst of it like the last guest at a party that never began.

"That was different," she said.

"How was it different?"

"Because—because Henry Kinneman didn't have anything to do with it, that's how. Henry's never failed at anything. Look at that house of his. Look at Bessie. Bessie Kinneman went to school with me, Ellery. She sat right across the aisle from me at the old Seminary, and she couldn't do fractions, she used to copy mine, and tonight she sat in that drawing room and told me she was having her dresses made in Chicago, and she asked me—" Mrs. Tabor's voice went up again, and this time it did not altogether come down, "she asked me, so sweetly, whether I didn't find Wilmot Street was getting a little *noisy* now. Noisy! As if she didn't know what she meant. As if I didn't know."

"Mattie—"

"And she looked at this dress. Don't tell me she didn't. I watched her do it."

Now there are in every marriage certain doors that both parties have agreed, without ever saying so, to leave shut. Mr. Tabor perceived, with the dismay of a man who hears a latch click behind him, that one of these doors had come open, and that through it were blowing all the small, cold winds of twenty-two years: the made-over silks, and the summers that had not been spent at the lakes, and the piano that had been rented and not bought, and the evenings when Mrs. Tabor had looked out of the window at the boarding-house across the way, where somebody was always practicing the cornet, and had said nothing at all.

"I didn't know you minded so much," he said, rather slowly.

"Minded!" said Mrs. Tabor. "Minded! Ellery, I've been minding since 1897."

She sat down then, quite suddenly, in the platform rocker, and the rocker, being a platform rocker, gave a long complaining creak and moved backward several inches, which spoiled what would otherwise have been a dramatic effect. She did not seem to notice it. She sat with the gloves crushed in her lap and looked at the black marble mantel, and two tears stood in her eyes and did not fall, for she was a woman of considerable self-government and did not intend that they should.

"Lucy's nineteen," she said, more quietly. "Do you know who she goes with? She goes with the Gorham girl, and the Peabody girls, and the Gorham girl's father keeps a feed store. And Bessie Kinneman's daughter is going East to school next fall, and the young men that come to her house have their own automobiles, and Lucy sees all that, and she comes home and she doesn't say anything, and that's worse than if she did. She's getting to be like me. She's learning not to say anything. And I thought, tonight, sitting there, I thought, here it is at last. Here's the chance. Here's Henry Kinneman holding out his hand, and all Ellery has to do is take it, and in three years—" She broke off. "And you went in that library and told him it was flat."

Mr. Tabor did not reply. He went to the window and drew back the lace curtain a little and looked out into the brown fog, where the lamp across the street made a blur, and somewhere far off a switch engine in the yards was bumping freight cars together with a sound like a giant's furniture being moved. He stood there a long time, so long that Mrs. Tabor glanced at him once, sidewise, and then, when he did not turn, glanced again.

"Mattie," he said at last, without turning, "did I ever tell you about the brickyard?"

"What brickyard?"

"I didn't, then." He let the curtain fall. "Before we were married. The year before. I was twenty-six, and I'd saved up eight hundred dollars, which was a good deal of money for a young fellow then, and a man named Pruett came to me—you wouldn't remember him; he left town—and he had a brickyard out on the river road, and he said the town was going to grow, which it was, and it was going to be built of brick, which it was, and he wanted a partner. And I put in the eight hundred dollars. And I put in two hundred more that I borrowed from my father, that he'd been saving to have his teeth fixed. And the river came up that spring, the way it did in those days, and the kilns went under, and Pruett went to Kansas City, and that was the end of it."

Mrs. Tabor stared at him.

"You never told me that."

"No."

"Why didn't you?"

He came back from the window and stood again upon the hearth rug, but not as a man about to address a lodge. He looked, for a moment, almost as if he did not know where to put his hands.

"I was ashamed of it," he said simply. "And I was courting you, and I didn't want you to know I was the kind of a fool that could lose a thousand dollars in one wet spring. And afterward, when we were married, there didn't seem to be any time that was right for it. My father never did get his teeth fixed, Mattie. He went around for seven years with his mouth like that, and he never said one word to me about it, not one, and every Sunday at dinner I'd watch him eat, and I'd think, that's my brickyard." He paused. "I made up my mind, then, that I wasn't ever going to put anybody's teeth into a hole in the ground again. Not my father's, and not yours, and not Lucy's."

The radiator knocked once more, and was still.

Mrs. Tabor looked down at the gloves in her lap. She smoothed them out, finger by finger, the way she had taken them off, only gently now, and she seemed to be giving the operation more of her attention than it strictly required.

"Henry Kinneman isn't Pruett," she said, but her voice had lost its edge, and she seemed to be saying it more to herself than to him.

"No," said Mr. Tabor. "I expect he isn't. I expect Henry'll make money out of Kinneman Heights, Mattie. I expect he's right about the town, more than likely, and I'm wrong, and in ten years there'll be houses out there and a car line and Bessie'll be telling somebody else what she paid for her rugs. Henry's a smart man. But Henry's got his money in it, and if it goes, Henry's got the Boulevard house left over, and his bank stock, and his other property. If it goes for us, we've got nothing left over. We've got Wilmot Street with a mortgage on it, and Lucy's money gone, and me fifty years old and still adding up columns for Frick and Hammersley, only adding them up for the bank, too." He drew a long breath. "I'm not a brave man, Mattie. I know that. I guess you've known it a long while. But I'm not going to be brave with your money and Lucy's. If that's a fault, it's the one I've got."

For some time after this Mrs. Tabor made no answer. The fog pressed softly at the windows. Lord Byron continued to regard the distance with an expression that suggested he, at least, had never been obliged to consider a mortgage. And Mrs. Tabor, sitting in her platform rocker in her twice-made-over silk, was conscious of a strange and not altogether welcome sensation, the sensation of a woman who has marched up to a fortress with banners flying and found the garrison already out on the drawbridge, unarmed, holding out its hat.

It is one of the hardest things in life to go on being angry with a person who has just told you the truth, and Mrs. Tabor, being a woman of spirit, did not intend to give up all at once. She rocked a little, and the rocker creaked.

"Bessie will be insufferable," she said.

"I expect so."

"She'll tell everybody you turned it down. She'll tell it so that it sounds as though you were afraid."

"I was afraid," said Mr. Tabor.

"Well, you needn't say so," said his wife, with some return of asperity. "There's no reason on earth to go around *saying* things like that." She rose and laid the gloves on the center table and stood looking down at them. "And that dress of Bessie's," she added, irrelevantly, "was too young for her. It was meant for a girl of twenty. With her neck."

Mr. Tabor, who was a wise man in the limited and patient way of men who keep books, perceived that the war was not won and would not, perhaps, ever be won, but that hostilities had for the present been suspended, and that he would do well to make no claims upon the territory. He turned down the gas until the flame was a small blue bead.

"It's late, Mattie," he said.

"I know it's late."

She went into the hall, and he followed her, and she paused again at the foot of the stair, with her hand on the newel post, in the dim light from the transom. He thought for a moment she was going to say something more about Henry Kinneman; but she did not. She looked at him, instead, in an odd, considering way, as though he were a man she had passed every day on the street for twenty-two years and had just now, for the first time, troubled to look at closely.

"Your father," she said. "Did he really never get his teeth fixed?"

"Never did."

"Poor old man," said Mrs. Tabor. She went up two steps and stopped. "Ellery, you should have told me. About the brickyard."

"I know it."

"I'd have married you anyway."

He said nothing to this; there did not seem to be anything that would do. But he stood in the hall below and watched her go up, slowly, one hand lifting the hem of the dove-colored silk, and when she had reached the landing and turned out of sight, he went back into the sitting room and stood for a while in the dark beside the window, looking out at the fog. Somewhere to the north, beyond the Boulevard, beyond the arc-lamps and the stone houses and the end of the car line, Henry Kinneman's four hundred flat acres lay out under the night, waiting to be made into Heights. Mr. Tabor thought about them for some time. Then he went out to the kitchen, and down the cellar steps, and shook down the furnace, which did not need it, and banked it for the night with great care, as though it were the most important thing in the world.

When Mr. Walter Lindley stepped down from the parlor car at the Union Station, with his gray spats a little dusty from the platform and his gloves held in one hand in the manner of a man who has lived for twenty-two years where gloves are held, he looked about him with the expression of one who comes to bestow a kindness. He had been a boy in this town, and it is the habit of men who have gone away to believe that the places they left have been waiting, rather wistfully, for their return. He was prepared to be gentle with it. He was prepared to find it small, and to forgive it for being small, and perhaps even to say a pleasant word or two about its quaintness to anyone who might ask him.

The town, however, had not been waiting. It had been growing, which is a thing towns do when no one is watching them, and it had grown in the particular way of Midland towns, which is to say outward and upward and blackward all at once. The smoke lay upon it like a damp shawl. From the station steps Mr. Lindley could see, where he remembered a livery stable and a vacant lot full of burdock and old tomato cans, a building of eleven stories, sooty already at the cornices, with a sign upon its roof advertising a brand of chewing gum in letters taller than a man. He was conscious of a slight sense of injury, as though someone had rearranged the furniture of his own room without consulting him.

"Walt! Walt Lindley! Here! Over here, you old sinner!"

The voice came from beside a large and very shiny automobile, and it belonged to a large and rather shiny gentleman in a brown suit, who was waving a straw hat with such vehemence that two porters and a lady with a canary in a cage turned to look at him. Mr. Lindley recognized his cousin, Ames Ruddock, partly by the voice, which had not changed, and partly by the ears, which had not changed either, though everything between them had.

The last time the cousins had seen each other, Ames had been a lank youth of nineteen with a celluloid collar and a habit of laughing through his nose; he had been, in fact, a creature of elbows. Now he had arrived at that condition of comfortable expansion which a certain kind of Midland man attains at forty and maintains, with the aid of a good cook and a sedentary business, until the end. His waistcoat described a gentle and confident arc. A heavy gold chain crossed it like a bridge over a prosperous river. His face was pink and broad and pleased with itself, and when he seized his cousin's hand he pumped it as though he expected water.

"Well, sir!" said Ames. "Well, sir! Twenty-two years! I says to Hattie this morning, I says, 'Hattie, I bet you I won't know him,' and here I knew you clear across the platform. You haven't changed a particle, Walt. Not a particle!"

This was untrue, and both men knew it; but it was the kind of untruth that is an office of friendship, and Mr. Lindley accepted it graciously, returning it with interest.

"Nor you, Ames," he said. "I'd have known you anywhere."

"Well, I don't know about that," said Ames, patting the arc of his waistcoat with a modest pride, as though it were an achievement he had worked for. "Put on a little weight, maybe. Hattie says it's the cooking. Get in, get in! Fellow'll take your grip. How do you like the car? Just got her in April. Six cylinders. She'll do forty on the boulevard if the police aren't looking." He winked enormously. "You folks in New York, I guess you're used to all this. I guess this looks pretty small to you."

"Not at all," said Mr. Lindley, sincerely, for he had never owned an automobile and was not certain how one got into it. "Not at all. It's a very handsome machine."

"Well, she's no slouch," Ames admitted, and the fellow put the grip in, and they set off with a jerk and a roar and a smell of gasoline that Mr. Lindley found, to his surprise, rather exhilarating.

There is a curious contest that goes on, silently and without malice, between any two men who were boys together and who have taken different roads. Each wishes to be assured that his own road was the better one; and yet each wishes, too, out of some old loyalty he could not have named, that the other has not done badly. The result is that each boasts a little and is ashamed of boasting, and then, because he is ashamed, boasts a little more to cover it. Mr. Lindley, riding down Washington Street beside his cousin, found himself mentioning that he lunched, as a rule, at a club on Forty-fourth Street, and that the club had a great many distinguished members, a number of whom he knew to speak to. Ames received this information with a respectful "Is that so?" and then mentioned, in his turn, that he was president of the Hardware Dealers' Association of the state, and had been for three terms, and that the governor had shaken hands with him at the last convention and called him by name.

"He did? By name?" said Mr. Lindley, impressed in spite of himself.

"Called me 'Ames,'" said his cousin. "'Ames,' he says, just like that. Of course," he added, out of fairness, "he'd been told it beforehand. But still."

"Still," Mr. Lindley agreed.

They passed the courthouse, which had been the grandest building in the world when they were boys and which now crouched, gray and apologetic, among neighbors that overtopped it by several stories. They passed the corner where old Mr. Heim's candy shop had stood, and where now there was a moving-picture theater with a great deal of electric light and a poster of a young woman being tied to a railroad track by a gentleman in a black mustache. Mr. Lindley turned his head to look at it.

"Heim's," he said. "Heim's was right there."

"Heim's!" cried Ames, delighted. "You remember Heim's? Licorice whips, a penny apiece! And the horehound! Old man Heim died, I guess it's fifteen years ago. His boy sold out and went to Detroit. They say he's in the automobile business. Doing fine."

"Everybody seems to be doing fine," said Mr. Lindley, a little wistfully.

"Well, it's a growing town," said Ames, with the air of a man explaining a virtue. "That's what it is. It's a growing town."

The Ruddock house stood on one of the new streets in the north part of town, where twenty years before there had been a cornfield and a swimming hole in Fall Creek, and where now there were rows of houses of a style the builders called "Colonial," which meant that they had white pillars in front of them and were not colonial in any other particular. Mrs. Ruddock met them at the door, a plump, kindly, anxious lady who had evidently been up since daybreak preparing for the visitor, and who shook his hand and said she had heard ever so much about him and hoped he would make himself right at home. Behind her, upon the stairway, there appeared for one moment a young girl of perhaps seventeen, with her hair done up in a style that was plainly an experiment, who looked at Mr. Lindley with that expression of polite and absolute indifference which youth reserves for persons over thirty, and then vanished upward with a rustle of skirts.

"That's Dorothy," said Mrs. Ruddock. "She's at the age. You know."

Mr. Lindley, who had no children and did not know, nevertheless nodded with every appearance of understanding.

The dinner—it was called dinner, though it was served at half past twelve, and Mr. Lindley had long since been taught to call such a meal lunch—was of a size that alarmed him. There was fried chicken, and there were mashed potatoes in a mound like a small snowy hill with a lake of gravy at the summit, and there were hot biscuits and sweet corn and sliced tomatoes and three kinds of preserves and, at the end, a peach pie of such amplitude and dignity that it seemed less a dessert than a monument. Mr. Lindley ate with a kind of desperate courtesy. Ames ate with simple happiness. Dorothy, who had come down at the last moment with her hair done in a different style, ate almost nothing and gazed at the window, as though she expected someone to appear in it.

"Walt and I," said Ames to his wife, through a biscuit, "were just like brothers. Weren't we, Walt? Just like brothers. Lived next door to each other on Clayton Street, his folks and mine. You remember the old barn, Walt?"

"I remember the barn," said Mr. Lindley.

"We had a show in it once," Ames went on, turning to his daughter. "A regular show, admission five cents or ten pins. Walt was the villain. He had a mustache made out of burnt cork, and it run down his face when he got hot. And I was the hero, and I was supposed to rescue the girl, only the girl went home in the middle because her mother called her, and we didn't have any girl to rescue, so I rescued the dog instead."

"Papa," said Dorothy, with a faint and weary shudder, "you've told that."

"Well, Cousin Walt hasn't heard it," said Ames.

"Cousin Walt," said Dorothy, "was in it."

There was a slight pause, during which Mrs. Ruddock passed the preserves with great energy to everyone at once.

After dinner Ames proposed that they take a drive "around the old stamping ground," and Mr. Lindley, who felt that if he sat still he would very likely fall asleep, agreed at once. They climbed into the six-cylinder car and went roaring southward, and as they went, a silence settled upon them that was not unfriendly but was full of things neither knew quite how to say. The boasting had worn itself out somewhere about the second piece of pie. Each had established his credentials; each was satisfied that the other was not a failure; and now they were simply two men of forty-one, in a hot automobile, going to look at the place where they had been boys.

Clayton Street, when they reached it, was not so much changed as diminished. The great elms that had arched over it were mostly gone, cut down to make way for wires, and the few that remained looked thin and dusty and discouraged. The houses were the same houses, but they had a shrunken and ashamed appearance, like old gentlemen who have come down in the world and are wearing their good clothes too long. Several of them had signs in their windows: "Rooms," and "Table Board," and, in one, "Madame Zara, Readings, Your Future Revealed." The Lindley house had become a boarding house, and a man in shirtsleeves sat on the porch with his feet on the railing, reading a newspaper. The Ruddock house next door had been torn down entirely, and in its place stood a long, low building of yellow brick with a wide door and a sign that said "Ajax Garage—Tires—Repairs."

Ames stopped the car at the curb, and the two men sat looking.

"Well," said Ames at last. "There she is."

"Where was the barn?" asked Mr. Lindley.

Ames pointed with his straw hat to the back of the garage. "Right about where that fellow's fixing that tire," he said. "The hayloft was right about where that grease-pit is. I guess."

They got out of the car, for no particular reason, and stood on the sidewalk. The man on the porch of the boarding house looked at them over his newspaper with mild suspicion and then went back to reading. A small boy came out of the garage, eating an apple and regarding the automobile with the profound and silent reverence that small boys of that period reserved for automobiles, and Ames, in a sudden expansion of spirit, gave him a nickel for no reason whatever. The boy took it without a word, looked at it, looked at Ames, decided that grown people were not to be understood, and went away.

"You remember Minnie Hoyle?" said Mr. Lindley, abruptly.

He had not intended to say it. It had been somewhere in his mind all day, and perhaps for twenty-two years, and it came out of him now as though the sidewalk itself had spoken.

Ames turned and looked at him, and an odd expression came over his broad pink face—an expression that was, for one moment, almost young.

"Minnie Hoyle," he said slowly. "Lived in the yellow house on the corner. Had a blue hair-ribbon. Do I remember Minnie Hoyle!" He laughed, but the laugh did not go through his nose as it used to; it stayed somewhere in his chest. "Walt, I'll tell you something. I'll tell you something I never told a living soul. You know why I didn't speak to you the last summer before you went East? You know why I wouldn't go to the train to see you off?"

"I always supposed," said Mr. Lindley carefully, "it was on account of the fight. The one behind the barn."

"Well, it was on account of the fight," Ames admitted, "but what was the fight on account of? It was on account of Minnie Hoyle! You'd took her to the Sunday-school picnic out at Broad Ripple, and you'd took her in a canoe, and you'd come back with her hair-ribbon in your pocket. I saw it. I saw it sticking out. And I knew right then she'd given it to you, and that was the end of me, and I went home and I like to died."

Mr. Lindley stared at his cousin.

"Ames," he said, "she didn't give it to me. It came off in the canoe and blew into the water, and I fished it out with my paddle, and I put it in my pocket to dry, and I forgot it. She never asked for it back. She never so much as spoke to me the whole way home. She talked the entire afternoon about you."

"About me?"

"About you. About how you'd recited 'The Charge of the Light Brigade' at the school exhibition, and how you'd made the gestures. She said you had a wonderful presence. I went home," said Mr. Lindley, with dignity, "and I like to died myself."

The two men looked at each other on the sidewalk in front of the Ajax Garage, and the man on the boarding-house porch lowered his newspaper again, because it seemed to him that something was happening, though he could not have said what.

"Well, I'll be—" said Ames. "Well, I will be—! All this time!" He began to laugh, and this time it did go through his nose, exactly as it had at nineteen, and Mr. Lindley, after a moment, began to laugh too, though he had not laughed in just that way for a very long while; in New York one laughed in a more restrained manner, as befitted a member of a club on Forty-fourth Street. They laughed until Ames had to take out a large handkerchief and wipe his eyes, and the small boy with the apple came back out of the garage to watch them, apparently in hope of another nickel.

"What became of her?" asked Mr. Lindley, when he could.

"Minnie? Why, she married Doc Pruitt. The dentist. Got an office in the Lemcke Building. Five children. I see her at church sometimes." Ames reflected. "She's got real heavy."

"Has she?"

"Heavier than me," said Ames, with a certain satisfaction.

They got back into the automobile, but Ames did not start it at once. He sat with his hands upon the wheel, looking at the garage where the barn had been, and when he spoke again his voice had dropped into a lower register, as the voices of large, hearty men sometimes do when they are about to say something they would not say before their families.

"Walt," he said, "I'll tell you something else. When you went East, I used to think about you. I used to read the New York papers down at the library, just to see what was going on where you were. Broadway and all. Opera. I used to think, there's Walt, he's going to the opera, he's eating in those restaurants, and here I am selling stove-bolts. I used to think you'd got the best of it. I guess I've thought that, off and on, for twenty years."

Mr. Lindley was silent for a moment. He thought of his rooms on Thirty-eighth Street, which were very tasteful and very quiet, and of the club where he knew a number of distinguished members to speak to and none of them to speak to about anything that mattered; and he thought of the opera, to which he had gone perhaps three times in twenty-two years, and had fallen asleep twice. He thought of Mrs. Ruddock passing the preserves to everyone at once, and of the peach pie, and of Dorothy at the window waiting for someone to appear in it.

"Ames," he said, "I don't know that I'd say I'd got the best of it."

Ames turned and looked at him.

"You don't?"

"I don't know that I would," said Mr. Lindley.

Ames considered this for some time, his brow working with the effort of it. He was not, perhaps, a man much given to reflection, but he was a man of kind instincts, and his instincts told him now that something had been offered him which he must not take too eagerly, nor yet refuse.

"Well," he said at last, slowly, "I guess maybe nobody does. Get the best of it, I mean. I guess maybe it all comes out about even." Then, because this was very near to philosophy, and philosophy made him uneasy, he cleared his throat and added briskly, "Anyhow, you're going to stay over Sunday. Hattie's got a roast. And I want you to see the store. We put in a new front last spring. Plate glass, the whole width. You won't see a front like that this side of Chicago."

"I'd like to see it," said Mr. Lindley, and found that he meant it.

The six cylinders roared, and the automobile moved away from the curb with a jerk that threw both gentlemen back against the leather. The small boy, disappointed of his second nickel, threw his apple-core after them with a fine contempt, and missed. Behind them the man on the boarding-house porch folded his newspaper, yawned, and observed to nobody in particular that there went a couple of fellows who had had a drink or two, by the looks of them; for it is the way of the world to misread the faces of men who have just found, in front of a garage, a boyhood they had supposed was lost.

And upon the corner, where the yellow house had stood and where there now stood a drugstore with a soda fountain, a stout lady in a purple hat came out with a parcel of tooth powder under her arm, and paused, and peered after the receding automobile with an expression of vague and troubled recognition. But the smoke was thick that afternoon, as it generally was, and the automobile was soon lost in it; and Mrs. Pruitt, after a moment, shook her head, decided she must have been mistaken, and went home to see about supper.

At a quarter before six o'clock on a certain Thursday in May, Roderick Dunlap, aged ten years and three months, was discovered by no one sitting on the roof of the woodshed, whither he had withdrawn in the manner of statesmen who, foreseeing a change of administration, find it convenient to visit the provinces. He was not doing anything. He was merely there, his knees drawn up to his chin and his eyes fixed upon the alley gate with an expression which, upon an older and more celebrated countenance, might have been taken for philosophic detachment. Upon Roderick's it was simply dread.

There is a quality in the air of a house wherein a boy has lately done something. The house itself appears to know it. The very windows take on a look, and the kitchen door, opening to let out the cook's cat, opens with a sort of significance, and closes again with more. Grown people pass from room to room upon errands that seem ordinary enough, yet the boy, who is attuned to these vibrations as a hound is to weather, perceives that every one of them is thinking about him. He knows, moreover, though nobody has said so, at precisely what hour the matter will come to a head. In Roderick's household that hour was the hour of his father's return from the office, and it was now approaching with the dreadful punctuality of all things that are not wanted.

Roderick had already been spoken to by his mother, briefly, at about three in the afternoon. She had come out upon the side porch with her hand at her throat and had said, "Roderick, is it true? Is it possible?" and then, without waiting for any answer, had gone in again, and Roderick had heard her telephoning to someone in a high, unnatural voice. Since that time no one had said anything to him whatever, which was much worse. His sister Florence, who was fourteen and had lately taken to wearing her hair in a manner she believed to resemble that of a person in a magazine, had passed beneath the woodshed half an hour ago, and, glancing upward, had permitted herself a single remark.

"Well, I certainly wouldn't be in your shoes," Florence had said. "Not for a million dollars I wouldn't."

Roderick had made no reply, beyond a slight motion of the lips which, had it been audible, would not have been fit for the ears of a young lady. He was considering whether it might not, after all, be best to run away and join the navy, an institution which he understood to be indifferent to a man's past. The difficulty was that he did not know precisely where the navy kept itself, and it was nearly supper time.

At seven minutes before six the front gate clicked.

Roderick did not see his father enter, but he heard the gate, and the sound went through him as the knell goes through the condemned. He flattened himself somewhat against the shingles and listened. He heard the front door open and close; he heard, very faintly, his mother's voice rising in the hall, not loud, but with that peculiar rapid urgency which wives employ when they have been holding a thing in all afternoon; and then he heard nothing at all for a long time, which he rightly interpreted as the sound of his father being told.

Mr. Ellsworth Dunlap was a gentleman of forty-four, inclined to stoutness and to the evening paper, and he had come home that afternoon wanting nothing in the world so much as his slippers, his armchair, and twenty minutes of silence in which to discover what the Senate had been doing. He was not, by nature, a stern man. He had, indeed, a secret and rather shameful tendency to laugh at things which his wife considered serious, and he had long ago learned to disguise this tendency behind a cough, a frown, and an abrupt interest in the condition of his fingernails. But he was a man who valued his possessions, and among his possessions there was none he had valued more than his overcoat.

It was a dark-blue overcoat of a heavy and superior cloth, with a collar of Persian lamb, and it had been made for him in Chicago by a tailor who had since died, so that it could never be replaced. Mr. Dunlap had worn it four winters and had looked forward to wearing it four more. He was attached to it in that inarticulate, faithful way in which men become attached to old hats, old dogs, and old opinions; and when his wife, standing close to him in the dim hall, with her voice dropped to a stricken whisper, told him what had become of it, he did not immediately speak. He set down his umbrella with great care, as if it, too, might be given away if he were not watchful, and he looked at the hatrack for some moments.

"To a tramp," he said at last.

"To a tramp, Ellsworth! To a perfectly strange tramp at the back door! I'd put it in the closet under the stairs only this morning, meaning to have Lena pack it away in camphor tomorrow, and he must have taken it right out of there the minute my back was turned. Mrs. Hollister saw the man going up the alley with it over his arm. She said he was the dirtiest-looking creature she ever laid eyes on. She said he had it on before he got to the corner."

"In May," said Mr. Dunlap.

"I don't know what you mean, 'in May.'"

"I mean," said Mr. Dunlap heavily, "that it was seventy-eight degrees by the bank thermometer at noon, and if a man wanted an overcoat on a day like this he must have wanted it pretty bad." He coughed. "Where is he?"

"Where is who? The tramp?"

"Roderick."

"I think he's on the woodshed. He's been there ever since. Ellsworth, you'll have to speak to him. I simply can't. I've been all to pieces since three o'clock. And it isn't only the coat; it's the principle of the thing. He might have given away anything. He might have given away the silver."

Mr. Dunlap, who doubted that even a tramp would have accepted the Dunlap silver, which had been a wedding present from an aunt of uncertain taste, refrained from saying so. He went to the back door, opened it, and addressed the air in the general direction of the woodshed.

"Roderick!"

There was no response, though there was a slight sound of shingles.

"Roderick! You come down off there this minute and come into the library."

Then, without waiting to see whether he was obeyed, Mr. Dunlap withdrew into the house, and went into the library, and sat down in his armchair, and did not take up his newspaper. This last circumstance, more than any other, will convey to the reader the gravity of the occasion.

Roderick was some time in arriving. It is not a long way from a woodshed roof to a library, but there are distances that cannot be measured with a tape, and Roderick traversed this one by a route of his own devising, which included a visit to the pump, an inspection of a hole beneath the grape arbor where something might conceivably have been living, and a pause of some duration upon the back steps, during which he endeavored, by rubbing one shoe upon the opposite stocking, to give himself the appearance of a boy who has always been good. He then entered the kitchen, where Lena, the cook, regarded him with a solemn and portentous eye and said, "Well, now!" in a manner that chilled him; and so, at length, by way of the dining room, he came to the library door and stood in it.

"Come in," said Mr. Dunlap. "Come in and shut the door."

Roderick came in and shut the door. He did this with an elaborate gentleness, as if the door were an invalid, and then he stood beside it, with his hands behind him and his head somewhat on one side, gazing at a point on the wall about a foot above his father's head. His face had assumed an expression of pure and patient inquiry, such as might be worn by a person who has been called in from his studies to settle some trifling point of fact, and who is perfectly willing to oblige, but hopes it will not take long.

"Roderick," said Mr. Dunlap, "where is my overcoat?"

Roderick appeared to give the question his most earnest consideration.

"Which one?" he asked.

"Which one!" Mr. Dunlap repeated, and there was a dangerous pause. "I have exactly one overcoat, Roderick. Or I had exactly one overcoat until this afternoon. I am asking you where it is."

"Well," said Roderick, "I guess the man's got it."

"What man?"

"Well, the man that came to the back door. I guess he's got it. I gave it to him."

"Ah!" said Mr. Dunlap. "You gave it to him. And will you be good enough to tell me what in the name of common sense possessed you to give my overcoat, my good overcoat, to a total stranger at the back door?"

Roderick shifted his weight from one foot to the other. His eyes descended from the wall and rested upon the carpet, which had a pattern of large, involved roses, and he began, very slowly, to trace one of them with the toe of his shoe.

"Well, he said he was cold," he said.

"Cold! On a day like this?"

"Well, he said he had a chill. He said he got a fever in the Philippines, fighting, and it comes back on him every once in a while, and when it comes he gets a chill so bad his teeth go like this." Here Roderick, abandoning the rose, gave a vivid and alarming demonstration with his jaw. "He said sometimes it nearly kills him. He said he was a soldier in the war, and he got shot twice, and they never even gave him a pension or anything, and he said nobody cares about an old soldier. He said that's the way it is in this world."

"Did he show you where he was shot?"

"No, sir. He said it was where he couldn't show it."

Mr. Dunlap coughed. It was a long and rather complicated cough, and at the end of it he found it necessary to examine his fingernails with great attention.

"And so," he said presently, "on the strength of this affecting history, you went to the closet under the stairs and took out my overcoat, and gave it to him."

"Well, yes, sir. I didn't have anything else."

"You might," said Mr. Dunlap, "have given him your own coat, if you were so bent upon philanthropy."

"Well, I thought about that," said Roderick, with candor, "but it wouldn't fit him. He was a pretty big man. And anyway," he added, "mine's got a tear in it."

Mr. Dunlap was silent. It began to be borne in upon him, as it is borne in upon most fathers sooner or later, that he was engaged in a contest with an intelligence which, though inferior to his own in nearly every respect, possessed one formidable advantage: it did not in the least perceive that it had done anything wrong. He was considering how best to bring this perception home when Roderick, encouraged by the silence, produced his strongest card.

"Anyway," he said, lifting his eyes for the first time and fixing them on his father's with the clear, untroubled gaze of the righteous, "Mrs. Bascom said to."

"Mrs. Bascom?" Mr. Dunlap was startled. "Mrs. Bascom said to give away my overcoat?"

"Well, not exactly your overcoat. But she said to. In Sunday school. She said it was in the Bible. She said if somebody asks for your coat, you ought to give him your cloak, too. She said that was what we were supposed to do, and if we didn't, we weren't any better than the Pharisees. She said it Sunday before last. You can ask anybody."

Here was a difficulty indeed. Mr. Dunlap was a vestryman, and he had himself, upon more than one occasion, spoken warmly in favor of a fuller and more practical application of Christian principles to the affairs of daily life. He had not, however, anticipated that the first practical application in his own household would be made with his own overcoat; and he found himself, for the moment, in the uncomfortable position of a general who discovers that the enemy has captured his artillery and is turning it upon him.

"Roderick," he said, choosing his words, "it is perfectly true that we ought to be generous. Nobody is saying that we oughtn't. But the passage you mention refers to giving away one's own coat. Not somebody else's. Do you understand the difference?"

Roderick thought it over.

"Well, but it was in our house," he said.

"It was in our house, but it was not your coat."

"Well, but you're my father."

Mr. Dunlap was obliged to cough again.

At this juncture the library door opened, and Mrs. Dunlap, who had found it impossible to remain in the hall any longer, came in and sat down upon the edge of the sofa, with an air of having come merely to lend moral support and of having no intention of saying anything. This intention she maintained for perhaps four seconds.

"Did you ask him about the knife?" she said.

"What knife?"

"He's got a knife," said Mrs. Dunlap darkly. "Florence saw it. The man gave it to him."

Mr. Dunlap turned upon his son a look of deepening suspicion.

"Roderick, did that man give you something?"

Roderick's hand went, involuntarily and in spite of himself, to his trousers pocket, and was arrested there, too late.

"Well, he didn't give it to me exactly," he said. "It was just, he said I'd been so nice to an old soldier he wanted me to have something to remember him by. He said it was a soldier's knife. He said he carried it all through the war."

"Let me see it."

Slowly, with the reluctance of one who surrenders the last relic of a cherished friendship, Roderick drew forth the object and laid it upon his father's palm. It was a small knife with a handle of imitation bone, from which a portion of the imitation had come away, and it possessed a single blade, which, when Mr. Dunlap with some difficulty pried it open, proved to be broken off about halfway along its length. Upon the remaining surface of the handle could be discerned, by careful scrutiny, the words "Souvenir of Atlantic City."

Mr. Dunlap regarded this article for a considerable time.

"So," he said at last, "you have traded an overcoat that cost me sixty-five dollars, with a genuine Persian lamb collar, for half of a souvenir penknife."

"I didn't trade it," Roderick protested, with real feeling. "I gave it. It was charity. He just gave me the knife afterward. That's different."

"It is indeed different," said Mr. Dunlap. "It is a great deal worse. If you had traded it, I could at least have had the satisfaction of thinking you'd been cheated. As it is——" He stopped abruptly, and a look of sudden and genuine horror came over his face. He sat up in his chair. "Clara," he said, "Clara, the letter!"

"What letter?"

"Judge Wheelock's letter! The one I promised faithfully to mail to Washington back in March! I put it in the inside pocket of that overcoat the morning of the big snow, and I never thought of it again until this minute!"

Mrs. Dunlap uttered a small cry. Roderick, who had no idea who Judge Wheelock was, nevertheless perceived that matters had taken a decided turn for the worse, and he resumed his study of the carpet roses with an intensity that suggested he might at any moment be called upon to pass an examination in them.

For some moments nobody spoke. Mr. Dunlap was occupied with a vision of himself explaining to Judge Wheelock, who was a person of no humor whatever, that the letter upon which so much depended had been, for two months, in the pocket of a coat which was now walking about the countryside upon the back of a veteran of a war in which he had very probably never served. Then he rose. He was not, as has been said, a stern man, but there are limits, and he had reached them.

"Roderick," he said, "go up to your room."

Roderick's face expressed the purest astonishment, as though such a sentence had never before been pronounced in the history of jurisprudence.

"Before supper?"

"You will have your supper in your room. Bread and milk. And you will stay there until I come up to talk to you, and when I do come up, you will have thought very carefully about the difference between what belongs to you and what belongs to other people. Do you understand me?"

"Yes, sir," said Roderick. Then, after a pause, in a voice in which the bitterness of all unappreciated benefactors since the beginning of the world was distinctly audible, he added, "I was only trying to be good."

He went out. He closed the door behind him, once more with that elaborate gentleness, and they heard him ascend the stairs, very slowly, one step at a time, with a pause of several seconds upon each, in the manner of a martyr mounting to the place of his execution and wishing all concerned to understand clearly what was being done to him.

Upstairs, in his room, Roderick sat down upon the bed and gazed out of the window at the darkening yard, and in a little while his sorrows took shape and became a vision. He saw, upon some not distant afternoon, a magnificent carriage drawn by four white horses coming to a halt before the Dunlap gate; and from it there descended a tall gentleman in a silk hat and a dark-blue overcoat with a Persian lamb collar, whom Roderick instantly recognized, beneath the disguise of wealth, as the old soldier. The old soldier, it appeared, had been a millionaire all along, who went about the country in rags for the purpose of testing the human heart; and he had found but one heart in all his wanderings that was true. He came up the front walk, while the whole neighborhood gathered at the fence, and he laid upon Roderick's shoulder a hand that glittered with diamonds, and he said, in a voice that carried as far as the Hollisters' side porch, "This is the boy." And then, turning to Mr. Dunlap, who stood behind him pale and humbled, he said, "Sir, you have punished a hero." Mr. Dunlap, in this vision, wept.

Roderick found it a very satisfactory vision, and he ran through it several times, with improvements.

Meanwhile, in the library below, Mrs. Dunlap had turned to her husband with an expression of earnest severity.

"Ellsworth, I do hope you didn't let him see you laughing."

"Laughing!" said Mr. Dunlap. "I lose my overcoat and Judge Wheelock's letter in the same afternoon, and you think I'm laughing?" He coughed. "Where would I find anything to laugh at in that?"

"You coughed four times. I counted."

"I have," said Mr. Dunlap with dignity, "a slight irritation of the throat." He picked up his newspaper, opened it, and held it before his face for some time without turning a page. Presently his shoulders were observed to move slightly.

"Ellsworth!"

"It was the part about the Pharisees," said Mr. Dunlap from behind the paper, in a muffled voice. "I'm sorry, Clara. I can't help it. It was the Pharisees."

At half past eight that evening, when Lena had cleared the dining table and Mrs. Dunlap was upstairs writing a long letter to her sister upon the subject of boys in general, Mr. Dunlap went quietly into the kitchen and cut a large wedge of the cherry pie which had been intended for the next day's dinner. He looked about him with some furtiveness, placed the pie upon a saucer, and carried it up the back stairs, which were seldom used and did not creak. He was gone some twenty minutes, and when he came down again the saucer was empty and he was humming. It is to be recorded that the talk upon the difference between what belongs to oneself and what belongs to other people had been delivered, and that it had been, in its way, a very good talk, though it had wandered, toward the end, into a long and circumstantial account of a certain gold watch, the property of Mr. Dunlap's grandfather, and of what had become of it in the summer of 1869, and of the remarkable ferret for which it had been exchanged.

Here is an excerpt of Booth Tarkington's writing, to show you their style:

We debate sometimes what is to be the future of this nation when we think that in a few years public affairs may be in the hands of the fin-de-siècle gilded youths we see about us during the Christmas holidays. Such foppery, such luxury, such insolence, was surely never practised by the scented, overbearing patricians of the Palatine, even in Rome’s most decadent epoch. In all the wild orgy of wastefulness and luxury with which the nineteenth century reaches its close, the gilded youth has been surely the worst symptom. With his airs of young milord, his fast horses, his gold and silver cigarette-cases, his clothes from a New York tailor, his recklessness of money showered upon him by indulgent mothers or doting grandfathers, he respects nothing and nobody. He is blase if you please. Watch him at a social function, how condescendingly he deigns to select a partner for the popular waltz or two step, how carelessly he shoulders older people out of his way, with what a blank stare he returns the salutation of some old acquaintance whom he may choose in his royal whim to forget! The unpleasant part of all this is that the young women he so condescendingly selects as partners for the dance greet him with seeming rapture, though in their hearts they must feel humiliated by his languid hauteur, and many older people beam upon him almost fawningly if he unbends so far as to throw them a careless, disdainful word! One wonders what has come over the new generation. Of such as these the Republic was not made. Let us pray that the future of our country is not in the hands of these fin-de-siècle gilded youths, but rather in the calloused palms of young men yet unknown, labouring upon the farms of the land. When we compare the young manhood of Abraham Lincoln with the specimens we are now producing, we see too well that it bodes ill for the twentieth century— George yawned, and tossed the clipping into his waste-basket, wondering why his aunt thought such dull nonsense worth the sending. As for her insinuation, pencilled upon the border, he supposed she meant to joke—a supposition which neither surprised him nor altered his lifelong opinion of her wit. He read her letter with more interest:
... The dinner your mother gave for the Morgans was a lovely affair. It was last Monday evening, just ten days after you left. It was peculiarly appropriate that your mother should give this dinner, because her brother George, your uncle, was Mr. Morgan’s most intimate friend before he left here a number of years ago, and it was a pleasant occasion for the formal announcement of some news which you heard from Lucy Morgan before you returned to college. At least she told me she had told you the night before you left that her father had decided to return here to live. It was appropriate that your mother, herself an old friend, should assemble a representative selection of Mr. Morgan’s old friends around him at such a time. He was in great spirits and most entertaining. As your time was so charmingly taken up during your visit home with a younger member of his family, you probably overlooked opportunities of hearing him talk, and do not know what an interesting man he can be. He will soon begin to build his factory here for the manufacture of automobiles, which he says is a term he prefers to “horseless carriages.” Your Uncle George told me he would like to invest in this factory, as George thinks there is a future for automobiles; perhaps not for general use, but as an interesting novelty, which people with sufficient means would like to own for their amusement and the sake of variety. However, he said Mr. Morgan laughingly declined his offer, as Mr. M. was fully able to finance this venture, though not starting in a very large way. Your uncle said other people are manufacturing automobiles in different parts of the country with success. Your father is not very well, though he is not actually ill, and the doctor tells him he ought not to be so much at his office, as the long years of application indoors with no exercise are beginning to affect him unfavourably, but I believe your father would die if he had to give up his work, which is all that has ever interested him outside of his family. I never could understand it. Mr. Morgan took your mother and me with Lucy to see Modjeska in “Twelfth Night” yesterday evening, and Lucy said she thought the Duke looked rather like you, only much more democratic in his manner. I suppose you will think I have written a great deal about the Morgans in this letter, but thought you would be interested because of your interest in a younger member of his family. Hoping that you are finding college still as attractive as ever, Affectionately, Aunt Fanny. George read one sentence in this letter several times. Then he dropped the missive in his wastebasket to join the clipping, and strolled down the corridor of his dormitory to borrow a copy of “Twelfth Night.” Having secured one, he returned to his study and refreshed his memory of the play—but received no enlightenment that enabled him to comprehend Lucy’s strange remark. However, he found himself impelled in the direction of correspondence, and presently wrote a letter—not a reply to his Aunt Fanny. Dear Lucy: No doubt you will be surprised at hearing from me so soon again, especially as this makes two in answer to the one received from you since getting back to the old place. I hear you have been making comments about me at the theatre, that some actor was more democratic in his manners than I am, which I do not understand. You know my theory of life because I explained it to you on our first drive together, when I told you I would not talk to everybody about things I feel like the way I spoke to you of my theory of life. I believe those who are able should have a true theory of life, and I developed my theory of life long, long ago. Well, here I sit smoking my faithful briar pipe, indulging in the fragrance of my tobacco as I look out on the campus from my many-paned window, and things are different with me from the way they were way back in Freshman year. I can see now how boyish in many ways I was then. I believe what has changed me as much as anything was my visit home at the time I met you. So I sit here with my faithful briar and dream the old dreams over as it were, dreaming of the waltzes we waltzed together and of that last night before we parted, and you told me the good news you were going to live there, and I would find my friend waiting for me, when I get home next summer. I will be glad my friend will be waiting for me. I am not capable of friendship except for the very few, and, looking back over my life, I remember there were times when I doubted if I could feel a great friendship for anybody—especially girls. I do not take a great interest in many people, as you know, for I find most of them shallow. Here in the old place I do not believe in being hail-fellow-well-met with every Tom, Dick, and Harry just because he happens to be a classmate, any more than I do at home, where I have always been careful who I was seen with, largely on account of the family, but also because my disposition ever since my boyhood has been to encourage real intimacy from but the few. What are you reading now? I have finished both “Henry Esmond” and “The Virginians.” I like Thackeray because he is not trashy, and because he writes principally of nice people. My theory of literature is an author who does not indulge in trashiness—writes about people you could introduce into your own home. I agree with my Uncle Sydney, as I once heard him say he did not care to read a book or go to a play about people he would not care to meet at his own dinner table. I believe we should live by certain standards and ideals, as you know from my telling you my theory of life. Well, a letter is no place for deep discussions, so I will not go into the subject. From several letters from my mother, and one from Aunt Fanny, I hear you are seeing a good deal of the family since I left. I hope sometimes you think of the member who is absent. I got a silver frame for your photograph in New York, and I keep it on my desk. It is the only girl’s photograph I ever took the trouble to have framed, though, as I told you frankly, I have had any number of other girls’ photographs, yet all were only passing fancies, and oftentimes I have questioned in years past if I was capable of much friendship toward the feminine sex, which I usually found shallow until our own friendship began. When I look at your photograph, I say to myself, “At last, at last here is one that will not prove shallow.” My faithful briar has gone out. I will have to rise and fill it, then once more in the fragrance of My Lady Nicotine, I will sit and dream the old dreams over, and think, too, of the true friend at home awaiting my return in June for the summer vacation. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. When he came home in June his friend was awaiting him; at least, she was so pleased to see him again that for a few minutes after their first encounter she was a little breathless, and a great deal glowing, and quiet withal. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. Lucy and her father were living at the Amberson Hotel, while Morgan got his small machine-shops built in a western outskirt of the town; and George grumbled about the shabbiness and the old-fashioned look of the hotel, though it was “still the best in the place, of course.” He remonstrated with his grandfather, declaring that the whole Amberson Estate would be getting “run-down and out-at-heel, if things weren’t taken in hand pretty soon.” He urged the general need of rebuilding, renovating, varnishing, and lawsuits. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.
