column307:
Here is an excerpt of Booth Tarkington's writing, to show you their style:

We debate sometimes what is to be the future of this nation when we think that in a few years public affairs may be in the hands of the fin-de-siècle gilded youths we see about us during the Christmas holidays. Such foppery, such luxury, such insolence, was surely never practised by the scented, overbearing patricians of the Palatine, even in Rome’s most decadent epoch. In all the wild orgy of wastefulness and luxury with which the nineteenth century reaches its close, the gilded youth has been surely the worst symptom. With his airs of young milord, his fast horses, his gold and silver cigarette-cases, his clothes from a New York tailor, his recklessness of money showered upon him by indulgent mothers or doting grandfathers, he respects nothing and nobody. He is blase if you please. Watch him at a social function, how condescendingly he deigns to select a partner for the popular waltz or two step, how carelessly he shoulders older people out of his way, with what a blank stare he returns the salutation of some old acquaintance whom he may choose in his royal whim to forget! The unpleasant part of all this is that the young women he so condescendingly selects as partners for the dance greet him with seeming rapture, though in their hearts they must feel humiliated by his languid hauteur, and many older people beam upon him almost fawningly if he unbends so far as to throw them a careless, disdainful word! One wonders what has come over the new generation. Of such as these the Republic was not made. Let us pray that the future of our country is not in the hands of these fin-de-siècle gilded youths, but rather in the calloused palms of young men yet unknown, labouring upon the farms of the land. When we compare the young manhood of Abraham Lincoln with the specimens we are now producing, we see too well that it bodes ill for the twentieth century— George yawned, and tossed the clipping into his waste-basket, wondering why his aunt thought such dull nonsense worth the sending. As for her insinuation, pencilled upon the border, he supposed she meant to joke—a supposition which neither surprised him nor altered his lifelong opinion of her wit. He read her letter with more interest:
... The dinner your mother gave for the Morgans was a lovely affair. It was last Monday evening, just ten days after you left. It was peculiarly appropriate that your mother should give this dinner, because her brother George, your uncle, was Mr. Morgan’s most intimate friend before he left here a number of years ago, and it was a pleasant occasion for the formal announcement of some news which you heard from Lucy Morgan before you returned to college. At least she told me she had told you the night before you left that her father had decided to return here to live. It was appropriate that your mother, herself an old friend, should assemble a representative selection of Mr. Morgan’s old friends around him at such a time. He was in great spirits and most entertaining. As your time was so charmingly taken up during your visit home with a younger member of his family, you probably overlooked opportunities of hearing him talk, and do not know what an interesting man he can be. He will soon begin to build his factory here for the manufacture of automobiles, which he says is a term he prefers to “horseless carriages.” Your Uncle George told me he would like to invest in this factory, as George thinks there is a future for automobiles; perhaps not for general use, but as an interesting novelty, which people with sufficient means would like to own for their amusement and the sake of variety. However, he said Mr. Morgan laughingly declined his offer, as Mr. M. was fully able to finance this venture, though not starting in a very large way. Your uncle said other people are manufacturing automobiles in different parts of the country with success. Your father is not very well, though he is not actually ill, and the doctor tells him he ought not to be so much at his office, as the long years of application indoors with no exercise are beginning to affect him unfavourably, but I believe your father would die if he had to give up his work, which is all that has ever interested him outside of his family. I never could understand it. Mr. Morgan took your mother and me with Lucy to see Modjeska in “Twelfth Night” yesterday evening, and Lucy said she thought the Duke looked rather like you, only much more democratic in his manner. I suppose you will think I have written a great deal about the Morgans in this letter, but thought you would be interested because of your interest in a younger member of his family. Hoping that you are finding college still as attractive as ever, Affectionately, Aunt Fanny. George read one sentence in this letter several times. Then he dropped the missive in his wastebasket to join the clipping, and strolled down the corridor of his dormitory to borrow a copy of “Twelfth Night.” Having secured one, he returned to his study and refreshed his memory of the play—but received no enlightenment that enabled him to comprehend Lucy’s strange remark. However, he found himself impelled in the direction of correspondence, and presently wrote a letter—not a reply to his Aunt Fanny. Dear Lucy: No doubt you will be surprised at hearing from me so soon again, especially as this makes two in answer to the one received from you since getting back to the old place. I hear you have been making comments about me at the theatre, that some actor was more democratic in his manners than I am, which I do not understand. You know my theory of life because I explained it to you on our first drive together, when I told you I would not talk to everybody about things I feel like the way I spoke to you of my theory of life. I believe those who are able should have a true theory of life, and I developed my theory of life long, long ago. Well, here I sit smoking my faithful briar pipe, indulging in the fragrance of my tobacco as I look out on the campus from my many-paned window, and things are different with me from the way they were way back in Freshman year. I can see now how boyish in many ways I was then. I believe what has changed me as much as anything was my visit home at the time I met you. So I sit here with my faithful briar and dream the old dreams over as it were, dreaming of the waltzes we waltzed together and of that last night before we parted, and you told me the good news you were going to live there, and I would find my friend waiting for me, when I get home next summer. I will be glad my friend will be waiting for me. I am not capable of friendship except for the very few, and, looking back over my life, I remember there were times when I doubted if I could feel a great friendship for anybody—especially girls. I do not take a great interest in many people, as you know, for I find most of them shallow. Here in the old place I do not believe in being hail-fellow-well-met with every Tom, Dick, and Harry just because he happens to be a classmate, any more than I do at home, where I have always been careful who I was seen with, largely on account of the family, but also because my disposition ever since my boyhood has been to encourage real intimacy from but the few. What are you reading now? I have finished both “Henry Esmond” and “The Virginians.” I like Thackeray because he is not trashy, and because he writes principally of nice people. My theory of literature is an author who does not indulge in trashiness—writes about people you could introduce into your own home. I agree with my Uncle Sydney, as I once heard him say he did not care to read a book or go to a play about people he would not care to meet at his own dinner table. I believe we should live by certain standards and ideals, as you know from my telling you my theory of life. Well, a letter is no place for deep discussions, so I will not go into the subject. From several letters from my mother, and one from Aunt Fanny, I hear you are seeing a good deal of the family since I left. I hope sometimes you think of the member who is absent. I got a silver frame for your photograph in New York, and I keep it on my desk. It is the only girl’s photograph I ever took the trouble to have framed, though, as I told you frankly, I have had any number of other girls’ photographs, yet all were only passing fancies, and oftentimes I have questioned in years past if I was capable of much friendship toward the feminine sex, which I usually found shallow until our own friendship began. When I look at your photograph, I say to myself, “At last, at last here is one that will not prove shallow.” My faithful briar has gone out. I will have to rise and fill it, then once more in the fragrance of My Lady Nicotine, I will sit and dream the old dreams over, and think, too, of the true friend at home awaiting my return in June for the summer vacation. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. When he came home in June his friend was awaiting him; at least, she was so pleased to see him again that for a few minutes after their first encounter she was a little breathless, and a great deal glowing, and quiet withal. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. Lucy and her father were living at the Amberson Hotel, while Morgan got his small machine-shops built in a western outskirt of the town; and George grumbled about the shabbiness and the old-fashioned look of the hotel, though it was “still the best in the place, of course.” He remonstrated with his grandfather, declaring that the whole Amberson Estate would be getting “run-down and out-at-heel, if things weren’t taken in hand pretty soon.” He urged the general need of rebuilding, renovating, varnishing, and lawsuits. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

column308:
Mrs. Wesley Pruitt had been married twenty-six years, and in that time she had learned that there are two kinds of silence in a household after supper. One is the comfortable kind, wherein a husband turns the pages of the *Evening Courier* and a wife darns, and neither has anything to say because neither has anything to conceal. The other kind is louder than a brass band, though nobody but the two people in the room can hear it. On this particular October evening the sitting-room of the Pruitt house on Delaware Street was filled from the carpet to the plaster rosette in the ceiling with the second kind, and Mrs. Pruitt sat in the midst of it with a sock drawn over the wooden egg in her left hand. For the space of a quarter of an hour she had not set a stitch.

Mr. Pruitt, on the other side of the lamp, read his newspaper with a thoroughness that would have done credit to a proof-reader. He had read the advertisements of the Bon Ton Store, wherein ladies' walking-skirts of English melton were offered at three dollars and ninety-eight cents. He had read the death notices, the river stages at Cincinnati, and a column on the habits of the Patagonian ostrich. He was now reading, for the second time, a notice that the Third Ward Republican Club would meet on Thursday evening at Odd Fellows' Hall. Within his own recollection he had never before cared when the Third Ward Republican Club met, nor where.

"Wesley," said Mrs. Pruitt.

"Mm," said Mr. Pruitt.

"Wesley, I'd like you to put down that paper."

He lowered it perhaps three inches, so that his eyebrows and the upper half of his spectacles came over the top of it like the sun rising over a low and cloudy horizon. "What is it, Mattie? I'm reading."

"I know you're reading. You've been reading since half-past seven, and you haven't turned a page since eight. I'd like you to put it down."

Mr. Pruitt considered this. He was a short, stoutish man of fifty-four, with a grey moustache that drooped somewhat at the corners and gave him, even in his happiest moods, the air of a walrus who had received disappointing news. He had been called "a solid man" by the town for so many years that he had come to believe it himself, and it was a belief he was not at present in a position to give up without a struggle. He folded the *Courier* with great care, creasing it along its natural lines as though it were a document of some legal consequence, and laid it upon his knee.

"Well?" he said.

Mrs. Pruitt took up her needle, looked at it, and put it down again. She was a thin woman, with the alert and somewhat apprehensive prettiness that a certain kind of girl carries with her into her fifties, like a parasol she has forgotten to close; and she had a way, when she was disturbed, of touching the brooch at her throat with the tips of her fingers, as if to make sure it was still there. She touched it now.

"I saw Mrs. Gutherie at Woman's Guild this afternoon," she said.

"Did you?" said Mr. Pruitt. "Well, that's nothing new. You see Mrs. Gutherie every Wednesday."

"She asked after your health."

"Very kind of her."

"She asked after it," Mrs. Pruitt went on evenly, "in a way I didn't care for. She asked after it the way people do when somebody in the family's been to the doctor and everybody knows it but the family. And then she said she supposed I must be anxious, these days—with everything. And I said, 'With everything, Mrs. Gutherie?' And she looked at me as if I'd been caught taking the last croquette off the plate, and she said, 'Oh, I'm sure I didn't mean a thing,' and went over to talk to Mrs. Lamphier about the rummage sale."

"Mrs. Gutherie," observed Mr. Pruitt, "is a woman who never in her life meant a thing and never in her life said anything else."

"Her husband," said Mrs. Pruitt, "is a vice-president of the Merchants' National Bank."

There was a pause. In the kitchen, Delia, the hired girl, could be heard dropping a stove-lid with the peculiar emphasis of a person who would rather be at a dance; and somewhere in the upper part of the house their daughter Ella was practising "The Maiden's Prayer" upon the upright piano, and arriving at the difficult passage in the left hand with the steady inevitability of a train approaching a washed-out trestle.

"I know what Henry Gutherie is," said Mr. Pruitt. "I've known Henry Gutherie since he was clerking in Dorsey's dry-goods and wore a celluloid collar to church."

"Wesley, have you been to the bank?"

"I go to the bank every day of my life. A man in business goes to the bank."

"You know what I mean."

He did know what she meant, and he knew she knew he knew it, and this triangle of knowledge so oppressed him that he took off his spectacles and began to polish them with his handkerchief, breathing on each lens in turn with a slow and deliberate thoroughness, as if he had been commissioned by the State to see that they were clean.

"Mattie," he said, "there are some things that are a man's business, and some that are a woman's. I've never asked you how you run the house—"

"You asked me last March why we needed a new boiler in the cellar."

"That was different."

"I don't see how."

"Well, it was. A boiler is—it's a household matter, but it's also a matter of plumbing, and plumbing's—" He perceived that he was in difficulties, and abandoned the boiler altogether. "What I mean to say is, I don't come home and trouble you with every little thing that goes on down at the store."

"No," said Mrs. Pruitt. "You don't. You haven't come home and troubled me with a single thing that goes on at the store since about the first of July. Before that, you used to tell me everything—how many kegs of nails went to the Logansport people, and what old Mr. Hibben said about the price of barbed wire, and all of it, all through supper, till I could have screamed. And then in July you stopped. You just stopped, Wesley. You've talked about the weather and the Philippines and the new pastor's wife's hats, and you've sat behind that paper every night like—like a man in a duck-blind."

Mr. Pruitt put his spectacles back on. Behind them his eyes had a look that his wife had not seen there in a long time—not since, in fact, the winter of 1893, when the panic had come down upon the town like a late frost upon an orchard, and men had walked about the streets with their hands in their pockets and their chins in their collars, not speaking much. She had been younger then and had not seen the look for what it was. She saw it now.

"It's that new store," she said, more gently. "Isn't it? That Kessler's."

He made a small motion with his hand, as of a man brushing away a fly that was not there.

"Kessler's," he said, "is a department store. They sell everything from hair-ribbons to kitchen ranges, and they buy it all from Chicago in carload lots, and they don't care if they make a cent on a keg of nails so long as the woman who comes in for the nails goes out with a parlour lamp and three yards of dotted swiss. That's their system. They call it a system." He pronounced the word as though it were the name of a disease. "My father sold hardware on Washington Street for thirty-one years and I've sold it there for twenty-two more, and we never had a system. We had a stock, and we stood behind it, and when a man bought a saw from Pruitt and Son he knew he could come back in ten years and get it set. That used to be enough."

"And it isn't enough any more?"

"It doesn't appear to be," said Mr. Pruitt.

Upstairs, Ella reached the difficult passage, faltered, went back four bars, and attacked it again with a kind of desperate gallantry. Neither of her parents heard her.

"How much did you borrow?" Mrs. Pruitt asked.

Her husband looked at her with a strange expression—partly of injury, partly of relief, and partly of that mild astonishment with which men occasionally discover that the women they have married possess the faculty of arithmetic.

"Who said I borrowed anything?"

"Nobody said it. Mrs. Gutherie didn't say it in the loudest voice I ever heard. How much, Wesley?"

"Mattie, I don't think it's a thing you need—"

"How much?"

He named a sum. It was not, as such sums go, an enormous one; there were men on Pennsylvania Street who lost as much in a bad afternoon on the Board of Trade and drove out to the Country Club the next morning in their new automobiles without so much as a crease in their brows. But to Mrs. Pruitt, who had been brought up to regard a mortgage in much the same light as a cancer, and who had once wept for an entire evening because Wesley had bought a set of encyclopaedias on the instalment plan, it fell upon the sitting-room like a piece of the ceiling. Her fingers went to the brooch and stayed there.

"Against what?" she said at last.

He did not answer.

"Against what, Wesley? A bank doesn't lend money on a man's good name any more. Henry Gutherie wouldn't lend his own mother car-fare on her good name. Against what?"

Mr. Pruitt looked at the carpet, a Brussels of a large and confident pattern, in which red cabbage-roses had been flourishing for eighteen years without regard to the vicissitudes of trade. He looked at the marble-topped table and the lamp with the painted globe. He looked at the walnut what-not in the corner, with its shells from Atlantic City and its little china shepherdess who had lost her crook in 1891 and never complained of it. He did not look at his wife.

"The house," he said.

It is one of the singular things about a tense conversation between married people that its most dangerous moment is not always the moment of the blow, but the moment just after, when the one who has struck it waits to see what will come back. Mr. Pruitt waited. He had, in the course of the long summer, rehearsed this scene a good many times—in the back office of the store, among the smells of oil and binder-twine; on the long walk home under the maples; even, now and then, at three o'clock in the morning, lying on his back and staring at the faint square of the window. In all these rehearsals his wife had wept. Sometimes she had wept quietly, and sometimes she had wept with great violence and had gone to her mother's in Greencastle and not come back; but she had always wept, and he had always been, at the end, a man more sinned against than sinning, who had shouldered his burden alone in order to spare her.

Mrs. Pruitt did not weep. She sat for a considerable time without saying anything, and then she put the sock and the darning-egg into her work-basket, and closed the lid of the basket, and folded her hands upon it.

"You might have told me," she said.

"I didn't want you worried."

"You didn't want me worried." She repeated it slowly, as if she were examining it for flaws, like a piece of china at an auction. "So you let me sit through Woman's Guild with Lettie Gutherie looking at me as if I had a black-bordered handkerchief in my reticule. You let me order Ella's winter coat from Indianapolis—the one with the caracul collar, Wesley, the one I told you about and you said, 'Get it, Mattie, get it, the girl's only young once.' You let me think we could afford that. You let me go on about having the front porch screened in the spring. You let me—" She stopped, and her voice, which had remained very steady, wavered upon some small obstacle and recovered. "You let me be a fool in front of the whole town, and you call that not wanting me worried."

"I thought I'd have it straightened out," said Mr. Pruitt. "I thought by Christmas—"

"By Christmas!"

"There's the fall trade from the farmers. There always is. When the corn's in, they come to town and they buy. Stoves, mostly, and stove-pipe, and harness hardware. I thought if the fall trade was what it used to be—"

"And is it?"

He moved his shoulders in a gesture that might have been a shrug and might have been only the settling of a tired man in an uncomfortable chair.

"The interurban," he said. "They've got the interurban out to Lebanon now, and up past Noblesville. A farmer gets on the car in the morning, and he's in Indianapolis by ten o'clock, and he can go round all the big stores and get back home for supper. Why should he hitch up a team and drive into our town to buy a stove from me? He can't think of a reason, and I'm hanged if I can think of one for him." He made a short, unhappy sound that was meant to be a laugh. "I sat down there in July and I added up the books, and I added them up again, and they came out the same way both times. I guess they'd have come out the same way if I'd added them up a hundred times. A column of figures is the most obstinate thing God ever made, Mattie. You can't argue with it and you can't bluff it and you can't—you can't keep it from your wife, either, it appears."

"No," she said. "It appears not."

He looked at her then, for the first time since he had folded the paper; and something in her face—it was not anger, exactly, though there was anger in it, and it was not pity, though there was that too—made him look away again quickly, the way a man looks away from a bright window.

"I suppose," he said, with a stiffness that was meant for dignity and did not quite arrive there, "you think I've made a pretty poor showing of it."

"I think," said Mrs. Pruitt, "that you've made a pretty poor showing of being married. That's what I think. Wesley Pruitt, I didn't marry the hardware store. I didn't marry your father's thirty-one years on Washington Street. If I'd wanted to marry a keg of nails I could have had my choice of them. I married you, and I married you for better or worse, and I stood up in front of Dr. Haskell and a hundred and forty people and said so, and I meant it, and you know I meant it." Her voice rose a little. "And here you've gone and had the worse all to yourself since July, like—like a boy with a bag of candy he won't pass round! As if it were yours! As if you had any right to it!"

This was a view of the matter which had not occurred to Mr. Pruitt in any of his rehearsals, and it disconcerted him a good deal more than tears would have done. He opened his mouth, closed it, and opened it again.

"I don't see," he said finally, "how you can call it candy."

"Oh, you don't see!" said Mrs. Pruitt. "No, I don't suppose you do. Men never do. A man thinks if he carries everything himself, he's being noble. He thinks he's Atlas, holding up the world. And all the while his wife is walking around underneath it, not knowing it's there, and bumping her head on it every time she stands up straight, and wondering what in the world's the matter with her."

There was a pause.

"I never thought of it like that," said Mr. Pruitt humbly.

"Well, think of it now."

He thought of it. Upstairs, by some miracle of persistence, Ella had at last achieved the difficult passage and was proceeding toward the end of "The Maiden's Prayer" with the reckless confidence of a person who has crossed a river on the ice and does not intend to look back. In the kitchen Delia had finished with the stove and could be heard on the back porch, conversing in low and spirited tones with somebody who was presumably the iceman's younger brother and certainly not the iceman. The clock on the mantel, a black marble one shaped like a small Greek temple, which had been a wedding present from Mr. Pruitt's Aunt Sophronia and had never kept correct time for a single day in twenty-six years, struck nine with great solemnity at a quarter of.

"Mattie," said Mr. Pruitt.

"What?"

"I'm sorry."

She did not answer at once; but the hand that had been at the brooch came down and lay upon the arm of her chair, and after a moment he reached across the lamp-table and covered it with his own. It was a thing he had not done, outside of church and the photographer's, in a good many years, and he did it awkwardly, nearly knocking over the lamp.

"Mind the lamp," said Mrs. Pruitt; but she did not take her hand away.

"What are we going to do?" he asked her. It was, though neither of them remarked it, the first time since July that he had said "we."

"Well," said Mrs. Pruitt, and her voice took on a brisk and practical note, as if the subject were a church supper that had run short of ham, "the first thing is, Ella's coat goes back. She can wear last year's another winter, and I'll put new braid on it, and if she cries she can cry. Girls of seventeen are made to cry; it's good for their complexions. The porch can wait. And I've been thinking for two years that we don't need Delia six days a week, and you know yourself she's not worth her board on Thursdays, with that boy hanging round the back porch."

"Mattie, I didn't mean for you to—"

"And the second thing," she went on, paying him no attention whatever, "is that to-morrow morning you're going down to the store, and I'm going with you."

Mr. Pruitt stared at her. "To the store? What for?"

"To look at those books you've been adding up," said his wife. "I kept Papa's accounts for him for six years before I married you, and he never lost a dollar he didn't mean to. A column of figures may be obstinate, Wesley, but I never yet saw one that couldn't be made to listen to reason if it was spoken to firmly enough."

He continued to stare at her, and as he stared, the walrus droop of his moustache appeared, very slowly, to lift a little at the corners—not much; it was not a moustache much given to lifting; but enough.

"Well, I'll be—" said Mr. Pruitt, and stopped, being a church-member.

"You'll be at breakfast at seven," said Mrs. Pruitt, and took the sock out of her work-basket again.

He sat watching her for some time. Then, because he was a man and could not help it, and because a certain portion of the dignity that had deserted him earlier in the evening seemed to be returning by the back stairs, he cleared his throat.

"Of course," he said, "I'd have told you myself, by Christmas, if Henry Gutherie's wife hadn't—"

"Of course you would," said Mrs. Pruitt placidly, without looking up from her darning. "Pass me the scissors, Wesley. They're under your paper."

He passed them to her; and it was not until he had picked up the *Courier* again, and opened it, and found himself reading for the third time that the Third Ward Republican Club would meet on Thursday at Odd Fellows' Hall, that it occurred to him to wonder how long his wife had actually known—and whether, in point of fact, Mrs. Gutherie had told her anything at all. He considered asking. He looked at her over the top of the paper, at her bent head and her quick, unhurried needle and the small, composed line of her mouth; and he decided, with what may have been the first real wisdom he had shown since July, that he would not.

Here is an excerpt of Booth Tarkington's writing, to show you their style:

We debate sometimes what is to be the future of this nation when we think that in a few years public affairs may be in the hands of the fin-de-siècle gilded youths we see about us during the Christmas holidays. Such foppery, such luxury, such insolence, was surely never practised by the scented, overbearing patricians of the Palatine, even in Rome’s most decadent epoch. In all the wild orgy of wastefulness and luxury with which the nineteenth century reaches its close, the gilded youth has been surely the worst symptom. With his airs of young milord, his fast horses, his gold and silver cigarette-cases, his clothes from a New York tailor, his recklessness of money showered upon him by indulgent mothers or doting grandfathers, he respects nothing and nobody. He is blase if you please. Watch him at a social function, how condescendingly he deigns to select a partner for the popular waltz or two step, how carelessly he shoulders older people out of his way, with what a blank stare he returns the salutation of some old acquaintance whom he may choose in his royal whim to forget! The unpleasant part of all this is that the young women he so condescendingly selects as partners for the dance greet him with seeming rapture, though in their hearts they must feel humiliated by his languid hauteur, and many older people beam upon him almost fawningly if he unbends so far as to throw them a careless, disdainful word! One wonders what has come over the new generation. Of such as these the Republic was not made. Let us pray that the future of our country is not in the hands of these fin-de-siècle gilded youths, but rather in the calloused palms of young men yet unknown, labouring upon the farms of the land. When we compare the young manhood of Abraham Lincoln with the specimens we are now producing, we see too well that it bodes ill for the twentieth century— George yawned, and tossed the clipping into his waste-basket, wondering why his aunt thought such dull nonsense worth the sending. As for her insinuation, pencilled upon the border, he supposed she meant to joke—a supposition which neither surprised him nor altered his lifelong opinion of her wit. He read her letter with more interest:
... The dinner your mother gave for the Morgans was a lovely affair. It was last Monday evening, just ten days after you left. It was peculiarly appropriate that your mother should give this dinner, because her brother George, your uncle, was Mr. Morgan’s most intimate friend before he left here a number of years ago, and it was a pleasant occasion for the formal announcement of some news which you heard from Lucy Morgan before you returned to college. At least she told me she had told you the night before you left that her father had decided to return here to live. It was appropriate that your mother, herself an old friend, should assemble a representative selection of Mr. Morgan’s old friends around him at such a time. He was in great spirits and most entertaining. As your time was so charmingly taken up during your visit home with a younger member of his family, you probably overlooked opportunities of hearing him talk, and do not know what an interesting man he can be. He will soon begin to build his factory here for the manufacture of automobiles, which he says is a term he prefers to “horseless carriages.” Your Uncle George told me he would like to invest in this factory, as George thinks there is a future for automobiles; perhaps not for general use, but as an interesting novelty, which people with sufficient means would like to own for their amusement and the sake of variety. However, he said Mr. Morgan laughingly declined his offer, as Mr. M. was fully able to finance this venture, though not starting in a very large way. Your uncle said other people are manufacturing automobiles in different parts of the country with success. Your father is not very well, though he is not actually ill, and the doctor tells him he ought not to be so much at his office, as the long years of application indoors with no exercise are beginning to affect him unfavourably, but I believe your father would die if he had to give up his work, which is all that has ever interested him outside of his family. Mr. Morgan took your mother and me with Lucy to see Modjeska in “Twelfth Night” yesterday evening, and Lucy said she thought the Duke looked rather like you, only much more democratic in his manner. Dear Lucy: No doubt you will be surprised at hearing from me so soon again, especially as this makes two in answer to the one received from you since getting back to the old place. I hear you have been making comments about me at the theatre, that some actor was more democratic in his manners than I am, which I do not understand. You know my theory of life because I explained it to you on our first drive together, when I told you I would not talk to everybody about things I feel like the way I spoke to you of my theory of life. I believe those who are able should have a true theory of life, and I developed my theory of life long, long ago. Well, here I sit smoking my faithful briar pipe, indulging in the fragrance of my tobacco as I look out on the campus from my many-paned window, and things are different with me from the way they were way back in Freshman year. I can see now how boyish in many ways I was then. I believe what has changed me as much as anything was my visit home at the time I met you. So I sit here with my faithful briar and dream the old dreams over as it were, dreaming of the waltzes we waltzed together and of that last night before we parted, and you told me the good news you were going to live there, and I would find my friend waiting for me, when I get home next summer. I will be glad my friend will be waiting for me. It is the only girl’s photograph I ever took the trouble to have framed, though, as I told you frankly, I have had any number of other girls’ photographs, yet all were only passing fancies, and oftentimes I have questioned in years past if I was capable of much friendship toward the feminine sex, which I usually found shallow until our own friendship began. I will have to rise and fill it, then once more in the fragrance of My Lady Nicotine, I will sit and dream the old dreams over, and think, too, of the true friend at home awaiting my return in June for the summer vacation. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

column308:
Ellery Vane came home in the first week of October, after an absence of three years and some months, and he came home with a mustache. It was not a large mustache, nor a dark one; in certain lights it was not visible at all, and in others it gave to his upper lip merely the effect of having been insufficiently attended to. But he was conscious of it at every moment, as a man newly knighted is conscious of his title, and he touched it frequently, with the side of his forefinger, in a manner he had acquired from a Hungarian gentleman upon the Boulevard Saint-Michel.

He had been in Paris "studying architecture," as his family put it to callers, though Ellery himself preferred to say that he had been "living." His letters home had borne this out. They had been long letters, written upon thin foreign paper in a hand that grew larger and more sloping as the months went by, and they had dealt principally with cafés, with the opinions of persons named Achille and Bertrand upon the subject of art, and with Ellery's own opinions upon the subject of nearly everything. His mother had read them aloud at Sunday dinners, and his Aunt Lavinia Gilmore, who lived three squares farther out upon Fennimore Street, had borrowed them and read them aloud at Sunday dinners of her own. Thus it happened that the Gilmore family knew a great deal about Achille and Bertrand, and somewhat more than Ellery suspected about Ellery.

On the afternoon of his second day at home he walked out Fennimore Street to call upon his aunt and her family. It was a walk he had taken, as a boy, perhaps two thousand times, generally at a run and often pursued; but he took it now at the deliberate gait of a man who has seen the Seine by moonlight and does not expect to be much astonished by anything in his native town. He carried a stick. Nobody in the town carried a stick except old Judge Brattle, who was lame, and Ellery was aware that he attracted notice. He was not displeased to attract it. A grocer's boy upon a bicycle wobbled perilously in turning to look at him, and Ellery bore the incident with composure.

He was thinking, as he walked, of his cousin Hattie.

He remembered her perfectly. She had been thirteen when he went away, a long, thin, freckled creature with two braids of hair the colour of wet straw, and knees that were usually skinned. She had followed him about from the time she could walk. She had fetched and carried for him, kept his secrets, lied for him to her mother and his, and been permitted, in return, to hold the rope while he climbed things. On the day he left for New York and the steamer she had wept so violently on the station platform that the conductor had asked whether the young lady was ill. Ellery had been touched by this, though embarrassed; and on the voyage over, gazing upon the Atlantic, he had more than once thought of her with a melancholy that he found not unpleasant.

He was prepared, therefore, to be very kind to Hattie. He would not crush her. He would let her see, gently, how far apart the years had carried them; he would tell her a little of the world, as much as was suitable for a young girl; and he would perhaps bring her, on some later occasion, one of the small engravings he had in his trunk, and explain it to her. He composed, as he went, the first thing he would say to her. It was to be, "Well, Tadpole!" said with a sort of weary fondness, and accompanied by a pat upon the head.

The Gilmore house had not changed, except that it seemed to have grown smaller, as such houses do, and there was a new iron fence along the front, with spikes. Ellery opened the gate, which squealed exactly as it always had, and was proceeding up the walk when a small boy in a sailor blouse rose from behind the hydrangea bush and regarded him with deep suspicion.

"Who you?" said the small boy.

"I," said Ellery, "am your cousin. You must be Wilfred."

"I'm Buster," said the small boy. "What's that on your lip?"

Ellery did not answer. He went up the steps and rang the bell, while Buster, at a distance of several feet behind him, made a careful study of the stick, the gloves, the coat, and the mustache, and appeared to arrive at an unfavourable verdict upon all four.

The door was opened by a young lady.

She was a tall young lady, in a dress of some soft grey stuff with a great deal of white at the throat. Her hair, which was neither the colour of wet straw nor of dry, but of something warmer than either, was done high upon her head in the manner of the drawings in the illustrated weeklies, and her face beneath it was of a kind that Ellery, had he encountered it in the Luxembourg Gardens, would have described in a letter home as "a type." There was not a freckle in it anywhere. She looked at him for a moment with polite inquiry, and then her eyes widened and she laughed.

"Why, Ellery!" she said. "It's Ellery! Mother! Mother, it's Ellery, and he's got a cane!"

Ellery's hand, which had been rising toward the level at which he had intended to pat her head, changed its course in some confusion and went to his hat. He removed the hat. He bowed—the bow was from the Boulevard Saint-Michel also—and said, "Ah—how do you do?" which was not at all what he had meant to say.

"How do I do?" cried Hattie. "Oh, my! Come in, come in! Don't stand there being foreign on the porch; the Pettibones are looking. Buster, go get your father out of the cellar. Tell him Cousin Ellery's here."

"I don't think he's Cousin Ellery," said Buster darkly. "I think he's a man."

"Go along!"

Buster went along, though not swiftly, and Ellery found himself in the front hall, where the same hat-rack held out the same antlers, and where there was the same smell, compounded of furnace and furniture polish and something baking, that had been the smell of his Aunt Lavinia's house for as long as he could remember. It affected him unexpectedly. He had been prepared to find it provincial; he found it, instead, so precisely and overwhelmingly familiar that for an instant he forgot his mustache altogether, and stood with his hat in his hand looking about him like a boy who has come home late for supper.

Then his aunt was upon him, a stout, flushed, voluble lady with flour on her forearms, who embraced him without regard for his coat and declared that he was thin, that he was pale, that he was the image of his poor grandfather, and that he must stay to supper because there was a chicken. Behind her, by degrees, came his Uncle Henry Gilmore, a large, slow, bald man in his shirt-sleeves, who had been attending to the furnace and who now shook hands with his nephew and looked at him over his spectacles with an expression that Ellery could not quite read.

"Well, well," said Uncle Henry. "Back from Paris, France."

"Yes, sir."

"How'd you leave it?"

"Leave it, sir?"

"Paris. Was it about where it ought to be when you came away?"

Ellery said, with a slight smile, that he believed Paris was much as usual; and Uncle Henry said, "That's good," and nodded several times, as though a weight had been lifted from his mind. Hattie made a small sound and turned it into a cough.

They put him in the front parlour, in the best chair, which was a mahogany rocker with a crocheted thing upon its back, and his aunt went away to the kitchen, calling over her shoulder that she would be back in two minutes and that nobody was to say anything interesting until she came. Uncle Henry, after standing a moment, observed that he would just go wash up, and went. Ellery was left alone with his cousin.

She sat down upon the sofa opposite him, folded her hands in her lap, and looked at him with an air of the frankest enjoyment. It was not an air he had anticipated. He had been ready for awe; he had been ready even for a little shyness, which he would have known how to dispel. He was not ready to be enjoyed. He touched his mustache.

"You've grown up, Hattie," he said, with what he hoped was an indulgent kindliness.

"So have you," she returned. "At least, you've grown something."

Ellery chose not to notice this. He leaned back in the rocker, crossed his knees, and allowed his gaze to travel about the room, slowly, as though appraising it. "It's curious," he said, "coming back. Everything seems so—so small. One gets used, over there, to a different scale of things. The proportions are different. I remember Bertrand saying to me once—"

"Bertrand's the one with the red beard," said Hattie, "that lives on a barge."

Ellery paused. "Why—yes. How did you—"

"And Achille's the one that painted the picture of the onion and the Salon wouldn't take it, and he said the jury were all bourgeois pigs, and you agreed with him. And there was a Hungarian count, only you weren't sure he was a count, and he borrowed forty francs from you and went to Vienna." She ticked them off upon her fingers. "Aunt Mattie used to bring your letters over every Sunday afternoon, and Mother read them out loud after supper. Father liked the one about the onion best. He made her read it twice."

Ellery felt himself growing warm about the ears. It occurred to him for the first time—and it was a novel and disagreeable idea—that his letters, which he had written in solitude and in a mood of some exaltation, had been received not in solitude at all, but by a circle of relatives sitting about a lamp after a heavy supper; and that some of those relatives had perhaps not been exalted.

"Your father," he said stiffly, "is hardly in a position to judge of painting."

"Oh, he didn't judge it," said Hattie. "He just liked it. He said he'd always thought there ought to be more pictures of onions, and he was glad somebody'd finally got round to it. He used to say it at the store." She laughed again, and then, seeing his face, she leaned forward quickly and put her hand upon his sleeve. "Oh, Ellery, don't! I didn't mean to make fun. We loved the letters, truly. You can't think how dull it is here in the winter, and every Sunday there'd be something new from you—it was like a serial in a magazine. I used to wonder what was going to happen to you next. Honestly I did."

The hand upon his sleeve was a very different hand from the grubby one that used to hold the rope. Ellery looked at it, and then at her, and for the space of a breath he was not altogether sure what he felt. It was not displeasure. It resembled, in some respects, the sensation of a man who has stepped confidently down a stair in the dark and found one step fewer than he expected.

"Did you?" he said.

"Of course I did. I used to think about you sitting at those little tables on the sidewalk, with everybody talking French, and wish I could see it. Is it really like that? With the little tables?"

"Yes," said Ellery. "It's really like that." And then, because she was looking at him with such straightforward interest, he forgot for a moment to be a man of the world, and began to tell her about the little tables—not as he had told it in his letters, with Achille's opinions and Bertrand's, but about the way the waiters swept the sawdust in the mornings, and the old woman who sold violets at the corner of the Rue Soufflot and called everybody "mon petit," and how cold his room had been in February, so that he had worn his overcoat to bed and once, for three days, his hat. Hattie laughed at the hat, and he found that he did not mind her laughing at it; he laughed himself, and the mustache, for the time being, was forgotten.

"You never wrote about the hat," she said.

"No," said Ellery. "I don't suppose I did."

"Why not? It's the best part."

He considered this, and was unable to answer it, and therefore changed the subject. "But you haven't told me anything about yourself," he said. "What have you been doing all this while?"

"Oh, me!" said Hattie. "Nothing. Growing up, Mother says. I finished at Miss Parkhurst's in June, and I've been to a good many parties, and I'm in a Browning club, only I don't understand Browning, and neither does anybody else in it except Mrs. Tolliver, and I'm not sure about her. And I've learned to ride a bicycle. Do you remember the old tree-house in the Pettibones' maple?"

"Remember it!" said Ellery. "I built it."

"You did not," said Hattie promptly. "I built it. You sat on the fence and told me where to put the boards."

"I supervised it," said Ellery, with dignity. "That is the function of an architect."

"Well, the architect fell out of it," said Hattie, "the very first day, and broke his collar-bone, and I had to run for Doctor Spence, and you made me promise to say you'd been pushed by the Kittredge boy."

"I was pushed," said Ellery.

"You were not! You were showing off. You stood up on the edge to show me how a man on a ship looks for whales, and the board went." She was laughing so that she had to put her handkerchief to her eyes. "And I told the whole neighbourhood the Kittredge boy did it, and Mr. Kittredge whipped him, and I've felt wicked about it ever since. I saw him at the Pettibones' dance last spring—he's a great tall thing now, with a moustache too—and I very nearly told him."

"I hope you didn't."

"No. I thought I'd better wait and ask you first. You always did decide those things."

Ellery looked at her sharply, but she was quite grave. He found, in that moment, a strong desire to hear more about the Kittredge boy—particularly about his moustache, and whether it was larger than his own, and why he had been at the Pettibones' dance, and with whom he had danced there—but he did not see how the inquiry could be decently made, and while he was considering the matter, there came a tremendous double knock at the front door, of the sort that announces either a telegraph messenger or a young man who has been there often before.

Hattie rose with a slight change of colour that Ellery did not fail to observe. "That'll be—excuse me just a minute," she said, and went out into the hall.

Ellery heard the door open, and a man's voice, cheerful and loud, inquiring whether it was too early; and Hattie's voice, lower, saying something he could not make out; and then the man's voice again, inquiring, with what seemed to Ellery an unnecessary heartiness, "The cousin from Paris? No! Well, bring him on—I want to see him!" And before Ellery had altogether composed himself in the rocker, the doorway was filled by a large, pink, extremely healthy young man in a brown suit, with a straw hat in one hand and a box of candy in the other.

"Ellery, this is Mr. Kittredge," said Hattie. "Lew, this is my cousin, Mr. Vane."

Ellery rose. He did not bow, this time; he found that he had no desire at all to bow. He shook hands. Mr. Kittredge's grip was of the sort that is described in the advertisements of physical culture establishments, and when it released him, Ellery stood for a moment flexing his fingers covertly behind his back.

"Mighty glad to know you," said Mr. Kittredge. "Heard a lot about you. Hattie used to read me your letters." He grinned broadly. "That fellow with the onion—say, I'd give a dollar to see that onion!"

Ellery said, in a voice which he endeavoured to make quite pleasant, that he believed the onion had been painted over.

"No! What with?"

"With—I believe it was a portrait of his landlady."

Mr. Kittredge appeared to find this the finest thing he had ever heard. He threw back his head and laughed so that the prisms on the parlour lamp shivered; and from the dining-room, where he had evidently been listening, there came an answering rumble that Ellery recognized as his Uncle Henry. Hattie looked from one young man to the other with an expression which, had Ellery been in a condition to read it, he would have seen to be compounded in nearly equal parts of anxiety and delight.

Mr. Kittredge sat down upon the sofa, which received him with a groan, and Hattie sat down beside him—not very near beside him, Ellery noted, but nearer than she had been sitting before. The box of candy lay between them. Ellery resumed the rocker.

"You'll find the old town changed some," said Mr. Kittredge genially.

"It seems to me," said Ellery, "not very much changed."

"Oh, it's changed! Why, we've got the electric cars clear out to the Fair Grounds now, and they're talking about paving Fennimore Street with brick, all the way. And there's three new buildings downtown over five stories. You'll have to go see the new Commerce Block—you being an architect. It's a corker."

"I shall make a point of it," said Ellery.

"Six stories and a basement," said Mr. Kittredge, "and an elevator that'll take you right up to the roof. And the whole front's pressed brick, with stone trimmings, and the name cut right in over the door in letters this high. I've got an office on the fourth floor." He paused modestly. "Insurance."

"Indeed," said Ellery.

It was at this point, and while Ellery was searching for some remark about pressed brick that would be at once courteous and annihilating, that he chanced to glance at his cousin, and found her looking at him. She was not laughing now. Her eyes, which he remembered as having been of no particular colour, were grey, and quite steady, and they held in them something that was at the same time an appeal and a challenge—as if she were asking him, without words, whether he was going to be decent; and as if she rather thought he was, but was not entirely sure.

Ellery looked at her for a moment. Then he turned to Mr. Kittredge.

"I'm told," he said, "that I owe you an apology."

Mr. Kittredge stared. "Me? What for?"

"About eleven years ago," said Ellery, "I fell out of a tree-house, and it was given out that you had pushed me. You hadn't. I was showing off, and the board went. I believe you suffered for it."

Mr. Kittredge's mouth opened slowly. He looked at Ellery, and then at Hattie, who had turned a deep and becoming pink, and then back at Ellery; and then a great light broke over his large, honest face, and he smote his knee with a blow that made the candy box leap.

"Well, I'll be—!" he cried. "Well, I'll be—! I always said I never did it! I always said so! The old man licked me in the woodshed and I told him all the way through I never did it, and he said that made it worse!" He turned upon Hattie. "And you knew it all the time!"

"I was only eight," said Hattie faintly.

"Eight! You were going on nine if you were a day!" But he was laughing, and he reached across and shook Ellery's hand again, with no diminution of pressure. "Mr. Vane, you're all right. I don't care what anybody says—you're all right!"

Ellery, nursing his fingers, did not inquire what anybody said. He had a general notion, and he found that he no longer cared to have it particularized.

Supper was a long affair and a loud one. There was the chicken, and there were hot biscuits, and three kinds of preserves, and a cake upon which his Aunt Lavinia had caused to be inscribed, in pink icing, the word WELCOME, the last two letters somewhat crowded against the edge. Buster, who was seated next to Ellery, ate steadily throughout and spoke only once, to inquire whether they had chicken in France, and on being told that they had, to observe that he did not believe it. Uncle Henry asked about the onion, and laughed until he had to be pounded upon the back. Mr. Kittredge stayed, as it appeared he usually did on Thursdays, and told a long story about a fire at the Commerce Block, in which nobody had been hurt and which seemed chiefly remarkable for the conduct of the elevator. And Ellery, to his own surprise, found himself telling about the hat he had worn to bed, and about the violet woman, and about the Hungarian count, whom he presented now not as an exotic acquaintance but as a man who had got away with forty francs of his money; and the table liked it better than anything in the letters.

It was late when he rose to go. Hattie came with him to the door, and out upon the porch, where the October night was sharp and still and the arc light at the corner made the maple leaves look as if they had been cut out of paper. Inside, Mr. Kittredge could be heard explaining something to Uncle Henry with great energy.

"Ellery," said Hattie, "that was nice of you. About the tree-house."

"It was true," said Ellery.

"I know. But you needn't have said it. I've always felt so mean."

He drew on his gloves slowly. "Is he—" he began, and stopped. "Is Mr. Kittredge a—a particular friend of yours?"

Hattie looked out at the arc light. "He's very kind," she said. "And he's coming along awfully well in the insurance business. Father thinks a great deal of him."

"Ah," said Ellery.

"But nothing's settled," she said quickly. "Nothing at all. I'm only nineteen."

"Of course," said Ellery. He did not know why this news should cheer him as it did, and he decided not to examine the matter. He took up his stick from where it leaned against the railing, looked at it for a moment as though he had never seen it before, and then, on an impulse, held it out to her.

"Would you give this to Buster?" he said. "I believe he'd like to have it. I don't think I'll need it."

Hattie took it, wondering. "Why, Ellery—"

"Good-night, Tadpole," said Ellery, and went down the steps and out through the gate, which squealed after him.

He walked home slowly. At the corner, under the arc light, he paused and drew the side of his forefinger once across his upper lip, thoughtfully, as a man might test the edge of a razor; and the next morning, to the profound relief of his mother and the open disappointment of the grocer's boy, it was gone.

Here is an excerpt of Booth Tarkington's writing, to show you their style:

We debate sometimes what is to be the future of this nation when we think that in a few years public affairs may be in the hands of the fin-de-siècle gilded youths we see about us during the Christmas holidays. Such foppery, such luxury, such insolence, was surely never practised by the scented, overbearing patricians of the Palatine, even in Rome’s most decadent epoch. In all the wild orgy of wastefulness and luxury with which the nineteenth century reaches its close, the gilded youth has been surely the worst symptom. With his airs of young milord, his fast horses, his gold and silver cigarette-cases, his clothes from a New York tailor, his recklessness of money showered upon him by indulgent mothers or doting grandfathers, he respects nothing and nobody. He is blase if you please. Watch him at a social function, how condescendingly he deigns to select a partner for the popular waltz or two step, how carelessly he shoulders older people out of his way, with what a blank stare he returns the salutation of some old acquaintance whom he may choose in his royal whim to forget! The unpleasant part of all this is that the young women he so condescendingly selects as partners for the dance greet him with seeming rapture, though in their hearts they must feel humiliated by his languid hauteur, and many older people beam upon him almost fawningly if he unbends so far as to throw them a careless, disdainful word! One wonders what has come over the new generation. Of such as these the Republic was not made. Let us pray that the future of our country is not in the hands of these fin-de-siècle gilded youths, but rather in the calloused palms of young men yet unknown, labouring upon the farms of the land. When we compare the young manhood of Abraham Lincoln with the specimens we are now producing, we see too well that it bodes ill for the twentieth century— George yawned, and tossed the clipping into his waste-basket, wondering why his aunt thought such dull nonsense worth the sending. As for her insinuation, pencilled upon the border, he supposed she meant to joke—a supposition which neither surprised him nor altered his lifelong opinion of her wit. He read her letter with more interest:
... The dinner your mother gave for the Morgans was a lovely affair. It was last Monday evening, just ten days after you left. It was peculiarly appropriate that your mother should give this dinner, because her brother George, your uncle, was Mr. Morgan’s most intimate friend before he left here a number of years ago, and it was a pleasant occasion for the formal announcement of some news which you heard from Lucy Morgan before you returned to college. At least she told me she had told you the night before you left that her father had decided to return here to live. It was appropriate that your mother, herself an old friend, should assemble a representative selection of Mr. Morgan’s old friends around him at such a time. He was in great spirits and most entertaining. As your time was so charmingly taken up during your visit home with a younger member of his family, you probably overlooked opportunities of hearing him talk, and do not know what an interesting man he can be. He will soon begin to build his factory here for the manufacture of automobiles, which he says is a term he prefers to “horseless carriages.” Your Uncle George told me he would like to invest in this factory, as George thinks there is a future for automobiles; perhaps not for general use, but as an interesting novelty, which people with sufficient means would like to own for their amusement and the sake of variety.
