I hear you have been making comments about me at the theatre, that some actor was more democratic in his manners than I am, which I do not understand. You know my theory of life because I explained it to you on our first drive together, when I told you I would not talk to everybody about things I feel like the way I spoke to you of my theory of life. I believe those who are able should have a true theory of life, and I developed my theory of life long, long ago. Well, here I sit smoking my faithful briar pipe, indulging in the fragrance of my tobacco as I look out on the campus from my many-paned window, and things are different with me from the way they were way back in Freshman year. I can see now how boyish in many ways I was then. I believe what has changed me as much as anything was my visit home at the time I met you. So I sit here with my faithful briar and dream the old dreams over as it were, dreaming of the waltzes we waltzed together and of that last night before we parted, and you told me the good news you were going to live there, and I would find my friend waiting for me, when I get home next summer. I will be glad my friend will be waiting for me. I am not capable of friendship except for the very few, and, looking back over my life, I remember there were times when I doubted if I could feel a great friendship for anybody—especially girls. I do not take a great interest in many people, as you know, for I find most of them shallow. Here in the old place I do not believe in being hail-fellow-well-met with every Tom, Dick, and Harry just because he happens to be a classmate, any more than I do at home, where I have always been careful who I was seen with, largely on account of the family, but also because my disposition ever since my boyhood has been to encourage real intimacy from but the few. What are you reading now? I have finished both “Henry Esmond” and “The Virginians.” I like Thackeray because he is not trashy, and because he writes principally of nice people. My theory of literature is an author who does not indulge in trashiness—writes about people you could introduce into your own home. I agree with my Uncle Sydney, as I once heard him say he did not care to read a book or go to a play about people he would not care to meet at his own dinner table. I believe we should live by certain standards and ideals, as you know from my telling you my theory of life. Well, a letter is no place for deep discussions, so I will not go into the subject. From several letters from my mother, and one from Aunt Fanny, I hear you are seeing a good deal of the family since I left. I hope sometimes you think of the member who is absent. I got a silver frame for your photograph in New York, and I keep it on my desk. It is the only girl’s photograph I ever took the trouble to have framed, though, as I told you frankly, I have had any number of other girls’ photographs, yet all were only passing fancies, and oftentimes I have questioned in years past if I was capable of much friendship toward the feminine sex, which I usually found shallow until our own friendship began. When I look at your photograph, I say to myself, “At last, at last here is one that will not prove shallow.” My faithful briar has gone out. I will have to rise and fill it, then once more in the fragrance of My Lady Nicotine, I will sit and dream the old dreams over, and think, too, of the true friend at home awaiting my return in June for the summer vacation. Friend, this is from your friend, G.A.M. George’s anticipations were not disappointed. When he came home in June his friend was awaiting him; at least, she was so pleased to see him again that for a few minutes after their first encounter she was a little breathless, and a great deal glowing, and quiet withal. Their sentimental friendship continued, though sometimes he was irritated by her making it less sentimental than he did, and sometimes by what he called her “air of superiority.” Her air was usually, in truth, that of a fond but amused older sister; and George did not believe such an attitude was warranted by her eight months of seniority. Lucy and her father were living at the Amberson Hotel, while Morgan got his small machine-shops built in a western outskirt of the town; and George grumbled about the shabbiness and the old-fashioned look of the hotel, though it was “still the best in the place, of course.” He remonstrated with his grandfather, declaring that the whole Amberson Estate would be getting “run-down and out-at-heel, if things weren’t taken in hand pretty soon.” He urged the general need of rebuilding, renovating, varnishing, and lawsuits. But the Major, declining to hear him out, interrupted querulously, saying that he had enough to bother him without any advice from George; and retired to his library, going so far as to lock the door audibly.

“Second childhood!” George muttered, shaking his head; and he thought sadly that the Major had not long to live. However, this surmise depressed him for only a moment or so. Of course, people couldn’t be expected to live forever, and it would be a good thing to have someone in charge of the Estate who wouldn’t let it get to looking so rusty that riffraff dared to make fun of it. For George had lately undergone the annoyance of calling upon the Morgans, in the rather stuffy red velours and gilt parlour of their apartment at the hotel, one evening when Mr. Frederick Kinney also was a caller, and Mr. Kinney had not been tactful. In fact, though he adopted a humorous tone of voice, in expressing his sympathy for people who, through the city’s poverty in hotels, were obliged to stay at the Amberson, Mr. Kinney’s intention was interpreted by the other visitor as not at all humorous, but, on the contrary, personal and offensive. George rose abruptly, his face the colour of wrath. “Good-night, Miss Morgan. Good-night, Mr. Morgan,” he said. “I shall take pleasure in calling at some other time when a more courteous sort of people may be present.”

“Look here!” the hot-headed Fred burst out. “Don’t you try to make me out a boor, George Minafer! I wasn’t hinting anything at you; I simply forgot all about your grandfather owning this old building. Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor! I won’t—” But George walked out in the very course of this vehement protest, and it was necessarily left unfinished. Mr. Kinney remained only a few moments after George’s departure; and as the door closed upon him, the distressed Lucy turned to her father. She was plaintively surprised to find him in a condition of immoderate laughter.

“I didn’t—I didn’t think I could hold out!” he gasped, and, after choking until tears came to his eyes, felt blindly for the chair from which he had risen to wish Mr. Kinney an indistinct good-night. His hand found the arm of the chair; he collapsed feebly, and sat uttering incoherent sounds.

“Papa!”

“It brings things back so!” he managed to explain, “This very Fred Kinney’s father and young George’s father, Wilbur Minafer, used to do just such things when they were at that age—and, for that matter, so did George Amberson and I, and all the rest of us!” And, in spite of his exhaustion, he began to imitate: “Don’t you try to put me in the light of a boor!” “I shall take pleasure in calling at some time when a more courteous sort of people—” He was unable to go on. There is a mirth for every age, and Lucy failed to comprehend her father’s, but tolerated it a little ruefully.

“Papa, I think they were shocking. Weren’t they awful!”

“Just—just boys!” he moaned, wiping his eyes. But Lucy could not smile at all; she was beginning to look indignant. “I can forgive that poor Fred Kinney,” she said. “He’s just blundering—but George—oh, George behaved outrageously!”

“It’s a difficult age,” her father observed, his calmness somewhat restored. “Girls don’t seem to have to pass through it quite as boys do, or their savoir faire is instinctive—or something!” And he gave away to a return of his convulsion. She came and sat upon the arm of his chair. “Papa, why should George behave like that?”

“He’s sensitive.”

“Rather! But why is he? He does anything he likes to, without any regard for what people think. Then why should he mind so furiously when the least little thing reflects upon him, or on anything or anybody connected with him?” Eugene patted her hand. “That’s one of the greatest puzzles of human vanity, dear; and I don’t pretend to know the answer. In all my life, the most arrogant people that I’ve known have been the most sensitive. The people who have done the most in contempt of other people’s opinion, and who consider themselves the highest above it, have been the most furious if it went against them. Arrogant and domineering people can’t stand the least, lightest, faintest breath of criticism. It just kills them.”

“Papa, do you think George is terribly arrogant and domineering?”

“Oh, he’s still only a boy,” said Eugene consolingly. “There’s plenty of fine stuff in him—can’t help but be, because he’s Isabel Amberson’s son.” Lucy stroked his hair, which was still almost as dark as her own. “You liked her pretty well once, I guess, papa.”

“I do still,” he said quietly.

“She’s lovely—lovely! Papa—” she paused, then continued—“I wonder sometimes—” “What?”

“I wonder just how she happened to marry Mr. Minafer.”

“Oh, Minafer’s all right,” said Eugene. “He’s a quiet sort of man, but he’s a good man and a kind man. He always was, and those things count.”

“But in a way—well, I’ve heard people say there wasn’t anything to him at all except business and saving money. Miss Fanny Minafer herself told me that everything George and his mother have of their own—that is, just to spend as they like—she says it has always come from Major Amberson.”

“Thrift, Horatio!” said Eugene lightly. “Thrift’s an inheritance, and a common enough one here. The people who settled the country had to save, so making and saving were taught as virtues, and the people, to the third generation, haven’t found out that making and saving are only means to an end. Minafer doesn’t believe in money being spent. He believes God made it to be invested and saved.”

“But George isn’t saving. He’s reckless, and even if he is arrogant and conceited and bad-tempered, he’s awfully generous.”

“Oh, he’s an Amberson,” said her father. “The Ambersons aren’t saving. They’re too much the other way, most of them.”

“I don’t think I should have called George bad-tempered,” Lucy said thoughtfully. “No. I don’t think he is.”

“Only when he’s cross about something?” Morgan suggested, with a semblance of sympathetic gravity.

“Yes,” she said brightly, not perceiving that his intention was humorous. “All the rest of the time he’s really very amiable. Of course, he’s much more a perfect child, the whole time, than he realizes! He certainly behaved awfully to-night.” She jumped up, her indignation returning. “He did, indeed, and it won’t do to encourage him in it. I think he’ll find me pretty cool—for a week or so!” Whereupon her father suffered a renewal of his attack of uproarious laughter.

Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can. Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.

The return of Mrs. Horace Bassett and her daughter, after an absence of seven years in Dresden, was a thing the town had been expecting for a fortnight, and had been discussing for a month; and by the time the two ladies actually descended from the afternoon train, the Dresden years had been so thoroughly examined upon so many front porches that there was hardly anything left in them for the travellers themselves to report. It was known that Mrs. Bassett had gone abroad "for the girl's education," and that this was a polite way of saying she had gone abroad because Horace Bassett's will had left her more money than she could comfortably spend in a town where everybody knew how much it was. It was known that the girl had studied the piano under a gentleman with a long name and a short temper; that she had been "presented somewhere"; and that she spoke German "like a native," a phrase which the town employed with great respect and some uneasiness, since nobody in it was qualified to judge.

"She'll come home stuck-up," said Mrs. Lemuel Harkins, who had been to Chicago twice and therefore understood the effects of travel. "They always do. She'll call the depot the station, and she'll say 'Fancy!' at everything, and she won't know a soul she used to play with."

"Florence Bassett?" said Mrs. Harkins's sister-in-law, doubtfully. "Why, she was the worst little tomboy on Sycamore Street! She used to fight boys."

"That's just the kind," Mrs. Harkins returned, with the calm of a prophet whose prophecies are not subject to review. "That's exactly the kind that comes home stuck-up worst of all."

Among those who agreed with Mrs. Harkins, and indeed went somewhat beyond her, was Florence Bassett's cousin, Mr. Walter Kittredge, aged twenty-one, who had lately been taken into his father's hardware business with a desk of his own, and who had in consequence begun to wear a stiff collar on week-days. Walter had not been consulted upon the question of his cousin's return; nobody had thought it necessary; but he had his own views of it, and they were formed upon recollections so vivid that seven years had not dimmed them in the least.

He remembered, for one thing, that at the age of eleven his cousin had bitten him. It had happened during a dispute over the ownership of a croquet mallet, and though Walter, at thirteen, had been very decidedly in the right, Florence had settled the matter in a manner which left the mark of her small, even teeth upon his wrist for a week, and left him, moreover, with no recourse; for a boy who complains that a girl has bitten him is not much better off than if he had been bitten by a boy and said nothing. He remembered also that she had once locked him in the Bassetts' smoke-house during the whole of a Sunday-school picnic, to which she had then gone in his place, wearing his cap; that she had told the entire neighbourhood he wrote poetry, which was true, and therefore unforgivable; and that upon the morning of her departure for Germany she had leaned out of the carriage window and called back to him, before a crowd of witnesses, "Good-bye, Walter! Don't cry!"—he had not been crying, and had not the least intention of it, but the crowd had looked at him, and one of the witnesses had been Ida Mae Purcell.

Seven years had not softened these memories; rather, they had been preserved, as such things are, in a kind of moral alcohol, and Walter could take any one of them out and examine it at his leisure, and frequently did. He had decided, therefore, that when his cousin came home he would be polite to her. He would be politer to her than to anybody else in town. He would be so polite that she would perceive at once how completely he had outgrown her, and how little he cared whether she had come home or stayed in Dresden till she was ninety.

"You'll go over there this evening, Walter," his mother said at supper, on the day of the arrival. "Your Aunt Clara will expect it. Florence is your own first cousin, and the only one you've got on my side."

"Yes'm," said Walter. "I'd intended to." And he added, with the air of a man of affairs whose evenings are mortgaged, "I can spare about half an hour."

His father looked up from his plate with an expression which Walter did not care for, and which he chose not to see.

He dressed with a care that would have surprised him if he had noticed it. He put on the gray suit he had bought in the spring and had worn only to church, and a new straw hat with a band of maroon silk; he selected, after some hesitation, a necktie of a quiet blue, as being more suitable to a person who had outgrown everything; and he brushed his hair until it lay upon his head with the smoothness of a seal's. Then, before the mirror, he practised a bow—not a deep bow, which might have been taken for eagerness, but a slight, grave inclination, such as a man of the world might bestow upon a relative he had not thought of in years. He practised it a good many times. Whatever he had outgrown, he had not yet outgrown the habit of rehearsal.

The Bassett house stood two squares farther out on Sycamore Street, a tall, narrow brick with a cupola and a cast-iron deer upon the lawn; and it had been kept open in the family's absence by an old couple who had let the deer rust and the grass go to seed, so that the house had about it, in the soft June dusk, an air of having been asleep and of not yet being sure it wished to wake up. There were lights in the lower windows, however, and the sound of a piano—a rapid, intricate, foreign sort of music, which seemed to Walter, as he came up the walk, exactly the kind of thing that would be played by a person who said "Fancy!" He set his jaw.

His Aunt Clara opened the door herself, and kissed him, and cried out that he had grown to be a perfect giant, and that he looked like his grandfather, and that she wouldn't have known him on the street; all of which Walter received with the patience of a nephew; and then she turned and called, "Florence! Here's Walter!"

The music stopped. There was a moment's pause, during which Walter prepared his bow; and then a young lady came out of the parlour into the lamplight of the hall, and Walter's bow, for some reason he was never afterward able to explain, did not take place at all.

It was not that she was tall, though she was taller than he had expected; nor that she was dressed in something white and simple which nevertheless did not look as if it had been made in the town, or anywhere near it; nor even that she was pretty, a quality which Walter had been fully prepared to discount. It was rather that she was so entirely unlike anything his recollection had provided for. He had come armed against a freckled little girl with a bang cut straight across her forehead and a temper to match; and here was a grave young woman with smooth dark hair and a gentle mouth, who held out her hand to him and said, in a low voice with something faintly strange in its cadences:

"How do you do, Walter. It's very good of you to come."

Walter took the hand. He found it necessary to say something, and what he said was, "Well—well, I should say so!" which was not at all what he had meant, and which had, moreover, no discoverable relation to anything. He felt his ears grow warm, and he released her hand rather too quickly, as though it had been the croquet mallet.

"Come into the parlour, both of you," said Mrs. Bassett comfortably. "I've got to see about the trunks; the expressman has put them all in the wrong rooms. You two can talk." And she departed upstairs with the air of a woman who has done a kindly thing and does not mean to stay to be thanked for it.

The parlour still smelled of having been shut up; the furniture had been uncovered that afternoon, and the linen dust-sheets lay folded in a heap in one corner, like the ghosts of the seven years retired to await their summons. Florence sat down upon the piano stool, and Walter, after considering several chairs, took the one that was farthest from her and also the least comfortable. He placed his new straw hat upon his knee, and, finding nothing else to do with his hands, held it there.

"You've changed a great deal," she said.

"Oh, I don't know," said Walter, with what he intended for careless ease. "A man gets older, of course. Business, and all that. I'm with my father now, you know—in the store." He coughed slightly. "Hardware."

"Yes, Aunt Ellen wrote us. She said you had a desk."

There was nothing in this remark to which a reasonable person could take exception; yet Walter had a vague, uncomfortable feeling that the desk had been diminished by being mentioned. He looked at his cousin narrowly; but she was regarding him with an expression of perfect seriousness.

"I expect you'll find the town pretty slow," he said, "after Europe."

"Oh, no. I've been thinking about it all the way over—on the ship, and all the way from New York. I don't think I thought about anything else."

"Well, I expect you'll find it's changed some, anyhow," Walter said, a little loftily, for he was determined to show her that the town, too, had gone on without her. "We've got the trolley out as far as the Fair Grounds now. And they've paved Main Street with brick, clear from the courthouse to the canal bridge. And the Opera House burned down two years ago, and they've built a new one with electric lights and a gallery and everything. It seats eleven hundred."

"Eleven hundred!" she said. "Fancy!"

Walter started. He had been waiting for that word with the grim satisfaction of a man who has predicted an earthquake; and now that it had come, he discovered that it had not been spoken in the least as he had expected. She had said it, he could not help perceiving, very much as a girl of eleven might have said "Golly!"—and there was in her eyes, as she said it, a sudden gleam that he remembered. It was the gleam that had preceded the smoke-house.

"Look here," he said, sitting up. "You're not making fun of the Opera House?"

"Making fun of it? Walter! I'm dying to see it. Is the fire-escape still on the outside, where the old one was—the one you climbed up the night of the Uncle Tom's Cabin show, and got caught by the marshal, and said you were looking for your little sister?"

"I never did any such—" Walter began; and stopped, because he had. "Well, anyhow, that was a long time ago," he said.

"And you haven't got a little sister. That was what made the marshal so cross." She clasped her hands about one knee, a posture not taught, he was sure, in Dresden. "Walter, does Ida Mae Purcell still live next door to you?"

"She's married," said Walter shortly.

"Married! Ida Mae! To whom?"

"Fellow named Spink. He sells insurance."

"Not Elmer Spink? The one that always had his mouth open?"

"I believe his name is Elmer," said Walter, with dignity; and then, because there are things a man cannot be dignified about forever, he added: "He's still got it open, mostly."

Florence laughed aloud—a quick, delighted, wholly undignified laugh that seemed to blow the seven years out of the room as a draught blows out a candle; and Walter, to his own great astonishment, found that he was laughing too.

It is a curious property of laughter shared between persons who have been children together that it leaves them, for the moment, children again; and in the next quarter of an hour the two cousins travelled farther back than the train had brought Miss Bassett from New York. She wished to know everything; and Walter, who had come prepared to tell her nothing, told it all. He told her that old Mr. Tubbs, who had kept the candy store, was dead, and that the store was now a barber shop, which seemed to both of them a kind of sacrilege; that the Methodist minister who had preached the forty-minute sermons had gone to Iowa, where, it was hoped, they were shorter; that the swimming hole below the Harkness mill had been filled in, because a boy had been drowned there—"not anybody we knew," Walter added hastily, seeing her face; that the town had a Country Club now, with golf, and that the men who played it wore knickerbockers and were stared at by farmers; and that Mrs. Lemuel Harkins had been telling everybody Florence would come home stuck-up.

"Did she?" said Florence, much interested. "And what did you tell everybody, Walter?"

Walter found the question a difficult one. "Oh, I didn't say much of anything," he answered—which was true, as far as it went, for he had said what he had to say chiefly to himself.

"I expect you thought I would, though."

"Well—" said Walter. He turned the straw hat round once upon his knee. "Well, you've been to a good many places."

"I've been to a good many places," she agreed. "And I've seen a great many things, and heard a great deal of music, and met a great many people who were very kind to us; and I've learned to speak German, though not nearly so well as everybody here seems to think. But do you know what I used to do, Walter, the first year, when I was homesick? I used to sit by the window in the pension—that's a kind of boarding-house—and say over the names of all the streets in this town, one after another, starting at the river. Water Street, Front Street, Mulberry, Sycamore, Locust—I used to say them the way you'd say your prayers. And when I got to the end I'd start over."

Walter looked at her. She was not laughing now; and there was something in her face that he did not altogether understand, except that it made him wish, rather abruptly, that he had not practised the bow.

"I never thought you'd be homesick," he said. "You didn't act it. You told me not to cry."

"Did I?" She seemed honestly surprised. "When?"

"When you went away. You leaned out of the carriage window. Everybody heard you."

She looked at him for a moment; then her eyes widened, and the corners of her mouth began, against her evident wishes, to tremble. "Walter! You haven't remembered that all this time?"

"No," said Walter. "No—of course not. I just happened to think of it."

"You have! You've remembered it for seven years!" She put both hands over her mouth; but it was no use; she rocked upon the piano stool in a manner which would certainly have distressed the gentleman with the long name. "Oh, Walter, I'm sorry—I am sorry—but you looked so—you had on that striped blouse—and your face was all red—and Ida Mae was there—"

"Ida Mae Purcell," said Walter coldly, "is now Mrs. Elmer Spink, and her opinions are of no interest to anybody."

This seemed to make matters worse. Walter watched his cousin with the expression of a man who has been robbed and is now required to stand by while the burglar enjoys himself; but presently, finding that he could not maintain it, he gave up and laughed with her, though not quite so heartily.

"You weren't crying, were you?" she asked, when she could ask anything.

"Certainly not."

"I was," said Florence. "All the way to the depot. Mamma had to give me her handkerchief, and then she had to borrow the driver's. I only called back to you so you wouldn't see."

There was a pause. Walter, who had not anticipated this information and was not prepared for it, examined the maroon band of his straw hat with some attention.

"Well," he said, at length, "that was a long time ago, too."

"Yes," she said. "It was."

Through the open window there came the sound of somebody's lawn-sprinkler, turning in the dark with its small, patient, revolving whisper, and the smell of wet grass and of the honeysuckle that had overrun the Bassetts' side fence during the years when nobody had been at home to stop it. A trolley car went by at the foot of the street, its bell clanging, and a light flickered blue upon the wire above it.

"That's the trolley," said Walter, with some pride. "You can hear it from here."

"Walter," said his cousin, rising suddenly, "is the old barn still there?"

"Why, yes. Nobody's used it. Mr. Brady's been keeping his garden tools in it."

"Let's go look!"

"In the dark?"

"There's a moon. Come on!"

And before Walter could object that a man in a gray suit and a new straw hat did not go poking about barns at night, she had gone out through the dining-room and the kitchen, where old Mrs. Brady looked up from the dishpan with a cry of "Mercy!", and was down the back steps and across the yard; and Walter, perforce, went after her—holding his hat, it must be confessed, rather than wearing it, as if he expected to need both hands for something.

The barn stood at the back of the lot, against the alley, and in the white light of the moon it looked smaller than it should have looked, as all the scenes of our childhood do when we return to them, having been built, apparently, for people of a different size. The door stuck, as it always had; Walter put his shoulder to it with a vigour he had not known he possessed, and it gave with a groan, and they stood together upon the threshold, breathing the old smell of hay-dust and harness leather and mice, which had not changed in the least.

"It's the same," Florence said softly. "Oh, it's just the same."

"Mr. Brady's got his lawn-mower in it," Walter pointed out.

"That doesn't matter. Walter—the post. The one by the ladder."

He knew which post she meant; he had known, he discovered, ever since she had first mentioned the barn. He struck a match, and they bent over it together, and there it was, cut deep into the soft old wood with a jack-knife that had afterward been lost in the cistern: two sets of initials, one above the other, F. B. and W. K., and beneath them, in letters considerably less steady, the solemn words, "SWORN ENEMYS FOR EVER."

The match burned down to Walter's fingers, and he dropped it with an exclamation. In the darkness that followed, they could be heard laughing again; and if a passer-by in the alley had chanced to hear them, he might have supposed, from the sound of it, that the barn was occupied by two children who ought long since to have been in bed.

"You spelled 'enemies' wrong," said Florence.

"I did not. You cut that part. I did the initials."

"I did the initials. You did the part that was spelled wrong. I remember perfectly, because I told you it was wrong, and you said it didn't matter, because enemies didn't care about spelling."

Walter was silent a moment, in the dark. "Well, I guess I was right about that, anyhow," he said.

They came back across the yard more slowly than they had gone, by the light of the moon and the kitchen window; and at the back steps Florence paused, and turned to him.

"Walter," she said, "you know what I was afraid of, all the way home on the train? I was afraid everybody would be different. I was afraid you'd be grown up, and dignified, and that you'd bow to me."

Walter felt the warmth come into his ears again, and was grateful for the darkness. "Bow?" he said. "What would I want to bow for?"

"I don't know. I was just afraid of it. But you haven't changed a bit, Walter. Not one single bit."

He received this with mixed emotions. For a moment he was inclined to consider it an insult, since it reduced his desk, his stiff collar, and the whole of his twenty-one years to nothing; but she had said it in so peculiar a tone—a tone, it seemed to him, of such distinct relief—that he found himself, upon reflection, inclined to consider it something else. He did not know precisely what. He went home, an hour and a half after his arrival (having spared, it appeared, a little more than the half hour he had intended), still turning the question over; and he was so absorbed in it that he passed his own gate and had walked half a square beyond before he discovered his error.

His mother, who was sitting up for him with a magazine she had not read, looked at him over it as he came in.

"Well?" she said. "Has Florence come home stuck-up?"

"Stuck-up?" said Walter. He hung the new straw hat upon the hall rack with great care, and stood looking at it. "No," he said. "No, she hasn't. She's just about the same as she always was."

"Why, Walter! I thought you couldn't abide her."

"I can abide her all right," said Walter; and went upstairs, whistling, a little off the key, a rapid, intricate, foreign sort of tune.

His mother sat for some time looking at the stairs where he had gone; and then she laid down her magazine and laughed quietly to herself, for she had been a girl in that town once, and had a cousin of her own. Mrs. Lemuel Harkins, had she been present, would no doubt have declared that she had foreseen everything; but there are some prophecies that come true in a manner so unexpected that even the prophet does not recognize them, and Mrs. Harkins, as it happened, was not present.
