Mr. Harvey Tillotson, of the Tillotson Hardware and Implement Company, believed himself to be a firm parent, and in this belief he was supported by nobody except Mr. Harvey Tillotson. His wife did not share it, his sister-in-law openly derided it, and his son, Roscoe, eight years old and of a speculative turn, had long ago ceased to take it into account in any of his calculations. Nevertheless, Mr. Tillotson held to the conviction with that tenacity which men commonly reserve for the opinions most frequently disproved; and on a certain warm Saturday afternoon in June, when he came home from the store an hour earlier than usual and was met at the door by Mrs. Tillotson with a face of tragedy, he felt that the hour of firmness had at last arrived, and that he was the man for it.

"Harvey," said Mrs. Tillotson, "you've got to speak to him. I can't. I simply can't. I've tried, and I can't."

"What's he done?" Mr. Tillotson asked, setting down his hat upon the hall-tree with a certain grim deliberation, as a judge might lay aside his gavel before passing sentence.

"He's been exhibiting the baby."

"He's been what?"

"Exhibiting her! In the side yard, under the grape arbour, all afternoon! He had a sign, Harvey. He printed it on the back of the calendar from your own store, and he charged two cents admission, and one cent for children under six, and he called her—" Mrs. Tillotson's voice failed her, and she was obliged to sit down upon the lower step of the stairway. "He called her 'The Wild Infant of Borneo, Caught in the Jungle by Hand.'"

Mr. Tillotson did not immediately reply. It is to be recorded, in justice to him, that his first sensation was one of authentic horror; and it is to be recorded, in justice to the truth, that this was followed almost at once by another sensation, of quite a different kind, which he made haste to suppress, and which he succeeded in suppressing only by fixing his eyes very sternly upon the umbrella stand.

"Where was Nora?" he inquired, Nora being the hired girl.

"Nora was ironing. And I was lying down with one of my headaches, and Sister Hattie was at the Missionary Society, and the baby was out there in her carriage, asleep, and perfectly safe, I thought—and when I woke up and looked out of the window, there was a line, Harvey! A line of children clear to the alley! And Roscoe standing at the arbour with your old derby hat on, the one I gave to the ash man, and a cane, and shouting. I could hear him from upstairs. He was shouting that she lived on raw meat and could not be approached closer than the clothes-prop."

"Raw meat," Mr. Tillotson repeated, still regarding the umbrella stand. "Good heavens!"

"And the worst of it," his wife went on, with rising emotion, "the worst of it is that Mrs. Fenwick's little boy was in the line, and Mrs. Fenwick will tell everybody at the Euchre Club, and that dreadful Mrs. Coombs heard about it somehow and came over and paid two cents herself, and she laughed so that she had to hold on to the gate. Harvey, I'll never be able to hold up my head on this street again. You've got to speak to him. You've got to be severe with him. I mean really severe, Harvey—not the way you always are."

This last observation Mr. Tillotson affected not to hear. He straightened his waistcoat, cleared his throat with a sound intended to be ominous, and said, "Where is he?"

"He's in the kitchen, counting it."

"Counting what?"

"The money!" cried Mrs. Tillotson, and covered her face.

Mr. Tillotson went to the kitchen door and opened it. His son, seated at the end of the kitchen table with his feet wound about the rungs of his chair, was engaged in arranging a quantity of copper coins into little stacks of five, and Nora, at the ironing board, was watching him with the absorbed and deferential interest of one who has a small sum riding upon the outcome. Roscoe looked up, beheld his father, and did not appear in the least disconcerted; he merely placed one protecting hand over the largest stack, an instinctive gesture which did not escape his father's notice, and which, though slight, contributed something toward the hardening of the paternal heart.

"Roscoe," said Mr. Tillotson, "you will come with me into the library."

The word "library" was itself a portent. The room so designated by Mrs. Tillotson contained a set of the encyclopædia, purchased upon the instalment plan from a persuasive young man who had afterward been sought by the authorities of three states; a bust of Longfellow, a steel engraving of the Battle of Lookout Mountain, and a leather chair which Mr. Tillotson occupied in the evenings with the newspaper; and Roscoe had never been summoned into it except for purposes of judgment. He knew this; and he therefore paused, before descending from his chair, to sweep his coins into the pocket of his knickerbockers, where they hung like a plummet and caused him to walk with a slight list to starboard.

"Leave that money on the table," said his father.

"Somebody might take it."

"Nobody will take it. Nora will watch it."

Roscoe glanced at Nora with an expression that did not wholly flatter her, but he obeyed, and followed his father down the hall, past his mother, who rose from the stairway and fled upward as they approached, as if unable to bear the spectacle of what was about to occur.

In the library Mr. Tillotson seated himself in the leather chair, and Roscoe stood before him upon the hearth-rug, his hands behind him and his eyes resting upon the bust of Longfellow with an air of polite detachment. He was a stocky boy, with freckles distributed over him so generously that they seemed less a feature of his complexion than a substitute for it; his hair rose at the crown into a tuft which no application of water had ever subdued; and his expression, at most times, was that of a merchant who considers the market sound but intends to keep his own counsel about it.

Mr. Tillotson had, in the course of the walk from the kitchen, composed the opening of what he believed would prove a memorable address. It began, "Roscoe, there are some things a gentleman does not do," and proceeded, by stages he had not yet worked out but which he trusted would come to him, toward a stirring conclusion upon the sanctity of the home. He now delivered the first sentence, and found that the rest of it had departed.

"Roscoe," he said, "there are some things a gentleman does not do."

"Yes, sir," said Roscoe.

There was a pause.

"And this is one of them," said Mr. Tillotson.

"Which one?" Roscoe asked, with an appearance of honest inquiry.

"You know very well which one! Exhibiting your little sister! Charging money to look at her! Telling people she—telling people she lives on raw meat!"

"I didn't say she lived on it," Roscoe returned. "I said she *et* it. I didn't say she lived on it right along. Anyways, I only said that the first part of the afternoon. After that I said she et snakes."

"Snakes!"

"Small ones," said Roscoe, as one who would not exaggerate.

Mr. Tillotson found it necessary to look again at the Battle of Lookout Mountain, which hung conveniently above his son's head. It was a large engraving, full of smoke and fortitude, and he studied it for some moments before he trusted himself to proceed.

"Do you realize," he said at length, "what you have done to your mother? Do you realize that she will be ashamed to show her face to the neighbours? That Mrs. Coombs—"

"Mrs. Coombs paid," said Roscoe quickly. "She paid two cents, same as anybody. I didn't let her in for nothin', papa. She wanted to come in for one cent because she said she was only goin' to look with one eye, but I made her pay two."

"That is not the point!"

"Well, she *paid*," Roscoe insisted, evidently feeling that this circumstance was of a nature to reflect credit upon the establishment, and could not fail to soften any reasonable parent. "An' she laughed. She laughed more'n anybody. She said it was worth it."

Mr. Tillotson leaned forward in his chair and spoke with great slowness and gravity, as if each word were being lifted from a considerable depth. "Roscoe, your little sister is not a—a curiosity. She is not a wild animal. She is a member of this family. She is your own flesh and blood. How would *you* like it if somebody put *you* in a carriage and charged two cents to look at you?"

Roscoe considered this question with a fairness that did him honour. "I'd want half," he said.

"You'd want—"

"Half of it. I'd want half the money. That's fair, ain't it?" And then, perceiving from his father's face that some further consideration was demanded, he added generously: "I was goin' to give her some. I was goin' to buy her a rubber ring with a bell on it. I was, papa! I already promised her."

"You promised her? She's eleven months old!"

"Well, I told her, anyways," said Roscoe. "She looked like she heard me."

There is a point in every interview between a parent and a child at which the parent becomes aware that the conversation is not proceeding along the lines he had intended, and that he is, in some way he cannot quite define, being drawn into a negotiation rather than conducting a trial. Mr. Tillotson had now reached this point, and he recognized it, for he had reached it before, upon many similar occasions—so many, indeed, that a less sanguine man might have begun to perceive a pattern. He therefore did what he had always done, which was to grow louder.

"I will not have it argued!" he said. "There is nothing to argue about! What you did was wrong, and you know it was wrong, and you are going to be punished for it. Do you understand me, sir?"

"Yes, sir."

"Where did you get such an idea in the first place? Who put it into your head?"

Roscoe brightened, for this was a question he could answer with satisfaction. "At the circus," he said. "The one you took me to. In the side tent. There was the Wild Man of Borneo, an' he was in a cage, an' he et a chicken, all feathers an' everything, an' they charged ten cents. An' you paid it, papa. You paid for both of us. You said it was the best ten cents you ever spent."

Mr. Tillotson remembered saying this. He remembered it with painful distinctness, and he remembered also the circumstance that the Wild Man of Borneo, upon being prodded somewhat too enthusiastically by an onlooker, had addressed that onlooker in an accent strongly suggestive of County Cork; and he remembered how he himself had laughed upon the way home, and had repeated the Wild Man's observations, with embellishments, at the supper table, to the great displeasure of Sister Hattie. It now seemed to him that these recollections were not of a kind to strengthen his position, and he made haste to leave them.

"That," he said, "was entirely different."

"Why was it?"

"Because—because that man was paid to be a wild man. It was his profession. He was a grown person, and he chose to do it."

"Sister didn't care," Roscoe said. "She slept the whole time, nearly. Only when Elmer Pruitt poked her with a stick, an' then she just hollered a little, an' I took the stick away from him an' made him go to the end of the line, an' I wouldn't give him his money back, either."

"Elmer Pruitt poked her with a stick!"

"Not hard," said Roscoe. "It was a soft stick. It was a weed."

At this Mr. Tillotson rose from his chair, for a sudden vision of his daughter, small and pink and helpless under the grape arbour, assailed by the Pruitt boy—a child of notorious character, whose father was a Democrat—filled him with an emotion that, for the first time in the interview, was wholly uncomplicated. He took a turn about the room, stopped before the bust of Longfellow, and addressed it, though his remarks were intended for his son.

"Do you see what might have happened? Do you see what comes of such things? She might have been hurt. She might have been—anything might have happened! A baby! A little helpless baby, that can't speak for herself, that trusts everybody—and her own brother sets her out in the yard for every little ruffian in the neighbourhood to come and poke at with weeds! For two cents!"

He turned, and saw that Roscoe's lower lip had begun, very slightly, to protrude; and that the freckled face, hitherto so composed, so mercantile, had undergone a change. The eyes were fixed no longer upon Longfellow, but upon the hearth-rug, and they had grown suspiciously bright.

"I didn't let him hurt her," Roscoe said, in a voice not altogether steady. "I took it away. I said if anybody touched her again I'd knock their block off, an' I would of, too. I wouldn't let anybody hurt her. She's—" He stopped, and his chin worked. "She's *my* sister. I'd lick anybody."

Now, this was a declaration which Mr. Tillotson had not anticipated, and it disarmed him more completely than all the preceding argument; for he was a man of soft heart, as firm men frequently are, and he was moved, besides, by the obscure perception that his son, in his own fashion and by his own lights, had not been entirely without a sense of his responsibilities. He sat down again, rather heavily, in the leather chair, and for a time neither of them said anything at all. Somewhere in the house a door closed softly, and Mr. Tillotson suspected, correctly, that his wife had come part way down the stairs and was listening.

"Roscoe," he said at last, in a different tone, "come here."

Roscoe came, though not very near.

"Your sister," said Mr. Tillotson, "is too little to look after herself, and so you have to look after her. That's what it means to be an older brother. It doesn't mean making money out of her. It means taking care of her, even when there isn't anything in it for you. Especially then. Do you understand that?"

"Yes, sir," said Roscoe, and sniffed.

"And it means not making her ridiculous in front of people. She can't help being little. When she grows up she won't like to hear that she was shown under the grape arbour as a—as a wild infant, and that Mrs. Coombs paid two cents to look at her. People will tell her, you know. People in this town never forget anything of that kind. They'll be telling it when she's a young lady."

Roscoe appeared to receive this aspect of the matter with genuine concern, and he was silent for some time, digging the toe of one shoe into the hearth-rug. Then he looked up.

"Papa?"

"Well?"

"How much ought I to give her?"

"Give her?"

"Out of the money. If people are goin' to tell her, I guess she ought to have more'n a rubber ring. I took in sixty-one cents," Roscoe said, with an unconscious pride he could not altogether suppress even in his contrition, "an' then there was a button Elmer Pruitt give me that I didn't count. I guess she ought to have half. I guess she ought to have thirty cents an' the button."

Mr. Tillotson looked at his son for a long moment. He had a strong impulse, which he afterward confessed to nobody, to take the boy upon his knee; and a second impulse, which he confessed later to the members of the Wednesday Night Club amid a degree of hilarity that was quite unbecoming in men of their years, to ask for a percentage himself as the proprietor of the grape arbour. He yielded to neither. He was a firm parent, and he had come into the library to be firm, and he meant to go out of it having been so.

"The money," he said, "is going into the collection plate at church to-morrow. All of it. Every cent."

Roscoe's face fell, but he made no protest; he had, it seemed, expected something of the kind, and accepted it as merchants accept a disastrous turn of the market, with silence and a secret resolution to do better next time.

"And you are not to go to the Fourth of July picnic."

This was graver, and Roscoe's lip again protruded; but he only said, "Yes, sir."

"And you are to go upstairs to your mother and tell her you are sorry, and that you will never do such a thing again."

"Yes, sir."

"You may go."

Roscoe went to the door, and opened it, and paused upon the threshold, as if there were something further he wished to say. Then he appeared to think better of it, and went out; and Mr. Tillotson heard his footsteps ascend the stairs, a little more slowly than usual, and heard Mrs. Tillotson's voice, low and tremulous, meeting him at the landing. He sat back in the leather chair, and drew a long breath, and felt, upon the whole, that he had acquitted himself well. He had been firm; he had been just; he had even, he thought, been rather wise, at the end; and he determined to mention to his wife, at a suitable moment, that this was the way such things ought to be handled, and that perhaps in future she would see the advantage of leaving them to him.

In this agreeable frame of mind he remained for some minutes, until the sound of voices drew him to the library window, which overlooked the side yard. Roscoe, it appeared, had completed his errand of contrition with remarkable dispatch, and had descended by the back stairs, and was now standing beneath the grape arbour, the scene of his late enterprise, surrounded by four or five boys of the neighbourhood, among whom the father recognized, with displeasure, the unregenerate Elmer Pruitt.

"Did you get a lickin'?" Elmer was asking, with the eagerness of one who hopes for the worst.

"Naw," said Roscoe, with scorn. "He just talked."

"What'd he say?"

"Oh, a lot. He said I couldn't go to the picnic." Roscoe paused, and then added, in the tone of an expert reporting a technical observation: "He was mighty near laughin', though. Twice. I could tell."

"How could you tell?"

"He kep' lookin' at the pitcher of the war on the wall," Roscoe explained. "He always does that when he's goin' to laugh. Mamma says it's because he's ashamed to." He kicked thoughtfully at the clothes-prop. "Say, listen. I been thinkin'. Next Saturday, when sister's asleep again—no, I ain't goin' to show her. I promised. But I been thinkin' we could get Alfred Coombs's billygoat, an' paint him with stripes—"

Mr. Tillotson stepped back from the window. He stood for a moment in the middle of the library, his hands in his pockets, regarding, with a fixed and solemn gaze, the Battle of Lookout Mountain; and anyone observing him might have supposed that he was deeply moved by the heroism there depicted. His shoulders, in fact, were shaking.

The cold had come down out of the north in the night, and it had come to stay. It lay upon the land like a weight, pressing the smoke of the cabin chimney flat upon the snow and freezing the breath of the dogs into a fine white powder that sifted down upon their backs as they lay curled, noses under tails, in the lee of the woodpile. The spirit-thermometer nailed beside the door had stopped at sixty-two below, and Seth Gorham, coming in with an armful of spruce, had glanced at it and grunted and said nothing. There was nothing to say about sixty-two below. A man accepted it, as he accepted the long dark and the short grub and the silence that pressed upon the ears until they rang with the blood singing inside them.

He kicked the door shut behind him and the frost rolled in across the floor in a white wave and broke against the stove and vanished. He dumped the wood into the box and stood a moment with his back to the heat, beating his mittened hands together. He was a big man, broad in the shoulder and long in the arm, with a face burned dark by snow-glare and a short yellow beard that the frost had sheathed in ice. As the ice melted it dripped upon his parka, and he stripped the parka off and hung it on the peg and turned to look at his wife.

She was at the table, mending a moccasin by the light of a slush-lamp, and she did not look up. She was a small woman, and the two winters in the country had worn her down to bone and sinew, so that her wrists were thin as a child's and the cords stood out upon the backs of her hands when she drew the sinew through the moosehide. But there was nothing of the child in her face. The North had taken the softness out of it and left something else in its place, something gray-eyed and steady that Seth Gorham had come to know without ever quite putting a name to.

"Kilpatrick's gone on," he said.

"I heard his dogs."

"He's headed down to Dawson for his partners." He paused, and she drew the sinew through, and waited. "He says it's coarse gold, Edie. Coarse gold on bedrock at eleven feet. He says a man named Swanson panned eighty dollars from one pan, and the creek ain't half staked."

"He says," she answered.

It was not the words but the voice in which she said them, and the man heard it and felt the blood come up warm into his face. He crossed to the table and sat down across from her, and the bench creaked under his weight.

"I'm going," he said.

She set the moccasin down then and looked at him, and for a long moment neither of them spoke. The stove ticked as the iron expanded. Outside, one of the dogs whined in its sleep, and another answered it with a low growl, and then there was only the silence again, the vast and brooding silence of the frozen land that lay about the cabin for a thousand miles in every direction and seemed to lean against the walls and listen.

"It is sixty-two below," she said.

"I've traveled at sixty-two below."

"And at sixty-two below the runners drag like they was on sand, and the dogs won't make fifteen miles a day, and it is seventy miles to the Kalzas by the river trail and no trail broke past the forks. That's five days, Seth. Five days in, and five days back if there's nothing there. Ten days."

"There's something there."

"Ten days," she repeated, as though he had not spoken, "and what will you eat?"

He had known she would come to it, and he had his answer ready. "I'll take half."

She did not answer at once. She rose from the bench and went to the cache-shelf at the back of the cabin, and she lifted down the flour-sack and the bean-sack and the slab of bacon wrapped in its canvas, and she laid them on the table under the lamp, one beside the other, as a prosecutor lays out the evidence before the jury. Then she sat down again and folded her hands.

"Twenty-three pounds of flour," she said. "I weighed it this morning. Eleven pounds of beans. The bacon is maybe nine pounds, and half of that is rind. There's a little tea and no sugar and no baking powder at all. That is what we have, Seth, and it is the eleventh of February, and the ice won't go out of the Stewart until the middle of May, and no steamboat will come up from St. Michael until June. Take half of that and tell me what is left for me."

"You can get credit at the post."

"The post is out of flour. You know it is out of flour. Lavigne went down there Christmas week with gold in his poke and came back with nothing but a can of tomatoes and a bad temper."

"Then I'll bring grub back from the Kalzas."

"From where? From Swanson? From the creek that ain't half staked?" There was no mockery in her voice now; it was level and patient, and that was the worst of it. "If there's gold there, there's a hundred men there, Seth, and every one of them as hungry as you. A man doesn't sell flour on a new creek in February. He'd sooner sell his eyes."

The man got up and walked to the stove and stood looking down into it through the crack of the draft, where the fire showed red. He was angry, and he did not wish to be angry, for he knew the anger was a weakness and that she would see it for a weakness. But the gold-hunger was upon him, and it was an old hunger, older than himself, older than the country. It had driven men across the Plains in the fifties and over the Chilkoot in ninety-seven, and it had driven him, Seth Gorham, out of a dry-goods store in Stockton where he had measured calico for nine years and felt his manhood wasting from him like water from a cracked jar. He had come into the North with the hunger in him, and two winters of poor diggings and muskeg and frozen gravel that would not pay wages had not killed it. They had only made it fiercer. And now a stranger had come down the creek at dusk with frost on his eyebrows and gold in his talk, and the hunger had leaped up in the man like a fire when the door is opened upon it.

"Two winters," he said, without turning. "Two winters on this creek and what have we got? A hole in the ground and a pile of gravel that won't run four bits to the pan. I've thawed and dug and hoisted till my back's like to break, and you've cooked beans and mended moccasins and sat in this cabin in the dark, and what have we got for it? Nothing. Not a thing. Twenty-three pounds of flour." He swung around on her. "A man has got to take his chance when it comes, Edie. That's the game up here. That's the whole of it. The ones that struck it on Bonanza, they didn't sit by the stove and count their beans. They went. They got up and went when the word came, and they didn't stop to ask was it sixty below."

"And the ones that didn't strike it," she said quietly, "they went too."

"What do you mean by that?"

"I mean you've got one side of the ledger and not the other. You know the names of the men that struck it on Bonanza. Everybody knows them. But who knows the names of the men that went up the Koyukuk in the fall of ninety-seven on a word like Kilpatrick's word? Who knows the names of the men they found in the spring on the Teslin trail, sitting by a dead fire with their mittens off? Nobody, Seth. The North don't keep their names. It just keeps them."

He did not answer. He knew she spoke truth, for he had seen with his own eyes, the spring before, the thing that had come out of the snow at the mouth of Indian River when the thaw set in, and he did not like to remember it. But the knowledge did not cool him. It only made him stubborn, as a horse is made stubborn by the bit.

"I've made my mind up," he said.

"Have you?" She looked at him, and her gray eyes were unafraid. "Then sit down and let me unmake it, if I can. You owe me that much."

He sat down. He was not sure afterward why he did, for he had meant to go to the peg and take down his parka and go out to harness the dogs, and leave her to her figuring. But something in her voice brought him to the bench, and he sat with his great arms on the table and his fists clenched, and waited.

"What did Kilpatrick look like?" she asked.

"What's that to do with it?"

"Tell me."

He frowned. "A long, thin feller. Black whiskers. Had a scar acrost the back of his hand, here." He touched his own knuckles.

"And his outfit?"

"Five dogs. Mongrels, mostly. A Yukon sled."

"And what did he have on the sled?"

"How do I know what he had on the sled? His robe, and an axe, and his grub."

"How much grub?"

He started to answer, and then he stopped, and in the stopping she read her answer and went on.

"I saw it," she said. "I went out to give him the hot water for his tea, and I saw his sled. There was a sack on it, Seth, and it wasn't half full, and the rest was his robe and an axe and nothing else. A man that has just come seventy miles from a new strike, he's either got a good outfit or he's got none, and if he's got none he's half-starved. Kilpatrick wasn't starved. You saw him eat. He ate like a man that eats regular, but no more than a man that eats regular. And his dogs wasn't trail-worn. Their feet wasn't cut. I looked."

"You looked at his dogs' feet?"

"I looked."

The man stared at her. He had lived with this woman for six years, and he had thought that he knew her, but he had not known that she looked at the feet of a stranger's dogs.

"There's more," she said. "He asked how many dogs we had. You didn't hear it, for you were out at the woodpile. He asked it of me, offhand, while he drank his tea. And he asked who else was on the creek, and how far down was Lavigne's, and were there any others above us. And then you came in, and he told you his story, and he told it to you, Seth. He didn't tell it to me. He'd already found out what he wanted from me."

"What are you driving at?"

"I'm driving at this. A man that has found gold, he don't go peddling it from cabin to cabin. He keeps his mouth shut and goes to Dawson and records his claim and buys his grub and goes back. That's the law of it, and you know it as well as I do. But a man that wants to empty a creek, a man that wants every cabin from here to the Stewart standing empty with the doors shut and the owners seventy miles off and the caches full—" She stopped, and let him finish it for himself.

He sat very still. He was thinking of Kilpatrick's eyes, which had been black and quick and had not rested anywhere for long, and of the way the man had laughed, a little too loud, when he told of Swanson's eighty-dollar pan. He had not marked these things at the time. The gold had been in his ears like a roaring, and he had heard nothing else. But he remembered them now, and they came back to him with a cold certainty, as a man remembers in the morning the thin ice he had crossed in the dark.

And still the hunger would not lie down.

"You can't know it," he said heavily. "You're guessing. It could be true, Edie. It could be as true as Bonanza."

"It could."

"And if it is, and I sit here—"

"Then you'll have sat here," she said, "and you'll be alive, and so will I. And there'll be other strikes. There's always other strikes. The country is full of gold, Seth. It's the men that are scarce. It's the men that it uses up."

He got to his feet again and went to the window, which was a sheet of bottle-glass set in moss and frosted an inch thick, and he scraped a little hole in the frost with his thumbnail and looked out. There was nothing to be seen. The night was blind and black, and the cold pressed upon the glass so that his thumb ached where he had touched it. Somewhere out there was the creek, and beyond the creek the river, and beyond the river the long white hills rolling away to the Kalzas and the Pelly and the unknown country, silent, terrible, indifferent, waiting with the patience of a thing that has all of time to wait in. He felt it out there, and for the first time that night he felt it as she felt it, not as a treasure-house to be broken into but as a jaw that had closed upon many men and would close upon many more.

He turned from the window.

"And if I go anyway," he said. "If I take the dogs and half the grub and go."

She rose then, and she was so small beside him that she had to tip her head back to meet his eyes. But she met them.

"Then I go with you," she said.

"You can't. It's sixty-two below."

"I came over the Chilkoot in March with a sixty-pound pack. I poled a boat down Lake Lebarge in the ice and walked the last ninety miles to Dawson because you were sick with the fever and couldn't. I can travel at sixty-two below as well as you can, Seth Gorham, and maybe a little better, for I don't sweat my underclothes with hurrying and freeze in them after." She did not raise her voice. "The grub stays together. If you go, we both go, and we take all of it, and we both starve on the Kalzas or we both strike it rich. But I will not sit in this cabin with eleven pounds of flour and watch the door for a man that ain't coming back. I did that once, the winter you went to Circle. I won't do it again."

He looked down at her, and something moved in him that he could not have named, something deeper than anger and deeper than the gold-hunger, something that lay down at the roots of him where the oldest things lie. He had a sudden memory of her on the Dyea trail in the spring of ninety-seven, sitting on a pack in the slush with her skirt torn and her face blistered by the sun-glare off the snow, laughing because a mule had kicked over a Swede's whole outfit of stoves and the Swede was dancing in the snow with rage. She had been young then, and soft, and he had wondered whether she would last the Pass. She had lasted. She had lasted everything. And standing before him now in the yellow light of the slush-lamp, with the sinew of the moccasin still wound about her fingers, she seemed to him suddenly the very thing that the North could not use up: not strong as he was strong, in the shoulders and the back, but strong in some other way, with a strength that endured and endured and did not break.

For a long time he said nothing. Then, slowly, he went back to the table and sat down, and he put his big hands on the flour-sack and looked at it as though he had never seen it before.

"Twenty-three pounds," he said.

"Twenty-three."

"It ain't much."

"It's enough," she said, "if we're careful. It's enough to see the ice go out."

He nodded. He did not look at her. After a while she sat down too, and took up the moccasin, and drew the sinew through, and the stove ticked, and the cold leaned against the walls and listened. Once a dog howled, a long quavering wolf-howl that rose up into the night and was answered from across the creek, and Seth lifted his head; but it was only the dogs singing to the cold, as dogs will, and after a while they fell silent.

He did not sleep much that night. He lay in the bunk under the robes and listened to the frost cracking in the timber of the walls, sharp as rifle-shots, and to his wife's slow breathing, and to his own heart. The hunger was not dead in him. He knew that it would never be dead while he lived. But it lay down, as a dog lies down at the word of its master, sullen and watchful, and in the long black hours toward morning he made a kind of peace with it.

At the first gray of the dawn, which came at nearly ten o'clock and was no more than a paleness in the south, he dressed and went outside. The cold struck him in the face like a hand. His breath crackled as it left his lips, and his eyelashes froze together so that he had to pinch them apart with his mittened fingers. He went down to the creek where the trail came in, and he bent over it in the half-light, as an Indian bends over sign, and studied it.

Kilpatrick's sled had passed in the night. The tracks were plain in the dry, sandy snow, and the frost had not yet blurred them. But they did not lead down the creek toward the river and Dawson, as the man had said. They led up. They led up the creek toward Lavigne's cabin, and beyond Lavigne's to the next cabin, and the next, and the next.

Seth Gorham straightened up and stood for a long time looking at those tracks. Then he turned and went back to the cabin, and he stamped the snow from his moccasins and went in.

His wife was at the stove, frying bacon. She looked at him once, quickly, and then looked back at the pan.

He did not tell her what he had seen. And she, being a wise woman, and knowing that a man's pride is a tender thing in a hard country, did not ask.

The day had been without sun, and the night came down upon the land without warning, as night comes in the far North in the dead of the year. There was no twilight worth the name. The grey of the sky merely deepened, and thickened, and pressed lower upon the white hills until the hills and the sky were of one substance and there was no telling where the one left off and the other began. The cold was sixty below. It was a cold that did not bite so much as grip, and it gripped all things alike, the spruce trees that stood stiff and silent along the frozen creek, the ice that boomed now and again with a sound like distant artillery, and the man who toiled behind his dogs up the last mile of Henderson Creek toward the cabin that was his home.

His name was Ross Kerrigan, and he had been five winters in the country. He was a big man, deep of chest and long of arm, and the five winters had worn the softness out of him as the sea wears the softness out of a stone. His face, what showed of it between the fur of his cap and the ice-matted beard, was dark and seamed and hard. He trotted beside the sled with the easy, shambling gait of the man who has learned that the trail is long and that strength must be spent as a miser spends his gold. Six dogs strained in the traces before him, wolfish brutes with frost rimming their muzzles, and they too ran with that same economy of effort, for they too had learned the lesson of the trail.

It was Bright, the lead-dog, who first caught the scent. He flung up his head and whined, and the team faltered in its stride. Kerrigan spoke sharply and they went on, but Bright whined again, and swerved toward the right bank where the trail from the Stewart came down through the timber. Kerrigan, peering through the gloom, made out a dark shape upon the snow. It moved. It rose to its knees, and swayed, and fell forward again upon its face.

"Whoa!" Kerrigan cried, and he flung the brake into the snow and ran.

It was a man, as he had known it would be. Nothing else in all that frozen land would have fallen in such a fashion and striven so feebly to rise. The man was clad in a parka too thin for the season, and his mittens were of a cheap make, and one of them was gone, so that the bare hand clawed at the snow like a thing apart from him. Kerrigan seized him by the shoulders and turned him over. The face was white, dead white across the cheekbones and the nose, and the eyelashes were frozen together so that the man could not see.

"I'm all in," the man said thickly. "All in. Leave me be."

"Leave you be nothing," Kerrigan growled. "Get up. The cabin's a quarter mile. You can make a quarter mile."

He dragged the man to the sled and heaved him upon it, atop the sacks of flour and the bundled grub, and lashed him there with the sled-lashing. Then he cried to the dogs, and they sprang into the collars, and the sled lurched forward, and Kerrigan ran beside it with one hand upon the gee-pole and the other upon the stranger's chest, feeling, through the thin parka, the faint stir of breath that told him the man yet lived.

The cabin was dark and cold when they reached it, for Kerrigan had been three days away at Dawson. He carried the man inside as one would carry a sack of meal, and laid him on the bunk, and fell to work. He had a fire roaring in the stove within the minute. He tore the remaining mitten from the stranger's hand, and pulled off the moccasins and the socks beneath, and examined the feet with the grim thoroughness of a man who has seen many feet in his time and knows what the frost can do to them. The feet were sound. The hands were sound, though the bare one was white to the second knuckle. It was the face that had suffered, the cheeks and the nose, and Kerrigan went outside and came back with a double handful of snow and began to rub.

The man groaned and twisted under the treatment. The blood came back into the frozen flesh with a pain like fire, and he cursed, weakly at first and then with growing strength, and Kerrigan grinned in his beard to hear it, for a man who could curse like that was a man who was going to live.

"That'll do," Kerrigan said at last, and stood back to look at his work. The ice was melting from the stranger's lashes now, and running down his cheeks like tears, and he blinked and wiped at his eyes with the back of his hand and looked up at his rescuer for the first time.

He looked for a long while. Kerrigan, who was busy at the stove with the coffee-pot, felt the look and turned, and found himself staring into a pair of grey eyes that he had known once, a long time ago, in another world.

"Ross," the man said. "Ross Kerrigan. By God, it is you."

Kerrigan set down the coffee-pot. He crossed the cabin slowly and stood over the bunk and looked down. The face was gaunt and weather-beaten and older by a dozen years than the face he remembered, and there was a white scar across the chin that had not been there before. But the eyes were the same, and the shape of the mouth, and the stubborn set of the jaw that had been the mark of every man in the Harlan line for as far back as anybody could remember.

"Jim," he said. "Jim Harlan."

And then, because he was not a man of many words and did not know what other words to say, he sat down upon the edge of the bunk and put his great hand upon his cousin's shoulder and held it there.

It was eleven years since they had seen each other. They had been boys together on the old Harlan ranch in the Sonoma hills, where Ross had gone to live after his father died, and they had been more like brothers than cousins. They had hunted quail together in the chaparral and fished for trout in the canyon pools, and fought each other with bare fists behind the hay barn, and stood shoulder to shoulder against the town boys of Glen Ellen. Then Jim had run away to sea at seventeen, and Ross had drifted south to the oil fields and north to the lumber camps, and then farther north still, over the Chilkoot with the first rush, and the years had flowed between them like a wide river, and neither had written, for neither was the writing kind.

"How in thunder," Kerrigan said, when the coffee was boiling and the bacon was spitting in the pan and Jim was sitting up in the bunk with a blanket about his shoulders, "how in thunder did you come to be lying in the snow at the foot of my creek?"

Jim laughed, a short hard laugh that turned into a cough. "Looking for you," he said. "Heard in Dawson that a man named Kerrigan had a claim on Henderson. Figured there couldn't be two of that breed in the country. Started out yesterday morning. Wasn't figuring on the cold."

"Nobody figures on the cold," Kerrigan said. "It's the one thing in this country a man can't figure on. You came up light, Jim. That parka ain't fit for October, let alone January. And alone. You don't travel alone at sixty below. That's the first law of this country, and the men who break it are mostly dead."

"I know it now," Jim said soberly. "I didn't know it yesterday."

They ate in silence, as hungry men eat. Jim wolfed his bacon and beans and sourdough bread like a famished animal, and Kerrigan watched him and filled his plate again, and filled it a third time. Outside, the dogs had been fed and had burrowed into the snow, and the night had settled down over the land, black and soundless and immense. Within, the stove glowed red and the candle burned steadily on the table and the frost upon the single window thickened into fantastic ferns and forests of white.

When at last they had done, and the pipes were lighted, and the smoke hung blue beneath the low pole roof, Kerrigan spoke.

"Where've you been, Jim? Eleven years is a long time."

"Everywhere," Jim said. "Nowhere. The sea, mostly." He drew upon his pipe and stared into the open door of the stove where the fire roared and leaped. "I shipped first on a coaster out of San Francisco. Then a lumber schooner to Australia. Then I fell in with the sealers. Seven seasons I went sealing, Ross. Off the coast of Japan, and up through the Kuriles, and into the Bering Sea. Hard work and hard men. I've seen men killed for a pouch of tobacco, and boats lost in the fog with every soul in them, and a captain shot down on his own deck by his own mate. I've been wrecked twice. This"—he touched the white scar on his chin—"I got from a boat-steerer who thought I'd shorted him on his lay. He didn't think it long."

He spoke without boasting, flatly, as a man speaks of the weather, and Kerrigan nodded slowly. He had known such men and such lives. The North was full of them, men who had been hammered on the anvil of the world until there was nothing soft left in them, nothing but the iron.

"And you?" said Jim.

Kerrigan shrugged his great shoulders. "Oil, for a while. Then logging, up in the redwoods. Then here. I came over the pass in 'ninety-seven, packed a ton of outfit on my back in fifty-pound lots, built a boat at Lindeman out of green spruce and ran the White Horse with it. Staked on Bonanza and sold out for a song, staked on Hunker and lost the claim to a jumper while I was down with the scurvy. Then I came here." He jerked his head toward the window, toward the black night and the frozen creek beyond. "It's paying. Not a fortune. But it's paying. I'll go out in the spring with a sack."

"Going out where?"

Kerrigan did not answer at once. He smoked, and the silence lengthened.

"Home," he said at last. "I'd figured on home. On the ranch. I'd figured on buying a piece of land in the valley, and going to see my mother, and maybe—" He stopped. "Well. A man figures on a good many things in the long winter nights."

Jim's face had changed. He took his pipe from his mouth and turned it over in his fingers, slowly, as though it were a thing of great interest. When he spoke his voice was low.

"You don't know, then," he said. "Nobody wrote you."

"Nobody knew where to write. Know what?"

"Aunt Martha," said Jim. "Your mother, Ross. She died. Two years gone, in the spring. It was her heart. She went quick, in her sleep. There wasn't any pain to it."

Kerrigan did not move. He sat upon the upended box that served him for a chair, with his elbows upon his knees and his pipe in his hand, and he did not move, and his face did not change. Only the hand that held the pipe tightened upon it, and the knuckles stood out white beneath the brown skin, and the cold pipe-stem snapped with a little dry sound that was very loud in the silent cabin.

He looked down at the broken pieces in his palm. Then he put them on the table, carefully, side by side.

"Two years," he said.

"I'm sorry, Ross."

"Two years." Kerrigan stood up, and went to the window, and stood there with his back to his cousin, staring at the frost-ferns as though he could see through them to the dark land beyond. "And me up here digging in the muck, thinking of her. Thinking of the day I'd walk up the road with my poke on my belt and tell her she'd never want for anything again. Two years she's been in the ground, and I didn't know it."

He was silent for a long while. Jim did not speak. He was a man who had lived among hard men, and he knew that there are times when words are worth nothing, and that the kindest thing a man can do for another man is to hold his tongue and let him be.

At last Kerrigan turned from the window. His face was set, and his eyes were dry, and if there had been any weakness in him it was gone, or buried so deep that no man would ever find it.

"What else?" he said. "You didn't come seventeen hundred miles to the Yukon in the dead of winter in a summer parka just to tell me that. What else, Jim?"

Jim Harlan looked up at him, and there was something in his eyes that Kerrigan had never seen there before, not even when they had been boys and had fought behind the barn until the blood ran.

"Nell," Jim said.

The name hung between them in the smoky air. Kerrigan's jaw tightened under the beard.

"What about Nell?"

"I married her, Ross."

Kerrigan said nothing at all.

"I came home from the sealing four years back," Jim went on, and now the words came fast, tumbling over each other, as though they had been dammed up within him for a long time and must at last break loose. "I came home with my pay, and she was there, still at her father's place by the creek. She'd waited, Ross. Not for me. For you. She'd waited six years for you, and you never wrote her, not a line, and nobody knew where you were or whether you were alive or dead. She'd given you up. And I—I'd always cared for her. You knew that. You must have known it, back when we were boys. I asked her, and she said yes. I don't know that she loved me, not the way she'd loved you. But she said yes."

Kerrigan stood very still. "Go on," he said.

"We had three years. Good years. I quit the sea and worked the ranch with Uncle Dave, and we were happy enough. And then last winter—" Jim's voice broke, and steadied, and went on. "Last winter there was to be a child. And something went wrong. The doctor came out from Santa Rosa through the storm, but he came too late, and there wasn't anything he could do. Neither of them lived, Ross. Not Nell. Not the boy."

The fire crackled in the stove. Outside, far off down the creek, the ice boomed sullenly, and one of the dogs lifted its voice in a long, quavering howl that rose and rose and broke at last into silence.

"So I sold my share of the ranch to Uncle Dave," Jim said. "There wasn't anything to hold me there. I couldn't look at the place. And I thought—I don't know what I thought. That you had a right to know. That I'd done you a wrong, maybe, and ought to tell you to your face. That you were the only one left in the world who'd understand." He laughed again, that short hard laugh. "So I came north. And I damned near died at the foot of your creek. And here I am."

He stopped. He had said what he had come to say, and now he sat with the blanket about his shoulders, and waited, and his grey eyes were steady on his cousin's face.

Kerrigan came back from the window. He came slowly across the cabin, his big body casting a great shadow upon the log wall in the candlelight, and he stood over Jim Harlan as he had stood over him in the snow. Jim did not flinch. He had faced death too many times to flinch now, and if his cousin's fist had come down upon him he would have taken it, and asked no quarter, and given none.

But Kerrigan's fist did not come down. Instead he reached out and took his cousin's frost-bitten hand, the one that had lost its mitten, and turned it over in his own and looked at it, at the white flesh and the blistering knuckles.

"You'll lose the skin off these two fingers," he said. "Nothing worse. You were lucky."

Then he sat down heavily upon the box again, and was silent for a long while, staring into the fire.

"I loved her, Jim," he said at last. "I loved her, and I left her, and I never wrote her a line. I told myself I'd write when I'd made my stake. When I had something to show. Every winter I told myself that, and every winter I didn't write. A man gets so he can't. The country gets into him. The trail, and the cold, and the gold that's always just under the next foot of muck. He forgets there's anything else in the world." He shook his head slowly. "You didn't do me any wrong. I did it to myself. And I did it to her. If there's any wrong in this, it's mine."

"Ross—"

"No." Kerrigan held up his hand. "No. Let it lie. She's dead, and my mother's dead, and the boy's dead, and there isn't anything you nor I nor any man can do about it. That's the way of things. The strong live a while and the weak go under, and in the end it's all one, and the snow covers everything. I've seen it a hundred times in this country. A man learns not to curse what can't be helped."

He reached for the coffee-pot on the stove and filled both their cups, and handed one to his cousin, and Jim took it in his good hand.

"You'll stay," Kerrigan said. It was not a question. "There's work enough on the claim for two. I've been short-handed since my partner went out in the fall. We'll thaw and dig through the winter and sluice in the spring, and when the river opens, we'll see."

"See what?"

Kerrigan shrugged. "Whatever there is to see. Maybe we'll go out together. Maybe we'll go on down the river to Nome. There's talk of gold on the beaches there, gold a man can scoop up with a pan. Maybe we'll go back to the sea, the both of us. I don't know. A man doesn't need to know. That's one thing this country's taught me. You live to the next meal and the next mile, and you let the rest take care of itself."

Jim Harlan looked at his cousin across the rim of the tin cup, and for the first time since he had opened his eyes in that cabin, the hardness went out of his face, and he looked, for a moment, like the boy who had fished the canyon pools long ago in the warm green hills.

"All right, Ross," he said. "I'll stay."

They talked far into the night after that, as men will who have been long apart and have much to tell. They talked of the old ranch, and of Uncle Dave and his bad leg, and of the quail coveys in the chaparral, and of the time they had stolen old man Beggs's rowboat and been carried out through the Golden Gate on the ebb tide and nearly drowned. Jim told of typhoons off the coast of Japan, and of a Russian prison on the Commander Islands where he had lain three months on black bread and water, and of seal rookeries where the beasts lay so thick upon the rocks that a man could not see the stone beneath them. And Kerrigan told of the Chilkoot in the spring of 'ninety-eight, when the avalanche had come down at the Scales and buried threescore men alive, and of the long, mad stampedes by night across the frozen hills, and of the scurvy winter on Hunker, when he had lain in his bunk and watched his own gums go black and his teeth loosen in his head, and had lived because he had refused, out of sheer stubbornness, to die.

They did not speak again of Nell, nor of Kerrigan's mother. Those things had been said, and there was no need to say them twice. They lay between the two men now like a buried thing, not forgotten, but put away, as the dead are put away in that country, beneath the snow and the frozen earth, until the spring.

The candle burned down and guttered out, and Kerrigan did not light another. The fire sank to a red glow in the stove. And at last Jim Harlan's voice trailed off in the middle of a sentence, and his head fell back against the log wall, and he slept.

Kerrigan rose and drew the blanket up about his cousin's shoulders, as a woman might have done, and then stood for a long while in the dark cabin, listening to the steady breathing of the sleeping man. Outside, the cold had deepened. He could hear it, the faint crackling of the frost in the spruce trees, the small sharp sounds of a world contracting in the iron grip of the Northern night. Somewhere a dog stirred and whimpered in its sleep.

He was a hard man, and the country had made him harder. But there was a thing in him that night, standing in the darkness beside the last living soul in the world who shared his blood and his boyhood, that was not hard at all. It had no name that he knew, and he did not try to give it one. He only knew that he was no longer alone, and that the long winter that stretched before him, which a day ago had seemed a thing to be endured, was now a thing that two men might face together.

He threw another stick upon the fire and lay down upon the floor beside the stove, wrapped in his robe of rabbit-skin, and was asleep almost before the flame had caught.

And in the morning, when the grey light crept down over the white hills and the cold stood at sixty-two below, they went out together onto the creek, the big man and the lean one, and took up the pick and the shovel, and bent their backs to the frozen ground.

The cold had come down out of the north in the night, and it had come to stay. It lay upon the land like a hand, heavy and unhurried, and under it the land was still. The spruce stood black and motionless along the flanks of the hills, each bough bowed beneath its burden of frost. The river was a broad white road between them, frozen six feet down, and it gave forth no sound. There was no wind. There was no life. There was only the cold, and the pale sun that lifted itself for an hour above the southern skyline, looked wanly upon the desolation, and sank again as if ashamed of its own feebleness.

John Haskell came down the last ridge of his trap-line at three in the afternoon, and the twilight was already thickening in the valley. He had been gone since the gray before dawn. His beard was a mat of ice where his breath had frozen upon it, and the fur of his parka-ruff was white with rime. Behind him, at the end of a short line, plodded Baldy, the old lead-dog, who was too wise and too stiff of joint to be left at the cabin with the rest of the team, and who preferred, besides, the company of the man. The pack on Haskell's shoulders held two marten and a lynx, frozen hard as cordwood. It had been a fair day. He was thinking, as he came down the ridge, of the fire that would be roaring in the sheet-iron stove, and of the beans that the boy would have set to thaw, and of the boy himself, who would be watching at the window with his nose flattened against the single pane of glass that had cost an ounce of dust at Forty Mile.

He was thinking these things when he lifted his eyes and saw that there was no smoke rising from the cabin.

He stopped. Baldy stopped behind him and sat down in the snow and looked up at him with grave, inquiring eyes. For a long moment the man stood without moving, and in that moment a great many thoughts passed through his brain, swift and cold and orderly, as was the way with thoughts in that country. A man who has lived long in the North learns to think so, for the North does not forgive the man who thinks slowly, and it does not forgive the man who thinks in a panic. There was a reason for the absence of smoke. There were many possible reasons. Some of them were small and some of them were large, and one or two of them were so large that he would not look at them yet. He would look at them when he had to and not before.

Then he went down the slope at a run, the pack thudding against his back and the old dog loping beside him.

The door of the cabin stood shut. That was a good sign. He flung it open and went in, and the air inside was the air of a cellar, and the stove was dull and black, and the boy was not there. On the table the beans stood in their pot, frozen solid. The boy's moccasins were gone from the nail behind the stove. His mittens were gone. His little parka of squirrel-skin, which his mother had sewn for him in the last winter of her life, was gone. And on the two pegs above the door, where the rifle should have been, there was nothing at all.

Haskell went out again. He did not hurry now. In the failing light he circled the cabin once, bent low, his eyes on the snow, and on the far side, beyond the cache, he found what he sought: the small, deep prints of a child's moccasins leading away toward the river. And beside them, here and there, the round dimple where the butt of the rifle had been rested, for the rifle was long and heavy, and the boy who carried it was seven years old.

There were other tracks, too, older ones, crossing the boy's trail at an angle and running on ahead of it, light and delicate, the toes spread wide. Haskell looked at them and understood. A fox had come down in the night to nose about the cache, and the boy had seen its tracks in the morning, and the boy had gone after it.

"The young fool," Haskell said aloud, and his voice sounded strange to him in the vast silence. "The young fool."

But there was no anger in his voice yet. There was only the cold, careful measuring of the trail ahead and the light that remained.

He took the trail with Baldy at his heels. It led down the bank and out upon the river and along the river for half a mile, close under the shore, where the fox had run and the boy had followed. At a place where the river bent there was an overflow, where water had forced up through a crack in the ice and spread itself beneath the snow and frozen again, and frozen only thinly. Here the fox tracks swerved wide, for the fox knew. And here the boy's tracks did not swerve, for the boy did not know. Haskell saw where the small feet had broken through the snow-crust into the water that lay hidden beneath it, saw the wild scramble of tracks where the boy had floundered out, and his heart stood still in his breast.

Then he saw that the tracks led back toward the cabin, by a different way, across a point of land, and that they were running tracks, and that they were not yet staggering. And a little further, under a spruce, he saw the place where the boy had stopped, and had pulled off a mitten, and had broken off dry twigs from beneath the lower boughs, and had heaped them together. There were three burnt matches lying on the snow. There was a small black scar where a fire had been kindled and had caught and had burned, and the snow about it had been trampled flat by small feet stamping, stamping, stamping, while the circulation came back into them.

Haskell stood and looked at that blackened place for some time. Something moved in his face beneath the ice of his beard, but there was none to see it save the old dog.

He found the boy two hundred yards further on. He was sitting in the snow at the foot of the bank below the cabin, the rifle across his knees, too spent to climb. His face was gray beneath the hood of the squirrel-skin parka, and there were white patches on his cheeks where the frost had bitten. But he lifted his head when he heard his father coming, and he did not cry.

Haskell did not speak. He picked up the rifle and slung it on his shoulder beside the pack. He picked up the boy and carried him up the bank and into the cabin, and set him on the bunk. Then, before he did any other thing, he knelt and pulled the moccasins from the boy's feet, and the socks beneath them, and looked at the feet. They were red, not white. He pressed the toes one after another between his thumb and finger and watched the blood come back into the places he had pressed. He let out a long breath. Then he rubbed the boy's cheeks with snow until the white patches were gone and the boy was whimpering with the pain of returning blood. Only when that was done did he build the fire.

He built it with care, as he did all things. He shaved the kindling thin, and laid it crosswise, and laid the heavier sticks above it, and touched the match to the shavings, and fed the flame until it roared up the stovepipe and the iron began to tick and glow. Then he set the beans on to thaw, and put water in the kettle for tea, and hung the frozen marten and the lynx from the rafters where they would soften for skinning. The boy watched him from the bunk. The man's back was broad and slow-moving, and it told the boy nothing, and the boy watched it as a young animal watches the larger animal that holds its fate.

At last Haskell turned around. He pulled the stool from beneath the table and set it before the bunk and sat down upon it, his hands upon his knees. The firelight played upon his face, which was lean and weather-blackened and seamed by the frost of many winters. His eyes were gray, the color of river ice, and they rested upon the boy's face and did not move from it.

"Davy," he said.

"Yes, sir."

"Where was the fire?"

The boy's lip trembled. He looked at the stove, which was glowing now, and then back at his father.

"I let it go out," he said.

"You let it go out." Haskell said the words slowly, as though he were turning them over in his hand and weighing them, the way he weighed gold dust on the little brass scales. "You were left to keep the fire. That was your work. I go to the traps, and you keep the fire. That is the way it is between us. I told you that."

"Yes, sir."

"And you let it go out, and you took the rifle, and you went down on the river after a fox."

The boy said nothing. There was nothing to say. He had known, from the moment he had broken through the snow into the water and felt it close upon his ankles like the jaws of a trap, that there would be nothing to say. He had known it while he fumbled with the matches, while he lost the first and the second to his shaking fingers, while he cupped the third in his bare hands and prayed over it as his mother had taught him to pray. He had known it all the long way back, running on feet that had gone dead beneath him. He had been more afraid of this moment than of the cold.

"What is the thermometer?" Haskell asked.

The boy's eyes went to the window, beside which the spirit thermometer hung on its nail outside the glass. He could not see it from where he sat, and he did not need to.

"I don't know," he said.

"Then I'll tell you. It was fifty-eight below at noon. It's colder now. At fifty below, spit crackles in the air before it hits the snow. At sixty, a man's breath freezes and falls to the ground with a sound like sand. You've heard that sound."

"Yes, sir."

"Do you know what fifty-eight below means to a man with wet feet?"

The boy's eyes filled. He shook his head.

Haskell leaned forward. The firelight caught the hard planes of his face and threw them into relief, and his voice, when he spoke again, was low and even and terrible in its evenness.

"It means he has ten minutes. Maybe fifteen if he's lucky and strong. If he gets a fire going in that time, he lives. If his fingers go before he can strike the match, or if the snow falls off a bough and puts out his fire, or if he's a fool and builds it in the wrong place, then he dies. He doesn't die at once. First his feet go, and he can't feel them, and he stamps and stamps and they won't come back. Then his hands go, and he can't hold the matches. Then he gets sleepy. He gets warm, Davy. He sits down in the snow, and he feels warm, and he thinks he'll rest a little before he goes on. And he doesn't go on. In the spring somebody finds him when the snow goes off, if the wolverines haven't found him first."

The boy was crying now, silently, the tears running down cheeks that still burned from the frost.

"I knew a man like that," Haskell went on, and he did not soften. "His name was Pete Lavoie. He was a big man, bigger than me. Strong as an ox. He'd been in the country eleven years, and he knew all there was to know about cold. And one day on the Sixtymile he went through an overflow, the same as you did today. He built his fire under a spruce. And the heat of the fire loosened the snow on the boughs above, and it came down and put out the fire. And Pete Lavoie had no more matches dry enough to strike, and his hands were gone. We found him three days after. He was sitting with his back to the tree, and he was smiling."

He stopped. The fire roared in the stove. Outside, somewhere up the hillside, a spruce split open with the frost, and the report of it came down through the still air like a pistol shot.

"You were lucky," Haskell said. "That's all you were. Lucky. The North gave you one chance today, and you took it. But it doesn't give that chance twice, and it doesn't give it to fools. It doesn't care that you're seven years old. It doesn't care that you're my boy. It doesn't care that your mother is dead and you're all I've got left of her. It doesn't care about anything. It's just the cold, and the cold has one law, and the law is that the man who breaks it dies."

The boy put his face in his hands and sobbed aloud now, great tearing sobs that shook his small body. And the man sat on the stool and watched him and did not reach out to him, though the reaching was in him, though every muscle in his arms ached with the reaching. For he knew the North better than he knew anything, and he knew that it was not enough that the boy should be sorry. Sorrow was a soft thing, and it melted away like the frost on the window when the stove got hot. The lesson must go deeper than sorrow. It must go down into the bone and into the blood, down to where the boy's body would remember it on some far day when his mind had forgotten, when he stood alone on some frozen trail with no father coming down the ridge to find him.

"Stop crying," he said.

The boy choked and swallowed and tried to stop. It was a long time before he could.

"Now look at me."

The boy lifted his wet face.

"Why did you go after the fox?"

The boy's chin quivered. He spoke so low that the man had to bend to hear him.

"I wanted to get it for you. I wanted to shoot it and skin it and have it hanging up when you came home. So you'd see I could. So you'd see I could do things."

Haskell sat back. For a long moment he did not speak, and the boy, watching him, could not read what was in his face. It was in the man's mind that he had heard those words before, in another voice, in another place. They had been his own words. He had spoken them forty years before to his own father, in a sod house on the Dakota prairie, after he had taken the shotgun to go after wolves that had been killing the calves, and had come home in a blizzard with two fingers frozen and no wolves. His father had beaten him with a harness strap that night until he could not sit, and he had hated his father for a month. Only later, when he was grown and had buried men who had not been beaten soon enough or hard enough, had he understood.

He looked at the boy's small hands, which were still red and swollen with the cold. He looked at the squirrel-skin parka that Mary had sewn. And he made up his mind.

"Stand up," he said.

The boy stood up on the floor of the cabin in his bare feet, trembling. He thought that he was to be whipped, and he braced himself for it, as a young dog braces itself before a blow, and he did not try to run.

"Get your moccasins," Haskell said. "Dry ones. The ones on the nail."

The boy obeyed, wondering. When he had pulled them on, his father handed him the axe.

"There's wood to cut," Haskell said. "You let the fire go out, and the fire burned nothing all day, and so there was no wood used. But tonight it will burn twice as hard to make the cabin warm again, and I have been on the trail since dawn. So you'll cut it. You'll cut enough to fill the box behind the stove, and enough to stack beside the door, and you'll do it now, before supper. And while you're cutting, you'll think about Pete Lavoie."

"Yes, sir."

"And tomorrow, when I go to the traps, you'll keep the fire. And the day after that. And every day until I tell you different. And you'll not touch the rifle again until I put it in your hands myself."

"Yes, sir."

"Go on, then."

The boy went out into the darkness, and the cold took him by the throat. Haskell sat on the stool and listened to the sound of the axe, slow and uneven at first, the sound of a small boy swinging a tool too heavy for him; then steadier, as the boy found the rhythm of it. He sat a long time, listening. Old Baldy came and laid his gray muzzle on the man's knee, and the man put his hand on the dog's head and kept it there.

When the boy came in at last, staggering under an armload of split spruce, his face was red with the cold and wet with sweat beneath the hood, and his eyes were dry. He stacked the wood in the box behind the stove, neatly, with the ends squared, as he had seen his father do. Then he went out for another armload, and another. When the box was full and the stack beside the door rose to the height of his shoulder, he stood before his father and waited.

Haskell looked at the woodbox. He looked at the stack. He looked at the boy.

"That'll do," he said.

They ate the beans together at the table, and the bacon that Haskell fried, and the sourdough bread, and they drank their tea scalding hot from tin cups. Neither of them spoke. When the meal was done, the boy washed the plates in the basin without being told, and dried them, and set them upon the shelf. Then he crawled into his bunk beneath the robes of rabbit-skin and turned his face to the log wall.

Haskell banked the fire for the night and blew out the candle. In the darkness he sat on the edge of his own bunk, unlacing his moccasins, and he heard the boy's breathing, which was not yet the breathing of sleep.

"Davy," he said.

"Yes, sir."

"The fire you built under the spruce. Down on the point."

The boy was silent, waiting.

"You built it in the open, clear of the boughs. You used dry twigs from underneath, where the snow doesn't reach. You built it small and fed it slow." He paused. "That was well done. Your mother would have been proud of that fire."

There was no answer from the other bunk. But after a time the man heard the breathing change, and deepen, and grow slow and even, and he knew that the boy slept.

He did not sleep himself for a long while. He lay on his back in the dark and listened to the cold. It was a living thing, the cold, and it prowled about the cabin in the night, and pressed its great face against the logs, and tried the door. Now and again the frost cracked a tree on the hillside, and once, far off, a wolf howled, and the dogs in their kennel answered it with a long, quavering chorus that rose and died away into the silence. And the man lay and listened and thought of the small, deep tracks going down to the river, and of the three burnt matches lying on the snow, and of how near it had been, and of how small a thing it is, after all, that stands between a man and the dark.

He thought, too, that the boy would hate him for a while, as he had hated his own father. That was right. That was the way of it. The young must hate the old for a time, for the old stand between them and the world and say no, and the young cannot see the world yet for what it is. But the boy would grow, and the cold would teach him the rest, and one day, God willing, on some far trail, he would understand.

The fire ticked in the stove. The boy slept. And outside, under the cold stars, the white land lay silent and waited, as it had always waited, as it would wait when they were both long gone, patient and pitiless and without end.
