Here is an excerpt of Jack London's writing, to show you their style:

Not but that I was afloat in a safe craft, for the Martinez was a new ferry-steamer, making her fourth or fifth trip on the run between Sausalito and San Francisco. The danger lay in the heavy fog which blanketed the bay, and of which, as a landsman, I had little apprehension. In fact, I remember the placid exaltation with which I took up my position on the forward upper deck, directly beneath the pilot-house, and allowed the mystery of the fog to lay hold of my imagination. A fresh breeze was blowing, and for a time I was alone in the moist obscurity—yet not alone, for I was dimly conscious of the presence of the pilot, and of what I took to be the captain, in the glass house above my head. I remember thinking how comfortable it was, this division of labour which made it unnecessary for me to study fogs, winds, tides, and navigation, in order to visit my friend who lived across an arm of the sea. It was good that men should be specialists, I mused. The peculiar knowledge of the pilot and captain sufficed for many thousands of people who knew no more of the sea and navigation than I knew. On the other hand, instead of having to devote my energy to the learning of a multitude of things, I concentrated it upon a few particular things, such as, for instance, the analysis of Poe’s place in American literature—an essay of mine, by the way, in the current Atlantic. Coming aboard, as I passed through the cabin, I had noticed with greedy eyes a stout gentleman reading the Atlantic, which was open at my very essay. And there it was again, the division of labour, the special knowledge of the pilot and captain which permitted the stout gentleman to read my special knowledge on Poe while they carried him safely from Sausalito to San Francisco. A red-faced man, slamming the cabin door behind him and stumping out on the deck, interrupted my reflections, though I made a mental note of the topic for use in a projected essay which I had thought of calling “The Necessity for Freedom: A Plea for the Artist.” The red-faced man shot a glance up at the pilot-house, gazed around at the fog, stumped across the deck and back (he evidently had artificial legs), and stood still by my side, legs wide apart, and with an expression of keen enjoyment on his face. I was not wrong when I decided that his days had been spent on the sea.

“It’s nasty weather like this here that turns heads grey before their time,” he said, with a nod toward the pilot-house.

“I had not thought there was any particular strain,” I answered. “It seems as simple as A, B, C. They know the direction by compass, the distance, and the speed. I should not call it anything more than mathematical certainty.”

“Strain!” he snorted. “Simple as A, B, C! Mathematical certainty!” He seemed to brace himself up and lean backward against the air as he stared at me. “How about this here tide that’s rushin’ out through the Golden Gate?” he demanded, or bellowed, rather. “How fast is she ebbin’? What’s the drift, eh? Listen to that, will you? A bell-buoy, and we’re a-top of it! See ’em alterin’ the course!” From out of the fog came the mournful tolling of a bell, and I could see the pilot turning the wheel with great rapidity. The bell, which had seemed straight ahead, was now sounding from the side. Our own whistle was blowing hoarsely, and from time to time the sound of other whistles came to us from out of the fog.

“That’s a ferry-boat of some sort,” the new-comer said, indicating a whistle off to the right. “And there! D’ye hear that? Blown by mouth. Some scow schooner, most likely. Better watch out, Mr. Schooner-man. Ah, I thought so. Now hell’s a poppin’ for somebody!” The unseen ferry-boat was blowing blast after blast, and the mouth-blown horn was tooting in terror-stricken fashion.

“And now they’re payin’ their respects to each other and tryin’ to get clear,” the red-faced man went on, as the hurried whistling ceased. His face was shining, his eyes flashing with excitement as he translated into articulate language the speech of the horns and sirens. “That’s a steam-siren a-goin’ it over there to the left. And you hear that fellow with a frog in his throat—a steam schooner as near as I can judge, crawlin’ in from the Heads against the tide.” A shrill little whistle, piping as if gone mad, came from directly ahead and from very near at hand. Gongs sounded on the Martinez. Our paddle-wheels stopped, their pulsing beat died away, and then they started again. The shrill little whistle, like the chirping of a cricket amid the cries of great beasts, shot through the fog from more to the side and swiftly grew faint and fainter. I looked to my companion for enlightenment.

“One of them dare-devil launches,” he said. “I almost wish we’d sunk him, the little rip! They’re the cause of more trouble. And what good are they? Any jackass gets aboard one and runs it from hell to breakfast, blowin’ his whistle to beat the band and tellin’ the rest of the world to look out for him, because he’s comin’ and can’t look out for himself! Because he’s comin’! And you’ve got to look out, too! Right of way! Common decency! They don’t know the meanin’ of it!” I felt quite amused at his unwarranted choler, and while he stumped indignantly up and down I fell to dwelling upon the romance of the fog. And romantic it certainly was—the fog, like the grey shadow of infinite mystery, brooding over the whirling speck of earth; and men, mere motes of light and sparkle, cursed with an insane relish for work, riding their steeds of wood and steel through the heart of the mystery, groping their way blindly through the Unseen, and clamouring and clanging in confident speech the while their hearts are heavy with incertitude and fear. The voice of my companion brought me back to myself with a laugh. I too had been groping and floundering, the while I thought I rode clear-eyed through the mystery.

“Hello! somebody comin’ our way,” he was saying. “And d’ye hear that? He’s comin’ fast. Walking right along. Guess he don’t hear us yet. Wind’s in wrong direction.” The fresh breeze was blowing right down upon us, and I could hear the whistle plainly, off to one side and a little ahead.

“Ferry-boat?” I asked. He nodded, then added, “Or he wouldn’t be keepin’ up such a clip.” He gave a short chuckle. “They’re gettin’ anxious up there.” I glanced up. The captain had thrust his head and shoulders out of the pilot-house, and was staring intently into the fog as though by sheer force of will he could penetrate it. His face was anxious, as was the face of my companion, who had stumped over to the rail and was gazing with a like intentness in the direction of the invisible danger. Then everything happened, and with inconceivable rapidity. The fog seemed to break away as though split by a wedge, and the bow of a steamboat emerged, trailing fog-wreaths on either side like seaweed on the snout of Leviathan. I could see the pilot-house and a white-bearded man leaning partly out of it, on his elbows. He was clad in a blue uniform, and I remember noting how trim and quiet he was. His quietness, under the circumstances, was terrible. He accepted Destiny, marched hand in hand with it, and coolly measured the stroke. As he leaned there, he ran a calm and speculative eye over us, as though to determine the precise point of the collision, and took no notice whatever when our pilot, white with rage, shouted, “Now you’ve done it!” On looking back, I realize that the remark was too obvious to make rejoinder necessary.

“Grab hold of something and hang on,” the red-faced man said to me. All his bluster had gone, and he seemed to have caught the contagion of preternatural calm. “And listen to the women scream,” he said grimly—almost bitterly, I thought, as though he had been through the experience before. The vessels came together before I could follow his advice. We must have been struck squarely amidships, for I saw nothing, the strange steamboat having passed beyond my line of vision. The Martinez heeled over, sharply, and there was a crashing and rending of timber. I was thrown flat on the wet deck, and before I could scramble to my feet I heard the scream of the women. This it was, I am certain,—the most indescribable of blood-curdling sounds,—that threw me into a panic. I remembered the life-preservers stored in the cabin, but was met at the door and swept backward by a wild rush of men and women. What happened in the next few minutes I do not recollect, though I have a clear remembrance of pulling down life-preservers from the overhead racks, while the red-faced man fastened them about the bodies of an hysterical group of women. This memory is as distinct and sharp as that of any picture I have seen. It is a picture, and I can see it now,—the jagged edges of the hole in the side of the cabin, through which the grey fog swirled and eddied; the empty upholstered seats, littered with all the evidences of sudden flight, such as packages, hand satchels, umbrellas, and wraps; the stout gentleman who had been reading my essay, encased in cork and canvas, the magazine still in his hand, and asking me with monotonous insistence if I thought there was any danger; the red-faced man, stumping gallantly around on his artificial legs and buckling life-preservers on all comers; and finally, the screaming bedlam of women. This it was, the screaming of the women, that most tried my nerves. It must have tried, too, the nerves of the red-faced man, for I have another picture which will never fade from my mind. The stout gentleman is stuffing the magazine into his overcoat pocket and looking on curiously. A tangled mass of women, with drawn, white faces and open mouths, is shrieking like a chorus of lost souls; and the red-faced man, his face now purplish with wrath, and with arms extended overhead as in the act of hurling thunderbolts, is shouting, “Shut up! Oh, shut up!” I remember the scene impelled me to sudden laughter, and in the next instant I realized I was becoming hysterical myself; for these were women of my own kind, like my mother and sisters, with the fear of death upon them and unwilling to die. And I remember that the sounds they made reminded me of the squealing of pigs under the knife of the butcher, and I was struck with horror at the vividness of the analogy. These women, capable of the most sublime emotions, of the tenderest sympathies, were open-mouthed and screaming. They wanted to live, they were helpless, like rats in a trap, and they screamed. The horror of it drove me out on deck. I was feeling sick and squeamish, and sat down on a bench. In a hazy way I saw and heard men rushing and shouting as they strove to lower the boats. It was just as I had read descriptions of such scenes in books. The tackles jammed. Nothing worked. One boat lowered away with the plugs out, filled with women and children and then with water, and capsized. Another boat had been lowered by one end, and still hung in the tackle by the other end, where it had been abandoned. Nothing was to be seen of the strange steamboat which had caused the disaster, though I heard men saying that she would undoubtedly send boats to our assistance. I descended to the lower deck. The Martinez was sinking fast, for the water was very near. Numbers of the passengers were leaping overboard. Others, in the water, were clamouring to be taken aboard again. No one heeded them. A cry arose that we were sinking. I was seized by the consequent panic, and went over the side in a surge of bodies. How I went over I do not know, though I did know, and instantly, why those in the water were so desirous of getting back on the steamer. The water was cold—so cold that it was painful. The pang, as I plunged into it, was as quick and sharp as that of fire. It bit to the marrow. It was like the grip of death. I gasped with the anguish and shock of it, filling my lungs before the life-preserver popped me to the surface. The taste of the salt was strong in my mouth, and I was strangling with the acrid stuff in my throat and lungs. But it was the cold that was most distressing. I felt that I could survive but a few minutes. People were struggling and floundering in the water about me. I could hear them crying out to one another. And I heard, also, the sound of oars. Evidently the strange steamboat had lowered its boats. As the time went by I marvelled that I was still alive. I had no sensation whatever in my lower limbs, while a chilling numbness was wrapping about my heart and creeping into it. Small waves, with spiteful foaming crests, continually broke over me and into my mouth, sending me off into more strangling paroxysms. The noises grew indistinct, though I heard a final and despairing chorus of screams in the distance, and knew that the Martinez had gone down. Later,—how much later I have no knowledge,—I came to myself with a start of fear. I was alone. I could hear no calls or cries—only the sound of the waves, made weirdly hollow and reverberant by the fog. A panic in a crowd, which partakes of a sort of community of interest, is not so terrible as a panic when one is by oneself; and such a panic I now suffered. Whither was I drifting? The red-faced man had said that the tide was ebbing through the Golden Gate. Was I, then, being carried out to sea? And the life-preserver in which I floated? Was it not liable to go to pieces at any moment? I had heard of such things being made of paper and hollow rushes which quickly became saturated and lost all buoyancy. And I could not swim a stroke. And I was alone, floating, apparently, in the midst of a grey primordial vastness. I confess that a madness seized me, that I shrieked aloud as the women had shrieked, and beat the water with my numb hands. How long this lasted I have no conception, for a blankness intervened, of which I remember no more than one remembers of troubled and painful sleep. When I aroused, it was as after centuries of time; and I saw, almost above me and emerging from the fog, the bow of a vessel, and three triangular sails, each shrewdly lapping the other and filled with wind. Where the bow cut the water there was a great foaming and gurgling, and I seemed directly in its path. I tried to cry out, but was too exhausted. The bow plunged down, just missing me and sending a swash of water clear over my head. Then the long, black side of the vessel began slipping past, so near that I could have touched it with my hands. I tried to reach it, in a mad resolve to claw into the wood with my nails, but my arms were heavy and lifeless. Again I strove to call out, but made no sound. The stern of the vessel shot by, dropping, as it did so, into a hollow between the waves; and I caught a glimpse of a man standing at the wheel, and of another man who seemed to be doing little else than smoke a cigar. I saw the smoke issuing from his lips as he slowly turned his head and glanced out over the water in my direction. It was a careless, unpremeditated glance, one of those haphazard things men do when they have no immediate call to do anything in particular, but act because they are alive and must do something.

The danger lay in the heavy fog which blanketed the bay, and of which, as a landsman, I had little apprehension. In fact, I remember the placid exaltation with which I took up my position on the forward upper deck, directly beneath the pilot-house, and allowed the mystery of the fog to lay hold of my imagination. A fresh breeze was blowing, and for a time I was alone in the moist obscurity—yet not alone, for I was dimly conscious of the presence of the pilot, and of what I took to be the captain, in the glass house above my head. I remember thinking how comfortable it was, this division of labour which made it unnecessary for me to study fogs, winds, tides, and navigation, in order to visit my friend who lived across an arm of the sea. It was good that men should be specialists, I mused. The peculiar knowledge of the pilot and captain sufficed for many thousands of people who knew no more of the sea and navigation than I knew. On the other hand, instead of having to devote my energy to the learning of a multitude of things, I concentrated it upon a few particular things, such as, for instance, the analysis of Poe’s place in American literature—an essay of mine, by the way, in the current Atlantic. Coming aboard, as I passed through the cabin, I had noticed with greedy eyes a stout gentleman reading the Atlantic, which was open at my very essay. And there it was again, the division of labour, the special knowledge of the pilot and captain which permitted the stout gentleman to read my special knowledge on Poe while they carried him safely from Sausalito to San Francisco. A red-faced man, slamming the cabin door behind him and stumping out on the deck, interrupted my reflections, though I made a mental note of the topic for use in a projected essay which I had thought of calling “The Necessity for Freedom: A Plea for the Artist.” The red-faced man shot a glance up at the pilot-house, gazed around at the fog, stumped across the deck and back (he evidently had artificial legs), and stood still by my side, legs wide apart, and with an expression of keen enjoyment on his face. I was not wrong when I decided that his days had been spent on the sea.

“It’s nasty weather like this here that turns heads grey before their time,” he said, with a nod toward the pilot-house.

“I had not thought there was any particular strain,” I answered. “It seems as simple as A, B, C. They know the direction by compass, the distance, and the speed. I should not call it anything more than mathematical certainty.”

“Strain!” he snorted. “Simple as A, B, C! Mathematical certainty!” He seemed to brace himself up and lean backward against the air as he stared at me. “How about this here tide that’s rushin’ out through the Golden Gate?” he demanded, or bellowed, rather. “How fast is she ebbin’? What’s the drift, eh? Listen to that, will you? A bell-buoy, and we’re a-top of it! See ’em alterin’ the course!” From out of the fog came the mournful tolling of a bell, and I could see the pilot turning the wheel with great rapidity. The bell, which had seemed straight ahead, was now sounding from the side. Our own whistle was blowing hoarsely, and from time to time the sound of other whistles came to us from out of the fog.

“That’s a ferry-boat of some sort,” the new-comer said, indicating a whistle off to the right. “And there! D’ye hear that? Blown by mouth. Some scow schooner, most likely. Better watch out, Mr. Schooner-man. Ah, I thought so. Now hell’s a poppin’ for somebody!” The unseen ferry-boat was blowing blast after blast, and the mouth-blown horn was tooting in terror-stricken fashion.

“And now they’re payin’ their respects to each other and tryin’ to get clear,” the red-faced man went on, as the hurried whistling ceased. His face was shining, his eyes flashing with excitement as he translated into articulate language the speech of the horns and sirens. “That’s a steam-siren a-goin’ it over there to the left. And you hear that fellow with a frog in his throat—a steam schooner as near as I can judge, crawlin’ in from the Heads against the tide.” A shrill little whistle, piping as if gone mad, came from directly ahead and from very near at hand. Gongs sounded on the Martinez. Our paddle-wheels stopped, their pulsing beat died away, and then they started again. The shrill little whistle, like the chirping of a cricket amid the cries of great beasts, shot through the fog from more to the side and swiftly grew faint and fainter. I looked to my companion for enlightenment.

“One of them dare-devil launches,” he said. “I almost wish we’d sunk him, the little rip! They’re the cause of more trouble. And what good are they? Any jackass gets aboard one and runs it from hell to breakfast, blowin’ his whistle to beat the band and tellin’ the rest of the world to look out for him, because he’s comin’ and can’t look out for himself! Because he’s comin’! And you’ve got to look out, too! Right of way! Common decency! They don’t know the meanin’ of it!” I felt quite amused at his unwarranted choler, and while he stumped indignantly up and down I fell to dwelling upon the romance of the fog. And romantic it certainly was—the fog, like the grey shadow of infinite mystery, brooding over the whirling speck of earth; and men, mere motes of light and sparkle, cursed with an insane relish for work, riding their steeds of wood and steel through the heart of the mystery, groping their way blindly through the Unseen, and clamouring and clanging in confident speech the while their hearts are heavy with incertitude and fear. The voice of my companion brought me back to myself with a laugh. I too had been groping and floundering, the while I thought I rode clear-eyed through the mystery.

“Hello! somebody comin’ our way,” he was saying. “And d’ye hear that? He’s comin’ fast. Walking right along. Guess he don’t hear us yet. Wind’s in wrong direction.” The fresh breeze was blowing right down upon us, and I could hear the whistle plainly, off to one side and a little ahead.

“Ferry-boat?” I asked. He nodded, then added, “Or he wouldn’t be keepin’ up such a clip.” He gave a short chuckle. “They’re gettin’ anxious up there.” I glanced up. The captain had thrust his head and shoulders out of the pilot-house, and was staring intently into the fog as though by sheer force of will he could penetrate it. His face was anxious, as was the face of my companion, who had stumped over to the rail and was gazing with a like intentness in the direction of the invisible danger. Then everything happened, and with inconceivable rapidity. The fog seemed to break away as though split by a wedge, and the bow of a steamboat emerged, trailing fog-wreaths on either side like seaweed on the snout of Leviathan. I could see the pilot-house and a white-bearded man leaning partly out of it, on his elbows. He was clad in a blue uniform, and I remember noting how trim and quiet he was. His quietness, under the circumstances, was terrible. He accepted Destiny, marched hand in hand with it, and coolly measured the stroke. As he leaned there, he ran a calm and speculative eye over us, as though to determine the precise point of the collision, and took no notice whatever when our pilot, white with rage, shouted, “Now you’ve done it!” On looking back, I realize that the remark was too obvious to make rejoinder necessary.

“Grab hold of something and hang on,” the red-faced man said to me. All his bluster had gone, and he seemed to have caught the contagion of preternatural calm. “And listen to the women scream,” he said grimly—almost bitterly, I thought, as though he had been through the experience before. The vessels came together before I could follow his advice. We must have been struck squarely amidships, for I saw nothing, the strange steamboat having passed beyond my line of vision. The Martinez heeled over, sharply, and there was a crashing and rending of timber. I was thrown flat on the wet deck, and before I could scramble to my feet I heard the scream of the women. This it was, I am certain,—the most indescribable of blood-curdling sounds,—that threw me into a panic. I remembered the life-preservers stored in the cabin, but was met at the door and swept backward by a wild rush of men and women. What happened in the next few minutes I do not recollect, though I have a clear remembrance of pulling down life-preservers from the overhead racks, while the red-faced man fastened them about the bodies of an hysterical group of women. This memory is as distinct and sharp as that of any picture I have seen. It is a picture, and I can see it now,—the jagged edges of the hole in the side of the cabin, through which the grey fog swirled and eddied; the empty upholstered seats, littered with all the evidences of sudden flight, such as packages, hand satchels, umbrellas, and wraps; the stout gentleman who had been reading my essay, encased in cork and canvas, the magazine still in his hand, and asking me with monotonous insistence if I thought there was any danger; the red-faced man, stumping gallantly around on his artificial legs and buckling life-preservers on all comers; and finally, the screaming bedlam of women. This it was, the screaming of the women, that most tried my nerves. It must have tried, too, the nerves of the red-faced man, for I have another picture which will never fade from my mind. The stout gentleman is stuffing the magazine into his overcoat pocket and looking on curiously. A tangled mass of women, with drawn, white faces and open mouths, is shrieking like a chorus of lost souls; and the red-faced man, his face now purplish with wrath, and with arms extended overhead as in the act of hurling thunderbolts, is shouting, “Shut up! Oh, shut up!” I remember the scene impelled me to sudden laughter, and in the next instant I realized I was becoming hysterical myself; for these were women of my own kind, like my mother and sisters, with the fear of death upon them and unwilling to die. And I remember that the sounds they made reminded me of the squealing of pigs under the knife of the butcher, and I was struck with horror at the vividness of the analogy. These women, capable of the most sublime emotions, of the tenderest sympathies, were open-mouthed and screaming. They wanted to live, they were helpless, like rats in a trap, and they screamed. The horror of it drove me out on deck. I was feeling sick and squeamish, and sat down on a bench. In a hazy way I saw and heard men rushing and shouting as they strove to lower the boats. It was just as I had read descriptions of such scenes in books. The tackles jammed. Nothing worked. One boat lowered away with the plugs out, filled with women and children and then with water, and capsized. Another boat had been lowered by one end, and still hung in the tackle by the other end, where it had been abandoned. Nothing was to be seen of the strange steamboat which had caused the disaster, though I heard men saying that she would undoubtedly send boats to our assistance. I descended to the lower deck. The Martinez was sinking fast, for the water was very near. Numbers of the passengers were leaping overboard. Others, in the water, were clamouring to be taken aboard again. No one heeded them. A cry arose that we were sinking. I was seized by the consequent panic, and went over the side in a surge of bodies. How I went over I do not know, though I did know, and instantly, why those in the water were so desirous of getting back on the steamer. The water was cold—so cold that it was painful. The pang, as I plunged into it, was as quick and sharp as that of fire. It bit to the marrow. It was like the grip of death. I gasped with the anguish and shock of it, filling my lungs before the life-preserver popped me to the surface. The taste of the salt was strong in my mouth, and I was strangling with the acrid stuff in my throat and lungs. But it was the cold that was most distressing. I felt that I could survive but a few minutes. People were struggling and floundering in the water about me. I could hear them crying out to one another. And I heard, also, the sound of oars. Evidently the strange steamboat had lowered its boats. As the time went by I marvelled that I was still alive. I had no sensation whatever in my lower limbs, while a chilling numbness was wrapping about my heart and creeping into it. Small waves, with spiteful foaming crests, continually broke over me and into my mouth, sending me off into more strangling paroxysms. The noises grew indistinct, though I heard a final and despairing chorus of screams in the distance, and knew that the Martinez had gone down. Later,—how much later I have no knowledge,—I came to myself with a start of fear. I was alone. I could hear no calls or cries—only the sound of the waves, made weirdly hollow and reverberant by the fog. A panic in a crowd, which partakes of a sort of community of interest, is not so terrible as a panic when one is by oneself; and such a panic I now suffered. Whither was I drifting? The red-faced man had said that the tide was ebbing through the Golden Gate. Was I, then, being carried out to sea? And the life-preserver in which I floated? Was it not liable to go to pieces at any moment? I had heard of such things being made of paper and hollow rushes which quickly became saturated and lost all buoyancy. And I could not swim a stroke. And I was alone, floating, apparently, in the midst of a grey primordial vastness. I confess that a madness seized me, that I shrieked aloud as the women had shrieked, and beat the water with my numb hands. How long this lasted I have no conception, for a blankness intervened, of which I remember no more than one remembers of troubled and painful sleep. When I aroused, it was as after centuries of time; and I saw, almost above me and emerging from the fog, the bow of a vessel, and three triangular sails, each shrewdly lapping the other and filled with wind. Where the bow cut the water there was a great foaming and gurgling, and I seemed directly in its path. I tried to cry out, but was too exhausted. The bow plunged down, just missing me and sending a swash of water clear over my head. Then the long, black side of the vessel began slipping past, so near that I could have touched it with my hands. I tried to reach it, in a mad resolve to claw into the wood with my nails, but my arms were heavy and lifeless. Again I strove to call out, but made no sound. The stern of the vessel shot by, dropping, as it did so, into a hollow between the waves; and I caught a glimpse of a man standing at the wheel, and of another man who seemed to be doing little else than smoke a cigar. I saw the smoke issuing from his lips as he slowly turned his head and glanced out over the water in my direction. It was a careless, unpremeditated glance, one of those haphazard things men do when they have no immediate call to do anything in particular, but act because they are alive and must do something.

column308:
The cabin stood on the bench above the river, a squat thing of unbarked spruce logs chinked with moss, and the snow lay against its north wall to the eaves. Within, the air was close and heavy with the smell of drying socks and bacon grease and the resinous breath of the stove, which glowed a dull cherry-red along its sides and ticked and muttered to itself like a live creature. Outside, there was no sound at all. The cold had taken all sound and crushed it, as it crushed everything that lived in the land. It was the cold of the deep winter, when the sun no longer troubled to lift itself above the southern hills, and the spirit thermometer nailed by the door had shrunk its red thread down to the mark of sixty-two below and gone into hiding there.

Clem Rawlins sat on an upturned box near the stove, mending a dog-harness with a sail-needle and a length of rawhide. He was a large man, loose-jointed and deliberate, with a face weathered to the colour of old saddle-leather, and a beard in which the frost of his last trip to the woodpile still glistened and was slowly turning to water. His hands were scarred and swollen at the knuckles, yet they moved with a nicety that seemed foreign to them, drawing the rawhide through, pulling it taut, testing it, and drawing it through again. He did not look up. He had not looked up for some minutes, though he knew his wife was watching him from the bunk where she sat with her mending idle in her lap.

She was a slender woman, not yet thirty, and the North had not been able to take from her the delicacy that had been bred into her by three generations of New England gentlefolk. It had sharpened her face, and it had put a fine line at either corner of her mouth, and it had roughened the hands she was so careful to keep in her lap; but it had not touched her eyes, which were grey and steady and, at this moment, very bright.

"You are mending that harness," she said at last, "as though it were the most natural thing in the world."

"It's got to be mended," he answered. "Wheel-dog chewed through the belly-band last night. Bright's a fool for leather."

"You know what I mean, Clem."

He drew the rawhide through once more and pulled it taut. "I know what you mean."

The stove ticked. A burning stick settled with a soft crunch, and a little spurt of flame showed for an instant through a crack in the door and was gone. Somewhere outside, far down the river, a dog lifted its voice in the long, sorrowful howl of the wolf-breed, and another took it up, and another, until the whole night seemed to be filled with that ancient lament, which was old when men first crouched over fires in caves, and which was a protest against existence itself. Then it died away, and the silence came back, heavier than before.

"Sixty-two below," Edith said. "I looked at it when you came in with the wood. Sixty-two, and falling. And you mean to start in the morning."

"Before the morning. Four o'clock. Lafferty's comin' by with his team, an' we'll travel together."

"Lafferty!" There was scorn in her voice, and something sharper than scorn. "Lafferty, who froze three toes off on the Stewart last winter because he was too proud to build a fire. A fine companion for a journey of eighty miles."

"Lafferty's all right. He learned his lesson. A man don't forget a thing like that."

"No," she said, "I suppose he doesn't. He has only seven toes to remind him."

He looked up then, and there was a glint of humour in his eyes, the slow humour of the man who has lived much in silence and is not easily stirred. But it faded when he saw her face. She was not jesting. She was white about the mouth, and her hands had clasped themselves together in her lap so tightly that the knuckles stood out.

"Edie," he said, and laid the harness across his knees. "Listen to me. You heard what Johnson said, same as me. Coarse gold on Little Salmon Fork, an' the gravel runnin' a dollar to the pan on bed-rock. A dollar to the pan! I've been five years in this country, an' I've never seen the like of that, not on Bonanza, not anywhere. An' there's not twenty men know of it yet. By the end of the week there'll be two hundred, an' by spring there'll be two thousand, an' every foot of ground worth havin' will be staked from the mouth to the head of the creek. It's now or it's never. You know that."

"I know that it is sixty-two below zero."

"It's been colder. I've travelled at seventy."

"And you have told me yourself what it is like. You have told me of the men you found sitting by the trail with their backs against a tree, smiling, as if they had only stopped to rest. You told me the cold put them to sleep, and they were glad of it. You told me that, Clem, sitting on that very box."

He was silent. He took up the harness again, looked at it, and put it down.

It was the way of the man, and of all men of his kind, to meet an argument as he met a hill on the trail: to put his head down and lean his weight into it and go on, without much thinking, because the hill was there and the other side of it was where he wished to be. Thought was a luxury of soft lands and long evenings. In the North a man lived by his muscles and by a certain dumb wisdom of the body that had come down to him from far-off ancestors who had hunted the mammoth and the cave-bear, and who had survived because they did not stop to reason why. Clem Rawlins did not know this. He knew only that the creek was there, and the gold was in the creek, and that something in him strained toward it as a dog strains toward the meat-cache. But he knew, too, dimly, that there was another thing in the cabin with him, a thing not to be met head-down, and it troubled him.

"I'll be careful," he said.

"Careful!" She laughed, a short, hard little laugh that had no mirth in it. "Every man who ever died on the trail meant to be careful. The land does not care how careful you mean to be. You taught me that also."

"Then what d'you want me to do?" His voice rose, not in anger yet, but in the bewilderment of a strong man who finds his strength of no use to him. "Sit here an' let the others take it? Sit here an' watch Olsen an' the Maloney boys come back in the spring with their pokes full, an' me with nothin' but a woodpile to show for the winter? We've been livin' on beans an' sour-dough for two years, Edie. You've been wearin' that same dress since the ice went out. Look at your hands."

She did not look at her hands. She looked at him.

"I have not complained of my hands," she said quietly.

"No. You ain't complained. That's just it." He stood up, abruptly, and the box went over behind him with a clatter. He did not stoop to right it. The cabin was too small for him when he stood, and his head came within a few inches of the ridge-pole, from which hung a frozen ham and a bundle of candles and a pair of snowshoes, and the shadows of these things swung across the log walls as he moved. "You ain't never complained. You came into this country with me when you could've stayed back home an' married some lawyer with a brick house an' a buggy. You came in over the Chilcoot with a pack on your back like a squaw, an' you ain't complained once. An' what've I given you for it? A shack an' a stove an' a winter that never ends. I want to give you somethin' better, an' I've got a chance to do it, the first real chance, an' you won't let me take it."

"I have not said I won't let you."

"You're sayin' it now. With your eyes you're sayin' it."

She rose also, and stood facing him across the narrow space between the bunk and the stove. She was a full head shorter than he, and slight, and he could have lifted her with one arm; yet for that moment it seemed to him that she was the larger of the two, and he was the one who must look up.

"Then hear what I say with my mouth," she said. "I did not come into this country for gold. I did not climb the Chilcoot because I wanted a brick house or a buggy. I had a brick house. I had three of them, if you will remember, and I left them, and my mother has not written to me since. I came because I wanted you, Clem, and because I believed that wherever you were, I should be content. And I have been content. I have been content with beans and sour-dough and this one dress, and I would be content with them for twenty years more. But I will not be content with a widow's weeds. I will not sit in this cabin through the rest of the winter, listening for a team that will not come, and then go out in the spring with the first boat and tell your sister that you died for a dollar to the pan."

He stared at her. The colour had come up into her face now, two red spots high on the cheekbones, and her breath came quickly, as though she had been running.

"That's woman's talk," he said, and knew as he said it that it was the wrong thing.

"Yes," she said. "It is woman's talk. And the creek, and the gold, and the cold, and the men who sit down by the trail and smile, that is man's talk, I suppose. Very well. I have listened to man's talk for five years. I have learned it. Shall I talk it to you? Shall I tell you about the weight of a full pack on a fourteen-mile portage, or the way the ice sounds before it goes out from under a sled? I know these things now. I know them as well as you. But you have never troubled to learn my talk, Clem. You have never asked."

The harness had slipped from where he had laid it and fallen to the floor, and he looked down at it as though it belonged to someone else. A queer thing was happening within him. It was as though a door he had never known existed had swung open in some back room of his being, and a cold draught was blowing through it, and he could not tell where the draught came from nor how to shut it out. He had faced men with knives and guns. He had faced a grizzly in the Pelly country with nothing in his hand but an axe. He had faced the White Silence itself, alone, with his matches gone and his feet freezing, and had come through, because the thing to be done was plain and he had done it. But here there was nothing plain. Here was only this woman, whom he loved with a love that was half worship and half bewilderment, and who stood before him now like a stranger.

"I'm askin' now," he said slowly. "What is it you want, Edie?"

For a long moment she did not answer. The fire had burned low, and the stove ceased its ticking, and the cold began to creep in at the base of the door, a thin white rime forming on the inner side of the threshold log. Then she turned away from him and sat down again on the edge of the bunk, and when she spoke, her voice was very tired.

"I want you to want something else," she said. "Something besides the creek. Something besides the next creek after that, and the one after that. Do you think I do not know you? If you find gold on Little Salmon Fork, will you be done? Will you take me Outside and buy me the brick house? You will not. You will hear of another strike on another creek, and you will go to it, and another after that, until one winter the land takes you. It is not the gold you want. I have watched you. It is the going. It is the trail and the cold and the danger. You love them more than you love any woman. You cannot help it, and I do not think I blame you for it. But I cannot make myself love them too, and I am tired, Clem, I am so tired of waiting to lose you."

He did not answer at once, for there was no answer. She had named the thing he had never named to himself, and he recognized it as a man recognizes his own face in a glass after long absence, with a little shock of strangeness. It was true. He had told himself it was the gold. He had told her it was the gold. But in the nights on the trail, crouched over his fire with the dogs curled in the snow about him and the aurora flaring overhead in great silent sheets of green and rose, he had known a fierce and solitary joy that had nothing to do with gold. It was the joy of the living thing that pits itself against the vast indifference and is not destroyed. It was the joy of the wolf that runs at the head of the pack in the moonlight. It was a joy older than speech, and it was in his blood, and he could no more cast it out than he could cast out the blood itself.

He righted the box and sat down on it heavily, with his great scarred hands hanging between his knees.

"I can't help what I am," he said.

"I know," she answered. "I have said I know."

"If I don't go, I'll be thinkin' about it all winter. I'll be sittin' here hatin' myself. Hatin' you, maybe, a little. I don't want that."

"Nor do I."

"Then what're we to do?"

She looked at him then, and something had changed in her face. The colour had gone out of it again, and the softness with it, and what remained was a hardness he had seen before only in the faces of men who had wintered on the Arctic coast and come back. It was the face the North gives to those who have measured themselves against it and have not been broken, and it sat strangely on her delicate features, and it frightened him more than her anger had.

"You will go," she said. "I knew from the first that you would go. I think I knew when Johnson came to the door. I only wanted you to know that I knew, and that I had not deceived myself. That is all. That was all I wanted."

"Edie—"

"No. Let me finish." She drew a breath. "You will go, and I will pack your grub tonight, because Lafferty will not think of it and you will forget the tea. And I will look at the thermometer every hour while you are gone, and I will not sleep, and I will not complain. And when you come back, if you come back, I will be here. But I will not pretend any longer that I am content, and I will not let you pretend that it is for me you go. It is not for me. Say it, Clem. Say that it is not for me."

The silence stretched between them. Outside, very faintly, there came a sound like a pistol-shot, and then another, as the great spruce trees on the hillside split their hearts open in the frost. Clem lifted his head and listened to it, and then he looked at his wife, and his lips moved twice before the words would come.

"It ain't for you," he said.

She nodded, once, as though he had confirmed a figure in an account-book. Then she rose and went to the cache-shelf by the door, and began to take down the sacks of flour and beans and the slab of bacon wrapped in burlap, and to lay them out upon the table in a neat row. Her movements were quick and sure. She did not look at him. He watched her for a while, the lamplight falling across her bent head and her thin, busy hands; and he thought that he had never seen anything so lonely in all his life, not on the barrens of the Mackenzie, not in the long night of the Arctic coast, as this woman measuring out tea into a canvas bag at sixty-two below.

He bent and picked up the harness from the floor. The rawhide was still threaded through the needle. He drew it through once more, and pulled it taut, and tested it. It held. Everything held, in this country, until the moment it did not.

At four o'clock Lafferty's team came up the bench, the dogs wreathed in their own frozen breath, and Lafferty's voice cried out hoarsely in the darkness. Clem went out with his pack and his sled. The door closed behind him, and the cold that had entered with its opening hung for a long time in the cabin, a pale mist along the floor, before the stove could eat it up. Edith stood by the window, where the frost had grown thick as a man's thumb upon the glass, and she scraped a little hole in it with her fingernail and put her eye to the hole. She could see nothing. She could hear, for a little while, the whine of the runners and the yelping of the dogs; and then she could not hear them; and then there was nothing in all the world but the silence, and the ticking of the stove, and the red thread of the thermometer creeping downward, notch by notch, toward the bottom of the glass.

Here is an excerpt of Jack London's writing, to show you their style:

Not but that I was afloat in a safe craft, for the Martinez was a new ferry-steamer, making her fourth or fifth trip on the run between Sausalito and San Francisco. The danger lay in the heavy fog which blanketed the bay, and of which, as a landsman, I had little apprehension. In fact, I remember the placid exaltation with which I took up my position on the forward upper deck, directly beneath the pilot-house, and allowed the mystery of the fog to lay hold of my imagination. And I was alone, floating, apparently, in the midst of a grey primordial vastness. When I aroused, it was as after centuries of time; and I saw, almost above me and emerging from the fog, the bow of a vessel, and three triangular sails, each shrewdly lapping the other and filled with wind. Where the bow cut the water there was a great foaming and gurgling, and I seemed directly in its path. I tried to cry out, but was too exhausted. The bow plunged down, just missing me and sending a swash of water clear over my head. Then the long, black side of the vessel began slipping past, so near that I could have touched it with my hands. I tried to reach it, in a mad resolve to claw into the wood with my nails, but my arms were heavy and lifeless. Again I strove to call out, but made no sound. I saw the smoke issuing from his lips as he slowly turned his head and glanced out over the water in my direction. The store of Martin Dorsey stood on Broadway, three doors above the corner, and it was a good store, as stores went in Oakland in those days. It sold nails by the keg and rope by the coil, lamp-chimneys and stove-blacking, axes, saws, and the hundred small iron necessities by which men hold their houses together against the weather. Martin Dorsey had built it up himself, from nothing, by patience and by a careful counting of pennies. He was thirty-four years old, and he had begun to grow a little heavy about the middle, and a little careful about the stairs. He wore a white collar six days in the week, and on the seventh he wore a stiffer one and went to church with his wife and his two small daughters. He was, in short, a man who had arrived. He had made his peace with the world, and the world, in its indifferent fashion, had made its peace with him.

It was late in the afternoon of a grey October day, and he was standing behind the counter with a pencil behind his ear, checking an invoice of carriage-bolts, when the door opened and a man came in out of the drizzle. Martin glanced up with the ready smile of the shopkeeper, and then the smile went stiff upon his face, and the pencil slipped from his fingers and rolled across the counter and fell to the floor.

The man who had entered was lean. That was the first thing, and it was the thing that remained afterward. He was lean as a wolf is lean at the end of winter, with the leanness that is not hunger merely but a sort of distillation, as though all that was soft and needless had been boiled out of him and only the essential fibre left. His face was burned a deep and permanent brown, and across the left cheek, from the bone to the corner of the jaw, ran a white seam of old scar. His eyes were grey and very pale against the brown of his skin, and they had in them a curious quality of distance, as of eyes long accustomed to looking at far things across white spaces. He wore a suit of good cloth that sat upon him awkwardly, like harness upon an animal that has never known harness; and he stood just inside the door, his feet planted wide, and looked at Martin Dorsey and grinned.

"Hello, Mart," he said.

"Jim," said Martin. "Jim Calloway. Good God."

He came around the end of the counter, and the two men gripped hands. Martin felt the hand that closed upon his own, and felt also that something was wrong with it. He looked down. The third and fourth fingers were gone at the second joint, and the stumps were puckered and shiny.

"Frost," said Jim Calloway, following his glance. "Up on the Stewart, in the winter of 'ninety-nine. Sixty-eight below, and a mitten I'd lost through the ice. I was lucky to save the rest. There was a Swede with me lost both feet." He laughed shortly, and the laugh had no mirth in it, nor any bitterness either. It was merely a statement, the way a man might laugh in remarking upon the price of flour.

"Nine years," said Martin. "Nine years, Jim, and never a word. Your mother—"

"I know about my mother," the other said quietly. "I got the letter. It was fourteen months old when I got it. It came in over the ice with the mail-carrier to Forty Mile, and he'd had it in his pack since the fall before." He paused, and the pale eyes went past Martin to the window, where the rain was streaking the glass. "There wasn't anything to be done about it, Mart. There wasn't anything a man could do."

Martin Dorsey, who was a kindly man and an emotional one, felt something rise in his throat; but his cousin's face forbade it, and he swallowed it down. He turned and called to the boy who swept out the back room, and told him to mind the store; and then he took his hat and his coat from the peg, and the two of them went out together into the drizzle.

They did not discuss where they would go. It was not necessary. Their feet carried them down Broadway and across the tracks and on toward the water, by the same streets they had run as boys, barefooted and ragged, when the world was young and every day was a battle to be fought and won. The smell of the estuary came up to meet them, the old smell of mud-flats and tar and rotting piles and the salt breath of the tide; and Martin Dorsey, who had not walked this way in years, felt it go into him like strong drink.

The saloon stood where it had always stood, at the foot of the wharf, a crazy little shack of weathered boards that leaned toward the water as if it were tired of standing. Inside, it was dim and smelled of stale beer and sawdust and wet wool. A pair of longshoremen were drinking at the bar, and in the corner an old man with a white beard slept with his head upon his arms. The barkeeper was a stranger. The old one, Jim said, would be dead; and he spoke it with the same flat finality with which he had spoken of the Swede's feet.

They took a table by the window, where they could see the grey water and the grey masts of the scow schooners lying at the wharf, and Jim Calloway ordered whiskey, and drank his at a gulp, and ordered again.

"You've done well, Mart," he said, looking across at his cousin with those far-seeing eyes. "I saw the sign. 'M. Dorsey, Hardware.' It's a good sign. Gold letters. And you've put on flesh."

Martin laughed, a little uncomfortably, and set his hands upon his stomach. "Annie feeds me," he said. "I married, Jim. Annie Holt—you'll remember her, she lived on Fifth Street, by the gas-works. We've two girls. Six and four. The older one reads already." He spoke with a sudden shy pride, as a man speaks of the one thing in his life that he is sure of. "And the store pays. It pays well. I've a house on Myrtle Street, with a garden, and a man to tend it on Saturdays."

"That's good," said Jim Calloway. "That's good, Mart." And he said it as if he meant it, and he did mean it; and yet there was something in the saying of it that made Martin Dorsey look at him sharply, for he had the feeling that his cousin was looking at him from a great way off, from across some wide and frozen distance, as one might look at a lighted window from the outer dark.

"And you?" said Martin. "Tell me about yourself. They said you'd struck it. Old Cassidy, who came down in 'ninety-nine, said you had a claim on Bonanza and were taking out a thousand a day."

Jim Calloway turned his glass slowly around and around upon the wet table. "Cassidy was a liar," he said. "But not by much. I struck it. I struck it twice. The first time I lost it, and the second time I kept it. I've got money in the bank in Seattle, Mart, more than this whole street would sell for. I could buy your store and never notice the hole it made."

He said it simply, without boasting, and then he fell silent, and his eyes went out the window to the water.

Now Martin Dorsey had always been the slower of the two. As boys it was Jim who had led, and Martin who followed; Jim who had first slipped the moorings of a borrowed skiff and gone out across the estuary in the dark, to where the oyster-beds lay on the flats and the fish patrol prowled with its lanterns; Jim who had first shipped before the mast, at sixteen, on a sealing schooner bound for the Japan coast; Jim who had first gone north, in the great stampede, when the whole Pacific seaboard went mad with the word of gold. Martin had followed him in most things, but he had not followed him north. He had been afraid. He knew it, and had always known it, and the knowledge had lain in him all these years like a small stone in a shoe, that a man grows used to and forgets until some chance pressure brings it back. It came back now, sitting across the table from this lean and scarred stranger who was his cousin, and he felt again the old shame, and with it a stir of something else, something hot and restless that he had thought long dead.

"Tell me about it," he said. "Tell me all of it, Jim."

And Jim Calloway told him.

He told it badly at first, haltingly, as men do who have lived long alone and have lost the habit of speech. But the whiskey loosened him, and the old familiar smell of the estuary, and the face of his cousin across the table; and presently the words came, and the dingy saloon fell away, and Martin Dorsey saw the North.

He saw the Chilkoot Pass in the winter of 'ninety-seven, a black line of men crawling up the white face of the mountain like ants upon a sugar-loaf, bent double beneath their packs, falling and rising and falling again, and some of them not rising. He saw the lakes, and the boats built of green lumber whipsawed from the forest, and the White Horse Rapids where the boats went down and the men in them. He saw the long winter night, when the sun did not rise at all, but only a pale glow along the southern sky at noon, and the cold came down out of the stars like a thing alive and predatory, and the trees cracked like rifle-shots in the frost. He saw men go mad from the silence of it, and men go mad from scurvy and from loneliness and from gold. He saw a man shot dead across a card-table in Dawson, over a dispute of eleven dollars, and nobody so much as stopping the game.

"And there was Kearney," Jim said, and stopped.

"Who was Kearney?"

"My partner. Big Irishman out of Butte. Hard-rock miner. He could carry two hundred pounds up the Pass and come down singing." Jim Calloway poured himself another drink and did not drink it. "We were coming out from the Stewart, the two of us, in the spring of nineteen-hundred, with the dogs. The ice was going out. We knew it was going, but we had to cross. We'd been eating dog for a week. He went through about fifty yards from the shore, him and the sled and four of the dogs. I got a pole to him. I had him by the hand. I had him by the hand, Mart, and the current took him out from under the ice, and I couldn't hold him. It was the hand with the fingers gone, you see. I couldn't get the grip."

He sat looking at the stumps of his fingers, turning them a little in the grey light from the window, as though they belonged to someone else and he were curious about them.

"That's how it is up there," he said at last. "It don't care. That's the thing you learn first, and you learn it hard. The cold don't care, and the river don't care, and the long dark don't care. A man's nothing. He's a little bit of warm meat moving across the snow, and the whole country's just waiting for him to stop moving. And the strong ones last a while, and the weak ones don't, and in the end they all go down. Kearney was the strongest man I ever knew. It didn't make any difference."

Martin Dorsey sat very still. Outside, the tide was setting in, and he could hear it lapping and sucking among the piles beneath the floor. A scow schooner was coming up the estuary under a patched mainsail, and a man at her tiller was singing something in a hoarse, tuneless voice. It came to Martin, sitting there, that all his life he had been safe; that he had built walls about himself, of brick and timber and nails by the keg and invoices of carriage-bolts, and had lived within the walls and called it living; and that all the while, outside, there had been this other thing, this vast and pitiless indifference which his cousin had looked upon face to face, and which had taken the fingers from his hand and the man from his grip and had put into his eyes that pale, far, unforgetting look.

"I've never done anything," Martin said suddenly. His voice surprised him. It was harsher than he meant. "I've never done one damned thing, Jim. I sell nails."

Jim Calloway looked at him for a long moment, and then he laughed, and this time there was something warm in the laugh, the first warmth Martin had heard in him.

"You poor fool," he said. "You poor, blind fool. Do you know what I thought about, Mart, all those winters? Lying in a cabin on the Stewart with the frost an inch thick on the inside of the door, and the candle froze so hard it wouldn't light, and Kearney snoring in the other bunk? I thought about this." He swept his maimed hand about him, at the dingy saloon, at the grey estuary, at the rain. "I thought about the smell of the mud-flats at low tide. I thought about your mother's kitchen on Sunday, and the pies on the window-sill. I thought about a house with a garden and a woman in it and children. I thought about it till I near went crazy with it. And here you've had it all along, and you sit there and tell me you've never done anything."

"But you've lived," said Martin. "You've lived, Jim. You've been out there where it's real."

"Real!" The other snorted, and leaned back in his chair. "It's all real, man. The cold's real, sure. But so's your two girls. So's the little one that reads. You think I wouldn't trade every ounce of dust in Seattle for one of 'em?" He stopped, and his face hardened, and the warmth went out of him as quickly as it had come. "No," he said slowly. "No, that ain't true either. I wouldn't trade. That's the hell of it. I couldn't if I wanted. I've gone too far out. A man gets out there in the white and the silence, and he gets the taste of it, and after that he's spoiled for anything else. I've been down here two weeks, Mart. Two weeks in a hotel with a feather bed and a bath-tub and a nigger to black my boots. And I can't sleep. The bed's too soft, and the walls are too close, and there's too much noise in the streets, and the people are all soft and white and talking about nothing. I lie awake at night and listen for the wolves."

He laughed again, short and hard. "There's a ship sails Thursday for Nome. I've got passage on her."

They sat for a while without speaking. The old man in the corner woke, and lifted his head and looked about him with bleared eyes, and put it down again. The longshoremen paid for their drinks and went out, and the door banged behind them, and a gust of wet wind came in and stirred the sawdust on the floor.

It was dusk when they left the saloon. The rain had stopped, and a wind had come up out of the west, out of the Golden Gate and the open sea beyond, and it was tearing the clouds into long grey rags and driving them inland over the hills. The two men walked down the wharf and along the waterfront, not speaking, past the coal-bunkers and the lumber-yards and the shabby boarding-houses where the sailors slept, until they came to the place where the old boatyard had been. The boatyard was gone. There was a brickyard in its place, and a fence of new boards. But beyond the fence, where the marsh began, lying over on her side in the mud with the tide creeping in about her, was the hulk of a sloop.

Jim Calloway stopped and stared, and then he gripped his cousin's arm with his maimed hand.

"It's her," he said. "Mart, by God, it's the Sea Swallow."

And so it was. Her mast was gone, and her deck was stove, and the green weed hung from her planking like the hair of a drowned woman; but the lines of her were the same, the long clean sheer of her that they had loved as boys, when they had pooled their stolen earnings and bought her from a drunken Greek for forty dollars and gone out in her across the bay in the teeth of the west wind, reefed down to the last point and the water boiling white along her lee rail, and the two of them in the cockpit soaked to the skin and yelling like savages for the sheer joy of being alive.

They stood side by side and looked at her, and the tide crept higher about her rotting ribs, and the wind came hard and cold from the sea.

"She was a good boat," Martin Dorsey said at last, and his voice was not steady.

"She was the best," said Jim Calloway.

And then, because there was nothing more to be said, and because both of them understood it, they turned and walked back toward the lights of the town. At the corner of Broadway they shook hands, and Martin felt again the strange, maimed grip, and held it a moment longer than he needed to.

"You'll come to supper," he said. "Before Thursday. Annie will want to see you. And the girls."

"I'll come," said Jim Calloway. But they both knew that he would not.

Martin Dorsey walked home to Myrtle Street through the windy dark. The lamps were lit in the house, and through the front window he could see his wife moving about the dining-room, setting the table, and the small fair head of his elder daughter bent over a book beneath the lamp. He stood at the gate a long time, looking in. Behind him, far off across the roofs of the town, he could hear the moaning of the west wind and, fainter still, the deep and hollow note of a steamer's whistle going out upon the tide toward the open sea. Something stirred in him, something old and wild and half-forgotten, that tugged at him like the ebb tugging at a moored boat. He stood and felt it pull, and his hands gripped the cold iron of the gate.

Then his daughter looked up from her book and saw him through the glass, and her face broke into light, and she waved. And Martin Dorsey opened the gate and went up the walk and into the warm house, and shut the door behind him upon the wind and the dark and the far crying of the whistle.

Here is an excerpt of Jack London's writing, to show you their style:

Not but that I was afloat in a safe craft, for the Martinez was a new ferry-steamer, making her fourth or fifth trip on the run between Sausalito and San Francisco. The danger lay in the heavy fog which blanketed the bay, and of which, as a landsman, I had little apprehension. In fact, I remember the placid exaltation with which I took up my position on the forward upper deck, directly beneath the pilot-house, and allowed the mystery of the fog to lay hold of my imagination. A fresh breeze was blowing, and for a time I was alone in the moist obscurity—yet not alone, for I was dimly conscious of the presence of the pilot, and of what I took to be the captain, in the glass house above my head. I remember thinking how comfortable it was, this division of labour which made it unnecessary for me to study fogs, winds, tides, and navigation, in order to visit my friend who lived across an arm of the sea. It was good that men should be specialists, I mused. The peculiar knowledge of the pilot and captain sufficed for many thousands of people who knew no more of the sea and navigation than I knew. On the other hand, instead of having to devote my energy to the learning of a multitude of things, I concentrated it upon a few particular things, such as, for instance, the analysis of Poe’s place in American literature—an essay of mine, by the way, in the current Atlantic. Coming aboard, as I passed through the cabin, I had noticed with greedy eyes a stout gentleman reading the Atlantic, which was open at my very essay. And there it was again, the division of labour, the special knowledge of the pilot and captain which permitted the stout gentleman to read my special knowledge on Poe while they carried him safely from Sausalito to San Francisco. A red-faced man, slamming the cabin door behind him and stumping out on the deck, interrupted my reflections, though I made a mental note of the topic for use in a projected essay which I had thought of calling “The Necessity for Freedom: A Plea for the Artist.” The red-faced man shot a glance up at the pilot-house, gazed around at the fog, stumped across the deck and back (he evidently had artificial legs), and stood still by my side, legs wide apart, and with an expression of keen enjoyment on his face. I was not wrong when I decided that his days had been spent on the sea.

“It’s nasty weather like this here that turns heads grey before their time,” he said, with a nod toward the pilot-house.

“I had not thought there was any particular strain,” I answered. “It seems as simple as A, B, C. They know the direction by compass, the distance, and the speed. I should not call it anything more than mathematical certainty.”

“Strain!” he snorted. “Simple as A, B, C! Mathematical certainty!” He seemed to brace himself up and lean backward against the air as he stared at me. “How about this here tide that’s rushin’ out through the Golden Gate?” he demanded, or bellowed, rather. “How fast is she ebbin’? What’s the drift, eh? Listen to that, will you? A bell-buoy, and we’re a-top of it! See ’em alterin’ the course!” From out of the fog came the mournful tolling of a bell, and I could see the pilot turning the wheel with great rapidity. The bell, which had seemed straight ahead, was now sounding from the side. Our own whistle was blowing hoarsely, and from time to time the sound of other whistles came to us from out of the fog.

“That’s a ferry-boat of some sort,” the new-comer said, indicating a whistle off to the right. “And there! D’ye hear that? Blown by mouth. Some scow schooner, most likely. Better watch out, Mr. Schooner-man. Ah, I thought so. Now hell’s a poppin’ for somebody!” The unseen ferry-boat was blowing blast after blast, and the mouth-blown horn was tooting in terror-stricken fashion.

“And now they’re payin’ their respects to each other and tryin’ to get clear,” the red-faced man went on, as the hurried whistling ceased. His face was shining, his eyes flashing with excitement as he translated into articulate language the speech of the horns and sirens. “That’s a steam-siren a-goin’ it over there to the left. And you hear that fellow with a frog in his throat—a steam schooner as near as I can judge, crawlin’ in from the Heads against the tide.” A shrill little whistle, piping as if gone mad, came from directly ahead and from very near at hand. Gongs sounded on the Martinez. Our paddle-wheels stopped, their pulsing beat died away, and then they started again. The shrill little whistle, like the chirping of a cricket amid the cries of great beasts, shot through the fog from more to the side and swiftly grew faint and fainter. I looked to my companion for enlightenment.

“One of them dare-devil launches,” he said. “I almost wish we’d sunk him, the little rip! They’re the cause of more trouble. And what good are they? Any jackass gets aboard one and runs it from hell to breakfast, blowin’ his whistle to beat the band and tellin’ the rest of the world to look out for him, because he’s comin’ and can’t look out for himself! Because he’s comin’! And you’ve got to look out, too! Right of way! Common decency! They don’t know the meanin’ of it!” I felt quite amused at his unwarranted choler, and while he stumped indignantly up and down I fell to dwelling upon the romance of the fog. And romantic it certainly was—the fog, like the grey shadow of infinite mystery, brooding over the whirling speck of earth; and men, mere motes of light and sparkle, cursed with an insane relish for work, riding their steeds of wood and steel through the heart of the mystery, groping their way blindly through the Unseen, and clamouring and clanging in confident speech the while their hearts are heavy with incertitude and fear. The voice of my companion brought me back to myself with a laugh. I too had been groping and floundering, the while I thought I rode clear-eyed through the mystery.

“Hello! somebody comin’ our way,” he was saying. “And d’ye hear that? He’s comin’ fast. Walking right along. Guess he don’t hear us yet. Wind’s in wrong direction.” The fresh breeze was blowing right down upon us, and I could hear the whistle plainly, off to one side and a little ahead.

“Ferry-boat?” I asked. He nodded, then added, “Or he wouldn’t be keepin’ up such a clip.” He gave a short chuckle. “They’re gettin’ anxious up there.” I glanced up. The captain had thrust his head and shoulders out of the pilot-house, and was staring intently into the fog as though by sheer force of will he could penetrate it. His face was anxious, as was the face of my companion, who had stumped over to the rail and was gazing with a like intentness in the direction of the invisible danger. Then everything happened, and with inconceivable rapidity. The fog seemed to break away as though split by a wedge, and the bow of a steamboat emerged, trailing fog-wreaths on either side like seaweed on the snout of Leviathan. I could see the pilot-house and a white-bearded man leaning partly out of it, on his elbows. He was clad in a blue uniform, and I remember noting how trim and quiet he was. His quietness, under the circumstances, was terrible. He accepted Destiny, marched hand in hand with it, and coolly measured the stroke. As he leaned there, he ran a calm and speculative eye over us, as though to determine the precise point of the collision, and took no notice whatever when our pilot, white with rage, shouted, “Now you’ve done it!” On looking back, I realize that the remark was too obvious to make rejoinder necessary.

“Grab hold of something and hang on,” the red-faced man said to me. All his bluster had gone, and he seemed to have caught the contagion of preternatural calm. “And listen to the women scream,” he said grimly—almost bitterly, I thought, as though he had been through the experience before. The vessels came together before I could follow his advice. We must have been struck squarely amidships, for I saw nothing, the strange steamboat having passed beyond my line of vision. The Martinez heeled over, sharply, and there was a crashing and rending of timber. I was thrown flat on the wet deck, and before I could scramble to my feet I heard the scream of the women. This it was, I am certain,—the most indescribable of blood-curdling sounds,—that threw me into a panic. I remembered the life-preservers stored in the cabin, but was met at the door and swept backward by a wild rush of men and women. What happened in the next few minutes I do not recollect, though I have a clear remembrance of pulling down life-preservers from the overhead racks, while the red-faced man fastened them about the bodies of an hysterical group of women. This memory is as distinct and sharp as that of any picture I have seen. It is a picture, and I can see it now,—the jagged edges of the hole in the side of the cabin, through which the grey fog swirled and eddied; the empty upholstered seats, littered with all the evidences of sudden flight, such as packages, hand satchels, umbrellas, and wraps; the stout gentleman who had been reading my essay, encased in cork and canvas, the magazine still in his hand, and asking me with monotonous insistence if I thought there was any danger; the red-faced man, stumping gallantly around on his artificial legs and buckling life-preservers on all comers; and finally, the screaming bedlam of women. This it was, the screaming of the women, that most tried my nerves. It must have tried, too, the nerves of the red-faced man, for I have another picture which will never fade from my mind. The stout gentleman is stuffing the magazine into his overcoat pocket and looking on curiously. A tangled mass of women, with drawn, white faces and open mouths, is shrieking like a chorus of lost souls; and the red-faced man, his face now purplish with wrath, and with arms extended overhead as in the act of hurling thunderbolts, is shouting, “Shut up! Oh, shut up!” I remember the scene impelled me to sudden laughter, and in the next instant I realized I was becoming hysterical myself; for these were women of my own kind, like my mother and sisters, with the fear of death upon them and unwilling to die. And I remember that the sounds they made reminded me of the squealing of pigs under the knife of the butcher, and I was struck with horror at the vividness of the analogy. These women, capable of the most sublime emotions, of the tenderest sympathies, were open-mouthed and screaming. They wanted to live, they were helpless, like rats in a trap, and they screamed. The horror of it drove me out on deck. I was feeling sick and squeamish, and sat down on a bench. In a hazy way I saw and heard men rushing and shouting as they strove to lower the boats. It was just as I had read descriptions of such scenes in books. The tackles jammed. Nothing worked. One boat lowered away with the plugs out, filled with women and children and then with water, and capsized. Another boat had been lowered by one end, and still hung in the tackle by the other end, where it had been abandoned. Nothing was to be seen of the strange steamboat which had caused the disaster, though I heard men saying that she would undoubtedly send boats to our assistance. I descended to the lower deck. The Martinez was sinking fast, for the water was very near. Numbers of the passengers were leaping overboard. Others, in the water, were clamouring to be taken aboard again. No one heeded them. A cry arose that we were sinking. I was seized by the consequent panic, and went over the side in a surge of bodies. How I went over I do not know, though I did know, and instantly, why those in the water were so desirous of getting back on the steamer. The water was cold—so cold that it was painful. The pang, as I plunged into it, was as quick and sharp as that of fire. It bit to the marrow. It was like the grip of death. I gasped with the anguish and shock of it, filling my lungs before the life-preserver popped me to the surface. The taste of the salt was strong in my mouth, and I was strangling with the acrid stuff in my throat and lungs. But it was the cold that was most distressing. I felt that I could survive but a few minutes. People were struggling and floundering in the water about me. I could hear them crying out to one another. And I heard, also, the sound of oars. Evidently the strange steamboat had lowered its boats. As the time went by I marvelled that I was still alive. I had no sensation whatever in my lower limbs, while a chilling numbness was wrapping about my heart and creeping into it. Small waves, with spiteful foaming crests, continually broke over me and into my mouth, sending me off into more strangling paroxysms. The noises grew indistinct, though I heard a final and despairing chorus of screams in the distance, and knew that the Martinez had gone down. Later,—how much later I have no knowledge,—I came to myself with a start of fear. I was alone. I could hear no calls or cries—only the sound of the waves, made weirdly hollow and reverberant by the fog. A panic in a crowd, which partakes of a sort of community of interest, is not so terrible as a panic when one is by oneself; and such a panic I now suffered. Whither was I drifting? The red-faced man had said that the tide was ebbing through the Golden Gate. Was I, then, being carried out to sea? And the life-preserver in which I floated? Was it not liable to go to pieces at any moment? I had heard of such things being made of paper and hollow rushes which quickly became saturated and lost all buoyancy. And I could not swim a stroke. And I was alone, floating, apparently, in the midst of a grey primordial vastness. I confess that a madness seized me, that I shrieked aloud as the women had shrieked, and beat the water with my numb hands. How long this lasted I have no conception, for a blankness intervened, of which I remember no more than one remembers of troubled and painful sleep. When I aroused, it was as after centuries of time; and I saw, almost above me and emerging from the fog, the bow of a vessel, and three triangular sails, each shrewdly lapping the other and filled with wind. Where the bow cut the water there was a great foaming and gurgling, and I seemed directly in its path. I tried to cry out, but was too exhausted. The bow plunged down, just missing me and sending a swash of water clear over my head. Then the long, black side of the vessel began slipping past, so near that I could have touched it with my hands. I tried to reach it, in a mad resolve to claw into the wood with my nails, but my arms were heavy and lifeless. Again I strove to call out, but made no sound. The stern of the vessel shot by, dropping, as it did so, into a hollow between the waves; and I caught a glimpse of a man standing at the wheel, and of another man who seemed to be doing little else than smoke a cigar. I saw the smoke issuing from his lips as he slowly turned his head and glanced out over the water in my direction. It was a careless, unpremeditated glance, one of those haphazard things men do when they have no immediate call to do anything in particular, but act because they are alive and must do something.
