The whistle at the Bessemer mill had blown for the change of shift at six o'clock, and it was nearly half-past seven before Janos Halasz came up the hill to the row of company houses where he lived. He was not drunk, as his wife had half feared he might be, for it was a Saturday, and there were eleven saloons between the mill gate and the foot of Shanty Hill, each of them lit up and roaring like a furnace. But he walked with his head down and his hands thrust deep into the pockets of his coat, and when he came in at the door he did not look at her, nor at the baby who lay on the bed in the corner, but went and sat down upon the box by the stove and stared at the floor.

Erzsi had his supper waiting for him. It was a pot of cabbage soup with a piece of pork in it the size of a man's two fingers, and a loaf of the gray bread that came from the company store at six cents. She had been keeping it warm for an hour, and the cabbage had gone soft and stringy, and the smell of it filled the room. The room was perhaps ten feet by twelve, and it served them as kitchen and parlor and bedroom all at once. Behind a curtain made of two flour sacks sewn together there was another room, smaller still, and in this slept the two boarders, Ferenc and old Mihaly, who paid them three dollars a week apiece and without whom the family could not have lived at all. The boarders were not at home tonight, it being Saturday. They would come in at two or three in the morning, and one of them would be sick on the step, as he had been last Saturday and the Saturday before that; and Erzsi would lie awake listening to him and thinking about the rent.

The rent was eleven dollars a month. It was taken out of Janos's pay by the company, before ever he saw it, and so was the bill at the company store, and so was the dollar a month for the company doctor, who came when he pleased and who had not come at all when the baby was born. There were many people in the outside world who believed that the steel workers of the Monongahela valley were well paid—had not the newspapers said so, and had not the president of the corporation himself declared, at a banquet in New York where the terrapin had cost four dollars a plate, that the American workingman was the most prosperous in the world? Janos Halasz earned two dollars and ten cents for a turn of twelve hours, and he worked seven days in the week, and every second Sunday he worked the "long turn" of twenty-four hours, when the shifts were changed about. When everything had been deducted that the company chose to deduct, there was left to him in a good month perhaps thirty dollars, and with this he had to feed and clothe his wife and himself and his two children, and to send something back to his old mother in the village beyond Kassa, who had sold her cow to pay his passage to America.

Erzsi put the soup before him and he did not touch it. She stood waiting, with her hands wrapped in her apron, and the fear that had been in her all day rose up and caught her by the throat.

"Janos," she said, "what is it? You have been laid off?"

He shook his head.

"Then you are hurt? Something has happened at the mill?"

"Nothing has happened," he said. "Let me be."

But she could not let him be. She had been married to him for six years, and she knew every shade of his silences, and this one was new to her. It was not the silence of weariness, which was the one she knew best of all—that dull, stupefied silence of a man who has stood for twelve hours before the mouth of a converter, with the heat beating upon him till the sweat ran down into his shoes and the flame of the blow roaring in his ears like the end of the world. This was something else; there was a hardness in it, and a kind of shame. And so she pulled the other box up beside him and sat down and put her hand upon his knee.

"Tell me," she said.

He was a long time about it. He took the spoon and stirred the soup, and watched the bits of cabbage go round, and then he laid the spoon down again. At last he said, without looking up, "Kinney spoke to me today."

Kinney was the foreman of the blowing floor—a big, red-faced Irishman with a voice like a steam whistle, who had come up from the ranks himself and had forgotten everything about the ranks except how to drive them. Erzsi had seen him once, on the day of the accident to Gyula Toth, when he had stood over the body and cursed because the converter would be shut down for half an hour.

"What did he say?" she asked.

"He said that there is talk among the men. About the union."

Erzsi's hand tightened upon his knee. Everybody in Shanty Hill knew about the talk of the union; it was whispered over the back fences and in the corners of the saloons, and at the Greek Catholic church after mass, when the men stood about in their Sunday collars. There was an organizer who had come up from Pittsburgh, a thin young man with spectacles who spoke Hungarian very badly and Slovak rather better, and who held meetings in the back room of Novak's hall until the company had bought Novak's hall, and after that in the woods above the slag dump. Two men had been discharged already for going to these meetings; one of them had been beaten by the deputies and put on a train with a ticket to Cleveland, and his wife had gone after him with the children a week later, carrying everything they owned in a bedsheet.

"He asked if you went to the meetings?" Erzsi said, and her voice was a whisper.

"No. He did not ask me that." Janos laughed, a short ugly sound. "He knows who goes. He knows everything. He wanted something else."

"What then?"

Janos lifted his head and looked at her for the first time, and she saw that his eyes were red, and not from the heat of the converter.

"He wants me to tell him who goes," he said. "He wants me to go myself, and sit with them, and listen, and come back and tell him the names. He says he will put me on the ladle crane. That is three dollars and forty cents the turn, Erzsi. Three dollars and forty cents. And he says that there will be something besides, five dollars at the end of each month, from the office, that nobody needs to know about."

There was a long silence in the room. Outside, somewhere down the hill, a man was singing in a drunken voice, and a dog was barking, and over everything, so constant that one ceased to hear it, there came the pounding of the mill—the rumble of the blooming rolls, the clang of the cars, the deep, shuddering breath of the blast furnaces, which never stopped, by day or by night, from one year's end to the next. The sky over the river was red with the glare of them, and the light came in at the one small window and lay upon the floor in a dull smear, like blood that had been wiped up carelessly.

Erzsi did not speak at once. She was doing sums in her head; she could not help it, any more than she could help breathing. For six years she had been doing these sums, morning and night, until they had become a part of the very fabric of her mind. Three dollars and forty cents instead of two dollars and ten—that was one dollar and thirty cents more in each turn, and there were thirty turns in the month, and that was thirty-nine dollars; and the five dollars besides made forty-four. Forty-four dollars more in a month! It was more than they had now altogether. It meant the rent paid on the first, and no more slips of paper from the company store with the figures in red ink. It meant shoes for little Jozsi, who had been going barefoot since September, though there had been frost upon the slag heaps these two weeks. It meant—her eyes went in spite of herself to the bed in the corner, where the baby lay breathing with that small, harsh, rattling sound that had kept her awake for five nights now—it meant a real doctor, a doctor from Pittsburgh, and medicine that was not a bottle of colored water with a company label on it.

Janos saw where her eyes had gone, and his face twisted.

"Yes," he said, bitterly. "I know. Do you think I did not think of that? I thought of nothing else all the afternoon. I stood on the floor and watched the blow, and I said to myself, the little one is coughing, and Kinney is offering money, and what is a name? A name is nothing. They know the names already, most of them. What harm is it if I tell them what they know?"

"And what did you tell him?" Erzsi asked.

"I told him I would think."

She let out her breath. She had not known that she was holding it. And then, because she was a woman who had been hungry, and who had watched her children be hungry, and who had learned in a hard school that it is the poor who pay for every pride, she said the thing that she would afterwards have given her right hand not to have said.

"Janos," she said, "it is not as if you were a union man yourself. You have never signed anything. You have never even been to the woods. What do you owe to these people?"

He turned on her so suddenly that she shrank back.

"What do I owe them?" he cried. "What do I owe to Gyula Toth, who was burned in the face so that his own wife screamed when they brought him home? What do I owe to Pista Varga, who has worked on the floor for nine years and has not had one Sunday in all that time to go to church, and is coughing like the baby there, only it is the dust in his lungs and no doctor in the world can cure that? What do I owe to the men who stand next to me in the heat, and drink out of the same bucket, and carry each other out when they fall down? You ask me what I owe them!"

"Hush," she said, "you will wake the children."

But Jozsi was awake already; she could see the gleam of his eyes from the pallet on the floor where he slept, beneath the window. He was five years old, and he had learned already that when his father raised his voice it was best to lie very still and pretend to be asleep. There are children all over the world who learn this lesson, in the tenements of New York and in the back streets of Manchester and in the mill towns of the valley; and they learn it before they learn their letters, and they never forget it.

Janos lowered his voice, but it was no less fierce.

"Do you know what they do to a man who carries tales?" he said. "Do you know what they called Sandor Kis, who did it last year at the Edgar Thomson works? They called him the dog's son, and they spat when he went by, and in the end somebody dropped a pig of iron on his foot from the charging floor, and nobody saw who did it, and he is walking with a crutch now in Homestead, and the company will not give him even a job at the gate. That is what happens to a spotter. And that is the best that happens. The worst is that you have to live with yourself."

"And what happens to a man who will not be a spotter?" Erzsi said. Her voice was low and steady now, but her hands were shaking in her lap. "I will tell you. Kinney asked you, and you would not, and so Kinney knows you are not his man. Do you think he will forget it? He will find a reason. He will say you were slow on the blow, he will say you were drunk, he will say you spoke back to him. And then you will have no job at all, and we will have no house, because the house belongs to the company, and they will put our things in the road the same as they did to the Kovacs. And where will we go then, with the winter coming and the baby sick? Will the union feed us? The union has no money. The young man with the spectacles has no money. He has a room in Pittsburgh and a clean shirt, and when it is finished he will go away to another town and talk to other men, and we will be in the road!"

She had not meant to cry, but now the tears came, and she put her apron over her face. Janos sat and looked at her, and the anger went out of him, and left him gray and old. He was twenty-nine years old, and there were times, like this one, when he looked fifty.

"Erzsi," he said, after a while, "listen to me."

She did not take the apron from her face.

"You think I do not know all that? I know it better than you. I have known it since I came across the water. In the old country it was the count, and his stewards, and the gendarmes with feathers in their hats, and you took off your cap when they rode by, and you said, yes, your honor, and no, your honor, and you starved quietly. And then we heard about America. The agent came to the village with his pictures—do you remember? The houses with gardens, and the men in collars, and the wages written large, so that the old women crossed themselves. A free country, he said. A man is a man in America, he said. And we came. And what is it here? It is the count again, only now he lives in New York and nobody has ever seen his face, and his stewards are called superintendents, and his gendarmes are called the Coal and Iron Police, and instead of feathers they have clubs. And it is the same thing, only worse, because in the old country at least the count did not pretend he was our friend."

She took the apron down and looked at him. He had never talked to her like this before; she did not know that he had these thoughts in him. It was as if a stranger had come and sat down by her stove.

"Where did you learn to talk so?" she said.

"In the woods," he said simply. "Above the slag dump."

And then she understood, and the room seemed to turn about her.

"You have been going," she whispered. "All this time—the Sundays when you said you were sleeping at Mihaly's cousin's—"

"Three times," he said. "Only three. And I have not signed. But I have been listening, and I have been thinking. And when Kinney came to me today and put his hand on my shoulder, and smiled at me with his big teeth, and talked to me as if we were brothers, I knew that he had seen me there, or somebody had seen me and told him. And I knew that he was not asking me. He was telling me. Either I am his dog, or I am finished."

Erzsi sat very still. The baby coughed, a long racking cough that ended in a thin wail, and she got up and went to the bed and lifted it, and held it against her shoulder, and walked up and down the narrow space between the stove and the curtain, patting the small back with her worn hand. The child was hot to the touch, hotter than it had been in the morning; she could feel the heat of it through her dress. She thought of the doctor from Pittsburgh, and of the medicine, and of the forty-four dollars, and she thought of Sandor Kis walking on his crutch in Homestead, and of men spitting when Janos went by, and of Janos sitting on this box night after night, not looking at her, not looking at anyone, with that hard shame in his eyes growing harder every day until there was nothing left of him but the shame. And she understood, in that moment, a thing which the gentlemen who write about labor in the magazines have never understood, and never will—that the choice which the company had put before her husband was not a choice between riches and poverty, nor even between bread and hunger, but between two kinds of death; and that it was the same choice which it put before every man in the valley, every day of his life, so softly that most of them never knew they were choosing at all.

"What will you do?" she said at last.

Janos was a long time answering.

"I do not know," he said. "Tell me what to do, Erzsi. You have a better head than I have. You always had. Tell me, and I will do it."

It was the cruelest thing he could have said to her, and he did not know it. She stood with the sick child against her breast, and the light of the furnaces lay red upon the floor, and the mill pounded on and on beneath them like the heart of some great beast that fed upon the bodies of men. She looked at her husband's hands, lying open upon his knees, the palms seamed with old burns and the knuckles swollen; and she looked at the eyes of her son, gleaming at her silently from the pallet beneath the window; and she knew that whatever she said now, he would remember it, and she would remember it, for as long as either of them lived.

"Eat your soup," she said. "It is getting cold."

He looked at her, and then he picked up the spoon and began to eat, slowly, mechanically, as a man eats who does not taste anything. She walked up and down with the baby, and the baby coughed and quieted and coughed again, and the drunken man down the hill had stopped singing.

When he had finished she took the bowl from him and set it in the basin, and then she came and stood in front of him.

"Monday," she said, "you will go to Kinney, and you will tell him that you have thought, and that you cannot do it, because you are a slow man with words and you would make mistakes with the names. Tell him you are stupid. They believe that of us; let them believe it. Perhaps he will let it go, and perhaps he will not. If he does not—" her voice faltered, and then went on—"if he does not, there is my cousin Marika in Johnstown, at the car works. She has written that they are taking men. It is not much. It is nothing. But it is not this."

Janos bowed his head, and she saw his shoulders shake. She put her free hand upon his hair, which was stiff with the dust of the mill, and stood so for a long time.

"And the little one?" he said, very low.

"I will take him to the Sisters at the hospital in Braddock," she said. "They do not ask for money first. Mrs. Toth told me."

She did not tell him what else Mrs. Toth had told her—that the Sisters were kind, but that the ward was full of children from the valley with the same cough, and that half of them did not come home. There are some things a woman carries by herself.

Outside, the whistle blew for some change of shift in some other department; it was impossible, in Shanty Hill, to know which. The red light flickered upon the window as a furnace was tapped down by the river, and for a moment the whole room was lit up—the stove and the boxes and the flour-sack curtain, and the man with his head bowed, and the woman standing over him with the child in her arms—like a picture of the Holy Family that some mad painter had set down in the pit of hell. And then the glare died away, and the room was dark again, and the mill went on pounding, as it would pound tomorrow, and the day after, and the year after that, making steel for the bridges and the skyscrapers and the battleships of the richest nation in the world.

It was a little after six o'clock on a Saturday evening in November when Thomas Wolak got down from the interurban car at the foot of Furnace Street, with a cardboard valise in one hand and a paper sack of oranges in the other. He stood for a minute upon the corner, looking about him, and he could hardly believe that this was the place where he had been born. Nine years he had been gone, and in nine years the town of Calder had grown as a cancer grows. Where there had been a meadow with a creek running through it, and a grove of willows where the boys used to swim, there was now a slag-dump forty feet high, gray and smoking, and beyond it the new open-hearth sheds of the Calder Steel and Wire Company, with their six stacks pouring out a smoke that was orange where the light of the furnaces caught it and black everywhere else. The creek was still there, but it ran in a culvert of cement, and it was the color of rust, and it smelled of acid. It had been made into a sewer, as everything in Calder sooner or later was made into a sewer, for the convenience of those who owned the town.

Thomas had come to see his cousin Anna. They had been raised in the same house, for Anna's father had died in the Shamokin mines when she was four years old, and her mother had brought her to Calder and taken in washing and boarded with Thomas's people. The two children had slept in the same trundle-bed until they were too big for it, and had gone to the parish school together, and had stolen apples together from the orchard of the superintendent, and had been whipped together for it. When Thomas was seventeen, and had been fired from the wire-drawing mill for talking back to a foreman, he had gone West to seek his fortune; and Anna had cried for two days, and had made him promise to write. He had written, at first, every month, and then every three months, and then hardly at all. It was not that he had forgotten her; but the life of a migratory worker is not one which lends itself to correspondence. A man who sleeps in box-cars and in "jungles" beside the railroad tracks, who follows the wheat harvest from Oklahoma to the Dakotas and then goes into the lumber camps of Washington for the winter, has no address to give, and seldom the price of a stamp; and as for what he has to tell, it is mostly of a kind he would rather his folks did not know.

He found the house by asking. It was on Slag Row, which was not the name the Company had given it, but the name everybody used. It was one of forty frame dwellings built in a double line along an unpaved road, each exactly like the rest, each painted the same dull red, which was the cheapest paint that could be bought, and each with a privy in the rear and a pump that served four families. The houses had been put up in a hurry, during the boom of 1906, and they had been intended to last ten years; they were now in their fourteenth, and they leaned against one another like drunken men. The rent was eleven dollars a month, and it was taken out of the pay envelope before the workingman ever saw it; so that if he lost his job, he lost his home on the same day, and there was a clause in the lease to that effect, which none of the tenants had read, since few of them could read English.

Thomas knocked, and the door was opened by a little girl of perhaps seven, with a dirty face and a pair of enormous brown eyes, who stared at him and then ran away screaming, "Mama! Mama! There's a man!" And then a woman came out of the kitchen, wiping her hands upon her apron; and Thomas stood in the doorway and looked at her, and for a moment he did not know her.

He had left a girl of sixteen, plump and rosy, with yellow braids wound about her head and a laugh that you could hear across the schoolyard. He saw before him a woman whom he would have taken to be forty, thin and stooping, with a face that was gray and lined, and hair that had been yellow and was now the color of dust. Her hands were red and swollen, and two of the knuckles were wrapped in rags. Only her eyes were the same; and when she saw who it was, they filled with tears, and she gave a cry and flung her arms about him, and stood there sobbing against his shoulder, while the little girl peeped from behind the stove and two smaller children came crawling out from somewhere to see what the matter was.

"Tomek! Tomek!" she kept saying, using the old name that nobody had called him by in nine years. "Oh, God, I thought you was dead! I thought you was dead somewhere and nobody would ever tell me!"

She drew him into the kitchen and made him sit down, and she bustled about to make coffee, laughing and crying at the same time, and stopping every minute to touch his arm, as if to make sure that he was real. The kitchen was a room perhaps ten feet square, and it served as dining-room and sitting-room and laundry as well. There was a cook-stove in one corner, and a table covered with oilcloth, and four chairs, of which one had a broken back; there was a wash-tub on a bench, full of gray water, and a line strung across the ceiling, upon which hung a row of children's underclothes, steaming in the heat. The window looked out upon the mill, and the glare of the furnaces came through it and played upon the wall, so that the room was never wholly dark, day or night; and there was a fine black grit that lay upon everything, upon the table and the dishes and the sills, and that crunched under your feet when you walked. Anna said that she swept it out three times a day, and it was back again in an hour. It got into the food, and into the children's lungs, and into the very pores of the skin; it was the dust of the Calder Steel and Wire Company, which had paid a dividend of twenty-two per cent the previous year.

Thomas gave the oranges to the children, who had never had oranges except at Christmas, and who did not know at first what to do with them. Then he sat and drank his coffee, which was weak, and watched his cousin as she moved about the room; and he asked her the questions that he dreaded to ask.

She told him the story, a little at a time, as women of her kind tell such stories, without complaining, as if it were the weather they were speaking of. She had married Joe Pastor, did Thomas remember him? the tall fellow who used to play the accordion at the weddings. Joe had a good job then, a heater's helper in the blooming-mill, at twenty-six cents an hour, and they had thought themselves rich. They had been married in the church, and had a real wedding, with a band, and had gone in debt a hundred and forty dollars for it, which had taken them two years to pay. Then the babies had come, one every year or so; there were five living, and two in the cemetery on the hill. The first one had died of what the doctor called the summer complaint, which was the name given in Calder to the disease that came from drinking milk that was not fit to drink. The second one had died in the influenza, two years ago, when there was a house on Slag Row where every soul had died, and the Company had nailed up the doors and burned the bedding in the road.

And Joe? Thomas asked; and Anna was silent for a while, and then she said that Joe was in the front room, lying down. He had been hurt.

It had happened eighteen months ago. There had been a hot-metal spill in the converter department; a ladle had tipped, because a crane-chain had been worn and nobody had replaced it, the foreman having been told that the department was running over its budget for the quarter. Two men had been burned to death, and Joe had been caught by the splash, across the legs and the lower part of the body. He had been six weeks in the Company hospital, and when he came out he could walk only with crutches, and the pain never left him. The Company doctor had certified that he was fit for light work, and he had been given a job as a watchman at twelve dollars a week; and then, after three months, there had been a slack season, and the watchman's job had been abolished, and Joe had been told that there was nothing for him. He had gone to see a lawyer about damages, a man who came around to the houses after every accident and offered to take such cases for half of what he got; and the lawyer had looked into it and said that there was nothing to be done, because Joe had signed a release in the hospital, when he was out of his head with morphine, accepting a hundred and fifty dollars in full settlement of all claims. Joe did not remember signing it; but there was his name upon the paper, and two witnesses, both of them employees of the Company, and that was the end of it.

"So now I take in washing," said Anna. "Like Mama did. You remember how Mama used to stand at the tub? I used to think, when I was a girl, I would never do that. I would never get my hands like hers." She held up her own hands, and laughed, a little laugh that was worse than tears. "Well, now I got them."

She did the washing for the families of the foremen and the clerks who lived on the hill, in the brick houses with the lawns in front. She got seventy-five cents a basket, and she could do six baskets a week, if the children did not get sick and if she did not get sick herself. The oldest boy, Stanley, who was twelve, worked after school as a "picker" at the scrap-yard, sorting iron from the trash, and brought home a dollar and a half a week; and he was going to quit school in the spring and go into the mill, because the law said he could not go in until he was fourteen, but the Company did not ask to see any papers, and there were plenty of boys of twelve in the mill. There was nothing else that could be done. The rent was eleven dollars a month, and coal was nine dollars a ton, and flour had gone up to where you could not believe it; and Joe needed medicine, and the doctor wanted two dollars a visit. They owed the Company store sixty-three dollars, and the store would not let them have any more credit, so that she had to buy for cash in Polish Town, a mile and a half away, and carry it home.

Thomas sat and listened, and his hands, which lay upon the oilcloth, clenched themselves slowly into fists. He had seen a great deal of misery in nine years; he had seen men frozen to death in box-cars, and men beaten insensible by railroad "bulls," and men shot down by deputies in a strike in the lumber camps; but there was something about this that struck him harder than all of it. It was his own people; it was the girl who had stolen apples with him, who had laughed so that you could hear her across the schoolyard. And he saw, as clearly as if it had been written out upon the wall, what was going to become of her. She would go on standing at the tub, year after year, until her back gave out or her lungs gave out; and the boy would go into the mill and be maimed as his father had been, or killed outright, or else would grow up hard and bitter and take to drink; and the little girl with the brown eyes would go into the wire-mill at fourteen, and marry at seventeen, and have a baby every year, and stand at her own tub, and so on and on, generation after generation, so long as there were steel-mills in Calder, and men who owned them, and men who had to work in them or starve.

Presently Joe came limping in from the front room, having heard voices. He was a tall man still, but he was so thin that his clothes hung upon him as upon a scarecrow, and his face was the face of a man who has not slept a whole night through in a year and a half. He shook hands with Thomas, and sat down carefully, laying his crutches against the table, and said that he was glad to see him, and that Anna had talked of him often. Then he asked, as the people of Calder always asked, whether Thomas had come back to work in the mill; and when Thomas said no, he had only come to visit, Joe looked at him curiously, and Anna asked him what he was doing now, out there in the West.

Then it was Thomas's turn to tell his story; and he told it to them, sitting at the oilcloth table, with the children gathered about him, sucking their oranges and listening with wide eyes, while the glare of the furnaces flickered upon the wall.

He told them how he had gone out with eleven dollars in his pocket, and how it had been stolen from him the first week, in a lodging-house in Pittsburgh. He told them of the harvest fields, where a man worked from four in the morning until dark, under a sun that knocked men over like ninepins, for two dollars and a half a day; and how, when the harvest was done, the farmers called the sheriff to drive the hands out of the county, so that they should not be a charge upon the taxpayers through the winter. He told them of the lumber camps, where the men slept in bunk-houses with two hundred others, in blankets that crawled with vermin, and ate food that a dog would have turned from; and where, if a man was crushed by a falling tree, they buried him in the woods and took the price of his coffin out of his last wages. He told them of the employment agencies in Spokane and Seattle, which sold jobs to the workers for a fee, and had an arrangement with the foremen to fire the men as soon as they were hired, so that there should be a constant procession of new victims, and a new fee every time. He told them how he had gone hungry, and slept in the rain, and been jailed for vagrancy, which meant for having no money; and how he had been beaten by a policeman in Fresno for standing on a soap-box and reading aloud the Declaration of Independence.

Anna gasped at this. "For reading that? But that is the American paper! That is what they teach in the school!"

Thomas laughed, not pleasantly. "Yes," he said. "They teach it in the school. But you try reading it on a street-corner, to a crowd of working-men who haven't had their wages, and see what happens to you. There's a part in it about how when a government gets to be destructive of life and liberty, the people have a right to alter or abolish it. The cops don't like that part."

And then he told them the thing that was the real news he had brought with him, the thing that had changed his life. He told them how, in the jail at Fresno, he had met a man, an old lumberjack with one eye, who had talked to him all one night through the bars; and how this man had explained to him, simply and plainly, as one explains a sum in arithmetic, why it was that the world was the way it was. Why it was that men who did all the work had nothing, and men who did no work had everything. Why it was that there were slack seasons, when the warehouses were full of goods and the people starved because they had produced too much. Why it was that the Calder Steel and Wire Company could pay a dividend of twenty-two per cent, and at the same time could not afford to replace a worn crane-chain. It was not because the owners were wicked men, though some of them were; it was because of the system under which they lived, which made it profitable to grind the worker down and unprofitable to treat him as a human being. So long as the mills belonged to a few, and the few ran them for profit, so long would there be Slag Rows, and crippled men, and children going into the mill at twelve. And the only way out was for the workers to stand together, all of them, the steel-men and the miners and the lumberjacks and the harvest hands, the Americans and the Poles and the Italians and the Negroes; and to take the mills and run them for the use of those who did the work.

He talked for a long time, more earnestly than he had meant to; and when he stopped, he saw that Joe was staring at him, and that there was a strange light in his tired face.

"There was a man used to talk like that in the blooming-mill," said Joe slowly. "Before the strike last year. A Hungarian. They took him away and nobody saw him no more." He was silent for a while, and then he said, "I used to think he was crazy. Now I don't know. I lie in there at night, and the pain don't let me sleep, and I think about it. I gave them eight years. I never missed a day. And they take my legs, and they give me a hundred and fifty dollars that I don't remember, and they throw me out. And they go on making steel. I hear the whistle every morning." He struck the table with his open hand, so that the cups rattled. "Somebody should do something!"

"Somebody will," said Thomas. "Us. There isn't anybody else."

Anna sat with her swollen hands folded in her lap, looking from one to the other of them; and Thomas could see the fear in her eyes, the fear that was bred into the very bones of the people of Calder, who had seen men taken away, and strikes broken by the state troopers riding down the road with clubs, and whole families evicted into the snow. But he could see something else too, something that he remembered from long ago, when she had stood up in the schoolyard to a bully twice her size, because he was twisting the arm of a smaller boy. It was buried deep now, under fourteen years of the tub and the washboard, of babies and debts and the black grit of the mill; but it was not dead.

"Tomek," she said at last, very low, "you will stay? A little while?"

He said that he would stay. He had meant to stay only over Sunday, but he said that he would stay the winter, and get a job in the mill if they would have him, and help with the rent. He did not tell her the rest of what was in his mind; that there was work to be done in Calder, and that he had come home to do it.

They made a bed for him on the kitchen floor that night, with quilts that Anna's mother had brought from Shamokin, and he lay there looking up at the red glare upon the ceiling and listening to the roar of the furnaces, which went on without ceasing, a sound like the breathing of some vast beast that was never satisfied. He thought of all the people sleeping in the forty red houses of Slag Row, and in the thousand other houses like them in Calder, and in the ten thousand other towns like Calder from one end of the land to the other; of the millions of men and women and children who fed that beast with their bodies, and who did not know that they were many and it was one. He thought of the old one-eyed lumberjack in the Fresno jail, and of the words he had said at dawn, when they came to take him out: "It's a long fight, boy. But it's the only one worth fighting." And somewhere toward morning, when the whistle blew for the day shift and he heard the tramp of feet going past in the dark, he fell asleep, with his fists still clenched upon the quilt.

The town of Brennan's Ford lay in a crook of the river, where the water came down brown and sluggish from the hills, and where, for eleven miles along either bank, the furnaces of the Allegheny Consolidated Steel Company sent up their columns of smoke by day and their pillars of fire by night. There was no hour of the twenty-four in which the sky above it was clean; there was no house in it, from the shanties on the flats to the frame cottages on Furnace Hill, upon whose window-sills one might lay a white handkerchief without lifting it black. The people who lived there had long since ceased to notice this; they breathed the soot as they breathed the air, and they washed their faces on Saturday night and went to Mass on Sunday morning, and on Monday the soot came back, as the shift whistle came back, and the foreman, and the rent.

In one of the cottages on Furnace Hill, the third from the end of a row of fourteen, each of which was painted the same color of dull red by the company that owned it, lived Andras Halas, a puddler's helper, with his wife Zuzka and their four children. The cottage had three rooms, and for these three rooms the family paid eleven dollars a month, which was deducted from Andras's wages before he ever saw them, so that he had the curious experience, every second Saturday, of being handed an envelope which contained less money than he had earned, together with a slip of paper explaining why. There were other deductions besides the rent; there was a deduction for the company doctor, whom the family had seen once in two years, and a deduction for the company insurance, which paid nothing unless a man was killed outright in the mill and paid very little then; and there was the account at the company store, which was never quite paid off, and which grew a little every winter and shrank a little every summer, but never by so much as it had grown.

Andras had come from the Zemplén country, in the northern part of Hungary, nine years before, and he had come because an agent of the steamship companies had told the people of his village that in America a strong man might earn two dollars a day and live like a lord. Andras was a strong man; he had shoulders like a draft horse and hands that could bend a horseshoe, and he had believed the agent, as a strong man will believe anything that promises him a fair return for his strength. He had found work within a week of landing, and he had been grateful for it; and he had worked ever since, twelve hours a day and seven days a week, with a twenty-four-hour shift every second Sunday when the day and night turns changed over, so that he slept in his own bed perhaps four nights out of seven and saw his children awake perhaps two hours out of the twenty-four. He was thirty-four years old now, and there were white streaks in his mustache, and a cough that came upon him in the mornings and shook him like a tree in a gale; and when he looked at himself in the bit of broken mirror that hung over the wash-basin, he saw a man of fifty.

The eldest of his children was a boy named Ferko, who was seven years old in the fall of that year. He was a thin, dark little fellow, with great serious eyes that seemed too large for his face, and he had the habit, which his mother found exasperating, of standing perfectly still and staring at things, as if he expected them to explain themselves to him. He went to the parish school in the mornings, where a tired nun taught him to read English out of a book about a boy who had a pony, and in the afternoons he was supposed to help his mother with the younger ones, of whom there were three: Juli, who was five, and Pista, who was three, and the baby, who had not yet been given a pet name because Zuzka had buried one baby already and did not like to grow too fond of this one too soon.

It was the end of November, and the cold had come down out of the hills early that year. There had been a hard frost every night for a week, and the river had ice along its edges, and in the mornings the windows of the cottage were furred over with white so thick that Ferko could write his name upon it with his finger, which he did, laboriously, every morning, because the nun had told him that a boy who could write his name was on the way to becoming an American. The cottage was heated by a single iron stove in the kitchen, and the stove burned coal, and the coal had to be bought from the company store at a price which was precisely one dollar a ton higher than the price at which the same coal could be bought in Pittsburgh, eighteen miles away. Why this should be so, Andras had never been able to understand; he had once asked a man in the mill, an Irishman who read newspapers, and the Irishman had laughed and said that it was so because the company owned the store, and the railroad, and the coal mine, and the houses, and the town council, and the priest, and very likely God Almighty as well; and Andras had crossed himself and gone away, not liking that sort of talk.

The coal that week had run very low. There was half a scuttle left in the shed behind the cottage, and it was Wednesday, and payday was not until the Saturday after next, and there was already a balance of thirty-one dollars against them on the books of the store. Zuzka had been banking the fire at night with ashes, and letting it go almost out in the middle of the day, and wrapping the baby in every rag she possessed; and still the baby coughed, a thin little whistling cough that Zuzka listened to in the dark with her hands clenched under the blanket. She had said nothing to Andras about the coal, because there was nothing Andras could do; he could not work more hours than there were, and he could not ask the store for more credit, because the store had refused him in October, and a man does not like to be refused twice.

But Ferko had seen. Ferko saw everything, standing still with his great eyes; he had seen his mother scrape the bottom of the scuttle, and he had seen her stand at the window with the baby against her shoulder, looking out at nothing; and he had heard the baby cough. And on Wednesday afternoon, instead of coming straight home from the parish school, he went down the hill to the railroad yards.

The yards of the Allegheny Consolidated lay along the river below the mills, a great flat waste of cinders and switches and sidings, where the coal cars came in from the mines in strings of forty and fifty, and stood waiting to be dumped into the bins that fed the furnaces. The cars were heaped high, and as they bumped and jolted over the switches, lumps of coal would fall from them and lie in the cinders between the tracks; and the children of the town, the Slovak children and the Hungarian children and the Polish and the Italian, had made it their business for twenty years to come down with sacks and buckets and gather up these lumps. It was forbidden; there were signs in four languages declaring it forbidden, and there were company policemen in blue coats with brass buttons whose duty it was to chase the children away. But the children came all the same, because their mothers were cold; and it was a thing everyone knew, that every winter one or two of them did not go home again, because a switch engine had come backing down a siding in the dusk with no one on the rear platform to see them.

Ferko had no sack, so he took off his jacket and tied the sleeves together to make one. He worked for an hour and a half, crawling between the rails with his hands bare, while the wind came off the river and cut through his thin shirt like a knife; and he gathered perhaps twenty pounds of coal, which was a great deal for a boy of seven to carry. Once a train of empties went by on the next track, so close that the wind of it knocked him flat upon the cinders, and he lay there with his face pressed into the ground and his heart pounding, and did not get up until it had gone. Once he saw a blue coat at the far end of the yard, and hid behind a stack of ties until it went away. And at last, when it was nearly dark, and the furnaces had begun to glow red along the river, he slung his bundle over his shoulder and set out up the hill, staggering under the weight of it, and as proud as any man who ever came home with his wages in his pocket.

He did not know that his father was at home. It was the week of the changeover, when Andras went from the day turn to the night turn, and he had come home at noon to sleep before going back at six; and he had slept badly, as he always did in the daytime, with the noise of the children and the light coming in at the edges of the blanket that was nailed over the window. He was sitting at the kitchen table in his undershirt, drinking a cup of coffee that was mostly chicory, when the door opened and Ferko came in.

The boy was black from head to foot. His face was black, and his hands were black, and the knees of his trousers were torn through and black underneath, and there was a long scratch across his cheek where a cinder had cut him, and a little trickle of blood had run down from it and dried. He had no jacket on, and he was shaking so with the cold that his teeth chattered; but his eyes were shining, and he came across the room and laid his bundle on the floor at his mother's feet, and untied the sleeves, and showed her what was inside.

"For the baby," he said, in Hungarian. "So she can be warm."

Zuzka stared at the coal, and then she stared at the boy, and then she put her hand to her mouth. She did not say anything; it was Andras who spoke. He had set down his cup, and he was looking at his son with a face that had gone suddenly gray, under the grime that never entirely washed out of it.

"Where did you get that?" he said.

Ferko looked at him, and the shine went slowly out of his eyes. "From the yards," he said. "By the tracks. It falls off the cars, Apa. Nobody wants it. It just lies there."

"Come here."

The boy came, slowly. Andras took him by the shoulders, not roughly, but with hands so heavy that the child seemed to shrink beneath them; and he turned him around to the light of the lamp, and looked at the scratch upon his cheek, and at the torn trousers, and at the bare, black, bleeding hands.

"Who told you to go there?"

"Nobody, Apa."

"Did you see the policemen?"

"I hid," said Ferko. "Behind the wood. He didn't see me."

"And the trains? Did you see the trains?"

Ferko was silent. He was thinking of the train of empties, and the wind of it, and the cinders against his face; and something in his father's voice made him afraid to speak of it.

"Answer me," said Andras.

"One went by," the boy whispered. "Close. I fell down. But it didn't hit me, Apa. It didn't hit me."

Andras let go of him then, and stood up, and walked across the kitchen to the window, and stood there with his back to the room. It was a long time before he turned around; and when he did, Zuzka saw his face, and took the two younger children by the hand and led them into the other room, and shut the door.

Here, perhaps, it is necessary to explain something, for the benefit of those readers who have been raised in comfortable homes, and who may be inclined to judge Andras Halas by the standards of such homes. In comfortable homes, a parent who scolds a child for an act of loving generosity is thought to be a harsh and foolish parent, and very likely he is. But in comfortable homes there are no switch engines; and the parent does not have before his eyes, as Andras had before his eyes at that moment, the picture of a little body lying across a rail in the dusk, as he had seen one lying two winters before, the son of a Polish laborer named Wojcik, who had gone down for coal just as Ferko had gone, and whom they had brought up the hill afterward in a gunny sack because there was not enough of him left to carry any other way. Nor does the parent in a comfortable home know, as Andras knew, that the company kept lists; that the blue-coated policemen took down the names of the children they caught, and that the names went to the superintendent, and that the superintendent sent them on to the foremen, and that a man whose child was caught twice stealing the company's coal might find, on the following payday, that there was no longer any work for him at the Allegheny Consolidated, nor at any other mill in the valley, since the mills of the valley shared their lists as they shared their prices. These were the things that Andras knew; and they had been driven into him not by any reasoning, but by the slow, grinding pressure of nine years, as the shape of a stone is driven into the clay that lies beneath it. And when he spoke to his son, it was these things that spoke, and not his love; though his love was there underneath, as the fire is underneath the ashes, and it was his love that made his voice shake.

"Listen to me," he said. "You will never go there again. Do you hear me? Never. Not for coal, not for anything. If I hear that you have been there, I will beat you until you cannot sit down. I will take my belt to you. Do you understand?"

Ferko stared at him. His father had never beaten him; his father had scarcely ever raised his voice to him; his father was a great, slow, silent man who came and went at strange hours, and who sometimes, on the Sundays when he was at home, would take the boy on his knee and sing him songs from the old country in a deep, rumbling voice like the sound of the furnaces. The child could not understand what had happened. He had done a good thing; he had brought coal for the baby; and now his father stood over him with a face like the face of a stranger, and talked of belts.

"But the baby is cold," he said. His lip had begun to tremble. "Anyu said—I heard her. She said there was no more. And the baby coughs."

"That is not your business!" cried Andras; and he struck the table with his fist, so that the coffee cup jumped and fell over, and the brown stuff ran across the oilcloth and dripped onto the floor. "Do you hear me? It is not your business! I am the father in this house. I will get the coal. It is for me to do, not for you. You are a child; you are seven years old; you will go to school and learn to read and be an American, and you will not crawl around on the tracks like a rat for the company's leavings! Do you want to be killed? Do you want them to carry you home in a sack, like the Wojcik boy? Do you want your mother to stand at the window and see that?"

Ferko did not know about the Wojcik boy; he had been only five when it happened. But he knew what a sack was, and he knew what it meant to be carried home; and suddenly the wind of the train came back to him, and the cinders, and the great black wheels going by so close above his head, and the full meaning of what he had done broke upon him, as such meanings do break upon children, all at once and overwhelmingly. His face crumpled, and he began to cry, not loudly, but with a dreadful, silent shaking, as if something inside him had come loose.

And Andras stood and looked at him, and the anger went out of him all at once, as the air goes out of a bellows. He sat down heavily upon the bench, and put his elbows on the table, in the spilled coffee, and put his face in his hands. He was thinking—so far as a man so tired could be said to think—that the boy was right. The baby was cold. There was no more coal. And there would be no more coal until the Saturday after next, and then only if the store would give it; and in the meantime the baby would cough, and he would be at the mill, twelve hours at a stretch, feeding the furnaces that turned out steel rails for railroads, and steel beams for skyscrapers, and steel plates for battleships, enough steel to build a world; and his own child would be cold. And it seemed to him, in a dim and confused way, as he sat there, that there was something wrong in this, something monstrous, something which no amount of beating with belts could ever set right; but he could not have said what it was, nor whom to blame for it. The Irishman would have told him; but Andras had crossed himself and gone away.

He felt a small hand upon his arm, and looked up. Ferko was standing beside him, his face streaked with tears that had made white channels through the coal dust; and he was holding out, in his black, bleeding palm, the one thing he had that he thought might mend matters between them—a lump of coal, the largest one from the bundle, nearly as big as his fist.

"I won't go again, Apa," he said. "I promise. I won't go again."

Andras looked at the lump of coal for a long time. Then he took it, gently, and turned it over in his great scarred fingers, as though it were something he had never seen before. And then he put his arm around the boy and drew him close against his chest, coal dust and tears and all, and held him there, and said nothing at all, because there was nothing in any language that he knew which could have said what he felt.

After a while he got up and opened the door of the stove, and laid the lump of coal upon the dying embers, and then the rest of it, piece by piece, out of the knotted jacket. He did not send it back to the yards; he did not even think of doing so. The fire caught, and roared up red behind the iron door, and the warmth of it spread slowly out into the cold little kitchen. Zuzka came back with the children, and set the baby in her basket near the stove; and the baby stopped coughing, and slept. Ferko sat on the floor beside her, washing his hands in a basin of water that his mother had set to warm upon the stove-top, and wincing as the water found the cuts. At the door he stopped, and looked back at his son.

"Never again," he said. "You remember."

And this, right after Bunny had renounced the luxury of small lies! Also there was the mystery about Mamma’s friends. There were always gentlemen friends who came to see her while Bunny was there, and who might or might not be agreeable to Bunny. When he came home, Aunt Emma would ask him questions, from which it was evident that she wanted to know about these gentlemen friends, but didn’t want Bunny to know that she wanted to know. Bunny noticed that Dad never referred to such matters; he never asked any questions about Mamma, and Aunt Emma always did her asking out of Dad’s presence. All this had a peculiar effect upon Bunny. Just as Dad kept a safe deposit box at the bank, into which nobody ever looked but himself, so Bunny kept a secret place in his own mind. Outwardly, he was a cheerful and frank little fellow, if somewhat too mature for his years; but all the time he was leading a dual life—picking up ideas here and there, and carrying them off and hiding them, as a squirrel does nuts, so that he may come back at a later season and crack them open and nibble them. Some nuts were good and some were bad, and Bunny learned to judge them, and to throw away the bad ones. It was a dark corner of life, mysterious and rather hateful. In the beginning, Bunny was loyal to his father, not trying to find out what his father didn’t want him to know. But this could not continue indefinitely, for the mind automatically seeks understanding. It was not merely that the birds and the chickens and the dogs in the street gave you hints; it was not merely that every street-boy knew, and was eager to explain; it was that the stupid grown-ups themselves persisted in saying things which you couldn’t help getting. It was Aunt Emma’s fixed conviction that every lady was after Dad; “setting her cap at him,” or “making sheep’s eyes at him”—she had many such phrases. And Dad always showed a queer embarrassment whenever he had been the least bit polite to any lady; he seemed to be concerned lest Bunny should share Aunt Emma’s suspicions. The Bankside family was accustoming itself to the presence of a butler, and Mrs. Bankside had been proposed at the most exclusive of the ladies’ clubs. Efficiency was the watch-word out here in the West, and when you decided to change your social status, you put the job right through. Also, you might have trouble in marketing your oil, and would begin to think, how nice to have your own refinery, and be entirely independent. But independence had its price, for then you would have to provide enough oil to keep the refinery going, and you would want a chain of filling-stations to get rid of your products. It was a hard game for the little fellow; and no matter how big you got, there was always somebody bigger! But Dad had no kick just now; everything was a-comin’ his way a-whoopin’. “There’s thousands of ranches jist like that in California, son. Oil on top of the ground don’t mean anything special.”

“Well, Dad, you’ve always said you wanted to try some wild-catting; and you know, that’s the only way you’ll ever get what you talk about—a whole big tract that belongs to you, with no royalties to pay, and nobody to butt in. You sped along upon a fine paved road, but the land was haunted by the souls of old-time pioneers who had crossed it in covered wagons or with pack-mules, and had left their bones beside many a trail. Even now, you had to be careful when you went off into side-trails across these wastes; every now and then a car would get stuck with an empty radiator, and the people would be lucky to get out alive. You could get water if you sunk a deep well; and so there were fruit ranches and fields of alfalfa here and there. There came long stretches where the ground was white, like salt; that was alkali, Dad said, and it made this country a regular boob-trap. The would-be rancher would have to pull up the trees, and obliterate the traces of them, and set a real-estater to hunting for another boob. Strapped to the running-board of Dad’s car, on the right hand side where Bunny sat, was a big bundle wrapped in a water-proof cover; they were camping out—which meant that the mind of a boy was back amid racial memories, the perils and excitements of ten thousand years ago. Tightly clutched in Bunny’s two hands were a couple of repeating shot-guns; he held these for hours, partly because he liked the feel of them, and partly because they had to be carried in the open—if you shut them up in the compartment they would be “concealed weapons,” and that was against the law. Near the head of the valley a dirt road went off, and a sign said: “Paradise, eight miles.” They wound up a little pass, with mountains that seemed to be tumbled heaps of rock, of every size and color. There were fruit ranches, the trees now bare of leaves, with trunks calcimined white, and young trees with wire netting about them, to keep away the rabbits. The first rains of the season had fallen, and new grass was showing—the California spring, which begins in the fall. The pass broadened out; there were ranch-houses scattered here and there, and the village of Paradise—one street, with a few scattered stores, sheltered under eucalyptus trees that made long shadows in the late afternoon light. Dad drew up at the filling station, which was also a feed-store. “Can you tell me where is the Watkins ranch?”

“There’s two Watkinses,” said the man. “There’s old Abel Watkins—” “That’s the one!” exclaimed Bunny.

“He’s got a goat-ranch, over by the slide. It ain’t so easy to find. Was you plannin’ to get there tonight?”

“We shan’t worry if we get lost,” said Dad; “we got a campin’ outfit.” So the man gave them complicated directions. You took the lane back of the school-house, and you made several jogs, and then there were about sixteen forks, and you must get the right one, and you followed the slide that took the water down to Roseville, and it was the fourth arroyo after you had passed old man Tucker’s sheep-ranch, with the little house up under the pepper trees. And so they started and followed a winding road that had apparently been laid out by sheep, and the sun set behind the dark hills, and the clouds turned pink, and they dodged rocks that were too high for the clearance of the car and crawled down into little gullies, and up again with a constant shifting of gears. There was no need to ask about the quail, for the hills echoed with the melodious double call of the flocks gathering for the night.

Strapped to the running-board of Dad’s car, on the right hand side where Bunny sat, was a big bundle wrapped in a water-proof cover; they were camping out—which meant that the mind of a boy was back amid racial memories, the perils and excitements of ten thousand years ago. Tightly clutched in Bunny’s two hands were a couple of repeating shot-guns; he held these for hours, partly because he liked the feel of them, and partly because they had to be carried in the open—if you shut them up in the compartment they would be “concealed weapons,” and that was against the law. Near the head of the valley a dirt road went off, and a sign said: “Paradise, eight miles.” They wound up a little pass, with mountains that seemed to be tumbled heaps of rock, of every size and color. There were fruit ranches, the trees now bare of leaves, with trunks calcimined white, and young trees with wire netting about them, to keep away the rabbits. The first rains of the season had fallen, and new grass was showing—the California spring, which begins in the fall. The pass broadened out; there were ranch-houses scattered here and there, and the village of Paradise—one street, with a few scattered stores, sheltered under eucalyptus trees that made long shadows in the late afternoon light. Dad drew up at the filling station, which was also a feed-store. “Can you tell me where is the Watkins ranch?”

“There’s two Watkinses,” said the man. “There’s old Abel Watkins—” “That’s the one!” exclaimed Bunny.

“He’s got a goat-ranch, over by the slide. It ain’t so easy to find. Was you plannin’ to get there tonight?”

“We shan’t worry if we get lost,” said Dad; “we got a campin’ outfit.” So the man gave them complicated directions. You took the lane back of the school-house, and you made several jogs, and then there were about sixteen forks, and you must get the right one, and you followed the slide that took the water down to Roseville, and it was the fourth arroyo after you had passed old man Tucker’s sheep-ranch, with the little house up under the pepper trees. And so they started and followed a winding road that had apparently been laid out by sheep, and the sun set behind the dark hills, and the clouds turned pink, and they dodged rocks that were too high for the clearance of the car and crawled down into little gullies, and up again with a constant shifting of gears. There was no need to ask about the quail, for the hills echoed with the melodious double call of the flocks gathering for the night.
