Ed Corliss came home a little after eleven, and found the light still burning in the kitchen. That was a bad sign, and he knew it before he had got the key out of the lock. When Lucy was content with the world she went to bed at ten, and left a plate of something on the back of the stove with a saucer turned over it. When she was not content she sat up, and she would have the coffee-pot going, and her sewing-basket on the table, and a look on her face which said that she had been thinking things over.

"Hello, honey," he said, and kissed her on the side of the forehead, which was the part she offered him.

"Your supper's dried out," said Lucy. "I kept it hot till nine."

"I'm sorry. Old Pryor kept me."

"I know he did. Mrs. Pryor telephoned."

Ed had been in the act of hanging his hat on the nail behind the door, and he stopped with the hat in his hand. Mrs. Pryor was the wife of the managing editor of the Valley City *Evening Star*, and she had never in her life telephoned to the wife of a reporter. She was a large lady who belonged to the Woman's Club and the Daughters of something-or-other, and she spoke of "Mr. Pryor's young men" as the wife of a rancher might speak of the hired hands.

"What did she want?"

"She wanted to know if I would come to tea on Thursday. She said she had heard so much about me." Lucy bit off a thread, and looked at him. "She said Mr. Pryor thinks the world of you, and he has big plans for you, and she hoped I would do everything to help."

So that was how it stood. Ed sat down at the table, and Lucy got up and brought his plate, which held a pork chop and some fried potatoes, rather brown at the edges. He did not want to eat, but he understood that it would be considered a hostile act to refuse, so he took up his knife and fork and began. Lucy sat down across from him and resumed her sewing, which was a little dress for Junior, made over from one of her own. She sewed very fast, and did not look up, and he knew that she was waiting for him to tell her; and he knew also that she knew already, and that the telling was only a formality, like the reading of a will when everybody has been told what is in it.

"Pryor wants me to take the city desk," he said.

"Oh, Ed!" And now she did look up, and in spite of everything her face was bright, and she was pretty again, the way she had been at the Normal School when he had first seen her, playing the piano at the Christmas entertainment. "Ed, that's wonderful! How much?"

"Seventy-five a week."

"Seventy-five! Why, that's—" She did the sum in her head; she was always quicker than he was at sums. "That's more than half again. Ed, we could pay off the piano by spring. We could move out of this place. Mamma could come and stay with us, and not have to live with Fred and that wife of his."

"Yes," said Ed. "We could do a lot of things."

He went on eating the pork chop, and Lucy watched him, and the light went slowly out of her face.

"What's the matter?" she said. "Isn't it settled?"

"Not exactly."

"What do you mean, not exactly? Either he offered it to you or he didn't."

"He offered it to me. There's a condition."

---

It will be necessary at this point to explain something about the newspaper business, as it was carried on in Valley City and in some hundreds of other cities of the Republic. Ed Corliss had come into it with the idea, common among young men who have been editors of their college papers, that a newspaper was an institution for the gathering and publishing of news. He had been four years on the *Star*, and had learned that this was a very simple-minded view. A newspaper was a business, like a bank or a department store; it sold advertising space, and the price of the space depended upon the circulation, and the circulation was got by giving the people murders and divorces and baseball scores and comic strips. The news was a kind of bait, and the advertisers were the fish; and you did not, if you knew your business, put anything on the hook that would frighten away the fish.

Now the biggest advertisers in Valley City were the department stores, and the biggest of the department stores was owned by the same family that owned the Valley Packing Company, which operated the three canneries down by the railroad yards. And for nineteen days the women in those canneries had been out on strike. They were mostly Mexican women, and Portuguese, and a few Italians, and they had been getting twenty-two cents an hour for cutting peaches, and they wanted thirty; and what was more, they wanted somebody to do something about the foreman on the night shift at Number Two, who had a habit of choosing which girls would be kept on and which would be laid off, according to standards which had nothing to do with peaches. All this Ed knew, because he had been down there; he had talked with the women on the picket line, and had sat in the hall of the Sons of Italy and listened to the meetings, and had written stories which had been cut down to four inches and put on page eleven between an advertisement for corsets and a report of the Rotary Club luncheon.

What Mr. Pryor wanted now was something different. He wanted a series of six articles, to run on the front page, under the general heading "Who Is Behind the Cannery Trouble?" He had the answer to the question all ready; it was the Reds. There was a young woman organizer named Ruth Kessler who had come down from San Francisco, and there was a Russian Jew named Abramowitz who ran a cleaning-and-pressing shop on Fourth Street and was known to subscribe to radical papers; and out of these materials, together with a little imagination, Ed was to show the people of Valley City that the peach-cutters were not really discontented at all, but had been misled by paid agents of Moscow, who were seeking to destroy the American home. The district attorney was ready to act, Mr. Pryor said, as soon as public opinion had been "prepared."

---

Ed told his wife this, not all at once, but in pieces, between mouthfuls of the pork chop; and Lucy listened, and her needle went slower and slower, and finally stopped.

"Well," she said, "and what's so terrible about that?"

"It isn't true, Lucy."

"How do you know it isn't true?"

"Because I've been down there. I've talked to those women. They're not Reds; half of them can't read. They go to Mass every Sunday. They want eight cents an hour more, and they want that fellow Hoskins to keep his hands to himself. That's the whole of it."

"But the papers say—"

"The papers say what Pryor tells them to say. I *am* the papers, honey. I know how it's done."

Lucy put the little dress down on the table, and smoothed it out with both hands, as if it were very important that there should be no wrinkles in it.

"Ed," she said, "there's this girl Kessler. She's a Communist, isn't she?"

"I don't know. I suppose she may be. She's a member of some union."

"Mrs. Pryor says she's a Communist. She says she's been arrested in three states."

"Well, maybe she has. That doesn't make the peach-cutters Communists. That doesn't make twenty-two cents an hour a living wage."

"Nobody said anything about wages. You said yourself, it's this Kessler and the Russian man that Mr. Pryor wants you to write about. Well, if they're Reds, why shouldn't people know it?"

Ed had an answer to this, but he found it was not the sort of answer that could be made at half past eleven at night across a kitchen table to a tired woman who had been counting the payments on a piano. The answer was that it was the oldest trick in the world; that whenever working people asked for anything, the men who paid them would find somebody with a foreign name and an unpopular opinion, and make that person the issue, so that nobody would have to think about the eight cents. He had seen it done in the street-car strike two years ago, and in the trouble at the lumber mill; and he had written some of it himself, in his first year, before he had understood. But to explain all this would sound like a lecture, and Lucy hated to be lectured; she said he was getting to talk like a soap-box orator.

So instead he said, "Lucy, you don't know anything about Ruth Kessler."

That was a mistake, and he saw it at once. Lucy's face went white, and then very red, and she picked up the little dress again and began to sew at it furiously, although he could see that she was only pushing the needle in and out of the same place.

"No," she said. "I don't know anything about Ruth Kessler. But you do, don't you? You know a great deal about her."

"Lucy, for heaven's sake—"

"Mrs. Pryor says you've been seen with her. At the Greek's restaurant on Front Street. Twice."

---

Now here was a curious thing about the lives of men and women, which Ed Corliss had observed many times, but never so clearly as at this moment. You might be talking about something which concerned the welfare of several hundred human beings—their food, their rent, the shoes of their children; and all the while, underneath, there would be running another conversation, about something entirely different, which neither of you had mentioned; and sooner or later that other conversation would come up to the top, like oil coming up through water, and spread itself over everything. Ed perceived that Lucy had not sat up until eleven o'clock to talk about the city desk at all. She had sat up to talk about Ruth Kessler; and Mrs. Pryor, who was a shrewd woman in her way, had known exactly which string to pull.

"I had coffee with her," he said, "because I was interviewing her. That's my job. I've had coffee with the chief of police, and with the Japanese consul, and with that evangelist woman who was in town last spring. Did Mrs. Pryor think I was in love with the evangelist?"

"The evangelist was sixty years old."

"Well, Ruth Kessler is thirty-five, and she wears men's shoes, and she talks about nothing but the class struggle. I give you my word, Lucy, there's nothing to it."

"Then why do you call her Ruth?"

Ed opened his mouth, and closed it again. He had called her Ruth because everybody called her Ruth; because the women on the picket line called her Ruth, and the Italian men in the hall, and the old Russian in the pressing shop; because she was the sort of person to whom you did not say "Miss Kessler," any more than you would say "Miss" to a man. But he understood that this explanation, also, would not help him.

"All right," he said. "Miss Kessler. Have it your own way."

There was a silence. The alarm clock on the shelf over the sink ticked very loud, and from the bedroom came a small whimper, as Junior turned over in his crib, and then was still. Lucy sat with her eyes on her sewing, and Ed saw that there were tears on her lashes, and he felt suddenly like a brute, and also, at the same time, angry—angry at Mr. Pryor, and at Mrs. Pryor, and at the Valley Packing Company, and at the whole arrangement of things which made it necessary for a man to choose between his wife and his conscience across a kitchen table at midnight.

"Lucy," he said, more gently, "listen to me. Suppose I write these articles. Suppose I say what Pryor wants. Then the district attorney arrests Ruth—arrests Miss Kessler, and the old man in the pressing shop, and they get five years apiece under the syndicalism law, the way those fellows did in Sacramento. And the women go back to work at twenty-two cents, because they've got nobody to lead them, and they're scared to death. And Hoskins goes on picking out the girls he likes on the night shift. And I sit in the city editor's chair at seventy-five a week. Is that what you want me to do?"

"I want you to stop thinking about everybody in the world except your own family!"

She said it so loud that they both glanced toward the bedroom door; and then she went on, in a fierce whisper, which was worse than the loud voice.

"You talk about those women. What about me? I've been wearing the same coat for three winters, Ed. When I go to the Missionary Society, I sit in the back so nobody will look at it. I make Junior's clothes out of my old dresses. I haven't had my teeth fixed since we were married, and you know that one in the back aches every time it rains. And Mamma—you know what Fred's wife says to her. You know she cried the whole time she was here at Thanksgiving, because she has to go back there. And you want me to think about Mexican women in a cannery!"

"They've got teeth too, Lucy."

"Oh!" She threw the little dress on the table, and stood up, and went to the sink, and stood with her back to him, gripping the edge of it with both hands. "Oh, you're impossible! You always have an answer. You're so clever, and so good, and everybody else is so wicked. I suppose I'm wicked too, because I want a decent coat."

Ed sat and looked at her back. He was a fair-minded young man, and he could not deny that what she said about the coat was true, and about the tooth, and about her mother. He had made her certain promises, when they were married, about the kind of home they would have; and he had not kept them, because the *Star* paid forty-five dollars a week, and you could not keep promises on forty-five dollars a week, with a baby, and a piano, and a mother-in-law with a weak heart. There was nothing romantic about it; it was simply arithmetic, and Lucy was better at arithmetic than he was.

And yet the other side of it was arithmetic too. There were some four hundred women in the canneries, and if they got their eight cents an hour, that would come to something like seventy thousand dollars a year, taken out of the pockets of the family that owned the department store; and if they didn't get it, then that seventy thousand would go on into the pockets of the family, and some small part of it would come back through the advertising department of the *Star*, and some smaller part of that would come to Ed Corliss in the form of a raise in salary, and buy Lucy a new coat. He saw it with a sort of horrible clearness, like a diagram on a blackboard; the money flowing out of the women's hands and up through the pipes of the system, and dribbling down again here and there to those who made themselves useful. And he was being invited to make himself useful.

"Lucy," he said, "come and sit down."

She did not move.

"Please, honey."

She came, and sat down, but on the edge of the chair, as if she might get up again at any moment. She had wiped her eyes with the back of her hand, and her nose was a little red, and Ed thought that she looked about sixteen years old.

"I'm not saying you're wicked," he said. "God knows you've been a brick. I'm saying I've got to be able to look at myself when I shave in the morning. That's all."

"Other men do it. Mr. Pryor does it. He's a deacon in the Baptist church."

"I know he is."

"And Harry Wilkins wrote all those things about the street-car men, and now he's on the *Examiner* in Los Angeles at a hundred a week, and his wife has a car."

"I know that too."

"Then what makes you so different?"

It was a fair question, and Ed did not know the answer. He thought about it for a while, turning his fork over and over on the plate. Perhaps it was the face of a woman on the picket line, a thin Portuguese woman with a baby on her hip, who had shown him her hands, all cut and stained with the peach juice, and had said, in her broken English, "Look, mister. Twenty-two cent." Perhaps it was only stubbornness, the same stubbornness that had made him walk out of Sunday school at the age of eleven because the teacher said that the heathen would all go to hell. He did not know; but he knew that it was there, and that it would not go away for seventy-five dollars a week.

"I don't know, Lucy," he said. "I just can't do it."

"Then he'll fire you."

"He might."

"He *will*. Mrs. Pryor as good as said so. She said Mr. Pryor had been very patient, because he liked you, but there were some people on the paper who were not—not *sound*, she said. And she said she hoped you weren't one of them, because it would be such a pity, with a young wife and a baby."

So it had been put to Lucy as plainly as that; and Ed understood now why she had sat up, and why she was so frightened. It was not merely the coat. It was the forty-five dollars too; the floor that was under them, such as it was. And he understood also that Mrs. Pryor had done this quite deliberately, and had probably told her husband all about it at dinner; and that the two of them had sat in their big house on Magnolia Avenue and decided that the wife was the weak point, and that the way to get at a man was through his kitchen.

He reached across the table, and took Lucy's hand, which was rough from washing, and cold.

"Lucy," he said, "I'm going to ask you to trust me. I don't know yet what I'm going to do. Maybe there's some way out of it. Maybe I can tell Pryor I'll write about the strike, but I'll write it straight, and let him cut it how he likes. Maybe I can get on somewhere else. There's the *Herald* in Fresno; Joe Martin's been after me to come up there."

"The *Herald* pays forty."

"I know."

"And we'd have to move, and break the lease, and lose the deposit."

"I know, honey."

She did not take her hand away, but she did not press his, either. She sat looking at the little dress, lying on the table between them, with the needle still sticking in the hem; and Ed watched her, and wondered what she was thinking. He thought that perhaps he had never really known what Lucy was thinking, in all the four years; there was a place in her mind, as in his own, where she kept things, and did not show them to anybody.

"I'm going to Mrs. Pryor's on Thursday," she said at last.

"All right."

"I'm going to wear my blue silk, and I'm going to be very nice to her. And if she asks me about you, I'm going to tell her you're thinking it over."

"All right, Lucy."

"And you'd better *be* thinking it over, Ed Corliss." She took her hand away, and picked up the little dress, and folded it, and put it in the sewing-basket, and shut the lid with a snap. "Because I'm not going back to live with my mother and Fred, with a baby on my hip like one of your peach women. I'm not. You can be a hero if you want to, but you can't make me be one."

She went into the bedroom, and Ed heard her undressing in the dark, and the creak of the springs as she lay down; and he sat on at the kitchen table, under the bare electric bulb, with the cold pork chop bone in front of him and the clock ticking on the shelf. Outside, far off down by the railroad yards, a switch engine was whistling; and somewhere down there, he knew, there were four hundred women asleep in shacks and boarding houses, or lying awake, wondering how long they could hold out, and whether there would be anything to eat on Saturday. They did not know Ed Corliss, nor care about him, and if he wrote the articles they would never know who had written them. That was the convenience of the system; nobody ever had to see anybody's face.

He got up after a while, and turned off the light, and stood in the dark kitchen; and he thought that it was a strange world, in which the hardest thing a man could do was to tell the truth in print, and the easiest was to lie and be paid for it, and in which the person who would suffer most from his telling the truth was the person he loved best in the world, who was lying in the next room pretending to be asleep.

Here is an excerpt of Upton Sinclair's writing, to show you their style:

Soon after this it was time for Bunny to visit his mother. Bunny’s mother did not bear Dad’s name, as other boys’ mothers do; she was called Mrs. Lang, and lived in a bungalow on the outskirts of Angel City. There was an arrangement whereby she had a right to have Bunny with her one week in every six months; Bunny always knew when this time was approaching, and looked forward to it with mixed emotions. His mother was sweet, and gave him the petting which he missed at other times; “pretty little Mamma,” was her name for herself. But in other ways the visit was embarrassing, because there were matters supposed to be kept hidden from Bunny, but which he could not help guessing. Mamma would question him about Dad’s affairs, and Bunny knew that Dad did not wish his affairs talked about. Then too, Mamma complained that she never had enough money; Dad allowed her only two hundred dollars a month, and how could a young and charming grass-widow exist on such a sum? Her garage bill was always unpaid, and she would tell Bunny about it, and expect him to tell Dad—but Dad would evade hearing. And next time, Mamma would cry, and say that Jim was a tyrant and a miser. The situation was especially difficult just now, because Mamma had read about the new well in the papers, and knew just how much money Dad had; she unfolded to Bunny a plan, that he should try to persuade Dad to increase her allowance, but without having Dad suspect that she had suggested it. And this, right after Bunny had renounced the luxury of small lies! Also there was the mystery about Mamma’s friends. There were always gentlemen friends who came to see her while Bunny was there, and who might or might not be agreeable to Bunny. When he came home, Aunt Emma would ask him questions, from which it was evident that she wanted to know about these gentlemen friends, but didn’t want Bunny to know that she wanted to know. Bunny noticed that Dad never referred to such matters; he never asked any questions about Mamma, and Aunt Emma always did her asking out of Dad’s presence. All this had a peculiar effect upon Bunny. Just as Dad kept a safe deposit box at the bank, into which nobody ever looked but himself, so Bunny kept a secret place in his own mind. Outwardly, he was a cheerful and frank little fellow, if somewhat too mature for his years; but all the time he was leading a dual life—picking up ideas here and there, and carrying them off and hiding them, as a squirrel does nuts, so that he may come back at a later season and crack them open and nibble them. Some nuts were good and some were bad, and Bunny learned to judge them, and to throw away the bad ones. One thing was plain: there was something which men and women did, which they were all in a conspiracy to keep you from knowing that they did. It was a dark corner of life, mysterious and rather hateful. In the beginning, Bunny was loyal to his father, not trying to find out what his father didn’t want him to know. But this could not continue indefinitely, for the mind automatically seeks understanding. It was not merely that the birds and the chickens and the dogs in the street gave you hints; it was not merely that every street-boy knew, and was eager to explain; it was that the stupid grown-ups themselves persisted in saying things which you couldn’t help getting. It was Aunt Emma’s fixed conviction that every lady was after Dad; “setting her cap at him,” or “making sheep’s eyes at him”—she had many such phrases. And Dad always showed a queer embarrassment whenever he had been the least bit polite to any lady; he seemed to be concerned lest Bunny should share Aunt Emma’s suspicions. But the truth was, Bunny was irritated by his aunt, and learned to evade her questions, and not tell what Dad had said to the nice lady in the hotel at Lobos River, and whether or not the lady had had dinner with them. These worldly arts Bunny acquired, but all the time he was in secret revolt. Why couldn’t people talk plainly? Why did they have to be pretending, and whispering, and making you uncomfortable? Within a week after bringing in Ross-Bankside No. 1, Dad had a new derrick under way on the lease, and in another week he had it rigged up, and the old string of tools was on its way into the earth again. Also he had two new derricks under way, and two new strings in process of delivery. There would be four wells, standing on the four corners of a diamond-shaped figure, three hundred feet on the side. It was necessary to call house-movers, and take the Bankside homestead to another lot; but that didn’t trouble Mr. Bankside, who had already moved himself to an ocean-front palace near Dad, and bought himself a whole outfit of furniture, and a big new limousine, also a “sport-car,” in which to drive himself to the country club to play golf every afternoon. The Bankside family was accustoming itself to the presence of a butler, and Mrs. Bankside had been proposed at the most exclusive of the ladies’ clubs. Efficiency was the watch-word out here in the West, and when you decided to change your social status, you put the job right through. Dad and Bunny made another trip to Lobos River, and not without some difficulty they conquered the “jinx” in Number Two, and brought in a very good well. There were to be two more derricks here, and more tools to be bought and delivered. That was the way in the oil business, as fast as you got any money, you put it back into new drilling—and, of course, new responsibilities. You were driven to this by the forces inherent in the game. You were racing with other people, who were always threatening to get your oil. As soon as you had one well, you had to have “offset wells” to protect it from the people on every side who would otherwise get your oil. Also, you might have trouble in marketing your oil, and would begin to think, how nice to have your own refinery, and be entirely independent. But independence had its price, for then you would have to provide enough oil to keep the refinery going, and you would want a chain of filling-stations to get rid of your products. It was a hard game for the little fellow; and no matter how big you got, there was always somebody bigger! But Dad had no kick just now; everything was a-comin’ his way a-whoopin’. Right in the midst of his other triumphs it had occurred to him to take one of his old Antelope wells and go a little lower, and see what he found; he tried it—and lo and behold, at eight hundred feet farther down the darn thing went and blew its head off. They were in a new layer of oil-sands; and every one of these sixteen old wells, that had been on the pump for a couple of years, and were about played out, were ready to present Dad with a new fortune, at a cost of only a few thousand dollars each! But right away came a new problem; there was no pipe-line to this field, and there ought to be one. Dad wanted some of the other operators to go in with him, and he was going up there and make a deal. Then Bunny came to him, looking very serious. “Dad, have you forgotten, it’s close to the fifteenth of November.”

“What about it, son?”

“You promised we were going quail-shooting this year.”

“By gosh, that’s so! But I’m frightfully rushed jist now, son.”

“You’re working too hard, Dad; Aunt Emma says you’re putting a strain on your kidneys, the doctor has told you so.”

“Does he recommend a quail diet?” Bunny knew by Dad’s grin that he was going to make some concession. “Let’s take our camping things,” the boy pleaded, “and when you get through at Antelope, let’s come home by the San Elido valley.”

“The San Elido! But son, that’s fifty miles out of our way!”

“They say there’s no end of quail there, Dad.”

“Yes, but we can get quail a lot nearer home.”

“I know, Dad; but I’ve never been there, and I want to see it.”

“But what made you hit on that place?” Bunny was embarrassed, because he knew Dad was going to think he was “queer.” Nevertheless, he persisted. “That’s where the Watkins family live.”

“Watkins family—who are they?”

“Don’t you remember that boy, Paul, that I met one night when you were talking about the lease?”

“Gosh, son! You still a-frettin’ about that boy?”

“I met Mrs. Groarty on the street yesterday, and she told me about the family; they’re in dreadful trouble, they’re going to lose their ranch to the bank because they can’t meet the interest on the mortgage, and Mrs. Groarty says she can’t think what they’ll do. You know Mrs. Groarty didn’t get any money herself—at least, she spent her bonus money for units, and she isn’t getting anything out of them, and has to live on what her husband gets as a night watchman.”

“What you want to do about it?”

“I want you to buy that mortgage, Dad; or anything, so the Watkinses can stay in their home. It’s wicked that people should be turned out like that, when they’re doing the best they can.”

“There’s plenty o’ people bein’ turned out when they don’t meet their obligations, son.”

“But when it’s not their fault, Dad?”

column308:
Rodney Hale had been at the university just three weeks when he made up his mind to go and see his cousin Mattie; and it took him another week to find out where she lived, because nobody in his family would tell him. That was the way of it with the Dunlaps. They were his mother's people on her sister's side, and there had been a quarrel, so long ago that Rodney had been only twelve when it happened; and since then the name of Aunt Lou was spoken in the Hale household only in a certain tone of voice, the tone which grown-ups use for things that are sad, and also a little shameful, and also not to be inquired into by the young. Rodney had inquired, of course; but his mother would say, "Your Aunt Lou made her own choice, dear," and change the subject. His father would not say anything at all, but would look at his newspaper; and his father, being the president of the Hale Packing Corporation, with three canneries in the Santa Clara valley and a fourth going up at Modesto, had a great deal of newspaper to look at.

What Rodney knew was this. Aunt Lou had been the pretty one of the two sisters, and she had married a railroad man, a brakeman on the Southern Pacific. That had been bad enough. But then something else had happened, which had to do with money and with Rodney's father, and after that there were no more Christmas boxes and no more summer visits to the ranch at Los Gatos, where Rodney and Mattie had built a dam across the creek and caught crawdads in a tomato can. Rodney had cried about it at the time, and been told he was too big a boy to cry; so he had stopped crying, and put the matter away. But now he was nineteen, and a freshman at Berkeley, with a roadster of his own and an allowance of a hundred and fifty dollars a month, and he had discovered that a man who is old enough to drive a roadster is old enough to find out a few things for himself.

He found the address in the end through an old servant of his grandmother's, who still exchanged letters with Aunt Lou at Christmas. It was in West Oakland, down near the yards; and Rodney drove there on a Saturday afternoon in November, across the flats where the Chinese truck-gardens used to be, and through streets of little frame houses, all built alike, with the paint scaling off them and the yards full of chickens and children. The air smelled of coal-smoke, and every few minutes there came the clang and shudder of a switch-engine, and the long crash of freight-cars bumping one against another, like a row of dominoes going down. Rodney had never been in this part of town before, though he had lived all his life within forty miles of it; and he found that he was embarrassed by his roadster, which was a bright canary-yellow and had cost twenty-six hundred dollars, and which every child on the block came running to look at.

The house had a number painted on the step, and a geranium in a coffee-can on the porch rail. Rodney knocked, and stood waiting with his heart thumping, wondering what he was going to say, and whether they would even let him in. Then the door opened, and there stood a young woman in a gray skirt and a white shirtwaist, with her sleeves rolled up and flour on her hands; a tall girl, with a wide mouth and straight brows and a lot of brown hair pinned up anyhow. She looked at him, and then past him at the roadster, and then at him again.

"Well, for the land's sake," she said. "If it isn't Roddy!"

"Hello, Mattie," said Rodney; and suddenly he didn't know what to do with his hands.

"You've grown about a foot. Last time I saw you, you came up to here on me." She held a floury hand at the level of her chin. "Now look at you. Is that thing yours?"

"Dad gave it to me. When I went up to college."

"I'll bet he did." She said it without any meanness, just as a matter of observation; the way you would say it was going to rain. "Well, don't stand there; come in, and mind the step, it's loose. Mother's lying down, she's had one of her headaches. Pa's down at the lodge hall. I'm making a pie."

So Rodney went in, and sat on a kitchen chair while his cousin made a pie. It was a small kitchen, with a wood-stove and an oilcloth on the table and a calendar from a grocery store on the wall; and it was very clean, but everything in it was old, and had been mended. Rodney noticed that the chair he sat on had a leg wired together, and that the cup she gave him coffee in had a crack down the side; and he was ashamed of himself for noticing, and ashamed of his tweed suit, which he had bought because all the fellows at the fraternity house wore them. But Mattie did not seem to be ashamed of anything. She rolled out her dough with a beer bottle, because the rolling-pin had gone somewhere, and she talked to him as if they had seen each other the week before.

"You remember the dam?" she said.

"Do I! You fell in, and your dress was ruined, and you made me tell Aunt Lou it was my fault."

"It was your fault. You said the rock would hold."

"Well, it held for me."

"You weighed about as much as a wet cat." She laughed, a big, free laugh, with her head back. "And the crawdads. We had forty-one of them in that can, and you wanted to take them home in the automobile, and your mother wouldn't have it. You cried all the way to the gate."

"I didn't cry."

"You bawled like a calf, Roddy. Don't you go lying to me, now you're a college man."

So that was all right; and for a while they talked about the old times, the hay-barn and the swing, and the old horse called Dutch that wouldn't go past the Japanese man's strawberry patch without stopping to eat. It was strange to Rodney how much he remembered, once she set him going; things he had not thought about in seven years came crowding back, so that he felt like a boy again. But all the time there was something else waiting, which neither of them had touched; and at last Rodney asked about it, because he had made up his mind on the drive over that he would not go home without knowing.

"Mattie, what happened? Why did we stop coming?"

She was crimping the edge of the pie, and she went on crimping it for a while before she answered. "Don't they tell you?"

"They don't tell me anything. Mother says Aunt Lou made her own choice. Dad won't talk about it at all."

"No, I don't suppose he would." She set the pie in the oven, and shut the door with her knee, and wiped her hands on her apron; then she sat down across the table from him, and looked at him straight, the way she had looked at him when they were children and she wanted to know if he was telling the truth. "Well, you're grown now, and I guess you've got a right to know. You remember Pa had a leg?"

"Had a—?"

"Two legs, I mean. He's got one now. He lost the other one under a box-car at Roseville, the winter I was thirteen. They were making up a train in the yards, and it was dark, and the coupling was a bad one—it had been reported bad three times, and they hadn't fixed it, because fixing couplings costs money and brakemen don't. He went in between to set the pin, and the car rolled, and that was that."

Rodney sat with his mouth open. "Gosh, Mattie! I never knew a thing about it."

"No. Well, you weren't meant to." She folded her hands on the oilcloth. "You know how it goes when a man gets hurt on the railroad, Roddy? Probably you don't. I'll tell you. While he's lying in the company hospital, with the ether hardly out of him, there comes a nice man in a gray suit, very sympathetic, and he says the company's terribly sorry, and they want to do the right thing; and he's got a paper here, and a check for four hundred dollars, and if your Pa will just sign, he'll have the money that afternoon, and save all the bother of lawyers. And your Ma is sitting there crying, and the rent's due, and there's three children at home; so your Pa signs. And then afterward you find out what the paper was. It was a release; it said the company wasn't to blame, and he'd never bring suit. Four hundred dollars, for a leg and a job. They call that man the claim agent; and they pay him a bonus for every paper he gets signed."

Rodney had nothing to say to this; it was entirely outside his experience. He knew about railroads, of course; his father shipped forty carloads of canned apricots out of the valley every season, and the traffic manager of the Southern Pacific came to dinner sometimes, a jolly, red-faced man who played golf and told stories about the Chinese. But it had never occurred to Rodney that a railroad was a thing which might cut off a man's leg, and then send around a fellow in a gray suit to settle the matter for four hundred dollars.

"But what did that have to do with us?" he asked.

"Ma wrote to your father," said Mattie. "She asked him to lend us money for a lawyer. There was a lawyer in Sacramento who said the release could be broke, because Pa had been under the ether and didn't know what he was signing. He said there might be ten thousand dollars in it, maybe more. And your father wrote back—" she stopped.

"Go on. Please."

"He wrote back that he did a large business with the railroad, and he couldn't afford to be mixed up in a suit against them; and that he thought Ma had better take what was offered and be grateful; and he sent her a check for a hundred dollars. And Ma sent the check back to him in an envelope, torn in two. And that was the end of it."

There was a silence in the kitchen. The pie was beginning to smell, and out in the yards a switch-engine went by, and the cups rattled on the shelf. Rodney sat looking at the crack in his coffee-cup, and he felt the blood coming up into his face, and burning there, as if somebody had slapped him. He knew that it was true; he knew it the moment she said it, because it explained so many things—his mother's voice, and his father's newspaper, and the way the subject was always changed. It was just the sort of thing his father would do. Not out of meanness; Rodney's father was not a mean man; he gave a great deal to the Community Chest, and had his name on a bronze plaque at the hospital in San Jose. But he was a man who thought about business first, and he had a way of saying, "You've got to look at the whole picture, son," which meant that the people who got hurt were a very small part of the picture, and you couldn't let them spoil the rest of it.

"I'm sorry, Mattie," said Rodney, at last. "I'm awfully sorry."

"Well, it wasn't your doing. You were a kid."

"I know, but—" he did not know how to finish. "What did you do? After, I mean?"

"Oh, we got along." She shrugged her shoulders. "Pa got a job as crossing-watchman; they give those to the crippled men, it looks well, and it don't cost much. Ma took in sewing. I quit high school and went to work at the telephone exchange; I'm on the long-distance board now, I get eighteen a week. My brother Will's a machinist's helper at the Moore shipyard, and little Ellen's still in school, she's going to finish if it kills us. So you see, we're doing fine."

She said it with a kind of grim cheerfulness, as if daring him to pity her; and Rodney didn't dare. Instead he asked about the telephone exchange, and she told him. It was the first time he had ever thought about what was at the other end of a telephone; you took the receiver off the hook, and said "Number, please," and the number came, like a miracle of nature. But it seemed that the miracle consisted of a long row of girls sitting on stools, with head-sets clamped over their ears and their hands flying among the plugs, a hundred and fifty calls to the hour; and a supervisor walking up and down behind them, timing them with a watch, and writing down their names if they said anything except the phrases printed on a card. You were not allowed to speak to the girl beside you; you were not allowed to leave your stool except at the regular relief, and if you had to go to the toilet out of turn, you held up your hand like a child in school. A great many of the girls broke down after a few years, Mattie said, from the strain on their nerves; the company had a rest-room with a couch in it, and they would lie there and cry, and then go back to the board, because there was rent to pay.

"But we've got a union now," she added, and her eyes lit up. "We're getting it together, anyhow. There's a girl from Seattle, she came down last spring, and she's been talking to us at noon. The company don't like it; they had two girls fired last month, they said for being impertinent to a subscriber. But you can't fire everybody; who'd run the boards?"

"Are you in it?"

"Of course I'm in it. I'm the secretary of our local."

Rodney looked at her with a new kind of respect. He was thinking of the girls he knew; the girls who came to the dances at the fraternity house, in their beaded dresses, and talked about the football team and the new Paramount picture, and which sorority had the best house on Piedmont Avenue. He could not imagine any of them being secretary of anything, except perhaps the committee for a tea. And it came to him that Mattie, who had quit school at thirteen, knew a great deal more about the world than he did, who was going to be a Bachelor of Arts; she knew how it was put together, and who did the work, and who got the money. He had a sudden uncomfortable feeling that she knew a good deal about his father's canneries, too; and that if he asked her, she would tell him things he would rather not hear.

He did not ask. Instead, she asked him about college, and he told her: about the fraternity, and how the fellows had looked him over during rushing week, and how they had taken him because his father was Hale of Hale Packing; about the courses, which were mostly dull, except one in economics where the professor talked a great deal about the law of supply and demand. Mattie wanted to know what the law of supply and demand was, and Rodney explained it to her, as well as he could; how wages were fixed by the number of workers looking for jobs, and prices by the number of people wanting to buy, and how everything came out even in the end, by a sort of natural law, like gravitation.

"And does your professor say what law it was that fixed Pa's leg at four hundred dollars?" asked Mattie.

Rodney opened his mouth, and shut it again. "Well, I guess—I guess that would be supply and demand too. There were lots of brakemen."

"There's always lots of brakemen," said Mattie. "That's the trouble with being one."

Then the bedroom door opened, and Aunt Lou came out, holding on to the door-frame; a small, faded woman, with gray in her hair, and lines about her mouth, so that Rodney hardly knew her at first. She was the pretty one, his mother had always said; but she did not look pretty now, only tired. She stood staring at him, and Rodney got up, knocking over his chair, and picked it up again, and stood there red to the ears.

"Hello, Aunt Lou."

"Why, it's Rodney!" She came forward, and took both his hands, and looked up into his face, and her eyes filled with tears. "Rodney! Why, you look just like your grandfather. Does your mother know you're here?"

"No, ma'am," said Rodney. "I didn't tell her."

Aunt Lou's face did something complicated; it seemed to be pleased and frightened and sad, all at once. "Well," she said, "well—I guess that's your own business. Sit down, child. Mattie, did you give him coffee? Is that the cracked cup? For pity's sake, give him the good one."

"He don't mind the cracked cup, Ma. He's a college man; he's studying economics."

So then there was more coffee, in the good cup, which had roses on it; and presently there was a thumping on the porch, and Uncle Ned came in on his crutch, a big, heavy man with a red neck and a gray mustache; and he stood in the doorway and looked at Rodney a long time, without saying a word. Rodney stood up again, and waited, not knowing whether he was going to be thrown out of the house. But Uncle Ned only said, "So you're Hattie's boy," and hung his hat on a nail, and lowered himself into the rocking-chair by the stove, laying the crutch across his knees. "Drove that yeller wagon down here, did you? Half the kids on Pine Street are a-settin' in it."

"Gosh!" said Rodney, and started for the door; but Uncle Ned laughed, a short laugh, like a bark.

"Let 'em set. Won't hurt it none. Only thing like it most of 'em will ever set in." And then, looking at Rodney sideways, "How's your Pa?"

"He's fine, sir. He's building a new plant at Modesto."

"I read about it in the paper. Doin' well, ain't he?"

"Yes, sir."

"Well," said Uncle Ned, and rocked a while, and looked at the stove; and Rodney waited for the rest, but there wasn't any. That was all Uncle Ned ever said about Rodney's father, then or afterward. But Rodney understood that it was a great deal; and he went home that evening with more to think about than he had ever had in his life.

They had made him stay to supper; there was stew, and the pie, which was apple, and very good. Will came home from the shipyard, black to the elbows, and scrubbed himself at the sink, and turned out to be a lanky, cheerful fellow who wanted to know how many cylinders the roadster had, and what she would do on the straightaway; and little Ellen, who was fourteen, sat across the table and stared at Rodney the whole meal, as if he were a moving-picture actor. When it was over, Mattie walked him out to the car, and drove off the last of the children, who were sitting on the hood and taking turns at the horn. It was dark by now, and the street-lamps were lit, and a long freight was going by at the end of the block, the cars sliding past one after another, with the brakemen walking on top against the sky.

"Will you come back?" said Mattie.

"Of course I will. If you'll have me."

"Well, I'll have you. Only you'd better think about it first." She stood with her hand on the door of the roadster, looking at him; and for a moment she was the little girl on the creek bank again, daring him to cross on the rocks. "It's going to make trouble for you at home, Roddy. You know that, don't you?"

"I don't care."

"You will, though. You'll care a lot. You'll have to choose, sooner or later; that's the way it is. They'll make you." And then she laughed, and slapped the door of the car. "Go on, now. And next time, leave this thing at home and come on the street-car, like a human being. You're ruining the morals of the neighborhood."

So Rodney drove back to Berkeley, through the streets of little houses, and across the flats, and up the hill to the fraternity house, where the fellows were getting ready for a dance, and somebody was playing "Yes, Sir, That's My Baby" on the phonograph. Somebody yelled to him, wanting to know where he'd been all day; and Rodney said, "Oh, just visiting some relatives," and went upstairs to his room, and sat on the bed without turning on the light.

He was thinking about a great many things; about four hundred dollars, and a check torn in two, and a hundred and fifty girls on stools holding up their hands to go to the toilet; about the law of supply and demand, which was like gravitation, and which had never yet been known to make a box-car roll the other way. He was thinking that his father had known all this, and had sat at the head of the dinner table every night for seven years, carving the roast and asking Rodney about his grades. And under it all, he was thinking that Mattie was right, and he was going to have to choose; and he was afraid, because he did not know yet which way he would go.

Here is an excerpt of Upton Sinclair's writing, to show you their style:

Soon after this it was time for Bunny to visit his mother. Bunny’s mother did not bear Dad’s name, as other boys’ mothers do; she was called Mrs. Lang, and lived in a bungalow on the outskirts of Angel City. There was an arrangement whereby she had a right to have Bunny with her one week in every six months; Bunny always knew when this time was approaching, and looked forward to it with mixed emotions. His mother was sweet, and gave him the petting which he missed at other times; “pretty little Mamma,” was her name for herself. But in other ways the visit was embarrassing, because there were matters supposed to be kept hidden from Bunny, but which he could not help guessing. Mamma would question him about Dad’s affairs, and Bunny knew that Dad did not wish his affairs talked about. Then too, Mamma complained that she never had enough money; Dad allowed her only two hundred dollars a month, and how could a young and charming grass-widow exist on such a sum? Her garage bill was always unpaid, and she would tell Bunny about it, and expect him to tell Dad—but Dad would evade hearing. And next time, Mamma would cry, and say that Jim was a tyrant and a miser. The situation was especially difficult just now, because Mamma had read about the new well in the papers, and knew just how much money Dad had; she unfolded to Bunny a plan, that he should try to persuade Dad to increase her allowance, but without having Dad suspect that she had suggested it. And this, right after Bunny had renounced the luxury of small lies! Also there was the mystery about Mamma’s friends. There were always gentlemen friends who came to see her while Bunny was there, and who might or might not be agreeable to Bunny. When he came home, Aunt Emma would ask him questions, from which it was evident that she wanted to know about these gentlemen friends, but didn’t want Bunny to know that she wanted to know. Bunny noticed that Dad never referred to such matters; he never asked any questions about Mamma, and Aunt Emma always did her asking out of Dad’s presence. All this had a peculiar effect upon Bunny. Just as Dad kept a safe deposit box at the bank, into which nobody ever looked but himself, so Bunny kept a secret place in his own mind. Outwardly, he was a cheerful and frank little fellow, if somewhat too mature for his years; but all the time he was leading a dual life—picking up ideas here and there, and carrying them off and hiding them, as a squirrel does nuts, so that he may come back at a later season and crack them open and nibble them. Some nuts were good and some were bad, and Bunny learned to judge them, and to throw away the bad ones. One thing was plain: there was something which men and women did, which they were all in a conspiracy to keep you from knowing that they did. It was a dark corner of life, mysterious and rather hateful. In the beginning, Bunny was loyal to his father, not trying to find out what his father didn’t want him to know. But this could not continue indefinitely, for the mind automatically seeks understanding. It was not merely that the birds and the chickens and the dogs in the street gave you hints; it was not merely that every street-boy knew, and was eager to explain; it was that the stupid grown-ups themselves persisted in saying things which you couldn’t help getting. It was Aunt Emma’s fixed conviction that every lady was after Dad; “setting her cap at him,” or “making sheep’s eyes at him”—she had many such phrases. And Dad always showed a queer embarrassment whenever he had been the least bit polite to any lady; he seemed to be concerned lest Bunny should share Aunt Emma’s suspicions. But the truth was, Bunny was irritated by his aunt, and learned to evade her questions, and not tell what Dad had said to the nice lady in the hotel at Lobos River, and whether or not the lady had had dinner with them. These worldly arts Bunny acquired, but all the time he was in secret revolt. Why couldn’t people talk plainly? Why did they have to be pretending, and whispering, and making you uncomfortable? Within a week after bringing in Ross-Bankside No. 1, Dad had a new derrick under way on the lease, and in another week he had it rigged up, and the old string of tools was on its way into the earth again. Also he had two new derricks under way, and two new strings in process of delivery. There would be four wells, standing on the four corners of a diamond-shaped figure, three hundred feet on the side. It was necessary to call house-movers, and take the Bankside homestead to another lot; but that didn’t trouble Mr. Bankside, who had already moved himself to an ocean-front palace near Dad, and bought himself a whole outfit of furniture, and a big new limousine, also a “sport-car,” in which to drive himself to the country club to play golf every afternoon. The Bankside family was accustoming itself to the presence of a butler, and Mrs. Bankside had been proposed at the most exclusive of the ladies’ clubs. Efficiency was the watch-word out here in the West, and when you decided to change your social status, you put the job right through. Dad and Bunny made another trip to Lobos River, and not without some difficulty they conquered the “jinx” in Number Two, and brought in a very good well. There were to be two more derricks here, and more tools to be bought and delivered. That was the way in the oil business, as fast as you got any money, you put it back into new drilling—and, of course, new responsibilities. You were driven to this by the forces inherent in the game. You were racing with other people, who were always threatening to get your oil. As soon as you had one well, you had to have “offset wells” to protect it from the people on every side who would otherwise get your oil. Also, you might have trouble in marketing your oil, and would begin to think, how nice to have your own refinery, and be entirely independent. But independence had its price, for then you would have to provide enough oil to keep the refinery going, and you would want a chain of filling-stations to get rid of your products. It was a hard game for the little fellow; and no matter how big you got, there was always somebody bigger! But Dad had no kick just now; everything was a-comin’ his way a-whoopin’. Right in the midst of his other triumphs it had occurred to him to take one of his old Antelope wells and go a little lower, and see what he found; he tried it—and lo and behold, at eight hundred feet farther down the darn thing went and blew its head off. They were in a new layer of oil-sands; and every one of these sixteen old wells, that had been on the pump for a couple of years, and were about played out, were ready to present Dad with a new fortune, at a cost of only a few thousand dollars each! But right away came a new problem; there was no pipe-line to this field, and there ought to be one. Dad wanted some of the other operators to go in with him, and he was going up there and make a deal. Then Bunny came to him, looking very serious. “Dad, have you forgotten, it’s close to the fifteenth of November.”

“What about it, son?”

“You promised we were going quail-shooting this year.”

“By gosh, that’s so! But I’m frightfully rushed jist now, son.”

“You’re working too hard, Dad; Aunt Emma says you’re putting a strain on your kidneys, the doctor has told you so.”

“Does he recommend a quail diet?” Bunny knew by Dad’s grin that he was going to make some concession. “Let’s take our camping things,” the boy pleaded, “and when you get through at Antelope, let’s come home by the San Elido valley.”

“The San Elido! But son, that’s fifty miles out of our way!”

“They say there’s no end of quail there, Dad.”

“Yes, but we can get quail a lot nearer home.”

“I know, Dad; but I’ve never been there, and I want to see it.”

“But what made you hit on that place?” Bunny was embarrassed, because he knew Dad was going to think he was “queer.” Nevertheless, he persisted. “That’s where the Watkins family live.”

“Watkins family—who are they?”

“Don’t you remember that boy, Paul, that I met one night when you were talking about the lease?”

“Gosh, son! You still a-frettin’ about that boy?”

“I met Mrs. Groarty on the street yesterday, and she told me about the family; they’re in dreadful trouble, they’re going to lose their ranch to the bank because they can’t meet the interest on the mortgage, and Mrs. Groarty says she can’t think what they’ll do. You know Mrs. Groarty didn’t get any money herself—at least, she spent her bonus money for units, and she isn’t getting anything out of them, and has to live on what her husband gets as a night watchman.”

“What you want to do about it?”

“I want you to buy that mortgage, Dad; or anything, so the Watkinses can stay in their home. It’s wicked that people should be turned out like that, when they’re doing the best they can.”

“There’s plenty o’ people bein’ turned out when they don’t meet their obligations, son.”

“But when it’s not their fault, Dad?”

“It would take a lot of bookkeeping to figger jist whose fault it is; and the banks don’t keep books that way.” Then seeing the protest in Bunny’s face, “You’ll find, son there’s a lot o’ harsh things in the world, that ain’t in your power to change. You’ll jist have to make up your mind to that, sooner or later.”

“But Dad, there’s four children there, and three of them are girls, and where are they to go? Paul is away, and they haven’t any way to let him know what’s happened. Mrs. Groarty showed me a picture of them, Dad; they’re good, kind people, you can see they’ve never done anything but work hard. Honest, Dad, I couldn’t be happy if I didn’t help them. You said you’d buy me a car some day, and I’d rather you took the money and bought that mortgage. It’s less than a couple of thousand dollars, and that’s nothing to you.”

“I know, son; but then you’ll get them on your hands—” “No, they’re not like that, they’re proud; Mrs. Groarty says they wouldn’t take money from you, any more than Paul would. But if you bought the mortgage from the bank, they couldn’t help that. Or you might buy the ranch, Dad, and rent it back to them. Paul says there’s oil on that ranch—at least his Uncle Eby had seen it on top of the ground.”

“There’s thousands of ranches jist like that in California, son. Oil on top of the ground don’t mean anything special.”

“Well, Dad, you’ve always said you wanted to try some wild-catting; and you know, that’s the only way you’ll ever get what you talk about—a whole big tract that belongs to you, with no royalties to pay, and nobody to butt in. So let’s take a chance on Paradise, and drive through there and camp out a few days and get some quail, and we’ll see what we think of it, and we’ll help those poor people, and give your kidneys a rest at the same time.” So Dad said all right; and he went away thinking to himself: “Gosh! Funny kid!” The San Elido valley lay on the edge of the desert, and you crossed a corner of the desert to get to it; a bare wilderness of sun-baked sand and rock, with nothing but grey, dusty desert plants. You sped along upon a fine paved road, but the land was haunted by the souls of old-time pioneers who had crossed it in covered wagons or with pack-mules, and had left their bones beside many a trail. Even now, you had to be careful when you went off into side-trails across these wastes; every now and then a car would get stuck with an empty radiator, and the people would be lucky to get out alive. You could get water if you sunk a deep well; and so there were fruit ranches and fields of alfalfa here and there. There came long stretches where the ground was white, like salt; that was alkali, Dad said, and it made this country a regular boob-trap. The stranger from the East would come in and inspect a nice fruit ranch, and would think he was making a good bargain to get the land next door for a hundred dollars an acre; he would set out his fruit-trees and patiently water them, and they wouldn’t grow; nothing would grow but a little alfalfa, and maybe there was too much alkali for that. The would-be rancher would have to pull up the trees, and obliterate the traces of them, and set a real-estater to hunting for another boob. Strapped to the running-board of Dad’s car, on the right hand side where Bunny sat, was a big bundle wrapped in a water-proof cover; they were camping out—which meant that the mind of a boy was back amid racial memories, the perils and excitements of ten thousand years ago. Tightly clutched in Bunny’s two hands were a couple of repeating shot-guns; he held these for hours, partly because he liked the feel of them, and partly because they had to be carried in the open—if you shut them up in the compartment they would be “concealed weapons,” and that was against the law. Near the head of the valley a dirt road went off, and a sign said: “Paradise, eight miles.” They wound up a little pass, with mountains that seemed to be tumbled heaps of rock, of every size and color. There were fruit ranches, the trees now bare of leaves, with trunks calcimined white, and young trees with wire netting about them, to keep away the rabbits. The first rains of the season had fallen, and new grass was showing—the California spring, which begins in the fall. The pass broadened out; there were ranch-houses scattered here and there, and the village of Paradise—one street, with a few scattered stores, sheltered under eucalyptus trees that made long shadows in the late afternoon light. Dad drew up at the filling station, which was also a feed-store. “Can you tell me where is the Watkins ranch?”

“There’s two Watkinses,” said the man. “There’s old Abel Watkins—” “That’s the one!” exclaimed Bunny.

“He’s got a goat-ranch, over by the slide. It ain’t so easy to find. Was you plannin’ to get there tonight?”

“We shan’t worry if we get lost,” said Dad; “we got a campin’ outfit.” So the man gave them complicated directions. You took the lane back of the school-house, and you made several jogs, and then there were about sixteen forks, and you must get the right one, and you followed the slide that took the water down to Roseville, and it was the fourth arroyo after you had passed old man Tucker’s sheep-ranch, with the little house up under the pepper trees. And so they started and followed a winding road that had apparently been laid out by sheep, and the sun set behind the dark hills, and the clouds turned pink, and they dodged rocks that were too high for the clearance of the car and crawled down into little gullies, and up again with a constant shifting of gears. There was no need to ask about the quail, for the hills echoed with the melodious double call of the flocks gathering for the night.

“By gosh, that’s so! But I’m frightfully rushed jist now, son.”

“You’re working too hard, Dad; Aunt Emma says you’re putting a strain on your kidneys, the doctor has told you so.”

“Does he recommend a quail diet?” Bunny knew by Dad’s grin that he was going to make some concession. “Let’s take our camping things,” the boy pleaded, “and when you get through at Antelope, let’s come home by the San Elido valley.”

“The San Elido! But son, that’s fifty miles out of our way!”

“They say there’s no end of quail there, Dad.”

“Yes, but we can get quail a lot nearer home.”

“I know, Dad; but I’ve never been there, and I want to see it.”

“But what made you hit on that place?” Bunny was embarrassed, because he knew Dad was going to think he was “queer.” Nevertheless, he persisted. “That’s where the Watkins family live.”

“Watkins family—who are they?”

“Don’t you remember that boy, Paul, that I met one night when you were talking about the lease?”

“Gosh, son! You still a-frettin’ about that boy?”

“I met Mrs. Groarty on the street yesterday, and she told me about the family; they’re in dreadful trouble, they’re going to lose their ranch to the bank because they can’t meet the interest on the mortgage, and Mrs. Groarty says she can’t think what they’ll do. You know Mrs. Groarty didn’t get any money herself—at least, she spent her bonus money for units, and she isn’t getting anything out of them, and has to live on what her husband gets as a night watchman.”

“What you want to do about it?”

“I want you to buy that mortgage, Dad; or anything, so the Watkinses can stay in their home. It’s wicked that people should be turned out like that, when they’re doing the best they can.”

“There’s plenty o’ people bein’ turned out when they don’t meet their obligations, son.”

“But when it’s not their fault, Dad?”

“It would take a lot of bookkeeping to figger jist whose fault it is; and the banks don’t keep books that way.” Then seeing the protest in Bunny’s face, “You’ll find, son there’s a lot o’ harsh things in the world, that ain’t in your power to change. You’ll jist have to make up your mind to that, sooner or later.”

“But Dad, there’s four children there, and three of them are girls, and where are they to go? Paul is away, and they haven’t any way to let him know what’s happened. Mrs. Groarty showed me a picture of them, Dad; they’re good, kind people, you can see they’ve never done anything but work hard. Honest, Dad, I couldn’t be happy if I didn’t help them. You said you’d buy me a car some day, and I’d rather you took the money and bought that mortgage. It’s less than a couple of thousand dollars, and that’s nothing to you.”

“I know, son; but then you’ll get them on your hands—” “No, they’re not like that, they’re proud; Mrs. Groarty says they wouldn’t take money from you, any more than Paul would. But if you bought the mortgage from the bank, they couldn’t help that. Or you might buy the ranch, Dad, and rent it back to them. Paul says there’s oil on that ranch—at least his Uncle Eby had seen it on top of the ground.”

“There’s thousands of ranches jist like that in California, son. Oil on top of the ground don’t mean anything special.”

“Well, Dad, you’ve always said you wanted to try some wild-catting; and you know, that’s the only way you’ll ever get what you talk about—a whole big tract that belongs to you, with no royalties to pay, and nobody to butt in. So let’s take a chance on Paradise, and drive through there and camp out a few days and get some quail, and we’ll see what we think of it, and we’ll help those poor people, and give your kidneys a rest at the same time.” So Dad said all right; and he went away thinking to himself: “Gosh! Funny kid!” The San Elido valley lay on the edge of the desert, and you crossed a corner of the desert to get to it; a bare wilderness of sun-baked sand and rock, with nothing but grey, dusty desert plants. You sped along upon a fine paved road, but the land was haunted by the souls of old-time pioneers who had crossed it in covered wagons or with pack-mules, and had left their bones beside many a trail. Even now, you had to be careful when you went off into side-trails across these wastes; every now and then a car would get stuck with an empty radiator, and the people would be lucky to get out alive. You could get water if you sunk a deep well; and so there were fruit ranches and fields of alfalfa here and there. There came long stretches where the ground was white, like salt; that was alkali, Dad said, and it made this country a regular boob-trap. The stranger from the East would come in and inspect a nice fruit ranch, and would think he was making a good bargain to get the land next door for a hundred dollars an acre; he would set out his fruit-trees and patiently water them, and they wouldn’t grow; nothing would grow but a little alfalfa, and maybe there was too much alkali for that. The would-be rancher would have to pull up the trees, and obliterate the traces of them, and set a real-estater to hunting for another boob. Strapped to the running-board of Dad’s car, on the right hand side where Bunny sat, was a big bundle wrapped in a water-proof cover; they were camping out—which meant that the mind of a boy was back amid racial memories, the perils and excitements of ten thousand years ago. Tightly clutched in Bunny’s two hands were a couple of repeating shot-guns; he held these for hours, partly because he liked the feel of them, and partly because they had to be carried in the open—if you shut them up in the compartment they would be “concealed weapons,” and that was against the law. Near the head of the valley a dirt road went off, and a sign said: “Paradise, eight miles.” They wound up a little pass, with mountains that seemed to be tumbled heaps of rock, of every size and color. There were fruit ranches, the trees now bare of leaves, with trunks calcimined white, and young trees with wire netting about them, to keep away the rabbits. The first rains of the season had fallen, and new grass was showing—the California spring, which begins in the fall. The pass broadened out; there were ranch-houses scattered here and there, and the village of Paradise—one street, with a few scattered stores, sheltered under eucalyptus trees that made long shadows in the late afternoon light. Dad drew up at the filling station, which was also a feed-store. “Can you tell me where is the Watkins ranch?”

“There’s two Watkinses,” said the man. “There’s old Abel Watkins—” “That’s the one!” exclaimed Bunny.

“He’s got a goat-ranch, over by the slide. It ain’t so easy to find. Was you plannin’ to get there tonight?”

“We shan’t worry if we get lost,” said Dad; “we got a campin’ outfit.” So the man gave them complicated directions. You took the lane back of the school-house, and you made several jogs, and then there were about sixteen forks, and you must get the right one, and you followed the slide that took the water down to Roseville, and it was the fourth arroyo after you had passed old man Tucker’s sheep-ranch, with the little house up under the pepper trees. And so they started and followed a winding road that had apparently been laid out by sheep, and the sun set behind the dark hills, and the clouds turned pink, and they dodged rocks that were too high for the clearance of the car and crawled down into little gullies, and up again with a constant shifting of gears. There was no need to ask about the quail, for the hills echoed with the melodious double call of the flocks gathering for the night.
