The last of the guests, Mr. and Mrs. Gus Tellefson, had been sped down the cement walk with shouts of "Don't take any wooden nickels!" and "You folks come see us now!" and Harlan T. Quist stood in the vestibule of his Dutch Colonial residence on Fairmount Heights, rubbing his hands together and surveying the field of his triumph.

It had been, he was certain, a corking good party. The creamed chicken in patty-shells had been commended by Dr. Lyman Pruitt, who was a nose-and-throat man and a judge of such things. The cocktails, compounded of gin procured from a bootlegger named Ernie (a mighty decent sort of fellow, for a bootlegger, and a veteran besides), had been pronounced by Gus Tellefson to be "the real McCoy, absolutely the genuine article." And Harlan himself had told, with what he felt to be unusual pith and color, the story of how he had talked the traffic officer at Grand Avenue and Fourth Street out of a ticket by the simple device of asking after the officer's mother. Everyone had laughed. Mrs. Pruitt had laughed until she wiped her eyes with a lace handkerchief which, Harlan had noticed, was not so fine as the handkerchiefs his own wife carried.

He turned off the porch light, which was of wrought iron in the Spanish Mission manner and had cost eighteen dollars and a half at the Bon Ton Lighting Shoppe, and he turned off the lamp in the living room, which had a parchment shade painted with a galleon in full sail, and he wound the eight-day clock on the mantel, as he had wound it every Saturday night for eleven years, and he went up the stairs humming "Yes, Sir, That's My Baby" in a baritone which he believed to be pleasing.

Harlan T. Quist was forty-seven years old. He was the vice-president and sales manager of the Quist-Dorrance Furnace Company, makers of the Comfy-Glo Hot-Air Furnace ("Banishes Winter From the Modern Home!"), and he was a member of the Monarch City Athletic Club, the Kiwanis, the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks, the Chamber of Commerce, and the First Methodist Church, in roughly that order of devotion. He was a plump man, pink about the jowls, with a gold Elk's tooth on his watch-chain and rimless spectacles which he believed gave him a scholarly appearance on the rare occasions when he read anything longer than the American Magazine. He held that Monarch City, with its population of two hundred and sixty-one thousand souls (by the census of 1920, and a darn sight more by now, believe you me), was the finest little city of its size in the United States, possessing as it did the second-largest bicycle-sprocket works in the Middle West, a new nine-story hotel with running ice-water in every room, and a citizenry of such pep and progressiveness as was not to be found in your effete East nor yet in your sun-soaked California, whatever they might claim out there with their oranges.

He believed in Service, in Optimism, in the Republican Party, in the Protestant religion so long as it did not interfere with business, and in his wife.

His wife was sitting at her dressing-table when he came into the bedroom.

It was a pleasant room, as pleasant rooms were reckoned on Fairmount Heights. The twin beds were of walnut veneer, matched, with the new Slumber-King box springs that the advertisement had described as "Scientifically Engineered for the Restful Repose of the Busy Executive." There was a cretonne-covered chaise longue upon which no one had ever reclined. There was a reading lamp with a ruffled pink shade, and on the night table beneath it a copy of "The Sheik," a box of Whitman's chocolates, and a bottle of Pepso-Tonic, which Harlan took for his stomach after banquets. Upon the wall hung a colored print of a moonlit lake with a birch-bark canoe, and beside it a photograph of their daughter, Dorothy, in her cap and gown from the State Normal School. The radiator, which was not a radiator but the ornamental register of the Comfy-Glo, breathed warmly from the baseboard, and Harlan never entered the room without feeling, faintly but genuinely, that he had personally caused that warmth to be.

Edna Quist was brushing her hair. She was a slender woman, still pretty in a faded and watchful way, and her hair, which she had refused to bob despite the urgings of the Thursday Bridge Club, fell nearly to her waist. She brushed it slowly, and in the mirror her eyes did not move.

"Well, sir!" said Harlan, sitting on the edge of his bed and unlacing his shoes with a grunt. "Well, sir, that was what I call a real party! Did you see Doc Pruitt go after that chicken? Say, I thought he'd eat the platter! And Gus—I tell you, Gus Tellefson is one of the finest fellows in this town, and I don't care who knows it. Little rough around the edges, maybe. But a real he-man. A regular fellow." He paused, one shoe in his hand. "You were mighty quiet, though, Edna. I noticed it. Mrs. Pruitt noticed it too, I bet."

"Did she?"

"Well, I don't know as she *noticed* it, exactly. I just mean—a hostess, you know, she's supposed to sort of keep the ball rolling." He set the shoe down beside its mate with a precision he had learned in the Spanish-American War, in which he had not fought but for which he had trained for eleven weeks at Camp Alger. "Not that I'm criticizing. Darned if I'm criticizing. You did fine. Swell. Only I thought maybe you had a headache."

"I haven't a headache."

"Well, that's good. That's fine." He began to unbutton his vest. "You want some of that Pepso-Tonic? Good for anything that ails you. Says so right on the bottle."

Edna put down the hairbrush. It was a silver hairbrush, part of a set he had bought her for their twentieth anniversary at Bauer & Wicklund's, Jewelers & Silversmiths, and he had paid forty-two dollars for the set, not counting the engraving. She looked at him in the mirror, and then she turned on the little bench and looked at him directly, and he was briefly and inexplicably uncomfortable, as though he had come into the office and found the cashier going through the books.

"Harlan," she said, "do you know what I was thinking all through dinner?"

"Why, no. What?"

"I was thinking that I have heard you tell the story about the policeman on Grand Avenue eleven times."

He laughed, a short, uncertain bark. "Well, it's a good story! Everybody laughed, didn't they? Darned if Lyman didn't laugh till he choked."

"Lyman Pruitt has heard it four times. I counted. And Myrtle Pruitt laughed the way she always laughs, and I laughed the way I always laugh, and Gus said 'That's a good one, Harl, that's a pip,' the way he always says it. And I sat there, and I looked at all of us around the table, with the candles going and the patty-shells and the little silver nut-dishes I bought in Chicago, and I thought: we are all dead. We have been dead for years, and nobody has had the decency to tell us."

Harlan stared at her. His vest hung open, and his suspenders drooped about his hips like the flags of a surrendered garrison.

"Why, Edna! That's a—that's a terrible thing to say!"

"Yes. I suppose it is."

"Well, I don't see what you want to go and say a thing like that for! On a Saturday night, and all! After a party that went off fine!" He was aware that his voice had risen, and he lowered it, glancing toward the door as though the neighbors, the Wendell Kimballs, might be listening across the side lawn, which, considering the thinness of the walls and the habits of Mrs. Kimball, they very well might. "Look here, now. You're just tired, that's all. Woman runs herself ragged getting ready for a dinner party, she gets tired, she gets to thinking things. Natural as anything. Why, I read an article just the other day—it was in the Saturday Evening Post, or maybe it was Collier's—about how the Modern Woman, with all her responsibilities in the home and her clubs and so on, she's under a terrific nervous strain. Terrific. That's all this is."

"No," said Edna. "That isn't all it is."

He waited. She folded her hands in her lap, and he saw, with the minor surprise of a man who has not looked at his wife's hands for a decade, that they were no longer young hands, that there were small brown spots on the backs of them, like the spots on a pear.

"I want to go away for a while," she said.

"Go away? Go away where? You mean down to the Lake? Why, sure, we'll open the cottage early this year, soon as the ice is out. I've been meaning to get that new screen porch put on anyway—"

"I don't mean the Lake. I hate the Lake. I have hated the Lake for nineteen summers. I mean New York."

"New York!"

He said it as he might have said Moscow, or Gomorrah.

"Ruth Halloway has taken an apartment on Twelfth Street, in the Village. You remember Ruth. We roomed together at Northwestern. She's been writing to me. She's working for a publisher—she reads manuscripts, she says, and there are people who come in the evenings and talk about books and pictures and the theater, real talk, Harlan, not about who's going to get the contract for the new viaduct. She says there's a room I could have. For the winter. Just for the winter."

Harlan stood up. Then he sat down again. Then, because it seemed to be expected of him, he stood up a second time and walked to the window and looked out at the street, at the arc light on the corner, at the Kimballs' new Buick sedan parked in their drive with the nose sticking out as Wendell always left it, which Harlan had several times mentioned was a hazard to the public.

"Well, I'll be darned," he said to the window. "I'll be eternally darned."

"Harlan—"

"No, now, you just let me get this straight." He turned around, and he had found his voice, the voice which had addressed the Kiwanis on "The Furnace Industry and the Future of the American Home," the voice which had won the Muncie and Fort Wayne territories from the Ozark Heat-Rite people in 1922. "You just let me get this straight. You want to go off to New York City. By yourself. And live in Greenwich Village, with a bunch of—of free-lovers and Bolsheviks and long-haired poets who never did a lick of honest work in their lives—"

"Ruth is not a Bolshevik. She votes for Coolidge, if it's any comfort to you."

"—and leave your home, and your husband, and your church work, and your clubs, and everything we've built up in this town, for—what? For *talk*? Is that what you said? *Talk*?"

"Yes," said Edna. "For talk."

"Well, by golly!" He began to pace, which was difficult in that room, for there was the chaise longue at one end and the dressing table at the other and the twin beds took up most of the middle, so that he had to go around the foot of his own bed and back again, like a bear in the city zoo in Riverside Park. "By golly, if that don't beat all! Talk! You can get all the talk you want right here! What's the matter with the Thursday Club? What's the matter with the Women's Auxiliary? What's the matter with the Monarch City Fortnightly? Didn't they have a fellow come out from the University just last month and lecture on—on Browning, or one of those birds?"

"Professor Teague. On Tennyson. He read 'Crossing the Bar,' and Mrs. Gollmar fell asleep, and afterward they served chicken salad, and Mrs. Hennessey said to me that it was a real privilege to have culture brought right to our doors, and then she asked me whether I thought her new marcel made her look stout." Edna's voice was quite level. "It did, Harlan. It made her look very stout. And I told her it didn't. I have been telling people things that weren't so for twenty-three years, and I am beginning to forget which things are."

He stopped pacing.

"Now just what do you mean by that?"

"I mean—oh, I don't know what I mean. That's the point, don't you see? I don't know what I think about anything. I only know what I'm supposed to think. I'm supposed to think that this is a fine little city, and that the Comfy-Glo is a fine furnace, and that Dorothy has married a fine young man—"

"Well, she has! Clarence is a mighty fine young fellow! Doing darn well down at the bank, and he's only twenty-six—"

"Clarence Wheelock," said Edna, "has the soul of a cash register, and he talks to Dorothy as though she were a not very bright customer. And Dorothy has stopped playing the piano. Did you know that? She told me last Tuesday. She said Clarence said it made too much noise when he was reading the paper."

Harlan opened his mouth and closed it. He had, as it happened, rather admired Clarence's firmness in the matter of the piano, and he was confused to find this admiration, which had been a sound, solid, Republican sort of admiration, suddenly held up before him like a fish gone bad.

He sat down heavily on his bed. The Slumber-King springs received him in scientific silence.

"Edna," he said, and his voice had changed; it had lost the Kiwanis ring and taken on something smaller and more frightened, the voice of a boy in a country schoolhouse who has been called to the front of the room and does not know why. "Edna, is there—you can tell me—is there some fella?"

She laughed. It was not a pleasant laugh, and it was not an unkind one; it was simply tired.

"No, Harlan. There's no fellow."

"Because if there's some fella—some of these smooth birds from the East, maybe, with spats on—I'd want to know. I'd have a right to know."

"There is no one. There's only me. I'd like to find out if there is still anyone named Edna. I used to think there was. When I was at Northwestern I wrote verses—did you know that? I had two of them printed in the college magazine. One was about the lake at night. Lake Michigan, I mean. Not your lake. I have them in a box in the attic, under Dorothy's baby clothes. I took them out last week and read them, and they weren't very good, but they were *mine*, Harlan. Nobody told me to think them."

He looked at her for a long time, and in the silence they could hear the Comfy-Glo in the cellar, ticking and sighing as it consumed its nightly ration of Pocahontas lump coal.

Then Harlan Quist did what he had done, with great success, to every difficult customer, every recalcitrant banker, every county commissioner who had ever stood between him and a signed contract. He changed his approach.

"Now, look here, Edna," he said, and he crossed the narrow space between the beds and sat down on the cretonne bench beside her, crowding her a little, and put his arm around her shoulders. "Look here. I've been thinking. You've been cooped up. That's what it is. A man gets so darn busy—what with the business, and the Kiwanis, and the drive for the new Y.M.C.A. building—he don't always notice that the Little Woman's sort of out of sorts. That's my fault. I admit it. I'm big enough to admit it. And what I say is, we'll take a trip. You and me. How about California? We'll go out on the Santa Fe, take one of those drawing-rooms, see the Grand Canyon and the Big Trees and all. Henry Dorrance went out last year, and he says the climate'd knock your eye out. Or—say! Say, how about Florida? They tell me you can buy a lot down there in Coral Gables for practically nothing and turn it over in six months for double. We could look into that. Combine business with pleasure."

"I don't want to see the Big Trees, Harlan."

"Well, then, New York! Sure! Why not? I'll go with you! I've been meaning to get on to the Heating Engineers' convention, and that's in the spring, and I could swing it so we'd have a week, maybe ten days, and we'd stay at the Commodore, and see a couple of good shows—they say that Abie's Irish Rose is a scream—and you could look up this Ruth what's-her-name and have a real visit with her. How'd that be?"

Edna looked at her hands.

"That isn't what I meant."

"I know it isn't what you meant. But a person's got to be practical. Now you just think about it a minute. Think how it'd look. Mrs. Harlan T. Quist goes traipsing off alone to Greenwich Village for the whole winter. Why, the whole town'd be talking! Myrtle Pruitt'd have it all over the Country Club in two days! They'd say we were getting a divorce, that's what they'd say. And it'd get around to the trade. You know how it is. A man in my position—people judge a man by his home. They want to know he's got things running smooth. Henry Dorrance's always saying, 'Harl, a man's home is his best advertisement.'"

"Yes," said Edna. "He would say that."

"Well, it's true! You can't get around it. And then there's Dorothy. Think how she'd feel. And your Mother, at her age. And—and the expense, too, Edna. I'm not saying we can't afford it. We can afford anything we darn please, and I'm proud of it. But there's no sense throwing money away on some hall bedroom in the Village when you've got a nice home right here, with every modern convenience—the electric washer and the Frigidaire and the new radio console with the five tubes, that you said yourself you liked—"

He went on. He was, by profession and by temperament, a man who went on, and his arguments marched past her one by one, well-drilled and in good order: the arguments of Respectability, of Economy, of Family, of Civic Standing, of What People Would Say. He spoke of the Women's Auxiliary, which would not know how to get on without her. He spoke of the church bazaar. He spoke of her health, which he feared was not equal to the rigors of an Eastern winter, though it had survived forty-four Monarch City winters, which were of a ferocity famous throughout the Middle West. He spoke, at last, of himself, of how he would rattle around in the big house all alone, with nobody to come home to but Hilda the hired girl, and how he would not know where she kept his collar buttons.

And as he spoke Edna Quist felt the old walls rising about her—not the walls of the Dutch Colonial house on Fairmount Heights, with its sun-parlor and its two-car garage, but the other walls, the invisible ones, built of a thousand Thursday luncheons and a thousand Sunday dinners and a thousand evenings like this one, built of creamed chicken and patty-shells, of the eleven tellings of the story of the policeman on Grand Avenue, of her own small, practiced laughter. She felt them rise and close, gently, comfortably, like the warmth of the Comfy-Glo, and she thought that she ought to fight them, and she found that she did not know how.

"Perhaps," she said at last, "perhaps I'm tired. Perhaps you're right."

The Pullman from Chicago came into Vernon Falls at 4:52 in the afternoon. It was nineteen minutes late, which the Vernon Falls Clarion would not report, since the Clarion was devoted to the doctrine that nothing in Vernon Falls was ever late, small, or second-rate. The station was a new one, finished in 1924 at a cost of four hundred and eighty thousand dollars. It was built of a tawny brick which the architect had called Tuscan and the Chamber of Commerce called Progressive. Above its waiting-room a mural showed a Chippewa maiden handing a sheaf of wheat to a Railroad Engineer. The engineer looked embarrassed, as well he might, for the maiden was wearing remarkably little and he was wearing a great deal, including gauntlets.

Wendell Purdy stood on the platform beneath the mural. He had been standing there since 4:20, because he believed in Being On Hand.

He was forty-four. He was the proprietor of Purdy's Peerless Auto Laundry and Tire Emporium ("We Wash 'Em While You Wait — and You Won't Wait Long!"). He was a past vice-president of the Ever-Onward Luncheon Club, a deacon of the Second Methodist Church, and a man whose waistcoat had been let out twice in three years. His tailor called it Prosperity. His wife called it the Strawberry Shortcake. He wore a gray suit of a pattern which the clothier on Grant Avenue had described as "conservative yet snappy," a pearl-gray fedora, and an Ever-Onward button in his lapel the size of a dime. In his vest pocket were three cigars. Two of them were good, for his cousin. One was a cheap one, for himself. He was a little ashamed of this, and a little proud of the generosity.

He had not seen his cousin Harlan Fenstock in nineteen years.

In nineteen years Wendell had acquired a wife, two children, a six-room Dutch Colonial house in the Glenwood Heights addition, a seven-passenger sedan, a radio with a mahogany cabinet, a set of the Book of Knowledge, a lot in the Lakeview Cemetery, and a fixed opinion on every question of economics, theology, and the relative merits of the Republican and Democratic parties. In the same nineteen years, so far as Wendell could make out, Harlan had acquired New York.

They had been boys together on their grandmother's farm, eleven miles out on the Sauk River road. Wendell remembered the creek, and the hayloft, and a certain afternoon when Harlan had dared him to eat a green apple, and another afternoon when they had shot a crow with an air-rifle and then, horribly and without explanation, both cried. Those memories were the softest things Wendell owned, and he took them out seldom, as a man takes out a pocket-watch that has stopped. He was not sure what Harlan would remember. Harlan had gone to the University. Then he had gone to Chicago. Then he had gone to New York, where he did something with advertising which, according to his letters at Christmas, was "really rather more creative than it sounds."

Wendell had read the phrase aloud to his wife, Myrtis.

"Creative," he had said. "Well, I guess I'm pretty darn creative too, when it comes to figuring how to get a Hupmobile's whitewalls clean in four minutes flat."

Myrtis had said, "Now, Wen."

The train wheezed to a stop. Porters sprang down. A drummer in a checked suit got off, then a frightened old lady, then a woman in furs who looked as though she had been misdirected, then a dozen people who were plainly natives returning from the Twin Cities with parcels. And then, last of all, a slender man in a soft brown hat and a belted overcoat of a tweed so rough it might have been woven from Scotch thistles. He carried a stick. He paused on the step and regarded Vernon Falls with a face of grave, kindly, and entirely unendurable tolerance.

"Harl!" bellowed Wendell. "Harl Fenstock, you old son of a gun!"

He galloped down the platform. He seized his cousin's gloved hand in both of his own and pumped it, and wanted very much to embrace him, and did not, because men in Vernon Falls did not do that except at funerals and when very drunk.

"Wendell," said Harlan. "My dear old Wen. You haven't changed a particle."

That was a lie, and both of them knew it, and both of them were grateful for it.

"Well, you certainly have, Harl! Look at you! Regular Fifth Avenue sport! What's that, a cane? By golly, I didn't know anybody still carried a cane, outside of the movies. Here, give me that grip. No, sir, I insist! You're company. Car's right outside. Wait'll you see her. Nineteen twenty-six Packard Eight, and she rides like a feather bed on a cloud. I'll get you out to the house in eleven minutes, and that's counting the traffic signals. We got traffic signals now, Harl. Seven of 'em. Electric."

"Really?" said Harlan. "How very metropolitan."

Wendell heard nothing in this but approval. He beamed.

II

The drive from the station to Glenwood Heights was conducted by Wendell in the manner of a guide at a cathedral, with this difference: the guide at a cathedral sometimes admits that a window is not original.

"That's the new Elks Temple, there on your right. Three stories and a roof garden. Cost one hundred and ninety thousand dollars and every nickel raised by subscription. That's the Farmers and Merchants Bank, the one with the columns. They're Corinthian, I think, or else Ionic; anyway they're solid granite, not just stuck on. Over there, see that? That's where the old Opera House was, where we went to see the Uncle Tom show that time, remember? Tore it down. Putting up a filling station. Twelve pumps. Biggest in the state outside of Minneapolis. And that, Harl" (he slowed the Packard reverently) "that's the Washington Junior High. Steam heat, a gymnasium, a cafeteria, and a manual-training shop that'd make Henry Ford sit up and take notice. Our Junior goes there. Darn smart kid, too, if I do say so. Wants to be an aviator. I tell him, all right, son, but you learn to read a balance sheet first."

"Charming," said Harlan, and lit a cigarette from a flat silver case. It was a Turkish cigarette, oval, with a gold tip. Wendell observed it out of the corner of his eye as a farmer observes a stranger's prize bull: with suspicion, with envy, and with a half-formed resolve to get one like it.

"Still smoke cigars, Wen?"

"Well, I'll tell you. I had a couple of extra-fine ones for you. Havana filler. Fifteen-centers."

"I'm afraid I gave them up. Bad for the palate. One can't taste wine."

"Wine?" Wendell slowed the car again, not reverently this time. "You mean to say you folks in New York just plain drink wine? Out loud?"

"My dear Wendell, everybody in New York drinks wine. Out loud, as you say. There's a little place on West Fifty-second Street, run by a perfectly delightful old Neapolitan, where you knock three times—"

"Well, I'll be darned. Now, I don't say I'm a fanatic about it. Man to man, I've been known to take a little nip of something at the Country Club after eighteen holes. But I mean to say, as a principle. The Eighteenth Amendment's the law of the land, and while I may not hold with every jot and tittle, I—well, I'll be darned."

He brooded on it for a block and a half, and then decided, with relief, that it was the kind of thing that made a fellow a regular cosmopolitan. Harlan blew a fine blue ring at the windshield, and was content to be a regular cosmopolitan.

III

Myrtis Purdy had been cooking for two days.

She was a plump, quick, anxious woman with hair that had been marcelled that morning at the Bon Ton Beauty Parlor at a cost of seventy-five cents and a certain amount of pain. She had read in the Ladies' Home Companion an article titled "Entertaining the Sophisticated Guest: Little Touches That Tell." In obedience to it she had laid on the dining-room table a centerpiece of wax fruit, four candles in holders of imitation pewter, a dish of salted almonds, and a little card at each place. The cards bore the diners' names in her best Palmer Method hand. There were only five diners, and every one of them would have known where to sit blindfolded, but the Ladies' Home Companion had been firm.

The menu was cream of tomato soup, pot roast with brown gravy, mashed potatoes, creamed peas in little paper cups, Parker House rolls, and a salad. The salad was a canned pear half upon a lettuce leaf, filled with cream cheese and topped with a maraschino cherry, and Myrtis considered it the most artistic object she had ever made with her hands. After that there would be a lemon chiffon pie, and coffee in the demitasse cups that had been a wedding present and had never before been used.

Harlan was kind about everything. He was, if anything, too kind. He praised the soup, which was out of a can, as "a really honest soup," and praised the wax fruit as "so restful." When the salad arrived he looked at it for a long moment, as an explorer might look at the totem of a tribe whose customs he had promised to respect. Then he said, "Do you know, I haven't seen one of these in years."

Myrtis glowed. Junior, who was fourteen and had already decided that his cousin Harlan talked like a sissy, kicked his sister Lorene under the table, and Lorene kicked him back. Wendell carved the pot roast as though it were a municipal improvement.

"Well, Harl," he said, "tell us about the big town. Tell us how you fellows live. I suppose you've got a pretty nifty apartment."

"Two rooms in the Village. Rather bare, really. A Brancusi drawing, some books, a bed, a gas-ring. I don't believe in possessions, Wen. They possess you."

"Two rooms?" Myrtis was stricken. "Why, Mr. Fenstock—Harlan—don't you have any kitchen?"

"There's a delicatessen on the corner."

"And you don't—you aren't—" Myrtis fluttered toward the delicate subject, and Wendell rescued her with the tact of a fire-engine.

"Never got hitched, eh, Harl? Well, it's never too late. Now, I know a mighty fine little woman over at the First National, private secretary to old man Hackett, smart as a whip and a darn good cook, Myrtis says—"

"Wendell!"

"—and she's a Congregationalist, but I guess that's no bar."

Harlan smiled, and the smile was weary, a little sad, and very well practiced. "I'm afraid, Wen, that I've come to feel marriage, in the bourgeois sense, is a rather outworn institution. Oh, for you, of course—for people who are rooted—it's quite right. I envy you, really. But for those of us who've had to make our lives among ideas—"

"Ideas," said Wendell. "Well, sure. I've got ideas too, Harl. Plenty. Why, I'll tell you an idea I had just last month. Fellow brings his car in to the Emporium, and while it's getting washed, what's he do? Sits there. Reads an old Saturday Evening Post. Wastes time. Now, my idea is, why not give him a shoeshine while he waits? A shine and a wash, one price, ninety-five cents. Call it the Spic-and-Span Special. Took it up at the Ever-Onward, and old Doc Bivens—he's a dentist, but a mighty broad-gauged fellow—Doc says, Wen, he says, that's the kind of idea that built America. Now how's that for an idea?"

"Splendid," said Harlan gently. "Simply splendid."

Wendell looked at him sharply. For one moment something passed over his broad, pink, shaven face. It was not quite suspicion, not quite hurt. It was the expression of a large dog who believes he has been praised and has, in some obscure way, been laughed at. Then it was gone, and he passed the gravy.

IV

After dinner, while Myrtis and Lorene washed the demitasse cups with the care of archaeologists, and Junior was banished to his homework and immediately went to the garage to look at a magazine about racing motors, the cousins sat in the living-room.

It was a room in which nothing had been left to chance. There was a davenport in mulberry velour and two easy chairs to match. There was a floor-lamp with a parchment shade on which a galleon was painted in sienna, and a smoking-stand shaped like a butler. A spinet desk held no papers. A bookcase held the Book of Knowledge, the Collected Works of O. Henry, two volumes of Edgar Guest, a Bible, a Rotary-style manual of parliamentary procedure, and a copy of a novel about a beautiful Englishwoman in the Sahara which Myrtis had bought and Wendell had confiscated and then read in the bathroom. Over the fireplace, which had never held a fire, since it was supplied with a gas log of genuine imitation birch, hung a large tinted photograph of a Wisconsin lake at sunset.

Wendell turned on the radio. A tenor in Pittsburgh sang about a pal that he loved. Wendell turned it off.

"Well," he said.

"Well," said Harlan.

There was a silence. In Vernon Falls silence between two men was regarded as a mechanical failure, like a stalled engine, and Wendell cranked furiously.

"Business good, Harl?"

"Business? Oh, I suppose so. I've been writing copy for a face cream. 'The Secret of the Sphinx.' One rubs it in and becomes eternal, apparently. It pays rather absurdly. But of course it isn't my real work."

"What's your real work?"

Harlan was silent for some time. He looked at the tinted lake over the gas log.

"I'm writing a novel," he said at last. "I've been writing it for eleven years. It's about—well, it's about a young man from a town rather like this one, who goes to the city to find beauty, and—" He stopped. "It's not finished."

"Well, say, that's fine!" Wendell beamed with honest admiration. "A novel! Say, you ought to put me in it. Ha, ha! 'Wendell Purdy, the Car-Wash King.' Say, when it's done you send me a copy and I'll get Hoskins down at the News Stand to put it in the window with a sign. Local Boy Makes Good. Why, I bet we could sell fifty copies right here in Vernon Falls."

"Fifty," said Harlan. And then, oddly, he laughed: not the soft, superior laugh he had used at dinner, but a short, hoarse, almost boyish bark. "Fifty copies. Wen, that's more than anyone in New York has ever offered me."

Wendell did not know what to make of this, so he lit his cheap cigar. Harlan, after a moment, held out his hand.

"I don't suppose you'd still have one of those good Havanas?"

"Sure! Sure I have! Thought you said—"

"I'm on vacation from my palate."

They smoked. The smoke went up to the ceiling, where Myrtis would find it in the morning and say nothing.

V

It was Harlan, finally, who said, "Do you remember Grandmother's place?"

Wendell did not answer at once. He took the cigar out of his mouth and looked at the end of it. "Remember it? Harl, I drive by it every Sunday. Don't stop. Just drive by. A Swede family's got it now. They took out the orchard. Put in soy beans."

"The orchard's gone?"

"Yep. Every tree."

"The green apples," said Harlan.

"By golly, you remember that! You made me eat one and I was sick as a pup all night, and Grandma gave me castor oil and you sat on the end of the bed and read me Tom Sawyer to make up for it."

"I'd forgotten I did that."

"Well, you did. Read the whole darn thing. Took you about three nights."

Harlan said, very low, "And the crow."

Wendell did not say anything. A clock on the mantel, a gift from the Ever-Onward Club on the occasion of Wendell's vice-presidency, ticked with the efficiency of all things given by the Ever-Onward Club.

"I've thought about that crow," Harlan said, "more than I've thought about anything I learned at the University. We were so pleased with ourselves. And then we picked it up, and it was warm, and its eye was—it was looking at us. And you began to cry first."

"I did not. You did."

"Did I?"

"Well, maybe we both did." Wendell's voice had grown thick. "Funny thing, Harl. You get to be a grown man. You got a business and a house and a family and your name on the Chamber of Commerce letterhead. Fellows call you Wen and slap you on the back. You go to the luncheon on Thursdays and you sing 'Smile, Ever-Onward, Smile' and you mean it, by golly, you mean every word. And then sometimes, three in the morning, you wake up and you think, what's it all for? What's it all for, anyhow? And you think about that darn crow."

He stopped, shocked at himself. He had never said anything of the kind to anyone. Not to Myrtis. Not to Reverend Gillis. Certainly not to Doc Bivens, who would have prescribed a tonic and told the whole Ever-Onward Club by Thursday.

Harlan looked at him, and for the first time that evening there was no tolerance in his face, nor any amusement, nor any pose whatever. There was only a tired man of forty-five, with thinning hair and a novel he would never finish, sitting in a mulberry chair in a city he had fled.

"I know, Wen," he said. "In New York you wake up at three in the morning too. The only difference is that there's someone in the next apartment playing a phonograph, so you can pretend you're not lonely."

The two cousins sat and regarded each other across the smoking-stand shaped like a butler. Each, for one strange moment, saw the other clearly, and saw also, in the other, himself.

It was a dangerous moment. It might have led anywhere: to confession, to tears, even to the abolition of the Spic-and-Span Special. It was saved, as such moments in Vernon Falls are always saved, by the arrival of a woman with refreshments.

"I thought you boys might like a little snack," said Myrtis brightly. She bore a tray of fudge and two glasses of grape juice. "Lorene made the fudge. Now, Harlan, you have to tell me honestly if it's as good as what you get in New York."

"Better," said Harlan, and took a piece. "Far better."

And with that he was the gentleman from the Village again, wise and weary and amused. Wendell, having wiped his eyes in the act of pretending to blow his nose, was the past vice-president of the Ever-Onward Luncheon Club again. He cleared his throat with a sound like a truck shifting gears.

"Say, Harl. Tomorrow I'm going to show you the whole works. Drive you out to the new Country Club, then over to see the dam they're putting in at Kettle Rapids, then lunch at the Ever-Onward. It's Thursday, and you'll be my guest, and they'll make you stand up and say a few words. Tell 'em about New York. Tell 'em about the advertising game. Boys'll eat it up."

"I'd be delighted," said Harlan.

"And Saturday afternoon—" Wendell hesitated, as though about to propose something slightly indecent. "Saturday afternoon, if you're not too busy, I thought maybe we might just drive out the Sauk River road. Not stop, or anything. Just drive by."

"Yes," said Harlan. "I'd like that, Wen."

"Course, it's soy beans now."

"I know."

Myrtis looked from one to the other, aware of some current she could not name, and anxiously offered more fudge.

VI

Later, in the twin beds that Myrtis had bought on the advice of the Ladies' Home Companion ("Modern Sleeping for the Modern Couple"), Wendell lay awake.

"Your cousin's very refined, isn't he?" said Myrtis in the dark.

"Harl? Oh, sure. Sure. Kind of high-hat, but he don't mean anything by it. That's just New York. They all get that way." He considered. "Lives in two rooms, though. Two rooms and a gas-ring. Fellow his age. Myrt, you know, I believe old Harl's been kind of up against it."

"Do you think he liked the salad?"

"Liked it? He said he hadn't had one in years, didn't he? Shows you what those New York restaurants are." Wendell yawned enormously. "Tell you what. We'll have him out for a real feed Sunday. Fried chicken. Biscuits. Do him good."

He was nearly asleep when he spoke again, so softly that Myrtis was not certain she had heard.

"He read me Tom Sawyer, Myrt. Three whole nights."

Down the hall, in the guest-room, under a framed print titled "The Spirit of '76," Harlan Fenstock lay on his back and listened. Somewhere a dog barked. A Ford went past in second gear. The Northern Pacific freight called long and lonesome from the river bottoms. There was no phonograph in the next apartment, nobody playing anything at all, and nothing to keep him from knowing exactly what he was.

He lay there for a long while. Then, because he could think of nothing else to do, he got up, found a pencil and the back of an envelope, and in the light of the street-lamp began to write the first page of his novel over again.

He began it, this time,

column308:
At half-past three on a Sunday afternoon in October, Walter J. Pettibone of Pettibone & Swale, Insurance (Fire, Life, Casualty, Automobile, and Plate Glass), stood at the window of his living room on Elm Terrace Drive and looked out upon the street with the expression of a man who has been betrayed by his own flesh and blood.

It was a good street. Pettibone had said so many times, to clients, to his brother-in-law from Duluth, and once, with considerable feeling, to a visiting lecturer on Ancient Egypt who had not asked. The houses were of tapestry brick and stucco and Colonial clapboard. Each had a sun-parlor, a two-car garage, and a lawn upon which the owner spent his Saturday afternoons in a sweater that had been knitted for him by his wife and that he would not have worn downtown for a thousand dollars. The elms along the parkway had been planted in 1911 by the Elm Terrace Improvement Association, of which Pettibone had been Secretary-Treasurer, and he regarded them, not unreasonably, as partly his own work. They were turning yellow now. It was the sort of afternoon on which a man ought to be at peace with the world, with a good cigar and the comic section, and Pettibone was not at peace with the world. He was, he told himself, darned sore.

Behind him, in a living room furnished with a davenport of mulberry mohair, a radio cabinet of genuine walnut veneer, a floor lamp with a parchment shade on which a galleon perpetually set forth for nowhere, a set of the Little Leather Library which no one had opened since it was delivered, and a framed photograph of the Vernon Falls Forward Club's Annual Outing at Lake Minnetaska (1922), Mrs. Pettibone sat with her hands folded and her eyes red.

"I just don't know what got into him," said Mrs. Pettibone, for the fourth time.

"I'll tell you what got into him," said Pettibone. "Pure cussedness. That's what got into him."

He did not, in fact, know what had got into his son. But it was his conviction, formed through twenty years of addressing luncheon clubs, that a man who did not know something should state it with particular firmness.

The facts were these. For three weeks Walter J. Pettibone had been laboring, with all the craft at his command, to secure the account of the Second National Bank of Vernon Falls, the bank's new building on Commercial Avenue being nine stories high and therefore, in the language of his profession, "a mighty sweet piece of fire business." He had taken the cashier to lunch twice at the Hotel Pendleton. He had sent the vice-president a box of Havana Perfectos with a card reading "Just a little token from one go-getter to another." And he had, through the sustained and tactical efforts of Mrs. Pettibone at the Thursday Afternoon Literary Circle, at last secured the presence at Sunday dinner of Mrs. J. Lucius Krebs, wife of the president of the Second National, a widow-shaped woman of fifty-eight who was not a widow, who had been to Europe twice, and who referred to everything west of Chicago as "out here."

The dinner had been planned as carefully as a sales campaign. There had been cream of tomato soup, and a roast of beef, and mashed potatoes with a little well of gravy in the top of each portion, and creamed onions, and a molded salad of lime gelatine in which pieces of celery and pineapple were suspended like insects in amber, and a lemon meringue pie from the Ladies' Exchange which Mrs. Pettibone had been prepared to claim as her own. Pettibone had worn his new gray suit with the faint lavender stripe. He had told Mrs. Krebs, between the soup and the roast, that there was nothing like a strong, conservative banking institution to give a city backbone, and Mrs. Krebs had said that she supposed that was so, out here.

Everything had been going swell. That was the word Pettibone used afterward, in his bitterness: swell. And then, as Mrs. Pettibone was bringing in the pie, seven-year-old Willis Pettibone, who had been sitting in his Sunday suit of blue serge with his hair wetted flat, eating his creamed onions with the mournful thoroughness of a child who has been told that he will not get dessert unless he does, laid down his fork and looked across the table at the president's wife with an interest that was entirely scientific.

"Papa says," observed Willis, in his clear and carrying treble, "that you're a dried-up old hen that'd foreclose on her own grandmother, but we got to be nice to you on account of the bank."

There had followed a silence. It was not a long silence, as such things are measured by the clock on the mantel, but Pettibone afterward felt that he had aged in it. He had heard himself laugh, a strange high laugh like a horse whinnying, and say, "Ha, ha! Kids! The things they think up!" And Mrs. Krebs had said, "Indeed," and eaten one forkful of the lemon meringue pie and declared that it was very nice, and that she must be getting along, as Mr. Krebs did not like her to be out after dark, it being then a quarter to two in the afternoon.

Now Pettibone turned from the window.

"Where is he?"

"He's up in his room. Walter, I want you to promise me one thing. I want you to promise you won't lose your temper."

"Lose my temper! Who's losing his temper? I'm as calm as—I'm perfectly calm. But I'm going to talk to that young man, and I'm going to talk to him plain, and if he doesn't—"

"Because I was reading in the Home Companion—no, it was the Woman's Hearthside Monthly—there was a perfectly wonderful article by a doctor, a psychologist I think he was, and he says you mustn't ever just punish a child without making him understand. He says you've got to reason with them. He says the modern parent is a pal."

"Well, I'm reasonable. I'm the most reasonable man in this town. Anybody'll tell you so. You can ask anybody at the Forward Club." Pettibone was somewhat mollified. He believed in modern methods. He had a Dictaphone at the office, though his stenographer refused to use it, and he had installed an oil burner the year before at a cost of six hundred and forty dollars, and he often said that you couldn't run a business today the way your granddad did. He supposed you couldn't run a boy that way either.

"I'll reason with him," he said. "You send him down to the den."

The den was a small room at the back of the house which had been described by the architect as a "library-study" and by Pettibone as "my den" and by Mrs. Pettibone, privately, as "that room." It contained a mission oak desk at which Pettibone paid the household bills once a month with groans that could be heard in the kitchen; a leather armchair, cracked across the seat; a smoking stand with an ash tray held up by a bronze Indian; a set of golf clubs he had used four times; a framed certificate from the Mid-Continent Underwriters' Association attesting that Walter J. Pettibone had written over two hundred thousand dollars in life policies in the fiscal year 1923; and, on the wall above the desk, a lithograph in brown and gold entitled THE MAN WHO WINS, beneath which were printed a number of lines of verse to the effect that the man who wins is the man who thinks he can.

Pettibone sat down in the leather chair. Then he decided that sitting down was not sufficiently impressive, and stood up. Then he decided that a pal would sit down, and sat down again. He lit a cigar. He put it out. He took off his glasses, which were of tortoise shell and made him look, he believed, like a bank examiner, and put them on again.

The door opened with a slowness that was itself a kind of commentary, and Willis came in.

He was a thin, fair child with large ears and a manner of grave attention which his teachers at the Lincoln School mistook for intelligence and his mother mistook for spirituality. He had taken off his Sunday jacket. He stood just inside the door with his hands behind his back and regarded his father much as he had regarded Mrs. Krebs, with an air of honest curiosity as to what would happen next.

"Shut the door, son," said Pettibone.

Willis shut the door.

"Now come over here. No, over here. Stand right there where I can see you. Now." Pettibone cleared his throat. He had made, by his own count, one hundred and eleven speeches in the course of his career, including the address of welcome to the State Convention of Hardware Jobbers, and he had never begun one without clearing his throat. "Now, Willis, I want to have a real heart-to-heart talk with you. Man to man. Do you know why I want to have a talk with you?"

"Because I said what you said about Mrs. Krebs," said Willis.

This was not the way it was supposed to go. In Pettibone's experience, when you asked a prospect a question, the prospect said he didn't know, and then you told him. He felt obscurely that his son had jumped ahead in the sales talk.

"Well—yes. That's right. Now. I'm not going to scold you. I want you to understand that. Your daddy isn't angry." He was, at that moment, angrier than he had been since the Fourth of July in 1919, when a competitor named Hagstrom had beaten him for the presidency of the Forward Club by three votes, two of them, Pettibone had always suspected, purchased. "I just want you to understand something. Do you know what you did?"

"I said—"

"No, no, I don't mean what you said. I mean, do you understand what you did? You embarrassed your mother. You embarrassed a guest in this house. A very fine lady, a very prominent lady, a lady that's done a lot of good in this community. Why, Mrs. Krebs is on the board of the Children's Home and the Visiting Nurses and I don't know what all. And you hurt her feelings. Now how do you think that made her feel?"

Willis considered this.

"You said she didn't have any feelings," he said. "You said she had a cash register where her heart ought to be. You said it at breakfast. You said it to Mama when you were putting the sugar on your oatmeal."

Pettibone opened his mouth and closed it. He was conscious of a sensation he associated chiefly with the examination of his income tax returns by a young man from the Federal Government.

"Now, that's—now see here. That's entirely different. That was a private conversation. Between your mother and me. A man's got a right to say things in his own home, hasn't he? A man's got a right to—to speak his mind, in his own home, to his own wife, without some little pitcher with big ears going and blabbing it all over town."

"I didn't blab it all over town. I just said it to Mrs. Krebs."

"That's worse!"

"Why?"

"Because—" Pettibone stood up. He found that he had to stand up. He walked to the window, which looked out upon the garage and the ash cans, and turned back. "Because, son, you don't go telling people things like that. It isn't—it isn't nice."

"But you said it."

"I know I said it! I'm not denying I said it! I'm a man that'll stand behind every word I ever said! But there's a time and a place! Do you understand me? There's a time and a place for everything!"

Willis did not appear to understand him. He looked at his father with the expression of a reasonable creature who has been given an unreasonable rule and is trying, honestly, to find the sense in it.

"Miss Gundersen says," he offered, "that you should always tell the truth. She says George Washington never told a lie, not even about the cherry tree, and his father said he'd rather lose a thousand cherry trees than have his boy tell a lie. And she says if you tell a lie you go to the bad place, and Jesus doesn't like it."

Miss Gundersen was Willis's Sunday School teacher at the First Methodist Church, of which Pettibone was a trustee and to whose new organ fund he had contributed three hundred dollars, receiving in return a small brass plate. He felt that Miss Gundersen, whom he had never cared for, had a good deal to answer for.

"Well, Miss Gundersen is absolutely right. That's absolutely sound doctrine, and don't you ever forget it. You always tell the truth. Your daddy always tells the truth. Why, in the insurance game, a man's word is his bond. Honesty is the best policy—ha, ha, that's a good one, the best policy—but it's true, Willis. You remember that."

"Then why—"

"But," said Pettibone, raising his hand like a traffic officer, "there's such a thing as tact. You know what tact is? Tact is—tact is—well, it's knowing what to say and when to say it. It's being considerate of other folks. It's what you might call the oil in the machinery of life. Now, a man can be perfectly truthful and still be tactful. You see? You don't have to go around saying every little thing you think. Why, if everybody went around saying every little thing they thought, there wouldn't be a business left standing in this country, nor a church either, nor—" He stopped, aware that this was perhaps not the line of argument the psychologist in the Woman's Hearthside Monthly had had in mind.

"Is it tact," inquired Willis, "when you said you were glad to see Mrs. Krebs?"

"Certainly it was tact! I was glad to see her!"

"But you said—"

"Never mind what I said! I'm the one doing the talking here!"

There was a pause. In the kitchen Mrs. Pettibone could be heard washing the dinner dishes with an unnecessary clatter, a sound which Pettibone recognized as a wife's way of listening at a door without the vulgarity of actually doing so. Outside, a Buick went by on Elm Terrace Drive, and from somewhere down the block came the hoarse, determined voice of Mr. Orville Tebbetts, the Ford dealer, calling his dog.

Pettibone sat down again and mopped his forehead with a handkerchief bearing his initials, a Christmas present from his wife, who had bought it at Bunting's Department Store along with eleven others exactly like it. He was aware that he was not winning. It was a sensation he had felt before, across a desk, when a prospect had a brother-in-law in the business, and he had a salesman's dread of it. Moreover, beneath his annoyance, beneath his very real fear that the Second National's nine stories of fire risk had gone to Hagstrom, there stirred something else, something formless and unwelcome, which he did not examine. It may have been shame. Pettibone did not, as a rule, examine anything that might turn out to be shame. He regarded introspection as the sort of thing that was all right for poets and fellows in Greenwich Village, but which a real red-blooded businessman was too busy for.

He tried a new approach. It was a principle with him that when one approach failed you switched to another, and he had once delivered a talk on this subject to the Junior Chamber of Commerce under the title "Hit 'Em from Another Angle."

"Willis," he said, very gently, leaning forward with his elbows on his knees, the very picture of a Pal, "do you like this house?"

"Yes, Papa."

"You like your room? With the electric train and all?"

"Yes, Papa."

"And you like going to the movies Saturdays, and having ice cream sodas at Schlegel's, and the new sled your mother and I are going to get you for Christmas? That is—maybe going to get you."

Willis's attention, which had wandered toward the bronze Indian on the smoking stand, came back sharply.

"Yes, Papa."

"Well, where do you think all that comes from? You think it grows on trees? No, sir! It comes from your daddy working hard at the office. And part of working hard at the office is being nice to people. Being nice to folks like Mrs. Krebs, and Mr. Krebs, and lots of folks. Even if—well, even if maybe they're not the kind of folks you'd pick out to go fishing with. That's business, son. That's the way the world goes round. You understand now?"

Willis looked at him for a long moment. Something moved behind the grave eyes; it might have been comprehension, and it might have been only the passage of a small cloud of calculation across a sky that had hitherto been perfectly clear.

"You mean," he said slowly, "you have to say nice things to people so they'll give you money."

"Well—that's putting it kind of crude. But—yes. In a manner of speaking."

"Even if you don't mean it."

"Now, I didn't say that—"

"And it's tact."

"That's right. That's tact."

"And it isn't a lie."

Pettibone hesitated. Then, with the air of a man reaching for a hammer, he said, "No, it isn't a lie. It's just business."

Willis nodded. He appeared satisfied. He appeared, in fact, so entirely satisfied, so tranquil and so instructed, that his father felt a faint chill, as though somewhere a door had been left open.

"All right," said Pettibone, and slapped his knees, briskly, to signify that the meeting was adjourned. "Now you go and tell your mother you're sorry. And tomorrow after school, I want you to write a nice little letter to Mrs. Krebs, saying you're sorry, and that you didn't mean it, and your mother will help you with the spelling. You hear me?"

"Yes, Papa."

"And if anything like this ever happens again, young man, so help me, I'll take the hairbrush to you, psychology or no psychology. You get me?"

"Yes, Papa."

The boy went to the door. With his hand on the knob he turned back.

"Papa," he said, "if I write Mrs. Krebs a nice letter, can I still have the sled?"

Pettibone looked at him. For a moment the father in him, the obscure, uneasy, unexamined father, struggled with the businessman; and the businessman won, as he generally did, by a comfortable margin.

"We'll see," said Pettibone. "You write a good one, and we'll see."

When the door had closed, he sat for some time in the leather armchair with an unlighted cigar in his mouth, looking up at THE MAN WHO WINS. He felt tired. He felt as he did at the end of a long day at the State Convention, when he had shaken hands with three hundred men and remembered the names of most of them. But presently, as the cigar was lit and drawn upon and the blue smoke rose toward the ceiling, the tiredness gave way to a slow and spreading satisfaction. He had handled it. By golly, he had handled it, and handled it well. No yelling, no whipping, none of that old-fashioned stuff his own father had gone in for, out in the barn behind the farmhouse in Kanabec County. Reason. Psychology. A real modern heart-to-heart. The boy had come in sassy and gone out understanding something about life. That was what a dad was for.

That evening, over the cold roast beef, he said to Mrs. Pettibone, "Well, I guess I got through to him all right."

"I heard," said Mrs. Pettibone.

"Kid's got a head on his shoulders. You know that? Asked me some pretty sharp questions. Pretty darn sharp. I tell you, Flora, that boy's going to make a businessman."

Mrs. Pettibone said nothing. She was thinking of the article in the Woman's Hearthside Monthly, and she was trying to remember whether the psychologist had said anything about what you did if the child turned out to learn the lesson too well; but she could not remember, and presently she got up to see about the pie.

The assurance of Tanis Judique’s friendship fortified Babbitt’s self-approval. At the Athletic Club he became experimental. “Yuh, lil exercise.”

“Well, just about.”

Babbitt, under the name of “Old Georgie,” was now a pioneer of the Bunch, since each month it changed half its membership and he who could recall the prehistoric days of a fortnight ago, before Mrs. Absolom, the food-demonstrator, had gone to Indianapolis, and Mac had “got sore at” Minnie, was a venerable leader and able to condescend to new Petes and Minnies and Gladyses. At Carrie’s, Tanis did not have to work at being hostess. She was dignified and sure, a clear fine figure in the black chiffon frock he had always loved; and in the wider spaces of that ugly house Babbitt was able to sit quietly with her. He repented of his first revulsion, mooned at her feet, andhappily drove her home. Next day he bought a violent yellow tie, to make himself young for her. He knew, a little sadly, that he could not make himself beautiful; he beheld himself as heavy, hinting of fatness, but he danced, he dressed, he chattered, to be as young as she was... as young as she seemed to be. As all converts, whether to a religion, love, or gardening, find as by magic that though hitherto these hobbies have not seemed to exist, now the whole world is filled with their fury, so, once he was converted to dissipation, Babbitt discovered agreeable opportunities for it everywhere. He had a new view of his sporting neighbor, Sam Doppelbrau. The Doppelbraus were respectable people, industrious people, prosperous people, whose ideal of happiness was an eternal cabaret. Their life was dominated by suburban bacchanalia of alcohol, nicotine, gasoline, and kisses. They and their set worked capably all the week, and all week looked forward to Saturday night, when they would, as they expressed it, “throw a party;” and the thrown party grew noisier and noisier up to Sunday dawn, and usually included an extremely rapid motor expedition to nowhere in particular. One evening when Tanis was at the theater, Babbitt found himself being lively with the Doppelbraus, pledging friendship with men whom he had for years privily denounced to Mrs. Babbitt as a “rotten bunch of tin-horns that I wouldn’t go out with, not if they were the last people on earth.” That evening he had sulkily come home and poked about in front of the house, chipping off the walk the ice-clots, like fossil footprints, made by the steps of passers-by during the recent snow. Howard Littlefield came up snuffling.

“Still a widower, George?”

“Yump. Cold again to-night.”

“What do you hear from the wife?”

“She’s feeling fine, but her sister is still pretty sick.”

“Say, better come in and have dinner with us to-night, George.”

“Oh—oh, thanks. Have to go out.” Suddenly he could not endure Littlefield’s recitals of the more interesting statistics about totally uninteresting problems. He scraped at the walk and grunted. Sam Doppelbrau appeared.

“Evenin’, Babbitt. Working hard?”

“Yuh, lil exercise.”

“Cold enough for you to-night?”

“Well, just about.”

“Still a widower?”

“Uh-huh.”

Hazel Tibbets had been waiting for him since a quarter to six, and she had been waiting in the particular way of a woman who has decided to say nothing until she has said everything. She had set the table with the Haviland, which was reserved for the Methodist pastor and the Fourth of July. She had cooked pot roast, which he loved, and she had made a lemon pie, which he loved still more. To Lowell Tibbets, coming in at six-twenty with the evening *Delphos City Advocate-Times* under his arm and the smell of vulcanizing rubber in his clothes, these were not courtesies but omens. He had been married nineteen years. He knew lemon pie.

"Well, well, well, smells mighty good in here!" he boomed. He gave her the brisk dry kiss that he had given her every evening since the Harding administration, the kiss of a man punching a time-clock. "Say, you'll never guess who was in the shop to-day. Old Judge Lindquist, and he says to me, 'Tibbets, you're the only man in town that'll tell a fellow the truth about a battery.' Now how's that for a compliment, from a man that's been on the bench thirty years?"

"That's nice," said Hazel.

He hung his overcoat on the hall tree, a fumed-oak structure with four brass hooks and a beveled mirror, which they had bought in the second year of their marriage because it was exactly like the hall tree of the Ed Purdys, who had then been the most enviable couple on Ashland Avenue. The Purdys had since moved to Glendale Terrace, bought a sedan with wire wheels, and acquired a hall closet, and Lowell had long felt obscurely shamed by the hall tree without ever quite knowing why.

"Anything new?" he said, in the hearty voice of a man skating across ice he suspects is thin.

"Supper's ready."

They sat down. The dining-room was, like ten thousand other dining-rooms in Delphos City, a museum of good intentions. It had a plate-rail with four plates on it, painted with windmills; a buffet with a mirrored back, on which stood a silver-plated fruit-bowl containing no fruit; a print of a stag at bay, purchased because it had seemed manly; and a print of a girl with a lamb, purchased because it had seemed womanly. There was a chandelier of amber glass that hung on four brass chains and cast upon both of them the yellow, slightly bilious light of a railway waiting-room. Neither of them had looked at any of these objects in eleven years.

Lowell carved, with the flourishes of a man who feels that carving is among the masculine arts, like fishing and the discussion of tariffs. He talked. He talked of the new filling-station that Standard Oil was putting up at Eighth and Monroe, and of how it would be a darn good thing for the town, he didn't care who said otherwise, because a city that wanted to grow had to grow, and you couldn't stop progress any more than you could stop the Mississippi River, and of how Shorty Mulvane at the Kiwanis lunch had told the funniest story about a Swede and a mule—no, he wouldn't tell it now, it wasn't exactly a lady's story, but it certainly was a corker. He talked as a boy whistles past a cemetery, and all the while he watched her from beneath his eyebrows.

She ate very little. She cut her pot roast into small exact squares and moved them about her plate as though she were playing checkers with herself and losing.

"Something the matter, Hazel?"

"Why, no. What should be the matter?"

"I don't know. You seem kind of—you know—quiet."

"I'm always quiet. You've said so yourself. You've said I was about as lively as a hitching-post."

"Now, honey, I never said any such—well, maybe once, but that was a joke. Can't a fellow make a joke in his own house?"

"Certainly he can."

He returned to his pot roast with the injured air of a man who has offered peace and had it handed back to him without the wrapper. He thought, with a sense of grievance that comforted him, "Women! You never know where you are with 'em. Fellow works his head off all day, comes home tired, wants a little peace and quiet—" But beneath the grievance there stirred a small cold thing which was not grievance at all, and which he refused to look at.

It was when she brought in the lemon pie that she said it. She set it down before him, and she did not sit, but stood with her hands folded upon the back of her chair, like a witness who has been told she may step down and has elected to remain.

"Lowell, I went to the bank this afternoon."

He felt the cold thing move. He made his voice very casual. He made it so casual that it creaked. "Oh, yeah? What for?"

"I went to draw out the money for Chicago."

"For—oh. Oh, that."

"Yes. That."

He studied the pie. It had a beautiful meringue, browned at the peaks like the snowy summits of the Rockies in the colored advertisements of the Burlington Route. He wished that he were in the Rockies. He wished that he were in the shop, with the honest grease and the honest radiator hose, and old Gus singing "Barney Google" in the back.

"I was going to tell you about that," he said.

"Were you?"

"Sure I was! Why, sure! I was just waiting till—well, till the right time. You know how you get when a fellow springs things on you all of a sudden."

"Mr. Haskins told me there was eleven dollars and forty cents in the savings account. He was very nice about it. He said it in a low voice so the people at the next window wouldn't hear. He looked at me the way Dr. Pritchard looked at Mrs. Gundersen when he told her it was the gall-bladder."

"Now, Hazel—"

"There was six hundred and twelve dollars in that account in October. I know, because I put a good deal of it there. I put it there out of the house money, a dollar here and two dollars there, for three years. I made over my blue serge instead of buying a new one. I told Mrs. Purdy we didn't care for the movies any more, when she asked us to go."

"I know, honey, I know, and I appreciate it, I want you to know that, I certainly appreciate—"

"Where is it, Lowell?"

He laid down his fork. He had, after all, been a man of affairs for twenty years; he had sold batteries to farmers who did not want batteries, and tires to traveling-men who were convinced their old tires had another ten thousand miles in them; he had addressed the Kiwanis Club on "The Spirit of Service in the Automotive Accessory Field" and been warmly applauded. He was not going to be cross-examined in his own dining-room like a chicken-thief. He squared his shoulders. He became, by an effort of will that was almost visible, the Lowell Tibbets of the Kiwanis platform.

"Now you sit down, Hazel, and I'll explain the whole thing to you, and when you've heard it you'll see I've done the smartest thing I ever did in my life. Sit down, now. Come on."

She sat down, slowly, and the light of the amber chandelier fell on her face. It was a face which had been pretty in 1906 and which had since been not so much aged as overlooked—a face, he would have said if he had ever thought about it, which was "just Hazel's face," like the hall tree or the stag at bay. She looked at him now with an attention he could not recall in years, and he did not care for it.

"You know Glen Arbor Heights," he began.

"I know it's a cornfield out past the fairgrounds."

"It *was* a cornfield! Sure it was a cornfield! So was Chicago once a swamp, so was New York nothing but a lot of Indians! That's just exactly the point! Now you listen. Charley Wenzel—you know Charley, he's in the Kiwanis, he's a darn fine fellow, a real live wire—Charley's in with the syndicate that's developing that whole tract, and they're putting in sewers, and sidewalks, and an ornamental gateway with electric lights on it, and the street-car company is going to run a line clear out there inside of two years, Charley says, maybe eighteen months. And when that car-line goes in—" He spread his hands upon the tablecloth in a gesture of vast and fertile prophecy. "Why, Hazel, those lots are going to be worth three, four times what they're asking now. It's the coming residential section of this city. All the best people are going to be out there. You'll see. Why, Charley says the Purdys are thinking of building out there themselves."

"The Purdys have just built."

"Well—well, they're thinking of it, anyway, for an investment. And I got in on the ground floor. I got a corner lot, Hazel—a corner lot, on Arcadia Boulevard and Sylvan Way—for nine hundred dollars, with only six hundred down. Charley let me in at the pre-development price. As a personal favor. Why, he said to me, 'Lowell, I wouldn't do this for every man in town, but you're the kind of fellow we want out there.'"

"Arcadia Boulevard," said Hazel.

"That's what they're going to call it."

"Is there anything on Arcadia Boulevard now?"

"Well, there's—there's stakes. With little flags on 'em. They've got it all surveyed. You ought to see the plat, Hazel; they've got it all drawn out in colors, with the parks and the lagoon and everything."

"There's going to be a lagoon."

"That's what the plat says."

She was silent, and in her silence he felt, absurdly, as though he were back in the eighth grade at the Washington School, standing at the blackboard with a problem in long division that would not come out, while Miss Frisbie waited.

"Lowell," she said at last, very gently, "that was my money."

"Our money," he corrected her, with dignity. "In this family we've always shared and shared alike, I hope."

"It was the money for Chicago. You knew it was. You said I could go. You said it last spring, on the porch, after the Elks' picnic. You said, 'Sure, go ahead, old girl, do you good.' I've got the catalogue upstairs. I've had it in my bureau drawer since April. The Art Institute has a summer course in design and color for—for persons of mature years. It's six weeks. I was going to stay at the Y.W. I had it all figured out to the penny."

"Well, now, Hazel, I never said—exactly—I mean, I said you *could* go, sure, if things—if we could see our way—"

"You said 'Sure, go ahead, old girl.'"

He was nettled. He hated being quoted; it was like being shown a photograph of oneself in a bathing-suit. "Well, maybe I did, but a man can't be expected to remember every last little thing he says on a porch after a picnic. And anyway—" He found his ground and planted himself upon it with relief. "Anyway, I don't mind telling you, I never thought much of that idea in the first place. What would you want to go traipsing off to Chicago for, at your age, and fool around with paint-brushes with a lot of long-haired sissies and girls that smoke cigarettes? What would people think? What would the Purdys think? You'd be the talk of the town. Why, Ed Purdy'd kid the life out of me."

"I don't think Ed Purdy thinks about me at all."

"Well, he would if you went. And what's it for, anyway? You can't make a living at it. You can't sell it. It's not as if you were going to be a—a commercial artist, or something practical, drawing ads for Kuppenheimer suits. It's just—fooling. Now, a lot is different. A lot is real estate. Real estate's the foundation of everything in this country. You ask any banker. Ask Haskins. Land is the one thing they aren't making any more of."

"Mr. Haskins," said Hazel, "asked me if you'd bought in Glen Arbor Heights. He said a good many men had."

"There! You see? Everybody's in on it!"

"He didn't say it the way you say it."

Lowell pushed back his chair, rose, and went to the window. Across Ashland Avenue the bungalow of the Gottliebs showed a lighted parlor and the blue-gray flicker of their new radio, which could bring in Pittsburgh on a clear night. He could hear it faintly—an orchestra playing something with saxophones. He thought of the Gottliebs, who never quarreled, or at least never quarreled where you could hear them. He thought of how, if he were Gottlieb, he would be sitting in a Morris chair now with his shoes off, listening to Pittsburgh. He felt that Fate had been niggardly with him.

"I'll tell you what it is," he said to the window. "It's those women. That Mrs. Ainsworth, and that schoolteacher with the bangs, at your Thursday Club. They've been putting ideas into your head. Reading papers on Ibsen and all that highbrow junk. A woman gets to brooding, and first thing you know she wants to go off and *express* herself." He produced the word as though holding it up by the tail. "Well, I'm all for culture. Nobody can say Lowell Tibbets isn't for culture. I gave ten dollars to the Chautauqua last summer, didn't I? But there's a limit."

"Nobody put anything in my head, Lowell."

"Then where'd you get it?"

She did not answer for so long that he turned around. She was sitting with her hands in her lap, looking at the girl-with-a-lamb on the wall, and he saw, with a queer jolt, that she was not going to cry. He had been prepared for crying. He had his technique for crying; he would pat her shoulder, and say "There, there, old girl," and suggest that they drive out to the Lakeside Pavilion for a soda, and in the morning it would be gone, the way crying always was gone. But she was dry-eyed, and her voice when it came was level and rather tired, like that of a woman reading a recipe aloud.

"When I was seventeen I took drawing at the high school from Miss Ostrander. She said I had a feeling for line. Those were her words: a feeling for line. She said if I kept at it I might go to the Academy in Cincinnati. Then I met you at the Epworth League social, and you had that straw boater and the red bicycle, and you were going to own the biggest garage in the state. And I thought, well, I'll draw afterwards. Afterwards. And then there was Marjorie, and then Marjorie had the scarlet fever, and then your father died and we took your mother, and then it was the war, and then the shop was in trouble, and then it was—just afterwards. I've been waiting for afterwards for twenty-one years, Lowell. I'm forty-three. I thought maybe afterwards was now."

He was moved, and, being moved, he was alarmed, and, being alarmed, he grew angry; for in Lowell Tibbets, as in most of the leading citizens of Delphos City, there was no emotion so delicate that it could not be converted on short notice into indignation.

"Well, I like that! I like that fine! So I've been standing in your way for twenty-one years, have I? I've been some kind of a—a jailer, have I? Who's kept a roof over your head? Who bought you that electric washing-machine when old lady Shotwell down the block was still scrubbing on a board? Who took you to Excelsior Springs in 1921? I've worked like a dog for this family, and this is the thanks I get! A fellow tries to make a little money for his old age, tries to provide for his wife in case anything happens to him, and she throws it up at him that he wouldn't let her go off to Chicago and draw pictures!"

"I didn't say you stood in my way."

"You as good as said it!"

"I said I was waiting. That's different. You didn't do anything, Lowell. Nobody did anything. It just—went."

That was worse. He could have fought an accusation; he had been fighting accusations, from customers and wholesalers and the man from the Internal Revenue, all his life. But he did not know how to fight a thing that had just gone. He stood by the window with his hands thrust into his trouser-pockets, jingling his keys and a half-dollar and the little celluloid Kiwanis badge he always carried, and he felt, for an instant only, an emptiness under his breastbone like the feeling of an elevator dropping too fast. He thought of the corner lot on Arcadia Boulevard, of the stakes with their little flags snapping in the November wind over the stubble of last year's corn, and he had a quick, disloyal, and wholly unendurable vision of those stakes still standing there in 1935, with the flags gone gray, and nobody coming.

He shook it off. He was a Booster, and Boosters did not have visions of that sort; that was precisely what distinguished them from Knockers.

"Now see here," he said, in a voice he meant to be tender and which came out merely loud, "I'll tell you what we'll do. When I sell that lot—and it won't be long, mind you, Charley says there's already a fellow from Toledo sniffing around—when I sell it, I'll give you the whole six hundred back, and a hundred extra on top of that, and you can go to Chicago, or New York, or Paris, France, if you want to, and draw till you're black in the face. How's that? Isn't that fair? Isn't that a square deal?"

"When you sell it."

"Sure, when I sell it!"

"And when will that be?"

"Well—well, how should I know to the day? A year. Two, maybe. When the car-line goes in."

She rose, and began to gather the plates. She stacked them neatly, the Haviland ones, with the little gold rims worn thin from nineteen years of Methodist pastors and Fourth-of-July dinners. The lemon pie stood untouched in the center of the table, its meringue beginning, very slightly, to weep.

"Afterwards," she said.

"What's that?"

"Nothing, Lowell. Eat your pie. I made it for you."

"I don't want any darn pie."

"Then I'll put it in the ice-box."

She carried the plates into the kitchen. He heard the water run, and the clink of china in the dishpan, and then—and this, absurdly, was what he could not bear—he heard her begin to hum. It was not a sad tune. It was "Smiles," which they had danced to at the Armistice Ball at the Odd Fellows' Hall, and she hummed it with a dreadful placidity, as though she were alone in the house, as though she had been alone in it a long while.

He went into the living-room and sat down in his chair, the big leather one with the smoking-stand beside it, and he opened the *Advocate-Times*. He read that the Delphos City Chamber of Commerce anticipated the most prosperous year in its history. He read that a man in Kansas had been killed by a Holstein bull. He read an advertisement for Glen Arbor Heights—"Where Nature Smiles and Values Climb!"—and studied the drawing of a lagoon with swans upon it, and a girl in a cloche hat gazing at the swans, and a bungalow with a pergola, and he told himself that it was a mighty fine drawing, a professional drawing, the kind of drawing a person could make a real living at.

From the kitchen the humming went on.

He turned the page. He found that he had read the same paragraph about the Holstein bull three times, and that he had not the faintest idea what it said. He lit a cigar, a Flor de Delphos, three for a quarter, and it tasted of nothing whatever.

"Hazel!" he called. "Say, Hazel! What do you say we drive out to the Pavilion and get a soda?"

The humming stopped. The water ran. After a while she answered, pleasantly, from very far away, "No, thank you, Lowell. You go, if you like."

He did not go. He sat in the leather chair under the bridge-lamp with the fringed shade, the newspaper open upon his knees, and listened to the Gottliebs' radio bringing in, faintly and triumphantly, through the November dark, an orchestra in Pittsburgh which was playing, for the benefit of all America, a selection entitled "Happy Days."
