Here is an excerpt of Sinclair Lewis's writing, to show you their style:

The assurance of Tanis Judique’s friendship fortified Babbitt’s self-approval. At the Athletic Club he became experimental. Though Vergil Gunch was silent, the others at the Roughnecks’ Table came to accept Babbitt as having, for no visible reason, “turned crank.” They argued windily with him, and he was cocky, and enjoyed the spectacle of his interesting martyrdom. He even praised Seneca Doane. Professor Pumphrey said that was carrying a joke too far; but Babbitt argued, “No! Fact! I tell you he’s got one of the keenest intellects in the country. Why, Lord Wycombe said that—” “Oh, who the hell is Lord Wycombe? What you always lugging him in for? You been touting him for the last six weeks!” protested Orville Jones.

“George ordered him from Sears-Roebuck. You can get those English high-muckamucks by mail for two bucks apiece,” suggested Sidney Finkelstein.

“That’s all right now! Lord Wycombe, he’s one of the biggest intellects in English political life. As I was saying: Of course I’m conservative myself, but I appreciate a guy like Senny Doane because—” Vergil Gunch interrupted harshly, “I wonder if you are so conservative? I find I can manage to run my own business without any skunks and reds like Doane in it!” The grimness of Gunch’s voice, the hardness of his jaw, disconcerted Babbitt, but he recovered and went on till they looked bored, then irritated, then as doubtful as Gunch. He thought of Tanis always. With a stir he remembered her every aspect. His arms yearned for her. “I’ve found her! I’ve dreamed of her all these years and now I’ve found her!” he exulted. He met her at the movies in the morning; he drove out to her flat in the late afternoon or on evenings when he was believed to be at the Elks. He knew her financial affairs and advised her about them, while she lamented her feminine ignorance, and praised his masterfulness, and proved to know much more about bonds than he did. They had remembrances, and laughter over old times. Once they quarreled, and he raged that she was as “bossy” as his wife and far more whining when he was inattentive. But that passed safely. Their high hour was a tramp on a ringing December afternoon, through snow-drifted meadows down to the icy Chaloosa River. She was exotic in an astrachan cap and a short beaver coat; she slid on the ice and shouted, and he panted after her, rotund with laughter.... Myra Babbitt never slid on the ice. He was afraid that they would be seen together. In Zenith it is impossible to lunch with a neighbor’s wife without the fact being known, before nightfall, in every house in your circle. But Tanis was beautifully discreet. However appealingly she might turn to him when they were alone, she was gravely detached when they were abroad, and he hoped that she would be taken for a client. Orville Jones once saw them emerging from a movie theater, and Babbitt bumbled, “Let me make you ’quainted with Mrs. Judique. Now here’s a lady who knows the right broker to come to, Orvy!” Mr. Jones, though he was a man censorious of morals and of laundry machinery, seemed satisfied. His predominant fear—not from any especial fondness for her but from the habit of propriety—was that his wife would learn of the affair. He was certain that she knew nothing specific about Tanis, but he was also certain that she suspected something indefinite. For years she had been bored by anything more affectionate than a farewell kiss, yet she was hurt by any slackening in his irritable periodic interest, and now he had no interest; rather, a revulsion. He was completely faithful—to Tanis. He was distressed by the sight of his wife’s slack plumpness, by her puffs and billows of flesh, by the tattered petticoat which she was always meaning and always forgetting to throw away. But he was aware that she, so long attuned to him, caught all his repulsions. He elaborately, heavily, jocularly tried to check them. He couldn’t. They had a tolerable Christmas. Kenneth Escott was there, admittedly engaged to Verona. Mrs. Babbitt was tearful and called Kenneth her new son. Babbitt was worried about Ted, because he had ceased complaining of the State University and become suspiciously acquiescent. He wondered what the boy was planning, and was too shy to ask. Himself, Babbitt slipped away on Christmas afternoon to take his present, a silver cigarette-box, to Tanis. When he returned Mrs. Babbitt asked, much too innocently, “Did you go out for a little fresh air?”

“Yes, just lil drive,” he mumbled. After New Year’s his wife proposed, “I heard from my sister to-day, George. She isn’t well. I think perhaps I ought to go stay with her for a few weeks.” Now, Mrs. Babbitt was not accustomed to leave home during the winter except on violently demanding occasions, and only the summer before, she had been gone for weeks. Nor was Babbitt one of the detachable husbands who take separations casually. He liked to have her there; she looked after his clothes; she knew how his steak ought to be cooked; and her clucking made him feel secure. But he could not drum up even a dutiful “Oh, she doesn’t really need you, does she?” While he tried to look regretful, while he felt that his wife was watching him, he was filled with exultant visions of Tanis.

“Do you think I’d better go?” she said sharply.

“You’ve got to decide, honey; I can’t.” She turned away, sighing, and his forehead was damp. Till she went, four days later, she was curiously still, he cumbrously affectionate. Her train left at noon. As he saw it grow small beyond the train-shed he longed to hurry to Tanis.

“No, by golly, I won’t do that!” he vowed. “I won’t go near her for a week!” But he was at her flat at four. He who had once controlled or seemed to control his life in a progress unimpassioned but diligent and sane was for that fortnight borne on a current of desire and very bad whisky and all the complications of new acquaintances, those furious new intimates who demand so much more attention than old friends. Each morning he gloomily recognized his idiocies of the evening before. With his head throbbing, his tongue and lips stinging from cigarettes, he incredulously counted the number of drinks he had taken, and groaned, “I got to quit!” He had ceased saying, “I will quit!” for however resolute he might be at dawn, he could not, for a single evening, check his drift. He had met Tanis’s friends; he had, with the ardent haste of the Midnight People, who drink and dance and rattle and are ever afraid to be silent, been adopted as a member of her group, which they called “The Bunch.” He first met them after a day when he had worked particularly hard and when he hoped to be quiet with Tanis and slowly sip her admiration. From down the hall he could hear shrieks and the grind of a phonograph. As Tanis opened the door he saw fantastic figures dancing in a haze of cigarette smoke. The tables and chairs were against the wall.

“Oh, isn’t this dandy!” she gabbled at him. “Carrie Nork had the loveliest idea. She decided it was time for a party, and she ’phoned the Bunch and told ’em to gather round.... George, this is Carrie.”

“Carrie” was, in the less desirable aspects of both, at once matronly and spinsterish. She was perhaps forty; her hair was an unconvincing ash-blond; and if her chest was flat, her hips were ponderous. She greeted Babbitt with a giggling “Welcome to our little midst! Tanis says you’re a real sport.” He was apparently expected to dance, to be boyish and gay with Carrie, and he did his unforgiving best. He towed her about the room, bumping into other couples, into the radiator, into chair-legs cunningly ambushed. As he danced he surveyed the rest of the Bunch: A thin young woman who looked capable, conceited, and sarcastic. Another woman whom he could never quite remember. Three overdressed and slightly effeminate young men—soda-fountain clerks, or at least born for that profession. A man of his own age, immovable, self-satisfied, resentful of Babbitt’s presence. When he had finished his dutiful dance Tanis took him aside and begged, “Dear, wouldn’t you like to do something for me? I’m all out of booze, and the Bunch want to celebrate. Couldn’t you just skip down to Healey Hanson’s and get some?”

“Sure,” he said, trying not to sound sullen.

column308:
In every American family there is one cousin who has Gone East and one cousin who has Stayed, and it is the peculiar burden of each to believe that the other envies him. Elbert Hackett had stayed. He was the proprietor of Hackett's Cut-Rate Drug Emporium, with its Sanitary Soda Fountain ("Seventeen Flavors, All Pure"), and of two branch stores, one of them out on Euclid Boulevard where the new bungalows were going up like mushrooms after a warm rain. He was a director of the Wenonah City Kiwanis, a Thirty-second Degree Mason, and the owner of a sedan with a heater that worked. He was forty-six and thick through the middle, and he had a laugh that began low in his chest, considered the matter, and came out all at once.

His cousin Lyman Hackett had gone East. Twenty-two years ago Lyman had departed from the Rock Island depot with a cardboard suitcase and a copy of Emerson's Essays, and he had become, by reports that drifted back through Aunt Hattie's Christmas letters, "something big in advertising in New York." Now he was coming through Wenonah City on his way to the Coast, and he had wired, and Elbert had been unsettled for a week.

"I don't see why you're so het up about it," said Mrs. Hackett, on the evening before. "He's only your cousin."

"Only my cousin! Say, that's a good one! Why, Lyman and I were raised practically like brothers out at Grandpa's place. And I'm not het up. I just want him to see that we've got a city here that's on the map. Those New York fellows, they think everything west of Buffalo is Indians and cornstalks."

"Well, I hope he doesn't expect anything fancy. I'm going to give him the chicken à la king, and if that isn't good enough for him he can go eat at the Hotel Wenonah."

"Now, Ethel, nobody said anything about it not being good enough." He was silent, while she watched him across the darning-egg. "Say, maybe you better get some of those little cakes with the pink frosting from Schermerhorn's. Lyman always did have a sweet tooth."

He did not say that he had been rehearsing, while he shaved, a number of remarks about the population of Wenonah City (eighty-four thousand, by the last census, and a sure hundred thousand by 1930, if the Chamber of Commerce figures meant anything, and they did), nor that he had taken his good gray suit to be pressed, nor that he had several times, in the privacy of the prescription room, lifted his chin and said aloud, "Well, well, Lyman, old man, you're looking fine, fine!" in a voice that he believed to be casual.

The Overland Limited was eleven minutes late. Elbert spent the eleven minutes walking the length of the platform, looking at his watch, buying a cigar he did not want, and telling the baggage-man, whom he had never seen before, that he was meeting his cousin from New York. The baggage-man said, "That so?" and spat.

When the train came, with a grandeur of steam and a squealing of brakes that always made Elbert feel the world was larger than Wenonah City and slightly menacing, he did not at first recognize the man who descended from the Pullman. He was looking for a boy with large ears and a cowlick. He saw instead a slender man in a pearl-gray overcoat with a velvet collar, in a soft hat of a curious greenish shade, in spats. The man was gray at the temples, in a manner that suggested the grayness had been arranged by a barber. He carried a stick. Nobody in Wenonah City carried a stick except old Judge Pettibone, and he had the rheumatism.

"Elbert! My dear old thing!"

"Well, well, Lyman, old man, you're looking fine—fine!" said Elbert, and was dismayed to hear that it came out exactly as he had rehearsed it, and not casual at all.

They shook hands. They shook hands for a long time, because neither of them could think what to do next. Lyman's hand was dry and thin and had a ring on it, a seal ring with a crest. (Crest! Where the deuce did a Hackett get a crest? The only crest Grandpa Hackett ever had was on his rooster.)

"Here, let me take that grip. Car's right outside. Got a new sedan—Cadwell Six, they're making 'em right here in town, you know; best car on the market for the money, and I've driven 'em all."

"Really? How awfully nice," said Lyman.

II

Elbert had planned the route from the depot with the care of a general disposing his troops. He drove up Washington Avenue so that his cousin might observe the new Second National Bank, nine stories, with a frieze of terra-cotta eagles; he turned on Fourth Street to pass the Masonic Temple, which had cost three hundred and twelve thousand dollars, not including the pipe organ; he went a block out of his way to cross the new viaduct over the Burlington tracks, and he slowed down upon the viaduct so that Lyman might comprehend its length.

"That viaduct," said Elbert, "is eleven hundred and forty feet long. Reinforced concrete. They say it'll stand a thousand years."

"It's very—substantial," said Lyman. He gazed out at the freight yards, the elevator, the gas tank, the long rows of houses with their identical front porches and their identical porch swings creaking in the March wind. "You know, it rather reminds me of Dayton. Or is it Akron? One of those places. I had to go out to one of them last year for a client. Tire people."

Elbert felt a small cold spot form under his breastbone. He had been to neither Dayton nor Akron, but he had a notion, gathered from conversations at the Kiwanis luncheons, that they were not places a man said in that tone of voice.

"Well, of course, we're growing," he said. "We got a lot of pep in this town. You'd be surprised. We got the finest school system in the state, and the Chamber's after a new packing plant that'll mean two thousand jobs. Lot of these Eastern towns, they're just standing still, living on what their granddads did. Out here we're going ahead."

"I'm sure you are," said Lyman kindly.

It was the kindness that Elbert minded.

III

Mrs. Hackett had been ready for forty minutes and had spent the time removing and replacing the doily on the parlor table. She received Lyman in her blue crêpe de Chine with the beaded front, and she said, "Well, I've certainly heard a lot about you," in a voice that implied she had not altogether believed it.

Lyman bowed over her hand. He actually bowed, from the waist, and Junior Hackett, aged eleven, who was standing in the dining-room door, made a sound like a wet cork drawn from a bottle and was sent upstairs to wash.

At dinner Lyman praised the chicken à la king. He praised it too much. He said that it was quite as good as one could get at the Brevoort, and when Mrs. Hackett asked what the Brevoort was, he explained, with a gentle little laugh, that it was a hotel in the Village. "Greenwich Village, you know. Rather a quaint old place. All sorts of interesting people. Artists. Writers. I had dinner there just last month with a chap who writes for the Saturday Evening Post."

"Well, I declare," said Mrs. Hackett, and looked at her husband as though he had failed to dine with anyone who wrote for anything.

"Funny thing," said Elbert loudly, "I had a fellow in the store last week, traveling man for a big pharmaceutical house in St. Louis. He said he'd never seen a better-arranged fountain anywhere. Said we had 'em beat in Kansas City. Course, I don't take much stock in what those drummers say, but still—"

"I'm sure it's a splendid fountain," said Lyman.

Myrtle Hackett, who was sixteen and had been reading motion-picture magazines with an earnestness she had never brought to Caesar's Commentaries, asked whether Mr. Hackett—Cousin Lyman, she meant—had ever seen Rudolph Valentino in person. Lyman considered the question with the gravity of a judge.

"I believe I passed him once on Fifth Avenue," he said. "He's shorter than you'd think."

Myrtle sighed, and looked at her cousin with a reverence she had never extended to her father, who had once shaken hands with the Governor, and had a photograph to prove it.

IV

Afterward the two men withdrew to what Elbert called the Den. It had a leather couch, a mission-oak smoking stand, a mounted pickerel that Elbert had caught at Lake Okoboji in 1919, and a radio cabinet with three dials. Elbert closed the door, winked, and produced from behind the Encyclopedia Britannica (the set was complete, and had been purchased on the installment plan from a young man who said it would give the children a start in life) a bottle of Scotch whisky.

"Real stuff. Pre-war. Got it from a fellow I know." He was proud of this; he was a little frightened by it; he poured with the elaborate carelessness of a deacon at a stag party.

Lyman held his glass to the light. "Ah," he said. "Yes." He sipped. He did not say anything else about it, and Elbert, who had paid eleven dollars for the bottle, felt that something had again been taken from him.

He turned on the radio. He was very fond of the radio. He could get Pittsburgh on a clear night, and once he had got Havana, Cuba, and had told everybody at Kiwanis about it for a month. Tonight he got a great deal of crackling, a man selling chicken feed in Iowa, and a soprano from Chicago singing "The Rosary." He turned it off.

"Interference," he explained. "Sunspots or something. Some nights you can get New York clear as a bell."

"You can get New York in New York too," said Lyman, "but I can't say I recommend it." And for the first time he laughed as though he meant it, and Elbert, without understanding the joke, laughed too, and they were both suddenly more comfortable.

They lit cigars. The house grew quiet; they could hear Mrs. Hackett upstairs telling Junior that if she heard one more peep out of him, and Myrtle playing "Kitten on the Keys" on the parlor piano with the soft pedal down, out of respect for company.

"Remember," said Elbert slowly, "the old swimming hole down on Turkey Creek? Under the cottonwoods there, back of Grandpa's south forty?"

"Remember it! Good Lord!" Lyman put down his glass. Something happened to his face; the arranged look went out of it, and for a moment he was a boy with large ears. "Remember the time you threw my pants in the creek and I had to walk home through Mrs. Ochsner's pasture in nothing but my shirt? And that damn bull of hers—"

"And you climbed the windmill! Ha! Clean to the top! And Grandpa come out with a pitchfork—"

"He wasn't after the bull. He was after me."

They roared. They slapped their knees. Elbert had to wipe his eyes. He had not laughed like that since—he could not recall; certainly not at Kiwanis, where laughter was a duty performed at the correct moments, like the singing of "America."

"And Uncle Ed's old mare," said Lyman, "the one that would only go if you sang to her—"

"Daisy! Golly, I'd forgot Daisy. You had to sing 'Shall We Gather at the River,' and nothing else would do. Ed tried 'Turkey in the Straw' once and she sat right down in the road."

"Sat down! Like a dog!"

They were off again. They remembered the jackknife with the pearl handle that they had fought over when they were twelve, until Lyman got a bloody nose and Elbert a split lip and Grandma Hackett had made them sit on opposite ends of the porch until supper and think about Cain and Abel. They remembered the camp meeting at Prairie Center, and the evangelist with the glass eye, and how Lyman had gone forward to be saved and had been so frightened he had wet the sawdust. They remembered the girl who taught the Prairie Center school, Miss Lottie Brandt, with whom they had both been in love at fourteen, and to whom they had both given valentines, and who had married a veterinarian from Ottumwa.

"I wonder whatever became of Lottie," said Lyman.

"She's dead. Died of the flu in eighteen. Ma wrote me."

"Oh."

They were silent. The cigars had gone out. The clock in the hall, a Seth Thomas with Westminster chimes that Mrs. Hackett's mother had given them for their tenth anniversary, ruminated on the quarter hour.

V

It was Elbert who spoke first, and he spoke in a voice that was not his Kiwanis voice.

"Say, Lyman. You like it back there? New York, I mean?"

"Like it?" Lyman's hand went to his tie, which was of a dark red silk and had cost, though Elbert did not know it, a good deal more than Lyman could afford. "Oh, rather. One couldn't live anywhere else, after. The theaters. The people. The sense of being at the center of things. You can't imagine, Elbert. Out here you're—well, you're terribly comfortable, of course, and I think it's fine, I honestly do, but there's no—no stimulus."

"Uh-huh. I s'pose not." Elbert looked at the mounted pickerel. "Lot of money in that advertising game, I s'pose."

"Oh, money." Lyman waved his hand. The seal ring flashed. "Money's rather beside the point, you know. Though of course one does all right. One does all right." He reached for the bottle; Elbert observed that he poured himself a larger drink than before. "As a matter of fact, I'm rather—I'm between connections just at present."

"Between—?"

"Connections. I left Dodd, Blandish and Pyle last fall. Disagreement on policy. They wanted to go after the soap business with a perfectly vulgar sort of copy, and I simply wouldn't put my name to it. So I'm—looking about. That's partly why I'm going out to the Coast. There's a chap in Los Angeles, motion-picture publicity, who's frightfully anxious to have me."

Elbert did not altogether understand. He understood that a man who was looking about was a man without a job, and he understood that in Wenonah City there was a phrase for it, and the phrase was "out of work," and it was said of switchmen and of the Hunkies at the brickyard. He looked at his cousin's spats. He looked at the gray at the temples, and saw now that it was not so well arranged as he had thought, and that under it the skin was thin and tired, and that there was a small shaving cut on the jaw that had been touched with alum.

He was filled with a confusion of emotions which he would not have been able to name, and which, had they been named for him, he would have indignantly denied. He was sorry for Lyman. He was glad. He was ashamed of being glad. He was, above all, suddenly and enormously generous, with the generosity of a man who for twenty years has been made to feel small and is now offered the chance to be large.

"Say, look here, Lyman." He leaned forward, his elbows on his knees. "Now don't take this wrong. But I been thinking for some time I ought to have a real advertising man. The stores are getting too big for me to handle the newspaper copy myself, and I'm opening a fourth one out in Riverside Park in the spring. Now, a fellow with your experience, a New York man—why, you could write your own ticket. I'd start you at fifty a week, and there's a nice little house for rent on Oak Street, two doors from the Methodist church, with a sleeping porch and—"

He stopped. Lyman was smiling at him, and it was the kind smile again, the depot smile, the Dayton-or-Akron smile.

"My dear old thing. That's tremendously decent of you. Tremendously. But I couldn't, you know. I really couldn't. I'd go mad in a month. I'd be writing copy for corn plasters and—forgive me—I'd simply die."

"Oh, sure. Sure, I understand," said Elbert. "Just a thought."

And he was relieved, because he did not really want his cousin in Wenonah City, wearing spats to the Kiwanis luncheons and saying "my dear old thing" to the Exalted Ruler of the Elks; and he was hurt, because he had offered the best he had, the very best, the stores and the sleeping porch and the Methodist church, and it had been handed back to him as one hands back a child's drawing.

"Corn plasters are a mighty good line," he said, with dignity. "We sell a lot of 'em."

"I'm sure you do," said Lyman.

VI

The Overland Limited for the West departed at nine-forty in the morning. Mrs. Hackett gave Lyman the pink-frosted cakes from Schermerhorn's in a shoebox tied with string, and Lyman said that she was a perfect dear and that he would think of her at every mouthful. Myrtle asked him to send her a picture postcard of the Hollywood studios. Junior asked him whether he had ever seen a gangster, and Lyman said that he had seen dozens, and Junior's respect was complete.

On the platform the two cousins stood together in the wind. They did not know what to say, now that it was time to say good-by, and so they talked about the weather, which was raw, and about the train, which was on time, and about the prospects of the Wenonah City Hawks in the Western League, a subject in which Lyman had no interest and Elbert very little.

"Well," said Elbert. "Well, old man."

"Well, Elbert."

They shook hands. Then, for no reason that either of them could have given, Elbert put his arm around his cousin's narrow shoulders and gave them a squeeze, the way Grandpa Hackett used to do in the barn, smelling of harness and Star plug tobacco; and Lyman for an instant leaned against him, and his stick clattered on the planking.

"Daisy," said Lyman, picking it up, "would only go for 'Shall We Gather at the River.'"

"She sat right down in the road," said Elbert, and his voice creaked.

The conductor called. Lyman climbed into the Pullman, waved his gray glove from the window, and was carried westward into the plains with his shoebox of cakes and his crest.

VII

That noon, at the Kiwanis luncheon in the Rose Room of the Hotel Wenonah, Elbert Hackett sat at the table of the Membership Committee and helped himself to a second portion of mashed potatoes.

"Had my cousin staying with me," he announced. "Lyman Hackett. Big advertising man from New York. Just passing through on his way to the Coast. Some of the big motion-picture people are after him, offering him the moon. Fine fellow. Course, he's got some Eastern notions, but you can't hold that against a man. Wants to come out and see us again. Said he was surprised—downright surprised—at the way this town's going ahead."

"Well, that's the stuff," said Mr. Orrin Wheelock of the Wheelock Furniture Company. "Those Eastern fellows got to be shown."

At the same hour, in the dining car of the Overland Limited, somewhere west of Grand Island, Lyman Hackett was sharing a table with a hardware salesman from Omaha, to whom he had been explaining the Theatre Guild.

"My people," he observed, stirring his coffee, "are out in Wenonah City. My cousin rather owns the town, you know. Drugs. Chain of stores. Simply rolling in it. Wanted me to come in with him, as a matter of fact. I couldn't, of course. But he's a dear old thing. A dear old thing."

Here is an excerpt of Sinclair Lewis's writing, to show you their style:

The assurance of Tanis Judique’s friendship fortified Babbitt’s self-approval. At the Athletic Club he became experimental. Though Vergil Gunch was silent, the others at the Roughnecks’ Table came to accept Babbitt as having, for no visible reason, “turned crank.” They argued windily with him, and he was cocky, and enjoyed the spectacle of his interesting martyrdom. He even praised Seneca Doane. Professor Pumphrey said that was carrying a joke too far; but Babbitt argued, “No! Fact! I tell you he’s got one of the keenest intellects in the country. Why, Lord Wycombe said that—” “Oh, who the hell is Lord Wycombe? What you always lugging him in for? You been touting him for the last six weeks!” protested Orville Jones.

“George ordered him from Sears-Roebuck. You can get those English high-muckamucks by mail for two bucks apiece,” suggested Sidney Finkelstein.

“That’s all right now! Lord Wycombe, he’s one of the biggest intellects in English political life. As I was saying: Of course I’m conservative myself, but I appreciate a guy like Senny Doane because—” Vergil Gunch interrupted harshly, “I wonder if you are so conservative? I find I can manage to run my own business without any skunks and reds like Doane in it!” The grimness of Gunch’s voice, the hardness of his jaw, disconcerted Babbitt, but he recovered and went on till they looked bored, then irritated, then as doubtful as Gunch. He thought of Tanis always. With a stir he remembered her every aspect. His arms yearned for her. “I’ve found her! I’ve dreamed of her all these years and now I’ve found her!” he exulted. He met her at the movies in the morning; he drove out to her flat in the late afternoon or on evenings when he was believed to be at the Elks. He knew her financial affairs and advised her about them, while she lamented her feminine ignorance, and praised his masterfulness, and proved to know much more about bonds than he did. They had remembrances, and laughter over old times. Once they quarreled, and he raged that she was as “bossy” as his wife and far more whining when he was inattentive. But that passed safely. Their high hour was a tramp on a ringing December afternoon, through snow-drifted meadows down to the icy Chaloosa River. She was exotic in an astrachan cap and a short beaver coat; she slid on the ice and shouted, and he panted after her, rotund with laughter.... Myra Babbitt never slid on the ice. He was afraid that they would be seen together. In Zenith it is impossible to lunch with a neighbor’s wife without the fact being known, before nightfall, in every house in your circle. But Tanis was beautifully discreet. However appealingly she might turn to him when they were alone, she was gravely detached when they were abroad, and he hoped that she would be taken for a client. Orville Jones once saw them emerging from a movie theater, and Babbitt bumbled, “Let me make you ’quainted with Mrs. Judique. Now here’s a lady who knows the right broker to come to, Orvy!” Mr. Jones, though he was a man censorious of morals and of laundry machinery, seemed satisfied. His predominant fear—not from any especial fondness for her but from the habit of propriety—was that his wife would learn of the affair. He was certain that she knew nothing specific about Tanis, but he was also certain that she suspected something indefinite. For years she had been bored by anything more affectionate than a farewell kiss, yet she was hurt by any slackening in his irritable periodic interest, and now he had no interest; rather, a revulsion. He was completely faithful—to Tanis. He was distressed by the sight of his wife’s slack plumpness, by her puffs and billows of flesh, by the tattered petticoat which she was always meaning and always forgetting to throw away. But he was aware that she, so long attuned to him, caught all his repulsions. He elaborately, heavily, jocularly tried to check them. He couldn’t. They had a tolerable Christmas. Kenneth Escott was there, admittedly engaged to Verona. Mrs. Babbitt was tearful and called Kenneth her new son. Babbitt was worried about Ted, because he had ceased complaining of the State University and become suspiciously acquiescent. He wondered what the boy was planning, and was too shy to ask. Himself, Babbitt slipped away on Christmas afternoon to take his present, a silver cigarette-box, to Tanis. When he returned Mrs. Babbitt asked, much too innocently, “Did you go out for a little fresh air?”

“Yes, just lil drive,” he mumbled. After New Year’s his wife proposed, “I heard from my sister to-day, George. She isn’t well. I think perhaps I ought to go stay with her for a few weeks.” Now, Mrs. Babbitt was not accustomed to leave home during the winter except on violently demanding occasions, and only the summer before, she had been gone for weeks. Nor was Babbitt one of the detachable husbands who take separations casually. He liked to have her there; she looked after his clothes; she knew how his steak ought to be cooked; and her clucking made him feel secure. But he could not drum up even a dutiful “Oh, she doesn’t really need you, does she?” While he tried to look regretful, while he felt that his wife was watching him, he was filled with exultant visions of Tanis.

“Do you think I’d better go?” she said sharply.

“You’ve got to decide, honey; I can’t.” She turned away, sighing, and his forehead was damp. Till she went, four days later, she was curiously still, he cumbrously affectionate. Her train left at noon. As he saw it grow small beyond the train-shed he longed to hurry to Tanis.

“No, by golly, I won’t do that!” he vowed. “I won’t go near her for a week!” But he was at her flat at four. He who had once controlled or seemed to control his life in a progress unimpassioned but diligent and sane was for that fortnight borne on a current of desire and very bad whisky and all the complications of new acquaintances, those furious new intimates who demand so much more attention than old friends. Each morning he gloomily recognized his idiocies of the evening before. With his head throbbing, his tongue and lips stinging from cigarettes, he incredulously counted the number of drinks he had taken, and groaned, “I got to quit!” He had ceased saying, “I will quit!” for however resolute he might be at dawn, he could not, for a single evening, check his drift. He had met Tanis’s friends; he had, with the ardent haste of the Midnight People, who drink and dance and rattle and are ever afraid to be silent, been adopted as a member of her group, which they called “The Bunch.” He first met them after a day when he had worked particularly hard and when he hoped to be quiet with Tanis and slowly sip her admiration. From down the hall he could hear shrieks and the grind of a phonograph. As Tanis opened the door he saw fantastic figures dancing in a haze of cigarette smoke. The tables and chairs were against the wall.

“Oh, isn’t this dandy!” she gabbled at him. “Carrie Nork had the loveliest idea. She decided it was time for a party, and she ’phoned the Bunch and told ’em to gather round.... George, this is Carrie.”

“Carrie” was, in the less desirable aspects of both, at once matronly and spinsterish. She was perhaps forty; her hair was an unconvincing ash-blond; and if her chest was flat, her hips were ponderous. She greeted Babbitt with a giggling “Welcome to our little midst! Tanis says you’re a real sport.” He was apparently expected to dance, to be boyish and gay with Carrie, and he did his unforgiving best. He towed her about the room, bumping into other couples, into the radiator, into chair-legs cunningly ambushed. As he danced he surveyed the rest of the Bunch: A thin young woman who looked capable, conceited, and sarcastic. Another woman whom he could never quite remember. Three overdressed and slightly effeminate young men—soda-fountain clerks, or at least born for that profession. A man of his own age, immovable, self-satisfied, resentful of Babbitt’s presence. When he had finished his dutiful dance Tanis took him aside and begged, “Dear, wouldn’t you like to do something for me? I’m all out of booze, and the Bunch want to celebrate. Couldn’t you just skip down to Healey Hanson’s and get some?”

“Sure,” he said, trying not to sound sullen.

“I’ll tell you: I’ll get Minnie Sonntag to drive down with you.” Tanis was pointing to the thin, sarcastic young woman. Miss Sonntag greeted him with an astringent “How d’you do, Mr. Babbitt. Tanis tells me you’re a very prominent man, and I’m honored by being allowed to drive with you. Of course I’m not accustomed to associating with society people like you, so I don’t know how to act in such exalted circles!” Thus Miss Sonntag talked all the way down to Healey Hanson’s. To her jibes he wanted to reply “Oh, go to the devil!” but he never quite nerved himself to that reasonable comment. He was resenting the existence of the whole Bunch. He had heard Tanis speak of “darling Carrie” and “Min Sonntag—she’s so clever—you’ll adore her,” but they had never been real to him. He had pictured Tanis as living in a rose-tinted vacuum, waiting for him, free of all the complications of a Floral Heights. When they returned he had to endure the patronage of the young soda-clerks. They were as damply friendly as Miss Sonntag was dryly hostile. They called him “Old Georgie” and shouted, “Come on now, sport; shake a leg” ... boys in belted coats, pimply boys, as young as Ted and as flabby as chorus-men, but powerful to dance and to mind the phonograph and smoke cigarettes and patronize Tanis. He tried to be one of them; he cried “Good work, Pete!” but his voice creaked. Tanis apparently enjoyed the companionship of the dancing darlings; she bridled to their bland flirtation and casually kissed them at the end of each dance. Babbitt hated her, for the moment. He saw her as middle-aged. He studied the wrinkles in the softness of her throat, the slack flesh beneath her chin. The taut muscles of her youth were loose and drooping. Between dances she sat in the largest chair, waving her cigarette, summoning her callow admirers to come and talk to her. (“She thinks she’s a blooming queen!” growled Babbitt.) She chanted to Miss Sonntag, “Isn’t my little studio sweet?” (“Studio, rats! It’s a plain old-maid-and-chow-dog flat! Oh, God, I wish I was home! I wonder if I can’t make a getaway now?”) His vision grew blurred, however, as he applied himself to Healey Hanson’s raw but vigorous whisky. He blended with the Bunch. He began to rejoice that Carrie Nork and Pete, the most nearly intelligent of the nimble youths, seemed to like him; and it was enormously important to win over the surly older man, who proved to be a railway clerk named Fulton Bemis. The conversation of the Bunch was exclamatory, high-colored, full of references to people whom Babbitt did not know. Apparently they thought very comfortably of themselves. They were the Bunch, wise and beautiful and amusing; they were Bohemians and urbanites, accustomed to all the luxuries of Zenith: dance-halls, movie-theaters, and roadhouses; and in a cynical superiority to people who were “slow” or “tightwad” they cackled: “Oh, Pete, did I tell you what that dub of a cashier said when I came in late yesterday? Oh, it was per-fect-ly priceless!”

“Oh, but wasn’t T. D. stewed! Say, he was simply ossified! What did Gladys say to him?”

“Think of the nerve of Bob Bickerstaff trying to get us to come to his house! Say, the nerve of him! Can you beat it for nerve? Some nerve I call it!”

“Did you notice how Dotty was dancing? Gee, wasn’t she the limit!” Babbitt was to be heard sonorously agreeing with the once-hated Miss Minnie Sonntag that persons who let a night go by without dancing to jazz music were crabs, pikers, and poor fish; and he roared “You bet!” when Mrs. Carrie Nork gurgled, “Don’t you love to sit on the floor? It’s so Bohemian!” He began to think extremely well of the Bunch. When he mentioned his friends Sir Gerald Doak, Lord Wycombe, William Washington Eathorne, and Chum Frink, he was proud of their condescending interest. He got so thoroughly into the jocund spirit that he didn’t much mind seeing Tanis drooping against the shoulder of the youngest and milkiest of the young men, and he himself desired to hold Carrie Nork’s pulpy hand, and dropped it only because Tanis looked angry. When he went home, at two, he was fully a member of the Bunch, and all the week thereafter he was bound by the exceedingly straitened conventions, the exceedingly wearing demands, of their life of pleasure and freedom. He had to go to their parties; he was involved in the agitation when everybody telephoned to everybody else that she hadn’t meant what she’d said when she’d said that, and anyway, why was Pete going around saying she’d said it? Never was a Family more insistent on learning one another’s movements than were the Bunch. All of them volubly knew, or indignantly desired to know, where all the others had been every minute of the week. Babbitt found himself explaining to Carrie or Fulton Bemis just what he had been doing that he should not have joined them till ten o’clock, and apologizing for having gone to dinner with a business acquaintance. Every member of the Bunch was expected to telephone to every other member at least once a week. “Why haven’t you called me up?” Babbitt was asked accusingly, not only by Tanis and Carrie but presently by new ancient friends, Jennie and Capitolina and Toots. If for a moment he had seen Tanis as withering and sentimental, he lost that impression at Carrie Nork’s dance. Mrs. Nork had a large house and a small husband. To her party came all of the Bunch, perhaps thirty-five of them when they were completely mobilized. Babbitt, under the name of “Old Georgie,” was now a pioneer of the Bunch, since each month it changed half its membership and he who could recall the prehistoric days of a fortnight ago, before Mrs. Absolom, the food-demonstrator, had gone to Indianapolis, and Mac had “got sore at” Minnie, was a venerable leader and able to condescend to new Petes and Minnies and Gladyses. At Carrie’s, Tanis did not have to work at being hostess. She was dignified and sure, a clear fine figure in the black chiffon frock he had always loved; and in the wider spaces of that ugly house Babbitt was able to sit quietly with her. He repented of his first revulsion, mooned at her feet, andhappily drove her home. Next day he bought a violent yellow tie, to make himself young for her. He knew, a little sadly, that he could not make himself beautiful; he beheld himself as heavy, hinting of fatness, but he danced, he dressed, he chattered, to be as young as she was... as young as she seemed to be. As all converts, whether to a religion, love, or gardening, find as by magic that though hitherto these hobbies have not seemed to exist, now the whole world is filled with their fury, so, once he was converted to dissipation, Babbitt discovered agreeable opportunities for it everywhere. He had a new view of his sporting neighbor, Sam Doppelbrau. The Doppelbraus were respectable people, industrious people, prosperous people, whose ideal of happiness was an eternal cabaret. Their life was dominated by suburban bacchanalia of alcohol, nicotine, gasoline, and kisses. They and their set worked capably all the week, and all week looked forward to Saturday night, when they would, as they expressed it, “throw a party;” and the thrown party grew noisier and noisier up to Sunday dawn, and usually included an extremely rapid motor expedition to nowhere in particular. One evening when Tanis was at the theater, Babbitt found himself being lively with the Doppelbraus, pledging friendship with men whom he had for years privily denounced to Mrs. Babbitt as a “rotten bunch of tin-horns that I wouldn’t go out with, not if they were the last people on earth.” That evening he had sulkily come home and poked about in front of the house, chipping off the walk the ice-clots, like fossil footprints, made by the steps of passers-by during the recent snow. Howard Littlefield came up snuffling.

“Still a widower, George?”

“Yump. Cold again to-night.”

“What do you hear from the wife?”

“She’s feeling fine, but her sister is still pretty sick.”

“Say, better come in and have dinner with us to-night, George.”

“Oh—oh, thanks. Have to go out.” Suddenly he could not endure Littlefield’s recitals of the more interesting statistics about totally uninteresting problems. He scraped at the walk and grunted. Sam Doppelbrau appeared.

“Evenin’, Babbitt. Working hard?”

“Yuh, lil exercise.”

“Cold enough for you to-night?”

“Well, just about.”

“Still a widower?”

“Uh-huh.”

Here is an excerpt of Sinclair Lewis's writing, to show you their style:

The assurance of Tanis Judique’s friendship fortified Babbitt’s self-approval. At the Athletic Club he became experimental. Though Vergil Gunch was silent, the others at the Roughnecks’ Table came to accept Babbitt as having, for no visible reason, “turned crank.” They argued windily with him, and he was cocky, and enjoyed the spectacle of his interesting martyrdom. He even praised Seneca Doane. Professor Pumphrey said that was carrying a joke too far; but Babbitt argued, “No! Fact! I tell you he’s got one of the keenest intellects in the country. Why, Lord Wycombe said that—” “Oh, who the hell is Lord Wycombe? What you always lugging him in for? You been touting him for the last six weeks!” protested Orville Jones.

“George ordered him from Sears-Roebuck. You can get those English high-muckamucks by mail for two bucks apiece,” suggested Sidney Finkelstein.

“That’s all right now! Lord Wycombe, he’s one of the biggest intellects in English political life. As I was saying: Of course I’m conservative myself, but I appreciate a guy like Senny Doane because—” Vergil Gunch interrupted harshly, “I wonder if you are so conservative? I find I can manage to run my own business without any skunks and reds like Doane in it!” The grimness of Gunch’s voice, the hardness of his jaw, disconcerted Babbitt, but he recovered and went on till they looked bored, then irritated, then as doubtful as Gunch. He thought of Tanis always. With a stir he remembered her every aspect. His arms yearned for her. “I’ve found her! I’ve dreamed of her all these years and now I’ve found her!” he exulted. He met her at the movies in the morning; he drove out to her flat in the late afternoon or on evenings when he was believed to be at the Elks. He knew her financial affairs and advised her about them, while she lamented her feminine ignorance, and praised his masterfulness, and proved to know much more about bonds than he did. They had remembrances, and laughter over old times. Once they quarreled, and he raged that she was as “bossy” as his wife and far more whining when he was inattentive. But that passed safely. Their high hour was a tramp on a ringing December afternoon, through snow-drifted meadows down to the icy Chaloosa River. She was exotic in an astrachan cap and a short beaver coat; she slid on the ice and shouted, and he panted after her, rotund with laughter.... Myra Babbitt never slid on the ice. He was afraid that they would be seen together. In Zenith it is impossible to lunch with a neighbor’s wife without the fact being known, before nightfall, in every house in your circle. But Tanis was beautifully discreet. However appealingly she might turn to him when they were alone, she was gravely detached when they were abroad, and he hoped that she would be taken for a client. Orville Jones once saw them emerging from a movie theater, and Babbitt bumbled, “Let me make you ’quainted with Mrs. Judique. Now here’s a lady who knows the right broker to come to, Orvy!” Mr. Jones, though he was a man censorious of morals and of laundry machinery, seemed satisfied. His predominant fear—not from any especial fondness for her but from the habit of propriety—was that his wife would learn of the affair. He was certain that she knew nothing specific about Tanis, but he was also certain that she suspected something indefinite. For years she had been bored by anything more affectionate than a farewell kiss, yet she was hurt by any slackening in his irritable periodic interest, and now he had no interest; rather, a revulsion. He was completely faithful—to Tanis. He was distressed by the sight of his wife’s slack plumpness, by her puffs and billows of flesh, by the tattered petticoat which she was always meaning and always forgetting to throw away. But he was aware that she, so long attuned to him, caught all his repulsions. He elaborately, heavily, jocularly tried to check them. He couldn’t. They had a tolerable Christmas. Kenneth Escott was there, admittedly engaged to Verona. Mrs. Babbitt was tearful and called Kenneth her new son. Babbitt was worried about Ted, because he had ceased complaining of the State University and become suspiciously acquiescent. He wondered what the boy was planning, and was too shy to ask. Himself, Babbitt slipped away on Christmas afternoon to take his present, a silver cigarette-box, to Tanis. When he returned Mrs. Babbitt asked, much too innocently, “Did you go out for a little fresh air?”

“Yes, just lil drive,” he mumbled. After New Year’s his wife proposed, “I heard from my sister to-day, George. She isn’t well. I think perhaps I ought to go stay with her for a few weeks.” Now, Mrs. Babbitt was not accustomed to leave home during the winter except on violently demanding occasions, and only the summer before, she had been gone for weeks. Nor was Babbitt one of the detachable husbands who take separations casually. He liked to have her there; she looked after his clothes; she knew how his steak ought to be cooked; and her clucking made him feel secure. But he could not drum up even a dutiful “Oh, she doesn’t really need you, does she?” While he tried to look regretful, while he felt that his wife was watching him, he was filled with exultant visions of Tanis.

“Do you think I’d better go?” she said sharply.

“You’ve got to decide, honey; I can’t.” She turned away, sighing, and his forehead was damp. Till she went, four days later, she was curiously still, he cumbrously affectionate. Her train left at noon. As he saw it grow small beyond the train-shed he longed to hurry to Tanis.

“No, by golly, I won’t do that!” he vowed. “I won’t go near her for a week!” But he was at her flat at four. He who had once controlled or seemed to control his life in a progress unimpassioned but diligent and sane was for that fortnight borne on a current of desire and very bad whisky and all the complications of new acquaintances, those furious new intimates who demand so much more attention than old friends. Each morning he gloomily recognized his idiocies of the evening before. With his head throbbing, his tongue and lips stinging from cigarettes, he incredulously counted the number of drinks he had taken, and groaned, “I got to quit!” He had ceased saying, “I will quit!” for however resolute he might be at dawn, he could not, for a single evening, check his drift. He had met Tanis’s friends; he had, with the ardent haste of the Midnight People, who drink and dance and rattle and are ever afraid to be silent, been adopted as a member of her group, which they called “The Bunch.” He first met them after a day when he had worked particularly hard and when he hoped to be quiet with Tanis and slowly sip her admiration. From down the hall he could hear shrieks and the grind of a phonograph. As Tanis opened the door he saw fantastic figures dancing in a haze of cigarette smoke. The tables and chairs were against the wall.

“Oh, isn’t this dandy!” she gabbled at him. “Carrie Nork had the loveliest idea. She decided it was time for a party, and she ’phoned the Bunch and told ’em to gather round.... George, this is Carrie.”

“Carrie” was, in the less desirable aspects of both, at once matronly and spinsterish. She was perhaps forty; her hair was an unconvincing ash-blond; and if her chest was flat, her hips were ponderous. She greeted Babbitt with a giggling “Welcome to our little midst! Tanis says you’re a real sport.” He was apparently expected to dance, to be boyish and gay with Carrie, and he did his unforgiving best. He towed her about the room, bumping into other couples, into the radiator, into chair-legs cunningly ambushed. As he danced he surveyed the rest of the Bunch: A thin young woman who looked capable, conceited, and sarcastic. Another woman whom he could never quite remember. Three overdressed and slightly effeminate young men—soda-fountain clerks, or at least born for that profession. A man of his own age, immovable, self-satisfied, resentful of Babbitt’s presence. When he had finished his dutiful dance Tanis took him aside and begged, “Dear, wouldn’t you like to do something for me? I’m all out of booze, and the Bunch want to celebrate. Couldn’t you just skip down to Healey Hanson’s and get some?”

“Sure,” he said, trying not to sound sullen.

“I’ll tell you: I’ll get Minnie Sonntag to drive down with you.” Tanis was pointing to the thin, sarcastic young woman. Miss Sonntag greeted him with an astringent “How d’you do, Mr. Babbitt. Tanis tells me you’re a very prominent man, and I’m honored by being allowed to drive with you. Of course I’m not accustomed to associating with society people like you, so I don’t know how to act in such exalted circles!” Thus Miss Sonntag talked all the way down to Healey Hanson’s. To her jibes he wanted to reply “Oh, go to the devil!” but he never quite nerved himself to that reasonable comment. He was resenting the existence of the whole Bunch. He had heard Tanis speak of “darling Carrie” and “Min Sonntag—she’s so clever—you’ll adore her,” but they had never been real to him. He had pictured Tanis as living in a rose-tinted vacuum, waiting for him, free of all the complications of a Floral Heights. When they returned he had to endure the patronage of the young soda-clerks. They were as damply friendly as Miss Sonntag was dryly hostile. They called him “Old Georgie” and shouted, “Come on now, sport; shake a leg” ... boys in belted coats, pimply boys, as young as Ted and as flabby as chorus-men, but powerful to dance and to mind the phonograph and smoke cigarettes and patronize Tanis. He tried to be one of them; he cried “Good work, Pete!” but his voice creaked. Tanis apparently enjoyed the companionship of the dancing darlings; she bridled to their bland flirtation and casually kissed them at the end of each dance. Babbitt hated her, for the moment. He saw her as middle-aged. He studied the wrinkles in the softness of her throat, the slack flesh beneath her chin. The taut muscles of her youth were loose and drooping. Between dances she sat in the largest chair, waving her cigarette, summoning her callow admirers to come and talk to her. (“She thinks she’s a blooming queen!” growled Babbitt.) She chanted to Miss Sonntag, “Isn’t my little studio sweet?” (“Studio, rats! It’s a plain old-maid-and-chow-dog flat! Oh, God, I wish I was home! I wonder if I can’t make a getaway now?”) His vision grew blurred, however, as he applied himself to Healey Hanson’s raw but vigorous whisky. He blended with the Bunch. He began to rejoice that Carrie Nork and Pete, the most nearly intelligent of the nimble youths, seemed to like him; and it was enormously important to win over the surly older man, who proved to be a railway clerk named Fulton Bemis. The conversation of the Bunch was exclamatory, high-colored, full of references to people whom Babbitt did not know. Apparently they thought very comfortably of themselves. They were the Bunch, wise and beautiful and amusing; they were Bohemians and urbanites, accustomed to all the luxuries of Zenith: dance-halls, movie-theaters, and roadhouses; and in a cynical superiority to people who were “slow” or “tightwad” they cackled: “Oh, Pete, did I tell you what that dub of a cashier said when I came in late yesterday? Oh, it was per-fect-ly priceless!”

“Oh, but wasn’t T. D. stewed! Say, he was simply ossified! What did Gladys say to him?”

“Think of the nerve of Bob Bickerstaff trying to get us to come to his house! Say, the nerve of him! Can you beat it for nerve? Some nerve I call it!”

“Did you notice how Dotty was dancing? Gee, wasn’t she the limit!” Babbitt was to be heard sonorously agreeing with the once-hated Miss Minnie Sonntag that persons who let a night go by without dancing to jazz music were crabs, pikers, and poor fish; and he roared “You bet!” when Mrs. Carrie Nork gurgled, “Don’t you love to sit on the floor? It’s so Bohemian!” He began to think extremely well of the Bunch. When he mentioned his friends Sir Gerald Doak, Lord Wycombe, William Washington Eathorne, and Chum Frink, he was proud of their condescending interest. He got so thoroughly into the jocund spirit that he didn’t much mind seeing Tanis drooping against the shoulder of the youngest and milkiest of the young men, and he himself desired to hold Carrie Nork’s pulpy hand, and dropped it only because Tanis looked angry. When he went home, at two, he was fully a member of the Bunch, and all the week thereafter he was bound by the exceedingly straitened conventions, the exceedingly wearing demands, of their life of pleasure and freedom. He had to go to their parties; he was involved in the agitation when everybody telephoned to everybody else that she hadn’t meant what she’d said when she’d said that, and anyway, why was Pete going around saying she’d said it? Never was a Family more insistent on learning one another’s movements than were the Bunch. All of them volubly knew, or indignantly desired to know, where all the others had been every minute of the week. Babbitt found himself explaining to Carrie or Fulton Bemis just what he had been doing that he should not have joined them till ten o’clock, and apologizing for having gone to dinner with a business acquaintance. Every member of the Bunch was expected to telephone to every other member at least once a week. “Why haven’t you called me up?” Babbitt was asked accusingly, not only by Tanis and Carrie but presently by new ancient friends, Jennie and Capitolina and Toots. If for a moment he had seen Tanis as withering and sentimental, he lost that impression at Carrie Nork’s dance. Mrs. Nork had a large house and a small husband. To her party came all of the Bunch, perhaps thirty-five of them when they were completely mobilized. Babbitt, under the name of “Old Georgie,” was now a pioneer of the Bunch, since each month it changed half its membership and he who could recall the prehistoric days of a fortnight ago, before Mrs. Absolom, the food-demonstrator, had gone to Indianapolis, and Mac had “got sore at” Minnie, was a venerable leader and able to condescend to new Petes and Minnies and Gladyses. At Carrie’s, Tanis did not have to work at being hostess. She was dignified and sure, a clear fine figure in the black chiffon frock he had always loved; and in the wider spaces of that ugly house Babbitt was able to sit quietly with her. He repented of his first revulsion, mooned at her feet, andhappily drove her home. Next day he bought a violent yellow tie, to make himself young for her. He knew, a little sadly, that he could not make himself beautiful; he beheld himself as heavy, hinting of fatness, but he danced, he dressed, he chattered, to be as young as she was... as young as she seemed to be. As all converts, whether to a religion, love, or gardening, find as by magic that though hitherto these hobbies have not seemed to exist, now the whole world is filled with their fury, so, once he was converted to dissipation, Babbitt discovered agreeable opportunities for it everywhere. He had a new view of his sporting neighbor, Sam Doppelbrau. The Doppelbraus were respectable people, industrious people, prosperous people, whose ideal of happiness was an eternal cabaret. Their life was dominated by suburban bacchanalia of alcohol, nicotine, gasoline, and kisses. They and their set worked capably all the week, and all week looked forward to Saturday night, when they would, as they expressed it, “throw a party;” and the thrown party grew noisier and noisier up to Sunday dawn, and usually included an extremely rapid motor expedition to nowhere in particular. One evening when Tanis was at the theater, Babbitt found himself being lively with the Doppelbraus, pledging friendship with men whom he had for years privily denounced to Mrs. Babbitt as a “rotten bunch of tin-horns that I wouldn’t go out with, not if they were the last people on earth.” That evening he had sulkily come home and poked about in front of the house, chipping off the walk the ice-clots, like fossil footprints, made by the steps of passers-by during the recent snow. Howard Littlefield came up snuffling.

“Still a widower, George?”

“Yump. Cold again to-night.”

“What do you hear from the wife?”

“She’s feeling fine, but her sister is still pretty sick.”

“Say, better come in and have dinner with us to-night, George.”

“Oh—oh, thanks. Have to go out.” Suddenly he could not endure Littlefield’s recitals of the more interesting statistics about totally uninteresting problems. He scraped at the walk and grunted. Sam Doppelbrau appeared.

“Evenin’, Babbitt. Working hard?”

“Yuh, lil exercise.”

“Cold enough for you to-night?”

“Well, just about.”

“Still a widower?”

“Uh-huh.”

Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can. Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
