The house in which the Gersbachs had their two rooms stood upon the north side of Washington Street, a little below the crest of the hill, where the cable cars of the Powell Street line, coming up out of the hollow of the town, swung around the curve with a prolonged clashing of iron upon iron, and went grinding and lurching onward toward the Bay. All day long, and far into the night, the cable hummed in its slot beneath the cobbles, a low, unceasing note, monotonous, interminable, like the drone of some vast insect buried in the earth. It was the first sound Delia Gersbach heard upon waking and the last sound she heard before she slept. After four years she had ceased to notice it at all, as one ceases to notice the beating of one's own heart. Only when it stopped, as it did sometimes in the small hours when the power-house shut down for repairs, would she start up in her bed, wide awake and vaguely frightened, as if something had died in the night.

Anton Gersbach was a gripman upon that line. He was a huge, slow, blond German of thirty-five, with enormous shoulders, a thick red neck, and great hands, square-ended, hard as the wooden handles of the grip lever, the palms ridged and yellow with callous. His hair was cropped close to his round skull, and his mustache, stiff and colorless as dry straw, hung down over a mouth that was heavy and good-natured and a trifle stupid. He was not quick. He thought with difficulty, laboriously, one idea at a time, turning it over and over as he would have turned a stone in his fingers. But he was strong, and he was steady, and for eleven years he had stood in the front of the dummy, his feet planted wide, his two fists upon the lever, and had driven his car up the terrific grade of Powell Street and down again, two hundred times a month, and never a mishap. The company knew him for a good man. He was proud of that. It was the one thing in the world of which he was proud.

Delia was little and dark and quick, Irish to the finger-tips, with a narrow, pale face, black eyebrows that nearly met above her nose, and a small, tight mouth that could shut like a purse. She was a good manager. She bought her meat at the shop on Stockton Street where it was a cent cheaper by the pound, and she carried it home herself rather than pay the boy to bring it. She had a passion for order. The two rooms were scrubbed and blacked and polished till they shone; the stove was a mirror; the oilcloth upon the kitchen table had been washed so often that the pattern of blue tiles was nearly gone from it. Every Saturday night, when Anton brought home his wages, she counted the money out upon that table, coin by coin, sorting the silver from the gold, and put away into the tin box behind the flour bin what could be spared. There were a hundred and forty dollars in the box now. She knew the sum to the very nickel. She thought of it often during the day, at odd moments, while she ironed, while she peeled potatoes, and the thought of it warmed her like a little fire.

It was a Thursday, toward the end of October, a day of high wind and blowing dust, when the trade-wind came booming in through the Golden Gate and swept the hill-tops of the city clean. At six o'clock Delia had the supper ready—a stew of mutton and onions, a loaf of bread, a pot of coffee black as ink. The lamp was lit. The window rattled in its frame. Below, in the street, the cable hummed in its slot.

At a quarter past six she heard Anton's heavy tread upon the stairs, slow, deliberate, each step jarring the flimsy house. He came in, filling the doorway with his bulk, and hung his cap upon its nail, and said, as he said every evening:

"Well, Dele."

"Well," she answered.

He went to the sink and washed his hands and face, blowing and snorting in the water like a horse, and dried himself upon the roller towel, and sat down at the table. She put the stew before him. He began to eat at once, bending over his plate, shovelling the food into his mouth with his knife, chewing enormously, his jaws working with the steady, mechanical regularity of some great machine. Delia did not eat. She sat opposite him, her hands folded upon the oilcloth, and watched him. He did not notice. He never noticed. When he was eating he was conscious of nothing but the food.

"Anton," she said at length.

"Huh?"

"How was the road to-day?"

"All right," he said, with his mouth full. "Pretty good. Wind's bad on the hill."

"Was it?"

"Yes. Blows the dust in the slot. She drags some."

"Who was your conductor to-day?"

He paused. It was only for an instant, the fraction of an instant, his knife suspended half-way to his mouth. Then he went on eating.

"Schultz," he said. "Same as always."

Delia drew a long breath. Her small mouth shut tight. Her hands upon the oilcloth gripped one another till the knuckles whitened.

"You're a liar, Anton Gersbach," she said.

He stopped eating then. He laid down his knife and looked up at her, slowly, his small blue eyes wide and puzzled under their pale lashes. For a long moment he did not speak. The lamp flared and smoked a little. The window rattled. Down in the street a car came grinding up the grade, and the cable sang beneath it, a long, shrill, rising note, and then fell again to its eternal hum.

"What's that?" he said at last.

"You heard me. You're a liar. You ain't been on the road to-day. You ain't been on the road this week. You ain't been on the road since the Tuesday before last. Don't you go telling me no, because I know."

He stared at her stupidly. His great red face grew slowly redder, the blood creeping up from his thick neck into his cheeks and over his forehead to the roots of his cropped hair. He moved in his chair, and the chair creaked under him.

"Who told you?" he said.

"Never you mind who told me. Mrs. Flaherty told me, if you want to know, that's who told me, and her husband's in the barn, and he told her, and she come up here this afternoon and sat right there where you're sitting, and told me, and asked me how I liked it. Me! That didn't know a thing about it. Me, that's been putting up your dinner-pail every morning this ten days, and you taking it and going off with it down the stairs as big as life, and saying, 'Good-by, Dele,' and all the time—all the time—" Her voice rose and broke. "Where've you been? Where've you been going all day long, every day, with that dinner-pail?"

Anton looked down at his plate. He did not answer at once. It was very hard for him to find words; it had always been hard. Words did not come to him; he had to go and seek them out, one by one, as one gropes for tools in the dark.

"I been looking for a job," he said.

"A job! And you with a job! What did you do? What did they let you go for? Eleven years you been with them. Eleven years! What did you do?"

He was silent again. His huge hands lay upon the table on either side of his plate, palm downward, and Delia saw the fingers of them curl slowly inward, as though they closed upon something, upon the handle of a lever, perhaps, gripping, gripping, with all the force of his enormous strength.

"There was a kid," he said.

Delia did not move.

"There was a kid," he said again, in his slow, thick voice. "Down by Jackson Street. Little girl. Coming out from behind a wagon. I didn't see her. I couldn't see her, Dele. The wagon was there, see, a brewery wagon, standing, and she come out from behind it with a hoop, running after the hoop. I put on the brake. I put her on hard. I put her on so hard I bent the shoe. But it's steep there, Dele. It's steep there by Jackson. You don't stop a car on that grade, not like you'd stop a horse."

"Did you—was she—"

"No. She ain't dead. She got her leg broke. They took her to the Receiving Hospital. She'll get well, the doctor says. But her father's a man that knows a lawyer, and he come to the company, and the company says somebody's got to go. So it was me. I was the man on the grip." He lifted his hands a little from the table and let them fall again. "It wasn't my fault, Dele. I put the brake on. I put her on hard."

For a moment—only for a moment—something softened in Delia's narrow face. Her lips parted. She looked at the great hands lying there upon the worn oilcloth, so strong, so helpless, and it seemed as if she would reach out and touch them. But the moment passed. A thought had come to her, a little, sharp, cold thought, and her mouth shut again.

"Ten days," she said. "Ten days, and you never told me."

"I was going to tell you."

"When? When was you going to tell me? When the rent come due? When there wasn't nothing in the house to eat? Ten days, and you going off every morning with your pail, making a fool of me, letting me think—letting me put by—" She stopped short. Her eyes narrowed. She leaned forward across the table. "Anton. Where's your wages? Saturday. You brought me your wages Saturday. Eleven dollars. You put it right there on the table, and I counted it. Where'd you get it?"

He did not answer.

"Where'd you get it?"

Still he said nothing. He sat there motionless, his head lowered, his eyes upon his plate, his great shoulders hunched, like an ox that waits for the goad. And Delia, watching him, felt a sudden fear take hold of her, a fear that made her heart beat thick and fast. She rose from the table so quickly that her chair went over behind her with a clatter, and ran to the corner where the flour bin stood, and dragged it out from the wall, and thrust her arm in behind it, groping. Her fingers found the tin box. She drew it out and pried off the lid with her nails and turned it out upon the drain-board of the sink. The coins rang upon the wood, rolled, spun, and lay still. She counted them, her lips moving, her fingers flying, pushing the gold to one side and the silver to the other.

There were a hundred and twenty-nine dollars.

She counted them again. A hundred and twenty-nine. She turned and faced him, the empty box in her hand.

"You took it," she said. Her voice was very low. "You took it out of the box. Eleven dollars. You took my money out of my box and brought it to me and put it on the table and let me count it and put it back. Like it was your wages. Like it was—" She choked. "My money!"

"It ain't your money," said Anton slowly. "It's our money."

"It's my money! Who saved it? Who went without? Who walked to Stockton Street for the meat, and wore her old jacket two winters, and turned her skirt, and never had a thing, not a ribbon, not a thing, so's there'd be something put by? It's my money, every cent of it, and you went and took it, sneaking, behind my back, like a thief—like a common thief—"

"Dele—"

"Like a thief!"

Then, all at once, Anton Gersbach rose to his feet.

He rose slowly, heavily, his chair scraping back upon the floor, and stood upright in the little kitchen, and the lamp-light, striking upward, threw his shadow enormous upon the wall and the ceiling, so that it seemed to fill the room, to crowd it, to loom over the small, dark woman by the sink. His face was crimson. His small eyes had grown suddenly bright and hard. His hands hung at his sides, and they were shut, and Delia saw the cords stand out upon the backs of them like ropes.

For a long moment neither spoke. And in that silence, from somewhere very deep down within the man, from beneath the slow stupidity, the patience, the good-nature, the eleven years of steady and faithful toil, something stirred—something blind and ancient and evil, that had lain there all his life, asleep, and was not asleep now. Delia felt it. She could not have said what it was, but she felt it, as one feels the first faint tremor of the earth before the great shock comes. She shrank back against the sink. The empty tin box slid from her fingers and fell clanging to the floor.

"Don't you call me that," said Anton.

His voice was not loud. It was thick and low, and it seemed to come from his chest rather than his throat, a sort of rumble, a growl.

"Don't you call me that, Dele. I ain't a thief. I worked. Eleven years I worked. Every day, rain or shine, fog, wind, every day, up that hill and down again. You know how many people I took up that hill? I don't know. Nobody knows. Thousands. Millions, maybe. And never a mishap. Never once. And then one kid comes out from behind a wagon, and they say, 'Gersbach, you go.' Like that. 'You go.' And I go. I go down to the barn every morning and stand there with my pail and ask Rafferty is there anything, and he says no. And I go down to the docks and ask is there anything, and they say no. And I go out to the gas-works, and they say no. And I walk. All day I walk. I eat my dinner out of the pail sitting on a pile of lumber by the water. And I think, I can't tell Dele. I can't go home and tell Dele. Because I knew what you'd say. I knew you'd say about the money. That's all you think about. The money. The money in the box."

He took a step toward her. The floor shook.

"Well, I took it," he said. "I took eleven dollars out of the box. So you wouldn't know. So you wouldn't look like that. You're looking like that now, Dele. You're looking at me like I was dirt."

Delia did not answer. She could not. She stood pressed against the sink, her hands behind her, gripping the edge of the drain-board, her face white as paper, her black eyes fixed upon him. She was afraid. For the first time in the four years of their marriage she was afraid of her husband. She had never thought of him as a thing to be feared. He had been to her only a great, slow, harmless creature, a kind of beast of burden, that went out in the morning and came back at night and brought her its wages and ate its supper and slept. And now, all at once, she saw that he was something else as well. She saw the size of him, the bulk of him, the terrible strength of those hands that had held back a loaded car upon the steepest grade in the city. And she saw that there was nothing—nothing at all—between that strength and herself but some thin, frail thing, some habit, some custom, that might snap at any moment like a rotten thread.

And Anton saw that she was afraid.

He stopped. He stood quite still in the middle of the floor, his head lowered, breathing hard through his nose. The red ebbed slowly out of his face. His hands opened. He looked down at them, at his great, yellow, callused hands, as though he had never seen them before, as though they belonged to some one else; and a puzzled, troubled expression came into his small eyes, the expression of a dog that has bitten and does not know why.

"Dele," he said, in a different voice. "Dele, I wouldn't—you know I wouldn't—"

She did not move.

He turned away from her. He went back to the table and stood beside it, looking down at his half-eaten supper, at the stew grown cold upon the plate, with a film of white fat creeping over it. He put out one hand and touched the back of his chair, aimlessly, and drew it back again.

"I'll get a job," he said. "I'll get one, Dele. Rafferty says maybe at the Market Street line, after the first of the month. They want gripmen there. He says he'll put in a word."

Delia drew a long, shuddering breath. The color began to come back into her face, a little at a time. She let go of the drain-board. She stooped, slowly, and picked up the tin box from the floor, and turned to the sink, and began to gather up the coins, one by one, the gold and the silver, and drop them into it. Her fingers were shaking so that she could hardly hold them. A dime slipped from her hand and rolled away under the stove, and she got down upon her knees and fished for it with a hairpin until she found it, and put it in the box with the rest.

Anton watched her do it. He said nothing.

When the coins were all in, she pressed down the lid, and pushed the box back into its place behind the flour bin, and dragged the bin back against the wall. Then she stood up and smoothed her apron with both hands, and came back to the table, and picked up her fallen chair, and set it upright, and sat down in it.

"Sit down and eat your supper," she said. "It's getting cold."

He sat down. He took up his knife again. But he did not eat. He sat there with the knife in his hand, staring at the plate.

"Dele," he said at last.

"Well?"

"You ain't going to tell nobody? About the eleven dollars?"

"Who'd I tell?"

"Mrs. Flaherty."

"I ain't going to tell Mrs. Flaherty nothing," said Delia, and her small mouth shut tight again. "It's none of Mrs. Flaherty's business."

That was all. They did not speak of it again that night. Anton ate a little of the cold stew, and drank his coffee, and then sat for a long time by the stove in his stocking feet, smoking his pipe and looking at nothing. Delia washed the dishes and dried them and put them away, and wiped the oilcloth, and blacked the stove, and set the bread to rise for the morning. At ten o'clock they went to bed.

But Delia did not sleep. She lay upon her back in the darkness, her eyes wide open, listening to the heavy breathing of the man beside her—the long, slow, even breathing of a great animal at rest. The wind had fallen. The window was still. Down below in the street the cable hummed in its slot, low, unceasing, monotonous, the voice of the vast, blind machine that ran beneath the city, that never stopped, that never rested, that did not care. She lay and listened to it, and thought about the little girl who had come out from behind the brewery wagon, running after her hoop; and about the hands that had put on the brake, put it on hard, so hard they bent the shoe, and could not stop the car; and about the look that had come into her husband's face when he rose up out of his chair and stood over her with the lamp-light throwing his shadow on the wall.

She had seen something to-night. She did not know what it was. She had not the words for it. But she knew that it was there now, and that it had always been there, and that it would never go away again. It was down there in him, deep, deep down, beneath the good-nature and the patience and the slow, plodding stupidity, as the cable was down there beneath the cobbles—hidden, buried, out of sight, but alive, and moving, and strong, stronger than he, stronger than she, stronger than either of them.

Toward morning, a little before four, the power-house shut down. The humming in the street ceased. And in the sudden, enormous silence Delia Gersbach started up in her bed, her heart pounding, her hands clutching at the blankets, wide awake and terribly afraid, as if something, somewhere in the dark, had died in the night.

The *Sacramento* came into the slip at a quarter past eleven, grinding against the piles with a long groan of strained timbers, and the gangplank had not yet fairly touched the planks of the wharf before the crowd began to pour off her, jostling, hurrying, elbowing one another, a confused and multicoloured stream of humanity: drummers with sample cases, ranchers in from the valley in their Sunday black, Chinamen in blue blouses carrying bundles knotted in matting, women dragging children, a priest, two sailors already drunk, a man with a crate of live chickens. The smell of the bay came up through the cracks in the flooring, the smell of salt water and tar and rotting kelp, mingled with the reek of coal smoke from the funnels and the odour of the ferry restaurant, where they fried ham and onions all day long.

Henry Dittmar stood well back against the iron railing of the waiting room, out of the press, his hat in one hand and his handkerchief in the other, mopping at the inside of the band. He was a little man, plump, pink, and very clean, with a round face like a well-scrubbed apple, a sparse yellow moustache waxed at the points, and small blue eyes that blinked continually behind gold-rimmed spectacles. He wore his best suit of brown cheviot, a little tight now across the stomach, a celluloid collar, and a cravat of purple satin into which was thrust a horseshoe pin of imitation pearls. He was nervous. He shifted from one foot to the other. Every moment he put his hat on, and then, reflecting, took it off again and wiped the band. He was looking for his cousin Lorenz, whom he had not seen in eleven years.

"I won't know him," he muttered. "That's the way it goes. Eleven years. I won't know him at all."

But he knew him at once. Over the heads of the crowd, over the bobbing hats and the bundles and the shoulders, there appeared all at once a head—a huge, shaggy, red head, crowned with a battered slouch hat, set upon a neck like the trunk of a tree. It rose above the throng as a rock rises above the surf. It came on steadily, unhurried, the crowd parting before it and closing in behind it; and then the whole man emerged, and Henry Dittmar caught his breath.

Lorenz Kraft was enormous. He was six feet and three inches tall, and broad in proportion, a veritable giant, with a great thick chest that strained the buttons of his flannel shirt, and arms that hung from his shoulders like the limbs of an oak. His beard, a tangled mass of red, grew high upon his cheekbones and fell halfway to his belt. His face, where it showed, was burned to the colour of a brick. His hands—Henry saw them first of all, and never afterward forgot them—his hands were colossal, knotted, seamed, scarred, the nails broken and blackened, the palms horned with callus, hands that had swung the sledge and gripped the drill and wrestled the iron nozzles of the hydraulic monitors through ten winters in the Sierra. He carried an old carpetbag in one of them as though it had been a lady's reticule. He smelled of pine, of wet earth, of tobacco, of the smoking car.

He saw Henry. He stopped short. Then his mouth opened in the midst of the red beard, and he laughed, a tremendous laugh, a laugh like the bellowing of a steer, that rang against the iron girders of the roof, so that people turned around to stare.

"Heinie!" he shouted. "Heinie Dittmar, by Gott! Look at him! Look at the little fellow!"

He dropped the carpetbag. He caught Henry about the body and lifted him clear off his feet, crushing him against his chest, and Henry's hat fell off and rolled away under the feet of the crowd, and his spectacles were knocked sideways upon his nose, and the breath went out of him in a single gasp.

"Lorenz—Lorenz—my hat. Ach, my hat, Lorenz!"

The giant set him down, and, still roaring with laughter, plunged after the hat, retrieved it from beneath the very hoofs of a baggage truck, and clapped it upon Henry's head, down over his ears.

"There's your hat. Ha! ha! Same Heinie. Same old Heinie, always fussing. Say, you've got fat, ain't you? Look at the belly on him! You been eating your own sausages, I guess. Well, well, well!"

He stood off and looked at his cousin, his hands on his hips, and Henry, straightening his spectacles, looked up at him, and for a moment neither of them said anything at all. There was something in the moment that neither of them understood, something that took them both by the throat. They were remembering, both of them, a little village on the Weser, a schoolroom that smelled of chalk and wet woollen stockings, a grandfather with a white beard and a terrible temper, a mother who had been the sister of the other's mother. Eleven years. And the one had grown fat and the other had grown into a giant, and they had become strangers to each other.

Then Lorenz picked up his carpetbag. "Well," he said, "where do we eat?"

They went out through the great arch of the ferry building into the sunlight of Market Street. It was a brilliant day, one of those rare, clear Sundays of the early summer when the trade wind holds off till afternoon, and the whole city lay spread out before them, glittering, roaring, alive. The cable cars came rushing down the slot in long processions, the gripmen leaning upon their levers, the bells clanging incessantly. The cobbles rang under the iron tires of drays and hacks and delivery wagons. The sidewalks swarmed. There was a smell of horses, of hot asphalt, of roasting coffee from the warehouses along the Embarcadero, and from somewhere far up the street there came, faint and brassy, the music of a band.

Lorenz stood stock still upon the curb and stared.

"Say," he exclaimed, "ain't that a sight, though! Ain't that a sight! Why, it's all changed. Look at the buildings. Look at them cars. Why, the last time I was down here, there wasn't no cars like them at all. Say, ain't that a sight!"

"Come," said Henry, pulling at his sleeve. "Come, we'll take the Folsom Street car. Minna will have dinner ready. She's been cooking since six o'clock. Come, Lorenz."

But Lorenz would not take the car. He would walk. He wanted to see everything. He had been in the mountains, he said, so long that he had forgotten what a city looked like. So they walked, the little man and the big one, side by side, Henry trotting to keep pace, his short legs twinkling, and Lorenz striding along with his great slow strides, his head turning from side to side, stopping every moment to stare at a shop window, at a woman's hat, at a policeman, at a Chinaman with a basket of fish slung from a bamboo pole across his shoulders.

"Say, ain't that a sight!"

---

The delicatessen of Henry Dittmar stood upon Folsom Street, near the corner of Seventh, between a saloon and a shop where they repaired umbrellas. Over the door a sign, newly painted in gilt upon a black ground, read, "H. DITTMAR. DELICATESSEN. IMPORTED AND DOMESTIC." In the window, upon a slab of white marble, were arranged in rows the treasures of the establishment: great ruddy hams, wrapped in silver paper; links of sausage, red and brown and grey, hanging in festoons from a brass rod; a wheel of Swiss cheese, cut open to show its holes; jars of pickled herring, of sauerkraut, of red cabbage, of dill cucumbers floating in brine; a pyramid of tinned sardines; and in the very centre, upon a platter garnished with sprigs of parsley, a whole smoked salmon, its skin glistening like oiled bronze.

Henry paused before this window as they came up, and looked at it, and then looked at his cousin. He could not help it. He was proud.

"That's mine," he said. "All that."

Lorenz looked at the window, and then he looked at Henry, and then all at once he laughed again, his great bellowing laugh, and smote Henry upon the back so that the little man staggered.

"Well, now, if that ain't fine! Heinie with a store! Heinie with a gold sign! Say, I always said you'd get along, Heinie. I always said it. You was always the one to save your pennies. Ha! ha! Remember the time you had the twelve pfennigs in the stocking, and I took 'em and bought licorice, and you cried all day?"

"I remember," said Henry. He did not laugh.

They went in through the shop, where the smell was overpowering, a thick, rich, pungent smell of cheese and garlic and smoked meat and vinegar and sawdust, and through a door at the back into the living rooms. Here the smell was different. Here it was the smell of cooking—of roasting pork and boiling potatoes and stewing cabbage and baking bread, a smell that came out to meet them in a warm, moist wave and enveloped them like a blanket. Lorenz stopped on the threshold and drew a long breath through his nostrils, and his eyes closed.

"Ach, Gott!" he murmured. "That's cooking. That's real cooking. Ten years I been eating beans and sowbelly. Ten years."

Minna Dittmar came out of the kitchen, wiping her hands upon her apron. She was a large, fair, handsome woman, larger than her husband, with an enormous coil of flaxen hair upon the top of her head, and red forearms bared to the elbow, and a face that shone with heat and soap and good nature. Behind her came the children, three of them, in descending order of size, the girls in starched pinafores, the boy in a sailor suit, all of them flaxen like their mother, all of them staring at the giant in the doorway with round, frightened, fascinated eyes.

"So this is Cousin Lorenz," said Minna. "Welcome, Cousin Lorenz. Welcome. Sit down, sit down. Everything's ready. Henry, take his bag. Gretchen, Louisa, Fritzie, say good day to Cousin Lorenz."

"Good day, Cousin Lorenz," said the children all together, in a single breath, and then fled behind their mother's skirts.

Lorenz squatted down upon his heels. Even so his head was higher than theirs. He held out one of his enormous hands, palm upward, and in the hollow of it lay a nugget of gold the size of a bean, rough and yellow and gleaming.

"Who wants it?" he said. "Who's going to come and get it?"

It was the boy who came, at last, step by step, his finger in his mouth, and took the nugget with a quick snatch and ran away with it, shrieking with delight; and then the girls were not to be outdone, and there were nuggets for them too; and in five minutes the three of them were climbing over their cousin as though he had been a mountain, pulling at his beard, riding upon his shoulders, and Lorenz was roaring with laughter, and Minna was scolding, and Henry was standing in the corner with the carpetbag in his hand, blinking behind his spectacles, and smiling a little, uncertainly.

Then they sat down to dinner.

It was a prodigious meal. Minna had outdone herself. There was a soup, thick with barley and bits of marrow bone; there was a loin of pork, roasted brown and crackling, swimming in its own gravy; there were potatoes, boiled whole in their jackets and then rolled in butter and parsley; there was red cabbage cooked with apples and vinegar; there was a great dish of noodles; there were dill pickles from the shop, and a pot of mustard, and a loaf of black rye bread and another of white; there was a pitcher of steam beer, and when that was gone, another; and to end with there was a coffee cake, sprinkled with sugar and cinnamon, and coffee in a pot of blue enamel.

Lorenz ate as he did everything, enormously. He ate with his elbows on the table and his head bent low over his plate, shovelling the food into his mouth with his knife, tearing the bread in great chunks with his fingers, gnawing the pork bones till they were white, wiping his plate clean with a crust and holding it out again. He ate in silence, with a kind of ferocity, his jaws working steadily, his eyes fixed upon his food. The gravy ran into his beard. He drank the beer in long gulps, his head thrown back, his throat moving, and set down the glass with a thump and a sigh and wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. Three times Minna filled his plate, and three times he emptied it; and the children watched him in a kind of awe, their own forks forgotten in their hands; and Minna watched him with the deep, contented pride of a woman whose cooking is appreciated; and Henry, picking at a bit of cabbage, watched him with an expression that was half admiration and half something else, something he could not have named.

At last Lorenz pushed back his chair and loosened his belt and let out a great breath.

"That," he said solemnly, "was a dinner."

Then, the edge of his hunger gone, he began to talk.

He talked of the mountains, of the mines, of the camps where he had worked. He told them of the old days on the hydraulic claims, before the courts had shut them down, when he was a youngster and had worked the monitors at the North Bloomfield—the great iron nozzles, longer than a man, through which the water came roaring down from the ditches high up on the mountain, with a force that would cut a man in two if he got in front of it, that tore away the hillsides, that brought down whole forests, that washed the very mountains into the rivers, rocks and gravel and trees and all.

"You never seen nothing like it, Heinie," he said, his eyes shining. "You never seen nothing like it in your life. You'd stand there with the nozzle, and the water would go out of it like—like a solid thing, like a bar of iron, white, and you'd turn it on the bank, and the whole bank would just come down. Just come down, like that. A hundred feet of it. Trees as big as this house. And the noise of it! You couldn't hear yourself holler. And the mud running away down the canyon, red, like blood. Gott! It made you feel—it made you feel like you was bigger than the mountain. Like you was God Almighty."

He stretched out his enormous arms as though he still held the nozzle, and his fists clenched, and for an instant something came into his face, something hard and fierce and joyous, that made Minna draw the children a little closer to her chair.

"They stopped it," he said. "The farmers down in the valley went to the courts and they stopped it. Said it was spoiling the rivers. Well, maybe it was. Now I'm on a quartz mill up by Grass Valley. Feeding the stamps. It ain't the same."

Then he wanted to know about the family, about everyone, and Henry told him. Aunt Lottie was dead—had died in Bremen, three winters ago, of the lung fever. Uncle Fritz had gone to Milwaukee and kept a brewery and was rich. Cousin Anna had married a schoolmaster. And the grandfather—old Grandfather Kraft—

"He's alive yet," said Henry. "Ninety-one years old. He lives with Anna. He don't know anybody no more. He sits by the stove."

Lorenz was silent a moment. He turned his beer glass round and round in his huge fingers.

"I remember him," he said slowly. "I remember him good. You remember, Heinie, the time he killed the horse?"

Henry nodded. He remembered. They had been boys of eight or nine, the two of them, hiding in the hayloft, and they had seen it through a crack in the boards—the old man, white-bearded, enormous, in a rage over nothing, over a kick, a stumble, and his fist coming down once upon the horse's head, between the eyes, and the horse going down upon its knees and then over upon its side, and lying there, its legs moving a little, and then not moving at all. And the old man standing over it, breathing hard, his fist still clenched, and then all at once beginning to cry.

"He was a strong one," said Lorenz. "They say I take after him."

He said it simply, without boasting, as though stating a fact; but he looked down as he said it at his own hands, lying upon the cloth among the crumbs, and for a moment he was very still. And Henry, looking at those hands, felt a little chill go down his back, the same chill he had felt in the hayloft so many years before.

"That's the way it goes," he said, without knowing exactly what he meant.

---

Later, when the dishes had been cleared away and the children put down for their naps, the cousins went out and sat upon the back steps that led down into the little yard. It was a narrow yard, fenced in with high board fences, where Minna kept a few geraniums in tubs and a line of washing hung limp in the still air. Over the fences rose the backs of other houses, grey and weather-stained, with fire escapes and clotheslines and rows of windows; and from somewhere close by a man was practising upon a cornet, playing the same few bars of "The Last Rose of Summer" over and over, breaking down always at the same note.

Lorenz filled his pipe, a short black clay, and lit it, and the smoke went up in long blue spirals. Henry had a cigar, one of the good ones from the box in the shop. They smoked in silence. Already the afternoon was turning. The trade wind had come up, as it always did, and away to the westward, over the Twin Peaks, the fog was beginning to pour in, a great grey wall of it, rolling and tumbling, swallowing the hills one by one. The air grew cold. Henry turned up the collar of his coat.

"You've done good, Heinie," said Lorenz at last. "You've done real good. A store. A wife. Them kids. A gold sign." He drew upon his pipe. "I ain't got nothing. Nothing but what I can carry in that bag."

"You could have," said Henry. "You could come down here. You could go into business. There's lots of chances. I'd help you, Lorenz. I'd lend you—"

Lorenz shook his great head slowly.

"No," he said. "No, I couldn't stand it. All them walls. All them people. I'd bust out of it, Heinie. I'd do something. I don't know what. I get to feeling, sometimes—" He stopped. He looked down at his hands again. "No," he said. "The mountains is the place for me. There's room up there."

Again they were silent. The cornet broke down upon its note and began again. The fog had reached the Mission now, and the sun was a pale disc behind it, like a coin seen through dirty water.

"You remember," said Lorenz suddenly, "the fight we had? Down by the mill pond? Over the knife?"

"I remember."

"I near killed you, Heinie. I had you down in the mud and I was hitting you, and I couldn't stop. I couldn't stop. It was like something got into me. If old Hinrichs hadn't come along—" He reached over, with a gentleness strange in a hand so huge, and touched the little white scar that ran through Henry's left eyebrow. "That's mine," he said. "I gave you that."

"It don't matter," said Henry. "We was kids."

"It matters," said Lorenz. "I thought about it a lot. Up there, nights, in the bunkhouse. I thought about it a lot."

And Henry, sitting there in the cold with his good cigar going out between his fingers, looked up at his cousin's face, at the red beard and the burned skin and the small, deep-set, troubled eyes, and understood all at once that this enormous creature beside him was afraid—afraid of something in himself, something that had come down to him from the old man by the stove, from the old man's father, and his father before him, a thing in the blood, dark and strong and blind, that slept and woke and slept again. It was Saturday evening, and Lauritzen came home along Tehama Street with his week's wages in his pocket and the smell of the brewery still in his clothes.

He had driven the four-horse dray of the Golden Gate Brewing Company for eleven years, ever since he had come ashore off the barkentine *Thyra* with a canvas bag and no English. In all that time he had not missed a day. He was a huge, slow, blond Dane of forty, enormously strong, with a jaw like the bow of a scow and hands that hung to the middle of his thighs, red and calloused, the knuckles split and healed and split again from the handling of kegs. He walked heavily, rolling a little from side to side, as if the sidewalk were the deck of a ship. His mind was like his body, ponderous and deliberate. Ideas came to him one at a time, and he turned each over and over, as he might have turned a keg upon its rim, before he set it down. He was not quick to anger. But once his anger was roused it moved in him like the shifting of a heavy cargo in a gale, and there was no stopping it.

Tehama Street at that hour was full of noise and smells. The fog had come in from the ocean an hour before, and it lay along the roofs in a gray, wet blanket, so that the gas-lamps, just lighted, glowed through it with a round, sick yellow, like the yolks of eggs. From the open door of the German bakery on the corner came the warm reek of rye bread and caraway seed. A Chinese vegetable peddler went by, his baskets swinging from a pole, crying something nobody understood. Children played in the gutters, shrieking, chasing one another around the hydrants. A woman in a wrapper leaned from an upper window and called, "Mamie! Ma-a-mie!" over and over again, never changing her note. Down at the end of the street, in the direction of the bay, the steam whistle of a planing-mill blew for the end of the day, a long, hoarse bellow that went on and on, and then stopped all at once.

Lauritzen liked it all. He liked the smells and the noise and the fog. He liked to come home on a Saturday with his money in his pocket and his supper waiting. It was a good thing to have a home, to have a wife and a boy, to have four rooms on the second floor, over the harness-maker's, with a stove and a lamp and a clock. He turned in at his own door and climbed the stairs, his great boots shaking the house.

His wife met him in the hall. She was a little, thin, anxious woman, with a pinched, freckled face and hair the color of rope, who had been a laundress before he married her, and who still had the red, parboiled hands of her trade. Her name was Matilda, but he called her Tilly. She had a way of twisting her apron in her fingers when she was frightened, and she was twisting it now.

"Hello, Tilly," he said, in his deep, slow voice. "Supper ready?"

"Yes, Hans, it's ready. It's all ready." She did not move out of the way. She stood in the narrow hall, twisting her apron, looking up at him. "Hans—"

"Well?"

"Hans, now, don't you get mad. Promise me you won't get mad."

He stood there, slow, puzzled, looking down at her. "What's the matter?"

"It's—it's the ship," she said.

For a moment he did not understand. Then the idea came to him, slowly, ponderously, and settled into its place. He pushed by her without a word and went into the front room.

The ship was gone from the mantelpiece.

It had stood there for eleven years, between the clock and the china dog, in the very middle of the shelf, where the lamplight fell full upon it. It was the only thing he had brought from the old country. It was a little full-rigged ship in a bottle, a perfect thing, with three masts and every yard in its place, the sails of white silk no bigger than a thumbnail, the hull painted black with a red streak at the water-line, and a little gilt figurehead at the bow. It had been made by his grandfather, a sailmaker in Helsingør, through the long winter evenings, with tweezers and a bit of wire, and it had been given to Lauritzen on the day he first went to sea. He had carried it round the Horn twice. He had carried it through a typhoon in the China Sea. He had never let it out of his sight. And every Saturday night of his life in Tehama Street, after supper, he had taken it down from the mantelpiece and held it in his huge red hands, turning it slowly in the lamplight, looking at it, saying nothing, while his pipe went out. It was his treasure, his one beautiful thing, his link with the sea, with his boyhood, with the gray old town on the Sound where the ships went by.

It was gone. And there, upon the carpet beneath the mantelpiece, upon a sheet of newspaper where Tilly had swept them, lay the pieces: the broken green glass of the bottle, the snapped masts, the little silk sails crumpled and torn, the hull split down the middle, the little gilt figurehead lying by itself, face downward, a tiny, pitiful thing.

Lauritzen stood and looked at it. He did not move. His great arms hung at his sides. His jaw protruded. His small blue eyes, set deep beneath the heavy blond brows, stared and stared.

"Who done that?" he said at last.

Tilly had followed him into the room. She was twisting her apron faster now. "It was an accident, Hans. He didn't mean it. He just took it down to look at it, and it slipped."

"Who done that?"

"Eddie," she said in a whisper.

"Where is he?"

"Hans, now, he's only six. He's only a baby, Hans."

"Where is he?"

She did not answer. But her eyes went, in spite of herself, toward the door of the little back bedroom. Lauritzen turned and went toward it.

"Eddie," he called. "Come out here."

There was no answer. Lauritzen opened the door. It was dark in the room. There was the smell of the boy's clothes and of the damp wall-paper. The window gave upon the back yard, where the harness-maker's washing hung in the fog, motionless, like gray ghosts. And under the bed, pressed against the wall, Lauritzen could hear a little sound of breathing, quick and frightened, like the breathing of a small animal run to earth.

"Come out of there," said Lauritzen.

Slowly the boy came out. He crawled from under the bed on his hands and knees and stood up, his face white and dirty, his blond hair, so like his father's, rumpled and full of dust. He was a small, thin child, with his mother's freckles and his father's blue eyes, and he wore a pair of knickerbockers cut down from an old pair of his father's trousers and a calico shirt. He stood in the doorway, in the light from the front room, and looked up at his father, and his chin shook.

"Come in here," said Lauritzen.

The boy came into the front room. Lauritzen pointed to the newspaper on the floor, to the broken glass and the little torn sails.

"Who done that?"

The boy looked at the floor. His lips moved, but no sound came.

"Who done that?" said Lauritzen again, louder.

"The cat," said the boy.

There was a silence. In the silence the clock upon the mantelpiece ticked loudly, steadily, monotonously, and down in the street the woman in the wrapper called, "Mamie! Ma-a-mie!"

"The cat," repeated Lauritzen slowly.

"The cat done it," said the boy, his voice rising, shrill, eager. "The cat jumped up on the mantel, and she knocked it down. I seen her. I seen her do it, papa. It was the cat."

Then, all at once, it came over Lauritzen. It rose in him suddenly, out of nowhere, out of the very depths of him, a vast, blind, red anger, the anger of the brute. It was not the broken ship. It was the lie. The ship was a thing of glass and wood and silk; it was gone, and that was all; a man could bear that. But the lie was another matter. The lie stung him, maddened him. That his own boy, his own flesh, should stand there before him, small and dirty and frightened, and lie to his face, and blame the cat, and think that he, Lauritzen, was such a fool as to believe it! The blood rushed to his face. His neck swelled. His great hands closed, and the knuckles stood out white beneath the red skin. He took a step forward, and the floor shook.

"You lie to me!" he shouted. "You lie to me! You stand there and you lie to me!"

The boy shrank back against the wall. Tilly gave a little cry and ran forward and caught at her husband's arm.

"Hans! Hans! Don't you hurt him! Don't you lay a hand on him!"

Lauritzen shook her off without seeing her, as he might have shaken off a fly. He was not thinking. He could not think. The anger filled him, mounted in him, roared in his ears like surf on a reef. His right hand rose, slowly, heavily, the enormous red hand with the split knuckles, the hand that lifted kegs, that held four horses in on the Second Street hill, that could have broken a plank across its palm. It rose above the boy's head and hung there.

And at that moment, there in the little front room in Tehama Street, with the fog at the windows and the clock ticking on the mantelpiece, Lauritzen saw his father.

He saw him as plainly as though he stood there in the room: a short, square, terrible old man in a pea-jacket, with a gray beard and a face burned brown by forty years of weather, a ship-chandler on the waterfront at Helsingør, who drank aquavit in the back of his shop and beat his children with a rope's end. Lauritzen saw the rope's end. He saw it as plainly as he saw his own hand. It was a short length of tarred hemp, knotted at the end, that hung from a nail behind the counter among the blocks and the coils of rope and the tins of tar. He saw his father take it down. He heard the old man's voice, thick and harsh: "Liar! Liar! I'll teach you to lie!" He felt the blows again, across his back, his shoulders, his legs—he, a little boy of six, a little white-headed boy crouching in a corner among the smell of tar and hemp and oakum, screaming, screaming, while the ships went by on the gray Sound outside the window and nobody came.

It was the same. It was all the same. It was in him, this thing. It had been in his father, and in his father's father before him, and in all the long line of them back and back, heavy, stupid, violent men of the sea and the waterfront, who drank and fought and beat their children. It was the old evil, the hereditary taint, the brute that lived in the blood and came down from father to son like the color of the eyes or the shape of the jaw. It had lain asleep in him for years. He had not known it was there. And now it was awake, and it had him by the throat, and it raised his hand above the head of his little son as it had raised the rope's end above his own head thirty-four years before.

The boy looked up at the hand. He did not scream. He did not move. He only stood there against the wall, his small dirty face turned up, his chin shaking, his blue eyes wide and fixed, staring at the great red hand that hung over him. And Lauritzen, looking down, saw in those eyes the very look that had been in his own eyes in the chandler's shop at Helsingør, the look of a small animal that sees the blow coming and cannot get away.

The hand hung there. It trembled. The muscles of the great forearm stood out like cables. For a long moment, an eternity, it hung there, and the clock ticked, and Tilly stood with both hands pressed against her mouth, and down in the street the woman called "Mamie!" and the cable-car bell clanged on Folsom Street.

Then Lauritzen turned, with a hoarse, inarticulate sound in his throat, and brought the hand down with all his strength upon the table.

The whole room shook. The lamp jumped. The dishes that Tilly had laid for supper leaped and clattered, and a cup rolled off and broke upon the floor. The table, a heavy thing of pine, cracked across its top from edge to edge with a report like a pistol shot. The boy screamed then, once, shrilly, and covered his face with his arms.

Lauritzen stood with his hand still upon the split board, breathing heavily through his nose, like one of his own horses at the top of the hill. The anger was going out of him. He could feel it go, draining away slowly, like water from a scuttled boat, leaving him empty and tired and a little sick. His hand hurt. He looked at it stupidly. The knuckles were bleeding.

After a while he went over to the boy and got down upon his knees in front of him. It was a slow business, his getting down, for he was very large and very heavy, and the floor creaked beneath him. When he was down, his face was on a level with the boy's face. He took the boy's arms, gently, in his great hands, and drew them down from his face. The boy was crying now, without noise, the tears making clean streaks through the dirt on his cheeks.

"Eddie," said Lauritzen. His voice was hoarse. He stopped and cleared his throat, and began again, slowly, choosing the words one by one, for English was still hard for him when he was moved. "Eddie, you look at me. You look at papa."

The boy looked at him.

"The ship," said Lauritzen. "The ship, that don't matter. You hear? I don't care about the ship. It's broke. All right. It's broke. That's all. Things get broke. Ships get broke. I seen ships go to pieces off the Horn, big ships, bigger'n this house. That's all right. That ain't nothing." He paused, laboring. "But you don't lie to me. You don't never lie to me. You hear, Eddie? You do anything, you break anything, you come and tell me. You say, 'Papa, I done it.' And I don't hit you. I don't never hit you. But you don't lie. Not to me. Not to nobody. You hear?"

"Yes, papa," whispered the boy.

"Who done it?"

The boy's chin shook. He looked at the floor. He looked at his mother. He looked back at his father.

"I done it," he said. "I took it down to look at. And it was slippery. And it fell."

Lauritzen nodded slowly, heavily, several times.

"All right," he said. "That's good. That's all right, now."

He put out his hand and laid it upon the boy's head, the great red hand with the bleeding knuckles, and it covered the whole of the small rumpled head like a cap. He let it stay there a moment. Then he got up, slowly, his knees cracking, and went to the window and stood with his back to the room, looking out into the fog.

Tilly gathered the boy into her arms and carried him into the kitchen, whispering and crooning over him. Lauritzen heard her pumping water at the sink, heard the splash of it, heard the boy's voice, thin and broken, and Tilly's voice answering, low and soothing. He did not turn around.

The fog was very thick now. The gas-lamps were mere smudges of yellow. The street was quieter; the children had been called in to supper; the Chinese peddler was gone. Only the woman in the wrapper still leaned from her window, calling "Mamie!" into the gray void, and no Mamie came. Somewhere out on the bay a fog-horn was blowing, at long, regular intervals, a deep, mournful, bellowing note, like some great beast lost in the mist and calling for its mate.

Lauritzen listened to it. It made him think of the sea. It made him think of Helsingør, and the gray Sound, and the ships going by, and the chandler's shop with its smell of tar and hemp and oakum, and the rope's end on its nail behind the counter. He wondered if the rope's end was there still. He wondered if his father was alive. He had not heard in twenty years. It was a long way off, all that, a long way off and a long time ago. And yet it had been here, tonight, in this room, as near as the clock upon the mantel. It had been in his hand.

He shivered a little, a great slow shiver that went through the whole of his huge frame. He was afraid. It was the first time in many years that Lauritzen had been afraid of anything. He was not afraid of horses, or of men, or of the sea. But he was afraid now of the thing that was in him, the thing that had come down to him in the blood, that had lain sleeping all these years and had awakened tonight and raised his hand. He had beaten it this time. He did not know if he could beat it always. It was strong, stronger than he. It was old, older than he. It was patient. It could wait.

After a long time he turned from the window and got down again upon his knees, slowly, heavily, beside the sheet of newspaper upon the floor. One by one, with his enormous blunt fingers, he picked out the pieces of the little ship from among the broken glass: the split hull, the snapped masts, the yards no thicker than a broom-straw, the torn sails of white silk. Last of all he found the little gilt figurehead, lying face downward by itself, and he turned it over and looked at it. It was a woman with her arms crossed upon her breast, very small, very bright, the gilt worn thin in places where his grandfather's tweezers had held it, sixty years ago, in Helsingør.

He sat there upon the floor for a long while, turning the little figurehead over and over in the lamplight, while his supper grew cold on the split table and the clock ticked and the fog-horn bellowed out on the bay. Then he got up and put it in his waistcoat pocket, and went in to his supper.

In his office at San Francisco, seated before a massive desk of polished redwood, very ornate, Lyman Derrick sat dictating letters to his typewriter, on a certain morning early in the spring of the year. The subdued monotone of his voice proceeded evenly from sentence to sentence, regular, precise, businesslike.

“I have the honour to acknowledge herewith your favour of the 14th instant, and in reply would state——” “Please find enclosed draft upon New Orleans to be applied as per our understanding——” “In answer to your favour No. 1107, referring to the case of the City and County of San Francisco against Excelsior Warehouse & Storage Co., I would say——” His voice continued, expressionless, measured, distinct. While he spoke, he swung slowly back and forth in his leather swivel chair, his elbows resting on the arms, his pop eyes fixed vaguely upon the calendar on the opposite wall, winking at intervals when he paused, searching for a word.

“That's all for the present,” he said at length. Without reply, the typewriter rose and withdrew, thrusting her pencil into the coil of her hair, closing the door behind her, softly, discreetly. When she had gone, Lyman rose, stretching himself putting up three fingers to hide his yawn. To further loosen his muscles, he took a couple of turns the length of he room, noting with satisfaction its fine appointments, the padded red carpet, the dull olive green tint of the walls, the few choice engravings—portraits of Marshall, Taney, Field, and a coloured lithograph—excellently done—of the Grand Canyon of the Colorado—the deep-seated leather chairs, the large and crowded bookcase (topped with a bust of James Lick, and a huge greenish globe), the waste basket of woven coloured grass, made by Navajo Indians, the massive silver inkstand on the desk, the elaborate filing cabinet, complete in every particular, and the shelves of tin boxes, padlocked, impressive, grave, bearing the names of clients, cases and estates. He was between thirty-one and thirty-five years of age. Unlike Harran, he resembled his mother, but he was much darker than Annie Derrick and his eyes were much fuller, the eyeball protruding, giving him a pop-eyed, foreign expression, quite unusual and unexpected. His hair was black, and he wore a small, tight, pointed mustache, which he was in the habit of pushing delicately upward from the corners of his lips with the ball of his thumb, the little finger extended. As often as he made this gesture, he prefaced it with a little twisting gesture of the forearm in order to bring his cuff into view, and, in fact, this movement by itself was habitual. He was dressed carefully, his trousers creased, a pink rose in his lapel. His shoes were of patent leather, his cutaway coat was of very rough black cheviot, his double-breasted waistcoat of tan covered cloth with buttons of smoked pearl. An Ascot scarf—a great puff of heavy black silk—was at his neck, the knot transfixed by a tiny golden pin set off with an opal and four small diamonds. At one end of the room were two great windows of plate glass, and pausing at length before one of these, Lyman selected a cigarette from his curved box of oxydized silver, lit it and stood looking down and out, willing to be idle for a moment, amused and interested in the view. His office was on the tenth floor of the EXCHANGE BUILDING, a beautiful, tower-like affair of white stone, that stood on the corner of Market Street near its intersection with Kearney, the most imposing office building of the city. Below him the city swarmed tumultuous through its grooves, the cable-cars starting and stopping with a gay jangling of bells and a strident whirring of jostled glass windows. Drays and carts clattered over the cobbles, and an incessant shuffling of thousands of feet rose from the pavement. Around Lotta's fountain the baskets of the flower sellers, crammed with chrysanthemums, violets, pinks, roses, lilies, hyacinths, set a brisk note of colour in the grey of the street. But to Lyman's notion the general impression of this centre of the city's life was not one of strenuous business activity. It was a continuous interest in small things, a people ever willing to be amused at trifles, refusing to consider serious matters—good-natured, allowing themselves to be imposed upon, taking life easily—generous, companionable, enthusiastic; living, as it were, from day to day, in a place where the luxuries of life were had without effort; in a city that offered to consideration the restlessness of a New York, without its earnestness; the serenity of a Naples, without its languor; the romance of a Seville, without its picturesqueness. As Lyman turned from the window, about to resume his work, the office boy appeared at the door.

“The man from the lithograph company, sir,” announced the boy.

“Well, what does he want?” demanded Lyman, adding, however, upon the instant: “Show him in.” A young man entered, carrying a great bundle, which he deposited on a chair, with a gasp of relief, exclaiming, all out of breath: “From the Standard Lithograph Company.”

“What is?”

“Don't know,” replied the other. “Maps, I guess.”

“I don't want any maps. Who sent them? I guess you're mistaken.” Lyman tore the cover from the top of the package, drawing out one of a great many huge sheets of white paper, folded eight times. Suddenly, he uttered an exclamation: “Ah, I see. They ARE maps. But these should not have come here. They are to go to the regular office for distribution.” He wrote a new direction on the label of the package: “Take them to that address,” he went on. “I'll keep this one here. The others go to that address. If you see Mr. Darrell, tell him that Mr. Derrick—you get the name—Mr. Derrick may not be able to get around this afternoon, but to go ahead with any business just the same.” The young man departed with the package and Lyman, spreading out the map upon the table, remained for some time studying it thoughtfully. It was a commissioner's official railway map of the State of California, completed to March 30th of that year. Upon it the different railways of the State were accurately plotted in various colours, blue, green, yellow. However, the blue, the yellow, and the green were but brief traceries, very short, isolated, unimportant. At a little distance these could hardly be seen. The whole map was gridironed by a vast, complicated network of red lines marked P. and S. W. R. R. These centralised at San Francisco and thence ramified and spread north, east, and south, to every quarter of the State. From Coles, in the topmost corner of the map, to Yuma in the lowest, from Reno on one side to San Francisco on the other, ran the plexus of red, a veritable system of blood circulation, complicated, dividing, and reuniting, branching, splitting, extending, throwing out feelers, off-shoots, tap roots, feeders—diminutive little blood suckers that shot out from the main jugular and went twisting up into some remote county, laying hold upon some forgotten village or town, involving it in one of a myriad branching coils, one of a hundred tentacles, drawing it, as it were, toward that centre from which all this system sprang. The map was white, and it seemed as if all the colour which should have gone to vivify the various counties, towns, and cities marked upon it had been absorbed by that huge, sprawling organism, with its ruddy arteries converging to a central point. It was as though the State had been sucked white and colourless, and against this pallid background the red arteries of the monster stood out, swollen with life-blood, reaching out to infinity, gorged to bursting; an excrescence, a gigantic parasite fattening upon the life-blood of an entire commonwealth. However, in an upper corner of the map appeared the names of the three new commissioners: Jones McNish for the first district, Lyman Derrick for the second, and James Darrell for the third. Nominated in the Democratic State convention in the fall of the preceding year, Lyman, backed by the coteries of San Francisco bosses in the pay of his father's political committee of ranchers, had been elected together with Darrell, the candidate of the Pueblo and Mojave road, and McNish, the avowed candidate of the Pacific and Southwestern. Darrell was rabidly against the P. and S. W., McNish rabidly for it. Lyman was supposed to be the conservative member of the board, the ranchers' candidate, it was true, and faithful to their interests, but a calm man, deliberative, swayed by no such violent emotions as his colleagues. Osterman's dexterity had at last succeeded in entangling Magnus inextricably in the new politics. The famous League, organised in the heat of passion the night of Annixter's barn dance, had been consolidated all through the winter months. Its executive committee, of which Magnus was chairman, had been, through Osterman's manipulation, merged into the old committee composed of Broderson, Annixter, and himself. Promptly thereat he had resigned the chairmanship of this committee, thus leaving Magnus at its head. Precisely as Osterman had planned, Magnus was now one of them. The new committee accordingly had two objects in view: to resist the attempted grabbing of their lands by the Railroad, and to push forward their own secret scheme of electing a board of railroad commissioners who should regulate wheat rates so as to favour the ranchers of the San Joaquin. The land cases were promptly taken to the courts and the new grading—fixing the price of the lands at twenty and thirty dollars an acre instead of two—bitterly and stubbornly fought. But delays occurred, the process of the law was interminable, and in the intervals the committee addressed itself to the work of seating the “Ranchers' Commission,” as the projected Board of Commissioners came to be called. It was Harran who first suggested that his brother, Lyman, be put forward as the candidate for this district. At once the proposition had a great success. Lyman seemed made for the place. While allied by every tie of blood to the ranching interests, he had never been identified with them. He was city-bred. The Railroad would not be over-suspicious of him. He was a good lawyer, a good business man, keen, clear-headed, far-sighted, had already some practical knowledge of politics, having served a term as assistant district attorney, and even at the present moment occupying the position of sheriff's attorney. More than all, he was the son of Magnus Derrick; he could be relied upon, could be trusted implicitly to remain loyal to the ranchers' cause. The campaign for Railroad Commissioner had been very interesting. At the very outset Magnus's committee found itself involved in corrupt politics. The primaries had to be captured at all costs and by any means, and when the convention assembled it was found necessary to buy outright the votes of certain delegates. The campaign fund raised by contributions from Magnus, Annixter, Broderson, and Osterman was drawn upon to the extent of five thousand dollars. Only the committee knew of this corruption. The League, ignoring ways and means, supposed as a matter of course that the campaign was honorably conducted. For a whole week after the consummation of this part of the deal, Magnus had kept to his house, refusing to be seen, alleging that he was ill, which was not far from the truth. The shame of the business, the loathing of what he had done, were to him things unspeakable. He could no longer look Harran in the face. He began a course of deception with his wife. More than once, he had resolved to break with the whole affair, resigning his position, allowing the others to proceed without him. But now it was too late. He was pledged. He had joined the League. He was its chief, and his defection might mean its disintegration at the very time when it needed all its strength to fight the land cases. More than a mere deal in bad politics was involved. There was the land grab. His withdrawal from an unholy cause would mean the weakening, perhaps the collapse, of another cause that he believed to be righteous as truth itself. He was hopelessly caught in the mesh. Wrong seemed indissolubly knitted into the texture of Right. He was blinded, dizzied, overwhelmed, caught in the current of events, and hurried along he knew not where. He resigned himself. In the end, and after much ostentatious opposition on the part of the railroad heelers, Lyman was nominated and subsequently elected. When this consummation was reached Magnus, Osterman, Broderson, and Annixter stared at each other. Their wildest hopes had not dared to fix themselves upon so easy a victory as this. It was not believable that the corporation would allow itself to be fooled so easily, would rush open-eyed into the trap. How had it happened? Osterman, however, threw his hat into the air with wild whoops of delight. Old Broderson permitted himself a feeble cheer. Even Magnus beamed satisfaction. The other members of the League, present at the time, shook hands all around and spoke of opening a few bottles on the strength of the occasion. Annixter alone was recalcitrant.

“It's too easy,” he declared. “No, I'm not satisfied. Where's Shelgrim in all this? Why don't he show his hand, damn his soul? The thing is yellow, I tell you. There's a big fish in these waters somewheres. I don't know his name, and I don't know his game, but he's moving round off and on, just out of sight. If you think you've netted him, I DON'T, that's all I've got to say.” But he was jeered down as a croaker. There was the Commission. He couldn't get around that, could he? There was Darrell and Lyman Derrick, both pledged to the ranches. Good Lord, he was never satisfied. He'd be obstinate till the very last gun was fired. Why, if he got drowned in a river he'd float upstream just to be contrary. In the course of time, the new board was seated. For the first few months of its term, it was occupied in clearing up the business left over by the old board and in the completion of the railway map. But now, the decks were cleared. It was about to address itself to the consideration of a revision of the tariff for the carriage of grain between the San Joaquin Valley and tide-water. Both Lyman and Darrell were pledged to an average ten per cent. cut of the grain rates throughout the entire State. The typewriter returned with the letters for Lyman to sign, and he put away the map and took up his morning's routine of business, wondering, the while, what would become of his practice during the time he was involved in the business of the Ranchers' Railroad Commission. But towards noon, at the moment when Lyman was drawing off a glass of mineral water from the siphon that stood at his elbow, there was an interruption. Some one rapped vigorously upon the door, which was immediately after opened, and Magnus and Harran came in, followed by Presley.

“Hello, hello!” cried Lyman, jumping up, extending his hands, “why, here's a surprise. I didn't expect you all till to-night. Come in, come in and sit down. Have a glass of sizz-water, Governor.” The others explained that they had come up from Bonneville the night before, as the Executive Committee of the League had received a despatch from the lawyers it had retained to fight the Railroad, that the judge of the court in San Francisco, where the test cases were being tried, might be expected to hand down his decision the next day. Very soon after the announcement of the new grading of the ranchers' lands, the corporation had offered, through S. Behrman, to lease the disputed lands to the ranchers at a nominal figure. The offer had been angrily rejected, and the Railroad had put up the lands for sale at Ruggles's office in Bonneville. At the exorbitant price named, buyers promptly appeared—dummy buyers, beyond shadow of doubt, acting either for the Railroad or for S. Behrman—men hitherto unknown in the county, men without property, without money, adventurers, heelers. Prominent among them, and bidding for the railroad's holdings included on Annixter's ranch, was Delaney. The farce of deeding the corporation's sections to these fictitious purchasers was solemnly gone through with at Ruggles's office, the Railroad guaranteeing them possession. The League refused to allow the supposed buyers to come upon the land, and the Railroad, faithful to its pledge in the matter of guaranteeing its dummies possession, at once began suits in ejectment in the district court in Visalia, the county seat. It was the preliminary skirmish, the reconnaisance in force, the combatants feeling each other's strength, willing to proceed with caution, postponing the actual death-grip for a while till each had strengthened its position and organised its forces.

If you think you've netted him, I DON'T, that's all I've got to say.” But he was jeered down as a croaker. There was the Commission. He couldn't get around that, could he? There was Darrell and Lyman Derrick, both pledged to the ranches. Good Lord, he was never satisfied. He'd be obstinate till the very last gun was fired. Why, if he got drowned in a river he'd float upstream just to be contrary. In the course of time, the new board was seated. For the first few months of its term, it was occupied in clearing up the business left over by the old board and in the completion of the railway map. But now, the decks were cleared. It was about to address itself to the consideration of a revision of the tariff for the carriage of grain between the San Joaquin Valley and tide-water. Both Lyman and Darrell were pledged to an average ten per cent. cut of the grain rates throughout the entire State. The typewriter returned with the letters for Lyman to sign, and he put away the map and took up his morning's routine of business, wondering, the while, what would become of his practice during the time he was involved in the business of the Ranchers' Railroad Commission. But towards noon, at the moment when Lyman was drawing off a glass of mineral water from the siphon that stood at his elbow, there was an interruption. Some one rapped vigorously upon the door, which was immediately after opened, and Magnus and Harran came in, followed by Presley.

“Hello, hello!” cried Lyman, jumping up, extending his hands, “why, here's a surprise. I didn't expect you all till to-night. Come in, come in and sit down. Have a glass of sizz-water, Governor.” The others explained that they had come up from Bonneville the night before, as the Executive Committee of the League had received a despatch from the lawyers it had retained to fight the Railroad, that the judge of the court in San Francisco, where the test cases were being tried, might be expected to hand down his decision the next day. Very soon after the announcement of the new grading of the ranchers' lands, the corporation had offered, through S. Behrman, to lease the disputed lands to the ranchers at a nominal figure. The offer had been angrily rejected, and the Railroad had put up the lands for sale at Ruggles's office in Bonneville. At the exorbitant price named, buyers promptly appeared—dummy buyers, beyond shadow of doubt, acting either for the Railroad or for S. Behrman—men hitherto unknown in the county, men without property, without money, adventurers, heelers. Prominent among them, and bidding for the railroad's holdings included on Annixter's ranch, was Delaney. The farce of deeding the corporation's sections to these fictitious purchasers was solemnly gone through with at Ruggles's office, the Railroad guaranteeing them possession. The League refused to allow the supposed buyers to come upon the land, and the Railroad, faithful to its pledge in the matter of guaranteeing its dummies possession, at once began suits in ejectment in the district court in Visalia, the county seat. It was the preliminary skirmish, the reconnaisance in force, the combatants feeling each other's strength, willing to proceed with caution, postponing the actual death-grip for a while till each had strengthened its position and organised its forces.
