It was towards nine o'clock of a raw evening in November, and in the little kitchen of the Rasmussen cottage, on the flats below the Potrero, the supper things had not yet been cleared away. The room was small, low-ceiled, smelling of coffee and of fried onions and of the kerosene of the lamp, which stood in the middle of the table upon a square of oilcloth, its chimney smoked upon one side, its flame turned a little too high, so that a thin thread of soot went wavering up toward the ceiling. Everything about the place was clean, scrubbed, set in order with a kind of rigid and Scandinavian scrupulousness: the zinc of the sink burnished till it shone, the stove blackened and polished, the row of tin canisters upon the shelf above it, labelled in German characters, COFFEE, SUGAR, TEA, SALT, standing at exact intervals, like soldiers drawn up for inspection. A calendar from a ship-chandler's on East Street hung beside the door, and above the table a cheap clock in a case of stamped walnut ticked loudly, steadily, monotonously, filling up all the pauses of the talk.

Lena Rasmussen sat at one end of the table, her hands folded upon the oilcloth before her, her back very straight. She was a big, blonde, heavy-limbed woman of about thirty, with a great mass of straw-coloured hair twisted into a knot at the back of her head, and pale blue eyes, set wide apart, that looked out upon the world with a slow, deliberate, unwavering gaze. Her arms, bare to the elbow, were red from the washtub, the skin of her fingers puckered and seamed. There was something massive about her, something placid and immovable, a sense of weight, of rootedness, as of a thing that had grown up out of the ground and could not be shifted.

Opposite her, his chair tilted back against the wall, his thumbs hooked in the armholes of his waistcoat, sat her husband. Adolph Rasmussen was a foreman at the Butchertown tannery. Even here, in his own kitchen, washed and in his clean shirt, there clung to him faintly the odour of his trade, the acrid smell of bark and of lime and of raw hides steeping in the vats, an odour that no soap would ever wholly remove. He was a short man, thick through the chest and shoulders, with a bull neck that rose in a solid column from his collar, and a square, close-cropped head. His mustache was red, and he chewed upon the ends of it when he was perplexed. His hands, lying upon his knees, were enormous, the knuckles knotted, the nails broken and stained a deep, indelible brown.

For some moments neither had spoken. Outside, from the direction of the bay, the foghorn at Point Bonita, very far away, sounded its long, hoarse, melancholy note, and nearer at hand, upon the spur track that ran behind the cottage, a switch engine went by, coughing, the windows rattling in their frames, the lamp flame shuddering in its chimney.

“Well,” said Adolph at length, letting the front legs of his chair down upon the floor with a thump, “well, what do you say? I can't talk all night. Gerstle wants his answer Saturday. Saturday noon, he says. After that he goes to somebody else.”

“Let him go to somebody else,” said Lena.

She did not raise her voice. She did not move. Her hands remained folded upon the oilcloth, and her pale eyes continued to rest upon her husband's face with the same slow and unwinking scrutiny.

“There!” exclaimed Adolph, striking his knee with his open palm. “There! That's what I knew you'd say. That's what I told Gerstle you'd say. I says to him, I says, 'My wife, she don't understand business. She's never had nothing to do with business. She'll say no right off, without thinking, without listening.' That's what I told him.”

“I have listened,” answered Lena. “I listened to you last night, and I listened to you Sunday. I listen to you all the time. It's always Gerstle, Gerstle, Gerstle.”

“And why not Gerstle? Ain't he a smart man? Ain't he made money? Look at him. Look how he lives. He's got a house on Folsom Street with a bay window, and a piano, and his wife wears a sealskin sacque. Two years ago he hadn't a cent; he was clerking in a bottling works for twelve dollars a week. Now look at him.”

“I don't want to look at him.”

Adolph got up. He began to walk up and down the narrow space between the table and the stove, three steps one way, three steps the other, his heavy shoes creaking, his head lowered, his hands thrust deep into his pockets. The floor trembled under his weight. The canisters upon the shelf gave out a faint tinny clinking. Lena did not turn her head to follow him. She sat as she had been sitting, looking now at the place where he had been, at the empty chair still pushed back against the wall.

“Listen here,” he said, stopping abruptly at the end of the table and leaning upon it with both fists, so that the oilcloth creaked under his knuckles. “Listen here, Lena, I'm going to tell you once more, plain, so you got to understand. This dredging company, it's a sure thing. There ain't no chance about it. They got the land, they got the machinery coming from Chicago, they got an engineer from the East that knows all about it. All up and down the Feather River, all around Oroville, there's gold in the gravel, millions of dollars in gold, just lying there, waiting. The old miners, they couldn't get at it. They only scratched the top. But these dredges, they go right down to bedrock, and they scoop it up—tons and tons of it every day—and the gold comes out the bottom like—like flour out of a mill. Gerstle showed me the figures. I seen them with my own eyes. It's a sure thing, I tell you. A fool could see it.”

“Then let the fools put their money in.”

“Ach!” He flung himself away from the table. “You don't know nothing. You don't know what you're talking about. Here's a chance—a chance, I say—such as don't come to a man once in his life, and you sit there like a—like a block of wood and say no, no, no. What do you think we're going to do? Live here in this hole all our lives? Me working in that stink down there twelve hours a day, coming home smelling like a dead horse, for eighteen dollars a week? You think I like it? You think I want to do that till I'm an old man and can't work no more and they turn me off?”

“We do well enough,” said Lena. “We have enough to eat. We owe nobody.”

“Enough to eat!” he cried. “Enough to eat! Pigs have enough to eat.”

There was a silence. The clock ticked with exasperating loudness. In the stove a coal settled, and a little spurt of flame showed for an instant through the cracks of the lid, red, then died away. Lena unfolded her hands, smoothed the oilcloth before her with a slow and deliberate gesture, and folded them again.

“How much does Gerstle want?” she asked.

Adolph turned quickly. For an instant his face lit up, and he came back to the table, eager, hopeful, his little eyes shining.

“Twelve hundred,” he said. “Twelve hundred for the shares. That's a third interest in the first dredge. A third, Lena, think of that. And when that one pays—and it's going to pay the first season, Gerstle says—then we go in on the second, and the third. And in five years—in five years—”

“There is not twelve hundred dollars,” said Lena. “There is four hundred and eighty in the bank. You know that.”

“I know that. I know that. But there's the place at San Lorenzo.”

He had said it at last, and having said it, he stood still, watching her, his breath coming a little short, his big hands opening and shutting at his sides. Lena did not answer at once. Something had come into her face, something slow and hard and set, like water freezing. Her lips closed upon each other in a straight line. The colour mounted very gradually into her broad cheeks, and her eyes, which had never left his face, grew if anything paler, more fixed.

The place at San Lorenzo! It was hers. It had been her father's. Old Peter Jessen had come out from Schleswig in the 'sixties, had worked as a section hand upon the Central Pacific, had saved and pinched and starved, and at last had bought those eleven acres on the flat lands beyond San Leandro, toward the bay. He had planted them with cherries and apricots, had built a little house there of redwood boards, had dug a well and put up a windmill, and for twenty years had lived upon the place, working it with his own hands, from dawn to dusk, season after season, digging, pruning, spraying, irrigating, bent double over his trees until his back had grown crooked like the trunks of the old apricots themselves. And when he died he had left it to Lena, his only child, and it was leased now to a Portuguese who paid her ninety dollars a year, which went into the bank, every cent, and was never touched.

To Lena the place was not a thing of dollars and cents. It was the earth itself, the brown, warm, fecund earth, the soil out of which her people had come and to which they clung, generation after generation, with the blind, unreasoning tenacity of roots. In her mind she saw it now, in the dim kitchen, under the smoking lamp—the long, straight rows of trees, grey and bare at this season, standing in the wet furrows; the windmill turning slowly against the sky, its vane creaking; the little house with its sagging porch, and beyond it, flat and endless, the marshes going down to the bay, and the bay itself, leaden-coloured under the November clouds, and over all the smell of wet earth and of rotting leaves and of smoke from the burning of prunings. It was hers. It was the one thing in the world that was hers, that was solid, that could not be taken away. It did not go up and down like the prices in the newspapers. It did not depend upon Gerstle or upon engineers from the East or upon machinery coming from Chicago. It was there. It would always be there.

“No,” she said.

“Lena—”

“No.”

“Now, you listen here—”

“No.”

She said the word each time in the same tone, flat, level, without emphasis, without anger, and it fell upon Adolph's ears like the blows of a hammer, regular and inexorable. He stared at her. A dull red crept up from his collar, suffusing his thick neck, his cheeks, his forehead, to the roots of his cropped hair. He began to chew upon his mustache.

“It ain't doing nobody any good,” he burst out at last. “It's just lying there. Ninety dollars a year! Ninety dollars! What's that? Gerstle says we'd make that in a week, in a day maybe, once the dredge gets going. And there's a man in Hayward will buy the place—I asked—fifteen hundred cash, he'll give. Fifteen hundred! That's twelve hundred for the shares and three hundred over. And you sit there and say no.”

“You asked?” said Lena. “You went and asked a man to buy my father's place?”

“Well, why not? What harm is there in asking? A man's got a right to ask, ain't he?”

“It is not yours to sell.”

“It's mine as much as yours,” he cried. “Ain't I your husband? Ain't what's yours mine? That's the law, ain't it?”

“It is not the law,” answered Lena quietly. “I asked Mr. Lindquist at the bank when Father died. It is my property. My separate property, he said. Nobody can sell it but me.”

Adolph's jaw dropped. For a moment he could find nothing to say. That she should have thought of this, that she should have gone to the bank, to Lindquist, and asked, years ago, without telling him, coolly, deliberately, as though she had foreseen this very night—the idea was at once so unexpected and so humiliating that it struck him dumb. And then, all at once, the blood went to his head. A sudden and blind rage, the rage of the male thwarted, baffled, defied, surged up within him, primitive, brutal, unreasoning. His fists clenched. He leaned across the table toward her, his face close to hers, his breath, smelling of coffee and of the tannery, beating upon her cheek.

“So that's it,” he said thickly. “So that's what you been doing. Sneaking around behind my back. Going to the bank. Asking Lindquist. Asking him what? How to keep your husband from getting what's his? Is that it? Is that what you're thinking about all the time, sitting there so quiet, with your hands folded? Is it?”

Lena did not draw back. She did not so much as blink. She sat upright in her chair, enormous, motionless, her pale eyes looking straight into his inflamed and swollen face, and there was neither fear in her glance nor anger, but only that same slow, heavy, invincible obstinacy, the obstinacy of the peasant, of the soil, of a thing that has been planted and cannot be uprooted.

“Sit down, Adolph,” she said.

He did not sit down. He straightened himself, breathing hard, and stood glaring at her, his chest heaving, his big brown hands working at his sides. Behind him the shadow cast by the lamp loomed enormous upon the wall, distorted, misshapen, its head bent forward against the ceiling. For a long moment the two remained thus, facing each other across the narrow table, the man standing, the woman seated, while the clock ticked on and on, measuring off the seconds with mechanical indifference, and the lamp flame wavered, and the thread of soot went curling upward.

Then, from far off across the bay, the foghorn sounded again, long, hoarse, desolate, and as if the sound had broken some spell, Adolph turned away. He dropped heavily into his chair and sat there, his elbows on his knees, his head in his hands, his fingers buried in his hair.

“I want something,” he muttered. “That's all. I want something. I'm thirty-four. I been working since I was twelve. Twelve years old, in the shipyards at Copenhagen, carrying rivets. Then on the boats. Then here. Always working, working, working, and what have I got? What have I got to show? Nothing. A two-room house on the flats, by the railroad, where you can't sleep for the engines. And every day I go down there to the vats and stand in that stink, and the boss, he cusses me, and I cuss the men, and they hate me, and I come home and eat my supper and go to bed and get up and do it all over again. And other men, men no smarter than me—men like Gerstle—they get rich. They get rich just like that.” He snapped his huge fingers. “Why not me? Why not me, Lena? Ain't I as good as Gerstle?”

Something stirred in Lena's face, something softer, troubled, almost pitying. For an instant her hands moved upon the oilcloth as though she would have reached out toward him. But she did not. She only said, very low:

“It is not a question of good, Adolph.”

“Then what is it?”

She was silent a long time, searching for the words, her slow mind groping, turning the thing over and over. How could she tell him? How explain to him what she felt so profoundly and so dumbly—that the money Gerstle talked of was not real, that it was a thing of the air, of the newspapers, of figures written upon paper, that it came quickly and went quickly, like water poured upon sand; while the land was real, was solid, was a thing you could put your hand upon, and dig into, and that would feed you when everything else had failed? She had seen men like Gerstle before. The city was full of them, shifting, eager, voluble men, always with a scheme, always with a sure thing, rising and falling like corks upon the tide. To-day the house on Folsom Street with the bay window and the piano; to-morrow—who knew? The great current of the city's life swept them up and swept them down again, careless, indifferent, blind, and when they went under no one remembered their names. But the land remained.

“It is only that I am afraid,” she said at length.

“Afraid! Afraid of what?”

“That it will all go. And then there will be nothing. Not the money in the bank, not the place, nothing. And we will be old.”

“It won't go,” he insisted, raising his head. “I tell you it can't go. Gerstle says—”

“Gerstle says.” She shook her head slowly. “Always Gerstle says.”

Adolph got up again. But the rage had gone out of him now; he moved heavily, sullenly, like a beast that has charged and been turned back and has not yet decided whether to charge again. He went to the window and stood there, his back to her, his hands in his pockets, looking out. There was nothing to see. The fog had come in from the bay, thick, grey, wet, blotting out everything; only, a little distance off, the red lantern of a switch on the spur track glowed dimly through the murk like a single bloodshot eye. Down there, beyond the fog, the city lay sprawled upon its hills, roaring faintly, a huge, vague, ceaseless murmur, the voice of three hundred thousand lives grinding upon one another, struggling, scrambling, fighting for money, for place, for bread—the voice of a monstrous machine, indifferent to who was crushed between its wheels.

“Saturday noon,” Adolph said, without turning round. “He wants his answer Saturday noon.”

Lena rose. She began to gather up the supper dishes, stacking the plates one upon another, the cups upon the plates, slowly, methodically, her big red hands moving with a kind of deliberate and unhurried precision. She carried them to the sink and set them down, and took the kettle from the stove and poured the hot water over them, and the steam went up in a white cloud about her head.

“You have had my answer,” she said.

He swung about. For a moment it seemed as if the anger would return; his face darkened, his fists closed. But Lena had turned her back upon him and stood bent over the sink, her broad shoulders moving rhythmically as she washed the dishes, and there was in the very set of those shoulders something so solid, so final, so immovable, that his fury broke against it and fell back, impotent. He stood looking at her a moment longer. Then, without a word, he took his hat and coat from the peg beside the door, under the ship-chandler's calendar, and went out, slamming the door behind him so that the canisters clinked upon the shelf and the lamp flame leaped and quivered.

Lena did not look up. She went on washing the dishes, one after another, drying them, setting them back upon the shelf in their exact places. Only, when she came to the last cup, her hands were still for a long moment in the cooling water, and she stood with her head bowed, listening to his heavy footsteps going away down the plank sidewalk, growing fainter, fainter, until they were swallowed up in the fog and the vast murmur of the city.

The clock ticked on. Far out across the bay the foghorn sounded once more, hoarse, prolonged, insistent, like a warning that no one heeded.

Here is an excerpt of Frank Norris's writing, to show you their style:

In his office at San Francisco, seated before a massive desk of polished redwood, very ornate, Lyman Derrick sat dictating letters to his typewriter, on a certain morning early in the spring of the year. The subdued monotone of his voice proceeded evenly from sentence to sentence, regular, precise, businesslike.

“I have the honour to acknowledge herewith your favour of the 14th instant, and in reply would state——” “Please find enclosed draft upon New Orleans to be applied as per our understanding——” “In answer to your favour No. 1107, referring to the case of the City and County of San Francisco against Excelsior Warehouse & Storage Co., I would say——” His voice continued, expressionless, measured, distinct. While he spoke, he swung slowly back and forth in his leather swivel chair, his elbows resting on the arms, his pop eyes fixed vaguely upon the calendar on the opposite wall, winking at intervals when he paused, searching for a word.

“That's all for the present,” he said at length. Without reply, the typewriter rose and withdrew, thrusting her pencil into the coil of her hair, closing the door behind her, softly, discreetly. When she had gone, Lyman rose, stretching himself putting up three fingers to hide his yawn. To further loosen his muscles, he took a couple of turns the length of he room, noting with satisfaction its fine appointments, the padded red carpet, the dull olive green tint of the walls, the few choice engravings—portraits of Marshall, Taney, Field, and a coloured lithograph—excellently done—of the Grand Canyon of the Colorado—the deep-seated leather chairs, the large and crowded bookcase (topped with a bust of James Lick, and a huge greenish globe), the waste basket of woven coloured grass, made by Navajo Indians, the massive silver inkstand on the desk, the elaborate filing cabinet, complete in every particular, and the shelves of tin boxes, padlocked, impressive, grave, bearing the names of clients, cases and estates. He was between thirty-one and thirty-five years of age. Unlike Harran, he resembled his mother, but he was much darker than Annie Derrick and his eyes were much fuller, the eyeball protruding, giving him a pop-eyed, foreign expression, quite unusual and unexpected. His hair was black, and he wore a small, tight, pointed mustache, which he was in the habit of pushing delicately upward from the corners of his lips with the ball of his thumb, the little finger extended. As often as he made this gesture, he prefaced it with a little twisting gesture of the forearm in order to bring his cuff into view, and, in fact, this movement by itself was habitual. He was dressed carefully, his trousers creased, a pink rose in his lapel. His shoes were of patent leather, his cutaway coat was of very rough black cheviot, his double-breasted waistcoat of tan covered cloth with buttons of smoked pearl. An Ascot scarf—a great puff of heavy black silk—was at his neck, the knot transfixed by a tiny golden pin set off with an opal and four small diamonds. At one end of the room were two great windows of plate glass, and pausing at length before one of these, Lyman selected a cigarette from his curved box of oxydized silver, lit it and stood looking down and out, willing to be idle for a moment, amused and interested in the view. His office was on the tenth floor of the EXCHANGE BUILDING, a beautiful, tower-like affair of white stone, that stood on the corner of Market Street near its intersection with Kearney, the most imposing office building of the city. Below him the city swarmed tumultuous through its grooves, the cable-cars starting and stopping with a gay jangling of bells and a strident whirring of jostled glass windows. Drays and carts clattered over the cobbles, and an incessant shuffling of thousands of feet rose from the pavement. Around Lotta's fountain the baskets of the flower sellers, crammed with chrysanthemums, violets, pinks, roses, lilies, hyacinths, set a brisk note of colour in the grey of the street. But to Lyman's notion the general impression of this centre of the city's life was not one of strenuous business activity. It was a continuous interest in small things, a people ever willing to be amused at trifles, refusing to consider serious matters—good-natured, allowing themselves to be imposed upon, taking life easily—generous, companionable, enthusiastic; living, as it were, from day to day, in a place where the luxuries of life were had without effort; in a city that offered to consideration the restlessness of a New York, without its earnestness; the serenity of a Naples, without its languor; the romance of a Seville, without its picturesqueness. As Lyman turned from the window, about to resume his work, the office boy appeared at the door.

“The man from the lithograph company, sir,” announced the boy.

“Well, what does he want?” demanded Lyman, adding, however, upon the instant: “Show him in.” A young man entered, carrying a great bundle, which he deposited on a chair, with a gasp of relief, exclaiming, all out of breath: “From the Standard Lithograph Company.”

“What is?”

“Don't know,” replied the other. “Maps, I guess.”

“I don't want any maps. Who sent them? I guess you're mistaken.” Lyman tore the cover from the top of the package, drawing out one of a great many huge sheets of white paper, folded eight times. Suddenly, he uttered an exclamation: “Ah, I see. They ARE maps. But these should not have come here. They are to go to the regular office for distribution.” He wrote a new direction on the label of the package: “Take them to that address,” he went on. “I'll keep this one here. The others go to that address. If you see Mr. Darrell, tell him that Mr. Derrick—you get the name—Mr. Derrick may not be able to get around this afternoon, but to go ahead with any business just the same.” The young man departed with the package and Lyman, spreading out the map upon the table, remained for some time studying it thoughtfully. It was a commissioner's official railway map of the State of California, completed to March 30th of that year. Upon it the different railways of the State were accurately plotted in various colours, blue, green, yellow. However, the blue, the yellow, and the green were but brief traceries, very short, isolated, unimportant. At a little distance these could hardly be seen. The whole map was gridironed by a vast, complicated network of red lines marked P. and S. W. R. R. These centralised at San Francisco and thence ramified and spread north, east, and south, to every quarter of the State. From Coles, in the topmost corner of the map, to Yuma in the lowest, from Reno on one side to San Francisco on the other, ran the plexus of red, a veritable system of blood circulation, complicated, dividing, and reuniting, branching, splitting, extending, throwing out feelers, off-shoots, tap roots, feeders—diminutive little blood suckers that shot out from the main jugular and went twisting up into some remote county, laying hold upon some forgotten village or town, involving it in one of a myriad branching coils, one of a hundred tentacles, drawing it, as it were, toward that centre from which all this system sprang. The map was white, and it seemed as if all the colour which should have gone to vivify the various counties, towns, and cities marked upon it had been absorbed by that huge, sprawling organism, with its ruddy arteries converging to a central point. It was as though the State had been sucked white and colourless, and against this pallid background the red arteries of the monster stood out, swollen with life-blood, reaching out to infinity, gorged to bursting; an excrescence, a gigantic parasite fattening upon the life-blood of an entire commonwealth. However, in an upper corner of the map appeared the names of the three new commissioners: Jones McNish for the first district, Lyman Derrick for the second, and James Darrell for the third. Nominated in the Democratic State convention in the fall of the preceding year, Lyman, backed by the coteries of San Francisco bosses in the pay of his father's political committee of ranchers, had been elected together with Darrell, the candidate of the Pueblo and Mojave road, and McNish, the avowed candidate of the Pacific and Southwestern. Darrell was rabidly against the P. and S. W., McNish rabidly for it. Lyman was supposed to be the conservative member of the board, the ranchers' candidate, it was true, and faithful to their interests, but a calm man, deliberative, swayed by no such violent emotions as his colleagues. Osterman's dexterity had at last succeeded in entangling Magnus inextricably in the new politics. The famous League, organised in the heat of passion the night of Annixter's barn dance, had been consolidated all through the winter months. Its executive committee, of which Magnus was chairman, had been, through Osterman's manipulation, merged into the old committee composed of Broderson, Annixter, and himself. Promptly thereat he had resigned the chairmanship of this committee, thus leaving Magnus at its head. Precisely as Osterman had planned, Magnus was now one of them. The new committee accordingly had two objects in view: to resist the attempted grabbing of their lands by the Railroad, and to push forward their own secret scheme of electing a board of railroad commissioners who should regulate wheat rates so as to favour the ranchers of the San Joaquin. The land cases were promptly taken to the courts and the new grading—fixing the price of the lands at twenty and thirty dollars an acre instead of two—bitterly and stubbornly fought. But delays occurred, the process of the law was interminable, and in the intervals the committee addressed itself to the work of seating the “Ranchers' Commission,” as the projected Board of Commissioners came to be called. It was Harran who first suggested that his brother, Lyman, be put forward as the candidate for this district. At once the proposition had a great success. Lyman seemed made for the place. column308:
On a certain Sunday morning toward the end of August, Cyrus Bergen stood at the foot of Market Street, before the gates of the ferry depot, waiting for the eleven o'clock boat from Oakland. He had come down early, much too early, fearing to be late, and for upward of half an hour he had walked to and fro upon the planking with short, heavy steps. He stopped at intervals to consult his watch, a great hunting-case affair of yellow gold, and snapped the lid shut each time with a little click of satisfaction, as if the punctuality of the instrument were in some way a credit to himself. He was a man of thirty-eight, stout, comfortable, well-fed, with a round, smooth-shaven face, very pink about the jowls, and small, pale-blue eyes that blinked continually behind gold-rimmed spectacles. His hair, thin upon the crown, was carefully parted and brushed flat with pomade. Between his consultations of the watch he had the habit of drawing the heavy chain through his fingers, link by link, and rubbing the seal that hung from it, a cornelian carved with his initials, with the ball of his thumb, slowly, reflectively, as one might caress a favourite animal. He was dressed in his Sunday clothes: a frock coat of black broadcloth, a little tight across the stomach; trousers of grey stripe; a waistcoat of white duck, freshly laundered, with buttons of mother-of-pearl; a high collar; a cravat of plum-coloured satin pierced by a horseshoe pin; and a hat of black felt, new that summer. His shoes had been blacked that morning by his wife's own hands.

He was head clerk at Ruhlmann & Kneiss, ship chandlers, on Steuart Street. He had held the place eleven years. He owned his house on Twenty-second Street, out in the Mission, a narrow, two-story affair painted drab, with a bay window and a little garden of geraniums and calla lilies in front. He had a wife, two children, a parlour organ, a canary, and a burial lot in the Odd Fellows' Cemetery, paid for in full.

The day was fine. A wind came in from the bay, salt and brisk, and set the flags snapping upon the masts of the shipping. All along the water-front the life of the city's edge went forward even on the Sabbath, less noisily than on weekdays but with no real cessation: the drays rumbling empty over the cobbles, the hackmen lounging on their boxes and calling to one another, the boot-blacks, the newsboys crying the Sunday editions, the vendors of peanuts and tamales, the sailors in pairs and trios, rolling, uncertain, their caps on the backs of their heads. Beyond the depot the masts of the deep-water ships rose in a thicket against the sky, and from somewhere out on the bay a tug whistled, hoarse, prolonged, insistent.

Cyrus was not thinking of any of these things. He was thinking of his cousin Adolph, whom he had not seen in nine years, and of whom he had heard nothing at all in the last four, until the letter had come on Thursday. It was a short letter, written in pencil on a sheet torn from a ledger, without date and almost without punctuation. It said only that Adolph had come down from Seattle on the steamer, that he was stopping for a day or two with a man he knew in Oakland, and that he would cross over Sunday on the eleven o'clock boat if Cyrus cared to meet him. It was signed "Dolph." Nobody had called him that since they were boys together on the ranch at Petaluma.

The boat came in at last. Cyrus heard the thud and grind of her against the piles, the creak of the slip, the rattle of the apron let down. Then came the crowd, released all at once, pouring through the gates in a dense, jostling, many-coloured stream: families out for the day with baskets and parasols, young men in straw hats and blazers of striped flannel, their girls upon their arms, Chinamen in blue blouses, a priest, a soldier from the Presidio, a woman leading a pug dog by a ribbon, labourers in clean shirts, clerks, shop-girls, idlers, all the miscellaneous humanity of a holiday morning, laughing, calling out, hurrying on toward the cable cars that waited, clanging, at the head of the street.

Cyrus stood upon his toes, peering, blinking, anxious. He looked for a young man, slim, light-haired, with a quick, nervous way of moving his head, for that was how he remembered Adolph. He did not see him. The crowd thinned and the stragglers came through, and Cyrus began to fear that his cousin had changed his mind, or missed the boat, or had never meant to come at all.

Then a man stopped directly in front of him and said:

"Well, Cy."

Cyrus stared. The man before him was tall, much taller than he had any recollection of, and gaunt to the point of emaciation. He was burned by sun and wind to the colour of saddle-leather, and a beard, reddish and untrimmed, covered the lower half of his face. His cheek-bones stood out like knobs, and the eyes beneath the heavy brows were deep-set and very light, almost colourless, with a curious fixity of gaze, as of a man long accustomed to looking at great distances. He wore a pea-jacket of coarse blue stuff, much stained, a flannel shirt open at the throat, trousers of brown duck stuffed into boots that reached half-way to the knee, and a cap of some kind of fur, though the day was warm. Over one shoulder he carried a canvas bag, lashed with rope. But what Cyrus noticed most, then and afterward, were the hands, enormous, knotted, seamed with old cuts and scars, the knuckles swollen, two of the fingernails gone entirely. They were not the hands of a man at all. They were the hands of some creature that had been made to dig and to grip and to hold on.

"Dolph!" exclaimed Cyrus. "Why, Dolph, I'd never have known you. Why, upon my word!" He put out his own hand, soft, pink, a little damp. Adolph took it, and Cyrus felt his fingers swallowed up and crushed together in a grip that made him wince. "Well, well, well," he said, and could think of nothing else to say. "Well, well, well."

"I guess I've changed some," said Adolph.

"Changed! I should say you had. Why, you're as brown as an Indian. And that beard! Say, what would Aunt Bettina—" He checked himself. "But come along, come along. You'll have something to eat. I've thought it all out. We'll go to Schreiber's. You remember Schreiber's? No, you wouldn't. It's since your time. It's on Ellis Street. The best place in town for a Sunday dinner, and quiet. Minna wanted you to come out to the house, but I said no, I said we'd want to talk, you and me, just the two of us, the first time. She sends her regards. You'll come out to the house to-morrow. Here, let me take your bag."

"I'll carry it," said Adolph.

They boarded a car and rode up Market Street, Cyrus talking the whole way, pointing out the new buildings, the new hotel, the place where the old Bella Union had burned, the corner where a man had been shot the winter before. Adolph said little. He sat with his bag between his knees and his great hands folded upon it, and looked at the city going past with that fixed, colourless stare, neither interested nor bored, but watchful, the way an animal brought in from the woods might look at the walls of a room.

Schreiber's was a long, low-ceiled place, half restaurant, half beer-hall, with a sanded floor and tables of scrubbed pine set in rows. The walls were painted a dull red and hung with lithographs of the Rhine, of Kaiser Wilhelm, and of a stag at bay, along with a pair of antlers, a cuckoo clock, and a framed card bearing the motto "Wer nicht liebt Wein, Weib und Gesang." At the back was a bar of carved walnut, very dark and polished, with a mirror behind it and a row of steins upon a shelf, each with a pewter lid and each with a name painted upon it in Gothic letters. The air was heavy with the smells of beer, sauerkraut, roasting veal, and tobacco. At that hour the place was half full: German families mostly, the men in their shirt-sleeves, their coats hung upon the backs of their chairs, the women stout and red-armed, the children kicking their heels beneath the tables, and a waiter in a long white apron going to and fro with four mugs of beer in each fist.

Cyrus chose a table near the window and ordered, without consulting his cousin, because he knew the place, he said, and knew what was good: soup with dumplings, Wiener schnitzel, potato salad, red cabbage, rye bread, Limburger, and beer. He tucked his napkin into his collar and spread it carefully over the white waistcoat.

When the food came Adolph fell upon it. He ate with a kind of concentrated violence, his head down, his elbows wide, tearing the bread in his fingers and wiping the plate with it, chewing enormously, his jaws working, the cords standing out in his lean neck. He did not speak. He emptied the soup tureen, then the platter of schnitzel, then the bowl of potato salad. Cyrus ordered more, and Adolph ate that also. It was not greed exactly. It was something older and simpler than greed, an appetite that had no reference to pleasure, the brute instinct of a body that had starved and did not believe it would not starve again. Cyrus watched him, fascinated and a little disturbed. Upon the instant he remembered a dog they had had upon the ranch, a big yellow mongrel that had been lost in the hills for a fortnight one winter. When it came back it had eaten in just this way, with just this terrible, silent earnestness, glaring up at them over its dish.

At length Adolph pushed back his plate, drank off his beer at a draught, and wiped his beard with the back of his hand.

"That was good," he said. "I haven't eaten like that in—I don't know. A long time."

"Have another beer," said Cyrus. "Have a cigar." He took two from his waistcoat pocket, offered one, and lit them both with a sulphur match, sucking at his own with little popping noises. Then he leaned back, drew the watch-chain through his fingers, rubbed the seal, and looked at his cousin across the table, benevolent, expansive, a little moist about the eyes.

"Well, Dolph," he said, "and so here we are. Here we are. After all these years. It don't seem possible."

"No," said Adolph.

"I suppose you heard about Aunt Bettina?"

"No. I haven't heard anything. Nobody knew where to write me."

"She's dead. Three years ago February. It was her heart. She went very quick, at the last. She asked about you. She kept asking about you. We didn't know what to tell her." He paused, then added hurriedly, as if to cover the reproach in what he had said: "But she didn't suffer. Dr. Mott said she didn't suffer at all."

Adolph turned the cigar slowly in his fingers and looked at the end of it. He said nothing. His face showed nothing.

"And the ranch is sold," continued Cyrus. "That was the year after. Uncle Herman couldn't keep it up, not alone, not with prices what they were and the mortgage and all. A Portugee bought it, a dairyman, name of Silva. He's tore down the old barn and put up a creamery. You wouldn't know the place. He cut down the walnut trees along the creek, too, for firewood."

"The walnut trees," repeated Adolph.

"All of 'em. Every one."

There was a silence. In the corner the cuckoo clock whirred and struck the half hour, and at the next table a child began to cry and was hushed. Cyrus thought of the walnut trees, the great, spreading, grey-trunked trees along the creek bottom, where he and Dolph had built a raft one summer, and dammed the water, and caught crawfish with bits of bacon on a string, and where Dolph, who was the younger by two years but always the bolder, had fallen from the highest branch and broken his arm and never cried at all. He thought of the old barn with its smell of hay and harness-leather and the warm, heavy smell of the cows, and the loft where they used to hide on rainy days and tell each other stories of pirates and Indians and the gold diggings. They had sworn there once, in blood drawn with a pin, that they would go to the gold diggings together when they were men and come back rich. Cyrus had forgotten it until this moment.

"Do you remember," he said, "that knife? That knife with the bone handle that grandpa gave you? And we fought over it, out behind the woodpile, and you blacked my eye?"

Adolph looked up. For the first time something moved in the deep-set, colourless eyes, something faint and far off, like a light seen across a great stretch of snow.

"I remember," he said. "I've got it yet." He put one hand into the pocket of the pea-jacket and drew out a clasp-knife, the bone handle yellow and worn smooth, the blade ground down to half its width by years of sharpening. He laid it on the table between them. "It's been everywhere with me," he said. "It's about all I brought back."

Cyrus took up the knife and turned it over, and then he laid it down again, gently, as if it were something that might break.

"Tell me about it," he said. "Up there, I mean. The North. Was it as bad as they say?"

Adolph was silent so long that Cyrus thought he would not answer. When he did speak it was slowly, in a flat, even voice, without emphasis, without any colour at all, as a man might recite a list of figures.

"We went in over the Chilkoot in 'ninety-four," he said, "me and a Swede named Lindquist. Before the rush. We packed our outfit over the pass in eleven trips. It took us six weeks. We built a boat at Lake Bennett and went down the river. We staked on a creek off the Stewart. We worked it two winters. You thaw the ground with fires and dig out what you've thawed and then build the fires again. All winter. It's dark most of the day. Sixty below. Seventy. The cold gets into everything. It gets into your head. You stop thinking, after a while. You just work and eat and sleep. We got some gold, not much. Enough to keep on. The second winter Lindquist got the scurvy. His teeth came out. His legs turned black. I tried to get him out to Forty Mile, on a sled, but he died on the trail. I couldn't bury him, the ground was froze. I put rocks on him."

He drew upon the cigar and let the smoke go out slowly through his beard.

"Then the rush came, in 'ninety-seven. Thousands of 'em. The whole country was overrun. They jumped claims, they stole outfits, they shot each other over a sack of flour. I sold out for what I could get and went down to Dawson and worked for wages. Then I went over to Nome when they struck it on the beaches. It was the same there. It's the same everywhere, I guess. There's gold up there, Cy, gold enough to buy this whole town, but it don't belong to the men that dig it. It belongs to the country. The country holds onto it. It lets a man have a little, just enough to keep him there, and then it kills him or breaks him or drives him out. It don't care. That's the thing you learn. It don't care whether you live or die, no more than the ice in the river cares. You're just a thing to it, like a rock or a tree. Less."

He stopped and looked out the window at the street, the passing carriages, the people going up and down in their Sunday clothes.

"Then it's queer to come back here," he said, "and see all this, and everybody acting as if it mattered."

Cyrus did not know what to reply. He shifted in his chair. He drew the watch-chain through his fingers and rubbed the seal. Something in his cousin's voice, in the flat, dead, indifferent level of it, frightened him obscurely. It was as though a door had been opened upon a place outside the world he knew, a vast, white, silent place, without limit and without mercy, where the things he lived by—his house, his garden, his position at Ruhlmann & Kneiss, his burial lot in the Odd Fellows' Cemetery—meant nothing whatever, had no more weight or substance than the smoke of his cigar.

"Well, but you're back now," he said at last, with a forced heartiness. "That's the main thing. You're back, and you're among your own folks. And you won't go up there again, not if I have anything to say about it. Look here, Dolph, I've been thinking. There's a place at our house, in the shipping department. Old Kneiss would take you on in a minute if I said the word. It ain't much to start, sixty a month, but there's a future in it. You could board with us till you got settled. Minna's a fine cook. And the children—you haven't seen the children. Herman's seven and Lottie's going on five. You'd be their uncle, kind of. Cousin, I mean. What do you say?"

Adolph looked at him. He looked at the round, pink, earnest face, the gold spectacles, the napkin tucked into the high collar, the white duck waistcoat with its buttons of mother-of-pearl, the plump hand fingering the cornelian seal. He looked at him a long time, steadily, without unkindness, but without understanding, the way one looks at a picture of a place one has never been.

"That's good of you, Cy," he said. "I mean it. That's good of you. But I couldn't."

"Why not?"

"I don't know. I just couldn't. I'd go crazy, inside walls. I'm shipping out Wednesday on a lumber schooner for the Sound. After that I don't know. Maybe back north. Maybe the Islands. There's talk of the Philippines."

"But Dolph—"

"No," said Adolph. "It ain't any use."

He put the knife back into his pocket and stood up and slung the canvas bag across his shoulder. Cyrus paid the reckoning, fumbling with the change, and they went out together into the street.

The afternoon had grown warm. The sun lay broad and yellow upon the pavements, and the wind had dropped. Up and down the length of the street the Sunday crowds moved slowly, aimlessly, in a kind of happy torpor: couples arm in arm, families with children, girls in white dresses and hats heaped with flowers, young men with canes, all of them sauntering, gazing in at the shop windows, stopping to talk, to laugh, to buy candy or ice cream from the carts at the corners, everybody idle, contented, unthinking, everybody taking life easily, as though there were nothing in the world but this warm afternoon and this pleasant street and this long, leisurely, well-fed Sabbath of the great city.

At the corner of Market Street they stopped.

"Well," said Cyrus. "Well, Dolph."

"Good-bye, Cy."

"You'll write? You'll let us know where you are?"

"I'll try."

They shook hands. Once more Cyrus felt his fingers swallowed up in that tremendous grip, and once more he winced. Then Adolph turned and went off down the street toward the water, walking with a long, slouching, tireless stride, the bag upon his shoulder, his head above the heads of the crowd, so that Cyrus could follow him for a long time, the fur cap bobbing among the straw hats and the flowered bonnets, until at length the throng closed over him and he was gone.

Cyrus stood upon the corner, blinking. He took out his watch, opened it, looked at it without seeing the time, and snapped it shut. Then he drew the chain through his fingers, slowly, link by link, and rubbed the cornelian seal with the ball of his thumb.

He had a vague, troubled sense of having lost something, though he could not have told what. He thought of the walnut trees cut down for firewood, of the old barn, of the oath sworn in the hayloft with a pin. He thought of the Swede, Lindquist, lying under his rocks in that white, enormous, indifferent country at the top of the world. He thought of his own house in the Mission, the bay window, the geraniums, the parlour organ, the canary in its cage, and they seemed to him all at once very small and very fragile, a little heap of things a man had gathered about himself to keep out the cold, while all around, beyond the edges of the lighted city, beyond the bay and the hills and the shining sea, the vast forces of the world went forward, blind, colossal, implacable, grinding men to dust beneath them and taking no account. Here is an excerpt of Frank Norris's writing, to show you their style:

In his office at San Francisco, seated before a massive desk of polished redwood, very ornate, Lyman Derrick sat dictating letters to his typewriter, on a certain morning early in the spring of the year. The subdued monotone of his voice proceeded evenly from sentence to sentence, regular, precise, businesslike.

“I have the honour to acknowledge herewith your favour of the 14th instant, and in reply would state——” “Please find enclosed draft upon New Orleans to be applied as per our understanding——” “In answer to your favour No. 1107, referring to the case of the City and County of San Francisco against Excelsior Warehouse & Storage Co., I would say——” His voice continued, expressionless, measured, distinct. While he spoke, he swung slowly back and forth in his leather swivel chair, his elbows resting on the arms, his pop eyes fixed vaguely upon the calendar on the opposite wall, winking at intervals when he paused, searching for a word.

“That's all for the present,” he said at length. Without reply, the typewriter rose and withdrew, thrusting her pencil into the coil of her hair, closing the door behind her, softly, discreetly. When she had gone, Lyman rose, stretching himself putting up three fingers to hide his yawn. To further loosen his muscles, he took a couple of turns the length of he room, noting with satisfaction its fine appointments, the padded red carpet, the dull olive green tint of the walls, the few choice engravings—portraits of Marshall, Taney, Field, and a coloured lithograph—excellently done—of the Grand Canyon of the Colorado—the deep-seated leather chairs, the large and crowded bookcase (topped with a bust of James Lick, and a huge greenish globe), the waste basket of woven coloured grass, made by Navajo Indians, the massive silver inkstand on the desk, the elaborate filing cabinet, complete in every particular, and the shelves of tin boxes, padlocked, impressive, grave, bearing the names of clients, cases and estates. He was between thirty-one and thirty-five years of age. Unlike Harran, he resembled his mother, but he was much darker than Annie Derrick and his eyes were much fuller, the eyeball protruding, giving him a pop-eyed, foreign expression, quite unusual and unexpected. His hair was black, and he wore a small, tight, pointed mustache, which he was in the habit of pushing delicately upward from the corners of his lips with the ball of his thumb, the little finger extended. As often as he made this gesture, he prefaced it with a little twisting gesture of the forearm in order to bring his cuff into view, and, in fact, this movement by itself was habitual. He was dressed carefully, his trousers creased, a pink rose in his lapel. His shoes were of patent leather, his cutaway coat was of very rough black cheviot, his double-breasted waistcoat of tan covered cloth with buttons of smoked pearl. An Ascot scarf—a great puff of heavy black silk—was at his neck, the knot transfixed by a tiny golden pin set off with an opal and four small diamonds. At one end of the room were two great windows of plate glass, and pausing at length before one of these, Lyman selected a cigarette from his curved box of oxydized silver, lit it and stood looking down and out, willing to be idle for a moment, amused and interested in the view. His office was on the tenth floor of the EXCHANGE BUILDING, a beautiful, tower-like affair of white stone, that stood on the corner of Market Street near its intersection with Kearney, the most imposing office building of the city. Below him the city swarmed tumultuous through its grooves, the cable-cars starting and stopping with a gay jangling of bells and a strident whirring of jostled glass windows. Drays and carts clattered over the cobbles, and an incessant shuffling of thousands of feet rose from the pavement. Around Lotta's fountain the baskets of the flower sellers, crammed with chrysanthemums, violets, pinks, roses, lilies, hyacinths, set a brisk note of colour in the grey of the street. But to Lyman's notion the general impression of this centre of the city's life was not one of strenuous business activity. It was a continuous interest in small things, a people ever willing to be amused at trifles, refusing to consider serious matters—good-natured, allowing themselves to be imposed upon, taking life easily—generous, companionable, enthusiastic; living, as it were, from day to day, in a place where the luxuries of life were had without effort; in a city that offered to consideration the restlessness of a New York, without its earnestness; the serenity of a Naples, without its languor; the romance of a Seville, without its picturesqueness. As Lyman turned from the window, about to resume his work, the office boy appeared at the door.

“The man from the lithograph company, sir,” announced the boy.

“Well, what does he want?” demanded Lyman, adding, however, upon the instant: “Show him in.” A young man entered, carrying a great bundle, which he deposited on a chair, with a gasp of relief, exclaiming, all out of breath: “From the Standard Lithograph Company.”

“What is?”

“Don't know,” replied the other. “Maps, I guess.”

“I don't want any maps. Who sent them? I guess you're mistaken.” Lyman tore the cover from the top of the package, drawing out one of a great many huge sheets of white paper, folded eight times. Suddenly, he uttered an exclamation: “Ah, I see. They ARE maps. But these should not have come here. They are to go to the regular office for distribution.” He wrote a new direction on the label of the package: “Take them to that address,” he went on. “I'll keep this one here. The others go to that address. If you see Mr. Darrell, tell him that Mr. Derrick—you get the name—Mr. Derrick may not be able to get around this afternoon, but to go ahead with any business just the same.” The young man departed with the package and Lyman, spreading out the map upon the table, remained for some time studying it thoughtfully. It was a commissioner's official railway map of the State of California, completed to March 30th of that year. Upon it the different railways of the State were accurately plotted in various colours, blue, green, yellow. However, the blue, the yellow, and the green were but brief traceries, very short, isolated, unimportant. At a little distance these could hardly be seen. The whole map was gridironed by a vast, complicated network of red lines marked P. and S. W. R. R. These centralised at San Francisco and thence ramified and spread north, east, and south, to every quarter of the State. From Coles, in the topmost corner of the map, to Yuma in the lowest, from Reno on one side to San Francisco on the other, ran the plexus of red, a veritable system of blood circulation, complicated, dividing, and reuniting, branching, splitting, extending, throwing out feelers, off-shoots, tap roots, feeders—diminutive little blood suckers that shot out from the main jugular and went twisting up into some remote county, laying hold upon some forgotten village or town, involving it in one of a myriad branching coils, one of a hundred tentacles, drawing it, as it were, toward that centre from which all this system sprang. The map was white, and it seemed as if all the colour which should have gone to vivify the various counties, towns, and cities marked upon it had been absorbed by that huge, sprawling organism, with its ruddy arteries converging to a central point. It was as though the State had been sucked white and colourless, and against this pallid background the red arteries of the monster stood out, swollen with life-blood, reaching out to infinity, gorged to bursting; an excrescence, a gigantic parasite fattening upon the life-blood of an entire commonwealth. However, in an upper corner of the map appeared the names of the three new commissioners: Jones McNish for the first district, Lyman Derrick for the second, and James Darrell for the third. Nominated in the Democratic State convention in the fall of the preceding year, Lyman, backed by the coteries of San Francisco bosses in the pay of his father's political committee of ranchers, had been elected together with Darrell, the candidate of the Pueblo and Mojave road, and McNish, the avowed candidate of the Pacific and Southwestern. Darrell was rabidly against the P. and S. W., McNish rabidly for it. Lyman was supposed to be the conservative member of the board, the ranchers' candidate, it was true, and faithful to their interests, but a calm man, deliberative, swayed by no such violent emotions as his colleagues. Osterman's dexterity had at last succeeded in entangling Magnus inextricably in the new politics. The famous League, organised in the heat of passion the night of Annixter's barn dance, had been consolidated all through the winter months. Its executive committee, of which Magnus was chairman, had been, through Osterman's manipulation, merged into the old committee composed of Broderson, Annixter, and himself. Promptly thereat he had resigned the chairmanship of this committee, thus leaving Magnus at its head. Precisely as Osterman had planned, Magnus was now one of them. The new committee accordingly had two objects in view: to resist the attempted grabbing of their lands by the Railroad, and to push forward their own secret scheme of electing a board of railroad commissioners who should regulate wheat rates so as to favour the ranchers of the San Joaquin. The land cases were promptly taken to the courts and the new grading—fixing the price of the lands at twenty and thirty dollars an acre instead of two—bitterly and stubbornly fought. But delays occurred, the process of the law was interminable, and in the intervals the committee addressed itself to the work of seating the “Ranchers' Commission,” as the projected Board of Commissioners came to be called. It was Harran who first suggested that his brother, Lyman, be put forward as the candidate for this district. At once the proposition had a great success. Lyman seemed made for the place. While allied by every tie of blood to the ranching interests, he had never been identified with them. He was city-bred. The Railroad would not be over-suspicious of him. He was a good lawyer, a good business man, keen, clear-headed, far-sighted, had already some practical knowledge of politics, having served a term as assistant district attorney, and even at the present moment occupying the position of sheriff's attorney. More than all, he was the son of Magnus Derrick; he could be relied upon, could be trusted implicitly to remain loyal to the ranchers' cause. The campaign for Railroad Commissioner had been very interesting. At the very outset Magnus's committee found itself involved in corrupt politics. The primaries had to be captured at all costs and by any means, and when the convention assembled it was found necessary to buy outright the votes of certain delegates. The campaign fund raised by contributions from Magnus, Annixter, Broderson, and Osterman was drawn upon to the extent of five thousand dollars. Only the committee knew of this corruption. The League, ignoring ways and means, supposed as a matter of course that the campaign was honorably conducted. For a whole week after the consummation of this part of the deal, Magnus had kept to his house, refusing to be seen, alleging that he was ill, which was not far from the truth. The shame of the business, the loathing of what he had done, were to him things unspeakable. He could no longer look Harran in the face. He began a course of deception with his wife. More than once, he had resolved to break with the whole affair, resigning his position, allowing the others to proceed without him. But now it was too late. He was pledged. He had joined the League. He was its chief, and his defection might mean its disintegration at the very time when it needed all its strength to fight the land cases. More than a mere deal in bad politics was involved. There was the land grab. His withdrawal from an unholy cause would mean the weakening, perhaps the collapse, of another cause that he believed to be righteous as truth itself. He was hopelessly caught in the mesh. Wrong seemed indissolubly knitted into the texture of Right. He was blinded, dizzied, overwhelmed, caught in the current of events, and hurried along he knew not where. He resigned himself. In the end, and after much ostentatious opposition on the part of the railroad heelers, Lyman was nominated and subsequently elected. When this consummation was reached Magnus, Osterman, Broderson, and Annixter stared at each other. Their wildest hopes had not dared to fix themselves upon so easy a victory as this. It was not believable that the corporation would allow itself to be fooled so easily, would rush open-eyed into the trap. How had it happened? Osterman, however, threw his hat into the air with wild whoops of delight. Old Broderson permitted himself a feeble cheer. Even Magnus beamed satisfaction. The other members of the League, present at the time, shook hands all around and spoke of opening a few bottles on the strength of the occasion. Annixter alone was recalcitrant.

“It's too easy,” he declared. “No, I'm not satisfied. Where's Shelgrim in all this? Why don't he show his hand, damn his soul? The thing is yellow, I tell you. There's a big fish in these waters somewheres. I don't know his name, and I don't know his game, but he's moving round off and on, just out of sight. If you think you've netted him, I DON'T, that's all I've got to say.” But he was jeered down as a croaker. There was the Commission. He couldn't get around that, could he? There was Darrell and Lyman Derrick, both pledged to the ranches. Good Lord, he was never satisfied. He'd be obstinate till the very last gun was fired. Why, if he got drowned in a river he'd float upstream just to be contrary. In the course of time, the new board was seated. For the first few months of its term, it was occupied in clearing up the business left over by the old board and in the completion of the railway map. But now, the decks were cleared. It was about to address itself to the consideration of a revision of the tariff for the carriage of grain between the San Joaquin Valley and tide-water. Both Lyman and Darrell were pledged to an average ten per cent. cut of the grain rates throughout the entire State. The typewriter returned with the letters for Lyman to sign, and he put away the map and took up his morning's routine of business, wondering, the while, what would become of his practice during the time he was involved in the business of the Ranchers' Railroad Commission. But towards noon, at the moment when Lyman was drawing off a glass of mineral water from the siphon that stood at his elbow, there was an interruption. Some one rapped vigorously upon the door, which was immediately after opened, and Magnus and Harran came in, followed by Presley.

“Hello, hello!” cried Lyman, jumping up, extending his hands, “why, here's a surprise. I didn't expect you all till to-night. Come in, come in and sit down. Have a glass of sizz-water, Governor.” The others explained that they had come up from Bonneville the night before, as the Executive Committee of the League had received a despatch from the lawyers it had retained to fight the Railroad, that the judge of the court in San Francisco, where the test cases were being tried, might be expected to hand down his decision the next day. Very soon after the announcement of the new grading of the ranchers' lands, the corporation had offered, through S. Behrman, to lease the disputed lands to the ranchers at a nominal figure. The offer had been angrily rejected, and the Railroad had put up the lands for sale at Ruggles's office in Bonneville. At the exorbitant price named, buyers promptly appeared—dummy buyers, beyond shadow of doubt, acting either for the Railroad or for S. Behrman—men hitherto unknown in the county, men without property, without money, adventurers, heelers. Prominent among them, and bidding for the railroad's holdings included on Annixter's ranch, was Delaney. The farce of deeding the corporation's sections to these fictitious purchasers was solemnly gone through with at Ruggles's office, the Railroad guaranteeing them possession. The League refused to allow the supposed buyers to come upon the land, and the Railroad, faithful to its pledge in the matter of guaranteeing its dummies possession, at once began suits in ejectment in the district court in Visalia, the county seat. It was the preliminary skirmish, the reconnaisance in force, the combatants feeling each other's strength, willing to proceed with caution, postponing the actual death-grip for a while till each had strengthened its position and organised its forces.

It was a continuous interest in small things, a people ever willing to be amused at trifles, refusing to consider serious matters—good-natured, allowing themselves to be imposed upon, taking life easily—generous, companionable, enthusiastic; living, as it were, from day to day, in a place where the luxuries of life were had without effort; in a city that offered to consideration the restlessness of a New York, without its earnestness; the serenity of a Naples, without its languor; the romance of a Seville, without its picturesqueness. As Lyman turned from the window, about to resume his work, the office boy appeared at the door.

“The man from the lithograph company, sir,” announced the boy.

“Well, what does he want?” demanded Lyman, adding, however, upon the instant: “Show him in.” A young man entered, carrying a great bundle, which he deposited on a chair, with a gasp of relief, exclaiming, all out of breath: “From the Standard Lithograph Company.”

“What is?”

“Don't know,” replied the other. “Maps, I guess.”

“I don't want any maps. Who sent them? I guess you're mistaken.” Lyman tore the cover from the top of the package, drawing out one of a great many huge sheets of white paper, folded eight times. Suddenly, he uttered an exclamation: “Ah, I see. They ARE maps. But these should not have come here. They are to go to the regular office for distribution.” He wrote a new direction on the label of the package: “Take them to that address,” he went on. “I'll keep this one here. The others go to that address. If you see Mr. Darrell, tell him that Mr. Derrick—you get the name—Mr. Derrick may not be able to get around this afternoon, but to go ahead with any business just the same.” The young man departed with the package and Lyman, spreading out the map upon the table, remained for some time studying it thoughtfully. It was a commissioner's official railway map of the State of California, completed to March 30th of that year. Upon it the different railways of the State were accurately plotted in various colours, blue, green, yellow. However, the blue, the yellow, and the green were but brief traceries, very short, isolated, unimportant. At a little distance these could hardly be seen. The whole map was gridironed by a vast, complicated network of red lines marked P. and S. W. R. R. These centralised at San Francisco and thence ramified and spread north, east, and south, to every quarter of the State. From Coles, in the topmost corner of the map, to Yuma in the lowest, from Reno on one side to San Francisco on the other, ran the plexus of red, a veritable system of blood circulation, complicated, dividing, and reuniting, branching, splitting, extending, throwing out feelers, off-shoots, tap roots, feeders—diminutive little blood suckers that shot out from the main jugular and went twisting up into some remote county, laying hold upon some forgotten village or town, involving it in one of a myriad branching coils, one of a hundred tentacles, drawing it, as it were, toward that centre from which all this system sprang. The map was white, and it seemed as if all the colour which should have gone to vivify the various counties, towns, and cities marked upon it had been absorbed by that huge, sprawling organism, with its ruddy arteries converging to a central point. It was as though the State had been sucked white and colourless, and against this pallid background the red arteries of the monster stood out, swollen with life-blood, reaching out to infinity, gorged to bursting; an excrescence, a gigantic parasite fattening upon the life-blood of an entire commonwealth. However, in an upper corner of the map appeared the names of the three new commissioners: Jones McNish for the first district, Lyman Derrick for the second, and James Darrell for the third. Nominated in the Democratic State convention in the fall of the preceding year, Lyman, backed by the coteries of San Francisco bosses in the pay of his father's political committee of ranchers, had been elected together with Darrell, the candidate of the Pueblo and Mojave road, and McNish, the avowed candidate of the Pacific and Southwestern. Darrell was rabidly against the P. and S. W., McNish rabidly for it. Lyman was supposed to be the conservative member of the board, the ranchers' candidate, it was true, and faithful to their interests, but a calm man, deliberative, swayed by no such violent emotions as his colleagues. Osterman's dexterity had at last succeeded in entangling Magnus inextricably in the new politics. The famous League, organised in the heat of passion the night of Annixter's barn dance, had been consolidated all through the winter months. Its executive committee, of which Magnus was chairman, had been, through Osterman's manipulation, merged into the old committee composed of Broderson, Annixter, and himself. Promptly thereat he had resigned the chairmanship of this committee, thus leaving Magnus at its head. Precisely as Osterman had planned, Magnus was now one of them. The new committee accordingly had two objects in view: to resist the attempted grabbing of their lands by the Railroad, and to push forward their own secret scheme of electing a board of railroad commissioners who should regulate wheat rates so as to favour the ranchers of the San Joaquin. The land cases were promptly taken to the courts and the new grading—fixing the price of the lands at twenty and thirty dollars an acre instead of two—bitterly and stubbornly fought. But delays occurred, the process of the law was interminable, and in the intervals the committee addressed itself to the work of seating the “Ranchers' Commission,” as the projected Board of Commissioners came to be called. It was Harran who first suggested that his brother, Lyman, be put forward as the candidate for this district. At once the proposition had a great success. Lyman seemed made for the place. While allied by every tie of blood to the ranching interests, he had never been identified with them. He was city-bred. The Railroad would not be over-suspicious of him. He was a good lawyer, a good business man, keen, clear-headed, far-sighted, had already some practical knowledge of politics, having served a term as assistant district attorney, and even at the present moment occupying the position of sheriff's attorney. More than all, he was the son of Magnus Derrick; he could be relied upon, could be trusted implicitly to remain loyal to the ranchers' cause. The campaign for Railroad Commissioner had been very interesting. At the very outset Magnus's committee found itself involved in corrupt politics. The primaries had to be captured at all costs and by any means, and when the convention assembled it was found necessary to buy outright the votes of certain delegates. The campaign fund raised by contributions from Magnus, Annixter, Broderson, and Osterman was drawn upon to the extent of five thousand dollars. Only the committee knew of this corruption. The League, ignoring ways and means, supposed as a matter of course that the campaign was honorably conducted. For a whole week after the consummation of this part of the deal, Magnus had kept to his house, refusing to be seen, alleging that he was ill, which was not far from the truth. The shame of the business, the loathing of what he had done, were to him things unspeakable. He could no longer look Harran in the face. He began a course of deception with his wife. More than once, he had resolved to break with the whole affair, resigning his position, allowing the others to proceed without him. But now it was too late. He was pledged. He had joined the League. He was its chief, and his defection might mean its disintegration at the very time when it needed all its strength to fight the land cases. More than a mere deal in bad politics was involved. There was the land grab. His withdrawal from an unholy cause would mean the weakening, perhaps the collapse, of another cause that he believed to be righteous as truth itself. He was hopelessly caught in the mesh. Wrong seemed indissolubly knitted into the texture of Right. He was blinded, dizzied, overwhelmed, caught in the current of events, and hurried along he knew not where. He resigned himself. In the end, and after much ostentatious opposition on the part of the railroad heelers, Lyman was nominated and subsequently elected. When this consummation was reached Magnus, Osterman, Broderson, and Annixter stared at each other. Their wildest hopes had not dared to fix themselves upon so easy a victory as this. It was not believable that the corporation would allow itself to be fooled so easily, would rush open-eyed into the trap. How had it happened? Osterman, however, threw his hat into the air with wild whoops of delight. Old Broderson permitted himself a feeble cheer. Even Magnus beamed satisfaction. The other members of the League, present at the time, shook hands all around and spoke of opening a few bottles on the strength of the occasion. Annixter alone was recalcitrant.

“It's too easy,” he declared. “No, I'm not satisfied. Where's Shelgrim in all this? Why don't he show his hand, damn his soul? The thing is yellow, I tell you. There's a big fish in these waters somewheres. I don't know his name, and I don't know his game, but he's moving round off and on, just out of sight. If you think you've netted him, I DON'T, that's all I've got to say.” But he was jeered down as a croaker. There was the Commission. He couldn't get around that, could he? There was Darrell and Lyman Derrick, both pledged to the ranches. Good Lord, he was never satisfied. He'd be obstinate till the very last gun was fired. Why, if he got drowned in a river he'd float upstream just to be contrary. In the course of time, the new board was seated. For the first few months of its term, it was occupied in clearing up the business left over by the old board and in the completion of the railway map. But now, the decks were cleared. It was about to address itself to the consideration of a revision of the tariff for the carriage of grain between the San Joaquin Valley and tide-water. Both Lyman and Darrell were pledged to an average ten per cent. cut of the grain rates throughout the entire State. The typewriter returned with the letters for Lyman to sign, and he put away the map and took up his morning's routine of business, wondering, the while, what would become of his practice during the time he was involved in the business of the Ranchers' Railroad Commission. But towards noon, at the moment when Lyman was drawing off a glass of mineral water from the siphon that stood at his elbow, there was an interruption. Some one rapped vigorously upon the door, which was immediately after opened, and Magnus and Harran came in, followed by Presley.

“Hello, hello!” cried Lyman, jumping up, extending his hands, “why, here's a surprise. I didn't expect you all till to-night. Come in, come in and sit down. Have a glass of sizz-water, Governor.” The others explained that they had come up from Bonneville the night before, as the Executive Committee of the League had received a despatch from the lawyers it had retained to fight the Railroad, that the judge of the court in San Francisco, where the test cases were being tried, might be expected to hand down his decision the next day. Very soon after the announcement of the new grading of the ranchers' lands, the corporation had offered, through S. Behrman, to lease the disputed lands to the ranchers at a nominal figure. The offer had been angrily rejected, and the Railroad had put up the lands for sale at Ruggles's office in Bonneville. At the exorbitant price named, buyers promptly appeared—dummy buyers, beyond shadow of doubt, acting either for the Railroad or for S. Behrman—men hitherto unknown in the county, men without property, without money, adventurers, heelers. Prominent among them, and bidding for the railroad's holdings included on Annixter's ranch, was Delaney. The farce of deeding the corporation's sections to these fictitious purchasers was solemnly gone through with at Ruggles's office, the Railroad guaranteeing them possession. The League refused to allow the supposed buyers to come upon the land, and the Railroad, faithful to its pledge in the matter of guaranteeing its dummies possession, at once began suits in ejectment in the district court in Visalia, the county seat. It was the preliminary skirmish, the reconnaisance in force, the combatants feeling each other's strength, willing to proceed with caution, postponing the actual death-grip for a while till each had strengthened its position and organised its forces.
