There is a certain hour in the domestic life of those who have but recently attained to a small measure of comfort when the very things which they have gathered about them, the carpets, the plush-covered chairs, the clock upon the mantel with its gilt cherub, seem to take on a voice and to speak of the effort which they cost. Such an hour had come, though she did not so phrase it to herself, to Ida Brannock. On this particular evening in November, in the year 1897, she sat in the front room of the four-room flat on Wells Street which she and her husband had occupied for something over two years, and waited for him to come home.

The room itself was not without a certain pretension. There was a Brussels carpet of a dull red figure, purchased on the installment plan from a house on State Street, and a lamp with a painted china shade, roses upon a ground of cream, which had been a wedding gift from her aunt in Elgin. There were lace curtains at the two windows, and between them a small walnut table on which reposed a family Bible, never opened, and a volume of Longfellow, opened rarely. Over all this the gas jet, turned low, cast a yellowish and uncertain light, so that the corners of the room were obscure and the cherub upon the clock seemed to be poised above a kind of darkness. It was a room, in short, such as ten thousand others in that city, the expression of a modest hope and of a hunger for respectability which is, after all, one of the most constant of the forces that move the human heart.

Ida Brannock was at this time twenty-seven years of age, a woman of medium height, rather full of figure, with brown hair which she wore drawn back and coiled in the fashion of the day, and with gray eyes which, in her girlhood, had been considered fine. She was not, by any means, a woman of intellect. She had little knowledge of books, and less of the great currents of commercial and social life which swept about her and of which she was, in her small way, a creature. But she had a strong, practical sense of what was due her, and a very clear notion of what constituted a proper home and a proper station in life. She had been raised in a small town in Illinois, the daughter of a harness-maker, and the city, when she came to it at nineteen, had seemed to her a vast and glittering thing, full of carriages and fine houses and women in sealskin, all of which she had desired with that dumb, insistent longing which is the portion of so many.

On this evening she was disturbed, and the disturbance had its origin in a conversation which she had held that afternoon with her sister's husband, one Albert Fenske, a clerk in a commission house on South Water Street. Fenske had dropped in, as he sometimes did, on his way to collect a bill in the neighborhood, and in the course of an idle quarter-hour he had remarked, with that kind of heavy jocularity which some men affect when they suspect they are conveying unwelcome news, that he had seen Howard twice that week "going into Coffey's place over on La Salle Street," and had asked whether Howard was "getting to be a regular plunger." Ida had not known what Coffey's place was, and had said so. Fenske, perceiving perhaps that he had gone too far, had explained with some reluctance that it was a bucket-shop, a place where small men bought and sold wheat and pork on margin, without, as he put it, "ever seeing a bushel of the stuff." He had added that a good many fellows "got cleaned out there," and then, catching her look, had hastened to say that very likely Howard was only watching the board, as a great many did, for the amusement of it.

But Ida was not deceived. She knew, with that instinct which is so often keener in women than reason itself, that her husband did not go anywhere for amusement which cost him nothing. And she knew, too, of the fourteen hundred dollars in the Illinois Trust and Savings Bank, the fruit of four years of saving on his part and two on hers, the money which was to make the first payment upon a cottage in Ravenswood, with a porch and a bit of lawn and a lilac bush by the gate, such as she had seen in the advertisements of the real-estate men and had dreamed of on many an evening in this very chair.

At a quarter past seven she heard his step upon the stairs. It was a heavy step, slower than usual, and there was something in its very slowness that confirmed her fears. The door opened, and Howard Brannock came in, removing his derby hat and hanging it upon the hook in the narrow hallway with a care which was almost elaborate.

He was a man of thirty-two, of good height and fair build, with a full brown mustache which he kept well trimmed and a face which might have been called handsome had it not been for a certain softness about the chin and a restless, seeking quality in the eyes. He was employed as a bookkeeper by a wholesale hardware concern on Lake Street at a salary of eighteen dollars a week, and he had for some years been possessed of the notion, common enough among men of his class and time, that he was destined for something better. He had watched the great operators of the Board of Trade, men whose names appeared daily in the papers, whose carriages stood at the curb on Jackson Street, and he had said to himself, as so many have said, that it needed only a little capital, a little nerve, a little luck. Alas, the city is full of such reasoning, and the outcome of it is written in the faces of a thousand clerks who once believed it.

"You're late," said Ida, without rising.

"Yes, I had to stay over a little. Hendricks wanted the November accounts gone over." He came into the room and stood near the table, looking down at the volume of Longfellow as though he had never seen it before.

"Your supper's on the back of the stove. It's likely dried out by now."

"That's all right. I'm not very hungry."

She looked at him steadily, and he, feeling her gaze, turned and went toward the window, where he stood looking down into the street. Below, the lamps had been lit, and a car went clanging by toward the river, its windows full of tired faces.

"Howard," she said, after a moment, "Albert was here this afternoon."

"Was he?" He did not turn. "What did he want?"

"He didn't want anything. He was collecting a bill over on Division Street and he stopped in." She paused. "He said he'd seen you going into some place on La Salle Street. Coffey's, he called it."

There was a silence in which the clock upon the mantel could be heard ticking with a kind of metallic precision. Howard Brannock's back, broad in its gray sack coat, did not move, but she saw his hand, which hung at his side, close slowly and then open again.

"Well," he said at last, "what of it? A lot of men go in there."

"What do they go in there for?"

"Oh, to watch the board. To see how the market's going. It's interesting, if you understand it."

"Albert says it's a bucket-shop. He says men lose their money there."

He turned now, and she saw that his face was flushed, with that dull flush which comes to a man who is at once ashamed and angry, and who does not know which feeling he had best give way to.

"Albert Fenske had better mind his own business," he said. "What does he know about it? He's been checking crates of cabbages for eleven years, and he'll be checking them for eleven more. That's all he'll ever amount to."

"That isn't what I asked you," she said, and her voice, though low, had in it a hardness which he had not often heard. "I asked you what you went there for."

He was silent again. The truth was that he had been preparing, all the way home on the car, a number of explanations, each more plausible than the last, and now, confronted by her quiet, insistent gaze, he found that none of them would do. It is one of the curious facts of our nature that the lie which seems so smooth in the mind becomes rough and unmanageable in the presence of the one to whom it is to be told, as though the very air between two persons who have shared a bed and a table for years were charged with some chemic property hostile to deceit.

"I've been trading a little," he said finally. "In wheat."

"With what?"

"Why, with—" He stopped, and then, as though plunging into cold water, went on. "With some of the money in the bank. I didn't want to say anything until I'd made something on it. I thought I'd surprise you."

Ida rose. She did not do so quickly, but with a kind of deliberation, placing her hands upon the arms of the chair and lifting herself as though she had suddenly grown older. She stood facing him across the little table, and the light of the china lamp fell upon her face, which had gone quite white.

"How much of it?" she asked.

"Now, Ida, see here—"

"How much of it, Howard?"

"About eleven hundred," he said.

She did not cry out. She did not, for a moment, say anything at all. She only stood there looking at him, and he, unable to meet her eyes, looked at the carpet, at the red figure of it which was already beginning to wear thin before the door, and which they had not yet finished paying for.

"Eleven hundred dollars," she said at last, as though repeating a sum in a lesson. "And how much of it have you got left?"

"Well, that's just it. It isn't exactly gone. Not the way you think. The market went against me this last week. Everybody was caught. There was a big crowd in from New York, Leiter's crowd, and they ran it up, and then they let it down, and a lot of men who know a great deal more than I do were wiped out. But it's bound to come back. Everybody says so. If I'd had a little more margin I could have held on, and then—"

"Then it's gone," she said.

"It's not gone. I tell you, it's—" He broke off, for he saw that it was useless, and a kind of weariness came over him. He sat down heavily in the rocker by the window, the rocker which had been her mother's, and put his hands over his face. "Yes," he said. "It's gone."

Now it would be easy to say of Ida Brannock that she was hard, and that in this hour, when her husband sat broken before her, she ought to have gone to him and put her hand upon his shoulder and said that it did not matter, that they were young and could save again. There are women who would have done so, and there are moralists who would have praised them. But the forces which govern the human heart are not so simply ordered. In Ida Brannock the desire for the little house in Ravenswood had been for two years the very center of her being, the thing about which all her thoughts revolved, as the planets revolve about the sun. She had denied herself a new winter coat for it. She had turned her old brown silk twice. She had walked when she might have ridden, and had bought the cheaper cuts at the butcher's, and had sat in this room, evening after evening, building in her mind the porch and the lilac bush and the white curtains of a home which should be truly her own. And now this man, in a few weeks, in a place she had never seen, among men she did not know, had taken that dream and cast it away, as one might throw a handful of coppers to a beggar in the street. It was not in her to forgive it, not then.

"You took it," she said, and her voice shook now, "without saying a word to me. Half of that was mine. I saved it. I saved it out of the housekeeping, a quarter here and fifty cents there, and you knew it. And you took it and gave it to those—those gamblers."

"They're not gamblers," he said, lifting his head. "That's just where you're wrong. It's business. It's the way all the big men made their money. Do you think Armour got where he is by keeping books at eighteen a week? Do you think Phil Armour ever sat in a four-room flat on Wells Street counting quarters?"

"I don't care how Armour got where he is. I care about what you did."

"I did it for you as much as for me. Can't you see that? I wanted to get you out of this. I wanted you to have something better than a cottage out on the prairie with the trains going by. I wanted—" He made a vague, helpless gesture with his hand, a gesture which seemed to include the whole of the city beyond the window, its lights, its towers, its great houses along the Lake Shore Drive, all that he had longed for and could not reach. "I wanted to be somebody," he said.

There was in his voice, as he said this, a note so genuine and so pitiful that for an instant she was moved in spite of herself. For she, too, had wanted to be somebody. She, too, had looked at the carriages and the sealskin and the great stone houses and had felt that burning, inarticulate hunger which the city awakens in all who come to it. But the feeling passed, and in its place there came a colder thought, one which had lain dormant in her mind for a long while and which now, under the stress of the moment, rose to the surface.

"You've always wanted to be somebody," she said. "You wanted it when you married me. You told me then you'd be a head bookkeeper inside of three years, and then you'd go into business for yourself. That was seven years ago."

"Well, and whose fault is that? Have I had a chance? Has anybody ever given me a chance?"

"Charley Pettibone had his drugstore on Clark Street by the time he was twenty-eight," she said quietly. "He's got two now. His wife has a girl to do the work."

He stared at her. The name of Charles Pettibone had not been spoken between them in a long time, but he knew it well enough. Pettibone had paid court to Ida in the year before her marriage, a small, bald, careful young man with gold-rimmed spectacles, and she had chosen Howard instead, because Howard was tall and well set up and had a way of talking about the future which made it seem very near and very bright.

"So that's it," he said slowly, and he got up out of the rocker. "You're sorry you didn't take him. That's what you've been thinking all along."

"I didn't say that."

"You didn't have to say it. I can see it in your face." He came a step nearer, and his voice rose. "Well, you can go to him if you like. You can go to him tonight. I dare say he'd take you, if his wife didn't mind."

"Howard!"

"Oh, I know what you think of me. I've known it for a year. You think I'm a failure. You think I'm no better than Albert Fenske. You sit here and count your quarters and look at me across the table, and you think, 'He'll never get anywhere. He'll never be anything.' Well, maybe you're right. Maybe I won't. But I tried. That's more than you can say for Fenske. I tried."

He stood breathing heavily, his face dark, his hands trembling, and she, confronted by this sudden outburst, drew back against the table. It was not that she was afraid of him; he had never struck her, nor, in all likelihood, would he ever do so. It was rather that she saw in him now, for the first time clearly, a thing which she had half-perceived before and had refused to look at: the weakness that lay beneath his large manner, the desperate, flailing desire of a man who feels the world slipping past him and cannot lay hold of it. And seeing this, she felt, not pity exactly, nor contempt exactly, but something compounded of both, a kind of chill, as though a door had been opened somewhere in the house and a draft had come in.

"You tried," she said, "with my money."

He turned away from her, as though she had struck him. He went to the window again and stood there, his forehead almost touching the cold glass, and for a long while neither of them spoke. In the kitchen the kettle, which she had left at the back of the stove, began to sing faintly. Out in the street a man was calling an extra, his voice rising thin and shrill above the noise of the traffic, and the sound of it, coming up through the window, seemed to her like a voice from another world, a world of great events in which she and her husband had no part at all.

"What are we going to do?" she said at last.

"I don't know." He did not turn. "There's three hundred left. We can start again."

"Start again," she repeated. "I'm twenty-seven, Howard."

"I know how old you are."

"I'll be thirty-one before we have it back. If we ever do."

He made no answer. What answer, indeed, could he have made? The arithmetic of their lives was plain enough, written out in the eighteen dollars which came in each Saturday and the seventeen and some cents which went out before the next. He knew it as well as she. He had known it, in some dim region of his mind, even as he stood before the blackboard in Coffey's place with the chalk-boy marking up the quotations and the ticker clattering and the other men about him, clerks and barbers and small shopkeepers like himself, all staring upward with the same hungry, hopeful faces. He had known it, and he had not let himself know it. Such is the nature of desire, which is a blind force, older than reason, and which will not be stayed by any sum in arithmetic.

"I'm going to bed," said Ida.

She went past him, without looking at him, and into the little bedroom at the back, and he heard her moving about there, heard the creak of the bureau drawer and the sound of her shoes being set upon the floor. He did not follow her. He stood at the window, looking down at the lights, at the cars going by, at the people hurrying home through the cold, each to his own small room and his own small hope, and he thought of the men in the carriages along Michigan Avenue, and of the house in Ravenswood which would not now be bought, and of the face of Charles Pettibone behind his gold-rimmed spectacles.

After a while he went into the kitchen and took the plate from the back of the stove. The meat had dried and curled at the edges, and the potatoes were hard. He sat down at the oilcloth-covered table and ate a little, not because he was hungry, but because it was there and it was something to do. The kettle had boiled dry and he lifted it off and set it on the sink.

In the bedroom Ida Brannock lay in the dark with her eyes open. She was not crying. She had thought that she would cry, but the tears did not come. Instead she lay there, quite still, and listened to the sounds of him in the kitchen, the scrape of the fork upon the plate, the creak of the chair, and she thought of nothing very clearly. Only, now and again, there rose before her the picture of a porch with a lilac bush beside it, and then the picture faded, and in its place there was only the dark, and the faint, steady ticking of the clock in the front room, which went on and on, indifferent, measuring out the hours of their lives as it would measure out the hours of whatever lives came after them.

For what, after all, can be said of such a pair? That he was weak, and she was hard? That he dreamed too largely, and she too narrowly? These are words, and they explain nothing. They were two small creatures caught in the vast machinery of a city which promised everything and gave, to the many, so little; and they had wanted what the city taught them to want, and they had not got it. In that, at least, they were not alone. Ten thousand lamps burned that night along the streets of Chicago, and beneath many of them, in many such rooms, the same question was being asked, in the same low, bitter voices, and was receiving the same answer, which is no answer at all.

It was on a raw afternoon in the latter part of November, 1897, when the wind off the lake had that peculiar, searching quality which makes the stranger in Chicago draw his coat about him and wonder why any one should choose to live in such a place, that Henry Lutz, aged thirty-four, and late of St. Louis, Kansas City, Omaha, and a dozen other points between, stepped down from a Cottage Grove Avenue car and turned westward into a street of brownstone and red-brick residences which, to his eye, represented everything that a man of reasonable ambition might wish for himself and seldom attain. He was not poorly dressed. Indeed, to the casual observer, he might have passed for a traveling man of the better sort, one who sold, let us say, a line of cigars or men's furnishings to the larger houses and was paid accordingly. He wore a brown overcoat of good cut, if somewhat thin at the cuffs, a derby hat which had been brushed that morning with especial care, and a pair of tan shoes which, though they had been resoled twice, still retained a certain air of confidence. His mustache was neatly trimmed, his collar fresh. Only one who knew how much of a man's estate may be carried upon his back, and how little remain behind it, would have suspected that the eleven dollars and forty cents in his pocket represented the whole of his present fortune.

He was going to see his cousin Dora, whom he had not laid eyes upon in nearly fourteen years.

It is a curious thing, this matter of kinship, and how it persists in the mind long after the conditions which gave it meaning have dissolved. Here was a woman whom he had known as a girl of fifteen, with heavy brown braids and a disposition to tease, on a farm outside of Wapakoneta, Ohio, where their two families, the Lutzes and the Kesslers, had been for years in that close and somewhat quarrelsome intimacy which marks the relations of German-American farmers who have intermarried and who share a church, a threshing machine, and a common grievance against the price of wheat. He had gone away at twenty, restless, eager, convinced that the world held something for him which the flat fields of Auglaize County could not provide. She had married, a few years later, a young man named Fennimore, a clerk in a wholesale hardware house in Toledo, and had removed with him first to Cleveland and then to Chicago, where, as Henry had heard in the irregular and uncertain way that news travels among scattered relatives, Fennimore had prospered. He was now, it appeared, a member of the firm of Ashby, Fennimore & Company, dealers in builders' hardware, with offices on Lake Street, and the address which Henry had obtained from an aunt in Lima indicated a house of some pretension.

He found it presently, a three-story structure of gray stone, with a bay window on the first floor and a flight of broad steps leading up to a door of heavy oak, glazed in its upper half with beveled glass. There was a small plot of lawn before it, brown now with the season, and an iron fence of ornamental design. Henry stopped before it and surveyed it with that mingled feeling of admiration and resentment which the sight of another's success so commonly evokes in those who have not succeeded. It was a fine house. There could be no doubt of that. It was the kind of house which he himself had imagined owning, at various times in his career, when some scheme or other had seemed about to bear fruit—when he had been selling stock in a mining company in Colorado, for instance, or when he had had a quarter interest in a billiard parlor in Kansas City, or when, for a brief and glorious season, he had been the western representative of a firm which manufactured a patent washing machine. None of these ventures had come to anything. The mine had proved to be little more than a hole in the side of a mountain; the billiard parlor had been closed by the police for reasons which he preferred not to dwell upon; and the washing machine had been found, upon extended trial by the housewives of Nebraska, to tear the clothes. And so here he was, at thirty-four, with eleven dollars and forty cents and a good overcoat, standing before his cousin's house and wondering how he should be received.

He mounted the steps and rang. The door was opened by a maid in a black dress and white cap, a young Swedish girl with a broad, impassive face, who took his card—he had had a few printed in St. Louis, in better days, bearing simply the legend *Henry J. Lutz* and nothing more, which he had found to be a decided convenience—and showed him into a front parlor while she went to announce him.

The room in which he found himself was furnished in that heavy and somewhat oppressive taste which was then considered the mark of solid prosperity. There was a carpet of deep red, figured with great medallions of gold and green; there were chairs and a sofa upholstered in plush of a darker shade; there were lace curtains at the windows, held back by cords of crimson silk; there was a piano of rosewood, upon which stood a number of photographs in silver frames; and there was a mantel of carved oak, surmounted by a mirror, before which a clock of black marble, flanked by two bronze figures representing, so far as Henry could make out, Commerce and Agriculture, ticked with a slow and dignified regularity. Over all hung a faint odor of furniture polish and of something cooking in a distant kitchen. Henry stood in the middle of this splendor, his hat in his hand, and felt himself, for the first time in many months, to be what he actually was—a man without a place.

He heard a rustle upon the stairs, and then she was in the doorway.

She was larger than he had remembered—that was his first thought—fuller of figure, with a matronly ampleness about the bust and hips which the close-fitting gown of plum-colored silk which she wore did nothing to disguise. Her hair, still brown, but with here and there a thread of gray, was done up high upon her head in the fashion of the day. Her face had broadened somewhat and lost the rosy, freckled quality of girlhood, taking on in its place a certain smoothness and self-possession which comes to women who have been for some years secure in their position. But her eyes were the same—a clear, rather light blue, with a quick, observing look in them—and when she saw him her mouth opened in an expression of genuine pleasure which went far toward dispelling his uneasiness.

"Why, Henry Lutz!" she exclaimed, coming forward with both hands extended. "As I live! I couldn't believe it when Anna brought up your card. I said to myself, it can't be—not Henry. Why, I haven't seen you since—since when?"

"Since your sister Lena's wedding," said Henry, taking her hands and holding them a moment. "That was in eighty-three. You had on a blue dress with white ruffles, and you danced with Gus Mohr until your mother made you sit down."

"Oh, my!" she laughed, coloring a little. "Do you remember that? Gus Mohr! I'd forgotten all about him. Well, sit down, sit down. Let me look at you. My, but you've changed. You've filled out. You used to be as thin as a rail. And that mustache! I don't think I'd have known you on the street."

They sat down, she upon the sofa and he in one of the plush chairs opposite, and for a moment neither of them spoke, each engaged in that silent and somewhat embarrassed appraisal which inevitably follows upon the meeting of two persons who were once familiar and have since become strangers. It is not easy, after a long absence, to bridge the gulf of years. Each brings to the encounter an image of the other fixed at some point in the past, and each is obliged to reconcile that image with the reality which sits before him. Dora saw a man somewhat heavier than the boy she had known, with lines about his eyes which spoke of late hours and uncertain fortune, but with the same air of easy, half-humorous assurance which had always distinguished him from the other young men of the neighborhood. Henry saw a woman who had settled into her life as into a comfortable chair, and who looked out upon the world from it with a calm, if not entirely incurious, contentment.

"Well," she said at last, "and where have you been all this time? Aunt Minna wrote me once that you were in Denver, and then somebody said Omaha, and then I didn't hear anything at all for years. I thought maybe you'd gone to California."

"I've been around," said Henry, with a wave of his hand which was intended to suggest the breadth and variety of his experience. "Denver, yes. Omaha. Kansas City for a good while. St. Louis lately. I've been in a number of things—mining, the selling end, one thing and another. A man has to keep moving out there if he wants to get ahead."

"And have you got ahead?" she asked, with the directness which he now recalled as having been characteristic of her even as a girl.

He laughed. "Well, I'm not a millionaire yet, if that's what you mean. But I've done pretty well. I can't complain." He glanced about the room with an appreciative eye. "Not as well as you, though, Dora. This is a fine place you've got here. A mighty fine place. Ed must be doing well."

"Oh, Edward does very well," she said, with a little air of pride which she made no effort to conceal. "He's been with the firm eleven years now, and he was made a partner three years ago. They do a big business. They furnished all the hardware for the new Marquette Building, you know, and for a lot of those big places downtown. Edward works awfully hard. He's hardly ever home before seven." She paused, and then added, with a touch of the old teasing manner, "You ought to have stayed in Ohio and married some nice girl, Henry, and gone into business in Lima or somewhere. You'd have been a rich man by now."

"Maybe," said Henry. "Maybe not. I never could stand it there. You know how it was. Nothing but corn and hogs and Sunday school."

"I know," she said, and for a moment a curious, reflective look came into her face. "I didn't like it either, not really. But I think about it sometimes. Do you remember the creek back of Grandpa Kessler's place, and how we used to go down there in the summer and catch crawfish under the stones? And the time you fell in and Grandpa whipped you for getting your Sunday pants wet?"

"I remember," said Henry, smiling. "And the time you and Lena hid my shoes in the haymow and I had to walk home barefoot through the stubble."

"Oh, we were awful!" she laughed. "And do you remember old Mrs. Brockschmidt, who used to come over and sit in the kitchen and tell Mother about her liver?"

They were off, then, upon that stream of reminiscence which flows so readily between those who share a common past, and for the better part of half an hour they talked of nothing else—of the farm, of the church, of the long drives into town on Saturday afternoons, of the threshing dinners and the barn dances and the winter evenings when the snow lay deep over the fields and the whole family gathered about the great iron stove in the sitting room. They spoke of relatives—who had died, who had married, who had gone away. Uncle Fritz was dead, it appeared, of a stroke, three years since. Cousin Augusta had married a Methodist, to the great scandal of the family, and moved to Indianapolis. Lena had five children now and lived in Sidney, where her husband kept a feed store. The old Kessler farm had been sold to a man named Huffman, who had torn down the barn and built a new one of a design which Dora, who had heard of it from her mother, described as "perfectly hideous."

It is in such moments that one perceives how much of what we call the self is merely a deposit of circumstance, laid down layer upon layer by the slow action of time and place. These two, sitting in a Chicago parlor amid the trappings of a prosperity which belonged to only one of them, had once been children together in a world so different from the present that it seemed almost to belong to another age. And yet that world lived still in each of them, beneath all the later accretions of experience—in the turn of a phrase, in a trick of laughter, in a sudden softening of the eyes at the mention of a name. Neither of them had chosen the course which life had taken. Henry had been drawn away by a restlessness which he could no more have resisted than a filing can resist the magnet; Dora had been carried along by the steady current of a conventional marriage to a man who happened to possess the particular combination of industry and caution which the commercial world rewards. And now here they were, the one up and the other down, and neither could have said with any certainty why it should be so.

Presently the maid came in with a tray upon which were a silver teapot, cups of thin china, and a plate of small cakes, and Dora poured for him with the practiced grace of a woman who has learned the ritual of hospitality from observation and repetition rather than from birth. Henry, holding the delicate cup in his large hand, felt again that sense of being out of his element, and the conversation, as if in sympathy, turned from the past to the present.

"And are you married, Henry?" she asked.

"No," he said. "I came close once or twice. But it never seemed to work out. A man in my line, moving around the way I do—it's not fair to a woman."

"What is your line, exactly?" she asked. "You said mining, and selling. But what are you doing now?"

It was the question he had been dreading, and he had prepared an answer for it, but now that it came he found himself, under the steady gaze of those light blue eyes, curiously reluctant to give it. The truth was that he was doing nothing at present. He had come up from St. Louis on the strength of a letter from an acquaintance who had promised him a place with a firm that dealt in office fixtures, and he had found on his arrival that the place had been filled. He had been in the city four days, living at a cheap hotel on Van Buren Street, and he had walked the streets of the business district until his feet ached, calling upon one firm after another, and receiving everywhere the same polite and indifferent refusal. Times were better than they had been in ninety-three and ninety-four, but there were still more men than places, and a man of thirty-four with no particular trade and a somewhat checkered history was not in great demand. It had been in a moment of discouragement, the evening before, sitting alone in his narrow room with the gas jet flaring and the noise of the elevated trains beating against the window, that he had remembered his cousin Dora and resolved to look her up.

He had not, he told himself, come to ask her for anything. He had merely come to see her, for old times' sake. But he knew, in that obscure and uncomfortable region of the mind where we keep the truths we do not care to examine, that this was not altogether so. He had come because he was lonely and because he was afraid, and because somewhere in the back of his thoughts there lurked the hope that Edward Fennimore, partner in a prosperous hardware firm, might know of something—might, if properly approached, put in a word for a cousin by marriage who was temporarily at loose ends.

"Just now," he said, setting down his cup, "I'm looking around a little. I came up from St. Louis to take a position with a concern here, but it fell through. Nothing serious. I've got a couple of other things in view."

She looked at him a moment without speaking, and he had the uncomfortable impression that she saw more than he intended her to see—the thin cuffs of the overcoat, perhaps, or the resoled shoes, or something in his face which belied the easy confidence of his manner. Women of her type, he reflected, are seldom deceived for long about such matters. They have an instinct for the economic status of others which is as sure as a banker's.

"I see," she said slowly. And then, in a different tone, brisker and more practical, "Well, you'll stay to supper, of course. Edward will be home by seven, and I want him to meet you. He's heard me speak of you. I've told him about the time you rode the Schaefers' bull."

"I don't want to put you out," said Henry.

"Put me out! Nonsense. We've got a leg of lamb, and there's more than enough. Besides," she added, with a little smile, "Edward knows a great many people in this town. If you're looking around, it wouldn't hurt you to talk to him."

Henry felt the blood come into his face, and he looked down at the carpet, at the great gold and green medallions, which seemed suddenly to swim a little before his eyes. It was what he had wanted, of course. It was what he had come for, though he would not have admitted it. And yet now that it was offered—freely, generously, without his having to ask—he experienced a sensation which was not entirely gratitude. There was something in it of humiliation, too, the humiliation of the man who has gone out into the world to conquer it and has come back, years later, to warm himself at the fire of those who stayed behind and prospered by the very virtues he had scorned. He had always considered himself a little superior to his Ohio relatives—cleverer, bolder, more alive to the possibilities of life. And here was Dora, who had never been farther from home than Chicago, who had married a hardware clerk and spent her days ordering the meals and arranging the furniture, offering to help him find a job.

But the feeling passed, as such feelings do in those who have been long buffeted by necessity. Pride is a luxury, and Henry Lutz, with eleven dollars and forty cents in his pocket and a hotel bill coming due on Saturday, was not in a position to indulge it.

"That's mighty kind of you, Dora," he said, looking up. "I'd like to meet Ed. I'd like it fine."

"Then that's settled," she said, and rose, shaking out the folds of her silk gown. "I'll just go and tell Hilda to set another place. You make yourself comfortable. There are some papers on the table there, and the new *Harper's*. I won't be a minute."

She went out, and Henry was left alone in the darkening parlor. The short November day was drawing to its close, and through the lace curtains he could see the lamplighter making his way along the street, touching the posts one by one into a pale and wavering flame. Across the way the windows of the houses opposite were beginning to glow, and he could see, here and there, the figures of people moving within—women drawing curtains, a man reading beside a lamp, a child pressing its face against the glass. It was the hour at which the city gathers itself in, when those who have homes go to them, and those who have none become, for a little while, more acutely conscious of the lack.

He thought of his room on Van Buren Street, with its iron bed and its cracked washbasin and its single window looking out upon an airshaft. He thought of the men he had seen that morning, standing in a line outside a employment agency on Clark Street, their collars turned up against the wind, their faces gray and patient. He thought of the farm in Ohio, of the creek and the crawfish and the great iron stove, and of the boy he had been, who had looked out across the flat fields and believed that the world was waiting for him. It had not been waiting. It had not, so far as he could tell, so much as noticed his arrival. And yet here, in this warm room, with the clock ticking upon the mantel and the smell of roasting lamb drifting in from the kitchen, he felt for a moment something which he had not felt in a long time—a sense of being connected to something, of belonging, however tenuously, to a family and a past.

Was it chance, he wondered, that had made the difference between him and Dora? Or was it something in the blood, some hidden quality of temperament which had fitted her for the steady, plodding life of the household and unfitted him for anything but wandering? He did not know. No one, perhaps, could know. Life seemed to him in that moment a vast and indifferent machine, which caught people up and carried them hither and yon according to laws which none of them understood, setting one down in a stone house on the South Side and another in a hotel room on Van Buren Street, and caring nothing for the merits or demerits of either.

He heard the front door open, and a man's voice in the hall, heavy and cheerful, asking for Mrs. Fennimore. Henry rose, straightened his coat, touched his mustache, and composed his face into an expression of easy assurance. Whatever else he had lost, he had not lost that. It was, after all, his stock in trade.

In that region of the West Side of Chicago which lies between Halsted Street and the river, where, in the early nineties, the small frame cottages of the working-poor stood shoulder to shoulder with the sheds of coal-dealers and the soot-darkened walls of planing-mills, there lived at this time a family by the name of Gerber, consisting of Otto Gerber, a man of perhaps thirty-eight years, his wife Anna, some four years younger, and their two children, a girl of eleven named Freda and a boy of seven called Willie. The house which they occupied, or rather the lower half of it, for the upper floor was let to a Bohemian tailor and his wife, was of that drab, unpainted, weather-greyed variety so common to the neighborhood, with a narrow porch the boards of which had long since begun to curl and spring, and a yard which in summer bore nothing more hopeful than a few clumps of dusty plantain and a single ailanthus tree that grew, as such trees will, with a kind of desperate vigor out of the very cinders. The rent was nine dollars a month. Gerber, who was employed as a packer in the shipping-room of a wholesale hardware concern on Lake Street, earned eleven dollars a week, out of which, by dint of the most rigid economy on the part of his wife, a few dollars were laid aside at the end of each month against that dreaded day of illness or layoff which hangs, like a sword of the very cheapest metal, above every such household.

Gerber himself was not an unkindly man, but he was a narrow and, in a sense, a frightened one. He had been born in a village near Kassel and brought to this country at the age of nine, and his earliest memories were of a father, a cooper by trade, who had beaten him with a barrel-stave for the least infraction and who had held, with all the dull tenacity of the European peasant, that the child is a wild thing which must be broken as a colt is broken, or it will run to ruin. The elder Gerber had died of drink in a boarding-house on Canal Street, a circumstance which, oddly enough, had done nothing to shake the son's faith in the father's principles but had rather confirmed it, for Otto had reasoned, in so far as he reasoned at all, that if so stern a man could come to so wretched an end, how much more need was there of sternness in a world so full of snares. He was a member of a small Lutheran congregation which met in a converted store on Jefferson Street, and from its pastor, a thin, sallow, consumptive-looking man with a fixed belief in the total depravity of the human heart, he had imbibed a set of notions as to sin, punishment, and the inevitable descent of the unchecked soul which colored, as a dye colors water, every one of his relations with his family. He was, in short, one of those countless millions who, having been given no means of thinking for themselves, take over entire the moral furniture of their fathers and their preachers and live among it, cramped and uneasy, all their days, never once suspecting that it might be rearranged or thrown out altogether.

Now it so chanced that on a certain evening in late October, when the first raw winds from the lake were beginning to rattle the loose sashes of the cottage and to send the dry leaves of the ailanthus skittering along the board walk, Mrs. Gerber, having occasion to go to the cracked sugar-bowl on the top shelf of the kitchen cupboard, wherein she was accustomed to keep the small change against the milkman and the iceman, discovered that a nickel was missing. She counted the coins twice, then a third time, standing on her toes beside the cupboard with the lamp-light falling upon her plain, broad, somewhat anxious face; and then, with a sinking of the heart which she could not have explained, she replaced the lid and stood looking at the floor. There had been thirty-five cents. There were now thirty. She was certain of it, for she had counted the money only that morning, after paying the baker, and had made a little mental note, as was her habit, of exactly what remained. Freda, she knew, would not have touched it; the girl was of a timid and conscientious disposition, too much so, perhaps, for her own good. There remained only Willie.

It would be difficult to convey, to one who has never known the pinch of real want, the significance which so trifling a sum as five cents can assume in a household such as this. Five cents would buy a loaf of bread, or a quart of milk, or a pound of the cheaper cuts of soup-meat. It was, in the economy of the Gerbers, not nothing. But it was not the money alone which troubled Mrs. Gerber. She was a woman of a soft and yielding nature, who loved her children with that dumb, unreasoning, almost animal affection which is so frequently the portion of the overworked and the unlettered, and she knew, as surely as she knew that night would follow day, what would happen when her husband came home and learned of it. For a moment she thought of saying nothing. She could make up the sum somehow, out of the egg-money or the few pennies she saved by walking to the market on Maxwell Street rather than buying at the corner. But even as the thought arose, there arose with it the conviction, instilled by years of living under Gerber's roof and by her own unquestioning acceptance of the church's teaching, that to conceal such a thing would be to share in it, and that a boy who stole a nickel at seven might very well, unless checked, steal a horse at twenty and end upon the gallows. Such are the fears which the moralists of this world, with the best intentions in the world, have bred in the minds of simple people, so that love itself is made to stand guard against its own natural impulses.

Willie, meanwhile, was in the front room, sprawled upon the faded ingrain carpet before the base-burner, playing with a small tin whistle painted red and gold, which he had procured that afternoon at Schuessler's notion-store on Halsted Street for the sum of exactly five cents. He was a slight, fair-haired, round-cheeked child, with large grey eyes which had in them, at times, a look of dreamy speculation not at all common in the boys of that street, and a mouth which trembled easily. He had not, in the strict sense of the word, intended to steal. He had seen the whistle in Schuessler's window for a week past, lying among the jack-straws and the penny dolls and the sticks of horehound candy, and it had seemed to him, with that intensity of desire which only childhood and, perhaps, first love can know, the most beautiful object in the world. Other boys had whistles. Heinie Mueller, whose father kept a saloon, had two. And Willie, passing the window morning and evening on his way to and from the Foster School, had looked at it until the looking became a kind of ache, and the ache a kind of necessity, and the necessity, one afternoon when his mother was in the yard taking in the wash and the sugar-bowl stood within reach of a chair, a deed. He had not thought of it as stealing. He had scarcely thought at all. He had simply been drawn, as a filing is drawn to a magnet, by a force which he did not understand and could not have resisted had he tried. And is it not so, after all, with the greater part of what we are pleased to call our sins? We speak of will and choice, but how much of either is there in the infant mind, or, for that matter, in the adult one, when the chemic pull of desire is set against the thin and abstract prohibitions which have been laid upon us from without?

He had hidden the whistle in his blouse all through supper and had only now, believing himself unobserved, taken it out to look at it, not daring to blow upon it, but turning it over and over in his small fingers, admiring the bright paint and the little brass ring at the end. It was in this posture that his father found him.

Gerber had come in at half-past six, tired, his shoulders aching from the lifting of kegs of nails and crates of door-hinges, his hands grimed with the black oil of the warehouse. He had washed at the kitchen sink, eaten his supper of fried potatoes, rye bread, and a little boiled beef in silence, as was his custom, and was about to sit down with the Abendpost when his wife, standing by the stove with her hands twisted in her apron, told him, in a low voice and with her eyes averted, of the missing nickel. He listened without a word. Then he laid down the paper, rose heavily, and walked into the front room.

"Willie," he said.

The boy looked up, and seeing his father's face, closed his hand instinctively over the whistle. It was too late. Gerber had seen the flash of red and gold.

"What have you got there?"

"Nothing, Pa."

"Open your hand."

Slowly, with a kind of fascinated dread, the boy opened his fingers. The whistle lay upon his palm, absurdly small and bright in the yellow light of the lamp.

"Where did you get it?"

Willie did not answer. His lower lip had begun to tremble, and his eyes, enormous now, fixed themselves upon his father's waistcoat, upon the brass watch-chain that hung across it, upon anything but that heavy, reddened, accusing face above.

"I asked you where you got it."

"At Schuessler's."

"And where did you get the money to buy it?"

There was a long silence, during which the base-burner ticked and settled, and the wind, rising, flung a handful of leaves against the window. In the kitchen doorway Mrs. Gerber stood with one hand at her throat. Freda, who had been drying the dishes, had stopped with a plate in her hands and was watching with a white face.

"Out of the sugar-bowl," said Willie at last, in a whisper.

Gerber drew a long breath. It is to be said for him that he was not, in that instant, angry in the ordinary sense, or not merely angry. What he felt was something more complex and more dreadful: a kind of cold horror, as though he had looked into the face of his son and seen there, for the first time, the features of the thief, the drunkard, the outcast, all those dark figures which his pastor was forever summoning up from the pit and which his own father had seemed, in his last years, so terribly to resemble. It was as if the whole weight of his inherited fear had come down upon him at once, and with it a sense of personal failure, of having, somehow, through laxity or inattention, permitted the evil seed to take root in his own house. And this fear, being too large and too formless for him to understand, translated itself, as such fears will in men of his stamp, into the only form of action he knew.

"Stand up," he said.

The boy stood up.

"Do you know what you are?" Gerber said, and his voice, which was ordinarily rather flat and toneless, had taken on a curious hoarseness. "You are a thief. A dieb. Do you know what happens to thieves? They go to the Bridewell. They go to Joliet. They go to the gallows. Do you want to be like the men who sleep in the alleys on Canal Street? Do you want to be like that?"

"No, Pa."

"That money was for milk. For bread. For your sister and for you. Your mother works all day, she scrubs, she washes, she saves every penny, and you go and steal it out of the bowl like a—like a rat out of the grain-bin. For a whistle!" He snatched the toy from the boy's hand and held it up, and for a moment it seemed as though he would crush it in his fist. "For this you would steal from your own mother!"

The child began to cry, not loudly, but with a kind of choked, hiccoughing wretchedness which was more pitiful than any outcry.

"Otto," said Mrs. Gerber faintly from the doorway, "he is only seven. He did not think—"

"Be still," said Gerber, without turning his head. "It is because you would always have it that he did not think that he is what he is. At seven he takes a nickel. At ten what will he take? At fifteen? I know how it goes. I have seen it." And indeed, in his mind's eye, he did see it, not as an argument but as a picture: the long road downward, the saloon, the cell, the pauper's grave, all as vivid and as certain as the bricks of the warehouse wall.

He went to the corner behind the door, where there hung upon a nail a leather strap, a cast-off piece of harness which he had brought home from the shipping-room some years before and which had been used, though rarely, upon both the children. Freda, at the sight of it, set down her plate and slipped out into the back entry, her hands over her ears. Mrs. Gerber took a step forward and then stopped, for she knew it was useless, and she had besides, deep within her, that same dull conviction that what was being done was, however terrible, necessary and right.

What followed need not be described at length. It was, in its way, a scene common enough in that place and in that time, repeated nightly in ten thousand cottages and tenements up and down the land, wherever ignorance and fear and the rough moral code of the poor combined to make of the parent a kind of magistrate and of the child a criminal awaiting sentence. Gerber laid the boy across his knee and struck him six times with the strap, not with any great savagery, for he was not a savage man, but with a grim and measured deliberation that was in some ways worse, counting each stroke aloud in German as his own father had done. At each blow the child screamed. And at each blow something passed between them, father and son, which neither of them could have named, but which was to remain, in the case of the boy at least, a permanent part of the furniture of his mind: a sense of the world as a place of sudden and inexplicable violence, of a power which descended upon one out of the very sources of protection and love, and against which there was no appeal. For a child does not reason, as his elders suppose, from the punishment to the offense. He reasons, if at all, from the punishment to the punisher, and draws therefrom conclusions which no sermon and no strap can afterward undo.

When it was over, Gerber set the boy upon his feet and said, still in that hoarse, unnatural voice: "Now you will go to Schuessler tomorrow with this whistle, and you will give it back, and you will tell him you stole the money to buy it, and you will ask him for the nickel, and you will bring the nickel to your mother. Do you hear?"

"Yes, Pa," the boy sobbed.

"And then you will get down on your knees tonight and ask God to forgive you. Go to bed."

The child went, stumbling, into the small back bedroom which he shared with his sister, and Mrs. Gerber, after a moment's hesitation, followed him. Gerber hung the strap upon its nail, laid the whistle upon the shelf above the base-burner, and sat down again in his chair with the Abendpost. But he did not read it.

It is one of the curiosities of the human constitution that a man may do a thing with perfect conviction of its rightness and yet feel, immediately afterward, a kind of nausea of the spirit which belies that conviction utterly. Gerber sat with the paper open upon his knees, staring at the columns of black type without seeing them, and became aware, by slow degrees, of a sensation in his chest which was very like the sensation of having eaten something that disagreed with him. He was not given to introspection. He had never in his life asked himself, in so many words, whether the methods of his father and his pastor were the right ones; such a question would have seemed to him almost as impious as asking whether God existed. And yet there rose up in him now, unbidden and unwelcome, a memory of himself at seven or eight, in the low-ceilinged kitchen of the house at Kassel, standing before his own father with the barrel-stave raised above him, and of the peculiar quality of the terror he had felt then: not the fear of pain merely, though that was great enough, but a sense of being utterly alone, cut off from every source of comfort, an outcast in his own home. He remembered that he had hated his father. He had hated him for years, secretly and with a shamed and frightened intensity, and had never once, in all that time, been made any better by the beatings, but only more cunning in concealment. The thought came to him, dimly and confusedly, as a figure is glimpsed through fog, that perhaps Willie would now hate him in the same way, and that perhaps the strap had done nothing but teach the boy to hide his whistles better.

He thrust the thought away. It was the devil's thinking, the pastor would have said, the softness that leads to ruin. A boy must be taught. If he were not taught, what would become of him? And yet the nausea persisted, and with it a strange, half-formed longing, which he could not have expressed and would have been ashamed to acknowledge, to go into the back room and take the child in his arms.

He did not go. Men of his kind seldom do. The barriers which life erects between them and their own tenderer impulses are too high and too old, built up stone by stone out of the hard necessities of their own childhood and the grim sayings of their teachers, and the few who manage to climb over them do so only at the cost of a struggle for which they have neither the words nor the understanding. He sat on, while the lamp flickered and the wind moaned in the chimney and the clock on the shelf, a cheap affair of stamped walnut bought on installments at a store on Blue Island Avenue, ticked away the minutes with an indifference which seemed, to his troubled mind, almost malicious.

In the back bedroom Mrs. Gerber sat upon the edge of the narrow iron bed and stroked the boy's hair while he cried himself, by degrees, into exhaustion. She did not speak of the whistle or the nickel or of God. She murmured to him, instead, those small, meaningless, comforting sounds which mothers have murmured since the beginning of the world, and which say, more plainly than any words, that the thing which has been done to him is not the whole of the truth, that there is something else besides the strap and the counting and the cold voice. And the child, clinging to her apron, received this message as the parched earth receives rain, without understanding it, but taking it in nevertheless, so that it, too, became a part of him, set down beside the other in the dark storehouse of his mind, where the two would struggle together, unreconciled, for the rest of his days.

At last he slept, his cheeks still wet and his small fists clenched upon the coverlet. Mrs. Gerber rose, turned down the wick of the little lamp upon the washstand, and went back into the kitchen, where Freda was finishing the dishes in silence. In the front room her husband still sat with the paper upon his knees. She looked at him for a moment from the doorway, and something in the set of his shoulders, in the way his heavy, work-worn hands lay idle upon the newsprint, moved her to a pity which she could not have explained. She went to him and laid a hand, very lightly, upon his arm.

"He is asleep," she said.

Gerber nodded without looking up. "He must learn," he said, after a moment, but the words came out without conviction, almost as a question.

"Yes," said his wife. "He must learn."

And so they remained, the two of them, in the dim and shabby room, with the wind beating against the windows and the coal settling in the stove, each of them troubled and neither of them able to say why; while upon the shelf above the base-burner the little whistle lay where it had been put, red and gold and quite unconscious of the turmoil it had wrought, catching now and again in its bright paint a stray gleam from the lamp. What, after all, are we to make of such a scene? Who was here to blame? The child, who had merely wanted, as all life wants, that which seemed to him beautiful? The father, who had merely done, out of fear and love confusedly mingled, what he had been taught was right? The mother, the pastor, the dead cooper in the boarding-house on Canal Street, the long dark line of peasant forebears stretching back into the forests of Hesse? Or is it rather that we are all of us, parent and child alike, caught up in a vast and impersonal drift of forces which we neither made nor comprehend, the playthings of hungers and fears that were old before the race was young, and that what we call our moral judgments are, in the main, but the rough and hasty signals we fling to one another across the dark, hoping, against all evidence, that somehow they will be understood?

"You like to tease, don't you?"

Hence she was now keen, first to see if he were present, next to be sure that he gained no hint that she had seen him first, and lastly to act as grandly as possible for his benefit—a Hortensian procedure and type of thought that was exactly the thing best calculated to impress him. He gazed and there she was—tripping here and there in a filmy chiffon dance frock, shaded from palest yellow to deepest orange, which most enhanced her dark eyes and hair. And having exchanged a dozen or more "Oh, Hellos," and references with one and another to this, that and the other local event, she at last condescended to evince awareness of his proximity.

"Oh, here you are. You decided to come after all. I wasn't sure whether you would think it worth while. You've been introduced to everybody, of course?" She looked around as much as to say, that if he had not been she would proceed to serve him in this way. The others, not so very much impressed by Clyde, were still not a little interested by the fact that she seemed so interested in him.

"Yes, I met nearly everybody, I think."

"Except Freddie Sells. He came in with me just now. Here you are, Freddie," she called to a tall and slender youth, smooth of cheek and obviously becurled as to hair, who now came over and in his closely-fitting dress coat looked down on Clyde about as a spring rooster might look down on a sparrow.

"This is Clyde Griffiths, I was telling you about, Fred," she began briskly. "Doesn't he look a lot like Gilbert?"

"Why, you do at that," exclaimed this amiable person, who seemed to be slightly troubled with weak eyes since he bent close. "I hear you're a cousin of Gil's. I know him well. We went through Princeton together. I used to be over here before I joined the General Electric over at Schenectady. But I'm around a good bit yet. You're connected with the factory, I suppose."

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, who, before a youth of obviously so much more training and schooling than he possessed, felt not a little reduced. He began to fear that this individual would try to talk to him about things which he could not understand, things concerning which, having had no consecutive training of any kind, he had never been technically informed.

"In charge of some department, I suppose?"

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, cautiously and nervously.

"You know," went on Mr. Sells, briskly and interestingly, being of a commercial as well as technical turn, "I've always wondered just what, outside of money, there is to the collar business. Gil and I used to argue about that when we were down at college. He used to try to tell me that there was some social importance to making and distributing collars, giving polish and manner to people who wouldn't otherwise have them, if it weren't for cheap collars. I think he musta read that in a book somewhere. I always laughed at him." Clyde was about to attempt an answer, although already beyond his depth in regard to this. "Social importance." Just what did he mean by that—some deep, scientific information that he had acquired at college. He was saved a non-committal or totally uninformed answer by Sondra who, without thought or knowledge of the difficulty which was then and there before him, exclaimed: "Oh, no arguments, Freddie. That's not interesting. Besides I want him to meet my brother and Bertine. You remember Miss Cranston. She was with me at your uncle's last spring." Clyde turned, while Fred made the best of the rebuff by merely looking at Sondra, whom he admired so very much.

"Yes, of course," Clyde began, for he had been studying these two along with others. To him, apart from Sondra, Bertine seemed exceedingly attractive, though quite beyond his understanding also. Being involved, insincere and sly, she merely evoked in him a troubled sense of ineffectiveness, and hence uncertainty, in so far as her particular world was concerned—no more.

"Oh, how do you do? It's nice to see you again," she drawled, the while her greenish-gray eyes went over him in a smiling and yet indifferent and quizzical way. She thought him attractive, but not nearly as shrewd and hard as she would have preferred him to be. "You've been terribly busy with your work, I suppose. But now that you've come out once, I suppose we'll see more of you here and there."

"Well, I hope so," he replied, showing his even teeth. Her eyes seemed to be saying that she did not believe what she was saying and that he did not either, but that it was necessary, possibly amusing, to say something of the sort. And a related, though somewhat modified, version of this same type of treatment was accorded him by Stuart, Sondra's brother.

"Here she is now," added Gertrude a little spitefully, for she resented the fact that Sondra was so much better-looking than either she or her sister, and that she had expressed an interest in Clyde. "She'll be looking to see if you notice how pretty she looks, so don't disappoint her." The impact of this remark, a reflection of the exact truth, was not necessary to cause Clyde to gaze attentively, and even eagerly. For apart from her local position and means and taste in dress and manners, Sondra was of the exact order and spirit that most intrigued him—a somewhat refined (and because of means and position showered upon her) less savage, although scarcely less self-centered, Hortense Briggs. She was, in her small, intense way, a seeking Aphrodite, eager to prove to any who were sufficiently attractive the destroying power of her charm, while at the same time retaining her own personality and individuality free of any entangling alliance or compromise. However, for varying reasons which she could not quite explain to herself, Clyde appealed to her. He might not be anything socially or financially, but he was interesting to her. Hence she was now keen, first to see if he were present, next to be sure that he gained no hint that she had seen him first, and lastly to act as grandly as possible for his benefit—a Hortensian procedure and type of thought that was exactly the thing best calculated to impress him. He gazed and there she was—tripping here and there in a filmy chiffon dance frock, shaded from palest yellow to deepest orange, which most enhanced her dark eyes and hair. And having exchanged a dozen or more "Oh, Hellos," and references with one and another to this, that and the other local event, she at last condescended to evince awareness of his proximity.

"Oh, here you are. You decided to come after all. I wasn't sure whether you would think it worth while. You've been introduced to everybody, of course?" She looked around as much as to say, that if he had not been she would proceed to serve him in this way. The others, not so very much impressed by Clyde, were still not a little interested by the fact that she seemed so interested in him.

"Yes, I met nearly everybody, I think."

"Except Freddie Sells. He came in with me just now. Here you are, Freddie," she called to a tall and slender youth, smooth of cheek and obviously becurled as to hair, who now came over and in his closely-fitting dress coat looked down on Clyde about as a spring rooster might look down on a sparrow.

"This is Clyde Griffiths, I was telling you about, Fred," she began briskly. "Doesn't he look a lot like Gilbert?"

"Why, you do at that," exclaimed this amiable person, who seemed to be slightly troubled with weak eyes since he bent close. "I hear you're a cousin of Gil's. I know him well. We went through Princeton together. I used to be over here before I joined the General Electric over at Schenectady. But I'm around a good bit yet. You're connected with the factory, I suppose."

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, who, before a youth of obviously so much more training and schooling than he possessed, felt not a little reduced. He began to fear that this individual would try to talk to him about things which he could not understand, things concerning which, having had no consecutive training of any kind, he had never been technically informed.

"In charge of some department, I suppose?"

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, cautiously and nervously.

"You know," went on Mr. Sells, briskly and interestingly, being of a commercial as well as technical turn, "I've always wondered just what, outside of money, there is to the collar business. Gil and I used to argue about that when we were down at college. He used to try to tell me that there was some social importance to making and distributing collars, giving polish and manner to people who wouldn't otherwise have them, if it weren't for cheap collars. I think he musta read that in a book somewhere. I always laughed at him." Clyde was about to attempt an answer, although already beyond his depth in regard to this. "Social importance." Just what did he mean by that—some deep, scientific information that he had acquired at college. He was saved a non-committal or totally uninformed answer by Sondra who, without thought or knowledge of the difficulty which was then and there before him, exclaimed: "Oh, no arguments, Freddie. That's not interesting. Besides I want him to meet my brother and Bertine. You remember Miss Cranston. She was with me at your uncle's last spring." Clyde turned, while Fred made the best of the rebuff by merely looking at Sondra, whom he admired so very much.

"Yes, of course," Clyde began, for he had been studying these two along with others. To him, apart from Sondra, Bertine seemed exceedingly attractive, though quite beyond his understanding also. Being involved, insincere and sly, she merely evoked in him a troubled sense of ineffectiveness, and hence uncertainty, in so far as her particular world was concerned—no more.

"Oh, how do you do? It's nice to see you again," she drawled, the while her greenish-gray eyes went over him in a smiling and yet indifferent and quizzical way. She thought him attractive, but not nearly as shrewd and hard as she would have preferred him to be. "You've been terribly busy with your work, I suppose. But now that you've come out once, I suppose we'll see more of you here and there."

"Well, I hope so," he replied, showing his even teeth. Her eyes seemed to be saying that she did not believe what she was saying and that he did not either, but that it was necessary, possibly amusing, to say something of the sort. And a related, though somewhat modified, version of this same type of treatment was accorded him by Stuart, Sondra's brother.
