It was a little after seven of a raw March evening, with the wind coming up off the river in those long, damp gusts which in Dayton at that season seem to carry with them the very smell of the mills, when Howard Pell, having climbed the two flights of the narrow, linoleum-covered stairs to the flat which he and his wife had occupied for the better part of three years, paused outside the door with his hand upon the knob and did not at once turn it. For he knew, or at least strongly suspected, that she knew. Wilbur Teague's wife, a gossiping, inquisitive woman of the kind that always seems to be at a window or a back fence when anything of moment is passing, had been in the neighborhood that afternoon. And Teague himself, as Howard had learned only at five o'clock and over the telephone at the store, had at last confessed that the Miami Valley Tile & Brick Company, into which, upon his most solemn assurances, Howard had put four hundred and twenty dollars of their joint savings, was no more. A receiver had been named. There would be, as Teague phrased it with a kind of shamefaced brightness, "maybe ten cents on the dollar, maybe nothing." And this money (and here was the sting of it) was not, as one might say, Howard's alone, but rather the fruit of three years of Ida's turning and pinching, her made-over shirtwaists, her refusals of this and that, her steady, almost grim, putting by of a dollar here and fifty cents there against that day, not too far off as they had hoped, when they might take a small house of their own out on Salem Avenue.

He opened the door. The flat, small and close, with its one front room giving upon a dining room scarcely larger than a closet, and beyond that the kitchen, was lit by a single gas jet under a fluted glass globe, and in its yellowish light he could see her sitting not at the table, where the plates were laid and a dish of something stood covered, but by the window, with her hands in her lap. She did not rise. And that in itself, so contrary to her custom, which was to come forward and take his hat and say something, however slight, about the weather or the day, told him all that he needed to know.

"Well," he said, attempting a lightness which he by no means felt, and hanging up his hat and coat upon the bent-wire rack by the door, "it's a mean night out. I thought that car would never come." And then, since she still said nothing: "You've had your supper, I suppose?"

"No, I waited." Her voice was low and quite even, and yet there was in it a quality—a kind of flat, held-back stillness—which caused him to look at her more closely than he otherwise would have. She was a woman of twenty-eight, not handsome in any striking way but with a certain neat, firm, brown-haired comeliness, a straight back and steady gray eyes, the daughter of a Miamisburg harness-maker who had raised her to believe, as such men do, that a dollar saved was a dollar's worth of safety in a world which, as he had often said, "don't owe nobody nothin'." And in her, as Howard had long since come to realize, though without ever quite putting it into words, there was a strain of hard practicality which, while it had been at first a source of comfort to him, had of late become a kind of reproach. For he was not like that. He was, as he would have said himself, a man who believed in taking a chance now and then. How else did anybody ever get ahead? Look at the Pattersons! Look at the Deeds! Had they got where they were by putting dimes in a sugar bowl?

"Mrs. Teague was here," she said presently, and looked at him. "This afternoon. She came up to borrow a pattern, she said. Only she didn't want any pattern."

"Oh, she did, eh?" He came over and stood by the table, fingering the edge of the cloth. "Well, that woman! She'd talk the ears off a mule. I don't know what Wilbur ever—"

"Howard." She said it quietly, but it stopped him. "Don't. Don't talk about her. I want to know about the money."

There it was, then. And in the face of it, as so often happens with natures of his kind, which are more given to hoping and wishing than to any direct facing of things, he felt a sudden inward shrinking, a desire to put it off, to temporize, to find some way—any way—of making it seem less than it was. Perhaps if he told it in a certain way—as a mere setback, a thing which might yet right itself—

"Well, now, Ida," he began, drawing out a chair and sitting down heavily, his elbows on the table, "it isn't as bad as all that. I don't know what she told you, but you know how she is. There's been some trouble, sure. A receiver's been put in. But that don't mean—that doesn't mean the thing's dead. Lots of concerns go through a receivership and come out all right. Wilbur says—"

"Wilbur says!" There was a flash in her gray eyes now, and she half rose, then sat again. "What does Wilbur say? What has Wilbur ever said that came to anything? He said it was as safe as the bank. He said in a year it would be paying eight per cent. He said—you said—that we could have the house by fall. Do you remember that? You stood right there"—she pointed to the place by the door—"and you said it."

He did remember it. And the memory, as she evoked it, was not a little galling, for he had been very sure of himself that night, very much the man of affairs, explaining to her with a pencil on the back of an envelope just how the thing would work—the clay beds out near Miamisburg, the new kilns, the building that was going on everywhere in the city and must go on, the contracts which Teague's brother-in-law was certain to get. And she, though doubtful, though not a little troubled, had at last given in—not because she believed, as he now saw, but because he had wanted it so much and she had not wished to stand in his way. And now this!

"I know what I said," he answered, a little sullenly. "And I believed it. So did Wilbur. Do you think he'd have put in his own money if he hadn't? He put in more'n I did—six hundred. He's out more than we are."

"I don't care what Wilbur's out." She was looking at him steadily, and he saw now, or thought he saw, that she had been crying earlier, though there was no sign of it now except a certain faint swelling about the lids. "It isn't Wilbur's money I saved. It isn't Wilbur's money I went without a winter coat for. I wore that old brown thing two winters, Howard, two winters, and turned the collar, and you never even noticed. And the Christmas before last when Mamma wanted me to come down to Miamisburg and I didn't go because it was a dollar and forty cents on the interurban—" She stopped, her lips pressed together, and looked away out of the window, where the wind was rattling the loose sash and the arc light at the corner swung a little on its wire.

He said nothing. What was there to say? It was all true. And yet, sitting there under the hissing gas, with the smell of the covered dish—it was a stew of some kind, he could tell—coming faintly to him, he was conscious of something else rising in him, something not so much contrite as resentful. For, after all, was it his fault that the thing had failed? Could anyone have foreseen it? And had he not done it for her, too, for both of them? Did she think he liked being a salesman behind the hardware counter at Rike's at fifteen dollars a week, with old Brenneman looking over his shoulder all day and calling him "young man" at thirty-one? Did she think he liked coming home to these three rooms, with the Schaefers' baby crying through the wall at all hours, and the toilet in the hall shared by two families? He had wanted to get out of it—that was all—to be something, to have something. And for that she would now sit there and look at him as though he were a thief!

"Well, I suppose you think I did it on purpose," he said at last, harshly, and was himself a little startled at the tone. "I suppose you think I went out and threw it in the river."

"I didn't say that."

"You might as well have. You've been sitting there looking at me as if—as if I'd been caught robbing a till. I made a mistake. All right. Other men make mistakes. Do you think Patterson never made a mistake? He failed twice, did you know that? Twice. And look where he is now."

"You're not Mr. Patterson," she said, and then, seeing his face, added more gently but no less firmly: "I don't mean it that way, Howard. I only mean—we haven't got anything to fail with. We haven't got anything to fall back on. We had four hundred and twenty dollars, and that was all, and now we haven't got it. If I got sick—if you lost your place—"

"I'm not going to lose my place."

"You don't know that. Nobody knows that." She turned her hands over in her lap and looked down at them, those hands which had done the washing and the ironing and the scrubbing of these rooms for three years, and which were reddened a little at the knuckles now from the cold water of the tubs in the basement. "And it isn't only that," she went on, more slowly. "It's—why didn't you tell me? You knew it was going bad. You must have known. Mrs. Teague said Wilbur's been worried since January. Since January, Howard. And you never said one word. You let me go on thinking—I bought the paper for the front room, you remember, because I thought by next year we'd be moving anyhow and it didn't matter if it was cheap—"

And here, indeed, was the true center of her grievance, as he could now see, and it touched him more nearly than the loss itself. For it was true. He had known. Not certainly, perhaps, but he had known that Teague was uneasy, that there had been talk of a note falling due, of the bank being hard to deal with. And he had said nothing, partly from a hope (so characteristic of him) that it would all come right of itself, and partly—and this he did not like to acknowledge even to himself—from a reluctance to face just such a scene as this, with her steady eyes upon him and that faint, unspoken judgment in them which he had come to dread more than any outspoken reproach.

But there was something else, too, which had kept him silent through these weeks, and which now, as he sat there, rose up in his mind with a peculiar, unwelcome vividness, so that he could scarcely meet her look. For on several of those evenings since January when he had told her that he was kept late at the store taking inventory, he had not been at the store at all, but rather had walked, as if by accident, along Third Street past the little millinery shop of a Mrs. Lorraine Hollis, a widow of thirty or thereabouts, plump, fair-haired, quick of tongue and laughter, whom he had met first when she came into Rike's to buy a pair of shears. Nothing had come of it—nothing, at least, that he would have called anything. He had walked home with her twice, and once they had stopped in at the Phillips House for a glass of beer and a sandwich, and she had laughed at his stories in a way that Ida never did, and had looked at him across the little marble-topped table with a frank, warm, appraising interest which had set him up more than he could have said. It was nothing. And yet! And yet! It was not nothing, either, and he knew it. For in her presence he had felt himself to be what he wished to be—a man of some parts, some daring, some future—whereas here, in these three close rooms, under Ida's quiet gaze, he felt himself to be only Howard Pell, hardware clerk, who had lost four hundred and twenty dollars.

Did Ida know of this? Had Mrs. Teague, among her other offices, seen him on Third Street? The thought caused him a sudden chill, and he looked at her quickly, searchingly, to see if there were anything more in her face than he had yet read there. But no—she was looking at her hands still, and there was in her expression only that hurt, stubborn, puzzled sorrow which was all he had seen before.

"I didn't tell you," he said, more quietly now, "because I didn't want to worry you. I thought it might come out all right. I kept thinking any day Wilbur would say they'd got the money from the Columbus people. I didn't see any use in both of us worrying."

"Both of us!" She looked up. "Howard, it was my money too. Half of it. More than half, if you count what I made sewing for the Kuhns. Didn't I have a right to worry about it? Didn't I have a right to know?"

"Well, I suppose you did." He moved restlessly in his chair. "But what good would it have done? You couldn't have done anything."

"I could have known." She said it so simply that it disarmed him for a moment. And then, after a pause, in a lower voice, as though the thing were being drawn out of her against her will: "I don't think you tell me things, Howard. I don't think you have for a long time. You come home and you eat your supper and you read the Journal and you go to bed, and I don't know what you're thinking about. Sometimes I look at you and I think—I don't even know what he wants. I used to think I did."

This was dangerous ground, and he felt it so. There was in her words, though she could not have intended it, a kind of nearness to the very thing he most wished to keep hidden, and the effect upon him was to produce, as such nearnesses so often do in weak and self-protective natures, not candor but anger—a quick, defensive anger that seized upon the first weapon to hand.

"Well, what do you expect?" he burst out. "What do you want me to talk about? The price of stove bolts? Old Brenneman's liver? I'm tired when I come home. A man's tired. And then I come in and it's always—what did this cost, and did you remember to pay the gas man, and Mrs. So-and-so's got a new rug. Do you think that's interesting to a man? Do you think a man wants to come home to that every night?" He had risen and was standing now, one hand gripping the back of the chair. "Maybe if you'd talk about something else once in a while—maybe if you'd ever laugh at anything—"

He stopped, for he saw that he had gone too far—that he had said, in his anger, a thing which revealed more than he had meant, and which she, with that quick, intuitive perception which even the plainest women possess in such matters, had instantly caught. For she had gone quite white, and was looking at him now not with anger but with a kind of slow, dawning, terrible attentiveness, as one might look at a stranger who had suddenly spoken in a familiar voice.

"Laugh," she repeated. "You want me to laugh." And then, very quietly: "Who laughs, Howard? Who do you know that laughs?"

"Nobody. I didn't mean anything. I only meant—oh, the devil!" He turned away from her and walked to the window, where he stood with his back to her, looking down into the street, at the swaying arc light and the wet, black pavement and a lone figure in a slicker bending against the wind. His heart was pounding in a curious way. What a fool he was! What an utter fool! To have said that—to have let her see—and yet, what had she seen? Nothing. Nothing that she could name. And there was nothing to name. He had walked home with a woman twice. Was that a crime?

Behind him he heard her rise, and then, after a moment, heard the scrape of the cover being lifted from the dish on the table.

"It's cold," she said, in a voice that was flat and toneless again. "I'll put it back on the stove."

He did not turn. He heard her go into the kitchen, heard the rattle of the stove lid and the small sounds of her moving about, and he stood there, a prey to the most conflicting and unhappy emotions—shame, and resentment, and a kind of dull fear, and beneath them all, persisting in spite of everything, the faint, warm memory of that other face across the marble table, and the laughter, and the sense of being, for an hour, someone other than himself. Was he wicked to feel so? His mother, a Methodist of the strictest sort, would have said so, without a moment's hesitation. And Ida's father, with his "don't owe nobody nothin'," would have said worse. And yet what was a man to do with such feelings, which came to him unbidden and which he could no more put away than he could the color of his eyes?

For what is it, after all, that binds two such as these together, beyond the mere words of a minister and the dull necessity of rent and coal and bread? Is it love, in any sense the poets would allow? Or is it rather a kind of habit, a mutual dependence of weak upon weak, which holds only so long as no stronger lure presents itself to either? The chemistry of such unions is obscure. And it is often only in such moments as this, when some unlooked-for strain is put upon them, that their true composition is revealed—and that, too often, to the dismay of both.

Presently she came back and stood in the doorway of the dining room, wiping her hands upon her apron.

"It'll be ready in a minute," she said. And then, after a pause, not looking at him: "I'm going to ask Mrs. Kuhn if she has any more sewing. And I thought—there's a sign in the window at Elder's. They want girls for the Easter rush. In the shirtwaist department."

He turned then. "You're not going to work in any store," he said. "I won't have it."

"Somebody has to put it back." She lifted her eyes to his, and in them there was no anger now, only a kind of tired, settled resolution which was harder to face than any anger could have been. "We can't just—not have anything, Howard. I can't live like that. I'd lie awake."

He wanted to say something—to protest, to forbid, to assert himself in some fashion as the head of this household which he had so signally failed to protect. But the words would not come. For he knew, and she knew, and each knew that the other knew, that she was right; and that it would be her steadiness, and not his daring, which would bring them, if anything could, back to where they had been that night when he stood by the door with the pencil and the envelope and talked of the house on Salem Avenue.

"Well," he said at last, heavily, and sat down again at the table. "Do as you like."

She went back into the kitchen. And he sat there under the hissing gas, with his hands lying idle before him on the cloth, and listened to the wind at the loose sash, and thought—not of the money now, nor of Ida, nor even of Mrs. Hollis exactly, but of the vague, vast, glittering world which lay somewhere beyond these three rooms and this street and this town, where men of daring and luck went on to great things, and where, as it seemed to him at that moment, with a pang so keen as to be almost physical, he himself would never, never come.

Here is an excerpt of Theodore Dreiser's writing, to show you their style:

But in the interim, in connection with his relations with Roberta no least reference to Sondra, although, even when near her in the factory or her room, he could not keep his thoughts from wandering away to where Sondra in her imaginary high social world might be. The while Roberta, at moments only sensing a drift and remoteness in his thought and attitude which had nothing to do with her, was wondering what it was that of late was beginning to occupy him so completely. And he, in his turn, when she was not looking was thinking—supposing?—supposing—(since she had troubled to recall herself to him), that he could interest a girl like Sondra in him? What then of Roberta? What? And in the face of this intimate relation that had now been established between them? (Goodness! The deuce!) And that he did care for her (yes, he did), although now—basking in the direct rays of this newer luminary—he could scarcely see Roberta any longer, so strong were the actinic rays of this other. Was he all wrong? Was it evil to be like this? His mother would say so! And his father too—and perhaps everybody who thought right about life—Sondra Finchley, maybe—the Griffiths—all. And yet! And yet! It was snowing the first light snow of the year as Clyde, arrayed in a new collapsible silk hat and white silk muffler, both suggested by a friendly haberdasher—Orrin Short, with whom recently he had come in contact here—and a new silk umbrella wherewith to protect himself from the snow, made his way toward the very interesting, if not so very imposing residence of the Trumbulls on Wykeagy Avenue. It was quaint, low and rambling, and the lights beaming from within upon the many drawn blinds gave it a Christmas-card effect. And before it, even at the prompt hour at which he arrived, were ranged a half dozen handsome cars of various builds and colors. The sight of them, sprinkled on tops, running boards and fenders with the fresh, flaky snow, gave him a keen sense of a deficiency that was not likely soon to be remedied in his case—the want of ample means wherewith to equip himself with such a necessity as that. And inside as he approached the door he could hear voices, laughter and conversation commingled. A tall, thin servant relieved him of his hat, coat and umbrella and he found himself face to face with Jill Trumbull, who apparently was on the look-out for him—a smooth, curly-haired blonde girl, not too thrillingly pretty, but brisk and smart, in white satin with arms and shoulders bare and rhinestones banded around her forehead.

"No trouble to tell who you are," she said gayly, approaching and giving Clyde her hand. "I'm Jill Trumbull. Miss Finchley hasn't come yet. But I can do the honors just as well, I guess. Come right in where the rest of us are." She led the way into a series of connecting rooms that seemed to join each other at right angles, adding as she went, "You do look an awful lot like Gil Griffiths, don't you?"

"Do I?" smiled Clyde simply and courageously and very much flattered by the comparison. The ceilings were low. Pretty lamps behind painted shades hugged dark walls. Open fires in two connecting rooms cast a rosy glow upon cushioned and comfortable furniture. There were pictures, books, objects of art.

"Here, Tracy, you do the announcing, will you?" she called. "My brother, Tracy Trumbull, Mr. Griffiths. Mr. Clyde Griffiths, everybody," she added, surveying the company in general which in turn fixed varying eyes upon him, while Tracy Trumbull took him by the hand. Clyde, suffering from a sense of being studied, nevertheless achieved a warm smile. At the same time he realized that for the moment at least conversation had stopped. "Don't all stop talking on my account," he ventured, with a smile, which caused most of those present to conceive of him as at his ease and resourceful. At the same time Tracy added: "I'm not going to do any man-to-man introduction stuff. We'll stand right here and point 'em out. That's my sister, Gertrude, over there talking to Scott Nicholson." Clyde noted that a small, dark girl dressed in pink with a pretty and yet saucy and piquant face, nodded to him. And beside her a very de rigueur youth of fine physique and pink complexion nodded jerkily. "Howja do." And a few feet from them near a deep window stood a tall and yet graceful girl of dark and by no means ravishing features talking to a broad-shouldered and deep-chested youth of less than her height, who were proclaimed to be Arabella Stark and Frank Harriet. "They're arguing over a recent Cornell-Syracuse foot-ball game ... Burchard Taylor and Miss Phant of Utica," he went on almost too swiftly for Clyde to assemble any mental notes. "Perley Haynes and Miss Vanda Steele ... well, I guess that's all as yet. Oh, no, here come Grant and Nina Temple." Clyde paused and gazed as a tall and somewhat dandified-looking youth, sharp of face and with murky gray eyes, steered a trim, young, plump girl in fawn gray and with a light chestnut braid of hair laid carefully above her forehead, into the middle of the room.

"Hello, Jill. Hello, Vanda. Hello, Wynette." In the midst of these greetings on his part, Clyde was presented to these two, neither of whom seemed to pay much attention to him. "Didn't think we'd make it," went on young Cranston speaking to all at once. "Nina didn't want to come, but I promised Bertine and Jill or I wouldn't have, either. We were up at the Bagley's. Guess who's up there, Scott. Van Peterson and Rhoda Hull. They're just over for the day."

"You don't say," called Scott Nicholson, a determined and self-centered looking individual. Clyde was arrested by the very definite sense of social security and ease that seemed to reside in everybody. "Why didn't you bring 'em along? I'd like to see Rhoda again and Van, too."

"Couldn't. They have to go back early, they say. They may stop in later for a minute. Gee, isn't dinner served yet? I expected to sit right down."

"These lawyers! Don't you know they don't eat often?" commented Frank Harriet, who was a short, but broad-chested and smiling youth, very agreeable, very good-looking and with even, white teeth. Clyde liked him.

"Well, whether they do or not, we do, or out I go. Did you hear who is being touted for stroke next year over at Cornell?" This college chatter relating to Cornell and shared by Harriet, Cranston and others, Clyde could not understand. He had scarcely heard of the various colleges with which this group was all too familiar. At the same time he was wise enough to sense the defect and steer clear of any questions or conversations which might relate to them. However, because of this, he at once felt out of it. These people were better informed than he was—had been to colleges. Perhaps he had better claim that he had been to some school. In Kansas City he had heard of the State University of Kansas—not so very far from there. Also the University of Missouri. And in Chicago of the University of Chicago. Could he say that he had been to one of those—that Kansas one, for a little while, anyway? On the instant he proposed to claim it, if asked, and then look up afterwards what, if anything, he was supposed to know about it—what, for instance, he might have studied. He had heard of mathematics somewhere. Why not that? But these people, as he could see, were too much interested in themselves to pay much attention to him now. He might be a Griffiths and important to some outside, but here not so much—a matter of course, as it were. It was in the latter part of October, a gray and windy day with the leaves of the maples along Calhoun Street already gone brown and blowing in little eddies against the curbs, that Hubert Kessler, who for nearly eleven years had not set foot in Fort Wayne, found himself descending from the day coach of the Pennsylvania with a yellow grip in one hand and a folded newspaper in the other, and looking about him with that mingled curiosity and uneasiness which a man feels on returning to a place where once he was poor and obscure and is now, or so he likes to think, somewhat less so. He was thirty-four. He was employed, and had been for six years now, as a traveling representative of Holcomb, Pratt & Company of Chicago, wholesalers in men's furnishings, cravats, hosiery, and the like, and was known in a modest way along the Ohio and Indiana routes as a man who could "place goods," which, as he himself would have said, was something. He wore on this occasion a long brown overcoat of a fashionable cut, a derby of the same shade, and a pearl-gray four-in-hand into which was thrust a small horseshoe pin of brilliants—not real, but very effective, as he thought. And he carried himself with a kind of brisk, self-conscious assurance, the while within him there moved a quite different and far less certain mood.

For he had come, not on business exactly, although he had arranged his route so that he might call on two or three of the local haberdashers, but rather, and it was this which troubled him, to see his cousin Lottie—Charlotte Ruebsam that had been, now Mrs. Emil Fenske—whom he had not seen since the funeral of their grandmother, and of whom he had heard from his mother, in one of her long, rambling, pencil-written letters, that "things had not gone so well." Emil, the husband, a brakeman on the Nickel Plate, had lost the better part of his left foot under a coupling the winter before, and was now, it appeared, doing nothing, or next to nothing. There were three children. And Lottie herself was "taking in sewing." That was all. But it had been enough to stir in Hubert a peculiar, half-sentimental, half-guilty impulse which he could not have explained, even to himself, and which he had at first resisted, and then, as is the way with such impulses, yielded to.

Why should he go? What was she to him now? A cousin—yes. But there were other cousins, a dozen of them, scattered about Allen and Noble counties, whom he never troubled to see. And yet! And yet! There had been those summers at the old Ruebsam place, out on the St. Joe road, when he and Lottie, the two of them nearly of an age, had been so much together—wading in the creek below the sugar bush, hunting eggs in the haymow, sitting on the high seat of the wagon beside their grandfather on the way to market. And she had been, at that time, so much the more favored of the two of them—the pretty one, the quick one, the one whom the uncles and aunts made over, while he, a thin, long-shanked, freckled boy whose father drank and whose mother took in washing in Lima, had been regarded, as he very well knew, as a kind of poor relation, tolerated rather than welcomed. He could remember still, and with a curious little sting, how Aunt Hulda had once said in his hearing, "Lottie will marry well. You'll see. A girl like that." And how he himself had believed it, and had looked upon Lottie in her starched white dress and pink sash as upon one born to some higher and more fortunate sphere than he could ever hope to attain.

Well, and now? He was not rich, to be sure. But he had a room at the Briggs House in Chicago and a hundred and forty dollars a month and expenses, and a little over nine hundred dollars in the Continental Bank, and he was, as he told himself, "on his way." And Lottie—

He did not like to complete the thought. It was not pleasant to be pleased by another's misfortune, and he was not, he assured himself, pleased. Not in the least. And yet there was in him, as there is in most of us, a small, secret, unacknowledged sense of a balance having been somehow redressed—of life, that great and indifferent arbiter, having at last turned its scales in his favor. And this, while he would have denied it vigorously, colored and flavored his whole approach.

The house, when at last he found it, after inquiring twice of a grocer and a boy with a coaster wagon, was in Wells Street, or rather off it, in a short and unpaved lane that ran down toward the yards of the Nickel Plate—a narrow, two-story frame affair, gray once, but now weathered to no color at all, with a sagging porch and a small yard in which a few frost-blackened tomato vines still clung to their stakes. Smoke from the switch engines hung low over everything, and there was in the air that peculiar acrid odor of coal gas and cinders and wet ashes which belongs to such neighborhoods. Hubert, standing at the gate with his grip in his hand, felt suddenly and acutely conscious of his new overcoat and his gray tie and his horseshoe pin. They seemed, here, almost an affront. He half wished he had not worn them. And yet, he reflected, why not? He had earned them, hadn't he? He was not going to pretend to be what he was not.

He knocked. There was a sound of a child crying somewhere within, and then a quick step, and the door was opened by a woman whom, for the fraction of a second, he did not know at all. She was thin—much thinner than he would have believed—with a faded blue calico wrapper drawn about her, and her hair, which he remembered as a kind of bright chestnut that the sun turned almost to copper, was now dulled and drawn back carelessly into a knot. There were lines about her mouth, and her eyes—those same gray-green eyes that he had once thought so wonderful—looked out at him with a kind of startled and defensive inquiry, as though she expected a bill collector or an agent of some kind.

"Yes?" she said.

"Lottie," he said. "Don't you know me? It's Hubert. Hubert Kessler."

"Hubert!" She put a hand to her throat, and then to her hair, and then, as if realizing all at once the wrapper and the general disorder of her appearance, colored deeply. "Why, Hubert Kessler! For goodness' sake! I never—why, I wouldn't have known you. Come in. Come in. My, but you look—" She stopped, as though uncertain how to finish, and stepped back to let him pass. "You'll have to excuse how things are. I wasn't expecting anybody. I've got sewing all over."

"Oh, that's all right," he said quickly and with what he hoped was an easy and cordial air. "I just thought I'd drop around. I'm through here on business, you see. Just for the day. And Ma wrote me you were living here, so I thought—well, why not? It's been a long time."

"It has," she said. "My, yes. It's been a long time."

The front room into which she led him was small and low and cluttered—a treadle sewing machine near the window, with a half-finished dress of some cheap red stuff thrown across it, a horsehair sofa, worn shiny, two or three chairs that did not match, a base burner whose isinglass windows glowed a dull orange, and on the wall a colored lithograph of the Kaiser and another of the Sacred Heart. A small boy of perhaps four, with a dirty face and a thumb in his mouth, stood in the doorway to the kitchen staring at Hubert with round eyes, and from somewhere above came still the thin, querulous wail of a younger child.

"That's Rudy," said Lottie. "Say how-do to your cousin, Rudy. Your Ma's cousin, that is. He's bashful. The baby's upstairs. She's got a cold. And Elsie's at school." She moved the red dress from a chair and dusted the seat with her hand. "Sit down, Hubert. Here. I'll make some coffee. You'll have some coffee?"

"Well, if it isn't too much trouble."

"Oh, no trouble." And she disappeared into the kitchen, whence came presently the rattle of a stove lid and the sound of water being poured, while Hubert, seated stiffly upon the chair with his derby on his knee and his overcoat still on, looked about him and endeavored to compose his thoughts.

So this was Lottie! This was what had become of her—the pretty one, the favored one, of whom Aunt Hulda had said she would "marry well." It was incredible. And yet, now that he thought of it, was it so incredible after all? How many such girls had he not seen in his travels—in Lima, in Muncie, in Logansport, in Peru—girls who at seventeen had been the belles of their little worlds, and at thirty were drudges, worn and shapeless, with a brood of children and a husband who drank or was out of work or both? It was the way of things, apparently. Life gave and then it took away. And the thing that it gave—youth, beauty, a certain bloom and charm—was precisely the thing that it took away soonest, leaving nothing in its place unless one had been shrewd enough, or lucky enough, to exchange it in time for something more durable. Money, for instance. Or position. And Lottie had not been shrewd, evidently. She had married a brakeman.

And yet he was troubled. For there was something in the sight of her, so changed, so obviously worn, which reached back into his own past and stirred memories that he would just as soon have left undisturbed. That creek. That haymow. That afternoon—he could see it now as plainly as though it were yesterday—when she had kissed him, quite suddenly and without warning, behind the corncrib, and then run away laughing, and he had stood there, a gawky boy of fourteen, scarlet and trembling and not knowing what to think. He had never told anyone of that. He had scarcely let himself think of it in years. And yet here it was, rising up in him again, along with the smell of coal smoke and the wail of the sick child upstairs.

She came back presently with two cups of coffee, thick white cups such as are used in railroad lunchrooms, and a plate with some slices of coffee cake upon it, and she had, he noticed, taken a moment to smooth her hair and to pin a little brooch at the throat of her wrapper—a cheap thing of colored glass, but it touched him somehow, this little effort.

"Now," she said, seating herself on the edge of the sofa opposite him, and smiling for the first time—and in that smile he caught for an instant a glimpse of the old Lottie, quick and bright and teasing—"tell me all about yourself. My, but you've done well. Anybody can see that. Aunt Martha wrote me you were traveling for some big house in Chicago."

"Oh, well," he said, with a modesty which was not altogether sincere, "it's a pretty good house. Holcomb, Pratt. Men's furnishings, you know—ties and shirts and so on. I cover Indiana and part of Ohio. It's a pretty good territory." He hesitated, and then, because he could not help it, added: "I've done fairly well, I guess. They seem to think so."

"I should say you have." She looked at his overcoat, his tie, the pin, with frank and open admiration, and yet with something else, too, something wistful and a little sad, which he caught and which made him uncomfortable. "Who'd have thought it? You used to be so—well, so quiet, Hubert. Grandpa used to say you'd never amount to anything because you never talked."

"Did he?" He laughed, a little stiffly. "Well, I talk now. I have to. That's my business, talking."

"I guess it is." She sipped her coffee. "And you're not married?"

"No. Not yet." He did not explain that there had been, in Chicago, a Miss Ida Sorensen, a stenographer, with whom he had kept company for nearly two years, and whom he had dropped—not cruelly, as he told himself, but firmly—when it began to seem that she expected more of him than he was prepared to give. A man on the road could not marry. Or rather, a man who intended to rise could not saddle himself too soon. That was common sense.

"Well, you've got time," said Lottie. "Men have more time." And she looked down into her cup, and for a moment neither of them spoke.

"And Emil?" he ventured finally, since it seemed necessary to say something about him. "Ma wrote me he'd been hurt."

"Yes." Her face changed—hardened a little, as he thought. "Last February. It was icy, and he slipped between the cars down at the junction. They had to take off three of his toes and part of the foot. He's around now, with a cane. The company gave him two hundred dollars." She said this last with a kind of dry bitterness which was not like the Lottie he remembered. "Two hundred dollars. And they won't take him back. He's out now, looking. He's always out looking." She paused. "He'll get something. Watchman, maybe. Somebody told him the Bass foundry wanted a watchman."

"Sure he will," said Hubert, with that easy, professional optimism which he had cultivated for use upon dubious merchants. "Lots of places want watchmen."

But inwardly he was thinking: So that's the way it is. And how did she ever come to marry him in the first place? A brakeman! Lottie Ruebsam, who might have had—well, who might have had almost anybody, in those days. There had been a young fellow named Gebhardt, he remembered, whose father owned the feed store at New Haven, who had been crazy about her. And another, a schoolteacher. What had happened? Why had she thrown herself away?

As though she read his thought, she said, a little defiantly: "Emil's all right. He's good to me and the children. He don't drink—hardly at all. It's just been bad luck. Anybody can have bad luck."

"Of course. Of course they can." And he flushed slightly, as though she had caught him at something.

The child upstairs had stopped crying. Rudy, having apparently satisfied himself that this stranger was harmless, had crept forward and now stood at Hubert's knee, gazing up at the glittering pin. Hubert, with a sudden impulse, took a nickel from his vest pocket and held it out to the boy, who seized it and fled into the kitchen.

"You shouldn't," said Lottie. But she smiled.

And then, as if by mutual and unspoken consent, they turned away from the present, with its smoke and its sewing and its crippled husband, and began to speak of the old days—of Grandpa Ruebsam and his great white beard and his German Bible; of Aunt Hulda and her sharp tongue; of the Fourth of July picnic at Robison Park when Cousin August had fallen in the lake; of the old orchard and the cider press and the sugar camp in March. And as they talked, Lottie grew more animated, more like herself, or rather like that former self which Hubert carried in his memory, and her eyes brightened, and once she laughed outright, a clear and ringing laugh that seemed to belong to another time and place altogether. And Hubert, watching her, felt stirring in him again that old, confused admiration, mixed now with pity and with something else—a vague, troubling sense of loss, as though something which had once been possible to both of them had somehow slipped away unnoticed and could never be recovered.

"Do you remember," she said suddenly, with a sly, half-embarrassed look, "that time behind the corncrib?"

He started. So she remembered! He had supposed—he did not know what he had supposed. That it had meant nothing to her, perhaps. That she had forgotten it the next day.

"Why—yes," he said, coloring. "I guess I do."

"You were so funny. You turned as red as a beet." She laughed again, but more softly now, and looked away toward the window, where the gray light was already fading. "I was a silly thing in those days. I thought—oh, I don't know what I thought. That everything would be wonderful, I guess. Didn't you?"

"I guess so," he said. And then, because he did not know what else to say, and because the moment seemed suddenly too intimate, too fraught with a kind of meaning which he did not wish to examine: "Well, things don't always turn out the way you expect."

"No," she said. "They don't." And she sighed, a long, quiet sigh, and smoothed the faded calico over her knees.

It was dusk when he rose to go. He had an engagement, he said, with a Mr. Whitcomb of Whitcomb & Lutz at seven, which was true, and his train for Lima left at nine-forty. And at the door, with his grip in his hand and his derby once more upon his head, he hesitated, fumbling in his pocket. Should he? Would she be offended? He had thought of it all afternoon, off and on—ten dollars, say, or even twenty. It would mean nothing to him, comparatively. And to her—

"Lottie," he said awkwardly, "I wish you'd let me—I mean, for the children—" And he held out, folded small, a twenty-dollar bill.

She looked at it, and then at him, and for a moment he thought she would refuse. Her lips tightened, and there came into her eyes a flash of that old pride which he remembered. But then, as quickly, it was gone, and she took the bill and closed her hand upon it.

"Thank you, Hubert," she said quietly. "You always were—" She did not finish. "Come again, if you're ever through. Emil would like to meet you."

"I will," he said. "Sure I will."

But he knew, even as he said it, that he would not. And walking back up the dark lane toward Wells Street, with the switch engines coughing and clanking in the yards below and the smoke drifting low across the scattered lights, he was conscious of a strange mingling of emotions—relief, and pity, and a kind of complacent satisfaction in his own better fortune, and beneath all these, troubling and unresolved, a sense of something lost which he could not name. Was it his fault, any of it? No. Of course not. It was life—blind, indifferent, chemic life—which shuffled people about like cards and dealt them as it would. Some it raised, and some it cast down, and there was no reason in it that any man could see. He had been lucky, that was all. Or shrewd. Or both. And she had not.

And yet! That laugh of hers, so clear and young, in that dim and shabby room! And that brooch of colored glass pinned at her throat! He could not get them out of his mind. All the way to Whitcomb & Lutz, and afterward, sitting in the smoking car of the Pennsylvania with the dark fields of Allen County slipping past outside, he kept seeing them, and wondering—vaguely, uneasily, as men will wonder about such things and then forget them—whether, after all, it was so very fine a thing to be on one's way, if on the way one left behind so much that could never again be reached.

Here is an excerpt of Theodore Dreiser's writing, to show you their style:

But in the interim, in connection with his relations with Roberta no least reference to Sondra, although, even when near her in the factory or her room, he could not keep his thoughts from wandering away to where Sondra in her imaginary high social world might be. The while Roberta, at moments only sensing a drift and remoteness in his thought and attitude which had nothing to do with her, was wondering what it was that of late was beginning to occupy him so completely. And he, in his turn, when she was not looking was thinking—supposing?—supposing—(since she had troubled to recall herself to him), that he could interest a girl like Sondra in him? What then of Roberta? What? And in the face of this intimate relation that had now been established between them? (Goodness! The deuce!) And that he did care for her (yes, he did), although now—basking in the direct rays of this newer luminary—he could scarcely see Roberta any longer, so strong were the actinic rays of this other. Was he all wrong? Was it evil to be like this? His mother would say so! And his father too—and perhaps everybody who thought right about life—Sondra Finchley, maybe—the Griffiths—all. And yet! And yet! It was snowing the first light snow of the year as Clyde, arrayed in a new collapsible silk hat and white silk muffler, both suggested by a friendly haberdasher—Orrin Short, with whom recently he had come in contact here—and a new silk umbrella wherewith to protect himself from the snow, made his way toward the very interesting, if not so very imposing residence of the Trumbulls on Wykeagy Avenue. It was quaint, low and rambling, and the lights beaming from within upon the many drawn blinds gave it a Christmas-card effect. And before it, even at the prompt hour at which he arrived, were ranged a half dozen handsome cars of various builds and colors. The sight of them, sprinkled on tops, running boards and fenders with the fresh, flaky snow, gave him a keen sense of a deficiency that was not likely soon to be remedied in his case—the want of ample means wherewith to equip himself with such a necessity as that. And inside as he approached the door he could hear voices, laughter and conversation commingled. A tall, thin servant relieved him of his hat, coat and umbrella and he found himself face to face with Jill Trumbull, who apparently was on the look-out for him—a smooth, curly-haired blonde girl, not too thrillingly pretty, but brisk and smart, in white satin with arms and shoulders bare and rhinestones banded around her forehead.

"No trouble to tell who you are," she said gayly, approaching and giving Clyde her hand. "I'm Jill Trumbull. Miss Finchley hasn't come yet. But I can do the honors just as well, I guess. Come right in where the rest of us are." She led the way into a series of connecting rooms that seemed to join each other at right angles, adding as she went, "You do look an awful lot like Gil Griffiths, don't you?"

"Do I?" smiled Clyde simply and courageously and very much flattered by the comparison. The ceilings were low. Pretty lamps behind painted shades hugged dark walls. Open fires in two connecting rooms cast a rosy glow upon cushioned and comfortable furniture. There were pictures, books, objects of art.

"Here, Tracy, you do the announcing, will you?" she called. "My brother, Tracy Trumbull, Mr. Griffiths. Mr. Clyde Griffiths, everybody," she added, surveying the company in general which in turn fixed varying eyes upon him, while Tracy Trumbull took him by the hand. Clyde, suffering from a sense of being studied, nevertheless achieved a warm smile. At the same time he realized that for the moment at least conversation had stopped. "Don't all stop talking on my account," he ventured, with a smile, which caused most of those present to conceive of him as at his ease and resourceful. At the same time Tracy added: "I'm not going to do any man-to-man introduction stuff. We'll stand right here and point 'em out. That's my sister, Gertrude, over there talking to Scott Nicholson." Clyde noted that a small, dark girl dressed in pink with a pretty and yet saucy and piquant face, nodded to him. And beside her a very de rigueur youth of fine physique and pink complexion nodded jerkily. "Howja do." And a few feet from them near a deep window stood a tall and yet graceful girl of dark and by no means ravishing features talking to a broad-shouldered and deep-chested youth of less than her height, who were proclaimed to be Arabella Stark and Frank Harriet. "They're arguing over a recent Cornell-Syracuse foot-ball game ... Burchard Taylor and Miss Phant of Utica," he went on almost too swiftly for Clyde to assemble any mental notes. "Perley Haynes and Miss Vanda Steele ... well, I guess that's all as yet. Oh, no, here come Grant and Nina Temple." Clyde paused and gazed as a tall and somewhat dandified-looking youth, sharp of face and with murky gray eyes, steered a trim, young, plump girl in fawn gray and with a light chestnut braid of hair laid carefully above her forehead, into the middle of the room.

"Hello, Jill. Hello, Vanda. Hello, Wynette." In the midst of these greetings on his part, Clyde was presented to these two, neither of whom seemed to pay much attention to him. "Didn't think we'd make it," went on young Cranston speaking to all at once. "Nina didn't want to come, but I promised Bertine and Jill or I wouldn't have, either. We were up at the Bagley's. Guess who's up there, Scott. Van Peterson and Rhoda Hull. They're just over for the day."

"You don't say," called Scott Nicholson, a determined and self-centered looking individual. Clyde was arrested by the very definite sense of social security and ease that seemed to reside in everybody. "Why didn't you bring 'em along? I'd like to see Rhoda again and Van, too."

"Couldn't. They have to go back early, they say. They may stop in later for a minute. Gee, isn't dinner served yet? I expected to sit right down."

"These lawyers! Don't you know they don't eat often?" commented Frank Harriet, who was a short, but broad-chested and smiling youth, very agreeable, very good-looking and with even, white teeth. Clyde liked him.

"Well, whether they do or not, we do, or out I go. Did you hear who is being touted for stroke next year over at Cornell?" This college chatter relating to Cornell and shared by Harriet, Cranston and others, Clyde could not understand. He had scarcely heard of the various colleges with which this group was all too familiar. At the same time he was wise enough to sense the defect and steer clear of any questions or conversations which might relate to them. However, because of this, he at once felt out of it. These people were better informed than he was—had been to colleges. Perhaps he had better claim that he had been to some school. In Kansas City he had heard of the State University of Kansas—not so very far from there. Also the University of Missouri. And in Chicago of the University of Chicago. Could he say that he had been to one of those—that Kansas one, for a little while, anyway? On the instant he proposed to claim it, if asked, and then look up afterwards what, if anything, he was supposed to know about it—what, for instance, he might have studied. He had heard of mathematics somewhere. Why not that? But these people, as he could see, were too much interested in themselves to pay much attention to him now. He might be a Griffiths and important to some outside, but here not so much—a matter of course, as it were. And because Tracy Trumbull for the moment had turned to say something to Wynette Phant, he felt quite alone, beached and helpless and with no one to talk to. But just then the small, dark girl, Gertrude, came over to him.

"The crowd's a little late in getting together. It always is. If we said eight, they'd come at eight-thirty or nine. Isn't that always the way?"

"It certainly is," replied Clyde gratefully, endeavoring to appear as brisk and as much at ease as possible.

"I'm Gertrude Trumbull," she repeated. "The sister of the good-looking Jill," a cynical and yet amused smile played about her mouth and eyes. "You nodded to me, but you don't know me. Just the same we've been hearing a lot about you." She teased in an attempt to trouble Clyde a little, if possible. "A mysterious Griffiths here in Lycurgus whom no one seems to have met. I saw you once in Central Avenue, though. You were going into Rich's candy store. You didn't know that, though. Do you like candy?"

"Oh, yes, I like candy. Why?" asked Clyde on the instant feeling teased and disturbed, since the girl for whom he was buying the candy was Roberta. At the same time he could not help feeling slightly more at ease with this girl than with some others, for although cynical and not so attractive, her manner was genial and she now spelled escape from isolation and hence diffidence.

"You're probably just saying that," she laughed, a bantering look in her eyes. "More likely you were buying it for some girl. You have a girl, haven't you?"

"Why—" Clyde paused for the fraction of a second because as she asked this Roberta came into his mind and the query, "Had any one ever seen him with Roberta?" flitted through his brain. Also thinking at the same time, what a bold, teasing, intelligent girl this was, different from any that thus far he had known. Yet quite without more pause he added: "No, I haven't. What makes you ask that?" As he said this there came to him the thought of what Roberta would think if she could hear him. "But what a question," he continued a little nervously now. "You like to tease, don't you?"

"Who, me? Oh, no. I wouldn't do anything like that. But I'm sure you have just the same. I like to ask questions sometimes, just to see what people will say when they don't want you to know what they really think." She beamed into Clyde's eyes amusedly and defiantly. "But I know you have a girl just the same. All good-looking fellows have."

"Oh, am I good-looking?" he beamed nervously, amused and yet pleased. "Who said so?"

"As though you didn't know. Well, different people. I for one. And Sondra Finchley thinks you're good-looking, too. She's only interested in men who are. So does my sister Jill, for that matter. And she only likes men who are good-looking. I'm different because I'm not so good-looking myself." She blinked cynically and teasingly into his eyes, which caused him to feel oddly out of place, not able to cope with such a girl at all, at the same time very much flattered and amused. "But don't you think you're better looking than your cousin," she went on sharply and even commandingly. "Some people think you are." Although a little staggered and yet flattered by this question which propounded what he might have liked to believe, and although intrigued by this girl's interest in him, still Clyde would not have dreamed of venturing any such assertion even though he had believed it. Too vividly it brought the aggressive and determined and even at times revengeful-looking features of Gilbert before him, who, stirred by such a report as this, would not hesitate to pay him out.

"Why I don't think anything of the kind," he laughed. "Honest, I don't. Of course I don't."

"Oh, well, then maybe you don't, but you are just the same. But that won't help you much either, unless you have money—that is, if you want to run with people who have." She looked up at him and added quite blandly. "People like money even more than they do looks." What a sharp girl this was, he thought, and what a hard, cold statement. It cut him not a little, even though she had not intended that it should. But just then Sondra herself entered with some youth whom Clyde did not know—a tall, gangling, but very smartly-dressed individual. And after them, along with others, Bertine and Stuart Finchley.

"Here she is now," added Gertrude a little spitefully, for she resented the fact that Sondra was so much better-looking than either she or her sister, and that she had expressed an interest in Clyde. "She'll be looking to see if you notice how pretty she looks, so don't disappoint her." The impact of this remark, a reflection of the exact truth, was not necessary to cause Clyde to gaze attentively, and even eagerly. For apart from her local position and means and taste in dress and manners, Sondra was of the exact order and spirit that most intrigued him—a somewhat refined (and because of means and position showered upon her) less savage, although scarcely less self-centered, Hortense Briggs. She was, in her small, intense way, a seeking Aphrodite, eager to prove to any who were sufficiently attractive the destroying power of her charm, while at the same time retaining her own personality and individuality free of any entangling alliance or compromise. However, for varying reasons which she could not quite explain to herself, Clyde appealed to her. He might not be anything socially or financially, but he was interesting to her. Hence she was now keen, first to see if he were present, next to be sure that he gained no hint that she had seen him first, and lastly to act as grandly as possible for his benefit—a Hortensian procedure and type of thought that was exactly the thing best calculated to impress him. He gazed and there she was—tripping here and there in a filmy chiffon dance frock, shaded from palest yellow to deepest orange, which most enhanced her dark eyes and hair. And having exchanged a dozen or more "Oh, Hellos," and references with one and another to this, that and the other local event, she at last condescended to evince awareness of his proximity.

"Oh, here you are. You decided to come after all. I wasn't sure whether you would think it worth while. You've been introduced to everybody, of course?" She looked around as much as to say, that if he had not been she would proceed to serve him in this way. The others, not so very much impressed by Clyde, were still not a little interested by the fact that she seemed so interested in him.

"Yes, I met nearly everybody, I think."

"Except Freddie Sells. He came in with me just now. Here you are, Freddie," she called to a tall and slender youth, smooth of cheek and obviously becurled as to hair, who now came over and in his closely-fitting dress coat looked down on Clyde about as a spring rooster might look down on a sparrow.

"This is Clyde Griffiths, I was telling you about, Fred," she began briskly. "Doesn't he look a lot like Gilbert?"

"Why, you do at that," exclaimed this amiable person, who seemed to be slightly troubled with weak eyes since he bent close. "I hear you're a cousin of Gil's. I know him well. We went through Princeton together. I used to be over here before I joined the General Electric over at Schenectady. But I'm around a good bit yet. You're connected with the factory, I suppose."

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, who, before a youth of obviously so much more training and schooling than he possessed, felt not a little reduced. He began to fear that this individual would try to talk to him about things which he could not understand, things concerning which, having had no consecutive training of any kind, he had never been technically informed.

"In charge of some department, I suppose?"

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, cautiously and nervously.

"You know," went on Mr. Sells, briskly and interestingly, being of a commercial as well as technical turn, "I've always wondered just what, outside of money, there is to the collar business. Gil and I used to argue about that when we were down at college. He used to try to tell me that there was some social importance to making and distributing collars, giving polish and manner to people who wouldn't otherwise have them, if it weren't for cheap collars. I think he musta read that in a book somewhere. I always laughed at him." Clyde was about to attempt an answer, although already beyond his depth in regard to this. "Social importance." Just what did he mean by that—some deep, scientific information that he had acquired at college. He was saved a non-committal or totally uninformed answer by Sondra who, without thought or knowledge of the difficulty which was then and there before him, exclaimed: "Oh, no arguments, Freddie. That's not interesting. Besides I want him to meet my brother and Bertine. You remember Miss Cranston. She was with me at your uncle's last spring." Clyde turned, while Fred made the best of the rebuff by merely looking at Sondra, whom he admired so very much.

"Yes, of course," Clyde began, for he had been studying these two along with others. To him, apart from Sondra, Bertine seemed exceedingly attractive, though quite beyond his understanding also. Being involved, insincere and sly, she merely evoked in him a troubled sense of ineffectiveness, and hence uncertainty, in so far as her particular world was concerned—no more.

"Oh, how do you do? It's nice to see you again," she drawled, the while her greenish-gray eyes went over him in a smiling and yet indifferent and quizzical way. She thought him attractive, but not nearly as shrewd and hard as she would have preferred him to be. "You've been terribly busy with your work, I suppose. But now that you've come out once, I suppose we'll see more of you here and there."

"Well, I hope so," he replied, showing his even teeth. Her eyes seemed to be saying that she did not believe what she was saying and that he did not either, but that it was necessary, possibly amusing, to say something of the sort. And a related, though somewhat modified, version of this same type of treatment was accorded him by Stuart, Sondra's brother.

column307:
Here is an excerpt of Theodore Dreiser's writing, to show you their style:

But in the interim, in connection with his relations with Roberta no least reference to Sondra, although, even when near her in the factory or her room, he could not keep his thoughts from wandering away to where Sondra in her imaginary high social world might be. The while Roberta, at moments only sensing a drift and remoteness in his thought and attitude which had nothing to do with her, was wondering what it was that of late was beginning to occupy him so completely. And he, in his turn, when she was not looking was thinking—supposing?—supposing—(since she had troubled to recall herself to him), that he could interest a girl like Sondra in him? What then of Roberta? What? And in the face of this intimate relation that had now been established between them? (Goodness! The deuce!) And that he did care for her (yes, he did), although now—basking in the direct rays of this newer luminary—he could scarcely see Roberta any longer, so strong were the actinic rays of this other. Was he all wrong? Was it evil to be like this? His mother would say so! And his father too—and perhaps everybody who thought right about life—Sondra Finchley, maybe—the Griffiths—all. And yet! And yet! It was snowing the first light snow of the year as Clyde, arrayed in a new collapsible silk hat and white silk muffler, both suggested by a friendly haberdasher—Orrin Short, with whom recently he had come in contact here—and a new silk umbrella wherewith to protect himself from the snow, made his way toward the very interesting, if not so very imposing residence of the Trumbulls on Wykeagy Avenue. It was quaint, low and rambling, and the lights beaming from within upon the many drawn blinds gave it a Christmas-card effect. And before it, even at the prompt hour at which he arrived, were ranged a half dozen handsome cars of various builds and colors. The sight of them, sprinkled on tops, running boards and fenders with the fresh, flaky snow, gave him a keen sense of a deficiency that was not likely soon to be remedied in his case—the want of ample means wherewith to equip himself with such a necessity as that. And inside as he approached the door he could hear voices, laughter and conversation commingled. A tall, thin servant relieved him of his hat, coat and umbrella and he found himself face to face with Jill Trumbull, who apparently was on the look-out for him—a smooth, curly-haired blonde girl, not too thrillingly pretty, but brisk and smart, in white satin with arms and shoulders bare and rhinestones banded around her forehead.

"No trouble to tell who you are," she said gayly, approaching and giving Clyde her hand. "I'm Jill Trumbull. Miss Finchley hasn't come yet. But I can do the honors just as well, I guess. Come right in where the rest of us are." She led the way into a series of connecting rooms that seemed to join each other at right angles, adding as she went, "You do look an awful lot like Gil Griffiths, don't you?"

"Do I?" smiled Clyde simply and courageously and very much flattered by the comparison. The ceilings were low. Pretty lamps behind painted shades hugged dark walls. Open fires in two connecting rooms cast a rosy glow upon cushioned and comfortable furniture. There were pictures, books, objects of art.

"Here, Tracy, you do the announcing, will you?" she called. "My brother, Tracy Trumbull, Mr. Griffiths. Mr. Clyde Griffiths, everybody," she added, surveying the company in general which in turn fixed varying eyes upon him, while Tracy Trumbull took him by the hand. Clyde, suffering from a sense of being studied, nevertheless achieved a warm smile. At the same time he realized that for the moment at least conversation had stopped. "Don't all stop talking on my account," he ventured, with a smile, which caused most of those present to conceive of him as at his ease and resourceful. At the same time Tracy added: "I'm not going to do any man-to-man introduction stuff. We'll stand right here and point 'em out. That's my sister, Gertrude, over there talking to Scott Nicholson." Clyde noted that a small, dark girl dressed in pink with a pretty and yet saucy and piquant face, nodded to him. And beside her a very de rigueur youth of fine physique and pink complexion nodded jerkily. "Howja do." And a few feet from them near a deep window stood a tall and yet graceful girl of dark and by no means ravishing features talking to a broad-shouldered and deep-chested youth of less than her height, who were proclaimed to be Arabella Stark and Frank Harriet. "They're arguing over a recent Cornell-Syracuse foot-ball game ... Burchard Taylor and Miss Phant of Utica," he went on almost too swiftly for Clyde to assemble any mental notes. "Perley Haynes and Miss Vanda Steele ... well, I guess that's all as yet. Oh, no, here come Grant and Nina Temple." Clyde paused and gazed as a tall and somewhat dandified-looking youth, sharp of face and with murky gray eyes, steered a trim, young, plump girl in fawn gray and with a light chestnut braid of hair laid carefully above her forehead, into the middle of the room.

"Hello, Jill. Hello, Vanda. Hello, Wynette." In the midst of these greetings on his part, Clyde was presented to these two, neither of whom seemed to pay much attention to him. "Didn't think we'd make it," went on young Cranston speaking to all at once. "Nina didn't want to come, but I promised Bertine and Jill or I wouldn't have, either. We were up at the Bagley's. Guess who's up there, Scott. Van Peterson and Rhoda Hull. They're just over for the day."

"You don't say," called Scott Nicholson, a determined and self-centered looking individual. Clyde was arrested by the very definite sense of social security and ease that seemed to reside in everybody. "Why didn't you bring 'em along? I'd like to see Rhoda again and Van, too."

"Couldn't. They have to go back early, they say. They may stop in later for a minute. Gee, isn't dinner served yet? I expected to sit right down."

"These lawyers! Don't you know they don't eat often?" commented Frank Harriet, who was a short, but broad-chested and smiling youth, very agreeable, very good-looking and with even, white teeth. Clyde liked him.

"Well, whether they do or not, we do, or out I go. Did you hear who is being touted for stroke next year over at Cornell?" This college chatter relating to Cornell and shared by Harriet, Cranston and others, Clyde could not understand. He had scarcely heard of the various colleges with which this group was all too familiar. At the same time he was wise enough to sense the defect and steer clear of any questions or conversations which might relate to them. However, because of this, he at once felt out of it. These people were better informed than he was—had been to colleges. Perhaps he had better claim that he had been to some school. In Kansas City he had heard of the State University of Kansas—not so very far from there. Also the University of Missouri. And in Chicago of the University of Chicago. Could he say that he had been to one of those—that Kansas one, for a little while, anyway? On the instant he proposed to claim it, if asked, and then look up afterwards what, if anything, he was supposed to know about it—what, for instance, he might have studied. He had heard of mathematics somewhere. Why not that? But these people, as he could see, were too much interested in themselves to pay much attention to him now. He might be a Griffiths and important to some outside, but here not so much—a matter of course, as it were. And because Tracy Trumbull for the moment had turned to say something to Wynette Phant, he felt quite alone, beached and helpless and with no one to talk to. But just then the small, dark girl, Gertrude, came over to him.

"The crowd's a little late in getting together. It always is. If we said eight, they'd come at eight-thirty or nine. Isn't that always the way?"

"It certainly is," replied Clyde gratefully, endeavoring to appear as brisk and as much at ease as possible.

"I'm Gertrude Trumbull," she repeated. "The sister of the good-looking Jill," a cynical and yet amused smile played about her mouth and eyes. "You nodded to me, but you don't know me. Just the same we've been hearing a lot about you." She teased in an attempt to trouble Clyde a little, if possible. "A mysterious Griffiths here in Lycurgus whom no one seems to have met. I saw you once in Central Avenue, though. You were going into Rich's candy store. You didn't know that, though. Do you like candy?"

"Oh, yes, I like candy. Why?" asked Clyde on the instant feeling teased and disturbed, since the girl for whom he was buying the candy was Roberta. At the same time he could not help feeling slightly more at ease with this girl than with some others, for although cynical and not so attractive, her manner was genial and she now spelled escape from isolation and hence diffidence.

"You're probably just saying that," she laughed, a bantering look in her eyes. "More likely you were buying it for some girl. You have a girl, haven't you?"

"Why—" Clyde paused for the fraction of a second because as she asked this Roberta came into his mind and the query, "Had any one ever seen him with Roberta?" flitted through his brain. Also thinking at the same time, what a bold, teasing, intelligent girl this was, different from any that thus far he had known. Yet quite without more pause he added: "No, I haven't. What makes you ask that?" As he said this there came to him the thought of what Roberta would think if she could hear him. "But what a question," he continued a little nervously now. "You like to tease, don't you?"

"Who, me? Oh, no. I wouldn't do anything like that. But I'm sure you have just the same. I like to ask questions sometimes, just to see what people will say when they don't want you to know what they really think." She beamed into Clyde's eyes amusedly and defiantly. "But I know you have a girl just the same. All good-looking fellows have."

"Oh, am I good-looking?" he beamed nervously, amused and yet pleased. "Who said so?"

"As though you didn't know. Well, different people. I for one. And Sondra Finchley thinks you're good-looking, too. She's only interested in men who are. So does my sister Jill, for that matter. And she only likes men who are good-looking. I'm different because I'm not so good-looking myself." She blinked cynically and teasingly into his eyes, which caused him to feel oddly out of place, not able to cope with such a girl at all, at the same time very much flattered and amused. "But don't you think you're better looking than your cousin," she went on sharply and even commandingly. "Some people think you are." Although a little staggered and yet flattered by this question which propounded what he might have liked to believe, and although intrigued by this girl's interest in him, still Clyde would not have dreamed of venturing any such assertion even though he had believed it. Too vividly it brought the aggressive and determined and even at times revengeful-looking features of Gilbert before him, who, stirred by such a report as this, would not hesitate to pay him out.

"Why I don't think anything of the kind," he laughed. "Honest, I don't. Of course I don't."

"Oh, well, then maybe you don't, but you are just the same. But that won't help you much either, unless you have money—that is, if you want to run with people who have." She looked up at him and added quite blandly. "People like money even more than they do looks." What a sharp girl this was, he thought, and what a hard, cold statement. It cut him not a little, even though she had not intended that it should. But just then Sondra herself entered with some youth whom Clyde did not know—a tall, gangling, but very smartly-dressed individual. And after them, along with others, Bertine and Stuart Finchley.

"Here she is now," added Gertrude a little spitefully, for she resented the fact that Sondra was so much better-looking than either she or her sister, and that she had expressed an interest in Clyde. "She'll be looking to see if you notice how pretty she looks, so don't disappoint her." The impact of this remark, a reflection of the exact truth, was not necessary to cause Clyde to gaze attentively, and even eagerly. For apart from her local position and means and taste in dress and manners, Sondra was of the exact order and spirit that most intrigued him—a somewhat refined (and because of means and position showered upon her) less savage, although scarcely less self-centered, Hortense Briggs. She was, in her small, intense way, a seeking Aphrodite, eager to prove to any who were sufficiently attractive the destroying power of her charm, while at the same time retaining her own personality and individuality free of any entangling alliance or compromise. However, for varying reasons which she could not quite explain to herself, Clyde appealed to her. He might not be anything socially or financially, but he was interesting to her. Hence she was now keen, first to see if he were present, next to be sure that he gained no hint that she had seen him first, and lastly to act as grandly as possible for his benefit—a Hortensian procedure and type of thought that was exactly the thing best calculated to impress him. He gazed and there she was—tripping here and there in a filmy chiffon dance frock, shaded from palest yellow to deepest orange, which most enhanced her dark eyes and hair. And having exchanged a dozen or more "Oh, Hellos," and references with one and another to this, that and the other local event, she at last condescended to evince awareness of his proximity.

"Oh, here you are. You decided to come after all. I wasn't sure whether you would think it worth while. You've been introduced to everybody, of course?" She looked around as much as to say, that if he had not been she would proceed to serve him in this way. The others, not so very much impressed by Clyde, were still not a little interested by the fact that she seemed so interested in him.

"Yes, I met nearly everybody, I think."

"Except Freddie Sells. He came in with me just now. Here you are, Freddie," she called to a tall and slender youth, smooth of cheek and obviously becurled as to hair, who now came over and in his closely-fitting dress coat looked down on Clyde about as a spring rooster might look down on a sparrow.

"This is Clyde Griffiths, I was telling you about, Fred," she began briskly. "Doesn't he look a lot like Gilbert?"

"Why, you do at that," exclaimed this amiable person, who seemed to be slightly troubled with weak eyes since he bent close. "I hear you're a cousin of Gil's. I know him well. We went through Princeton together. I used to be over here before I joined the General Electric over at Schenectady. But I'm around a good bit yet. You're connected with the factory, I suppose."

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, who, before a youth of obviously so much more training and schooling than he possessed, felt not a little reduced. He began to fear that this individual would try to talk to him about things which he could not understand, things concerning which, having had no consecutive training of any kind, he had never been technically informed.

"In charge of some department, I suppose?"

"Yes, I am," said Clyde, cautiously and nervously.

"You know," went on Mr. Sells, briskly and interestingly, being of a commercial as well as technical turn, "I've always wondered just what, outside of money, there is to the collar business. Gil and I used to argue about that when we were down at college. He used to try to tell me that there was some social importance to making and distributing collars, giving polish and manner to people who wouldn't otherwise have them, if it weren't for cheap collars. I think he musta read that in a book somewhere. I always laughed at him." Clyde was about to attempt an answer, although already beyond his depth in regard to this. "Social importance." Just what did he mean by that—some deep, scientific information that he had acquired at college. He was saved a non-committal or totally uninformed answer by Sondra who, without thought or knowledge of the difficulty which was then and there before him, exclaimed: "Oh, no arguments, Freddie. That's not interesting. Besides I want him to meet my brother and Bertine. You remember Miss Cranston. She was with me at your uncle's last spring." Clyde turned, while Fred made the best of the rebuff by merely looking at Sondra, whom he admired so very much.

"Yes, of course," Clyde began, for he had been studying these two along with others. To him, apart from Sondra, Bertine seemed exceedingly attractive, though quite beyond his understanding also. Being involved, insincere and sly, she merely evoked in him a troubled sense of ineffectiveness, and hence uncertainty, in so far as her particular world was concerned—no more.

"Oh, how do you do? It's nice to see you again," she drawled, the while her greenish-gray eyes went over him in a smiling and yet indifferent and quizzical way. She thought him attractive, but not nearly as shrewd and hard as she would have preferred him to be. "You've been terribly busy with your work, I suppose. But now that you've come out once, I suppose we'll see more of you here and there."

"Well, I hope so," he replied, showing his even teeth. Her eyes seemed to be saying that she did not believe what she was saying and that he did not either, but that it was necessary, possibly amusing, to say something of the sort. And a related, though somewhat modified, version of this same type of treatment was accorded him by Stuart, Sondra's brother.
