It was not until the lamps had been brought in, and Bridges, with his inveterate air of having been, in the matter of the curtains, a party to some arrangement more delicate than any he would ever be asked to explain, had drawn them across the long grey windows and withdrawn, that Cecily Marchbank allowed herself to recognise that she had been waiting. She put it to herself, with a small inward wince at the commonness of the image, that she had been waiting very much as one waits at a station for a train one has been told is not coming. Her husband was in the house. She had heard him, a quarter of an hour since, let himself in below with that particular economy of sound which she had long ago learned to take for consideration and had lately, so lately that she could have named the very hour, begun to take for something else. He had gone, as he always went, to his own room. He would come, as he always came, when he had done whatever it was that a man did, at that hour, with his gloves and his letters and the half-dozen small certitudes of his day. And she would be there, as she was always there, in the low chair by the fire, with the book she had not read open upon her knee, to receive him. The whole thing was, she reflected, so beautifully in order that the order itself had come, in the course of the afternoon, to strike her as the most extraordinary circumstance of all.

For it was in the afternoon, and in this very room, that old Mr. Prothero had sat for twenty minutes on the edge of the yellow sofa and, in the gentlest manner in the world, taken the floor from under her. He had not, poor man, the least notion of what he did. That was precisely what she had found, while he was still there and she was still pouring out his tea, so nearly unbearable. Had he come with an intention she might have met it; one could always meet an intention, could turn it, could even, with a little luck, make a friend of it. But he had come with nothing but a paper to be signed and the remains of an affection for her father, and he had let the thing drop as one lets drop a glove, stooping to recover it with a little apologetic sound only after it had lain for a perceptible moment on the carpet between them. "And of course, my dear lady, in the matter of Mr. Vane's allowance, Mr. Marchbank's instructions continue exactly as before; you are not to give it a thought." She had given it, since, nothing else. She had given it the whole of the grey hour that followed his departure, and she was giving it now, with the fire hot on her cheek and her hands quite cold, the last of her attention before the door should open.

The door opened, and Hugh came in.

He came in, as she was afterwards to think, exactly as he would have come in on any day of the eleven years. That was the first of the things she had to take from him, and she took it, so to speak, without moving. He was a large, fair, quiet man, with the look, which strangers found reassuring and which she had once found so too, of having long since settled every question that could possibly be put to him and of being prepared, should a new one turn up, to settle it with the same mild thoroughness. He crossed to her, touched her hair with the lightest of hands, a touch that was hardly more than a recognition that she was there, and stood with his back to the fire, looking down at her book.

"You've got on with it?"

"Not in the least."

"Ah," he said, and seemed to accept the failure as he accepted most things, as a fact that took its place among other facts. "It's a dull book, perhaps."

"It's a perfectly brilliant book. It's I who have been dull." She closed it upon her finger, and then, as if the finger too were a sort of pretence, drew it out and laid the volume aside. "Mr. Prothero has been here."

She had meant to say it without emphasis, and she believed she had succeeded; but she saw, or thought she saw, in the very blankness with which he received it, that the absence of emphasis had itself been a kind of emphasis. He had always been able to hear what she did not say. It came over her now, with a slow, cold thoroughness, that she had for years been grateful for this.

"Has he, dear old thing? What did he want?"

"Oh, only my name to something. The Hampshire leases, I think. He was very kind." She paused, and then, because there was nothing for it but to go on, she went on. "He was particularly kind about you."

Hugh lifted his eyebrows by the smallest fraction. "About me?"

"About your instructions. He wished me to know that they continue exactly as before." She heard her voice give each word its full value, as one counts out coins upon a counter. "I wasn't, he said, to give it a thought."

There followed a silence in which the little French clock on the chimney-piece made itself heard as it had perhaps never before been permitted to. Hugh did not move. He continued to stand with his hands behind him, and the firelight, coming up from below, did odd things to the familiar planes of his face. They gave it, she thought, the look of a face seen for the first time, or rather, which was worse, of a face seen for the first time by someone who had known it always. She waited. It was her one advantage, she felt, that she could wait. And yet she perceived almost at once that it was not an advantage at all, since he could so evidently wait too, and could do it, besides, with a sort of large patience that made her own seem by comparison only a held breath.

"Well," he said at last, "you mustn't."

"Mustn't what?"

"Give it a thought. He was quite right."

"Oh, Hugh!" It broke from her before she could stop it, and she was sorry, for it was the note of the injured wife, and she had promised herself whatever else might happen not to strike that. "You don't suppose I can let it go at that?"

"I suppose," he said, "that you can do anything you like. You always could."

She looked at him. "Is that what you call it? That I could do anything I liked?"

"What else should I call it?"

"I should call it," she said, "that you let me."

He received this, she saw, as a man receives a blow he has been expecting for so long that its arrival is almost a relief. He moved away from the fire at last, went to the window, put a finger between the curtains as if to see whether it still rained, and came back. It was characteristic of him, she reflected, that even his agitation should take the form of a little tour of inspection.

"I'm not sure," he said, "that I follow you."

"You follow me perfectly. You've followed me for two years. That's just it, isn't it? You've followed me every step." She had risen without knowing it, and stood now with one hand on the back of her chair, facing him across the small bright space of the hearthrug. "When I first began to send it to Bertie, when I first sat at that table and wrote to Mr. Prothero that I wished a sum set aside, quarterly, from what my mother left me, and that I wished it done quietly, how long was it before you knew?"

"Does it matter?"

"It matters more than anything in the world."

He seemed to consider. It was, she thought, the dreadful fairness of him that he really did consider. He gave the question its due, as he gave everything its due. "Prothero came to me," he said at length, "within the month. He had to. You'll remember the amount you named."

"I remember it."

"And you'll remember, perhaps, what you had."

She did remember. She remembered with a clearness that made her colour. It had not, at the time, seemed to her a question of arithmetic at all. It had seemed a question of Bertie, of Bertie at Boulogne with his poor shabby wife and his worse than shabby name, of Bertie whom Hugh had said, three years before, in this very room and in the mildest of voices, that he could not again receive. She had not argued then. She had simply gone on, in the silence that followed, to do the thing she could not have done had she argued; and she had believed, she had been able for two years to believe, that she did it out of her own small store, by her own small sacrifice, in her own small secret. She had gone without things. She had been, in her quiet way, rather proud of the things she went without.

"It wasn't enough," she said.

"It wasn't half enough."

"And so you made it up."

"And so I made it up."

"Every quarter."

"Every quarter."

The repetitions fell between them like stones into a well, and she listened to each one strike. "And you never said a word."

"What word was there to say?"

"Oh!" She turned from him, and then, since there was nowhere in the room to turn to, turned back. "There were a thousand. There was only one that you mightn't have said, and that was precisely the one you chose: nothing at all."

He looked at her with an expression she could not at first read, and when she read it she wished she had not, for it was a kind of tenderness, and it was the last thing she could at that moment bear. "My dear," he said, "you had made up your mind not to tell me."

"Yes."

"You had made it up, I take it, because you knew what I thought."

"I knew what you had said."

"It comes to the same thing, between us. Doesn't it?" He waited, but she gave him nothing, and he went on. "Very well. You had decided, and you had decided against me. You had a perfect right to. Bertie is your brother. I had my reasons, and I don't withdraw them; but I never supposed they were reasons you were obliged to share. What was I to do? Come to you and say that I'd found you out? Make you account to me? Make you choose, after all, between giving the thing up and doing it under my eye, with my leave, as a thing I had graciously consented to? You'd have hated that."

"I should have hated it," she said, "less than this."

"Than what?"

"Than having done it under your eye without knowing your eye was there."

He was silent. The clock, which had been so loud, seemed to have stopped; she found herself glancing at it, absurdly, to be sure.

"You talk," he said slowly, "as if I'd been watching you."

"Haven't you?"

"I've been doing nothing in the world," he said, "but leaving you alone."

It was so exactly true, and so exactly the heart of the matter, that for a moment she could only stand and look at it. He had left her alone. He had left her alone with a completeness, a delicacy, a positive genius of abstention, that had allowed her to keep her secret and to be proud of it, to make her little sacrifices and to feel their sharpness, to sit across the table from him at dinner with her small superb consciousness of having outwitted him in the one matter in which she had ever opposed him. And all the while it had been he who paid. Not merely in money; she could have borne the money. He had paid in this, in the having to see her play at her poor brave game, and in the having to let her win it.

"Then what," she asked, very low, "have I been all this while? What have I been doing, if it wasn't what I thought?"

"You've been doing what you thought."

"No. I've been doing what you allowed me to think I was doing. It's not the same. You must see it's not the same."

"I see," he said, "that you'd rather I had stopped you."

"I'd rather you had stopped me than have carried me."

He took that, and she saw it go home. He had, she knew, a horror of phrases; he distrusted them as he distrusted foreigners and early hours. But this one he did not dismiss. He stood with it, so to speak, held up before him, and turned it in the light.

"Carried you," he repeated. "Is that how it looks?"

"How else can it look? I thought I was walking. I thought, Hugh, God forgive me, that I was rather fine at it. And all the time—" She broke off, for she had felt her voice begin to go, and she would not, she would not, have it go now. "All the time you had your arm under mine, and I never felt it. That's what I can't forgive. Not that you did it. That you did it so well."

"Would you have had me do it badly?"

"I'd have had you do it so that I knew."

"But then," he said, and for the first time there was something in his voice that was not quite steady, something she had never heard in it and could not have named, "then you'd have had nothing. Don't you see? It would have been mine. The whole thing, Bertie, and the money, and the being good to him in spite of me. It would have all been mine, done by my leave, paid for by my cheque, and you'd have stood by and been grateful. I didn't want your gratitude. I wanted you to have it. I wanted you to have the thing itself."

"The thing itself," she echoed. "And what was the thing itself?"

"The having done it alone."

"But I didn't do it alone. That's the one thing I didn't do."

"You did it in everything that mattered."

"Who," she asked, "was to say what mattered?"

He opened his lips, and then closed them again; and in the interval she understood that he had been about to say "I," and had seen in time that it was the one word which, of all words, would finish them. She watched him not say it. It was, she thought, almost the finest thing she had ever seen him do, and it was at the same time the thing which, more than any other, made her feel how entirely, how hopelessly, she had been living for two years inside the walls of his discretion, as one lives inside a house one has been told one owns.

She sat down again, because her knees, she found, had very little more to say in the matter. He remained standing. For a while neither spoke, and she was conscious of the room about them, the lamps, the books, the yellow sofa where Mr. Prothero had sat, as of so many witnesses who had been present at a great many scenes and had never yet been present at one quite like this.

"There's something else," she said presently, "that I want to ask you."

"Ask it."

"Is there anything, anything at all, of that sort, that you know and that I don't know you know?"

He looked at her for a long moment. "Of what sort?"

"Of the sort where you've seen, and said nothing, and made it up. Where you've stood behind me." She lifted her eyes to his. "I want to know how many of these rooms I've been living in."

He did not answer at once, and his not answering was, she felt, the worst answer he could have given and at the same time the most honest. When he spoke it was gently, with that terrible gentleness of his that seemed to have no bottom to it. "If I told you, should you be any happier?"

"I don't ask to be happier. I ask to know."

"Ah," he said, "but you see, my dear, that's just what I've never been able to manage: to give you the one without taking away the other."

She sat quite still. She heard the rain now, faintly, against the glass behind the curtains, and the sound of a cab in the street, and somewhere below the muffled closing of a door. It occurred to her, with a curious detachment, that she might at this moment rise and leave the room, the house, the whole beautiful ordered fabric of their life; and it occurred to her in the same instant that she would do nothing of the kind, and that he knew she would do nothing of the kind, and that he had known it, very possibly, before he came in. Yet the knowledge did not, as she would have expected, add to her humiliation. It seemed, rather, to have passed beyond humiliation into some other region altogether, a region where they stood, the two of them, for the first time on the same ground and could look at each other across it.

"Then what," she asked at last, "is there that you don't know?"

He considered this too. She could see him consider it, honestly, with his large fair face bent a little towards the fire, as though the answer might be found among the coals.

"What you'll do now," he said.

She let that settle. It settled, she thought, not as a stone settles but as something lighter, a feather, a flake of ash, turning once or twice in the warm air before it found the hearth.

"That," she said, "is what I don't know either."

He looked up quickly, and their eyes met; and for an instant, a single strange instant which she was afterwards to turn over a hundred times without wearing it out, something passed between them that was neither forgiveness nor its refusal, neither the old order restored nor the new one declared, but simply the recognition, on either side, that there was at last a thing in the world which neither of them knew and which they would have, from this hour, to find out together.

"Well," he said, very quietly, "that's something."

"Is it?"

"It's something," he repeated, "that we've never had before."

She did not reply. She reached instead for the book she had laid aside and opened it, at random, upon her knee, and looked down at the page without seeing it, while he, after a moment, sat down in the chair opposite and stretched his hands to the fire. They remained so until Bridges came to tell them that dinner was served. It was, she was to think afterwards, the first time in their life together that they had been so absolutely in the same place; and she could not for the life of her have said whether it was the bottom of something or the top.

It was not until the carriage had actually turned in at the gate, and the sound of its wheels on the gravel had come up to him through the open window with the peculiar flatness of a thing long expected, that Gilbert Treherne admitted to himself he had been, all the afternoon, rather more than merely attentive. He had told himself he was reading; he had a volume open on his knee to prove it; but the volume, he was aware, had been open at the same place since luncheon, and the place had nothing in it. What it had, if anything, was the light. That had been, through the long June hours, a kind of occupation in itself, the slow travelling of it across the faded carpet of the library, across the brass of the fender and the dull gilt of the frames, and he had followed it as a man in a waiting-room follows the hands of the clock, not because they tell him anything, but because they so beautifully refuse to.

He got up now, all the same, and he got up, he was conscious, with a promptness that would have amused her had she seen it. That was the first of his perceptions, and it struck him, even as he crossed the hall, as wonderfully characteristic of the whole situation that his first thought of her should be of what she would make of him. It had always been so. It had been so at nineteen, when she was seventeen and had made of him, by turns, a great many things he had never meant to be. It had been so through the eighteen years since, in which she had made of him, he could only suppose, nothing at all, or nothing beyond the occasional figure at the foot of a letter written at Christmas. He had kept her letters, and she had doubtless not kept his; it was the kind of difference that had once filled him with a sense of injury and that now, as he stood at the door and watched the horses pulled up, filled him only with a mild, a curious, an almost scientific interest.

She was out of the carriage before the man could get down, and that too was like her. It was like her, or like what she had been. She stood for a moment on the step with her hand still upon the door, looking up, not at him, but at the house, the long grey front of it with its row of windows and the clipped yew at either end. And it was in this moment, the moment before she had so much as found his face, that he had his chance at her, and took it, and was struck.

She was older, of course; that was the least of it. She was older as he was older, and he had braced himself for that as one braces oneself for a cold bath, with the knowledge that the shock, once over, would be over. What he had not braced himself for was that she should be, in some sense he could not at once have named, *more*. She had always been vivid; she was now, as it were, composed. The vividness was all there, he could see it in the very angle of her head; but it had been taken in hand, arranged, put to some use he could only guess at. She looked like a woman who had learned a great many things in places where he had never been, and who had come back, not to tell them, but to see whether they would still hold.

"Well," she said, when at last her eyes came down to him, "you've kept it."

He knew she meant the house. "I've done nothing else."

"Ah, that's not true. But it's charming of you to say it." She came up the two steps and gave him her hand, and then, as if the hand were insufficient, and with a little laugh at its insufficiency, her cheek. "Dear Gilbert. You look exactly as I knew you would."

"That's either very kind or very cruel."

"It's neither. It's only very true. It's what I came for."

He didn't ask her what she meant; he had learned, long ago, that the questions one asked her were the questions she had arranged for one to ask, and he preferred, on this occasion, to keep his own counsel a little longer. He took her in, and the servants took her things, and in the cool dimness of the hall she stood again and looked about her with the same air she had worn upon the step, the air, as he now made it out, of someone verifying an inventory.

"The clock," she said. "And Aunt Clementina's hideous Chinese bowl. And the smell, Gilbert. Do you know it has the same smell?"

"I'm afraid I've ceased to notice it."

"That's because you've never been away. One has to go away to have a smell at all." She turned to him with a sudden brightness. "I've had a great many smells since I saw you last."

"I don't doubt it. You must tell me about them."

"Oh, I shall tell you about everything. That is, about everything that can be told. And you'll tell me about the rest."

He found himself smiling at this, though he could not have said whether at her or at the formula. "The rest, my dear Maud, will hardly fill an afternoon."

"Then we'll take two," she answered; and on this she went up to take off her hat.

---

They had tea on the terrace, where the shadow of the house had by this time reached the edge of the lawn and stopped there, as if in deference to the cedar. She had changed into something grey and soft that made her, to his eye, both younger and more remote, and she sat with her cup in her lap and her gaze on the long slope of the garden, and for some minutes neither of them said anything at all. It was a silence he would not have dared to break, and that he was, in a manner, proud of; it seemed to him to prove that they could still have it, the old capacity for not needing to speak, and he cherished it as one cherishes a relic, with the faint fear that it might not bear handling.

It was she, naturally, who handled it.

"You've not married," she said.

"You knew that."

"I knew it in the sense of having been told. I didn't know it in the sense of having seen it. One has to see these things." She turned her eyes upon him with an expression of the frankest appraisal. "And now I see it. It's quite complete, isn't it? It's as finished as the house."

"You make me sound like a piece of furniture."

"No, no. Furniture is put somewhere. You've *placed* yourself, which is a very different thing. You've done it beautifully. I don't think I've ever seen anyone so perfectly where he meant to be."

He considered this. It was the sort of remark she had always had a genius for making, at once so flattering and so faintly appalling that one didn't know whether to bow or to protest; and he had, in the old days, generally done both, with the result of appearing a fool. He did neither now. He merely let it rest a moment between them, as one lets a coin lie on the table to see which side is up.

"And you," he said at last, "were you where you meant to be?"

She gave a short laugh. "Ah, that's the question, isn't it? That's the one I've been waiting for."

"Then I'm glad I've not disappointed you."

"You never did. That was precisely your—" But she stopped; she put down her cup; she seemed for an instant to look at what she had been about to say and to decide that it would keep. "I was in a great many places," she went on, in a different tone, "and in most of them I meant to be somewhere else. That's the condition, I suppose, of people who go abroad. They're always on the point of arriving."

"And Mr. Rainsford?"

He had wondered how he would manage the name, and he was conscious, now that it was out, of having managed it rather well. It had come with the right lightness and the right gravity, and it had come, above all, as a question, which left her free to make of it whatever she chose.

She made of it, for a moment, nothing. She looked down at her hands, which were clasped in her lap, and he saw that she wore still the ring he had never seen her put on.

"Edmund," she said presently, "was a very good man. You'd have liked him. Everyone liked him. He was the kind of man about whom there was nothing whatever to say except that one liked him, and I said it, you know, for fourteen years." She raised her eyes. "That's not a complaint. Don't think it a complaint. It's only a description."

"I didn't think it a complaint."

"No, you wouldn't. You'd think it something much worse. You'd think it a confession."

"Is it?"

"Oh," she said, with a fine vagueness, "everything one says to you is a confession. That's what makes you so dangerous." And then, as if she had gone further than she intended, she looked away again at the garden. "The cedar's grown."

"Trees do."

"Not all of them. Some of them stop. Some of them are struck." She paused. "Do you remember the evening of Aunt Clementina's party, when the band played and we all came out here because the drawing-room was so hot?"

He remembered it, as it happened, a good deal better than he had any wish to own. "There were so many of Aunt Clementina's parties."

"There was only one where the band played. She thought it vulgar afterwards and never had it again." Maud smiled. "You stood just there, by the urn. I was over by the cedar with that dreadful young man from the Foreign Office who wanted me to admire his moustache. And you never came over."

"I don't think I was asked."

"No," she said slowly. "No, you weren't. That was the point."

---

They walked, after tea, down through the garden, by the long border where the delphiniums were at their height and the bees went in and out of them with a sort of drowsy persistence, and on to the low wall at the bottom, beyond which the fields fell away towards the river. It was the old walk, the inevitable walk; they took it, he felt, as two people take a familiar road in the dark, not by seeing, but by remembering where the turns had been.

She asked him about the neighbours, and he told her; she asked him about the vicar, and the vicar's wife, and the Misses Pendle who had once seemed so old and who were, it appeared, older still and quite indestructible; and he answered her with a fullness that surprised himself. He had not known how much he had to tell. It had seemed to him, all these years, that nothing happened at Fallowfield, that the days fell one upon another like leaves in a still wood; and here he was, producing for her a whole history, a chronicle of small events, each of which, in the telling, took on a kind of shape it had not had in the living. He was aware that she was listening with the most delicate attention, and he was aware, too, that the attention was less to what he said than to the fact of his saying it, as if she were measuring, by the very abundance of his talk, the depth of the silence it had been accumulated in.

At the wall she stopped and laid her two hands upon the warm stone.

"You've been very happy," she said.

It was not a question, and he did not treat it as one. "I've been very quiet."

"It's the same thing, for you. It was always the same thing. That's what I couldn't—" Again she broke off. "That's what I didn't understand."

"And you understand it now?"

"I understand that I didn't understand it. That's as far as one gets, I think, at our time of life." She looked out over the fields. "When I went away, Gilbert, I thought I was going to find something. I didn't know what. I thought it was out there"—she made a small gesture towards the horizon, towards all the vague, glittering, unvisited distances of the world—"and that you, by staying, were simply refusing to look for it. I thought you were afraid."

"Perhaps I was."

"No. That's the thing. I've come back to find that you weren't. You simply didn't need to look, because you'd already—" She turned to him, and for the first time since her arrival there was something in her face that was neither arranged nor composed, something that looked out at him with the old, the unguarded, the dreadfully direct gaze of seventeen. "Had you, Gilbert? Had you already found it?"

He took his time. He had a sense, which he would afterwards recall with a kind of wonder, that the whole of the long afternoon, and indeed the whole of the long eighteen years, had been leading up to this one small question at the bottom of the garden; and that it was, therefore, a question that deserved a better answer than any he could on the instant supply. He looked at her hands on the wall. He looked at the ring.

"I'd found," he said at last, "that one could go on."

"Go on without?"

"Go on with what one had."

She was silent for a long moment. Then she said, very low: "And what had you?"

"Oh," he answered, with a lightness that cost him, he was afterwards to reflect, about as much as anything had ever cost him, "I had the house. I had the garden. I had the Misses Pendle." He paused, and then, because it was there and because she had come so far to hear it, he added: "And I had, you know, the knowledge that you were somewhere."

"Somewhere," she repeated.

"Somewhere having your smells."

She laughed, but the laugh was not quite steady. "That was enough for you?"

"It had to be. And it turned out, rather to my surprise, that it was."

---

They went back up the garden in the long gold light of the evening, slowly, and without much speech. He felt that something had been settled, though he could not have said precisely what; and he felt, too, that she felt it, and that she was turning it over, as she had always turned things over, to see what it was made of and how much it would bear. At the foot of the terrace steps she stopped once more, by the old stone urn, and put her hand upon its rim.

"This is where you stood," she said.

"So you tell me."

"And I was over there." She looked across the lawn at the dark spread of the cedar. "It's not very far, is it? I used to think it was the whole width of the world."

"It was, then."

"Yes." She was quiet. "It was, then. And now it's only a lawn." She turned to him with something that was very nearly the old brightness, though it had in it, he thought, a new and rather touching courage. "Do you know why I came back, Gilbert?"

"To see whether I'd kept the house."

"To see whether you'd kept *anything*. Whether there was anything left to keep." She drew a breath. "I've been a widow two years. I've been, in all that time, a great many places, and I've had, in all of them, a great many people being kind to me. And I found that the only person in the world to whom I wanted to say—" She stopped, and he saw her make, with an effort that was almost visible, the decision to go on. "To whom I wanted to say that I had been wrong, was you."

"Wrong about what?"

"About the width of the lawn."

He stood very still. The light was going off the top of the cedar now, and a blackbird, somewhere in the shrubbery, had begun its long liquid evening argument with itself. He was aware of an immense temptation, a temptation so large and so simple that it seemed to him for an instant to fill the whole garden, and he was aware too, and as distinctly, of the reasons, the fine, the many, the eighteen-years-accumulated reasons, against it. It was not that he did not feel what she offered. It was that he felt it so completely, and with so clear a sense of what it was worth, that he could not bear to take it at less than its value. And its value, he saw, its whole and beautiful value, lay just in its being offered here, at the foot of the steps, by the urn, in the last of the light, and in its being, so offered, already more than either of them could have hoped to have.

"My dear," he said gently, "you weren't wrong. You were only seventeen."

She looked at him for a long moment. Then something in her face gave way, not into tears, as he had half feared, but into a kind of smile, wan and comprehending and infinitely wise.

"And now I'm thirty-five," she said, "and you're thirty-seven, and it's a lawn."

"It's a very pretty lawn."

"It is. It's the prettiest lawn in England. You've kept it beautifully." She took her hand from the urn. "Shall we go in? I believe I've had, for one evening, as much as I can carry."

"And so much more than we came for," he said.

She paused on the step above him and looked down, and in the dusk he could not quite see her expression.

"Then we've had it, you know," she said.

"Had what?"

"Why, all of it. All of it—" she turned and went on up toward the lighted windows, so that the last words came back to him over her shoulder, faint and clear—"all of it but the thing itself."

He stood there a little longer, after she had gone in, alone by the urn in the deepening blue, and listened to the blackbird finish its argument; and it seemed to him, as he listened, that the bird had come at last, after so much debate, to a conclusion it could live with; and that it was, on the whole, and all things considered, not a bad one.

It was not till the door had fairly closed upon Mrs. Dacre-Wilmot, and the sound of her carriage had diminished, by the stages of a retreat to which Mrs. Stannard found herself attending with an almost morbid acuteness, into the general murmur of the Square, that she permitted herself to recognise how much, in the course of the last quarter of an hour, had been taken out of her hands. She stood for a moment where her visitor had left her, beside the little table on which the tea-things still kept up, in their silver and their porcelain, the brave pretence of an occasion that had gone off; and she was conscious, as she looked at them, of a queer reluctance to ring for their removal, as if to do so were to admit, before the servants at least, that there had been anything in the afternoon to remove. There had been, heaven knew, quite enough; there had been, in fact, precisely the one thing that she had spent the better part of three seasons in arranging should never, under any pressure, be produced; and it had been produced, with a lucidity she could only call appalling, by a person of seven who had come down, in a clean frock and with her hair freshly brushed, to be looked at.

She had wanted her to be looked at. That was the beauty of it, as Mrs. Stannard put the matter to herself with the irony that was perhaps her only immediate resource. She had expressly desired, for reasons she would not have cared to set forth at length even to her husband, that Mrs. Dacre-Wilmot should see the child, should take in, so to speak, the whole charming domestic picture, and should carry away from Bryanston Square an impression not merely of a pretty drawing-room and a punctual tea but of something finer and more settled, a household in which things were, as one said, *right*. Nina was, after all, a decidedly presentable small person; she had her father's grave grey eyes and a way of standing with her hands folded before her that the governess, Miss Pengelly, had cultivated with a patience her employer had more than once had occasion to bless. It had seemed the simplest thing in the world. One sent up word; the child appeared; the visitor said something gracious; the child said something prettier; and the whole little transaction left behind it that faint fragrance of the nursery which, as Mrs. Stannard had observed, softened even the hardest of her acquaintance. She had not, it was clear to her now, sufficiently considered what the child might say.

What Nina had said, after a pause in which she had appeared to take Mrs. Dacre-Wilmot in with a thoroughness her mother had at the time thought merely shy, was: "Are you the lady Mamma says one simply *has* to have?"

It had not, in the event, been followed by any catastrophe that a stranger would have recognised. Mrs. Dacre-Wilmot was a woman of the world, and the world had long since taught her, among its other lessons, the supreme one of not hearing. She had laughed; she had said "Dear little thing!" in a voice that was all sweetness and that rang, to her hostess's ear, with the clear cold note of a bell struck once; she had asked Nina whether she liked her lessons, and had received, Mrs. Stannard dimly remembered, some answer about the Kings of England; and she had stayed, with an exquisite observance of every decency, a full eight minutes longer than she would otherwise have stayed, before rising with the remark that she had "a hundred places" still to go. Mrs. Stannard knew perfectly what the eight minutes had meant. They had been a gift, and a gift of such a kind that the receiving of it was itself the humiliation. One could have borne, she reflected, a coldness, a stiffening, even an early departure; what one could scarcely bear was to be so beautifully let off.

She rang at last, not for the tea-things but for the child; and while she waited she moved, without quite knowing why, to the window, where the light of the March afternoon lay thin and colourless over the railings and the bare plane-trees, and where she could compose herself, as she would have said, with her back to the room. It was important to compose herself. She had a lively sense, which did her, she supposed, a certain credit, that whatever she said in the next few minutes would be said to a creature who would remember it, and who would remember it, moreover, not in the large approximate fashion of grown persons, who forgot the words and kept only the general tone, but with the terrible literalness of the very young, for whom the words were everything. She must therefore find the right words; and it was precisely here, as she stood drawing her fingers along the edge of the curtain, that she became aware of a difficulty she had not foreseen and that grew, the more she looked at it, into something like a small black abyss.

The difficulty was simply that Nina had told the truth.

It was not that Mrs. Stannard had ever, in so many terms, cultivated in her daughter a passion for veracity; she was not a woman of systems, and she had left the moral side of the nursery, as she had left its arithmetic, very largely to Miss Pengelly, who was the daughter of a Cornish clergyman and might be supposed to understand such things. But it had been understood, in a general way, between herself and the child, that one did not tell stories; and Nina, as her mother now remembered with a sort of chill, had once been deprived of jam for a week for maintaining, against all evidence, that the cat had broken a Chelsea shepherdess which had in point of fact been broken by Nina. The lesson had been learned; one had seen it learned; one had even, at the time, been rather touched by the gravity with which the child had afterwards owned to the smallest delinquencies. And now the lesson had come home, as lessons do, by the door one had least expected, and had walked into the drawing-room in a clean frock, and had looked Mrs. Dacre-Wilmot full in the face.

For she *had* said it. She had said it, Mrs. Stannard could even recall, at luncheon, a fortnight ago, to her husband, across a dish of cutlets, with Nina sitting between them in the high chair from which she had so lately graduated to a cushion; and she had said it, moreover, with a particular little emphasis, a turn of the voice she was rather proud of, which had made Edward look up and smile. "Oh, she's insufferable, of course, but she's one of the women one simply *has* to have." It had seemed at the time the most harmless of domestic sallies. It had been addressed to Edward, and Edward was, in the nature of things, the safest of receptacles; and the child had appeared to be wholly absorbed in the business of reducing a potato to its elements. One had not, it now appeared, reckoned with the elements of the child.

There was a light knock, and Nina came in, accompanied as far as the threshold by Miss Pengelly, whose face expressed in about equal parts a desire to be of use and a lively anxiety to be dismissed. Mrs. Stannard dismissed her with a look; and the door closed, with a softness that seemed to her to have in it something of the governess's own discretion, upon mother and daughter.

Nina advanced some three or four steps and stopped, as she had been taught to stop, with her hands folded. She did not look frightened. That, her mother afterwards thought, was perhaps the first thing that struck her, and struck her, oddly enough, as a kind of reproach. The child looked grave, and she looked attentive, and she had evidently understood from the summons, and from Miss Pengelly's manner on the stairs, that something was the matter; but she had not, it was plain, the faintest notion of what it might be, and she was waiting, with the exemplary patience of her years, to be told.

"Come here to me, Nina."

The child came, and Mrs. Stannard, who had meant to remain standing, found that she had sat down upon the sofa, so that their eyes were now nearly on a level. She had not intended this; she had intended something more in the manner of the bench, and she was conscious that by the mere fact of sitting she had already surrendered a position. But it was done, and she went on from where she was.

"Do you know why I have sent for you?"

Nina considered. "Is it because of the lady?"

"It is because of what you said to the lady."

There was a pause, in which Mrs. Stannard could see the child, as it were, going back over the ground. It was a curious thing to watch, and she watched it with an interest she could not entirely suppress even in the midst of her displeasure: the grey eyes travelling inward, the small brow faintly contracted, the lips moving very slightly as if repeating something under the breath. Then the brow cleared.

"I asked her if she was the one you have to have."

"You did. And it was very wrong of you."

Nina looked at her mother with an expression of the most complete and candid bewilderment. "But you said it, Mamma."

It was exactly what Mrs. Stannard had known she would say; she had heard it, in fact, a dozen times over in the course of her vigil at the window, and had prepared for it, she had supposed, a dozen answers. She found now that none of them would do. They had all been answers for a child who was being impertinent, or sly, or who was, in the vulgar phrase, "answering back"; and Nina was none of these things. She was simply stating a fact, and stating it, moreover, in the tone of one who offers, a little timidly, a piece of evidence that must, she supposes, settle the whole question in her favour.

"I said it to Papa," Mrs. Stannard returned, after a moment. "That is a very different thing."

"Why is it different?"

Ah, why indeed! Mrs. Stannard felt the question settle upon her with a weight out of all proportion to the small voice that had put it. She had a sudden vision, almost comic in its vividness, of herself attempting to explain to this personage of seven the whole elaborate system by which she and Edward, and Mrs. Dacre-Wilmot herself, and everyone they knew, contrived to live together in a state of reasonable comfort: the system of things said in one room and not in another, of things thought always and said never, of faces put on at the door and taken off again on the stairs. It was a system in which she had been bred, and which she had always regarded, so far as she regarded it at all, as merely the condition of civilised life; but it had never before occurred to her that it might require to be *explained*, and she was now made to feel, under the clear unwavering gaze of her daughter, that it would not explain well.

"Because," she said at last, "there are things one says to one's husband, or to one's very nearest friends, that are not meant to be said to anyone else. They are private. You understand what that means, Nina, *private*?"

"Like my diary that Miss Pengelly gave me?"

"Very like that."

"But it wasn't in a diary. You said it out loud, at luncheon." The child paused, and then added, with the air of one who desires above all things to be fair: "And Parkins was there. He was handing the potatoes."

Mrs. Stannard was silent. Parkins had been there; Parkins was always there; Parkins had, she supposed, been handing potatoes to the private utterances of the family for eleven years, and it had never once crossed her mind to regard him as a public. She was aware, very sharply, of a disposition to laugh, and of a stronger disposition, under it, to do something quite different; and she was aware too that she could do neither, that she was here, so to speak, in an official capacity, and that whatever the merits of the case the child must on no account be allowed to suppose that she had won it.

"Nina," she said, and she made her voice as grave as she knew how, "you are not to argue with me. You have done something that has given me a great deal of pain, and that has given pain, I am afraid, to Mrs. Dacre-Wilmot, who has always been very kind to you."

This last was not strictly true; Mrs. Dacre-Wilmot had, to her knowledge, never so much as looked at the child before that afternoon. But it served, she thought, the purposes of the occasion; and she was rewarded by seeing, for the first time, a faint change in Nina's face, a slight trembling at the corners of the mouth, which suggested that the idea of pain, at least, had reached her.

"Did it hurt her?"

"It must have hurt her very much."

"She didn't look hurt. She laughed."

"People often laugh," said Mrs. Stannard, "when they are hurt."

She had not meant to say this either; it had come out of her, as it were, of itself, and she heard it after it had been spoken with a curious little shock, as if it had been said by someone else in the room. The child received it in silence. She was looking, her mother saw, not at her face now but at some point a little below it, at the brooch, perhaps, or at nothing at all; and there was in her look something so considering, so deliberately and patiently occupied, that Mrs. Stannard had the odd impression of having handed her a parcel which she was now, very carefully, undoing.

"Then why," Nina asked presently, "do you have to have her?"

It was the question, of all questions, that Mrs. Stannard would have given most to be spared; and she was the less prepared for it that she had never, in the last three years, quite put it to herself. One had Mrs. Dacre-Wilmot because one had her; because everyone had her; because a house in which she did not appear was a house that people, after a season or two, somehow ceased to think of. It was a necessity of the same order as one's carriage, or one's box at the opera, or the particular shade of grey one's footmen wore; and to ask why one had her was, she obscurely felt, to ask why one had any of these things, which was a question that led, if one were so imprudent as to follow it, to regions where she had no wish to wander and certainly none to conduct her daughter.

"That," she said, "is not a thing for little girls to ask."

"Is it a thing for little girls to know?"

"It is not."

Nina appeared to accept this; or rather, her mother thought, she appeared to file it, to put it away in some small mental cabinet against a future occasion. It was impossible not to see that she had taken a step, that she had moved, in the course of these few minutes, into a region she had not inhabited before, and that she was looking about her with the grave curiosity of a traveller just arrived. Mrs. Stannard had a sudden and very painful sense of having been the one who opened the door.

She felt that she must bring the scene to an end, and that she must end it, if possible, with something that would have the air of a conclusion.

"You must understand, Nina," she began, with a firmness that cost her more than she would have cared to own, "that it is never kind, and never right, to repeat to people the things that are said about them. Even when they are true. *Especially* when they are true. Do you understand me?"

The child lifted her eyes. "Then it is wrong to say true things?"

"It is wrong to say *some* true things. To *some* people."

"But how shall I know which?"

Mrs. Stannard opened her lips to reply, and found that she had nothing whatever to say. How did one know which? She herself knew, she supposed; she knew as a bird knows its way south, without any notion of how she had come by the knowledge or of how it might be conveyed. It was the whole art of life as she had lived it, and she now perceived, with a kind of dismay, that it was an art without rules, without precepts, without anything at all that could be written down in a copy-book or recited to a governess; that it was learned, if it was learned at all, precisely by such scenes as the present one, by blunders and their consequences, by the slow accumulation of afternoons on which one had said the wrong thing and seen the faces change.

"You will learn," she said at last. "Everyone learns."

"Did you have to learn?"

"Yes."

"Did someone punish you?"

Mrs. Stannard looked at her. She had, in fact, a dim recollection of something of the kind, of a drawing-room in Hertfordshire and a tall aunt in purple and a sentence she had overheard about a curate, and of a dark half-hour afterwards in a room that smelt of camphor; but she had not thought of it for thirty years, and she was not sure that she wished to think of it now.

"I daresay," she said. "And that is why, Nina, though I am very sorry to do it, I am afraid that I must punish you too. You will not come down to dessert this evening, and you will not go with Miss Pengelly to the Zoological Gardens on Saturday."

It was, she knew, a severe sentence; the Zoological Gardens had been promised for a month, and the child had talked of nothing else. She waited for the tears she supposed must follow, and was prepared, in spite of herself, to be glad of them, since tears at least would have restored the situation to a footing she understood. But Nina did not cry. She stood for a moment quite still, her hands still folded, and then she said, in a very small but perfectly steady voice:

"Yes, Mamma."

There was a pause.

"You may go now, my dear."

The child turned obediently towards the door; but she had not reached it when she stopped, and looked back, and her mother saw that she was again in the act of considering, that she had found something more in the parcel and was examining it before she let it drop.

"Mamma."

"Well?"

"If I mustn't say it, may I still *think* it?"

Mrs. Stannard did not at once reply. The light at the window had faded while they talked, and the room, with its abandoned tea-table and its cooling silver, had taken on that grey, irresolute look which drawing-rooms wear in the half-hour before the lamps; and in the dimness the little figure by the door seemed to her both smaller than it had been and, in some fashion she could not have defined, more remote, as if it were already standing at a distance from which it would never quite come back.

"Ah, my darling," she said at last, and she was aware, as she said it, that her voice was not altogether under her control, "that is just what we all do."

Nina received this, too, with gravity; she nodded once, as if a doubtful point had been satisfactorily cleared up; and then she was gone, and Mrs. Stannard heard her small feet on the stairs, mounting steadily, without haste, towards the regions where Miss Pengelly waited with the Kings of England. She sat on alone in the darkening room for some minutes longer, and it was only when Parkins came in at last to light the lamps that she roused herself and rang, with an air of the most perfect composure, for the tea-things to be taken away.

Here is an excerpt of Henry James's writing, to show you their style:

Valentin de Bellegarde died tranquilly, just as the cold faint March dawn began to illumine the faces of the little knot of friends gathered about his bedside. An hour afterwards Newman left the inn and drove to Geneva; he was naturally unwilling to be present at the arrival of Madame de Bellegarde and her first-born. At Geneva, for the moment, he remained. He was like a man who has had a fall and wants to sit still and count his bruises. He instantly wrote to Madame de Cintré, relating to her the circumstances of her brother’s death—with certain exceptions—and asking her what was the earliest moment at which he might hope that she would consent to see him. M. Ledoux had told him that he had reason to know that Valentin’s will—Bellegarde had a great deal of elegant personal property to dispose of—contained a request that he should be buried near his father in the churchyard of Fleurières, and Newman intended that the state of his own relations with the family should not deprive him of the satisfaction of helping to pay the last earthly honors to the best fellow in the world. He reflected that Valentin’s friendship was older than Urbain’s enmity, and that at a funeral it was easy to escape notice. Madame de Cintré’s answer to his letter enabled him to time his arrival at Fleurières. This answer was very brief; it ran as follows:— “I thank you for your letter, and for your being with Valentin. It is a most inexpressible sorrow to me that I was not. To see you will be nothing but a distress to me; there is no need, therefore, to wait for what you call brighter days. It is all one now, and I shall have no brighter days. Come when you please; only notify me first. My brother is to be buried here on Friday, and my family is to remain here. C. de C.” As soon as he received this letter Newman went straight to Paris and to Poitiers. The journey took him far southward, through green Touraine and across the far-shining Loire, into a country where the early spring deepened about him as he went. But he had never made a journey during which he heeded less what he would have called the lay of the land. He obtained lodging at the inn at Poitiers, and the next morning drove in a couple of hours to the village of Fleurières. But here, preoccupied though he was, he could not fail to notice the picturesqueness of the place. It was what the French call a petit bourg; it lay at the base of a sort of huge mound on the summit of which stood the crumbling ruins of a feudal castle, much of whose sturdy material, as well as that of the wall which dropped along the hill to enclose the clustered houses defensively, had been absorbed into the very substance of the village. The church was simply the former chapel of the castle, fronting upon its grass-grown court, which, however, was of generous enough width to have given up its quaintest corner to a little graveyard. Here the very headstones themselves seemed to sleep, as they slanted into the grass; the patient elbow of the rampart held them together on one side, and in front, far beneath their mossy lids, the green plains and blue distances stretched away. The way to church, up the hill, was impracticable to vehicles. It was lined with peasants, two or three rows deep, who stood watching old Madame de Bellegarde slowly ascend it, on the arm of her elder son, behind the pall-bearers of the other. Newman chose to lurk among the common mourners who murmured “Madame la Comtesse” as a tall figure veiled in black passed before them. He stood in the dusky little church while the service was going forward, but at the dismal tomb-side he turned away and walked down the hill. He went back to Poitiers, and spent two days in which patience and impatience were singularly commingled. On the third day he sent Madame de Cintré a note, saying that he would call upon her in the afternoon, and in accordance with this he again took his way to Fleurières. He left his vehicle at the tavern in the village street, and obeyed the simple instructions which were given him for finding the château.

“It is just beyond there,” said the landlord, and pointed to the tree-tops of the park, above the opposite houses. Newman followed the first cross-road to the right—it was bordered with mouldy cottages—and in a few moments saw before him the peaked roofs of the towers. Advancing farther, he found himself before a vast iron gate, rusty and closed; here he paused a moment, looking through the bars. The château was near the road; this was at once its merit and its defect; but its aspect was extremely impressive. Newman learned afterwards, from a guide-book of the province, that it dated from the time of Henry IV. It presented to the wide, paved area which preceded it and which was edged with shabby farm-buildings an immense façade of dark time-stained brick, flanked by two low wings, each of which terminated in a little Dutch-looking pavilion capped with a fantastic roof. Two towers rose behind, and behind the towers was a mass of elms and beeches, now just faintly green. But the great feature was a wide, green river which washed the foundations of the château. The building rose from an island in the circling stream, so that this formed a perfect moat spanned by a two-arched bridge without a parapet. The dull brick walls, which here and there made a grand, straight sweep; the ugly little cupolas of the wings, the deep-set windows, the long, steep pinnacles of mossy slate, all mirrored themselves in the tranquil river. Newman rang at the gate, and was almost frightened at the tone with which a big rusty bell above his head replied to him. An old woman came out from the gate-house and opened the creaking portal just wide enough for him to pass, and he went in, across the dry, bare court and the little cracked white slabs of the causeway on the moat. At the door of the château he waited for some moments, and this gave him a chance to observe that Fleurières was not “kept up,” and to reflect that it was a melancholy place of residence. “It looks,” said Newman to himself—and I give the comparison for what it is worth—“like a Chinese penitentiary.” At last the door was opened by a servant whom he remembered to have seen in the Rue de l’Université. The man’s dull face brightened as he perceived our hero, for Newman, for indefinable reasons, enjoyed the confidence of the liveried gentry. The footman led the way across a great central vestibule, with a pyramid of plants in tubs in the middle of glass doors all around, to what appeared to be the principal drawing-room of the château. Newman crossed the threshold of a room of superb proportions, which made him feel at first like a tourist with a guide-book and a cicerone awaiting a fee. But when his guide had left him alone, with the observation that he would call Madame la Comtesse, Newman perceived that the salon contained little that was remarkable save a dark ceiling with curiously carved rafters, some curtains of elaborate, antiquated tapestry, and a dark oaken floor, polished like a mirror. He waited some minutes, walking up and down; but at length, as he turned at the end of the room, he saw that Madame de Cintré had come in by a distant door. She wore a black dress, and she stood looking at him. As the length of the immense room lay between them he had time to look at her before they met in the middle of it. He was dismayed at the change in her appearance. Pale, heavy-browed, almost haggard with a sort of monastic rigidity in her dress, she had little but her pure features in common with the woman whose radiant good grace he had hitherto admired. She let her eyes rest on his own, and she let him take her hand; but her eyes looked like two rainy autumn moons, and her touch was portentously lifeless.

“I was at your brother’s funeral,” Newman said. “Then I waited three days. But I could wait no longer.”

“Nothing can be lost or gained by waiting,” said Madame de Cintré. “But it was very considerate of you to wait, wronged as you have been.”

“I’m glad you think I have been wronged,” said Newman, with that oddly humorous accent with which he often uttered words of the gravest meaning.

“Do I need to say so?” she asked. “I don’t think I have wronged, seriously, many persons; certainly not consciously. To you, to whom I have done this hard and cruel thing, the only reparation I can make is to say, ‘I know it, I feel it!’ The reparation is pitifully small!”

“Oh, it’s a great step forward!” said Newman, with a gracious smile of encouragement. He pushed a chair towards her and held it, looking at her urgently. She sat down, mechanically, and he seated himself near her; but in a moment he got up, restlessly, and stood before her. She remained seated, like a troubled creature who had passed through the stage of restlessness.

“I say nothing is to be gained by my seeing you,” she went on, “and yet I am very glad you came. Now I can tell you what I feel. It is a selfish pleasure, but it is one of the last I shall have.” And she paused, with her great misty eyes fixed upon him. “I know how I have deceived and injured you; I know how cruel and cowardly I have been. I see it as vividly as you do—I feel it to the ends of my fingers.” And she unclasped her hands, which were locked together in her lap, lifted them, and dropped them at her side. “Anything that you may have said of me in your angriest passion is nothing to what I have said to myself.”

“In my angriest passion,” said Newman, “I have said nothing hard of you. The very worst thing I have said of you yet is that you are the loveliest of women.” And he seated himself before her again abruptly. She flushed a little, but even her flush was pale. “That is because you think I will come back. But I will not come back. It is in that hope you have come here, I know; I am very sorry for you. I would do almost anything for you. To say that, after what I have done, seems simply impudent; but what can I say that will not seem impudent? To wrong you and apologize—that is easy enough. I should not have wronged you.” She stopped a moment, looking at him, and motioned him to let her go on. “I ought never to have listened to you at first; that was the wrong. No good could come of it. I felt it, and yet I listened; that was your fault. I liked you too much; I believed in you.”

“And don’t you believe in me now?”

“More than ever. But now it doesn’t matter. I have given you up.” Newman gave a powerful thump with his clenched fist upon his knee. “Why, why, why?” he cried. “Give me a reason—a decent reason. You are not a child—you are not a minor, nor an idiot. You are not obliged to drop me because your mother told you to. Such a reason isn’t worthy of you.”

“I know that; it’s not worthy of me. But it’s the only one I have to give. After all,” said Madame de Cintré, throwing out her hands, “think me an idiot and forget me! That will be the simplest way.” Newman got up and walked away with a crushing sense that his cause was lost, and yet with an equal inability to give up fighting. He went to one of the great windows, and looked out at the stiffly embanked river and the formal gardens which lay beyond it. When he turned round, Madame de Cintré had risen; she stood there silent and passive. “You are not frank,” said Newman; “you are not honest. Instead of saying that you are imbecile, you should say that other people are wicked. Your mother and your brother have been false and cruel; they have been so to me, and I am sure they have been so to you. Why do you try to shield them? Why do you sacrifice me to them? I’m not false; I’m not cruel. You don’t know what you give up; I can tell you that—you don’t. They bully you and plot about you; and I—I”—And he paused, holding out his hands. She turned away and began to leave him. “You told me the other day that you were afraid of your mother,” he said, following her. “What did you mean?” Madame de Cintré shook her head. “I remember; I was sorry afterwards.”

“You were sorry when she came down and put on the thumbscrews. In God’s name what is it she does to you?”

“Nothing. Nothing that you can understand. And now that I have given you up, I must not complain of her to you.”

“That’s no reasoning!” cried Newman. “Complain of her, on the contrary. Tell me all about it, frankly and trustfully, as you ought, and we will talk it over so satisfactorily that you won’t give me up.” Madame de Cintré looked down some moments, fixedly; and then, raising her eyes, she said, “One good at least has come of this: I have made you judge me more fairly. You thought of me in a way that did me great honor; I don’t know why you had taken it into your head. But it left me no loophole for escape—no chance to be the common, weak creature I am. It was not my fault; I warned you from the first. But I ought to have warned you more. I ought to have convinced you that I was doomed to disappoint you. But I was, in a way, too proud. You see what my superiority amounts to, I hope!” she went on, raising her voice with a tremor which even then and there Newman thought beautiful. “I am too proud to be honest, I am not too proud to be faithless. I am timid and cold and selfish. I am afraid of being uncomfortable.”

“And you call marrying me uncomfortable!” said Newman staring. Madame de Cintré blushed a little and seemed to say that if begging his pardon in words was impudent, she might at least thus mutely express her perfect comprehension of his finding her conduct odious. “It is not marrying you; it is doing all that would go with it. It’s the rupture, the defiance, the insisting upon being happy in my own way. What right have I to be happy when—when”—And she paused.

“When what?” said Newman.

“When others have been most unhappy!”

“What others?” Newman asked. “What have you to do with any others but me? Besides you said just now that you wanted happiness, and that you should find it by obeying your mother. You contradict yourself.”

“Yes, I contradict myself; that shows you that I am not even intelligent.”

“You are laughing at me!” cried Newman. “You are mocking me!” She looked at him intently, and an observer might have said that she was asking herself whether she might not most quickly end their common pain by confessing that she was mocking him. “No; I am not,” she presently said.

“Granting that you are not intelligent,” he went on, “that you are weak, that you are common, that you are nothing that I have believed you were—what I ask of you is not heroic effort, it is a very common effort. There is a great deal on my side to make it easy. The simple truth is that you don’t care enough about me to make it.”

“I am cold,” said Madame de Cintré, “I am as cold as that flowing river.” Newman gave a great rap on the floor with his stick, and a long, grim laugh. “Good, good!” he cried. “You go altogether too far—you overshoot the mark. There isn’t a woman in the world as bad as you would make yourself out. I see your game; it’s what I said. You are blackening yourself to whiten others. You don’t want to give me up, at all; you like me—you like me. I know you do; you have shown it, and I have felt it. After that, you may be as cold as you please! They have bullied you, I say; they have tortured you. It’s an outrage, and I insist upon saving you from the extravagance of your own generosity. Would you chop off your hand if your mother requested it?”

But here, preoccupied though he was, he could not fail to notice the picturesqueness of the place.
