The church was simply the former chapel of the castle, fronting upon its grass-grown court, which, however, was of generous enough width to have given up its quaintest corner to a little graveyard. Here the very headstones themselves seemed to sleep, as they slanted into the grass; the patient elbow of the rampart held them together on one side, and in front, far beneath their mossy lids, the green plains and blue distances stretched away. The way to church, up the hill, was impracticable to vehicles. It was lined with peasants, two or three rows deep, who stood watching old Madame de Bellegarde slowly ascend it, on the arm of her elder son, behind the pall-bearers of the other. Newman chose to lurk among the common mourners who murmured “Madame la Comtesse” as a tall figure veiled in black passed before them. He stood in the dusky little church while the service was going forward, but at the dismal tomb-side he turned away and walked down the hill. He went back to Poitiers, and spent two days in which patience and impatience were singularly commingled. On the third day he sent Madame de Cintré a note, saying that he would call upon her in the afternoon, and in accordance with this he again took his way to Fleurières. He left his vehicle at the tavern in the village street, and obeyed the simple instructions which were given him for finding the château.

“It is just beyond there,” said the landlord, and pointed to the tree-tops of the park, above the opposite houses. Newman followed the first cross-road to the right—it was bordered with mouldy cottages—and in a few moments saw before him the peaked roofs of the towers. Advancing farther, he found himself before a vast iron gate, rusty and closed; here he paused a moment, looking through the bars. The château was near the road; this was at once its merit and its defect; but its aspect was extremely impressive. Newman learned afterwards, from a guide-book of the province, that it dated from the time of Henry IV. It presented to the wide, paved area which preceded it and which was edged with shabby farm-buildings an immense façade of dark time-stained brick, flanked by two low wings, each of which terminated in a little Dutch-looking pavilion capped with a fantastic roof. Two towers rose behind, and behind the towers was a mass of elms and beeches, now just faintly green. But the great feature was a wide, green river which washed the foundations of the château. The building rose from an island in the circling stream, so that this formed a perfect moat spanned by a two-arched bridge without a parapet. The dull brick walls, which here and there made a grand, straight sweep; the ugly little cupolas of the wings, the deep-set windows, the long, steep pinnacles of mossy slate, all mirrored themselves in the tranquil river. Newman rang at the gate, and was almost frightened at the tone with which a big rusty bell above his head replied to him. An old woman came out from the gate-house and opened the creaking portal just wide enough for him to pass, and he went in, across the dry, bare court and the little cracked white slabs of the causeway on the moat. At the door of the château he waited for some moments, and this gave him a chance to observe that Fleurières was not “kept up,” and to reflect that it was a melancholy place of residence. “It looks,” said Newman to himself—and I give the comparison for what it is worth—“like a Chinese penitentiary.” At last the door was opened by a servant whom he remembered to have seen in the Rue de l’Université. The man’s dull face brightened as he perceived our hero, for Newman, for indefinable reasons, enjoyed the confidence of the liveried gentry. The footman led the way across a great central vestibule, with a pyramid of plants in tubs in the middle of glass doors all around, to what appeared to be the principal drawing-room of the château. Newman crossed the threshold of a room of superb proportions, which made him feel at first like a tourist with a guide-book and a cicerone awaiting a fee. But when his guide had left him alone, with the observation that he would call Madame la Comtesse, Newman perceived that the salon contained little that was remarkable save a dark ceiling with curiously carved rafters, some curtains of elaborate, antiquated tapestry, and a dark oaken floor, polished like a mirror. He waited some minutes, walking up and down; but at length, as he turned at the end of the room, he saw that Madame de Cintré had come in by a distant door. She wore a black dress, and she stood looking at him. As the length of the immense room lay between them he had time to look at her before they met in the middle of it. He was dismayed at the change in her appearance. Pale, heavy-browed, almost haggard with a sort of monastic rigidity in her dress, she had little but her pure features in common with the woman whose radiant good grace he had hitherto admired. She let her eyes rest on his own, and she let him take her hand; but her eyes looked like two rainy autumn moons, and her touch was portentously lifeless.

“I was at your brother’s funeral,” Newman said. “Then I waited three days. But I could wait no longer.”

“Nothing can be lost or gained by waiting,” said Madame de Cintré. “But it was very considerate of you to wait, wronged as you have been.”

“I’m glad you think I have been wronged,” said Newman, with that oddly humorous accent with which he often uttered words of the gravest meaning.

“Do I need to say so?” she asked. “I don’t think I have wronged, seriously, many persons; certainly not consciously. To you, to whom I have done this hard and cruel thing, the only reparation I can make is to say, ‘I know it, I feel it!’ The reparation is pitifully small!”

“Oh, it’s a great step forward!” said Newman, with a gracious smile of encouragement. He pushed a chair towards her and held it, looking at her urgently. She sat down, mechanically, and he seated himself near her; but in a moment he got up, restlessly, and stood before her. She remained seated, like a troubled creature who had passed through the stage of restlessness.

“I say nothing is to be gained by my seeing you,” she went on, “and yet I am very glad you came. Now I can tell you what I feel. It is a selfish pleasure, but it is one of the last I shall have.” And she paused, with her great misty eyes fixed upon him. “I know how I have deceived and injured you; I know how cruel and cowardly I have been. I see it as vividly as you do—I feel it to the ends of my fingers.” And she unclasped her hands, which were locked together in her lap, lifted them, and dropped them at her side. “Anything that you may have said of me in your angriest passion is nothing to what I have said to myself.”

“In my angriest passion,” said Newman, “I have said nothing hard of you. The very worst thing I have said of you yet is that you are the loveliest of women.” And he seated himself before her again abruptly. She flushed a little, but even her flush was pale. “That is because you think I will come back. But I will not come back. It is in that hope you have come here, I know; I am very sorry for you. I would do almost anything for you. To say that, after what I have done, seems simply impudent; but what can I say that will not seem impudent? To wrong you and apologize—that is easy enough. I should not have wronged you.” She stopped a moment, looking at him, and motioned him to let her go on. “I ought never to have listened to you at first; that was the wrong. No good could come of it. I felt it, and yet I listened; that was your fault. I liked you too much; I believed in you.”

“And don’t you believe in me now?”

“More than ever. But now it doesn’t matter. I have given you up.” Newman gave a powerful thump with his clenched fist upon his knee. “Why, why, why?” he cried. “Give me a reason—a decent reason. You are not a child—you are not a minor, nor an idiot. You are not obliged to drop me because your mother told you to. Such a reason isn’t worthy of you.”

“I know that; it’s not worthy of me. But it’s the only one I have to give. After all,” said Madame de Cintré, throwing out her hands, “think me an idiot and forget me! That will be the simplest way.” Newman got up and walked away with a crushing sense that his cause was lost, and yet with an equal inability to give up fighting. He went to one of the great windows, and looked out at the stiffly embanked river and the formal gardens which lay beyond it. When he turned round, Madame de Cintré had risen; she stood there silent and passive. “You are not frank,” said Newman; “you are not honest. Instead of saying that you are imbecile, you should say that other people are wicked. Your mother and your brother have been false and cruel; they have been so to me, and I am sure they have been so to you. Why do you try to shield them? Why do you sacrifice me to them? I’m not false; I’m not cruel. You don’t know what you give up; I can tell you that—you don’t. They bully you and plot about you; and I—I”—And he paused, holding out his hands. She turned away and began to leave him. “You told me the other day that you were afraid of your mother,” he said, following her. “What did you mean?” Madame de Cintré shook her head. “I remember; I was sorry afterwards.”

“You were sorry when she came down and put on the thumbscrews. In God’s name what is it she does to you?”

“Nothing. Nothing that you can understand. And now that I have given you up, I must not complain of her to you.”

“That’s no reasoning!” cried Newman. “Complain of her, on the contrary. Tell me all about it, frankly and trustfully, as you ought, and we will talk it over so satisfactorily that you won’t give me up.” Madame de Cintré looked down some moments, fixedly; and then, raising her eyes, she said, “One good at least has come of this: I have made you judge me more fairly. You thought of me in a way that did me great honor; I don’t know why you had taken it into your head. But it left me no loophole for escape—no chance to be the common, weak creature I am. It was not my fault; I warned you from the first. But I ought to have warned you more. I ought to have convinced you that I was doomed to disappoint you. But I was, in a way, too proud. You see what my superiority amounts to, I hope!” she went on, raising her voice with a tremor which even then and there Newman thought beautiful. “I am too proud to be honest, I am not too proud to be faithless. I am timid and cold and selfish. I am afraid of being uncomfortable.”

“And you call marrying me uncomfortable!” said Newman staring. Madame de Cintré blushed a little and seemed to say that if begging his pardon in words was impudent, she might at least thus mutely express her perfect comprehension of his finding her conduct odious. “It is not marrying you; it is doing all that would go with it. It’s the rupture, the defiance, the insisting upon being happy in my own way. What right have I to be happy when—when”—And she paused.

“When what?” said Newman.

“When others have been most unhappy!”

“What others?” Newman asked. “What have you to do with any others but me? Besides you said just now that you wanted happiness, and that you should find it by obeying your mother. You contradict yourself.”

“Yes, I contradict myself; that shows you that I am not even intelligent.”

“You are laughing at me!” cried Newman. “You are mocking me!” She looked at him intently, and an observer might have said that she was asking herself whether she might not most quickly end their common pain by confessing that she was mocking him. “No; I am not,” she presently said.

“Granting that you are not intelligent,” he went on, “that you are weak, that you are common, that you are nothing that I have believed you were—what I ask of you is not heroic effort, it is a very common effort. There is a great deal on my side to make it easy. The simple truth is that you don’t care enough about me to make it.”

“I am cold,” said Madame de Cintré, “I am as cold as that flowing river.” Newman gave a great rap on the floor with his stick, and a long, grim laugh. “Good, good!” he cried. “You go altogether too far—you overshoot the mark. There isn’t a woman in the world as bad as you would make yourself out. I see your game; it’s what I said. You are blackening yourself to whiten others. You don’t want to give me up, at all; you like me—you like me. I know you do; you have shown it, and I have felt it. After that, you may be as cold as you please! They have bullied you, I say; they have tortured you. It’s an outrage, and I insist upon saving you from the extravagance of your own generosity. Would you chop off your hand if your mother requested it?”

The villa which Bernard Longstaff had taken for the autumn stood upon the slope of Bellosguardo, at a height from which Florence, at the hour of his return, lay below him like a thing composed and finished, a city that had long since said everything it had to say and was content to be listened to. He had come up the hill on foot, having dismissed his fly at the bottom of the last ascent, for he had an idea, which he would not have cared to examine very closely, that he wished to arrive slowly. The afternoon was at that stage of its decline in which the light seems less to fall than to linger; the cypresses along the wall had taken on a certain gravity of outline, and the olive-trees on the terraces below, with their silvery indifference, appeared to be thinking of something else. Longstaff thought of his wife. He had been thinking of her, indeed, ever since the morning, when, at the bankers' in the Via Tornabuoni, a clerk with a beautiful manner had handed him, along with his letters, a small piece of information which he had been at some trouble, during six weeks, to prevent from reaching her. The clerk had not meant it as information; he had meant it as a courtesy. But Longstaff knew enough of courtesies, and of the way they travel, to be aware that it would have reached her before him.

He found her, as he had half expected to find her, on the loggia that overlooked the garden. She was seated in one of the low cane chairs which the proprietor of the villa, an English lady of artistic tendencies now resident at Cannes, had distributed about the place with an evident faith in their picturesqueness, and she held in her lap a letter which she was not reading. She did not rise when he came out to her; she only turned her head, and he saw at once—it was the first thing he saw—that she had been waiting for him in a manner that was not the manner of the other days. There is a way of waiting that is a welcome, and there is a way that is a judgment; Agnes Longstaff had never before, to her husband's knowledge, practised the second, and she practised it now, he was obliged to admit, with a natural distinction which he could not help admiring even as he felt the chill of it.

"You walked up," she said. "I saw you from the wall. You stopped twice."

"I stopped to look at the view," said Longstaff. "It is a view that invites stopping."

"You have seen it every day for a month."

"That is just what makes it so good. One is always finding something more." He came and stood by the balustrade, and looked down, by way of illustrating his remark, upon the dim red mass of the Duomo; but he was conscious that the demonstration was not convincing, and he presently turned round and leaned against the stone, so that he faced her. "You have had a letter," he said.

"I have had a letter from Everard." She lifted it a little from her lap, not as if to offer it to him, but rather as one exhibits a piece of evidence in a court where the judge is known to be partial. "I think you know what is in it."

Longstaff had a moment of hesitation, which he afterwards regretted; for it was in that moment, he believed, that she made up her mind about him. "I can guess," he said.

"You needn't guess. I will tell you." She spoke very quietly; her voice, which was one of her charms, had kept all its softness, and it was only in a certain carefulness of articulation, as if each word were a small object that she was setting down on a table and did not wish to break, that he perceived the effort it cost her. "He writes to thank me. He thanks me very handsomely—Everard always thanks people handsomely; it is the one thing he does without being asked. He thanks me for my generosity, and for my delicacy, and for having managed it all so that he never needed to come to me with his hat in his hand. He says he knew I should understand that he could never have asked. He says that it has saved him, and that he shall never forget it. And he says that Mr. Pruett, of the firm in Lincoln's Inn, conveyed to him that the matter was arranged at my particular desire, and that I wished it never to be spoken of between us. So you see," she went on, with a faint smile which was the most painful thing he had yet seen in her face, "I have been very generous and very delicate, and I didn't know it."

Longstaff put his hands into his pockets, and then, as if he felt the attitude to be unbecoming, took them out again. "I asked Pruett to say that," he said. "I thought it would be easier for him."

"Easier for Everard?"

"Easier for everyone. He would have taken it from you. He would never have taken it from me."

"That is very true," said Mrs. Longstaff. "He would never have taken it from you. And so you gave it him in my name, and he took it, and now he thinks—he thinks—" She stopped, and he saw her hands close upon the letter, so that the thin foreign paper made a little dry crackle in the stillness. "I don't know what he thinks. I don't know what anyone thinks. That is what I have been sitting here all the afternoon trying to know."

It was not the first time, in the eighteen months of their marriage, that Bernard Longstaff had found himself in the presence of a sentiment in his wife which he could recognise without being able to share; but it was the first time that the sentiment had been directed against himself, and he became aware, as he stood there, that he had never quite measured how much of his happiness had rested on the assumption that it never would be. He was a man who had made, in his own country and by methods which he would have described as perfectly plain, a fortune which he would have described as perfectly comfortable; and he had brought to his marriage with an English girl of old name and slender means a conviction—it was hardly more conscious than the conviction that one breathes—that the possession of money laid upon its possessor no obligation so imperative as that of using it to make other people's lives easier. It had seemed to him the simplest thing in the world. I do not know that it was not, in itself, the simplest thing in the world; but he was now to learn that there are simplicities which, transplanted into certain soils, put out the most surprising roots.

"My dear," he said, "you are making a great deal of a very small matter. Your brother was in a hole. He was in a very considerable hole—I happen to know just how considerable, and I don't think you do, and I don't think you need. I had the means of getting him out of it, and I got him out. I did it in the way that seemed to me to give the least pain. If I made a mistake about the way, I'm sorry. But I'm not sorry I did it, and I don't believe that, when you have thought it over, you'll be sorry either."

"Ah, you don't believe!" she murmured. She looked away from him, out at the garden, where a fountain, choked with fallen leaves, was making a small, ineffectual effort to justify its existence. "That is what is so wonderful in you, Bernard—what I have always thought so wonderful. You believe that things come right if one only means them well. You believe that if one has the means, and the good intention, there's nothing else to be considered. And you're quite right, I daresay, in your own country. I've no doubt it's a much better country than mine. But you've married into mine."

"I married you," said Longstaff, with a promptness which he was afterwards glad of. "I didn't marry a country."

"Oh, but you did! That's just what you did—though I don't suppose you knew it, and I'm sure I didn't tell you. I didn't know it myself, very well. One never knows how much one belongs to things until somebody does something to them." She turned back to him, and her eyes, which were grey and usually rather slow in their movements, had in them now a kind of shining quickness that made him think, irrelevantly, of the surface of water just before rain. "Do you understand what you have done? You have made my brother your debtor without his knowing it, and you have made me his creditor without my knowing it, and you have made me a liar to him whether I speak or whether I hold my tongue. If I tell him the truth, he will feel that he has been tricked—that he has been fed out of a hand he would never have eaten from—and he will hate you, and he will never forgive me for having let him be humiliated. And if I don't tell him, then every time he looks at me with that dreadful gratitude in his face I shall know that I am taking credit for your money. I shall be wearing your generosity like a borrowed jewel and letting people admire it. Is that what you wanted for me?"

Longstaff was silent for some moments. He had a habit, in moments of difficulty, of looking at the matter in hand as if it were a piece of machinery whose working he did not yet understand but had every confidence of mastering, and he applied this habit now to his wife's speech. But he found, to his discomfort, that the machinery did not lend itself to inspection; it was all, as it were, inside. "I wanted you not to be troubled," he said at last. "That's the whole of what I wanted. You had been troubled about him—you know you had. You used to read his letters and put them away and say nothing, and I used to see your face. I couldn't stand it. I thought, here's a thing I can stop. And I stopped it."

"Without asking me."

"Without asking you—yes. Because if I had asked you, you'd have said no."

"Then you knew I should say no!" she cried; and there was in the exclamation something so nearly triumphant that he perceived he had put into her hand the very weapon she had been feeling for. "You knew it, and you did it notwithstanding. You knew what I should feel, and you decided that my feeling didn't count—that it was a sort of prejudice, a sort of old-world superstition, that a sensible man might very well step over, as one steps over a puddle. I don't say it wasn't a superstition. Perhaps it was. But it was mine, Bernard. You might have left me that."

He took a turn along the loggia, his footsteps sounding upon the old tiles with an emphasis which he had not intended and which seemed to him, as he heard it, rather vulgar. When he came back she had not moved; she sat with the letter in her lap, very upright, very pale, with the last of the daylight on her face, and he thought—it was a thought that came to him with a sort of pang, at the most inappropriate moment—that she had never looked so like the portrait of her great-grandmother which hung, darkened and cracked, in the dining-room of her father's house in Wiltshire. The resemblance had been pointed out to him on his first visit there, with a certain pride, by her father; and he had admired it then, without in the least understanding that what he was admiring was a family's whole conception of what was due to itself.

"Agnes," he said, standing before her, "I'll put it plainly, since we seem to be putting things plainly. Do you think I did it to buy something?"

She looked up at him, and for a moment he saw her hesitate; and he was grateful to her for the hesitation, for he knew that it meant she would not answer him with a phrase. "No," she said slowly. "I don't think you did it to buy anything. I think you did it because you're good—because you're kinder than anyone I have ever known. But that's just the dreadful part of it. If you had done it to buy something, I could have quarrelled with you and been done with it. But you did it out of kindness, and so I can't even quarrel. I can only sit here and feel—" she made a little gesture, opening her hands, and then letting them fall—"feel bought, without anyone's having bought me."

"That's nonsense," said Longstaff; but he said it without conviction, and she heard the absence of conviction as clearly as if it had been a note struck on the piano.

"Is it? Then tell me what I am to say to Everard. Tell me what I am to say to my father, when he hears of it—and he will hear of it; Everard will tell him, in the fulness of his heart. He will tell him that his sister has saved him, and my father will look at me across the table at Christmas and wonder where I found three thousand pounds. And then he will understand where I found it; and he will say nothing, because he is a gentleman; and I shall see him saying nothing, every day, for as long as he lives." She paused, and then added, in a lower voice, "You don't know what it is to see my father say nothing."

"I think I can imagine it," said Longstaff with a short laugh. He was aware, as he laughed, that he was angry; and the discovery surprised him so much that he stood for a moment quite still, examining it, as a man who has been struck in the dark stands still to find out where he is hurt. It was not his wife's reproaches that angered him; he could have borne those—he could have borne, he thought, almost any reproach that was simply a reproach. It was something else, something he could not have named, but which seemed to rise up from the very ground on which she stood: a sense that there was a whole province of feeling in which she lived, and in which he was a stranger, and that she had let him in, all these months, only as one lets in a visitor—with every courtesy, and with every door but one left open. "Look here," he said, more roughly than he had ever spoken to her. "I didn't marry your father, and I didn't marry your brother, and I certainly didn't marry the opinion of the county. I married you. And I thought—God knows I may have been wrong—I thought that when I married you, what was mine was yours, and that what troubled you troubled me. If that isn't so—if there's a part of you that's still Miss Vane of Hatherleigh, and that I'm not to touch—then I'd rather you told me so now. I'd rather know where the fences are."

The words were out before he had weighed them, and he saw them reach her. She did not flinch; she was not of a race that flinched. But a slow colour came into her face, and stayed there, and he understood that he had said a thing which was both less and more than he meant, and that she was taking it in its fullest sense.

"Do you think," she said, very low, "that I don't know there are fences? I have been walking along them ever since we were married. I have been trying—you can't think how I have been trying—to find the gate. And I thought, just lately, that I had nearly found it. And then this." She looked down at the letter. "It isn't the money, Bernard. You must believe that it isn't the money. It's that you went round. You went round me, as if I were one of the fences."

He was silent; and in the silence the bell of some convent in the valley began to ring for the evening office, thin and patient, as if it had been ringing in the same way for four hundred years and had no intention of hurrying now. Longstaff listened to it with a strange attention. He had a confused feeling that it was saying something to him, and that if he could only make out what it was saying he would know what to say to his wife; but the bell, like everything else in that old country, kept its meaning to itself.

"I went round," he said at last, "because I was afraid that if I went through, I should break something."

She raised her eyes to him quickly. "And you didn't think you would break something by going round?"

"I didn't think about it at all," said Longstaff, with a candour which cost him more than she knew. "That's the truth. I thought about Everard, and I thought about your face when you read his letters, and I thought about Pruett and how the thing could be fixed. I didn't think about the fences. I suppose I don't see them, half the time. I suppose that's the matter with me." He sat down, abruptly, in the cane chair beside hers, which received him with a creak of protest, and leaned forward, his elbows on his knees, looking at the tiles. "Well, what do you want me to do? I can't undo it. Everard has the money, and he's spent it, I daresay, or the people he owed have spent it for him. I can write to him and tell him the truth, if you like. I'll take it all on myself. I'll tell him you knew nothing about it, and that I'm a meddling Yankee who doesn't know any better. He'll believe that easily enough."

"You would do that?"

"I'd do a good deal more than that, if it would make you look at me as you did a week ago."

She was silent for a long moment, and he did not look at her; he had an instinct that if he looked at her she would not say what she was going to say. When at last she spoke, it was in a voice so changed that he hardly knew it—a voice from which all the careful articulation had gone, and in which there was nothing left but a kind of weariness that was almost tenderness.

"No," she said. "You shan't write to him. That would be worse. That would be the worst of all." She put out her hand, not to him, but to the arm of his chair, and let it rest there, at a small, precise distance from his own. "I shall have to carry it. I see that. I shall have to let him thank me, and say nothing, and be what he thinks I am. It will be a sort of penance, I suppose—a penance for having married a man who is better than my family and doesn't know it." She gave a little laugh, which broke in the middle. "Only you must never do it again, Bernard. You must never go round again. If you want to break something, break it. I would rather have it broken, and know."

Longstaff turned his head and looked at her hand on the arm of his chair, and then, very slowly, as if he were afraid of startling some shy creature, he put his own beside it—not upon it, but beside it, so that their fingers were almost touching. It was a small thing; it was the kind of thing which, a year before, he would not have thought worth the doing. But he had begun, that afternoon, to learn the value of small distances.

"I'll try," he said. "I don't promise I shall always see the fences. But when I don't, you must show me where they are."

"I'll show you," said his wife; and they sat there, side by side, without speaking, while the bell in the valley ceased, and the light went off the cypresses, and Florence, below them, withdrew into its own dimness, keeping, as it had always kept, a great deal more than it gave. It would be too much to say that they were reconciled; it was rather that they had each, for the first time, caught a glimpse of the other's country from the frontier, and had found it, if not more familiar, at least more worth the journey. Whether the journey would ever be made, I shall not undertake to say. But Longstaff, when he went in to dress for dinner, was aware that he had been, during the last hour, more nearly married than at any moment since the ceremony; and he was aware also—it was a reflection which he kept to himself—that it had cost him three thousand pounds, and that he did not in the least regret the price.

Valentin de Bellegarde died tranquilly, just as the cold faint March dawn began to illumine the faces of the little knot of friends gathered about his bedside. An hour afterwards Newman left the inn and drove to Geneva; he was naturally unwilling to be present at the arrival of Madame de Bellegarde and her first-born. At Geneva, for the moment, he remained. He was like a man who has had a fall and wants to sit still and count his bruises. He instantly wrote to Madame de Cintré, relating to her the circumstances of her brother’s death—with certain exceptions—and asking her what was the earliest moment at which he might hope that she would consent to see him. M. Ledoux had told him that he had reason to know that Valentin’s will—Bellegarde had a great deal of elegant personal property to dispose of—contained a request that he should be buried near his father in the churchyard of Fleurières, and Newman intended that the state of his own relations with the family should not deprive him of the satisfaction of helping to pay the last earthly honors to the best fellow in the world. He reflected that Valentin’s friendship was older than Urbain’s enmity, and that at a funeral it was easy to escape notice. Madame de Cintré’s answer to his letter enabled him to time his arrival at Fleurières. This answer was very brief; it ran as follows:— “I thank you for your letter, and for your being with Valentin. It is a most inexpressible sorrow to me that I was not. To see you will be nothing but a distress to me; there is no need, therefore, to wait for what you call brighter days. It is all one now, and I shall have no brighter days. Come when you please; only notify me first. My brother is to be buried here on Friday, and my family is to remain here. C. de C.” As soon as he received this letter Newman went straight to Paris and to Poitiers. The journey took him far southward, through green Touraine and across the far-shining Loire, into a country where the early spring deepened about him as he went. But he had never made a journey during which he heeded less what he would have called the lay of the land. He obtained lodging at the inn at Poitiers, and the next morning drove in a couple of hours to the village of Fleurières. But here, preoccupied though he was, he could not fail to notice the picturesqueness of the place. It was what the French call a petit bourg; it lay at the base of a sort of huge mound on the summit of which stood the crumbling ruins of a feudal castle, much of whose sturdy material, as well as that of the wall which dropped along the hill to enclose the clustered houses defensively, had been absorbed into the very substance of the village. The church was simply the former chapel of the castle, fronting upon its grass-grown court, which, however, was of generous enough width to have given up its quaintest corner to a little graveyard. Here the very headstones themselves seemed to sleep, as they slanted into the grass; the patient elbow of the rampart held them together on one side, and in front, far beneath their mossy lids, the green plains and blue distances stretched away. The way to church, up the hill, was impracticable to vehicles. It was lined with peasants, two or three rows deep, who stood watching old Madame de Bellegarde slowly ascend it, on the arm of her elder son, behind the pall-bearers of the other. Newman chose to lurk among the common mourners who murmured “Madame la Comtesse” as a tall figure veiled in black passed before them. He stood in the dusky little church while the service was going forward, but at the dismal tomb-side he turned away and walked down the hill. He went back to Poitiers, and spent two days in which patience and impatience were singularly commingled. On the third day he sent Madame de Cintré a note, saying that he would call upon her in the afternoon, and in accordance with this he again took his way to Fleurières. He left his vehicle at the tavern in the village street, and obeyed the simple instructions which were given him for finding the château.

“It is just beyond there,” said the landlord, and pointed to the tree-tops of the park, above the opposite houses. Newman followed the first cross-road to the right—it was bordered with mouldy cottages—and in a few moments saw before him the peaked roofs of the towers. Advancing farther, he found himself before a vast iron gate, rusty and closed; here he paused a moment, looking through the bars. The château was near the road; this was at once its merit and its defect; but its aspect was extremely impressive. Newman learned afterwards, from a guide-book of the province, that it dated from the time of Henry IV. It presented to the wide, paved area which preceded it and which was edged with shabby farm-buildings an immense façade of dark time-stained brick, flanked by two low wings, each of which terminated in a little Dutch-looking pavilion capped with a fantastic roof. Two towers rose behind, and behind the towers was a mass of elms and beeches, now just faintly green. But the great feature was a wide, green river which washed the foundations of the château. The building rose from an island in the circling stream, so that this formed a perfect moat spanned by a two-arched bridge without a parapet. The dull brick walls, which here and there made a grand, straight sweep; the ugly little cupolas of the wings, the deep-set windows, the long, steep pinnacles of mossy slate, all mirrored themselves in the tranquil river. Newman rang at the gate, and was almost frightened at the tone with which a big rusty bell above his head replied to him. An old woman came out from the gate-house and opened the creaking portal just wide enough for him to pass, and he went in, across the dry, bare court and the little cracked white slabs of the causeway on the moat. At the door of the château he waited for some moments, and this gave him a chance to observe that Fleurières was not “kept up,” and to reflect that it was a melancholy place of residence. “It looks,” said Newman to himself—and I give the comparison for what it is worth—“like a Chinese penitentiary.” At last the door was opened by a servant whom he remembered to have seen in the Rue de l’Université. The man’s dull face brightened as he perceived our hero, for Newman, for indefinable reasons, enjoyed the confidence of the liveried gentry. The footman led the way across a great central vestibule, with a pyramid of plants in tubs in the middle of glass doors all around, to what appeared to be the principal drawing-room of the château. Newman crossed the threshold of a room of superb proportions, which made him feel at first like a tourist with a guide-book and a cicerone awaiting a fee. But when his guide had left him alone, with the observation that he would call Madame la Comtesse, Newman perceived that the salon contained little that was remarkable save a dark ceiling with curiously carved rafters, some curtains of elaborate, antiquated tapestry, and a dark oaken floor, polished like a mirror. He waited some minutes, walking up and down; but at length, as he turned at the end of the room, he saw that Madame de Cintré had come in by a distant door. She wore a black dress, and she stood looking at him. As the length of the immense room lay between them he had time to look at her before they met in the middle of it. He was dismayed at the change in her appearance. Pale, heavy-browed, almost haggard with a sort of monastic rigidity in her dress, she had little but her pure features in common with the woman whose radiant good grace he had hitherto admired. She let her eyes rest on his own, and she let him take her hand; but her eyes looked like two rainy autumn moons, and her touch was portentously lifeless.

“I was at your brother’s funeral,” Newman said. “Then I waited three days. But I could wait no longer.”

“Nothing can be lost or gained by waiting,” said Madame de Cintré. “But it was very considerate of you to wait, wronged as you have been.”

“I’m glad you think I have been wronged,” said Newman, with that oddly humorous accent with which he often uttered words of the gravest meaning.

“Do I need to say so?” she asked. “I don’t think I have wronged, seriously, many persons; certainly not consciously. To you, to whom I have done this hard and cruel thing, the only reparation I can make is to say, ‘I know it, I feel it!’ The reparation is pitifully small!”

“Oh, it’s a great step forward!” said Newman, with a gracious smile of encouragement. He pushed a chair towards her and held it, looking at her urgently. She sat down, mechanically, and he seated himself near her; but in a moment he got up, restlessly, and stood before her. She remained seated, like a troubled creature who had passed through the stage of restlessness.

“I say nothing is to be gained by my seeing you,” she went on, “and yet I am very glad you came. Now I can tell you what I feel. It is a selfish pleasure, but it is one of the last I shall have.” And she paused, with her great misty eyes fixed upon him. “I know how I have deceived and injured you; I know how cruel and cowardly I have been. I see it as vividly as you do—I feel it to the ends of my fingers.” And she unclasped her hands, which were locked together in her lap, lifted them, and dropped them at her side. “Anything that you may have said of me in your angriest passion is nothing to what I have said to myself.”

“In my angriest passion,” said Newman, “I have said nothing hard of you. The very worst thing I have said of you yet is that you are the loveliest of women.” And he seated himself before her again abruptly. She flushed a little, but even her flush was pale. “That is because you think I will come back. But I will not come back. It is in that hope you have come here, I know; I am very sorry for you. I would do almost anything for you. To say that, after what I have done, seems simply impudent; but what can I say that will not seem impudent? To wrong you and apologize—that is easy enough. I should not have wronged you.” She stopped a moment, looking at him, and motioned him to let her go on. “I ought never to have listened to you at first; that was the wrong. No good could come of it. I felt it, and yet I listened; that was your fault. I liked you too much; I believed in you.”

“And don’t you believe in me now?”

“More than ever. But now it doesn’t matter. I have given you up.” Newman gave a powerful thump with his clenched fist upon his knee. “Why, why, why?” he cried. “Give me a reason—a decent reason. You are not a child—you are not a minor, nor an idiot. You are not obliged to drop me because your mother told you to. Such a reason isn’t worthy of you.”

“I know that; it’s not worthy of me. But it’s the only one I have to give. After all,” said Madame de Cintré, throwing out her hands, “think me an idiot and forget me! That will be the simplest way.” Newman got up and walked away with a crushing sense that his cause was lost, and yet with an equal inability to give up fighting. He went to one of the great windows, and looked out at the stiffly embanked river and the formal gardens which lay beyond it. When he turned round, Madame de Cintré had risen; she stood there silent and passive. “You are not frank,” said Newman; “you are not honest. Instead of saying that you are imbecile, you should say that other people are wicked. Your mother and your brother have been false and cruel; they have been so to me, and I am sure they have been so to you. Why do you try to shield them? Why do you sacrifice me to them? I’m not false; I’m not cruel. You don’t know what you give up; I can tell you that—you don’t. They bully you and plot about you; and I—I”—And he paused, holding out his hands. She turned away and began to leave him. “You told me the other day that you were afraid of your mother,” he said, following her. “What did you mean?” Madame de Cintré shook her head. “I remember; I was sorry afterwards.”

“You were sorry when she came down and put on the thumbscrews. In God’s name what is it she does to you?”

“Nothing. Nothing that you can understand. And now that I have given you up, I must not complain of her to you.”

There isn’t a woman in the world as bad as you would make yourself out. I see your game; it’s what I said. You are blackening yourself to whiten others. They have bullied you, I say; they have tortured you. It’s an outrage, and I insist upon saving you from the extravagance of your own generosity. Would you chop off your hand if your mother requested it?”

Lawrence Hilyard had lived in Rome for eleven years, and he had come, in that time, to regard the arrival of an American relative very much as a man who has built his house upon a quiet shore regards the announcement of a high tide. It was not that he disliked his relatives; he had a great tenderness for several of them, and an indulgent toleration for the rest. But he had arranged his life with a certain nicety, and he had a suspicion, founded upon some experience, that people who came from a distance to look at it were apt to handle it as they might have handled a piece of old lace in a shop, holding it up to the light, and asking what it was good for. When, therefore, he received a note from his cousin, Mrs. Penrose, informing him that she had reached the Hôtel de Londres the evening before, and that she should be "at home, in a manner of speaking," at four o'clock, he folded it with a sigh, which he immediately afterwards repudiated as ungracious, and put it into his pocket with a gesture of resolution.

He had not seen Caroline Penrose for something more than twelve years. She had been Caroline Hilyard when he last looked at her, and she had been twenty-two years old; she had worn a grey dress with a great many little buttons, and she had stood on the steps of her father's house in Albany, under the elm that dropped its leaves on the gravel, and given him her hand with a smile which he had thought, at the time, rather too composed. He remembered the smile better than the buttons, and the buttons better than anything she had said. He had gone to Europe a month afterwards; she had married, two years later, a gentleman of the name of Penrose, who was understood to be in railways; and Penrose, in the fulness of time, had died, leaving her, as Hilyard had gathered from his mother's letters, "very comfortably placed, and with nothing in the world to do." It was the last clause, I think, that had caused our friend his little sigh. A woman with nothing in the world to do might very conceivably undertake to do something with him.

He walked to the hotel through the long golden afternoon, which lay upon the old yellow walls like a varnish, and he took, without quite knowing why, the longer way, by the Piazza di Spagna, where the flower-sellers were sitting among their baskets on the great steps, and where an English family was disputing, with a cabman, a question of twenty centimes. He reflected that he had grown, in eleven years, very fond of these things; that they were, in a sense, his property; and that he had a right to be fond of them without justifying the attachment to anyone. He reflected also—for he was a man who reflected a good deal, and who was a little ashamed of it—that he was nevertheless extremely curious to know what his cousin would think of him.

She received him in a small salon on the second floor, with a balcony that looked over the street and a gilded clock that had stopped, apparently, in the reign of Gregory XVI. She was standing by the window when he came in, and she turned round slowly, as if she had been expecting him for a long time and could afford to take the last moment at her ease. He saw at once that she had changed, and he saw almost as quickly that she had changed less than he had feared. She was taller than he remembered—or perhaps it was only that she carried herself with a greater consciousness of her height—and she was dressed in black, with a little white at the throat, which gave her the air of a person who had lately come out of mourning and had not yet decided what to go into. Her face was thinner; the composure he remembered was there still, but it had acquired a sort of finish, like a surface that has been much handled. She held out both her hands.

"Well, Lawrence," she said, "you haven't run away."

"I never run away," said Hilyard. "I only go away, which is quite different. I take my time about it."

"You took twelve years," said Mrs. Penrose. "That is a good deal of time, even for you." And she looked at him with an attention which was frank without being in the least indiscreet, as one looks at a portrait of which one has heard a great deal and which one has been told is a good likeness. "You are very brown," she presently added. "And you have grown a beard. I am not sure that I approve of the beard."

"It was not grown for your approval," said Hilyard, laughing; "but if you had written sooner, I might have consulted you."

They sat down, she upon a little hard sofa covered with yellow damask, and he upon a chair which creaked, he thought, with a kind of reproach. For some minutes they talked of the things that people talk of who have a great many important matters to say and have not yet determined in what order to say them: of her voyage, which had been rough; of the Alps, which she had crossed in a diligence and found "overpowering, but a little too much like a picture"; of the hotel, which was dear; of her maid, who was homesick. Hilyard listened, and made the answers that occurred to him, and watched her the while with a curiosity which deepened by degrees into something that was almost anxiety. He had a sense that she was taking his measure, and that she was doing it with a skill which she had not possessed at twenty-two. In those days she had been a very direct young woman; she had asked questions as one throws a stone into a pond, for the simple pleasure of seeing the circles widen. Now she seemed to ask them as one drops a plummet, to find out how deep the water was.

"And you are really happy here?" she said at last, with an abruptness which was the first thing about her that seemed to him quite unchanged.

"Happy?" Hilyard repeated. "That is a large word. I am very comfortable. I have a good many things I care for, and very few that I dislike. I have an apartment in an old palace with a ceiling painted by somebody who was nearly as good as Guido; I have a few friends who don't bore me; I have the whole of Rome to walk about in. If that is happiness, I suppose I am happy."

"It sounds like a description of a very pleasant hotel," said Mrs. Penrose.

"Ah, you are severe!" he cried. "That is the American in you. You want everything to be good for something."

"And you want nothing to be good for anything but to be looked at. That is the—what shall I call it?—the Roman in you." She smiled, but the smile was not altogether a concession. "I don't say it is wrong, Lawrence. I only say it is very different from what you used to want."

"What did I use to want?" he asked.

She looked at him a moment before answering; and it struck him that she was deciding whether she might tell him the truth or whether it would be kinder to invent something. "You used to want to do things," she said. "You used to talk about the law, and about politics, and about making Albany a place that people would not be ashamed to come from. You used to make speeches to me under the elm—don't you remember?—about the duty of an educated man in a new country."

Hilyard coloured a little; he remembered the speeches perfectly, and he remembered, too, that they had been addressed less to the new country than to the young lady in the grey dress. "I was very young," he said. "I was very young and very solemn. It is a combination that produces a great many speeches."

"I liked them," said Mrs. Penrose simply. "I liked them better than anything you have said to-day."

He got up and went to the window, where the light was beginning to turn from gold to rose, and stood looking down into the street, at a priest in a broad hat who was walking slowly along the pavement with his hands behind him, and at a little girl who was carrying a great flask of wine almost as large as herself. He was conscious of a feeling which he could not immediately name, and which, when he did name it, he did not much like. It was the feeling of a man who has been told that his house is very handsome, but that it has been built upon the wrong foundation.

"You have come a long way to tell me that," he said, without turning round.

"I have come a long way for several reasons," his cousin answered. "That is not the chief of them. But since you ask it, I will confess that I wanted to see what you had become. I have wondered about it a great deal. One does wonder, you know, about the people one has—" And she paused.

"About the people one has refused?" said Hilyard, turning now and facing her with a smile that he meant to be easy and that he felt to be only brave.

Mrs. Penrose did not flinch; she had evidently expected the word, and she received it as a good fencer receives a thrust which he has invited. "I never refused you, Lawrence," she said quietly. "You never asked me. You talked to me about the duty of an educated man, and then you went to Europe. I have always thought it was the most curious proposal a woman ever had, if it was a proposal at all."

This was so exactly the truth, and so exactly the truth that he had spent twelve years in not looking at, that Hilyard was for a moment silent. Then he laughed—a short laugh, which had more of acknowledgment in it than of mirth. "You have the advantage of me," he said. "You have had time to put it into words. I have only had time to put it out of my mind."

"And have you succeeded?"

"Perfectly—until a quarter of an hour ago."

She looked at him with an expression which he could not quite read—something between compunction and amusement, with a third element behind both which he afterwards thought may have been relief. "I did not come to stir up old dust," she said. "Indeed I did not. I have a great deal of new dust of my own, and that is quite enough. I came because Aunt Hester is dead."

Hilyard sat down again, slowly. He had known that their aunt was ill—his mother's letters had mentioned it in the tone in which they mentioned the weather—but he had not known that she was dead, and the announcement affected him more than he would have supposed. Aunt Hester had been the grand personage of his childhood, a lady of formidable uprightness who lived in a square brick house at the top of the hill, with a garden full of box and a parlour full of mahogany, and who had given him, on his tenth birthday, a copy of Plutarch's Lives with the inscription, "To be read, not merely possessed." He had read it, in consequence, with a diligence which he had never since applied to anything; and it occurred to him now, with a little pang, that he had not written to her in three years.

"I am very sorry," he said. "I am sorrier than I can say. I ought to have known."

"You could not have known; it was very sudden at the last. She was in the garden one afternoon, cutting the dead heads off the roses, and she sat down on the bench by the sundial and did not get up again. It was the way she would have chosen, if she had been consulted. She did not like to be ill; she thought it was a want of character."

"That was so like her!" Hilyard murmured. "Everything was a question of character with her. I believe she thought the weather had a character, and that it was generally bad."

Mrs. Penrose smiled faintly. "She thought you had a character," she said; "and that it was very good—only wasted. She used to say so to me. She used to say that you were the only one of us who had any imagination, and that you had taken it to Europe as people take their money to a foreign bank, where they can never be sure of getting it back." She paused a moment, and then went on, in a lower and more deliberate tone, "She has left you the house, Lawrence."

Hilyard stared at her. "The house—on the hill?"

"The house on the hill, and the garden, and the mahogany, and a sum of money which is not large but which is quite sufficient to keep the house as she kept it. There is a condition attached to it. You must live in it—for at least half of every year. If you do not choose to live in it, it goes to the town, for a library."

There was a silence in the little salon, through which the voices of the street came up, thin and musical, like the voices of people in another world. Hilyard sat with his eyes fixed upon the stopped gilt clock, as if he expected it to begin going again and tell him what o'clock it was in his life. He was aware of a great many sensations at once—of surprise, of a certain tenderness, of a certain irritation, and, underlying all of these, of something that was not unlike fear.

"That is very like her, too," he said at last. "She has made me a present and set me an examination in the same breath."

"She would not have thought of it as an examination," said his cousin. "She would have thought of it as an opportunity."

"For the duty of an educated man in a new country?"

"Perhaps." Mrs. Penrose looked down at her hands, which were folded in her lap, and he noticed that she wore a ring which he did not remember, a plain band of gold, rather worn. "I was asked to tell you," she went on, "because I was going abroad, and because the lawyers thought it would be pleasanter for you to hear it from one of the family than to read it in a letter. And I was very willing to tell you. But I want you to understand, Lawrence, that I did not come to persuade you. I have no opinion about what you ought to do."

"You have a great many opinions," said Hilyard, "and I should think very poorly of you if you had not. You have been expressing them for the last half-hour with the utmost lucidity. You think I am wasting myself among painted ceilings."

She lifted her eyes to his, and he saw that they were full of a light which was neither quite amused nor quite grave. "I think," she said slowly, "that you have made a very pretty thing of your life, and that you are very much afraid someone will ask you what it is for. I don't ask it. I only notice that you are afraid."

He felt the justice of this with a sharpness which was almost physical; it was as if she had laid her finger upon a place which he had not known was sore until she touched it. But he was a man who had cultivated, in eleven years of Roman leisure, a very considerable degree of self-possession, and he did not allow the sensation to appear in his face. He merely leaned back in his creaking chair and regarded his cousin with an expression of humorous admiration.

"You have become very formidable, Caroline," he said. "You used to throw stones into ponds. Now you take soundings."

"Is that what you think?" she asked; and for the first time her composure seemed to waver a little, like the surface of water when a light wind passes over it. "I suppose it is true. One learns to take soundings when one has been nearly drowned." She stopped, and he waited; but she did not go on, and he understood, with that fine instinct of discretion which was one of the best things his foreign life had given him, that she had said as much as she intended about the late Mr. Penrose and the railways.

"I am sorry," he said gently. "I did not know."

"There was nothing to know—nothing, at least, that would have made a story. He was a good man in his way; it was only that his way was not mine. We were very civil to each other for nine years, and then he died, and I was very civil to his memory. That is all." She rose and went to the window, as he had done, and stood with her back to him, looking out at the rosy dusk which was gathering over the roofs. "I sometimes think," she said, without turning round, "that civility is the most dreadful thing in the world. It is like a very handsome house in which nobody lives."

Hilyard got up and stood beside her. Below them the lamps were beginning to be lighted, one by one, along the street, and the bells of a neighbouring church had begun to ring for the Ave Maria with a confused, sweet clamour, like a flock of birds rising together. He was aware that the moment was one of those which, if one does not take care, become memorable; and he was not sure that he wished to take care.

"And you think," he said, "that I have built myself a very handsome house in which nobody lives?"

"I think you have built yourself a very handsome house," said Mrs. Penrose, "and that you live in it quite alone. That is not the same thing, but it is not very different."

"And Aunt Hester's house—would that be any less lonely?"

She turned and looked at him, and he saw that her eyes were wet, though her voice was perfectly steady. "I don't know," she said. "I have told you that I have no opinion. I only know that it would be in Albany, and that I am going back to Albany in the autumn."

He took this in slowly, as one takes in a landscape which one has been looking at for some time without perceiving that it contained a figure. Then he laughed, very softly, and the laugh had in it, this time, no bravery at all, but only a kind of wondering humility.

"You said you had not come to persuade me," he said.

"I have not," his cousin answered, with a little flush which was the most becoming thing he had seen in her that afternoon. "I have come to tell you the news. What you do with it is your own affair. I should be sorry, Lawrence, if you went back for my sake; and I should be sorrier still if you stayed here for fear that I might think you had."

"That is a very delicate distinction," said Hilyard.

"It is the only one I have to offer you," she replied; and she held out her hand, as a sign that the interview was at an end.

He took it, and held it a moment longer than was strictly necessary, looking at the worn gold ring. "I shall come again to-morrow," he said. "I shall show you the painted ceiling, and you shall tell me that it is very pretty and not good for anything. And then—then we shall see."

"Then we shall see," Mrs. Penrose repeated; and she let him go.

He walked home through the dusk by the shortest way, which led him past nothing that he particularly cared for; and when he reached his apartment he stood for a long time in the great dim room, under the ceiling that had been painted by somebody nearly as good as Guido, and looked up at the faded gods and goddesses who were sporting there among their faded clouds. They had never seemed to him so beautiful, and they had never seemed to him so far away.

Here is an excerpt of Henry James's writing, to show you their style:

Valentin de Bellegarde died tranquilly, just as the cold faint March dawn began to illumine the faces of the little knot of friends gathered about his bedside. An hour afterwards Newman left the inn and drove to Geneva; he was naturally unwilling to be present at the arrival of Madame de Bellegarde and her first-born. At Geneva, for the moment, he remained. He was like a man who has had a fall and wants to sit still and count his bruises. He instantly wrote to Madame de Cintré, relating to her the circumstances of her brother’s death—with certain exceptions—and asking her what was the earliest moment at which he might hope that she would consent to see him. M. Ledoux had told him that he had reason to know that Valentin’s will—Bellegarde had a great deal of elegant personal property to dispose of—contained a request that he should be buried near his father in the churchyard of Fleurières, and Newman intended that the state of his own relations with the family should not deprive him of the satisfaction of helping to pay the last earthly honors to the best fellow in the world. He reflected that Valentin’s friendship was older than Urbain’s enmity, and that at a funeral it was easy to escape notice. Madame de Cintré’s answer to his letter enabled him to time his arrival at Fleurières. This answer was very brief; it ran as follows:— “I thank you for your letter, and for your being with Valentin. It is a most inexpressible sorrow to me that I was not. To see you will be nothing but a distress to me; there is no need, therefore, to wait for what you call brighter days. It is all one now, and I shall have no brighter days. Come when you please; only notify me first. My brother is to be buried here on Friday, and my family is to remain here. C. de C.” As soon as he received this letter Newman went straight to Paris and to Poitiers. The journey took him far southward, through green Touraine and across the far-shining Loire, into a country where the early spring deepened about him as he went. But he had never made a journey during which he heeded less what he would have called the lay of the land. He obtained lodging at the inn at Poitiers, and the next morning drove in a couple of hours to the village of Fleurières. But here, preoccupied though he was, he could not fail to notice the picturesqueness of the place. It was what the French call a petit bourg; it lay at the base of a sort of huge mound on the summit of which stood the crumbling ruins of a feudal castle, much of whose sturdy material, as well as that of the wall which dropped along the hill to enclose the clustered houses defensively, had been absorbed into the very substance of the village. The church was simply the former chapel of the castle, fronting upon its grass-grown court, which, however, was of generous enough width to have given up its quaintest corner to a little graveyard. Here the very headstones themselves seemed to sleep, as they slanted into the grass; the patient elbow of the rampart held them together on one side, and in front, far beneath their mossy lids, the green plains and blue distances stretched away. The way to church, up the hill, was impracticable to vehicles. It was lined with peasants, two or three rows deep, who stood watching old Madame de Bellegarde slowly ascend it, on the arm of her elder son, behind the pall-bearers of the other. Newman chose to lurk among the common mourners who murmured “Madame la Comtesse” as a tall figure veiled in black passed before them. He stood in the dusky little church while the service was going forward, but at the dismal tomb-side he turned away and walked down the hill. He went back to Poitiers, and spent two days in which patience and impatience were singularly commingled. On the third day he sent Madame de Cintré a note, saying that he would call upon her in the afternoon, and in accordance with this he again took his way to Fleurières. He left his vehicle at the tavern in the village street, and obeyed the simple instructions which were given him for finding the château.

“It is just beyond there,” said the landlord, and pointed to the tree-tops of the park, above the opposite houses. Newman followed the first cross-road to the right—it was bordered with mouldy cottages—and in a few moments saw before him the peaked roofs of the towers. Advancing farther, he found himself before a vast iron gate, rusty and closed; here he paused a moment, looking through the bars. The château was near the road; this was at once its merit and its defect; but its aspect was extremely impressive. Newman learned afterwards, from a guide-book of the province, that it dated from the time of Henry IV. It presented to the wide, paved area which preceded it and which was edged with shabby farm-buildings an immense façade of dark time-stained brick, flanked by two low wings, each of which terminated in a little Dutch-looking pavilion capped with a fantastic roof. Two towers rose behind, and behind the towers was a mass of elms and beeches, now just faintly green. But the great feature was a wide, green river which washed the foundations of the château. The building rose from an island in the circling stream, so that this formed a perfect moat spanned by a two-arched bridge without a parapet. The dull brick walls, which here and there made a grand, straight sweep; the ugly little cupolas of the wings, the deep-set windows, the long, steep pinnacles of mossy slate, all mirrored themselves in the tranquil river. Newman rang at the gate, and was almost frightened at the tone with which a big rusty bell above his head replied to him. An old woman came out from the gate-house and opened the creaking portal just wide enough for him to pass, and he went in, across the dry, bare court and the little cracked white slabs of the causeway on the moat. At the door of the château he waited for some moments, and this gave him a chance to observe that Fleurières was not “kept up,” and to reflect that it was a melancholy place of residence. “It looks,” said Newman to himself—and I give the comparison for what it is worth—“like a Chinese penitentiary.” At last the door was opened by a servant whom he remembered to have seen in the Rue de l’Université. The man’s dull face brightened as he perceived our hero, for Newman, for indefinable reasons, enjoyed the confidence of the liveried gentry. The footman led the way across a great central vestibule, with a pyramid of plants in tubs in the middle of glass doors all around, to what appeared to be the principal drawing-room of the château. Newman crossed the threshold of a room of superb proportions, which made him feel at first like a tourist with a guide-book and a cicerone awaiting a fee. But when his guide had left him alone, with the observation that he would call Madame la Comtesse, Newman perceived that the salon contained little that was remarkable save a dark ceiling with curiously carved rafters, some curtains of elaborate, antiquated tapestry, and a dark oaken floor, polished like a mirror. He waited some minutes, walking up and down; but at length, as he turned at the end of the room, he saw that Madame de Cintré had come in by a distant door. She wore a black dress, and she stood looking at him. As the length of the immense room lay between them he had time to look at her before they met in the middle of it. He was dismayed at the change in her appearance. Pale, heavy-browed, almost haggard with a sort of monastic rigidity in her dress, she had little but her pure features in common with the woman whose radiant good grace he had hitherto admired. She let her eyes rest on his own, and she let him take her hand; but her eyes looked like two rainy autumn moons, and her touch was portentously lifeless.

“I was at your brother’s funeral,” Newman said. “Then I waited three days. But I could wait no longer.”

“Nothing can be lost or gained by waiting,” said Madame de Cintré. “But it was very considerate of you to wait, wronged as you have been.”

“I’m glad you think I have been wronged,” said Newman, with that oddly humorous accent with which he often uttered words of the gravest meaning.

“Do I need to say so?” she asked. “I don’t think I have wronged, seriously, many persons; certainly not consciously. To you, to whom I have done this hard and cruel thing, the only reparation I can make is to say, ‘I know it, I feel it!’ The reparation is pitifully small!”

“Oh, it’s a great step forward!” said Newman, with a gracious smile of encouragement. He pushed a chair towards her and held it, looking at her urgently. She sat down, mechanically, and he seated himself near her; but in a moment he got up, restlessly, and stood before her. She remained seated, like a troubled creature who had passed through the stage of restlessness.

“I say nothing is to be gained by my seeing you,” she went on, “and yet I am very glad you came. Now I can tell you what I feel. It is a selfish pleasure, but it is one of the last I shall have.” And she paused, with her great misty eyes fixed upon him. “I know how I have deceived and injured you; I know how cruel and cowardly I have been. I see it as vividly as you do—I feel it to the ends of my fingers.” And she unclasped her hands, which were locked together in her lap, lifted them, and dropped them at her side. “Anything that you may have said of me in your angriest passion is nothing to what I have said to myself.”

“In my angriest passion,” said Newman, “I have said nothing hard of you. The very worst thing I have said of you yet is that you are the loveliest of women.” And he seated himself before her again abruptly. She flushed a little, but even her flush was pale. “That is because you think I will come back. But I will not come back. It is in that hope you have come here, I know; I am very sorry for you. I would do almost anything for you. To say that, after what I have done, seems simply impudent; but what can I say that will not seem impudent? To wrong you and apologize—that is easy enough. I should not have wronged you.” She stopped a moment, looking at him, and motioned him to let her go on. “I ought never to have listened to you at first; that was the wrong. No good could come of it. I felt it, and yet I listened; that was your fault. I liked you too much; I believed in you.”

“And don’t you believe in me now?”

“More than ever. But now it doesn’t matter. I have given you up.” Newman gave a powerful thump with his clenched fist upon his knee. “Why, why, why?” he cried. “Give me a reason—a decent reason. You are not a child—you are not a minor, nor an idiot. You are not obliged to drop me because your mother told you to. Such a reason isn’t worthy of you.”

“I know that; it’s not worthy of me. But it’s the only one I have to give. After all,” said Madame de Cintré, throwing out her hands, “think me an idiot and forget me! That will be the simplest way.” Newman got up and walked away with a crushing sense that his cause was lost, and yet with an equal inability to give up fighting. He went to one of the great windows, and looked out at the stiffly embanked river and the formal gardens which lay beyond it. When he turned round, Madame de Cintré had risen; she stood there silent and passive. “You are not frank,” said Newman; “you are not honest. Instead of saying that you are imbecile, you should say that other people are wicked. Your mother and your brother have been false and cruel; they have been so to me, and I am sure they have been so to you. Why do you try to shield them? Why do you sacrifice me to them? I’m not false; I’m not cruel. You don’t know what you give up; I can tell you that—you don’t. They bully you and plot about you; and I—I”—And he paused, holding out his hands. She turned away and began to leave him. “You told me the other day that you were afraid of your mother,” he said, following her. “What did you mean?” Madame de Cintré shook her head. “I remember; I was sorry afterwards.”

“You were sorry when she came down and put on the thumbscrews. In God’s name what is it she does to you?”

“Nothing. Nothing that you can understand. And now that I have given you up, I must not complain of her to you.”

“That’s no reasoning!” cried Newman. “Complain of her, on the contrary. Tell me all about it, frankly and trustfully, as you ought, and we will talk it over so satisfactorily that you won’t give me up.” Madame de Cintré looked down some moments, fixedly; and then, raising her eyes, she said, “One good at least has come of this: I have made you judge me more fairly. You thought of me in a way that did me great honor; I don’t know why you had taken it into your head. But it left me no loophole for escape—no chance to be the common, weak creature I am. It was not my fault; I warned you from the first. But I ought to have warned you more. I ought to have convinced you that I was doomed to disappoint you. But I was, in a way, too proud. You see what my superiority amounts to, I hope!” she went on, raising her voice with a tremor which even then and there Newman thought beautiful. “I am too proud to be honest, I am not too proud to be faithless. I am timid and cold and selfish. I am afraid of being uncomfortable.”

“And you call marrying me uncomfortable!” said Newman staring. Madame de Cintré blushed a little and seemed to say that if begging his pardon in words was impudent, she might at least thus mutely express her perfect comprehension of his finding her conduct odious. “It is not marrying you; it is doing all that would go with it. It’s the rupture, the defiance, the insisting upon being happy in my own way. What right have I to be happy when—when”—And she paused.

“When what?” said Newman.

“When others have been most unhappy!”

“What others?” Newman asked. “What have you to do with any others but me? Besides you said just now that you wanted happiness, and that you should find it by obeying your mother. You contradict yourself.”

“Yes, I contradict myself; that shows you that I am not even intelligent.”

“You are laughing at me!” cried Newman. “You are mocking me!” She looked at him intently, and an observer might have said that she was asking herself whether she might not most quickly end their common pain by confessing that she was mocking him. “No; I am not,” she presently said.

“Granting that you are not intelligent,” he went on, “that you are weak, that you are common, that you are nothing that I have believed you were—what I ask of you is not heroic effort, it is a very common effort. There is a great deal on my side to make it easy. The simple truth is that you don’t care enough about me to make it.”

“I am cold,” said Madame de Cintré, “I am as cold as that flowing river.” Newman gave a great rap on the floor with his stick, and a long, grim laugh. “Good, good!” he cried. “You go altogether too far—you overshoot the mark. There isn’t a woman in the world as bad as you would make yourself out. I see your game; it’s what I said. You are blackening yourself to whiten others. You don’t want to give me up, at all; you like me—you like me. I know you do; you have shown it, and I have felt it. After that, you may be as cold as you please! They have bullied you, I say; they have tortured you. It’s an outrage, and I insist upon saving you from the extravagance of your own generosity. Would you chop off your hand if your mother requested it?”
