Valentin de Bellegarde died tranquilly, just as the cold faint March dawn began to illumine the faces of the little knot of friends gathered about his bedside. An hour afterwards Newman left the inn and drove to Geneva; he was naturally unwilling to be present at the arrival of Madame de Bellegarde and her first-born. At Geneva, for the moment, he remained. He was like a man who has had a fall and wants to sit still and count his bruises. He instantly wrote to Madame de Cintré, relating to her the circumstances of her brother’s death—with certain exceptions—and asking her what was the earliest moment at which he might hope that she would consent to see him. M. Ledoux had told him that he had reason to know that Valentin’s will—Bellegarde had a great deal of elegant personal property to dispose of—contained a request that he should be buried near his father in the churchyard of Fleurières, and Newman intended that the state of his own relations with the family should not deprive him of the satisfaction of helping to pay the last earthly honors to the best fellow in the world. He reflected that Valentin’s friendship was older than Urbain’s enmity, and that at a funeral it was easy to escape notice. Madame de Cintré’s answer to his letter enabled him to time his arrival at Fleurières. This answer was very brief; it ran as follows:— “I thank you for your letter, and for your being with Valentin. It is a most inexpressible sorrow to me that I was not. To see you will be nothing but a distress to me; there is no need, therefore, to wait for what you call brighter days. It is all one now, and I shall have no brighter days. Come when you please; only notify me first. My brother is to be buried here on Friday, and my family is to remain here. C. de C.” As soon as he received this letter Newman went straight to Paris and to Poitiers. The journey took him far southward, through green Touraine and across the far-shining Loire, into a country where the early spring deepened about him as he went. But he had never made a journey during which he heeded less what he would have called the lay of the land. He obtained lodging at the inn at Poitiers, and the next morning drove in a couple of hours to the village of Fleurières. But here, preoccupied though he was, he could not fail to notice the picturesqueness of the place. It was what the French call a petit bourg; it lay at the base of a sort of huge mound on the summit of which stood the crumbling ruins of a feudal castle, much of whose sturdy material, as well as that of the wall which dropped along the hill to enclose the clustered houses defensively, had been absorbed into the very substance of the village. The church was simply the former chapel of the castle, fronting upon its grass-grown court, which, however, was of generous enough width to have given up its quaintest corner to a little graveyard. Here the very headstones themselves seemed to sleep, as they slanted into the grass; the patient elbow of the rampart held them together on one side, and in front, far beneath their mossy lids, the green plains and blue distances stretched away. The way to church, up the hill, was impracticable to vehicles. It was lined with peasants, two or three rows deep, who stood watching old Madame de Bellegarde slowly ascend it, on the arm of her elder son, behind the pall-bearers of the other. Newman chose to lurk among the common mourners who murmured “Madame la Comtesse” as a tall figure veiled in black passed before them. He stood in the dusky little church while the service was going forward, but at the dismal tomb-side he turned away and walked down the hill. He went back to Poitiers, and spent two days in which patience and impatience were singularly commingled. On the third day he sent Madame de Cintré a note, saying that he would call upon her in the afternoon, and in accordance with this he again took his way to Fleurières. He left his vehicle at the tavern in the village street, and obeyed the simple instructions which were given him for finding the château.

“It is just beyond there,” said the landlord, and pointed to the tree-tops of the park, above the opposite houses. Newman followed the first cross-road to the right—it was bordered with mouldy cottages—and in a few moments saw before him the peaked roofs of the towers. Advancing farther, he found himself before a vast iron gate, rusty and closed; here he paused a moment, looking through the bars. The château was near the road; this was at once its merit and its defect; but its aspect was extremely impressive. Newman learned afterwards, from a guide-book of the province, that it dated from the time of Henry IV. It presented to the wide, paved area which preceded it and which was edged with shabby farm-buildings an immense façade of dark time-stained brick, flanked by two low wings, each of which terminated in a little Dutch-looking pavilion capped with a fantastic roof. Two towers rose behind, and behind the towers was a mass of elms and beeches, now just faintly green. But the great feature was a wide, green river which washed the foundations of the château. The building rose from an island in the circling stream, so that this formed a perfect moat spanned by a two-arched bridge without a parapet. The dull brick walls, which here and there made a grand, straight sweep; the ugly little cupolas of the wings, the deep-set windows, the long, steep pinnacles of mossy slate, all mirrored themselves in the tranquil river. Newman rang at the gate, and was almost frightened at the tone with which a big rusty bell above his head replied to him. An old woman came out from the gate-house and opened the creaking portal just wide enough for him to pass, and he went in, across the dry, bare court and the little cracked white slabs of the causeway on the moat. At the door of the château he waited for some moments, and this gave him a chance to observe that Fleurières was not “kept up,” and to reflect that it was a melancholy place of residence. “It looks,” said Newman to himself—and I give the comparison for what it is worth—“like a Chinese penitentiary.” At last the door was opened by a servant whom he remembered to have seen in the Rue de l’Université. The man’s dull face brightened as he perceived our hero, for Newman, for indefinable reasons, enjoyed the confidence of the liveried gentry. The footman led the way across a great central vestibule, with a pyramid of plants in tubs in the middle of glass doors all around, to what appeared to be the principal drawing-room of the château. Newman crossed the threshold of a room of superb proportions, which made him feel at first like a tourist with a guide-book and a cicerone awaiting a fee. But when his guide had left him alone, with the observation that he would call Madame la Comtesse, Newman perceived that the salon contained little that was remarkable save a dark ceiling with curiously carved rafters, some curtains of elaborate, antiquated tapestry, and a dark oaken floor, polished like a mirror. He waited some minutes, walking up and down; but at length, as he turned at the end of the room, he saw that Madame de Cintré had come in by a distant door. She wore a black dress, and she stood looking at him. As the length of the immense room lay between them he had time to look at her before they met in the middle of it. He was dismayed at the change in her appearance. Pale, heavy-browed, almost haggard with a sort of monastic rigidity in her dress, she had little but her pure features in common with the woman whose radiant good grace he had hitherto admired. She let her eyes rest on his own, and she let him take her hand; but her eyes looked like two rainy autumn moons, and her touch was portentously lifeless.

“I was at your brother’s funeral,” Newman said. “Then I waited three days. But I could wait no longer.”

“Nothing can be lost or gained by waiting,” said Madame de Cintré. “But it was very considerate of you to wait, wronged as you have been.”

“I’m glad you think I have been wronged,” said Newman, with that oddly humorous accent with which he often uttered words of the gravest meaning.

“Do I need to say so?” she asked. “I don’t think I have wronged, seriously, many persons; certainly not consciously. To you, to whom I have done this hard and cruel thing, the only reparation I can make is to say, ‘I know it, I feel it!’ The reparation is pitifully small!”

“Oh, it’s a great step forward!” said Newman, with a gracious smile of encouragement. He pushed a chair towards her and held it, looking at her urgently. She sat down, mechanically, and he seated himself near her; but in a moment he got up, restlessly, and stood before her. She remained seated, like a troubled creature who had passed through the stage of restlessness.

“I say nothing is to be gained by my seeing you,” she went on, “and yet I am very glad you came. Now I can tell you what I feel. It is a selfish pleasure, but it is one of the last I shall have.” And she paused, with her great misty eyes fixed upon him. “I know how I have deceived and injured you; I know how cruel and cowardly I have been. I see it as vividly as you do—I feel it to the ends of my fingers.” And she unclasped her hands, which were locked together in her lap, lifted them, and dropped them at her side. “Anything that you may have said of me in your angriest passion is nothing to what I have said to myself.”

“In my angriest passion,” said Newman, “I have said nothing hard of you. The very worst thing I have said of you yet is that you are the loveliest of women.” And he seated himself before her again abruptly. She flushed a little, but even her flush was pale. “That is because you think I will come back. But I will not come back. It is in that hope you have come here, I know; I am very sorry for you. I would do almost anything for you. To say that, after what I have done, seems simply impudent; but what can I say that will not seem impudent? To wrong you and apologize—that is easy enough. I should not have wronged you.” She stopped a moment, looking at him, and motioned him to let her go on. “I ought never to have listened to you at first; that was the wrong. No good could come of it. I felt it, and yet I listened; that was your fault. I liked you too much; I believed in you.”

“And don’t you believe in me now?”

“More than ever. But now it doesn’t matter. I have given you up.” Newman gave a powerful thump with his clenched fist upon his knee. “Why, why, why?” he cried. “Give me a reason—a decent reason. You are not a child—you are not a minor, nor an idiot. You are not obliged to drop me because your mother told you to. Such a reason isn’t worthy of you.”

“I know that; it’s not worthy of me. But it’s the only one I have to give. After all,” said Madame de Cintré, throwing out her hands, “think me an idiot and forget me! That will be the simplest way.” Newman got up and walked away with a crushing sense that his cause was lost, and yet with an equal inability to give up fighting. He went to one of the great windows, and looked out at the stiffly embanked river and the formal gardens which lay beyond it. When he turned round, Madame de Cintré had risen; she stood there silent and passive. “You are not frank,” said Newman; “you are not honest. Instead of saying that you are imbecile, you should say that other people are wicked. Your mother and your brother have been false and cruel; they have been so to me, and I am sure they have been so to you. Why do you try to shield them? Why do you sacrifice me to them? I’m not false; I’m not cruel. You don’t know what you give up; I can tell you that—you don’t. They bully you and plot about you; and I—I”—And he paused, holding out his hands. She turned away and began to leave him. “You told me the other day that you were afraid of your mother,” he said, following her. “What did you mean?” Madame de Cintré shook her head. “I remember; I was sorry afterwards.”

“You were sorry when she came down and put on the thumbscrews. In God’s name what is it she does to you?”

“Nothing. Nothing that you can understand. And now that I have given you up, I must not complain of her to you.”

“That’s no reasoning!” cried Newman. “Complain of her, on the contrary. Tell me all about it, frankly and trustfully, as you ought, and we will talk it over so satisfactorily that you won’t give me up.” Madame de Cintré looked down some moments, fixedly; and then, raising her eyes, she said, “One good at least has come of this: I have made you judge me more fairly. You thought of me in a way that did me great honor; I don’t know why you had taken it into your head. But it left me no loophole for escape—no chance to be the common, weak creature I am. It was not my fault; I warned you from the first. But I ought to have warned you more. I ought to have convinced you that I was doomed to disappoint you. But I was, in a way, too proud. You see what my superiority amounts to, I hope!” she went on, raising her voice with a tremor which even then and there Newman thought beautiful. “I am too proud to be honest, I am not too proud to be faithless. I am timid and cold and selfish. I am afraid of being uncomfortable.”

“And you call marrying me uncomfortable!” said Newman staring. Madame de Cintré blushed a little and seemed to say that if begging his pardon in words was impudent, she might at least thus mutely express her perfect comprehension of his finding her conduct odious. “It is not marrying you; it is doing all that would go with it. It’s the rupture, the defiance, the insisting upon being happy in my own way. What right have I to be happy when—when”—And she paused.

“When what?” said Newman.

“When others have been most unhappy!”

“What others?” Newman asked. “What have you to do with any others but me? Besides you said just now that you wanted happiness, and that you should find it by obeying your mother. You contradict yourself.”

“Yes, I contradict myself; that shows you that I am not even intelligent.”

“You are laughing at me!” cried Newman. “You are mocking me!” She looked at him intently, and an observer might have said that she was asking herself whether she might not most quickly end their common pain by confessing that she was mocking him. “No; I am not,” she presently said.

“Granting that you are not intelligent,” he went on, “that you are weak, that you are common, that you are nothing that I have believed you were—what I ask of you is not heroic effort, it is a very common effort. There is a great deal on my side to make it easy. The simple truth is that you don’t care enough about me to make it.”

“I am cold,” said Madame de Cintré, “I am as cold as that flowing river.” Newman gave a great rap on the floor with his stick, and a long, grim laugh. “Good, good!” he cried. “You go altogether too far—you overshoot the mark. There isn’t a woman in the world as bad as you would make yourself out. I see your game; it’s what I said. You are blackening yourself to whiten others. You don’t want to give me up, at all; you like me—you like me. I know you do; you have shown it, and I have felt it. After that, you may be as cold as you please! They have bullied you, I say; they have tortured you. It’s an outrage, and I insist upon saving you from the extravagance of your own generosity. Would you chop off your hand if your mother requested it?”

Mr. Tressider had been told of the thing just before luncheon, and he had borne the telling with a composure that, it must be confessed, did him more credit as a host than as a parent. He had sat through the cutlets and the long, bland pudding opposite Mrs. Ventnor, who was to leave by the four o'clock train, and he had talked to her of the Lucerne hotels, of the price of hothouse grapes, and of a bishop they both knew, with a fluency he afterwards thought almost indecent. Mrs. Ventnor had talked too. She had even laughed, at moments, with a little clear ring that seemed to him to come from a great way off, as from the bottom of a well in which something precious had been dropped. When her fly came round to the door he handed her into it with all the forms. She gave him two fingers in a grey glove, said that Wrayford had been "most restful," and looked at him, as the wheels began to turn, in a manner that he took some pains, over the next quarter of an hour, not to interpret. Then he went into the library, rang the bell, and told the man that he should be glad if Miss Pellew would bring Miss Dorothea down at half-past four.

He had half an hour, therefore, and he spent it, characteristically, in walking up and down. The library at Wrayford was a long, low room with three deep windows on the garden. In October, at that hour, the light came in with a kind of reluctance, as if it had been asked to stay later than it liked and were making the best of it. Mr. Tressider was a man of forty-four, tall and slightly stooping, with a fine, rather worn face and the air (which he had never tried to get, and which was perhaps for that reason the more complete) of a person who has always been reasonable. He had been reasonable at Oxford, reasonable in his marriage, and reasonable, two years before, at his wife's death. People said of him, with an emphasis it would be hard to define, that he had "taken it beautifully." What he had taken beautifully, in the main, was the charge of a small daughter, then five years old and now seven. He had brought to the task the same gentle, deliberate intelligence with which he would have catalogued a collection of coins, and with something of the same faint fear of handling the objects too much.

The facts were simple enough, and Miss Pellew had laid them before him with a governess's exactness and a governess's evident relief at having someone to lay them before. On the previous afternoon Mrs. Ventnor, a lady of no great age and of a very great deal of manner, had found Dorothea alone in the yew walk and had been kind to her. In the course of that kindness she had asked the child, as ladies will, whether she was glad to have visitors at Wrayford. Dorothea had considered, and had replied that she was glad to have some visitors. Pressed, very charmingly, to say whether Mrs. Ventnor was among the happy number, she had answered with perfect candour that she did not know yet, but that papa said Mrs. Ventnor "came to look at the house as if she meant to buy it, and at him as if he were thrown in." Mrs. Ventnor, Miss Pellew reported, had said "Did he, dear?" in a voice of great sweetness. She had then gone indoors. She had come down to dinner in her best pearls and with a headache, and she had announced her departure, a day early, at breakfast.

Mr. Tressider had made the remark. That was the point at which his meditation always broke off, like a path ending suddenly at a ha-ha. He had made it, on the evening of Mrs. Ventnor's arrival, to his old friend Colonel Brabazon, over the last of the claret, in a tone he had supposed perfectly private and in a mood he would have called, if anyone had pressed him, playful. He had no recollection of the child being near. He seemed now to recollect, with an odd belated distinctness, a small white figure on the stairs and a door that had not been quite shut. The remark had struck him, at the moment of making it, as rather good. It struck him now as the kind of thing a man says once in his life and has to keep paying for.

It may be imagined, then, that the interview before him wore a complicated face. He was quite clear that the child must be spoken to. A child who repeats to a guest what has been said of the guest is a child who has done something very wrong. It was of no use to argue that the remark had been true; or rather, that it had been true was precisely what made the matter grave. But his clearness went no further than that, and beyond it lay a region he could not see into. He walked to the window and looked out at the long lawn, where a gardener was sweeping leaves into little heaps that the wind took apart again, one by one, with a sort of patient malice. He had a strong impression, which he did not try to put into words, that he himself was about to be swept up in very much the same way.

At half-past four exactly there was a knock, and Miss Pellew put her head in, very discreetly, and then drew it back. In its place, as if pushed gently from behind, Dorothea came into the room. The door closed upon her with a little click of finality. She stood just inside it, a small person in a dark blue frock with a white collar, her hands folded in front of her in an attitude that had evidently been recommended on the stairs. She was not a pretty child, people said, but she was going to be "interesting." Her father had never been quite sure what they meant by that. He saw it now, however. It lay in her eyes, which were large and grey and unblinking, and which she fixed on him, across the long room, with an expression of the most serious and attentive expectancy, as if he were going to do something remarkable and she would not for the world have missed it.

"Come here, Dolly," said Mr. Tressider.

She came the length of the room without hurrying, with a little touch of ceremony that he found extremely disconcerting, and stopped at a carefully judged distance from his chair. He had sat down, on a sudden instinct that it would be better to be lower. Even so their eyes were not level. He was conscious of looking down at her as from a pulpit, and the sensation did not help him.

"Do you know why I have sent for you?"

Dorothea considered. She always considered, which was one of the things about her that people found interesting. "Is it about Mrs. Ventnor?" she asked.

"It is about Mrs. Ventnor." He paused, and then, because it seemed the proper form, he added, "Miss Pellew has told me what you said to her yesterday, in the yew walk."

"Yes," said Dorothea simply. "I thought she would." The tone was not defiant. It was merely the tone of one who has observed how things generally fall out and sees no reason to be surprised when they do. Her father felt that the conversation had already got a little away from him.

"Then you know," he went on, more firmly, "that it was a very wrong thing to say."

"Was it wrong?" Dorothea asked. There was no impudence in the question. She asked it, if one may say so, scientifically, as she might have asked whether a certain mushroom were the kind one ate.

"It was very wrong indeed. It was unkind, and it was rude, and it made Mrs. Ventnor unhappy. She has gone away a day sooner than she meant to. Did you know that?"

"I saw the fly," said Dorothea. She looked down for a moment at her folded hands, and then up again. "Was she very unhappy, papa?"

Mr. Tressider hesitated. He had a fine regard for the truth, and he could not, with any regard for it at all, describe Mrs. Ventnor's state as one of unmixed grief. She had been, he thought, rather more angry than unhappy. Under the anger, too, there had been something he could only call satisfaction, as of a lady who has found a reason she would otherwise have had to invent. But this was not a distinction to lay before a child of seven, and he took refuge in a generality.

"People are always unhappy when they are told unkind things about themselves," he said.

"Even when they're true?" asked Dorothea.

It was the question he had seen coming, as one sees a carriage coming down a long straight road and has nothing to do but wait for it. "Especially when they are true," he said, and immediately felt that this was not at all what he had meant to say. "That is—what I mean is, Dolly, that whether a thing is true or not is not the only question. There are a great many true things that one must not say. It is not kind to say them, and it is not—it is not the custom."

Dorothea received this in silence. He saw that she was turning it over, and that she found it, like a new toy, a little puzzling in its working but by no means without interest. "Then why," she said presently, "did you say it to Colonel Brabazon?"

I will not pretend that Mr. Tressider was unprepared for this. He had foreseen it from the moment Miss Pellew left him. But there is a difference, as everybody knows, between foreseeing a blow and receiving it, and he received this one in a place he had not thought to guard. It was not that the child had caught him out. He had expected that. It was the perfect absence of triumph in the catching. She did not look at him as a small adversary who has scored a point. She looked at him as one who has asked a reasonable question and waits, with every confidence, for a reasonable answer. That confidence, indeed, was the most terrible part of it. He would have been a great deal more comfortable if she had been pert.

He got up and went to the fireplace, where nothing was burning, and stood with his back to it, as men do who wish to look as if there were a fire.

"That," he said, after a moment, "was a different thing."

"Why was it different?"

"Because Colonel Brabazon is my friend, and I was talking to him privately. I was not talking to Mrs. Ventnor. I did not mean it to go any further. When grown-up people talk together in that way, Dolly, they say things they would not say to anyone else, and the person they say them to understands that. It is a kind of—" he searched for the word, and found, with a slight sense of absurdity, that it was "—a kind of trust."

"Then I broke the trust," said Dorothea, slowly, as one who is getting the thing by heart.

"In a way. Yes. You heard something that was not meant for you, and you repeated it to the one person in the world who ought not to have heard it."

Dorothea looked at the carpet. It was an old Turkey carpet, a good deal worn in the middle, and she seemed to be studying the pattern with great attention, as though the answer to the whole difficulty might be woven into it somewhere if one only looked long enough. Her father watched her, and was aware of a feeling he would have been ashamed to confess and was equally unable to suppress: a sort of appalled admiration. She was so small, and she was thinking so hard.

"I didn't know it was a trust," she said at last. "I thought it was a joke. You laughed, and Colonel Brabazon laughed, and I thought, if it's a joke, Mrs. Ventnor might like it too. People like jokes." She raised her eyes. "But she didn't laugh."

"No," said Mr. Tressider. "She didn't laugh."

"Was it because it wasn't a good joke? Or because it was about her?"

"Because it was about her," he said. There was a short silence, and then, with a candour he had not known he possessed, he added, "It was not a very good joke either."

Dorothea looked at him with a new expression, which he could not at once make out. It might have been sympathy. It might also, he thought, have been the first faint dawning of a judgment. He was by no means sure which of the two he would have preferred.

"Then you were naughty too," she said.

It came out without the least malice, as a simple point of fact, a sum she had been working out and had now got to the bottom of. Mr. Tressider stood quite still before the empty grate. It came over him, with a force that was almost physical, that he had arrived at one of those moments a man may go through a whole life without meeting, and that most men, meeting them, contrive to slip past. He might have slipped past this one. Nothing would have been easier. He had only to say, in the voice his own father had used to him, that little girls did not speak so to their papas. He had only to send her back to Miss Pellew with a punishment, a supper of bread and milk, an early bed, a prohibition of the pony, and the thing would have been folded up and put away. There it would have lain, he knew, among the other things that had been folded up and put away in Dorothea's small, grave, unforgetting mind, and one day, perhaps years hence, she would take it out and look at it. He found he could not bear the thought of what she would see.

"Yes," he said. "I was naughty too."

He had not known how the words would sound until he heard them. They sounded, in the long low room, extraordinarily small and extraordinarily loud at once. Dorothea received them without visible emotion. She only unclasped her hands, which had been locked together all this while, and let them hang at her sides, as if a weight she had been holding had been taken from her.

"Then are we both to be punished?" she asked.

Mr. Tressider gave a short laugh, which he could not have stopped and did not try to. "I think I have been punished already," he said. "I had to sit through luncheon."

Dorothea did not understand this, and she very properly declined to pretend that she did. She waited.

He came back to his chair and sat down in it, and this time, on an impulse he did not examine, he leaned forward and took both her hands. They were cold. He realised, with a pang, that she had been a great deal more frightened than she had allowed him to see, and that the folded hands and the measured approach had been a sort of armour. She had put it on, poor small soldier, on the stairs.

"Listen to me, Dolly," he said. "I am going to tell you something, and I want you to remember it. It is not easy, and I am not sure that I understand it perfectly myself, so you must not mind if I say it badly. When I said that thing to Colonel Brabazon, I did wrong, because I said an unkind thing about a person who was a guest in my house and who had done me no harm. That she would never hear of it did not make it right. It only made it safe. Do you see the difference?"

Dorothea frowned. "I think so," she said, with great caution.

"And when you said it to Mrs. Ventnor, you did wrong too. But your wrong was a different wrong from mine, and in some ways—" he paused, and she saw him pause, and he saw that she saw it "—in some ways it was not so bad, because you did not know. And in other ways it was worse, because it hurt her, and mine did not. Do you see that?"

"Yes," said Dorothea. She seemed to see it a great deal better than he did.

"So I shall not punish you," he went on, "because I don't think it would be fair, and because I think you understand already. But I want you to do something for me. I want you to write to Mrs. Ventnor."

Dorothea's eyes widened. "To say I'm sorry?"

"To say you are sorry."

She considered this with her customary gravity. Then she put the question that her father, had he known her a little better, would have told himself she was bound to put. "Are you going to write to her too?"

Mr. Tressider looked at her for a long moment. Through the window behind her he could see the gardener, who had given up the struggle with the leaves and was trundling his barrow away down the walk, with an air of philosophic resignation that struck him, just then, as the wisest thing in the world. He thought of Mrs. Ventnor. He thought of the two fingers in the grey glove and of the way she had looked at him as the fly turned. He thought, with a clearness that was new to him and not wholly agreeable, of what such a letter would have to say, and what it could not possibly say, and of what Mrs. Ventnor, who was not a fool, would read between the lines. It would be, he perceived, the most difficult letter of his life. He perceived also, by some process he could not trace, that he was going to write it.

"Yes," he said. "I am going to write to her too."

Dorothea gave a little nod. It was the nod of a person who has had a matter put on a proper footing and is satisfied. Then, with a sudden lapse into her seven years, she came closer, leaned against his knee, and said in quite a different voice, a small, tired, confiding voice, "I didn't like her very much, papa."

"No," said Mr. Tressider. "I know you didn't."

"Did you?"

He hesitated, and then he laughed again, more gently this time, and put his hand on her hair. "I shall tell you that," he said, "when you are older."

She accepted the postponement, as children will accept anything that is offered with sufficient firmness, and presently, at a sign from him, she went back across the long room to the door. It was getting dusky now, and her small blue figure seemed to dwindle as it went, until at the threshold she turned and looked back at him with those large grey considering eyes. For a moment he had the singular impression that she was not seven at all, but very old, and that it was she who had sent for him.

"Papa," she said, "what shall I put in the letter?"

"Put the truth," said Mr. Tressider, and then, catching himself, he added, with a rueful smile she could not have seen in that light, "or as much of it, Dolly, as is kind."

She went out, and the door closed after her with the same little click as before. Mr. Tressider sat on for some time in the darkening library without ringing for the lamps. He was thinking, I believe, not so much of Mrs. Ventnor, nor even of Dorothea, as of the curious, almost comic reversal by which he had come down to administer a lesson and was going up to dress for dinner with one in his own pocket. He was a just man, and he did not resent it. But he was conscious, as he rose at last and went to the writing-table, that his daughter had been more interesting than he had bargained for. He was conscious also, which was perhaps the more uncomfortable reflection, that the people who called her so had been right.
