The Aldridges' brougham turned out of Fifth Avenue a little after eleven, and Margaret, who had sat through the drive with her hands folded upon the clasp of her small beaded bag, was conscious that her husband had not spoken since they left the Lorings' door. This was not in itself remarkable. Stephen Aldridge belonged to that class of men for whom silence in a closed carriage is a form of courtesy, a tacit acknowledgment that whatever had been worth saying had already been said, in a better light and to more appreciative listeners. He sat with his gloved hands upon the head of his stick, his profile, faintly illuminated at intervals by the passing lamps, presenting to her that look of tranquil competence which she had once thought the most reassuring thing in the world, and which she had lately come to regard as she might have regarded a handsome piece of furniture too large for the room.

She was aware of the letter in her bag as one is aware of a small burn on the finger: it did not hurt unless she touched it, and she could not keep from touching it. It had come by the second post, in a hand she had not seen for eleven years and had recognized before she had broken the seal, and she had carried it all day, through a luncheon at her mother's and a call upon a cousin and the long, glittering monotony of Mrs. Loring's dinner, with the peculiar sensation of a woman who has smuggled something through the customs and dares not look at the inspector.

The house in Sixty-third Street received them with its usual air of having been kept warm on purpose. The footman took Stephen's coat; Margaret's maid hovered at the turn of the stairs; and the library fire, which Stephen liked to find burning at whatever hour he came in, had been built up to a pitch of comfortable brightness that seemed to Margaret, as she stood in the doorway, almost an impertinence. She dismissed the maid with a word and followed her husband into the room.

He had gone at once to the hearth, where he stood, as was his habit, with one foot upon the fender and his eyes upon the clock, as if the hour itself were a guest whose punctuality he wished to commend. He was a man of forty-six, still slender, with the slightly faded fairness of those whom prosperity has preserved rather than enriched, and a way of smoothing his moustache with the knuckle of his forefinger when he was about to say something judicious.

"Mrs. Loring's terrapin," he observed, "is not what it was. I suspect she has changed her cook. One ought to say something to Loring, but one never knows how these things are taken."

Margaret had seated herself in the low chair at the other side of the fire. She drew off her gloves slowly, a finger at a time, and laid them on the arm of the chair.

"Stephen," she said, "I have had a letter."

He turned his head with the mild attentiveness he accorded to all her remarks, the attentiveness of a man who has never been surprised by his wife and does not expect to be.

"Yes?"

"From Philip Ormsby."

There was a pause, of the length in which a well-bred man decides what his face shall do. Stephen's face did nothing. He took his foot from the fender and stood upright, and the movement had about it something so deliberate, so evidently chosen in preference to some other movement, that she felt her heart contract.

"Ormsby," he repeated. "I had understood he was abroad."

"He is in Rome. He has been there for some years, I believe." She opened the bag and took out the letter, but did not offer it to him; she held it in her lap, the thin foreign paper crackling a little under her fingers. "He is ill. He says, in fact, that he is dying. The doctors have given him until the spring, or perhaps a little beyond it."

"I am very sorry to hear it," said Stephen; and she knew that he was, in the precise measure that the circumstances required.

"He asks me to come to him."

She had rehearsed the sentence so many times since the morning that it came out with a flatness that dismayed her. She had meant it to fall between them like a challenge, and it fell instead like a remark about the weather, and lay there on the hearth-rug, between his polished shoes and the hem of her grey satin gown, without either of them appearing to notice it.

Stephen sat down. He did so with care, drawing up the knees of his trousers, and when he was settled he looked at her across the firelight with an expression in which she could detect nothing but a grave and considerate kindness.

"Poor fellow," he said. "It is natural, I suppose, that a man in his situation should turn to old friends. You will write to him, of course. I should think a kind letter, not too long, would be the right thing. Perhaps you would like me to add a line."

It was so exactly what she had foreseen, so exactly the response that eleven years of marriage had trained her to expect, that for a moment she could only look at him. She had supposed, in the course of that long day, every possible answer from him except the one he had made, and she now perceived that she had supposed them all precisely in order to avoid supposing this one. Anger she could have met; jealousy she could have met; even ridicule she had a certain armour against. But this placid assumption that the letter required nothing more than another letter, that the summons of a dying man could be satisfactorily discharged by a few well-chosen sentences on her own engraved paper, left her standing, as it were, in an empty room with her weapons in her hands.

"I do not think," she said, "that a letter would be the right thing."

He raised his eyebrows very slightly.

"No? What, then?"

"I think I ought to go."

The clock on the mantelpiece, a small gilt affair that had been one of their wedding presents, chose this moment to strike the half-hour; and they both waited, with the instinctive politeness of people who do not interrupt, until it had finished.

"To Rome," said Stephen at length.

"To Rome."

"Alone?"

"I should take Parsons, naturally."

He smoothed his moustache with his knuckle. She watched the gesture as she might have watched a judge settling his robes.

"My dear Margaret," he said, "you must let me put the thing before you as it would appear to other people. I don't say it is how I see it myself; you know that I have never been a man to make difficulties. But you are not a girl, and you are not living in a vacuum. You are my wife, and Bessie's mother, and you have a position in this town which, I think you will allow, it has cost us both something to maintain. If you were to start for Italy in the middle of February, without me and without the child, to sit at the bedside of a man to whom, if you will forgive my saying so, it was very generally supposed at one time that you were engaged—"

"I was never engaged to him."

"I said it was supposed. I am not speaking of the facts. I am speaking of what Mrs. Loring would say to Mrs. Trent, and what Mrs. Trent would say to everybody else."

"And is that to decide it?"

"It need not decide it. But it must be considered. You have always considered it yourself, Margaret. I have never known you to be indifferent to it."

That was true, and the truth of it stung her more sharply than any reproach could have done. She had considered it all her life. She had been brought up to consider it as she had been brought up to say her prayers and to hold her fork in a particular way; and it had seemed to her, until this morning, as much a part of the natural order as the coming of Lent or the closing of the opera season. It was considering it, eleven years ago, that had made her send Philip Ormsby away with nothing in his hands but a vague and insubstantial future, and accept instead the solid and tangible present that Stephen Aldridge had offered her in his mother's drawing-room with the air of a man presenting a carefully drawn deed.

"You speak," she said, "as if the only thing that mattered were what people would say."

"Not the only thing. But a very real one. You and I did not invent the world we live in, my dear, and we are not likely to reform it. We can only live in it decently."

"Decently!" She heard her own voice rise, and lowered it at once, with a glance at the door, so deeply was the habit of the house ingrained in her. "Is it decent to let a man die alone, in a hired lodging, among strangers, because Mrs. Trent might find it amusing to talk about?"

"He is not, I imagine, quite alone. Ormsby always had a great many friends. And Rome is full of Americans at this season."

She looked at him, and for the first time in many years she tried to see him as a stranger might have seen him: the long, well-kept hands, the impeccable linen, the face that had never in her memory been disordered by any emotion it had not first examined and approved. She had once supposed that so much composure must be the surface of some deep reservoir of feeling, as the stillness of a lake is said to indicate its depth. She was no longer certain that the lake was not merely a very well-made pond.

"Stephen," she said slowly, "you have not once asked me whether I loved him."

He was silent for a moment. Then he leaned forward and, taking up the poker, rearranged a log that had no need of rearranging.

"No," he said. "I have not."

"Is it because you do not care?"

"It is because I have always known."

The words were spoken so quietly, with so little emphasis, that she did not at first take in their meaning. When she did, she felt the blood leave her face, and she was glad that the lamp stood behind her chair.

"You have always known," she repeated.

"Since before we were married. My dear Margaret, did you suppose I was blind? Everybody knew. Your mother knew; she told me, in fact, with a great deal of tact, that it had been a girlish fancy and was quite over. I did not believe it was quite over, but I believed it would be, in time. I thought that you were a sensible woman, and that you would make a sensible choice, and that the rest would take care of itself." He replaced the poker in its stand with a small, precise click. "I was right, I think. You did make a sensible choice. And the rest has taken care of itself, very well, on the whole."

"And the letters?" she said, hardly knowing why she asked it.

"What letters?"

"He wrote to me. Two or three times, in the first years. I kept them."

"I know you did," said Stephen gently. "They are in the rosewood box in your dressing-room, under the Valenciennes collar that belonged to your grandmother. Parsons mentioned it once, years ago, when the box was mislaid in moving. I told her to put it back exactly where she had found it and to say nothing to you."

Margaret sat very still. She had the sensation of a person who, having believed herself to be walking alone in a dark garden, discovers that someone has been holding a lantern behind her the whole way. All the small concealments of her married life, the sense of a private chamber into which she might retire and which belonged to her alone, the secret that had seemed to give her, in her own eyes, a certain depth and dignity, had been known, and catalogued, and tolerated, and put back in its place with the Valenciennes collar on top.

"You never said anything," she murmured.

"What was there to say? It was not the sort of thing one speaks of. I trusted you to be what you are, and you have never disappointed me."

She understood then, with a clearness that was almost a physical pain, that this was the most terrible thing he could have said to her, and that he had said it as a compliment. He had trusted her to be what she was; and what she was, it appeared, was a woman who kept a dead man's letters in a rosewood box and would never, under any provocation, take them out.

"And if I disappointed you now?" she said. "If I went to Rome?"

He considered the question with perfect seriousness, as he considered everything.

"I don't think you will," he said. "But if you feel strongly about it, there is no reason why you should not go, provided it is done in the right way." He paused, and she saw his face assume the faintly animated expression it wore when he was arranging a dinner or planning a journey. "As a matter of fact, I have been thinking for some time that we ought to go abroad again. Bessie is getting to an age when she ought to see something of Europe; her French is deplorable, and Miss Fenwick tells me she has no feeling whatever for art. We might go out at the beginning of March, spend a few weeks in Rome, and go on to Florence for Easter. I could get away from the office without much difficulty. You could see Ormsby as often as you liked; I would call on him myself, naturally. Nobody could find anything to say about that. It would be the most natural thing in the world."

He smiled at her, the kind, slightly tired smile of a man who has found a reasonable solution to an awkward problem and expects to be thanked for it.

Margaret looked down at the letter in her lap. She saw it all as he had described it: the steamer, the Grand Hotel, Bessie in her new travelling dress complaining of the cold in the galleries, Stephen consulting his Baedeker in the carriage, and herself, at an hour fixed in advance and announced to the concierge, mounting the stairs of some shabby palazzo to sit for twenty minutes at the bedside of a dying man, while her husband waited in the anteroom with his hat upon his knee and his watch in his hand. She saw Philip's eyes turn from her face to the doorway where Stephen stood, and she saw them understand everything, and forgive it, because he had always forgiven her everything; and she knew that she could not endure his forgiveness in that room.

"No," she said. "I don't think that would do."

"No?" Stephen looked genuinely puzzled. "I thought it was what you wanted."

"It was very kind of you to suggest it." She heard her voice come back to its accustomed pitch, the low, well-modulated voice in which she ordered dinners and declined invitations and condoled with acquaintances upon their bereavements; and she listened to it with a kind of detached wonder, as if it belonged to some other woman in the next room. "But I think, on the whole, you were right. A letter would be best."

He rose, with an air of relief so delicately suppressed that only eleven years of observation enabled her to detect it.

"I am sure it would. And you write such charming letters, Margaret. He will be touched by it, I know." He came round the hearth and bent over her chair, and she felt his lips, dry and cool, upon her forehead. "Don't sit up too late. You look tired. These long dinners are a strain; I sometimes think we go out too much."

"Perhaps we do."

"We might stay quietly at home next week. I'll tell Hobbs to refuse the Van Allens." He paused at the door, his hand upon the knob, and looked back at her with a sudden and almost boyish solicitude that she had not seen in his face for years. "You're not unhappy, are you, my dear?"

She looked up at him, and smiled.

"No," she said. "I am not unhappy."

When the door had closed behind him she sat for a long time without moving, the letter lying in her lap and the fire sinking slowly to a bed of crimson ash. The house was perfectly silent; it was a house in which silence was one of the things that money could buy, and Stephen had bought a great deal of it. She thought of the rosewood box upstairs, and of Parsons putting it back under the collar with her own scrupulous hands, and of Stephen standing by, approving; and she perceived that there was not a single corner of her life which had not been swept and dusted and set in order by someone who loved her.

At length she rose and went to the writing-table in the window, and took a sheet of her paper from the rack, and dipped her pen. *Dear Philip,* she wrote; and then she sat looking at the two words in the lamplight, and found that she could think of nothing to put after them that she had not been saying, in one form or another, every day of her married life.

Mrs. Townsend Haverly had always held that a drawing-room should be prepared for a visitor much as a countenance is prepared for a portrait: not so as to disguise its character, which would be both futile and vulgar, but so as to present that character in the most becoming light. On the April afternoon when her cousin was expected, she had accordingly spent the better part of an hour in moving a Sèvres jardinière from the console to the centre-table and back again, in drawing the brown velvet curtains a quarter of an inch closer against the glare of Fifth Avenue, and in considering, with a scrupulousness she would have been ashamed to acknowledge, whether the photograph of her late husband in its silver frame ought to stand upon the piano, where it had stood for eleven years, or be removed to the writing-table, where it might seem less to invite remark.

She left it at last upon the piano, reflecting that to move it would be to confess that she had thought of moving it; and Mrs. Haverly had lived too long among people to whom every confession was a currency not to know the value of withholding even the smallest coin.

It was twenty-two years since she had seen Katharine Rensford, who was now the Comtesse de Mauvilliers, and who had written from the Holland House, in a hand which seemed to Sophy to have grown at once larger and less legible, that she was "only in New York for a fortnight, darling, and should die if she did not see her dearest Sophy before anyone else." The phrase had a little troubled Mrs. Haverly, who knew that Kitty had been three days in the city already, and that the Lanyon girls, who were related to nobody in particular, had dined with her on the second; but she had answered with the cordial promptness which the occasion required, and had then sat for some time with the note in her lap, looking out at the slow procession of carriages and wondering what, after so long an interval, two women who had once shared a governess, a pony, and every secret of their girlhood could possibly find to say to each other.

For the separation had not been merely one of distance. Kitty had gone abroad in the autumn of the year in which she broke her engagement to Townsend Haverly, and she had gone, as the family put it, "under a cloud," though the cloud had never been precisely defined, and had dispersed itself, in the course of time, into that diffused and not unflattering vapour which in New York surrounded any woman who had done something unaccountable and married a foreigner afterwards. Sophy herself had married Townsend in the following spring. No one had ever suggested that there was anything unaccountable in that; and it had sometimes seemed to her, in the long and orderly years that followed, that the absence of any such suggestion was the one thing in her life she had never been able to forgive.

The bell sounded at a quarter past four, which was a quarter of an hour later than Kitty had named, and Mrs. Haverly, who had been standing by the window, sat down hastily in the chair beside the fire and took up a piece of needlework she had no intention of continuing. She heard the murmur of the parlour-maid in the hall, a rustle, a laugh that was at once familiar and estranged, like a tune heard in another key; and then the portières were parted, and her cousin came in.

Sophy's first impression was that Kitty had grown very small. She had been the taller of the two as girls, and had carried her height with a kind of indolent defiance which their grandmother had called "the Rensford slouch," and which the young men of that day had found irresistible; but the woman who now crossed the room with both hands outstretched seemed to have been, in some subtle way, compressed—as if the years, instead of adding to her, had pared her down to some essential and rather brittle core. She was dressed with an elegance which made Sophy's grey silk, chosen that morning with so much deliberation, seem suddenly provincial; and yet, as their hands met, Mrs. Haverly was aware, beneath the soft perfection of the suède, of a seam that had been carefully and invisibly mended.

"Sophy! My dear, my dear! And you haven't changed—not by a hair. It's monstrous of you. I came up the steps trembling, positively trembling, and here you sit as if I had gone out to the Stuyvesants' and come back again."

"It's you who have not changed, Kitty," said Mrs. Haverly, who knew it to be untrue, and who knew that her cousin knew it.

"Ah, don't! I have the glass to tell me otherwise, and a French glass is the most candid object in Europe." The Comtesse sank into the chair opposite, loosened the furs at her throat, and let her eyes travel about the room with a frank and leisurely curiosity that Sophy found herself following, chair by chair, as one follows the progress of an examiner through an essay one has written with too much care. "But the house! The dear old house. You've kept everything. There's Grandmamma's cabinet, and the Canalettos—or are they only school of?—and the very same bronze clock with the shepherdess who always looked as if she had lost something. Do you know, I've thought of that clock in the most unlikely places. In Biarritz once, at a perfectly dreadful ball, I thought of it for a whole quadrille."

"It keeps very good time," said Sophy, and immediately wished she had said something else.

Kitty laughed, not unkindly. "Of course it does. Everything here keeps good time. That was always the wonder of it."

The tea was brought in, and for some minutes the business of cups and sugar afforded them that shelter which the ritual of hospitality so obligingly provides for the unready. Mrs. Haverly poured, and asked about the voyage, and was told that it had been abominable; she asked about Paris, and was told that it was exactly the same, which was the most tiresome thing about it; she asked, with the faint lowering of the voice proper to the subject, about the late Comte, and was told that he had died very beautifully, in the odour of sanctity and under a cloud of debts, and that his relations had been charming about everything except the money.

"They are always charming, the French," said Kitty, stirring her tea. "It's their substitute for being kind. One gets used to it, as one gets used to their coffee. And then one comes home and finds people being kind without the least attempt at charm, and it's so overwhelming one could cry."

Sophy, uncertain whether this was meant for herself, took refuge in the family. There was a great deal of family to be got through, for twenty-two years had wrought among the Rensfords and their connections those changes which, viewed at close range, seem merely the slow erosions of time, but which, presented all at once to an absent eye, have the startling completeness of a landslip. Aunt Euphemia was dead, and had left her pearls to the Ladies' Missionary Society, to the lasting indignation of her nieces. Cousin Bertram had married a Miss Pruett of Philadelphia and had gone into the Church, which was thought on the whole a less conspicuous misfortune than the marriage. The old house at Newport had been sold to some people from Chicago, who had built a ballroom where the rose-garden used to be.

"Where the rose-garden used to be," Kitty repeated slowly. She set down her cup. "Do you remember the summer we hid in it all one afternoon, to avoid being taken to the Bellamys' clambake, and Grandmamma had the gardeners out looking for us with rakes, as if we had been a pair of strayed spaniels?"

"I remember that you hid," said Sophy, smiling in spite of herself. "I was only there because you had my hand."

"Yes—I always had your hand, hadn't I? You were so good about it. You let yourself be led into every scrape, and then you always got out of them so much better than I." She paused, and her glance, which had been wandering over the tea-things, came to rest, with apparent idleness, upon the piano. "That was Townsend's great argument for you, you know. That you got out of things so well."

There was a silence in which the bronze shepherdess, with her air of perpetual bereavement, measured out several seconds with unnecessary distinctness.

Mrs. Haverly had foreseen that the name would be spoken. She had even, in the sleepless hour before dawn, rehearsed a dozen ways of speaking it herself—lightly, gravely, with the tranquil possessiveness of the widow or the generous detachment of the victor—so that it might be got over at once and set aside, like an unavoidable call. But she had not foreseen that Kitty would speak it first, and in that tone; and she found that all her rehearsals had deserted her, leaving only the plain, unanswerable fact that her cousin had uttered a sentence she did not understand.

"His argument?" she said at last.

The Comtesse looked at her with a curious, half-incredulous attentiveness, the look of a traveller who, consulting a map in a foreign city, discovers that the street he is standing in has been renamed.

"Sophy," she said, "you can't mean that you never knew?"

"I don't know what you mean by knowing. I knew that you broke your engagement—that you went abroad. Everyone knew that."

"Everyone," said Kitty softly, "knew exactly what they were told, which was what my mother and your mother agreed to tell them. I broke the engagement, certainly. It was the only way to manage it decently. But I broke it because Townsend came to me one evening, on the verandah at Newport—with the band playing that idiotic waltz from *Les Cloches* all the while, I can hear it now—and told me, with the face of a man going to the scaffold, that he had made a mistake, and that it was you he cared for, and had always cared for, and that he would of course stand by his word if I wished it. If I wished it!" She gave a little laugh, in which there was more of the old Kitty than in anything she had yet said. "I was twenty, and I had been told I was the prettiest girl in Newport by everybody except the one man who had asked me to marry him. Do you suppose I could have stayed and watched? I went to Paris, and I married Raoul, who at least had the decency to prefer other women only after the wedding."

Mrs. Haverly did not answer. She was aware of sitting very still, with her hands folded upon the needlework in her lap, and of a sensation that was not so much pain as a kind of vast and silent rearrangement—as if the furniture of her entire existence were being moved, piece by piece, by invisible hands, and set down in positions that were at once utterly strange and unaccountably right.

For twenty-two years she had believed herself the second choice. She had believed it on her wedding-day, when Townsend's hand had trembled in hers and she had attributed the tremor to regret; she had believed it through the birth of her children, through the long, uneventful winters in this house and the long, uneventful summers at Lenox; she had believed it most of all on those evenings when he had looked up from his newspaper and regarded her for a moment with an expression she could never read, and which she had schooled herself to interpret as the patient tenderness of a man making the best of what remained to him. She had never reproached him. She had prided herself, indeed, on never reproaching him, and on keeping his house and rearing his sons and sitting at the foot of his table with a serenity so unbroken that no one—not even Townsend himself, she had hoped—could suspect the small, cold, unremitting ache beneath it. And she had built, out of that ache, a whole architecture of conduct: a reticence that her friends called dignity, a moderation in her pleasures that they called good taste, a refusal ever to ask for anything that they called, simply, Sophy's way. She had been, all her married life, a woman bravely making do; and it appeared that there had been nothing whatever to make do with.

"He never told me," she said, and was surprised to hear how steady her voice was.

"No," said Kitty. "I don't suppose he would have. He was so dreadfully honourable. I daresay he thought it would wound you to know that he had ever been engaged to anyone else on a misunderstanding—that it would make you feel you had been the cause of something. And you, I suppose, were too proud to ask." She leaned forward and laid her gloved hand, with its invisible mending, upon her cousin's. "My poor Sophy. What did you think, all those years?"

Mrs. Haverly looked at the hand, and then at the face above it—the face that had once been the prettiest in Newport, and that was now so skilfully composed, so admirably maintained, and so unmistakably tired. And it came to her, with that sudden lucidity which sometimes visits us at the very moment we are least able to make use of it, that her cousin had known all this for twenty-two years, and had written to her at Christmas and on her birthday and when the boys were born, in letters full of Paris and of nothing, and had never once seen fit to mention it.

"I thought," she said slowly, "what I suppose you meant me to think."

Kitty withdrew her hand. For an instant something flickered in her eyes—not guilt, exactly, for the Comtesse de Mauvilliers had long since passed beyond the jurisdiction of that particular tribunal, but a kind of rueful recognition, as of a player who sees that her opponent has at last understood the game.

"Ah, well," she said, "one has so little, Sophy. You had the house, and the children, and Townsend. I had only my version of the story. You can hardly blame me for keeping it."

"And now?"

"And now he's dead, and I'm old, and there's no longer anything to keep." She rose, drawing her furs about her with a gesture so graceful that it seemed rehearsed, and perhaps was. "Besides, I thought you ought to know. It seemed—what is it you say here?—the square thing. And I'm going back on the *Bretagne* on Saturday, so you needn't be troubled with me again."

Mrs. Haverly rose too, and the two women stood for a moment facing each other across the tea-table, with its silver and its thin china and its plate of untouched sandwiches—the whole small, bright apparatus of a civility that had survived, as such civilities do, the collapse of everything it had been designed to cover.

"You'll come and dine before you sail?" Sophy heard herself say.

"If I can, darling. You know how it is—there are a hundred people, and they all want to look at me and see how badly I've worn." Kitty bent and kissed her, lightly, upon either cheek, in the French fashion; and her lips were cool, and smelt faintly of violets. "You've worn so beautifully, Sophy. You always did. It was what he loved in you."

When the portières had fallen behind her, and the front door had closed, and the sound of the carriage wheels had been absorbed into the general murmur of the Avenue, Mrs. Haverly remained standing where her cousin had left her. The light was going; the parlour-maid would presently come in to draw the curtains and light the lamps, and to carry away the tea-things, and would find nothing unusual in the room except that the needlework had fallen to the floor. Sophy stooped and picked it up.

Then, after a moment, she crossed to the piano and took up the photograph in its silver frame. It was a good likeness, people had always said: the square, reserved face, the heavy moustache, the eyes that looked out from beneath their level brows with that expression she had never been able to read. She studied it now for a long time, as she might have studied a letter in a familiar hand which she had always supposed to be addressed to someone else.

She had been loved, it seemed. She had been loved for twenty-two years, steadily and in silence, by a man too scrupulous to speak of it and a wife too proud to inquire; and the knowledge, which would once have transfigured every hour of her life, arrived now like a legacy from a distant relation, too late to be spent and too large to be ignored. She did not know whether she was richer for it or poorer. She knew only that the room in which she stood—the room she had so carefully arranged that afternoon, to present its character in the most becoming light—had become, between one cup of tea and the next, a place she had never seen before.

She set the photograph down again, not upon the piano, but upon the writing-table, where it might be seen from her chair beside the fire; and then, as the parlour-maid came in with the lamp, she sat down and took up her needlework, and began, with fingers that were almost steady, to continue it.

Mrs. Austin Linthorne had never in her life been obliged to raise her voice, and she did not intend to begin on a Thursday.

Thursday was her day. For eleven years, ever since she had come as a bride to the high narrow house in East Twenty-third Street, the drawing-room curtains had been looped back on that afternoon at precisely three o'clock, the silver kettle set to murmur over its spirit-lamp, and the second-best Sèvres brought down from the pantry shelf; and for eleven years a certain number of ladies, never fewer than four and seldom more than nine, had mounted the brown-stone steps between half-past three and six to partake of these conveniences and of Mrs. Linthorne's conversation. It was a conversation that had been greatly praised, chiefly for what it omitted; and Mrs. Linthorne, who had been brought up to regard omission as the highest of the social arts, accepted the praise as her due, much as she accepted the deference of her cook and the punctuality of her husband's return from the club.

It was therefore with a sense of having been made the victim of something very like an act of God that she sat, at a quarter to seven on this particular Thursday, in the small upstairs sitting-room which she called her boudoir and her husband called "Augusta's office," and waited for her daughter to be brought to her.

The room was one in which she had always felt herself most completely in possession of her faculties. It was hung with a pale gray paper sprigged with violets, and furnished with a rosewood writing-table, a chaise-longue in faded rep, and a cabinet of small porcelain objects which had belonged to her grandmother Van Steen and which no one but herself was permitted to dust. On the mantel-shelf a gilt clock, supported by a reclining nymph of uncertain mythology, ticked with the soft insistence of a conscience that has long since ceased to expect a hearing. Mrs. Linthorne had placed herself in the straight chair beside the writing-table rather than on the chaise-longue, for she had a strong sense of the fitness of attitudes, and she did not think a reprimand could be properly administered from a reclining posture.

She heard the nursery door open on the floor above, and the brief, decisive descent of Miss Platt's boots upon the stair, followed by a lighter and more irregular patter that seemed to hesitate at every step and to be hurried on again by some invisible pressure. Then there was a knock, and the governess appeared in the doorway, holding by the hand a little girl of seven in a white muslin frock with a blue sash, whose face, beneath a smooth cap of fair hair, wore the look of studied blankness which children assume when they have been told in advance that they are to be spoken to.

"Thank you, Miss Platt. You may leave her with me."

Miss Platt, who had been in families where the reprimanding of children was done downstairs in the library by the father, and who privately considered the Linthorne arrangement a symptom of the general softening of New York, withdrew with a slight compression of the lips; and Mrs. Linthorne and her daughter were alone.

"Come here, Phoebe."

The child came, and stood at her mother's knee with her hands clasped behind her, a posture she had been taught to adopt when reciting the collects. Mrs. Linthorne observed it, and was faintly annoyed by it, without being able to say why; it was as though the little girl had come to the interview already dressed for it, and had thereby robbed it of some part of its spontaneity.

"Do you know why I have sent for you?"

"Yes, Mamma."

"Then perhaps you will tell me."

Phoebe's eyes, which were gray like her mother's and had the same trick of seeming to look past the person addressed toward some point of greater interest just over his shoulder, travelled slowly round the room and came to rest upon the reclining nymph.

"Because of what I said to Mrs. Rawle."

"Because of what you said to Mrs. Rawle," Mrs. Linthorne repeated, as if the words, once uttered in the child's treble, required to be restated in a register that would give them their proper weight.

It had happened at a little after five, at the hour when the room was fullest and when Mrs. Linthorne, with the instinct of a general who knows the precise moment at which reserves may be safely committed, had sent upstairs for her daughter. Phoebe was brought down on Thursdays as other households brought down their best Madeira: not often, not for long, and only for guests who could be trusted to appreciate the vintage. She had been led round the circle in her muslin and sash, had curtsied to old Mrs. Stuyvesant Rawle, who sat enthroned in the armchair nearest the fire with her niece Miss Pell beside her, and had been asked, in the tone of benevolent condescension which the elderly reserve for very young children and very poor relations, whether she was a good girl and minded what her mamma told her.

And Phoebe, standing before the old lady with her hands clasped behind her, had looked up into the large pale face beneath its towering arrangement of black lace and false curls, and had said, in a clear voice that carried to every corner of the room:

"Is Mr. Fenwick going to prison, like the thief in the Bible?"

Mrs. Linthorne, recalling the scene, was conscious once more of the peculiar quality of the silence that had followed. It had not been an empty silence; on the contrary, it had been crowded, as a church is crowded on Easter morning, with things that every one present had come expressly to see and was resolved not to be seen looking at. Mr. Bertram Fenwick was Mrs. Rawle's son-in-law; his affairs had been the subject of a paragraph in the evening papers of the previous Tuesday, and of a great many paragraphs, in a far more searching style, in every drawing-room between Washington Square and Murray Hill ever since. It was understood that there had been irregularities in the management of certain trust funds; it was understood that the family were doing what could be done; it was understood, above all, that nothing whatever was to be said. And the understanding had been so perfect, so universal, so beautifully observed, that Mrs. Rawle had been able to come to Mrs. Linthorne's Thursday in her best black lace, precisely as if Bertram Fenwick were still a vestryman of Grace Church and a director of the Knickerbocker Trust, and to be received there with a cordiality which was itself the most exquisite form of tact.

That this structure, so delicately raised by so many skilled and willing hands, should have been brought down in a single sentence by a child in a blue sash was a thing Mrs. Linthorne could not yet contemplate without a slight tightening at the base of her throat. Mrs. Rawle had not answered. She had merely looked at the child for a moment with an expression that Mrs. Linthorne did not care to remember, and had then turned to her niece and observed that the Academy exhibition was said to be very poor this year. Miss Pell had agreed that it was very poor. Mrs. Linthorne had rung for Miss Platt. And eleven minutes later, which was precisely as long as decency required and not a moment longer, Mrs. Rawle had risen, gathered her lace about her, and taken her leave, with a pressure of the hand so faint as to amount almost to an absence.

"I should like you to understand," Mrs. Linthorne now said, "that you have done a very unkind thing."

Phoebe considered this. "I didn't mean to be unkind, Mamma."

"I daresay you did not. That makes no difference whatever."

The child's eyes left the nymph and came round, with a kind of slow surprise, to her mother's face. It was evident that this was a proposition she had not before encountered, and that it had struck her as being, in some obscure way, unfair; and Mrs. Linthorne, who had herself been brought up on it, was surprised in turn to find that she could not immediately think how it was to be defended.

"What I mean," she went on, a little more quickly, "is that there are things which are unkind in themselves, whatever one may intend by them. To speak to Mrs. Rawle of Mr. Fenwick's misfortunes was one of those things."

"Is it a misfortune to go to prison?"

"Phoebe!"

"I only asked because Bridget said it was his own fault, and I thought a misfortune was when it wasn't anybody's fault, like Cousin Lavinia's lameness."

Mrs. Linthorne was silent for a moment. The name of Bridget had fallen into the conversation with the effect of a door opening in a draughty passage, and she was conscious of a small cold current that had not been there before.

"Bridget told you about Mr. Fenwick?"

"She told Miss Platt. In the nursery, when they thought I was asleep. She said her cousin was a waiter at the Brunswick and heard the gentlemen talking, and that Mr. Fenwick had taken money that belonged to widows and orphans, and that he would go to prison like the thief in the Bible, only there wouldn't be anybody to forgive him, because rich people never got forgiven unless they were found out first, and Mr. Fenwick had been found out too late." Phoebe paused, with the air of one who has rendered a difficult passage faithfully and hopes for credit on that account. "I wanted to know what it meant. And Mrs. Rawle is his mother-in-law, so I thought she would be sure to know."

It was a perfectly logical account, and Mrs. Linthorne recognized, with a sensation she did not care to examine, that it was also very likely an accurate one. Bertram Fenwick had taken the widows' money; that was the substance of all the conversations she had carefully not joined in during the past three days, and of the one, rather longer, which she had had with her husband on the subject the night before, behind the closed door of their bedroom. Austin had said that it was a bad business, and that Fenwick had always been too clever by half, and that he supposed the old lady would have to sell the Newport place; and she had said that it was very hard on poor Laura Fenwick, who had never known anything about anything; and they had both felt, without saying so, a certain mild and decorous satisfaction in the reflection that nothing of the kind could ever have happened in their own family, where the men had always been, if not clever, at least slow. Neither of them had suggested that what Fenwick had done was untrue. It had simply been agreed between them, as between all their acquaintance, that its truth was a matter of no social consequence whatever, and that the only fact of consequence was the attitude to be taken toward it.

How was one to explain this to a child of seven? Mrs. Linthorne, who had never before been required to explain it to anyone, since everyone she knew had been born understanding it, found herself groping for the terms of an argument whose premises had always seemed to her as self-evident as the multiplication table.

"Whether what Bridget said is true or not," she began, "has nothing to do with the matter."

"But if it's true—"

"It has nothing to do with it, Phoebe. Nothing whatever. You must try to understand that there are a great many things which are true and which are nevertheless never spoken of. Not in a drawing-room; not before people who would be hurt by them; not anywhere, by a well-brought-up little girl. A lady does not speak of things merely because they are true. She speaks of them only when it is—" she hesitated, and the word that came was not the word she had intended—"when it is convenient."

She heard it as she said it, and wished it unsaid; but the child had heard it too, and Mrs. Linthorne saw it go into her and lodge there, as a pebble drops into a well and is lost to sight while the sound of its falling still lingers in the air.

"When it is suitable," she amended.

"Yes, Mamma."

The child's tone was perfectly docile, and it was precisely this docility that Mrs. Linthorne found most disquieting. She had expected tears, or protestations, or at the least that obstinate wordless resistance which she remembered in herself at the same age, when her own mother had summoned her to account for having told the Bishop's wife that she smelt of camphor. She had been prepared to meet any of these with the firmness proper to the occasion. But Phoebe neither wept nor protested; she merely stood there with her hands behind her and her gray eyes fixed upon her mother's face, and seemed to be taking down the lesson as Miss Platt's pupils took down dictation, word by careful word, for later study.

Mrs. Linthorne remembered the Bishop's wife now with unexpected sharpness. She remembered her mother's dressing-room in the old house in Bond Street, with its smell of orris-root and its towering mahogany wardrobe, and her mother's voice, which had never been raised either, explaining to her that the Bishop's wife had a great deal to bear, and that a little girl who said such things would grow up to be a woman who was not asked anywhere. She remembered how she had understood, quite suddenly and with a kind of chill, that the offence lay not in the camphor but in the noticing of it; and how, from that day, she had begun to cultivate the habit of not noticing which had since become the very texture of her mind. She had not thought of it for thirty years; and she found it strange, and a little unpleasant, to discover the scene preserved in her memory with such clearness, like a fly in amber, or a fossil in a stone that one had always supposed to be merely a stone.

"You must understand," she said, more gently than she had meant to, "that Mrs. Rawle is a very old lady, and that she is very unhappy just now, and that she came to us today because she knew that she would be safe here. She trusted us. And you made her feel that she was not safe. That is what you did."

For the first time something moved in the child's face. Her lower lip drew in, and her eyes, which had remained fixed so steadily upon her mother, wavered and fell.

"I didn't know she was unhappy. She didn't look unhappy. She looked the way she always looks."

"That," said Mrs. Linthorne, "is because she is a lady."

Phoebe was silent; and her mother, watching the small fair head bent over the clasped hands, felt for a moment that she had said the most important thing she would ever say to her daughter, and was not at all certain whether it had been the right one.

But there remained the question of Bridget, and Mrs. Linthorne, who had a tidy mind, was not one to leave a question unsettled merely because it was disagreeable. Bridget had been the nursery-maid for two years. She was a stout, fresh-coloured young woman from County Clare, with a soft voice and a fund of stories about fairies and drowned sailors which Mrs. Linthorne had always mildly deprecated, and she was, as Mrs. Linthorne now perceived with perfect lucidity, a source of contamination. It was not merely that she had repeated what her cousin heard at the Brunswick. It was that she had done so in the hearing of a child, in a tone that conveyed, as such tones always did, a relish for the downfall of the rich which was the most dangerous of all the sentiments a servant could entertain. Mrs. Linthorne had no fear of anarchists; but she had a very clear sense of the way in which the foundations of things were undermined, not by bombs, but by nursery-maids.

"I shall have to speak to Bridget," she said.

Phoebe's head came up.

"What will you say to her?"

"That is not your affair. But I think you should know, Phoebe, so that you may remember it in future, that Bridget will not be able to stay with us after this."

The child stared at her. Mrs. Linthorne had anticipated some surprise; she had not anticipated the look that now came into Phoebe's eyes, which was not surprise at all, but a kind of slow and terrible comprehension, as though a curtain had been drawn back upon a room the child had always supposed to be empty and she had found it full of people sitting in the dark.

"Because of what I said?"

"Because of what she said. You only repeated it."

"But I was the one who repeated it. If I hadn't said it, you wouldn't have known."

"No," Mrs. Linthorne admitted, "I suppose I should not."

"Then it's my fault."

There was no answer to this, or none that Mrs. Linthorne cared to give. She looked at her daughter, and her daughter looked back at her; and in that look there passed between them a kind of knowledge which Mrs. Linthorne had always supposed to be the reward of maturity, and which she now saw, with a faint inward recoil, could be acquired in the space of a single evening by a child of seven in a blue sash. It was the knowledge that words were not merely words, but objects with weight and edges, which might be set down in a drawing-room and found, an hour later, to have broken something in the kitchen.

"You will be a good girl," said Mrs. Linthorne at last, "and you will not cry about it, and you will not say anything to Bridget. Miss Platt will see to your packing for the Easter visit to your grandmother; and when you come back there will be a new nurse, and we shall not speak of this again."

"Yes, Mamma."

"Now you may kiss me, and go up to bed."

The child came forward and lifted her face, and Mrs. Linthorne bent and kissed her on the forehead; and it seemed to her that the small cheek was cooler than usual, and that the arms which in other circumstances would have gone about her neck remained exactly where they were, clasped behind the muslin frock. Phoebe made her curtsy at the door, as she had been taught to do, and went out; and Mrs. Linthorne heard her steps upon the stair, no longer hesitant now but quite even and regular, mounting toward the nursery where Bridget, all unknowing, was laying out her nightgown before the fire.

When the steps had ceased, Mrs. Linthorne remained for some time in her straight chair beside the writing-table. The lamp had been lit by an unseen hand while she talked, and its light fell upon the cabinet of porcelain and drew from the little figures within it a cold and intermittent glitter, like the eyes of small animals in a hedgerow. The nymph on the mantel-shelf reclined, and the clock beneath her ticked. Mrs. Linthorne was aware of being tired, with a tiredness that seemed to have nothing to do with the hour or the exertions of the afternoon; and she was aware, too, of a sensation she could only describe to herself as a kind of dishonour, though she could not for the life of her have said in what the dishonour consisted. She had done exactly what her mother would have done. She had done what every woman of her acquaintance would have done. And the child had understood; that was the point; the child had understood perfectly, and would never make such a mistake again.

It occurred to her, with no particular emphasis, that she had always rather disliked Mrs. Rawle.

Presently she heard the street door close below, and her husband's voice in the hall, and his tread upon the stair. He came in, smelling faintly of cigars and the cold March evening, and stooped to kiss her cheek before taking up the evening paper from the table where the parlour-maid had laid it.

"Well, my dear? Anything happen today?"

Mrs. Linthorne folded her hands in her lap.

"Mrs. Rawle called," she said. "And Phoebe has been a little tiresome. I think we shall have to get a new nurse."

"Ah?" said Austin Linthorne, unfolding the paper; and the subject, like so many others in that well-ordered house, was allowed to sink back into the silence from which it should never have been permitted to emerge.

Here is an excerpt of Edith Wharton's writing, to show you their style:

There had never been such a June in Eagle County. Usually it was a month of moods, with abrupt alternations of belated frost and mid-summer heat; this year, day followed day in a sequence of temperate beauty. Every morning a breeze blew steadily from the hills. Toward noon it built up great canopies of white cloud that threw a cool shadow over fields and woods; then before sunset the clouds dissolved again, and the western light rained its unobstructed brightness on the valley. On such an afternoon Charity Royall lay on a ridge above a sunlit hollow, her face pressed to the earth and the warm currents of the grass running through her. Directly in her line of vision a blackberry branch laid its frail white flowers and blue-green leaves against the sky. Just beyond, a tuft of sweet-fern uncurled between the beaded shoots of the grass, and a small yellow butterfly vibrated over them like a fleck of sunshine. This was all she saw; but she felt, above her and about her, the strong growth of the beeches clothing the ridge, the rounding of pale green cones on countless spruce-branches, the push of myriads of sweet-fern fronds in the cracks of the stony slope below the wood, and the crowding shoots of meadowsweet and yellow flags in the pasture beyond. All this bubbling of sap and slipping of sheaths and bursting of calyxes was carried to her on mingled currents of fragrance. Every leaf and bud and blade seemed to contribute its exhalation to the pervading sweetness in which the pungency of pine-sap prevailed over the spice of thyme and the subtle perfume of fern, and all were merged in a moist earth-smell that was like the breath of some huge sun-warmed animal. Charity had lain there a long time, passive and sun-warmed as the slope on which she lay, when there came between her eyes and the dancing butterfly the sight of a man's foot in a large worn boot covered with red mud.

“Oh, don't!” she exclaimed, raising herself on her elbow and stretching out a warning hand.

“Don't what?” a hoarse voice asked above her head.

“Don't stamp on those bramble flowers, you dolt!” she retorted, springing to her knees. The foot paused and then descended clumsily on the frail branch, and raising her eyes she saw above her the bewildered face of a slouching man with a thin sunburnt beard, and white arms showing through his ragged shirt.

“Don't you ever SEE anything, Liff Hyatt?” she assailed him, as he stood before her with the look of a man who has stirred up a wasp's nest. He grinned. “I seen you! That's what I come down for.”

“Down from where?” she questioned, stooping to gather up the petals his foot had scattered. He jerked his thumb toward the heights. “Been cutting down trees for Dan Targatt.” Charity sank back on her heels and looked at him musingly. She was not in the least afraid of poor Liff Hyatt, though he “came from the Mountain,” and some of the girls ran when they saw him. Among the more reasonable he passed for a harmless creature, a sort of link between the mountain and civilized folk, who occasionally came down and did a little wood cutting for a farmer when hands were short. Besides, she knew the Mountain people would never hurt her: Liff himself had told her so once when she was a little girl, and had met him one day at the edge of lawyer Royall's pasture. “They won't any of 'em touch you up there, f'ever you was to come up.... But I don't s'pose you will,” he had added philosophically, looking at her new shoes, and at the red ribbon that Mrs. Royall had tied in her hair. Charity had, in truth, never felt any desire to visit her birthplace. She did not care to have it known that she was of the Mountain, and was shy of being seen in talk with Liff Hyatt. But today she was not sorry to have him appear. A great many things had happened to her since the day when young Lucius Harney had entered the doors of the Hatchard Memorial, but none, perhaps, so unforeseen as the fact of her suddenly finding it a convenience to be on good terms with Liff Hyatt. She continued to look up curiously at his freckled weather-beaten face, with feverish hollows below the cheekbones and the pale yellow eyes of a harmless animal. “I wonder if he's related to me?” she thought, with a shiver of disdain.

“Is there any folks living in the brown house by the swamp, up under Porcupine?” she presently asked in an indifferent tone. Liff Hyatt, for a while, considered her with surprise; then he scratched his head and shifted his weight from one tattered sole to the other.

“There's always the same folks in the brown house,” he said with his vague grin.

“They're from up your way, ain't they?”

“Their name's the same as mine,” he rejoined uncertainly. Charity still held him with resolute eyes. “See here, I want to go there some day and take a gentleman with me that's boarding with us. He's up in these parts drawing pictures.” She did not offer to explain this statement. It was too far beyond Liff Hyatt's limitations for the attempt to be worth making. “He wants to see the brown house, and go all over it,” she pursued. Liff was still running his fingers perplexedly through his shock of straw-colored hair. “Is it a fellow from the city?” he asked.

“Yes. He draws pictures of things. He's down there now drawing the Bonner house.” She pointed to a chimney just visible over the dip of the pasture below the wood.

“The Bonner house?” Liff echoed incredulously.

“Yes. You won't understand—and it don't matter. All I say is: he's going to the Hyatts' in a day or two.” Liff looked more and more perplexed. “Bash is ugly sometimes in the afternoons.” She threw her head back, her eyes full on Hyatt's. “I'm coming too: you tell him.”

“They won't none of them trouble you, the Hyatts won't. What d'you want a take a stranger with you though?”

“I've told you, haven't I? You've got to tell Bash Hyatt.” He looked away at the blue mountains on the horizon; then his gaze dropped to the chimney-top below the pasture.

“He's down there now?”

“Yes.” He shifted his weight again, crossed his arms, and continued to survey the distant landscape. “Well, so long,” he said at last, inconclusively; and turning away he shambled up the hillside. From the ledge above her, he paused to call down: “I wouldn't go there a Sunday”; then he clambered on till the trees closed in on him. Presently, from high overhead, Charity heard the ring of his axe. She lay on the warm ridge, thinking of many things that the woodsman's appearance had stirred up in her. She knew nothing of her early life, and had never felt any curiosity about it: only a sullen reluctance to explore the corner of her memory where certain blurred images lingered. But all that had happened to her within the last few weeks had stirred her to the sleeping depths. She had become absorbingly interesting to herself, and everything that had to do with her past was illuminated by this sudden curiosity. She hated more than ever the fact of coming from the Mountain; but it was no longer indifferent to her. Everything that in any way affected her was alive and vivid: even the hateful things had grown interesting because they were a part of herself.

“I wonder if Liff Hyatt knows who my mother was?” she mused; and it filled her with a tremor of surprise to think that some woman who was once young and slight, with quick motions of the blood like hers, had carried her in her breast, and watched her sleeping. She had always thought of her mother as so long dead as to be no more than a nameless pinch of earth; but now it occurred to her that the once-young woman might be alive, and wrinkled and elf-locked like the woman she had sometimes seen in the door of the brown house that Lucius Harney wanted to draw. The thought brought him back to the central point in her mind, and she strayed away from the conjectures roused by Liff Hyatt's presence. Speculations concerning the past could not hold her long when the present was so rich, the future so rosy, and when Lucius Harney, a stone's throw away, was bending over his sketch-book, frowning, calculating, measuring, and then throwing his head back with the sudden smile that had shed its brightness over everything. She scrambled to her feet, but as she did so she saw him coming up the pasture and dropped down on the grass to wait. When he was drawing and measuring one of “his houses,” as she called them, she often strayed away by herself into the woods or up the hillside. It was partly from shyness that she did so: from a sense of inadequacy that came to her most painfully when her companion, absorbed in his job, forgot her ignorance and her inability to follow his least allusion, and plunged into a monologue on art and life. To avoid the awkwardness of listening with a blank face, and also to escape the surprised stare of the inhabitants of the houses before which he would abruptly pull up their horse and open his sketch-book, she slipped away to some spot from which, without being seen, she could watch him at work, or at least look down on the house he was drawing. She had not been displeased, at first, to have it known to North Dormer and the neighborhood that she was driving Miss Hatchard's cousin about the country in the buggy he had hired of lawyer Royall. She had always kept to herself, contemptuously aloof from village love-making, without exactly knowing whether her fierce pride was due to the sense of her tainted origin, or whether she was reserving herself for a more brilliant fate. Sometimes she envied the other girls their sentimental preoccupations, their long hours of inarticulate philandering with one of the few youths who still lingered in the village; but when she pictured herself curling her hair or putting a new ribbon on her hat for Ben Fry or one of the Sollas boys the fever dropped and she relapsed into indifference. Now she knew the meaning of her disdains and reluctances. She had learned what she was worth when Lucius Harney, looking at her for the first time, had lost the thread of his speech, and leaned reddening on the edge of her desk. But another kind of shyness had been born in her: a terror of exposing to vulgar perils the sacred treasure of her happiness. She was not sorry to have the neighbors suspect her of “going with” a young man from the city; but she did not want it known to all the countryside how many hours of the long June days she spent with him. What she most feared was that the inevitable comments should reach Mr. Royall. Charity was instinctively aware that few things concerning her escaped the eyes of the silent man under whose roof she lived; and in spite of the latitude which North Dormer accorded to courting couples she had always felt that, on the day when she showed too open a preference, Mr. Royall might, as she phrased it, make her “pay for it.” How, she did not know; and her fear was the greater because it was undefinable. If she had been accepting the attentions of one of the village youths she would have been less apprehensive: Mr. Royall could not prevent her marrying when she chose to. But everybody knew that “going with a city fellow” was a different and less straightforward affair: almost every village could show a victim of the perilous venture. And her dread of Mr. Royall's intervention gave a sharpened joy to the hours she spent with young Harney, and made her, at the same time, shy of being too generally seen with him. As he approached she rose to her knees, stretching her arms above her head with the indolent gesture that was her way of expressing a profound well-being.

“I'm going to take you to that house up under Porcupine,” she announced.

“What house? Oh, yes; that ramshackle place near the swamp, with the gipsy-looking people hanging about. It's curious that a house with traces of real architecture should have been built in such a place. But the people were a sulky-looking lot—do you suppose they'll let us in?”

“They'll do whatever I tell them,” she said with assurance. He threw himself down beside her. “Will they?” he rejoined with a smile. “Well, I should like to see what's left inside the house. And I should like to have a talk with the people. Who was it who was telling me the other day that they had come down from the Mountain?” Charity shot a sideward look at him. It was the first time he had spoken of the Mountain except as a feature of the landscape. What else did he know about it, and about her relation to it? Her heart began to beat with the fierce impulse of resistance which she instinctively opposed to every imagined slight.

“The Mountain? I ain't afraid of the Mountain!” Her tone of defiance seemed to escape him. He lay breast-down on the grass, breaking off sprigs of thyme and pressing them against his lips. Far off, above the folds of the nearer hills, the Mountain thrust itself up menacingly against a yellow sunset.

“I must go up there some day: I want to see it,” he continued. Her heart-beats slackened and she turned again to examine his profile. It was innocent of all unfriendly intention.

“What'd you want to go up the Mountain for?”

“Why, it must be rather a curious place. There's a queer colony up there, you know: sort of out-laws, a little independent kingdom. Of course you've heard them spoken of; but I'm told they have nothing to do with the people in the valleys—rather look down on them, in fact. I suppose they're rough customers; but they must have a good deal of character.” She did not quite know what he meant by having a good deal of character; but his tone was expressive of admiration, and deepened her dawning curiosity. It struck her now as strange that she knew so little about the Mountain. She had never asked, and no one had ever offered to enlighten her. North Dormer took the Mountain for granted, and implied its disparagement by an intonation rather than by explicit criticism.

“It's queer, you know,” he continued, “that, just over there, on top of that hill, there should be a handful of people who don't give a damn for anybody.” The words thrilled her. They seemed the clue to her own revolts and defiances, and she longed to have him tell her more.

“I don't know much about them. Have they always been there?”

“Nobody seems to know exactly how long. Down at Creston they told me that the first colonists are supposed to have been men who worked on the railway that was built forty or fifty years ago between Springfield and Nettleton. Some of them took to drink, or got into trouble with the police, and went off—disappeared into the woods. A year or two later there was a report that they were living up on the Mountain. Then I suppose others joined them—and children were born. Now they say there are over a hundred people up there. They seem to be quite outside the jurisdiction of the valleys. No school, no church—and no sheriff ever goes up to see what they're about. But don't people ever talk of them at North Dormer?”

“I don't know. They say they're bad.” He laughed. “Do they? We'll go and see, shall we?” She flushed at the suggestion, and turned her face to his. “You never heard, I suppose—I come from there. They brought me down when I was little.”

“You?” He raised himself on his elbow, looking at her with sudden interest. “You're from the Mountain? How curious! I suppose that's why you're so different....” Her happy blood bathed her to the forehead. He was praising her—and praising her because she came from the Mountain!

“Am I... different?” she triumphed, with affected wonder.

“Oh, awfully!” He picked up her hand and laid a kiss on the sunburnt knuckles.

“Come,” he said, “let's be off.” He stood up and shook the grass from his loose grey clothes. “What a good day! Where are you going to take me tomorrow?”
