She was not in the least afraid of poor Liff Hyatt, though he “came from the Mountain,” and some of the girls ran when they saw him. Among the more reasonable he passed for a harmless creature, a sort of link between the mountain and civilized folk, who occasionally came down and did a little wood cutting for a farmer when hands were short. Besides, she knew the Mountain people would never hurt her: Liff himself had told her so once when she was a little girl, and had met him one day at the edge of lawyer Royall's pasture. “They won't any of 'em touch you up there, f'ever you was to come up.... But I don't s'pose you will,” he had added philosophically, looking at her new shoes, and at the red ribbon that Mrs. Royall had tied in her hair. Charity had, in truth, never felt any desire to visit her birthplace. She did not care to have it known that she was of the Mountain, and was shy of being seen in talk with Liff Hyatt. But today she was not sorry to have him appear. A great many things had happened to her since the day when young Lucius Harney had entered the doors of the Hatchard Memorial, but none, perhaps, so unforeseen as the fact of her suddenly finding it a convenience to be on good terms with Liff Hyatt. She continued to look up curiously at his freckled weather-beaten face, with feverish hollows below the cheekbones and the pale yellow eyes of a harmless animal. “I wonder if he's related to me?” she thought, with a shiver of disdain.

“Is there any folks living in the brown house by the swamp, up under Porcupine?” she presently asked in an indifferent tone. Liff Hyatt, for a while, considered her with surprise; then he scratched his head and shifted his weight from one tattered sole to the other.

“There's always the same folks in the brown house,” he said with his vague grin.

“They're from up your way, ain't they?”

“Their name's the same as mine,” he rejoined uncertainly. Charity still held him with resolute eyes. “See here, I want to go there some day and take a gentleman with me that's boarding with us. He's up in these parts drawing pictures.” She did not offer to explain this statement. It was too far beyond Liff Hyatt's limitations for the attempt to be worth making. “He wants to see the brown house, and go all over it,” she pursued. Liff was still running his fingers perplexedly through his shock of straw-colored hair. “Is it a fellow from the city?” he asked.

“Yes. He draws pictures of things. He's down there now drawing the Bonner house.” She pointed to a chimney just visible over the dip of the pasture below the wood.

“The Bonner house?” Liff echoed incredulously.

“Yes. You won't understand—and it don't matter. All I say is: he's going to the Hyatts' in a day or two.” Liff looked more and more perplexed. “Bash is ugly sometimes in the afternoons.” She threw her head back, her eyes full on Hyatt's. “I'm coming too: you tell him.”

“They won't none of them trouble you, the Hyatts won't. What d'you want a take a stranger with you though?”

“I've told you, haven't I? You've got to tell Bash Hyatt.” He looked away at the blue mountains on the horizon; then his gaze dropped to the chimney-top below the pasture.

“He's down there now?”

“Yes.” He shifted his weight again, crossed his arms, and continued to survey the distant landscape. “Well, so long,” he said at last, inconclusively; and turning away he shambled up the hillside. From the ledge above her, he paused to call down: “I wouldn't go there a Sunday”; then he clambered on till the trees closed in on him. Presently, from high overhead, Charity heard the ring of his axe. She lay on the warm ridge, thinking of many things that the woodsman's appearance had stirred up in her. She knew nothing of her early life, and had never felt any curiosity about it: only a sullen reluctance to explore the corner of her memory where certain blurred images lingered. But all that had happened to her within the last few weeks had stirred her to the sleeping depths. She had become absorbingly interesting to herself, and everything that had to do with her past was illuminated by this sudden curiosity. She hated more than ever the fact of coming from the Mountain; but it was no longer indifferent to her. Everything that in any way affected her was alive and vivid: even the hateful things had grown interesting because they were a part of herself.

“I wonder if Liff Hyatt knows who my mother was?” she mused; and it filled her with a tremor of surprise to think that some woman who was once young and slight, with quick motions of the blood like hers, had carried her in her breast, and watched her sleeping. She had always thought of her mother as so long dead as to be no more than a nameless pinch of earth; but now it occurred to her that the once-young woman might be alive, and wrinkled and elf-locked like the woman she had sometimes seen in the door of the brown house that Lucius Harney wanted to draw. The thought brought him back to the central point in her mind, and she strayed away from the conjectures roused by Liff Hyatt's presence. Speculations concerning the past could not hold her long when the present was so rich, the future so rosy, and when Lucius Harney, a stone's throw away, was bending over his sketch-book, frowning, calculating, measuring, and then throwing his head back with the sudden smile that had shed its brightness over everything. She scrambled to her feet, but as she did so she saw him coming up the pasture and dropped down on the grass to wait. When he was drawing and measuring one of “his houses,” as she called them, she often strayed away by herself into the woods or up the hillside. It was partly from shyness that she did so: from a sense of inadequacy that came to her most painfully when her companion, absorbed in his job, forgot her ignorance and her inability to follow his least allusion, and plunged into a monologue on art and life. To avoid the awkwardness of listening with a blank face, and also to escape the surprised stare of the inhabitants of the houses before which he would abruptly pull up their horse and open his sketch-book, she slipped away to some spot from which, without being seen, she could watch him at work, or at least look down on the house he was drawing. She had not been displeased, at first, to have it known to North Dormer and the neighborhood that she was driving Miss Hatchard's cousin about the country in the buggy he had hired of lawyer Royall. She had always kept to herself, contemptuously aloof from village love-making, without exactly knowing whether her fierce pride was due to the sense of her tainted origin, or whether she was reserving herself for a more brilliant fate. Sometimes she envied the other girls their sentimental preoccupations, their long hours of inarticulate philandering with one of the few youths who still lingered in the village; but when she pictured herself curling her hair or putting a new ribbon on her hat for Ben Fry or one of the Sollas boys the fever dropped and she relapsed into indifference. Now she knew the meaning of her disdains and reluctances. She had learned what she was worth when Lucius Harney, looking at her for the first time, had lost the thread of his speech, and leaned reddening on the edge of her desk. But another kind of shyness had been born in her: a terror of exposing to vulgar perils the sacred treasure of her happiness. She was not sorry to have the neighbors suspect her of “going with” a young man from the city; but she did not want it known to all the countryside how many hours of the long June days she spent with him. What she most feared was that the inevitable comments should reach Mr. Royall. Charity was instinctively aware that few things concerning her escaped the eyes of the silent man under whose roof she lived; and in spite of the latitude which North Dormer accorded to courting couples she had always felt that, on the day when she showed too open a preference, Mr. Royall might, as she phrased it, make her “pay for it.” How, she did not know; and her fear was the greater because it was undefinable. If she had been accepting the attentions of one of the village youths she would have been less apprehensive: Mr. Royall could not prevent her marrying when she chose to. But everybody knew that “going with a city fellow” was a different and less straightforward affair: almost every village could show a victim of the perilous venture. And her dread of Mr. Royall's intervention gave a sharpened joy to the hours she spent with young Harney, and made her, at the same time, shy of being too generally seen with him. As he approached she rose to her knees, stretching her arms above her head with the indolent gesture that was her way of expressing a profound well-being.

“I'm going to take you to that house up under Porcupine,” she announced.

“What house? Oh, yes; that ramshackle place near the swamp, with the gipsy-looking people hanging about. It's curious that a house with traces of real architecture should have been built in such a place. But the people were a sulky-looking lot—do you suppose they'll let us in?”

“They'll do whatever I tell them,” she said with assurance. He threw himself down beside her. “Will they?” he rejoined with a smile. “Well, I should like to see what's left inside the house. And I should like to have a talk with the people. Who was it who was telling me the other day that they had come down from the Mountain?” Charity shot a sideward look at him. It was the first time he had spoken of the Mountain except as a feature of the landscape. What else did he know about it, and about her relation to it? Her heart began to beat with the fierce impulse of resistance which she instinctively opposed to every imagined slight.

“The Mountain? I ain't afraid of the Mountain!” Her tone of defiance seemed to escape him. He lay breast-down on the grass, breaking off sprigs of thyme and pressing them against his lips. Far off, above the folds of the nearer hills, the Mountain thrust itself up menacingly against a yellow sunset.

“I must go up there some day: I want to see it,” he continued. Her heart-beats slackened and she turned again to examine his profile. It was innocent of all unfriendly intention.

“What'd you want to go up the Mountain for?”

“Why, it must be rather a curious place. There's a queer colony up there, you know: sort of out-laws, a little independent kingdom. Of course you've heard them spoken of; but I'm told they have nothing to do with the people in the valleys—rather look down on them, in fact. I suppose they're rough customers; but they must have a good deal of character.” She did not quite know what he meant by having a good deal of character; but his tone was expressive of admiration, and deepened her dawning curiosity. It struck her now as strange that she knew so little about the Mountain. She had never asked, and no one had ever offered to enlighten her. North Dormer took the Mountain for granted, and implied its disparagement by an intonation rather than by explicit criticism.

“It's queer, you know,” he continued, “that, just over there, on top of that hill, there should be a handful of people who don't give a damn for anybody.” The words thrilled her. They seemed the clue to her own revolts and defiances, and she longed to have him tell her more.

“I don't know much about them. Have they always been there?”

“Nobody seems to know exactly how long. Down at Creston they told me that the first colonists are supposed to have been men who worked on the railway that was built forty or fifty years ago between Springfield and Nettleton. Some of them took to drink, or got into trouble with the police, and went off—disappeared into the woods. A year or two later there was a report that they were living up on the Mountain. Then I suppose others joined them—and children were born. Now they say there are over a hundred people up there. They seem to be quite outside the jurisdiction of the valleys. No school, no church—and no sheriff ever goes up to see what they're about. But don't people ever talk of them at North Dormer?”

“I don't know. They say they're bad.” He laughed. “Do they? We'll go and see, shall we?” She flushed at the suggestion, and turned her face to his. “You never heard, I suppose—I come from there. They brought me down when I was little.”

“You?” He raised himself on his elbow, looking at her with sudden interest. “You're from the Mountain? How curious! I suppose that's why you're so different....” Her happy blood bathed her to the forehead. He was praising her—and praising her because she came from the Mountain!

“Am I... different?” she triumphed, with affected wonder.

“Oh, awfully!” He picked up her hand and laid a kiss on the sunburnt knuckles.

“Come,” he said, “let's be off.” He stood up and shook the grass from his loose grey clothes. “What a good day! Where are you going to take me tomorrow?”

The carriage had set them down at a quarter past eleven, and Julia Merriam, mounting the steps of the narrow brown house in East Thirty-eighth Street, was aware that her husband had not spoken since they left Mrs. Lorrimer's door. It was not unusual for Howard to be silent after a dinner; he had a way of folding up his sociability with his opera-hat, as if both were articles to be put away until the next occasion required them. But his silence tonight had a different quality. It was not the slack, comfortable muteness of a man who has talked enough. It was taut, watchful, and she had felt it beside her in the dark of the brougham as one feels the presence of a third person in a room.

The maid had left the gas burning low in the hall, and a single lamp in the library, where a fire, banked for the night, gave out a sullen glow between the brass dogs. Julia, who had meant to go straight upstairs, found herself pausing on the threshold. The room, with its rows of uncut sets in tooled calf, its engravings after Landseer, and the tall clock that had come to her from her grandmother's house in Bond Street, had always seemed to her the one corner of the house which was wholly hers; yet tonight, as Howard followed her in and closed the door behind him, she had the odd sensation of entering it as a visitor.

"You'll have a little brandy?" he said, moving toward the tray on the side-table. "Mrs. Lorrimer's champagne is always too sweet."

"No, thank you."

He poured a glass for himself, holding the decanter a little longer than was necessary, as though the act of pouring gave him a reason for keeping his back to her. She sat down in the low chair by the fire and drew off her gloves slowly, one finger at a time. It was a habit of hers when she wished to gain a moment, and she was conscious, even as she did it, that he knew the habit and would read it.

"It was a pleasant dinner," she said.

"Was it? I thought it rather long."

"Mrs. Lorrimer was very kind to me." She laid the gloves across her knee and smoothed them. "Kinder than usual, I thought. She took me aside after dinner and asked after my cousin Bayard. She wanted to know whether he was still at Newport, or whether he had come back to town for the winter."

Howard set down his glass. "And what did you tell her?"

"I told her I didn't know. Which was true." She looked up at him. "But it struck me as curious that she should ask. She has never shown the least interest in Bayard. And then Mrs. Hollis asked me the same thing in the cloak-room—almost in the same words. It was as if they had rehearsed it."

He gave a short laugh, which did not quite succeed. "Women will ask anything in a cloak-room."

"Yes; but not usually that."

She had not meant to say so much. She had meant, on the drive home, to keep her small accumulation of impressions to herself until she could sort and weigh them in the privacy of her own room, as she had sorted and weighed so many things in the eleven years of her marriage. It was her way to proceed by inference rather than by question, and Howard had always seemed grateful for her reticence, as men are grateful for any arrangement which spares them the necessity of explanation. But the evening had left her with a disquiet that refused to be laid aside: the faint, deliberate cordiality of women who had never before troubled to be cordial, the abrupt silence of two men by the smoking-room door when she passed with her hostess, the look—half curiosity and half compassion—which old Mrs. Dagonet had bent on her across the drawing-room, as one might look at a person who has not yet heard of a death in the family.

Howard had seated himself on the opposite side of the hearth, his long legs stretched toward the fender. He was a handsome man still, with the kind of good looks that wear well in the lamplight: a broad forehead, a short fair moustache, eyes of a mild and agreeable grey. She had once thought those eyes the most candid she had ever seen; it was only gradually that she had learned their candour to be a matter of colouring rather than of character.

"I suppose," he said, after a pause, "you'd better hear it from me than from Kate Hollis."

The clock in the corner ticked through a long interval before she answered. "Hear what, Howard?"

He turned his glass between his fingers, watching the firelight in it. "You know I've been rather deep in the Northern Lakes business."

"I know you've spoken of it."

"Well—it's gone wrong. Not altogether, not irretrievably; but it's gone wrong. There was a meeting of the directors this afternoon." He paused, as if to let the word *directors* carry its own weight of solemnity. "Fallowfield has bolted. Nobody knows quite where—Montreal, they think. And the books are not what they ought to be."

She sat very still. The phrase reached her slowly, as words reach one through a closed door. *The books are not what they ought to be.* She had heard it said of other men, at other dinners, in the lowered voices which New York reserved for the discussion of such accidents; and she remembered how, on those occasions, she had felt for the wives a pity so detached that it was almost a form of complacency.

"And you?" she said at last. "What has that to do with you?"

"My name is on the prospectus." He said it lightly, almost carelessly, with the air of a man mentioning that he had been caught in the rain. "As a director, you understand. I lent it to Fallowfield as a favour, two years ago, when he was getting the thing started. Everyone said it was as sound as the Bank of England. Your cousin Bayard himself went in for a time."

"Bayard got out a year ago."

He glanced at her quickly. "How do you know that?"

"Because he told me so. He came to tea one afternoon in the spring—you were at Lakewood—and he said he had sold his shares and advised his friends to do the same. I thought he had told you."

"He may have mentioned it." Howard shrugged. "Bayard is always selling out of something. He has the instincts of a grocer."

She let the remark pass. It was not the first time she had heard her cousin's prudence described in such terms, and she had long since ceased to defend him. Bayard Sellwood was ten years older than herself, a bachelor, very rich, and very dry; he had been her guardian in the years after her father's death, and had given her away at her wedding with an expression which she had afterward, in moments of private candour, recalled as one of resignation. He had never liked Howard; and Howard, she had always believed, had never cared whether Bayard liked him or not. It struck her now, with a small cold shock, that she might have been mistaken.

"How much is it?" she asked.

"How much is what?"

"How much do you stand to lose? Or—" she hesitated over the word, which seemed to her to belong to a vocabulary she had never expected to use—"how much are you liable for?"

He set down his glass on the little table at his elbow and leaned forward, clasping his hands between his knees. It was an attitude she had seen him take at the card-table when he was about to play a doubtful hand.

"That's just it, Julia. It isn't so much the money. The money could be managed, more or less, with time. It's the—the other thing. There's talk of an inquiry. Hollis and Penniman have been at the District Attorney's office half the day. If it comes to an inquiry, every director whose name is on that prospectus will have to answer for it; and you know what that means. One may be as innocent as a babe and still come out of it with a smell of the courts about one. And in our world—" he made a small, expressive movement of the hand—"one doesn't get rid of that smell."

She knew, indeed, what it meant. She had been born into that world and had breathed its air all her life; she knew how it closed ranks, how it drew in its skirts, how it could make a man vanish more completely by a mere averting of eyes than any court could do by sentence. She thought of the Lennox Bartletts, who had gone to live in Florence after the affair of the Trust Company, and of whom one now spoke only in the past tense, as of the dead.

"And what is it," she said slowly, "that Mrs. Lorrimer and Mrs. Hollis wished to know about my cousin?"

Howard was silent. The fire had sunk lower, and in the deepening shadow his face seemed to her suddenly older, the lines about the mouth more strongly marked, as though some inner support had been withdrawn.

"Bayard is a great friend of Judge Ferrier's," he said at length. "They were at Columbia together. And Ferrier, as it happens, has a good deal to say about whether the District Attorney goes forward or lets the matter drop. A word from the right quarter—not anything improper, you understand; simply a word to the effect that one's character is known, that one was imposed upon like everybody else—a word like that, at the right moment, might make all the difference."

"I see," said Julia.

She did see; and what she saw was not only the immediate fact, but a long perspective of facts behind it, stretching back through the years like an avenue of which she had hitherto seen only the near end. She saw why Mrs. Lorrimer had been kind, and why Mrs. Hollis had asked her question in the cloak-room: they were not inquiring after Bayard's health, but calculating, as the whole of their world was no doubt calculating tonight, whether Howard Merriam's wife had it in her power to save him, and whether she would choose to use it. She saw, too—and this was the sight that made her fingers tighten on the gloves in her lap—that Howard himself had been making the same calculation, perhaps for weeks, perhaps for months, while he talked to her at breakfast of the weather and the Opera and the new pair of bays he thought of buying.

"How long have you known?" she asked.

"Known what?"

"That it would come to this. That you would need Bayard."

He coloured slightly. "One doesn't know these things. One fears them, perhaps. I hoped until today that Fallowfield would pull through."

"But you feared it. Since the spring, at least. Since the time you were at Lakewood." She was looking at him steadily now, and she saw his eyes waver. "That was why you were so anxious that we should ask Bayard to dine in May. I remember you said you thought we had neglected him. I was touched by that, Howard. I thought you were doing it for me."

"Well, and if I was thinking of my own interests as well as yours—is that a crime? Our interests are the same, I suppose."

"Are they?" She heard her own voice with a kind of detached surprise; it was quiet and very clear, like the voice of someone reading aloud in another room. "I wonder. I have never been quite sure what your interests were. I don't think I have ever been asked to share them until tonight."

He stood up abruptly and went to the mantelpiece, where he stood with one hand on the marble, looking down at the dying fire. She noticed that he was careful not to disturb the little Sèvres figures that stood there—a shepherd and shepherdess which had belonged to her mother—and the trivial carefulness of the gesture seemed to her, in that moment, more revealing than anything he had said. He had always been careful of her things. He had been careful of her name, her connections, her cousin, her grandmother's clock; he had handled them all with the same deferential precision, as a man handles the property of a client.

"I don't think you're being quite fair, Julia," he said without turning. "I've never asked you for anything. I've never so much as hinted that your family might do something for me. You must allow that."

"Yes," she said, "I allow it. You have been very patient."

The word hung between them. He turned and looked at her, and for the first time that evening she saw in his face something which was neither embarrassment nor calculation, but a kind of startled resentment, as if she had struck him with a weapon he had not known she possessed.

"Patient! What do you mean by that?"

"I mean that you waited a long time before you needed what you married me for."

She had not known she was going to say it until the words were spoken; and when they were spoken they seemed to her to have been lying in her mind, fully formed, for years, like a letter written and never sent. The room was very silent. A coal fell in the grate, and the small sound made them both start.

Howard drew a long breath. "That is an ugly thing to say."

"It is an ugly thing to think. I have tried not to think it." She looked down at her hands. "I have tried for eleven years."

He came and stood before her, and she was aware of the effort he was making to master his voice; she had always admired, a little against her will, his capacity for self-command, which she had once mistaken for strength of feeling held in check. "Julia, listen to me. I don't deny that I was glad, when I married you, that you were—who you were. What man wouldn't have been? But that wasn't all of it, and you know it wasn't. You can't sit there and tell me you've been unhappy all these years. We've had a decent life together. We've been—" he searched for the word—"we've been comfortable."

"Yes," she said. "We have been comfortable."

He seemed to hear in the repetition something which made him pause. He looked at her for a moment in silence, and then, with a slight lift of the shoulders, he sat down again in the chair opposite, as if acknowledging that the matter could not be settled standing.

"Well," he said, in a lower tone, "I won't argue about what's past. It's the present I'm thinking of. I'm not asking you to do anything wrong. I'm only asking you to go and see your cousin—tomorrow, if possible—and tell him how matters stand. He'll listen to you. He's always been fond of you, in his dry way. And if he says a word to Ferrier, the whole thing may blow over in a week. If he doesn't—" He left the sentence unfinished, and the silence completed it more eloquently than any words.

Julia sat looking into the fire. She was thinking, oddly enough, not of the inquiry or the District Attorney or even of Howard, but of a summer afternoon long ago at her grandmother's place on the Hudson, when Bayard, then a grave young man of twenty-five, had found her crying in the boat-house because she had broken a china cup belonging to the set her grandmother valued above all her possessions. He had not scolded her, nor had he comforted her; he had simply taken the pieces from her and said, "We'll tell her together, shall we? Things are always easier to confess when one isn't alone." She had never forgotten the phrase, nor the dry, kind, slightly ironic look that went with it. And she knew, as surely as she knew anything, what that look would be tomorrow when she sat in his library in Washington Square and told him why she had come.

"He will do it," she said at last. "I think he will do it, if I ask him."

Howard's face cleared, and he leaned toward her with a quick, almost boyish movement of relief. "I knew you'd see it sensibly. You always do, in the end."

"But he will know," she went on, as if he had not spoken, "exactly why I have come. He will know that I came because you sent me. And he will look at me—" She stopped, and pressed her lips together. "He will look at me as he looked at me on the day I was married."

"My dear girl, what does it matter how Bayard looks at you? He's not a man of any imagination."

"No," she agreed. "He has no imagination. That is why he always sees things as they are."

Howard was silent. She knew that he did not understand her, and she knew too that it was no longer of any use to try to make him understand. The distance between them, which she had measured so often in secret and had always contrived to call by gentler names—reserve, habit, the natural separateness of two people who respected each other's privacy—lay open before her now, as plain as the width of the hearthrug that divided their chairs. It was not a distance which could be crossed by any word of hers or his. It had been there from the beginning, and she had furnished it, as one furnishes an empty room, with the decent upholstery of her own forbearance.

The clock in the corner gathered itself with a faint whirr and struck midnight. Howard rose, as though the sound released him, and stood looking down at her with an expression in which relief and uncertainty were curiously mingled.

"You'll go tomorrow, then?"

"Yes. I'll go tomorrow."

He hesitated, and then bent and kissed her forehead. It was the kiss he gave her every night at the foot of the stairs, neither warmer nor colder than usual; and she reflected, with a detachment which frightened her a little, that she would very likely receive it every night for the rest of her life, and that it would mean exactly what it had always meant.

"You're tired," he said. "Don't sit up."

"I won't be long."

When he had gone she sat on alone in the low chair, the gloves still lying across her knee. The fire had dwindled to a few red seams in a bed of ash, and the lamplight, falling on the rows of tooled calf, made them look as if they had been arranged to be seen rather than read. She thought of the women at Mrs. Lorrimer's, of their soft solicitude and their watchful eyes, and she knew that tomorrow, and for many tomorrows, she would meet those eyes with the same composure she had worn tonight, and that no one—not Kate Hollis, nor old Mrs. Dagonet, nor even Bayard himself—would ever be quite sure what lay behind it. That, at least, was a possession of which no one could deprive her: the right to be unreadable. She had come into it, she perceived, as one comes into an inheritance, by the death of something else.

She rose at last, laid the gloves on the table, and turned down the lamp. In the darkness the little Sèvres shepherd and shepherdess gleamed faintly on the mantel, bowing to each other across their few inches of marble, as they had bowed for a hundred years, in perfect courtesy and perfect separation.

Here is an excerpt of Edith Wharton's writing, to show you their style:

There had never been such a June in Eagle County. Usually it was a month of moods, with abrupt alternations of belated frost and mid-summer heat; this year, day followed day in a sequence of temperate beauty. Every morning a breeze blew steadily from the hills. Toward noon it built up great canopies of white cloud that threw a cool shadow over fields and woods; then before sunset the clouds dissolved again, and the western light rained its unobstructed brightness on the valley. On such an afternoon Charity Royall lay on a ridge above a sunlit hollow, her face pressed to the earth and the warm currents of the grass running through her. Directly in her line of vision a blackberry branch laid its frail white flowers and blue-green leaves against the sky. Just beyond, a tuft of sweet-fern uncurled between the beaded shoots of the grass, and a small yellow butterfly vibrated over them like a fleck of sunshine. This was all she saw; but she felt, above her and about her, the strong growth of the beeches clothing the ridge, the rounding of pale green cones on countless spruce-branches, the push of myriads of sweet-fern fronds in the cracks of the stony slope below the wood, and the crowding shoots of meadowsweet and yellow flags in the pasture beyond. All this bubbling of sap and slipping of sheaths and bursting of calyxes was carried to her on mingled currents of fragrance. The September of that year came into the valley with a languor that seemed to deny the turning of the season. The maples on the green at Wyndham Corners had not yet begun to redden, and the late roses against the Leland porch, which in other years would by now have been blackened by the first frost, hung their loosened petals in the windless air as if they had been forgotten by the calendar. Jane Leland, standing at the parlour window with her hand on the fold of the curtain, watched the road that came up from the station, and reflected that it was like her cousin to arrive on a day when everything looked its best, and like the place to have made ready for her without being asked.

She had been at the window for nearly half an hour, though the train was not due till four, and she was ashamed of her impatience in the way that people who have lived long alone are ashamed of any emotion that has no one to witness it. Twice she had gone back into the room to straighten the antimacassar on the high-backed chair by the fire, and once to the dining room to see that Ellen had remembered the seed-cake; and each time she had returned to the window with the sense of having betrayed something to the furniture. The parlour had been her mother's, and her grandmother's before that, and in the twenty-two years since Harriet had last sat in it nothing had been moved except by the slow subsidence of age. The horsehair sofa had sagged a little at one end, where old Mrs. Leland had lain through her final winter; the steel engraving of "The Landing of the Pilgrims" had acquired a brownish bloom under its glass; and the clock on the mantel, which had always lost four minutes in the day, lost them still. Jane had considered, in the week since Harriet's letter came, whether she ought to do something to the room: a new carpet, perhaps, or at least fresh muslin for the windows. But she had done nothing, partly because there was no money for carpets, and partly because some obscure pride forbade her to dress the house for an inspection. If Harriet found it shabby, she would at least find it what it had always been.

The hired carriage from the Wyndham livery came round the corner of the green a little before half-past four, and Jane, with a flutter she despised, let the curtain fall and went out into the hall. By the time she had opened the door the carriage had stopped, and a lady was being handed down by the livery boy with a deliberation that turned the small act into a ceremony. Jane's first impression was of colour, a dark rich violet, unlike anything that had been seen on the green at Wyndham Corners in her memory, and of a hat that seemed to have been designed with a view to its effect at a distance. Her second was that the lady inside the dress and beneath the hat was older than she had prepared herself to see.

"Jane! My dear, my dear Jane!"

The voice, at least, had not changed. It had the same high caressing lift that had once made the Wyndham boys turn on the church steps, and the same trick of dwelling on a name as though it were being tasted. Harriet came up the walk with both hands out, and Jane, who had meant to be composed, found herself held against a quantity of lace and enveloped in a scent she could not name, but which made her think of shuttered rooms in places she had never seen.

"You haven't altered in the least," Harriet declared, holding her off to look at her. "Not in the least. I should have known you anywhere."

Jane, who knew precisely how much she had altered, received this with the faint smile with which one accepts a coin of doubtful currency. "You'll want your tea," she said. "Ellen will see to the trunks."

"Trunks!" Harriet laughed. "There's only the one, and a dressing-case. I travel like a nun nowadays." She glanced back at the carriage, where the livery boy was struggling with a leather box of a magnitude that hardly bore out the claim, and then turned her eyes, with a quick sweeping movement that Jane remembered, over the front of the house, the fanlight, the brass knocker, the two lilacs that flanked the steps. "And here it all is," she said in a lowered tone. "Exactly as it was. Do you know, I used to dream about that knocker?"

In the parlour she would not sit down at once, but moved about the room touching things, the back of the sofa, the frame of the engraving, the spine of a book on the corner table, with a slow, appraising tenderness that Jane found more unsettling than criticism would have been. It was as if her cousin were walking through a museum in which she had once been a living exhibit, and Jane felt herself, with the rest of the furniture, being included in the collection.

"The clock," Harriet said, pausing before the mantel. "Does it still lose?"

"Four minutes a day."

"How perfectly delicious." She turned with a little rustle and sank at last into the high-backed chair, the very chair whose antimacassar Jane had twice straightened. "You can't think what it is, after Florence, after everything, to come into a room where the clock loses four minutes a day. It's like being let into the secret of eternity."

Jane poured the tea. She had always poured tea well, and she did it now with a particular care, as if her hands might speak for her where her tongue would not. She was conscious, as she passed the cup, of her own fingers, which were rough at the knuckles from the garden, and of Harriet's, which were ringed and white and very slightly swollen, so that the rings seemed to have grown into the flesh.

"Tell me about yourself," she said. "Your letters were so short, these last years."

"Were they? I suppose they were. One gets out of the way of writing; one's life becomes so cut up into pieces that there's no single piece large enough to send." Harriet stirred her tea and looked into it. "You know, of course, about Gerald."

"I saw the notice. I wrote to you."

"Yes, dear, you did. It was the only letter I kept." She said this simply, and Jane, who had expected some flourish, was disarmed. "Everyone else wrote about what a loss it was to art. You wrote about how he used to carry me over the brook at the Fosters' picnic. I had quite forgotten that. I cried over it for an hour."

There was a pause, in which the clock on the mantel ticked with its customary hesitation, and a late bee, blundering through the open window, bumped against the glass of the engraving and fell back stunned upon the sill.

"Was it very hard at the end?" Jane asked.

"Hard?" Harriet lifted her eyebrows. "Oh, the dying wasn't hard. Gerald did everything gracefully, even that. It was the living that had been hard, the last ten years." She set down her cup. "But I don't want to talk about that yet. I want to hear about Wyndham. I want to hear about everyone. Is old Dr. Prentiss still alive? And the Fosters, and that dreadful girl with the red hair who sang in the choir, what was her name?"

"Maud Bellows. She married a man from Springfield and has seven children."

"Seven! Good heavens. And she couldn't keep the alto line straight for the length of a hymn." Harriet laughed, and leaned back in her chair with an air of settling into an entertainment. "Go on. Tell me everything."

Jane told her. She told her of Dr. Prentiss, who had died in the blizzard of 'eighty-eight, driving out to a confinement on the Dorset road; of the Foster place, which had been sold to a man from Boston who had put a mansard on it; of the church, which had been given a new organ by subscription and had never since been able to find anyone to play it properly. She told it all in the dry, exact manner which she had learned from her father, who had been the village lawyer and had trusted no statement that could not be sworn to; and she was aware as she spoke that the history of twenty years in Wyndham Corners could be compressed into a quarter of an hour without serious omission. Harriet listened with an attention that seemed to Jane at first a kindness and afterward a kind of hunger. She asked questions about people Jane had supposed her to have forgotten; she remembered the colour of the Bellowses' front door and the name of the Fosters' dog; and when Jane spoke of the deaths, of old Mrs. Wheelock, of the two Turner boys in the diphtheria year, she was silent for a moment, as if she were adding them to some private account.

"And you," she said at last. "You've said nothing about yourself."

"There's nothing to say. You see how it is." Jane made a small gesture that took in the room, the garden beyond the window, the green with its unreddened maples. "Mother was ill for eleven years. After that there was the house to see to, and the Sunday school, and the Library Committee. One day goes into the next."

"Eleven years," Harriet repeated. She looked at her cousin with a sudden fixity, and Jane felt that something was being measured. "And there was never anyone? I used to think, when I went away, that you and Walter Ames..."

She left the sentence suspended, and Jane, who had long ago schooled herself against that name, was surprised to feel the old warmth come up into her face. It was absurd, at forty-six, to be betrayed by one's blood; but the blood, it seemed, had a longer memory than the will.

"Walter Ames married a girl from Pittsfield," she said. "They live in Albany. He has done very well."

"Ah." Harriet was silent; then she said, with a lightness that did not quite succeed: "He wrote to me once, you know. Years ago, the first winter we were in Rome. I never answered."

Jane looked at her. The room, which a moment before had been full of the soft drowsy light of the September afternoon, seemed to her to have grown suddenly very still, as if the furniture itself were listening.

"He wrote to you?"

"Oh, it was nothing. A foolish letter. He had heard that Gerald and I were... that things were not quite what they ought to be. He offered..." She broke off, and turned her rings slowly on her swollen fingers. "I don't know why I'm telling you this. I suppose because it's the kind of thing one can only say in a room like this, where nothing has happened for so long that anything one says seems already to belong to the past."

Jane did not answer at once. She was thinking, with a curious detachment, of a certain evening in the April before Harriet's marriage, when Walter Ames had walked home with her from the Wednesday prayer-meeting and had stood a long while at the gate without speaking, looking past her toward the lighted windows of the Durrell house, where Harriet was then staying. She had told herself at the time that he was shy; she had told herself so for several years afterward, until there was no longer any occasion to tell herself anything. Now, sitting across the tea-table from the cause of that silence, she found that the knowledge, so long postponed, had lost its power to wound and kept only its power to illuminate. It was as if a picture she had looked at every day had been turned a little toward the window, and she had seen for the first time what it represented.

"I'm glad you didn't answer," she said at last; and was surprised to discover that she meant it, and that she meant it not for Walter's sake, nor even for Harriet's, but for the sake of the girl from Pittsfield, whom she had never seen.

Harriet glanced at her quickly, as though she had expected something else; then she laughed, a short laugh without much mirth in it, and rose and went to the window.

"How green it all is," she said. "In Italy everything is brown by September. One forgets that the world can stay green so long."

They went out into the garden before supper, because Harriet wished to see the roses, and because Jane, who had begun to find the parlour oppressive, was glad of the excuse. The sun had dropped behind the steeple of the Congregational church, and the long shadow of it lay across the green and up the Leland lawn almost to the foot of the porch steps, so that the two women walked in and out of it as they went down the path. The air was full of the smell of the late phlox and of the dry, sweetish odour of fallen apples from the old tree by the wall, and somewhere beyond the hedge a cow-bell clanked at long intervals, as if marking a time slower than that of any clock.

Harriet walked with her skirt gathered in one hand, stooping now and then to look at a flower without touching it; and Jane, watching her, saw with a pang that she moved more heavily than her voice had led one to suppose, and that she paused, at the slight rise where the path turned toward the arbour, to recover her breath.

"Jane," she said abruptly, when they had reached the bench beneath the grape-vine, "I may as well tell you now. I haven't come for a visit."

Jane sat down beside her and waited.

"There's nothing left, you see. Gerald's pictures never sold, toward the end; people had stopped wanting that kind of thing, and he wouldn't paint any other kind. There were debts, a great many, and I've paid what I could. The villa went last spring. I've a little income from Mother's side, a very little, and I thought..." She looked away across the garden toward the house, whose windows were beginning to catch the reddening light. "I thought that if you would let me, I might stay. Not as a guest. I could pay something, and I could help with the house. I'm not so useless as I look."

There was a silence. The cow-bell clanked again beyond the hedge, and a robin, late in the season, ran across the grass with the quick, interrupted motion of a thought that cannot decide on its conclusion.

Jane was aware of many things at once. She was aware, first, of a sharp and humiliating relief, as though she had been released from some test she had expected to fail; for she had dreaded, more than she had admitted even to herself, that her cousin would come and look about her and go away again, carrying back to the larger world a picture of the narrow one that she, Jane, had never left. She was aware, next, of an obscure resentment that the life she had made out of her renunciations, a life whose very bareness she had come to regard as a kind of dignity, should now be wanted, and wanted as a refuge, by the one person who had always seemed to her to have chosen better. And beneath both of these, deeper than either, she was aware of something she could hardly name: a sense that the long, quiet years in which nothing had happened had been, after all, not an absence but a store; that she had been keeping the house, and the garden, and the clock that lost four minutes a day, against precisely such an evening as this.

"Of course you'll stay," she said.

Harriet turned to her, and Jane saw that her eyes were wet. "You say it as if it were nothing."

"It isn't nothing. But it's what the house is for." She paused, and then added, with the dry precision that was her father's: "You'll find it very dull."

"Dull!" Harriet caught her hand and held it. "My dear, you don't know. You can't know. I've had twenty years of things that weren't dull, and I'd give every one of them..." She broke off, and laughed again, unsteadily. "No, that's not true either. I wouldn't give them. That's the worst of it. I wouldn't give a single one of them, and yet I'd give anything to have had yours instead."

Jane looked down at the two hands, her own brown and roughened, her cousin's white and burdened with their sunken rings, lying together on the grey wood of the bench; and it seemed to her that she understood, for the first time, that neither of them had chosen at all, but that each had been chosen by some quality in herself that she had not known she possessed, and had afterward called the result by the name of choice. The thought did not sadden her. It had, rather, the cool and steadying effect of a fact long suspected and at last confirmed.

"Ellen will have supper on the table," she said, rising. "And you must be tired."

They walked back together through the darkening garden. The shadow of the steeple had spread until it covered the whole of the lawn, and the windows of the house, which a little while before had burned with the reflected sunset, were now only faintly luminous, like the eyes of someone half asleep. At the foot of the porch steps Harriet stopped and looked up at the fanlight, through which the lamp Ellen had lit in the hall shone with a mild and steady yellow.

"I used to think," she said, "that if I ever came back it would be because I had failed. And now I'm here, and I don't feel that I have failed at all. I only feel that I've come home late."

Jane said nothing. She went up the steps ahead of her cousin and held the door; and as Harriet passed in, with her violet skirts brushing the threshold that had worn smooth under the feet of four generations, Jane heard from the parlour the clock on the mantel strike seven, a little after the hour, as it always did.

Here is an excerpt of Edith Wharton's writing, to show you their style:

There had never been such a June in Eagle County. Usually it was a month of moods, with abrupt alternations of belated frost and mid-summer heat; this year, day followed day in a sequence of temperate beauty. Every morning a breeze blew steadily from the hills. Toward noon it built up great canopies of white cloud that threw a cool shadow over fields and woods; then before sunset the clouds dissolved again, and the western light rained its unobstructed brightness on the valley. On such an afternoon Charity Royall lay on a ridge above a sunlit hollow, her face pressed to the earth and the warm currents of the grass running through her. Directly in her line of vision a blackberry branch laid its frail white flowers and blue-green leaves against the sky. Just beyond, a tuft of sweet-fern uncurled between the beaded shoots of the grass, and a small yellow butterfly vibrated over them like a fleck of sunshine. This was all she saw; but she felt, above her and about her, the strong growth of the beeches clothing the ridge, the rounding of pale green cones on countless spruce-branches, the push of myriads of sweet-fern fronds in the cracks of the stony slope below the wood, and the crowding shoots of meadowsweet and yellow flags in the pasture beyond. All this bubbling of sap and slipping of sheaths and bursting of calyxes was carried to her on mingled currents of fragrance. Every leaf and bud and blade seemed to contribute its exhalation to the pervading sweetness in which the pungency of pine-sap prevailed over the spice of thyme and the subtle perfume of fern, and all were merged in a moist earth-smell that was like the breath of some huge sun-warmed animal. Charity had lain there a long time, passive and sun-warmed as the slope on which she lay, when there came between her eyes and the dancing butterfly the sight of a man's foot in a large worn boot covered with red mud.

“Oh, don't!” she exclaimed, raising herself on her elbow and stretching out a warning hand.

“Don't what?” a hoarse voice asked above her head.

“Don't stamp on those bramble flowers, you dolt!” she retorted, springing to her knees. The foot paused and then descended clumsily on the frail branch, and raising her eyes she saw above her the bewildered face of a slouching man with a thin sunburnt beard, and white arms showing through his ragged shirt.

“Don't you ever SEE anything, Liff Hyatt?” she assailed him, as he stood before her with the look of a man who has stirred up a wasp's nest. He grinned. “I seen you! That's what I come down for.”

“Down from where?” she questioned, stooping to gather up the petals his foot had scattered. He jerked his thumb toward the heights. “Been cutting down trees for Dan Targatt.” Charity sank back on her heels and looked at him musingly. She was not in the least afraid of poor Liff Hyatt, though he “came from the Mountain,” and some of the girls ran when they saw him. Among the more reasonable he passed for a harmless creature, a sort of link between the mountain and civilized folk, who occasionally came down and did a little wood cutting for a farmer when hands were short. Besides, she knew the Mountain people would never hurt her: Liff himself had told her so once when she was a little girl, and had met him one day at the edge of lawyer Royall's pasture. “They won't any of 'em touch you up there, f'ever you was to come up.... But I don't s'pose you will,” he had added philosophically, looking at her new shoes, and at the red ribbon that Mrs. Royall had tied in her hair. Charity had, in truth, never felt any desire to visit her birthplace. She did not care to have it known that she was of the Mountain, and was shy of being seen in talk with Liff Hyatt. But today she was not sorry to have him appear. A great many things had happened to her since the day when young Lucius Harney had entered the doors of the Hatchard Memorial, but none, perhaps, so unforeseen as the fact of her suddenly finding it a convenience to be on good terms with Liff Hyatt. She continued to look up curiously at his freckled weather-beaten face, with feverish hollows below the cheekbones and the pale yellow eyes of a harmless animal. “I wonder if he's related to me?” she thought, with a shiver of disdain.

“Is there any folks living in the brown house by the swamp, up under Porcupine?” she presently asked in an indifferent tone. Liff Hyatt, for a while, considered her with surprise; then he scratched his head and shifted his weight from one tattered sole to the other.

“There's always the same folks in the brown house,” he said with his vague grin.

“They're from up your way, ain't they?”

“Their name's the same as mine,” he rejoined uncertainly. Charity still held him with resolute eyes. “See here, I want to go there some day and take a gentleman with me that's boarding with us. He's up in these parts drawing pictures.” She did not offer to explain this statement. It was too far beyond Liff Hyatt's limitations for the attempt to be worth making. “He wants to see the brown house, and go all over it,” she pursued. Liff was still running his fingers perplexedly through his shock of straw-colored hair. “Is it a fellow from the city?” he asked.

“Yes. He draws pictures of things. He's down there now drawing the Bonner house.” She pointed to a chimney just visible over the dip of the pasture below the wood.

“The Bonner house?” Liff echoed incredulously.

“Yes. You won't understand—and it don't matter. All I say is: he's going to the Hyatts' in a day or two.” Liff looked more and more perplexed. “Bash is ugly sometimes in the afternoons.” She threw her head back, her eyes full on Hyatt's. “I'm coming too: you tell him.”

“They won't none of them trouble you, the Hyatts won't. What d'you want a take a stranger with you though?”

“I've told you, haven't I? You've got to tell Bash Hyatt.” He looked away at the blue mountains on the horizon; then his gaze dropped to the chimney-top below the pasture.

“He's down there now?”

“Yes.” He shifted his weight again, crossed his arms, and continued to survey the distant landscape. “Well, so long,” he said at last, inconclusively; and turning away he shambled up the hillside. From the ledge above her, he paused to call down: “I wouldn't go there a Sunday”; then he clambered on till the trees closed in on him. Presently, from high overhead, Charity heard the ring of his axe. She lay on the warm ridge, thinking of many things that the woodsman's appearance had stirred up in her. She knew nothing of her early life, and had never felt any curiosity about it: only a sullen reluctance to explore the corner of her memory where certain blurred images lingered. But all that had happened to her within the last few weeks had stirred her to the sleeping depths. She had become absorbingly interesting to herself, and everything that had to do with her past was illuminated by this sudden curiosity. She hated more than ever the fact of coming from the Mountain; but it was no longer indifferent to her. Everything that in any way affected her was alive and vivid: even the hateful things had grown interesting because they were a part of herself.

“I wonder if Liff Hyatt knows who my mother was?” she mused; and it filled her with a tremor of surprise to think that some woman who was once young and slight, with quick motions of the blood like hers, had carried her in her breast, and watched her sleeping. She had always thought of her mother as so long dead as to be no more than a nameless pinch of earth; but now it occurred to her that the once-young woman might be alive, and wrinkled and elf-locked like the woman she had sometimes seen in the door of the brown house that Lucius Harney wanted to draw. The thought brought him back to the central point in her mind, and she strayed away from the conjectures roused by Liff Hyatt's presence. Speculations concerning the past could not hold her long when the present was so rich, the future so rosy, and when Lucius Harney, a stone's throw away, was bending over his sketch-book, frowning, calculating, measuring, and then throwing his head back with the sudden smile that had shed its brightness over everything. She scrambled to her feet, but as she did so she saw him coming up the pasture and dropped down on the grass to wait. When he was drawing and measuring one of “his houses,” as she called them, she often strayed away by herself into the woods or up the hillside. It was partly from shyness that she did so: from a sense of inadequacy that came to her most painfully when her companion, absorbed in his job, forgot her ignorance and her inability to follow his least allusion, and plunged into a monologue on art and life. To avoid the awkwardness of listening with a blank face, and also to escape the surprised stare of the inhabitants of the houses before which he would abruptly pull up their horse and open his sketch-book, she slipped away to some spot from which, without being seen, she could watch him at work, or at least look down on the house he was drawing. She had not been displeased, at first, to have it known to North Dormer and the neighborhood that she was driving Miss Hatchard's cousin about the country in the buggy he had hired of lawyer Royall. She had always kept to herself, contemptuously aloof from village love-making, without exactly knowing whether her fierce pride was due to the sense of her tainted origin, or whether she was reserving herself for a more brilliant fate. Sometimes she envied the other girls their sentimental preoccupations, their long hours of inarticulate philandering with one of the few youths who still lingered in the village; but when she pictured herself curling her hair or putting a new ribbon on her hat for Ben Fry or one of the Sollas boys the fever dropped and she relapsed into indifference. Now she knew the meaning of her disdains and reluctances. She had learned what she was worth when Lucius Harney, looking at her for the first time, had lost the thread of his speech, and leaned reddening on the edge of her desk. But another kind of shyness had been born in her: a terror of exposing to vulgar perils the sacred treasure of her happiness. She was not sorry to have the neighbors suspect her of “going with” a young man from the city; but she did not want it known to all the countryside how many hours of the long June days she spent with him. What she most feared was that the inevitable comments should reach Mr. Royall. Charity was instinctively aware that few things concerning her escaped the eyes of the silent man under whose roof she lived; and in spite of the latitude which North Dormer accorded to courting couples she had always felt that, on the day when she showed too open a preference, Mr. Royall might, as she phrased it, make her “pay for it.” How, she did not know; and her fear was the greater because it was undefinable. If she had been accepting the attentions of one of the village youths she would have been less apprehensive: Mr. Royall could not prevent her marrying when she chose to. But everybody knew that “going with a city fellow” was a different and less straightforward affair: almost every village could show a victim of the perilous venture. And her dread of Mr. Royall's intervention gave a sharpened joy to the hours she spent with young Harney, and made her, at the same time, shy of being too generally seen with him. As he approached she rose to her knees, stretching her arms above her head with the indolent gesture that was her way of expressing a profound well-being.

“I'm going to take you to that house up under Porcupine,” she announced.

“What house? Oh, yes; that ramshackle place near the swamp, with the gipsy-looking people hanging about. It's curious that a house with traces of real architecture should have been built in such a place. But the people were a sulky-looking lot—do you suppose they'll let us in?”

“They'll do whatever I tell them,” she said with assurance. He threw himself down beside her. “Will they?” he rejoined with a smile. “Well, I should like to see what's left inside the house. And I should like to have a talk with the people. Who was it who was telling me the other day that they had come down from the Mountain?” Charity shot a sideward look at him. It was the first time he had spoken of the Mountain except as a feature of the landscape. What else did he know about it, and about her relation to it? Her heart began to beat with the fierce impulse of resistance which she instinctively opposed to every imagined slight.

“The Mountain? I ain't afraid of the Mountain!” Her tone of defiance seemed to escape him. He lay breast-down on the grass, breaking off sprigs of thyme and pressing them against his lips. Far off, above the folds of the nearer hills, the Mountain thrust itself up menacingly against a yellow sunset.

“I must go up there some day: I want to see it,” he continued. Her heart-beats slackened and she turned again to examine his profile. It was innocent of all unfriendly intention.

“What'd you want to go up the Mountain for?”

“Why, it must be rather a curious place. There's a queer colony up there, you know: sort of out-laws, a little independent kingdom. Of course you've heard them spoken of; but I'm told they have nothing to do with the people in the valleys—rather look down on them, in fact. I suppose they're rough customers; but they must have a good deal of character.” She did not quite know what he meant by having a good deal of character; but his tone was expressive of admiration, and deepened her dawning curiosity. It struck her now as strange that she knew so little about the Mountain. She had never asked, and no one had ever offered to enlighten her. North Dormer took the Mountain for granted, and implied its disparagement by an intonation rather than by explicit criticism.

“It's queer, you know,” he continued, “that, just over there, on top of that hill, there should be a handful of people who don't give a damn for anybody.” The words thrilled her. They seemed the clue to her own revolts and defiances, and she longed to have him tell her more.

“I don't know much about them. Have they always been there?”

“Nobody seems to know exactly how long. Down at Creston they told me that the first colonists are supposed to have been men who worked on the railway that was built forty or fifty years ago between Springfield and Nettleton. Some of them took to drink, or got into trouble with the police, and went off—disappeared into the woods. A year or two later there was a report that they were living up on the Mountain. Then I suppose others joined them—and children were born. Now they say there are over a hundred people up there. They seem to be quite outside the jurisdiction of the valleys. No school, no church—and no sheriff ever goes up to see what they're about. But don't people ever talk of them at North Dormer?”

“I don't know. They say they're bad.” He laughed. “Do they? We'll go and see, shall we?” She flushed at the suggestion, and turned her face to his. “You never heard, I suppose—I come from there. They brought me down when I was little.”

“You?” He raised himself on his elbow, looking at her with sudden interest. “You're from the Mountain? How curious! I suppose that's why you're so different....” Her happy blood bathed her to the forehead. He was praising her—and praising her because she came from the Mountain!

“Am I... different?” she triumphed, with affected wonder.

“Oh, awfully!” He picked up her hand and laid a kiss on the sunburnt knuckles.

“Come,” he said, “let's be off.” He stood up and shook the grass from his loose grey clothes. “What a good day! Where are you going to take me tomorrow?”

“Oh, don't!” she exclaimed, raising herself on her elbow and stretching out a warning hand.

“Don't what?” a hoarse voice asked above her head.

“Don't stamp on those bramble flowers, you dolt!” she retorted, springing to her knees. The foot paused and then descended clumsily on the frail branch, and raising her eyes she saw above her the bewildered face of a slouching man with a thin sunburnt beard, and white arms showing through his ragged shirt.

“Don't you ever SEE anything, Liff Hyatt?” she assailed him, as he stood before her with the look of a man who has stirred up a wasp's nest. He grinned. “I seen you! That's what I come down for.”

“Down from where?” she questioned, stooping to gather up the petals his foot had scattered. He jerked his thumb toward the heights. “Been cutting down trees for Dan Targatt.” Charity sank back on her heels and looked at him musingly. She was not in the least afraid of poor Liff Hyatt, though he “came from the Mountain,” and some of the girls ran when they saw him. Among the more reasonable he passed for a harmless creature, a sort of link between the mountain and civilized folk, who occasionally came down and did a little wood cutting for a farmer when hands were short. Besides, she knew the Mountain people would never hurt her: Liff himself had told her so once when she was a little girl, and had met him one day at the edge of lawyer Royall's pasture. “They won't any of 'em touch you up there, f'ever you was to come up.... But I don't s'pose you will,” he had added philosophically, looking at her new shoes, and at the red ribbon that Mrs. Royall had tied in her hair. Charity had, in truth, never felt any desire to visit her birthplace. She did not care to have it known that she was of the Mountain, and was shy of being seen in talk with Liff Hyatt. But today she was not sorry to have him appear. A great many things had happened to her since the day when young Lucius Harney had entered the doors of the Hatchard Memorial, but none, perhaps, so unforeseen as the fact of her suddenly finding it a convenience to be on good terms with Liff Hyatt. She continued to look up curiously at his freckled weather-beaten face, with feverish hollows below the cheekbones and the pale yellow eyes of a harmless animal. “I wonder if he's related to me?” she thought, with a shiver of disdain.

“Is there any folks living in the brown house by the swamp, up under Porcupine?” she presently asked in an indifferent tone. Liff Hyatt, for a while, considered her with surprise; then he scratched his head and shifted his weight from one tattered sole to the other.

“There's always the same folks in the brown house,” he said with his vague grin.

“They're from up your way, ain't they?”

“Their name's the same as mine,” he rejoined uncertainly. Charity still held him with resolute eyes. “See here, I want to go there some day and take a gentleman with me that's boarding with us. He's up in these parts drawing pictures.” She did not offer to explain this statement. It was too far beyond Liff Hyatt's limitations for the attempt to be worth making. “He wants to see the brown house, and go all over it,” she pursued. Liff was still running his fingers perplexedly through his shock of straw-colored hair. “Is it a fellow from the city?” he asked.

“Yes. He draws pictures of things. He's down there now drawing the Bonner house.” She pointed to a chimney just visible over the dip of the pasture below the wood.

“The Bonner house?” Liff echoed incredulously.

“Yes. You won't understand—and it don't matter. All I say is: he's going to the Hyatts' in a day or two.” Liff looked more and more perplexed. “Bash is ugly sometimes in the afternoons.” She threw her head back, her eyes full on Hyatt's. “I'm coming too: you tell him.”

“They won't none of them trouble you, the Hyatts won't. What d'you want a take a stranger with you though?”

“I've told you, haven't I? You've got to tell Bash Hyatt.” He looked away at the blue mountains on the horizon; then his gaze dropped to the chimney-top below the pasture.

“He's down there now?”

“Yes.” He shifted his weight again, crossed his arms, and continued to survey the distant landscape. “Well, so long,” he said at last, inconclusively; and turning away he shambled up the hillside. From the ledge above her, he paused to call down: “I wouldn't go there a Sunday”; then he clambered on till the trees closed in on him. Presently, from high overhead, Charity heard the ring of his axe. She lay on the warm ridge, thinking of many things that the woodsman's appearance had stirred up in her. She knew nothing of her early life, and had never felt any curiosity about it: only a sullen reluctance to explore the corner of her memory where certain blurred images lingered. But all that had happened to her within the last few weeks had stirred her to the sleeping depths. She had become absorbingly interesting to herself, and everything that had to do with her past was illuminated by this sudden curiosity. She hated more than ever the fact of coming from the Mountain; but it was no longer indifferent to her. Everything that in any way affected her was alive and vivid: even the hateful things had grown interesting because they were a part of herself.

“I wonder if Liff Hyatt knows who my mother was?” she mused; and it filled her with a tremor of surprise to think that some woman who was once young and slight, with quick motions of the blood like hers, had carried her in her breast, and watched her sleeping. She had always thought of her mother as so long dead as to be no more than a nameless pinch of earth; but now it occurred to her that the once-young woman might be alive, and wrinkled and elf-locked like the woman she had sometimes seen in the door of the brown house that Lucius Harney wanted to draw. The thought brought him back to the central point in her mind, and she strayed away from the conjectures roused by Liff Hyatt's presence. Speculations concerning the past could not hold her long when the present was so rich, the future so rosy, and when Lucius Harney, a stone's throw away, was bending over his sketch-book, frowning, calculating, measuring, and then throwing his head back with the sudden smile that had shed its brightness over everything. She scrambled to her feet, but as she did so she saw him coming up the pasture and dropped down on the grass to wait. When he was drawing and measuring one of “his houses,” as she called them, she often strayed away by herself into the woods or up the hillside. It was partly from shyness that she did so: from a sense of inadequacy that came to her most painfully when her companion, absorbed in his job, forgot her ignorance and her inability to follow his least allusion, and plunged into a monologue on art and life. To avoid the awkwardness of listening with a blank face, and also to escape the surprised stare of the inhabitants of the houses before which he would abruptly pull up their horse and open his sketch-book, she slipped away to some spot from which, without being seen, she could watch him at work, or at least look down on the house he was drawing. She had not been displeased, at first, to have it known to North Dormer and the neighborhood that she was driving Miss Hatchard's cousin about the country in the buggy he had hired of lawyer Royall. She had always kept to herself, contemptuously aloof from village love-making, without exactly knowing whether her fierce pride was due to the sense of her tainted origin, or whether she was reserving herself for a more brilliant fate. Sometimes she envied the other girls their sentimental preoccupations, their long hours of inarticulate philandering with one of the few youths who still lingered in the village; but when she pictured herself curling her hair or putting a new ribbon on her hat for Ben Fry or one of the Sollas boys the fever dropped and she relapsed into indifference. Now she knew the meaning of her disdains and reluctances. She had learned what she was worth when Lucius Harney, looking at her for the first time, had lost the thread of his speech, and leaned reddening on the edge of her desk. But another kind of shyness had been born in her: a terror of exposing to vulgar perils the sacred treasure of her happiness. She was not sorry to have the neighbors suspect her of “going with” a young man from the city; but she did not want it known to all the countryside how many hours of the long June days she spent with him. What she most feared was that the inevitable comments should reach Mr. Royall. Charity was instinctively aware that few things concerning her escaped the eyes of the silent man under whose roof she lived; and in spite of the latitude which North Dormer accorded to courting couples she had always felt that, on the day when she showed too open a preference, Mr. Royall might, as she phrased it, make her “pay for it.” How, she did not know; and her fear was the greater because it was undefinable. If she had been accepting the attentions of one of the village youths she would have been less apprehensive: Mr. Royall could not prevent her marrying when she chose to. But everybody knew that “going with a city fellow” was a different and less straightforward affair: almost every village could show a victim of the perilous venture. And her dread of Mr. Royall's intervention gave a sharpened joy to the hours she spent with young Harney, and made her, at the same time, shy of being too generally seen with him. As he approached she rose to her knees, stretching her arms above her head with the indolent gesture that was her way of expressing a profound well-being.

“I'm going to take you to that house up under Porcupine,” she announced.

“What house? Oh, yes; that ramshackle place near the swamp, with the gipsy-looking people hanging about. It's curious that a house with traces of real architecture should have been built in such a place. But the people were a sulky-looking lot—do you suppose they'll let us in?”

“They'll do whatever I tell them,” she said with assurance. He threw himself down beside her. “Will they?” he rejoined with a smile. “Well, I should like to see what's left inside the house. And I should like to have a talk with the people. Who was it who was telling me the other day that they had come down from the Mountain?” Charity shot a sideward look at him. It was the first time he had spoken of the Mountain except as a feature of the landscape. What else did he know about it, and about her relation to it? Her heart began to beat with the fierce impulse of resistance which she instinctively opposed to every imagined slight.

“The Mountain? I ain't afraid of the Mountain!” Her tone of defiance seemed to escape him. He lay breast-down on the grass, breaking off sprigs of thyme and pressing them against his lips. Far off, above the folds of the nearer hills, the Mountain thrust itself up menacingly against a yellow sunset.

“I must go up there some day: I want to see it,” he continued. Her heart-beats slackened and she turned again to examine his profile. It was innocent of all unfriendly intention.

“What'd you want to go up the Mountain for?”

“Why, it must be rather a curious place. There's a queer colony up there, you know: sort of out-laws, a little independent kingdom. Of course you've heard them spoken of; but I'm told they have nothing to do with the people in the valleys—rather look down on them, in fact. I suppose they're rough customers; but they must have a good deal of character.” She did not quite know what he meant by having a good deal of character; but his tone was expressive of admiration, and deepened her dawning curiosity. It struck her now as strange that she knew so little about the Mountain. She had never asked, and no one had ever offered to enlighten her. North Dormer took the Mountain for granted, and implied its disparagement by an intonation rather than by explicit criticism.

“It's queer, you know,” he continued, “that, just over there, on top of that hill, there should be a handful of people who don't give a damn for anybody.” The words thrilled her. They seemed the clue to her own revolts and defiances, and she longed to have him tell her more.

“I don't know much about them. Have they always been there?”

“Nobody seems to know exactly how long. Down at Creston they told me that the first colonists are supposed to have been men who worked on the railway that was built forty or fifty years ago between Springfield and Nettleton. Some of them took to drink, or got into trouble with the police, and went off—disappeared into the woods. A year or two later there was a report that they were living up on the Mountain. Then I suppose others joined them—and children were born. Now they say there are over a hundred people up there. They seem to be quite outside the jurisdiction of the valleys. No school, no church—and no sheriff ever goes up to see what they're about. But don't people ever talk of them at North Dormer?”

“I don't know. They say they're bad.” He laughed. “Do they? We'll go and see, shall we?” She flushed at the suggestion, and turned her face to his. “You never heard, I suppose—I come from there. They brought me down when I was little.”

“You?” He raised himself on his elbow, looking at her with sudden interest. “You're from the Mountain? How curious! I suppose that's why you're so different....” Her happy blood bathed her to the forehead. He was praising her—and praising her because she came from the Mountain!

“Am I... different?” she triumphed, with affected wonder.

“Oh, awfully!” He picked up her hand and laid a kiss on the sunburnt knuckles.

“Come,” he said, “let's be off.” He stood up and shook the grass from his loose grey clothes. “What a good day! Where are you going to take me tomorrow?”
