In the town of Pickerel, Ohio, which lies along the Wheeling and Lake Erie railroad not far from where the land begins to fall away toward the lake, there lived a man named Joe Hardesty and his wife Ellen. They lived in a frame house on Pearl Street, at the end where the sidewalk stopped and the road went on, dusty in summer and deep with mud in the spring, out past the cemetery and into the country. Joe Hardesty worked in the plow works by the tracks. He had worked there eleven years. He was a heavy man with a red neck and his hands were large and the backs of them were covered with fine yellow hairs that caught the light when he sat under the lamp in the evening, reading the Cleveland paper and turning the pages slowly as though the paper were a thing that might break.

Ellen Hardesty had been a schoolteacher before she married. She had taught for two years in a little brick schoolhouse out on the Turner Pike, and the children who had been in her school remembered her as a tall, thin woman with brown hair who sometimes stood for a long time by the window looking out at the fields and did not hear when they spoke to her. Then she would turn suddenly and her face would be red and she would be very kind to them for the rest of the day, as though she had done them some wrong.

It is a strange thing about people that live together for a long time in one house. They come to know each other's ways, the way a man clears his throat before he speaks, the sound of a woman's feet on the stairs, and they think they know everything there is to know. Then something happens, some little thing, and it is as though a door had opened in a wall where no door had been, and there is a dark room beyond and in the room something moving about.

This is the story of an evening in the fall of the year when Joe Hardesty came home from the plow works and found his wife sitting in the kitchen in the dark.

---

It was late in October. All day the wind had been blowing from the west and the leaves of the maple trees along Pearl Street had come down and lay in the gutters and against the fences, and when the wind blew they moved along the ground with a dry, whispering sound. Joe walked home from the works with his dinner pail in his hand. He walked as he always walked, with his head a little down and his shoulders hunched, and when he passed the house of Will Sommers, the drayman, Will called to him from the porch, and Joe lifted the hand that did not have the dinner pail in it but did not stop.

When he came into his own yard he saw that there was no light in the kitchen window. He stood for a moment by the gate. The thing was unusual. For eleven years there had been a light in the kitchen window when he came home, and the smell of supper cooking, and his wife's figure moving back and forth past the window. He thought she might be ill. Then he thought she might have gone to her sister's on Duane Street, and he felt a little anger rise in him because she had not told him. He went around to the back of the house and opened the kitchen door.

She was sitting at the table. In the gray light that came in at the window he could see her shape there, very straight in the chair, with her hands lying on the oilcloth before her. She did not move when he came in.

"Ellen," he said. "What's the matter? Are you sick?"

"No," she said. "I'm not sick."

He set the dinner pail down on the shelf by the door. He did not know what to do with his hands then, and he stood rubbing them together. The stove was cold. He could feel that it was cold. There was no fire in it at all.

"I'll light the lamp," he said.

"Don't," she said. "Not yet. Sit down a minute, Joe."

He sat down across the table from her. He was a man who did not like things to be out of their places and he felt uneasy. He thought of the supper that was not cooked and was ashamed that he should think of it. He looked at his wife's face, but in the dark it was only a pale shape, like a plate that has been set on a shelf in a dim room.

"I went down to the station today," she said.

"To the station? What for?"

"I don't know what for. I just went. I put on my hat and my good coat and I went down there and sat on the bench and waited for the two-forty to come in from Toledo. Then I watched it go out again."

Joe Hardesty said nothing. He put one of his big hands on the table and moved it slowly over the oilcloth as though he were smoothing out a wrinkle that was not there.

"Was there somebody on it you knew?" he asked.

"No. There wasn't anybody on it I knew. That's what I mean. There wasn't anybody."

---

It should be said here that Ellen Hardesty was the daughter of a man named Abner Pruett, who had kept a harness shop on Main Street in Pickerel for thirty years and who had died when Ellen was nineteen. He had been a small, silent man who wore a leather apron and smelled always of neat's-foot oil, and on Sunday afternoons he used to walk out alone along the railroad tracks for miles, stepping from tie to tie, and come back after dark with his shoes covered with cinders. No one ever knew where he went or why. Once, when Ellen was a child, he had taken her with him, and they had walked until the town was out of sight behind them and there was nothing but the shining rails going on and on between the cornfields. Her father had stopped then and stood looking along the tracks to where they came together at the edge of the sky. "There," he had said. "Do you see it?" She had looked and looked but she had seen nothing, only the rails and the fields and a crow flying. She had been afraid to tell him she saw nothing. "Yes," she had said, and he had taken her hand and they had walked back.

She had not thought of that day for years. But on this day, sitting on the bench at the station in her good coat, she had thought of it, and it had seemed to her that her whole life had been like that, like standing on the tracks beside her father and saying yes, yes, she saw it, when she saw nothing at all.

---

"I don't understand you, Ellen," Joe said. "What are you trying to say?"

"I'm not trying to say anything. I'm just telling you."

"You're telling me you went down to the station and watched a train."

"Yes."

"Well, what of it? A person can go down to the station. There's nothing wrong in that."

She laughed then, a short, sharp laugh, and the sound of it in the cold kitchen startled him so that he drew his hand back from the table. "No," she said. "There's nothing wrong in it. There's nothing wrong in anything. That's the trouble, Joe. You don't see. There's nothing wrong in anything and there's nothing right either. There's just the days."

He was silent. Outside the wind had risen again and a branch of the apple tree by the woodshed scraped against the side of the house. It made a sound like someone trying to get in. Joe Hardesty thought of the plow works, of the long shed where he worked, with the dust floating in the shafts of light that came down through the high windows and the noise of the machines that went on all day, so that a man could not hear himself think and did not want to. He thought that a man who worked all day had a right to come home and find a fire in the stove. Then he thought that it was not right of him to think that, not now. He did not know what was right to think.

"You've been sitting here all afternoon," he said. "In the cold."

"I came home and sat down and I didn't get up. I meant to. I kept saying to myself, now get up, Ellen, get up and make the fire, it's getting late, Joe will be coming. And I didn't get up."

"Why didn't you?"

"I don't know."

"You must know."

"I don't know, Joe. Can't you understand a person not knowing?"

He could not. That was the truth of it, and she could see that it was the truth of it, even in the dark. He was a man who had always known why he did a thing. He went to work because it was time to go to work. He came home because it was time to come home. He had married her because he had wanted her and she had been there, walking along Main Street on a Saturday evening in a white dress with a blue sash, and he had walked beside her and talked to her about the weather and the price of hogs and the new waterworks the town was building, and after a time she had let him take her arm. It had all been simple. Everything had been simple.

---

They sat for a long time. It grew darker in the kitchen until he could not see her at all, could only hear her breathing across the table. Once she moved her hand and it struck against the sugar bowl and the lid of the bowl rattled. Joe started at the sound.

"Joe," she said, "do you remember when we used to go walking out on the Turner Pike? Before we were married?"

"I remember."

"There was a place where the road went over a little bridge, by the Collier farm, and we used to stand on the bridge and look down at the creek. Do you remember that?"

"Yes."

"One night you asked me what I was thinking about. We were standing on the bridge and it was summer and there were frogs in the creek and you asked me what I was thinking about and I said nothing. Do you remember?"

"I don't remember that," he said.

"I wasn't thinking about nothing. I was thinking about something. I was thinking that if I could only say it to you, what I was thinking, then everything would be all right forever. And I couldn't say it. I tried and it wouldn't come. It was like my mouth was full of cotton. So I said nothing. And you said, well, I was thinking about you, and you kissed me, and I let you. And then it was too late."

"Too late for what?"

"For saying it."

He leaned forward in his chair. His big hands were clenched together on the table now and his knuckles hurt. "Well, say it now, then," he said, and his voice was louder than he had meant it to be. "Go on and say it. Whatever it is. I'm here. I'm sitting right here."

She did not answer. He could hear her breathing, quick and shallow, as though she had been running.

"I can't," she said at last. "It's gone. It's been gone a long time. I don't even know what it was anymore. That's what I found out today, sitting down there at the station. I found out I don't even know what it was."

---

There is a kind of loneliness that comes to people in small towns in the Middle West that is not like any other kind. It is not the loneliness of a man lost in a great city among strangers, nor of a man alone on a mountain or at sea. It is the loneliness of people who are known to everyone and to whom everyone is known, who have walked the same streets all their lives and said good morning to the same faces, and who wake suddenly in the night and lie in their beds and listen to the clock ticking in the hall and think, Who am I? What am I doing here? And there is no one to tell them. The wind goes through the bare trees and a dog barks somewhere far off and a train whistles out beyond the edge of town, going away, going toward Cleveland or Chicago or some place they have never seen, and that is all.

Ellen Hardesty had felt this loneliness for a long time without knowing what it was. She had felt it when she stood by the window of the little schoolhouse on the Turner Pike. She had felt it on her wedding night, lying awake beside Joe while he slept, listening to his heavy breathing and looking at the square of moonlight on the floor. She had felt it in the mornings, packing his dinner pail, putting in the bread and the cold meat and the piece of pie wrapped in a napkin, the same things every day, and snapping the lid shut. And on this day it had come up in her all at once, like water rising in a well, and she had put on her hat and her good coat and gone down to the station.

---

"Are you going to go away?" Joe asked.

He said it very quietly. She heard the fear in his voice and something in her went out to him, and she wanted to reach across the table and touch his hand. But she did not do it.

"No," she said. "Where would I go?"

"I don't know. Chicago. Your cousin is in Chicago."

"I'm not going to Chicago."

"Then what is it? What do you want, Ellen? You tell me what you want and I'll get it for you. If it's money, I've got some put by. More than you know. I've been saving. I was going to buy the lot next to the Weatherbys', to build on. We could build a better house. With a parlor, a real parlor. You could have a piano."

"I don't want a piano."

"Then what do you want?"

She stood up suddenly. He heard the chair scrape on the floor. She went to the window and stood there, and now he could see her again, a little, a dark shape against the lesser darkness of the window. Beyond her the yard was full of moving shadows where the wind shook the apple tree.

"I wanted you to come in," she said, "and see me sitting here in the dark, and not ask me if I was sick. I wanted you to come in and know. Without my saying anything. That's all. It's foolish. I know it's foolish."

Joe Hardesty sat at the table. He looked at the dark shape of his wife at the window and he felt something he had never felt before. It was as though there were a great weight on his chest. He thought that he ought to get up and go to her. He thought that if he went to her and put his arms around her, it might be all right. But his legs would not move. He sat there with his hands clenched on the oilcloth and he could not move.

"I'm not a smart man, Ellen," he said. "You knew that when you married me. I don't know about things like that. I work. I come home. I don't know what you want me to know."

"I know," she said. "It isn't your fault."

"Then whose fault is it?"

"Nobody's. It isn't anybody's fault. Don't you see, Joe? That's the worst of it. If it was somebody's fault, we could do something."

---

After a while he got up and lit the lamp. His hands shook as he struck the match, and the first match went out and he had to strike another. When the wick caught and the yellow light filled the kitchen they both looked at each other, blinking, like people who have come up out of a cellar. Her face was very white and there were marks under her eyes and she looked older than he had ever seen her look. He saw for the first time that there was gray in her hair, above the ears. He did not know when it had come there.

She looked at him too. She looked at his red neck and his heavy shoulders and his big hands with the yellow hairs on the backs of them, and at his face, which was frightened and puzzled, like the face of a boy who has been punished and does not know why. She thought, He is a good man. She thought it clearly, as though someone had spoken the words aloud in the kitchen. He is a good man, and I have lived with him eleven years, and I do not know him and he does not know me, and that is the way it is going to be.

"I'll make the fire," she said.

"No. Let me do it."

He went out to the woodshed. The wind caught at his coat as he crossed the yard and the branch of the apple tree whipped against the shed wall. He stood in the dark shed for a long time with his hands on the pile of split wood and did not gather any of it up. He thought of his own father, who had farmed a hundred and sixty acres south of town and who had never in his life said more than a dozen words at a time to Joe's mother, and of his mother, who had lived to be seventy and died in the front bedroom with her face to the wall. He had thought they were happy. It had never come into his mind to think anything else. Now he wondered. He stood in the woodshed and wondered about his father and his mother and about all the people in Pickerel, in all the houses along all the streets, sitting in their kitchens in the evening with the lamps lit. He wondered if they were all like this. He wondered if every one of them was sitting across a table from someone and could not say what they wanted to say.

It was a terrible thought and he did not want to have it. He gathered up an armload of wood and went back across the yard to the house.

---

When he came into the kitchen Ellen was standing by the stove. She had taken off her good coat at last and hung it on the hook behind the door and she was standing with her hands folded in front of her, waiting. He knelt down and opened the firebox and began laying in the kindling. He did it slowly and carefully, the way he did everything, and she stood above him and watched his big hands moving among the sticks of wood.

"Joe," she said.

"What?"

She did not say anything more. He looked up at her and waited, and she looked down at him, and for a moment it seemed to both of them that something was going to be said, something that would change everything. The lamp hissed on the table. The wind blew outside. Far off, out beyond the edge of town, a freight train was whistling for the crossing at Turner Pike, a long sound and then two short ones, going away.

"Nothing," she said. "I was just going to say the wood's damp. It won't draw well."

"It'll draw," he said. "Give it time."

He struck a match and held it to the paper under the kindling, and the flame caught and ran along the edge of the paper and climbed up into the sticks. They both watched it. When the fire was going he closed the firebox door and stood up, and his knees cracked, and he brushed the bits of bark from his trousers.

Ellen got the skillet down from its nail. She went to the pantry and came back with the potatoes and a knife and sat down at the table to peel them. Joe sat down across from her and picked up the Cleveland paper, which he had dropped on the chair when he came in, and opened it, and held it up before him. But he did not read it. He sat holding the paper and looking at it and over the top of it he could see the top of his wife's head, bent over the potatoes, and the gray in her hair above the ears, and her thin hands moving with the knife.

Neither of them spoke again. After a time the kitchen grew warm and the smell of frying potatoes filled the room, and the window grew black and gave back the image of the lamp and the table and the two people sitting there. Anyone passing along Pearl Street that night, going out toward the cemetery and the country, would have looked in and seen them and thought nothing of it. They would have seen only a man reading his paper and a woman cooking his supper in a lighted kitchen, the way it was in every house in Pickerel, the way it had always been.

The man who got off the evening train at Lenville that fall was named Tom Hartsel, and he had not been in the town for nineteen years. He stood on the station platform with a brown bag in his hand and looked about. There was the same water tank, the same pile of ties rotting beside the track, the same yellow building with the word FREIGHT painted on its side, though the paint had gone grey and was peeling. A boy sat on a baggage truck and swung his legs. He looked at Tom Hartsel and then looked away. Tom Hartsel was a stranger to him. He was a man in a city suit with a soft hat and a gold chain across his vest, and the boy, after one glance, went on swinging his legs and spitting on the boards of the platform.

Tom Hartsel was forty-one years old. He sold harness hardware, buckles and rings and snaps, for a firm in Chicago, and he had traveled over half of Indiana and all of Illinois and a good part of Iowa. He had sat in a great many hotel rooms. He had eaten a great many meals in railroad eating houses with other men like himself, men who talked loudly and told stories and laughed, and he had laughed with them. In the evenings, when the others had gone off somewhere, he sometimes sat alone by a window and looked out into a street of a town he did not know. It was then that something came into his mind. He could not have said what it was. It was a kind of hunger, but not a hunger of the belly. He would get up and walk about the room. He would take off his collar and put it on the dresser and look at it. Then he would go to bed.

Now he had come back to Lenville, and he did not know why he had come. He had a cousin there, Clara, who had been Clara Hartsel and was now Clara Moyer. She was a widow and lived on the Moyer place, two miles out on the Pike Road. He had written her a letter. In the letter he had said that he would be passing near and might stop. That was not true. He had not been passing near. He had gone a long way out of his road to come to Lenville, and he had told his firm a lie about it.

He did not hire a rig at the livery. He walked. It was a cool evening and the light was going out of the sky. He went along Main Street past the bank and past Hagerty's hardware store, where he had once, as a boy, bought a jackknife with a horn handle, and then he went out past the last houses and into the country. The corn had been cut and stood in shocks in the fields. Here and there a pumpkin lay yellow on the ground between the shocks. A dog barked at a farmhouse and then was quiet. Tom Hartsel walked with his bag in his hand and his shoes, which were new and had been bought in Peoria, began to hurt his feet. He did not mind. He walked on, and as he walked he thought of his cousin Clara.

There is a thing that happens sometimes between two people when they are young. It is not love, exactly, though it may be mistaken for love. It is more as though for a moment, a minute or an hour, two people stand outside of the life about them and look at each other and know that they are alone and that the other one is alone also. Afterward they go back into life and are what they were. But the moment stays. It stays in them like a stone in the bed of a creek, and the water of their lives goes over it and goes over it and it is always there.

When Tom Hartsel was a boy of fourteen, his father had died, and he had been sent out to the farm of his uncle, Clara's father, to work. Clara was a year younger than he was. She was a thin girl with large hands and red hair that would not stay in its braids, and she had a way of standing very still and looking at a thing, a bird or a cloud or a man driving along the road, as though she were trying to get the inside of it. Her father was a hard man. He worked his hired men and he worked his own children and he worked Tom Hartsel, and at night they were all too tired to talk.

One day in August, a storm had come up very quickly out of the west while Tom and Clara were in the far field turning hay. They ran for the barn. The rain caught them before they got there, and they came into the barn soaked through, and they stood together in the wide door and looked out. The rain came down so hard that the house, only a little way across the barnyard, could not be seen. There was nothing in the world but the barn and the rain and the two of them. The lightning cracked. Clara did not say anything. She put out her hand and took hold of Tom's wrist, and she held it, and they stood that way. Then the rain stopped and the sun came out and the hens came out of the woodshed and began to scratch, and Clara let go of his wrist and went to the house. That was all. Nothing had been said. Two years later Tom Hartsel went away to Cleveland to work in a factory, and later to Chicago, and he had not seen his cousin since.

He had thought of that afternoon a great many times. In hotel rooms in Galesburg and Keokuk and Terre Haute he had thought of it. He had been married, for three years, to a woman in Chicago who had afterward gone away with a man who owned a cigar store, and while he was married he had thought of it. It was not that he wanted his cousin. It was something else. He wanted to know what had happened in the barn door. He wanted to know if she remembered.

---

The Moyer house stood back from the road behind two big maple trees. It was a frame house painted white, and there was a porch across the front. A light was burning in one of the windows. Tom Hartsel went in at the gate and up the path, and before he got to the porch steps the door opened and a woman came out.

She was a large woman. That was the first thing he saw. He had been thinking of a thin girl with red hair, and here was a woman of forty, broad in the hips, with her hair, still reddish but faded and streaked with grey, done up tight on her head. She wore an apron. She stood on the porch with her large hands folded across the apron and looked at him.

"Well," she said. "Tom."

"Hello, Clara," he said.

They shook hands. Her hand was hard and dry. He thought that she was going to say something more, and he waited, but she only stood and looked at him, as she had used to look at things, as though she were trying to get the inside of him. Then she laughed, a short laugh, and said, "You'll want your supper. I kept it warm."

He went into the house and sat at the kitchen table and she gave him fried potatoes and side meat and bread and a dish of applesauce. She did not eat. She sat across from him and watched him eat. There was a clock on the shelf over the stove, and it ticked loudly. Tom Hartsel ate, and he said that the potatoes were good, and she said that they were only potatoes. He asked about the farm and she told him. She had a man, a German named Shultz, who worked the land on shares. He lived in the tenant house down by the creek. The wheat had been poor that year but the corn was fair. She had forty hens. She sold eggs in town.

"It's a lonely life, I guess," he said.

"I don't know," she said. "I don't think about it."

When he had finished eating she took his plate and washed it at the sink. He sat at the table and watched her back. He took out a cigar and then put it back into his pocket. He did not know whether she would want him to smoke in her kitchen. He began to rub his thumb against one of the buttons of his vest. It was a habit he had. When he was talking to a harness maker in some town and the harness maker would not buy, he rubbed his thumb against the button, round and round, and went on talking.

"I've been all over," he said. "Illinois, Iowa. I was in Kansas City once."

"Were you?" she said, without turning around.

"It's a big place. Bigger than you'd think. There's stockyards there. The smell of it, you can smell it all over the town." He stopped. He had not meant to talk about the stockyards in Kansas City. He did not know why he had begun.

She dried the plate and put it on the shelf.

"Let's go sit on the porch," she said. "It's not too cold yet."

---

They sat on the porch in the dark. She sat in a rocking chair and he sat on the top step with his back against a post. He lit his cigar. The fields lay out before them, grey under the starlight, and the shocks of corn stood in rows like men waiting for something. Down by the creek a light burned in the tenant house where the German lived. Once a wagon went by on the road, and a man on the seat called out, "Evening, Mis' Moyer," and she called back, "Evening, Ed," and the wagon went on and the sound of it died away.

For a long time neither of them said anything. Tom Hartsel smoked his cigar. He thought that now, in the dark, it would be easy to say what he had come to say. He thought that he would say, "Clara, do you remember the day it rained, when we stood in the barn door?" It was a simple thing to say. He said it over in his mind several times. But each time he came to the place where he should have opened his mouth, something stopped him. It was as though there were a hand on his throat.

"You heard about Uncle Will," Clara said.

"No," he said. "What about him?"

She told him. Uncle Will Hartsel, who had kept the harness shop in Lenville, a strange coincidence, Tom Hartsel thought, since he himself now sold harness hardware, had died the winter before. He had been found in the back of his shop, sitting in a chair, and he had been dead two days. Nobody had missed him. He had not had a customer in two days.

"He used to give me licorice," Tom Hartsel said.

"He gave all the children licorice," she said.

They were silent again. Tom Hartsel thought of Uncle Will sitting dead in the back of his shop among the smells of leather and oil. He thought of himself sitting in hotel rooms. He thought that one day he too would be found sitting somewhere, in a hotel room in some town in Iowa, and that a clerk would find him, and that nobody else would know. It was a foolish thought and he put it away from him.

"You were married," Clara said.

"Yes."

"I heard that. Mother had it in a letter. Before she died."

"It didn't come to anything," he said. "She went off."

"I'm sorry."

"No," he said. "It was all right. I don't know. It was all right."

He wanted to tell her about it. He wanted to tell her how it had been, how he and the woman had lived in two rooms on the West Side of Chicago, and how in the evenings, when he was home from the road, they had sat across from each other at the table and had nothing to say, and how sometimes he would look at her and she would look at him and it was like two people looking at each other through a thick pane of glass. He wanted to tell her that it had not been the woman's fault. He wanted to tell her that it had been nobody's fault, that it was the way things were, that people were shut up in themselves like hens in a coop and could not get out. But he did not tell her any of this. He sat on the step and smoked his cigar.

"Moyer was a good man," Clara said. "He was older than me, you know. Fifteen years. He didn't say much. He'd come in from the fields and eat his supper and sit right there where you're sitting and smoke his pipe. Then he'd go to bed. That was all, every night. Eleven years." She rocked in her chair. "I used to wonder what he thought about. Sitting there. I never asked him."

"Why didn't you?"

"I don't know," she said. "I thought he'd tell me if he wanted me to know."

Tom Hartsel took the cigar out of his mouth and looked at the end of it. The coal glowed red in the dark. He thought that now was the time. Now she had opened a door, a little way, and he could go in at it.

"Clara," he said.

"What?"

He did not say anything. He sat with the cigar in his hand. Then he said, "That German. Shultz. Is he a good worker?"

"Yes," she said. "He's all right."

---

Later he could not remember how long they sat there. The cigar went out and he did not light it again. The light in the tenant house by the creek went out. A little wind came up and moved the dry leaves of the maple trees, and some of the leaves came down and fell on the porch and on the steps. One fell on Tom Hartsel's knee and he picked it up and held it.

He began to talk. He did not intend to. It was as though something in him had been wound up tight for a long time and now came loose. He talked about the towns he had been in. He told her about a town in Illinois where there was a man who kept a harness shop and who also kept a crow in a cage, and the crow could say three words, and the man had told Tom Hartsel that the crow was the only friend he had. He told her about a woman he had seen once, standing alone at night on a bridge over a river in Iowa, and how he had wanted to go up to her and speak to her and had not done it, and how in the morning he had looked in the newspaper to see if a woman had been found in the river and had felt foolish. He told her about the hotel rooms, the iron beds and the pitchers of water and the pictures on the walls, always the same pictures, a stag standing in a lake, a ship in a storm. He talked faster and faster. His voice became high and strange to him, like the voice of another man.

"I don't know what it's all for," he said. "That's what I want to know. A man goes along. He goes from one town to another town. He sells buckles. He eats his dinner. What's it for? I sit in those rooms and I think, there must be something. There must be something a man could say to another person, and then it would be all right. Do you know what I mean? Do you, Clara?"

He stopped. He was breathing hard, as though he had been running. He was ashamed. He thought that she would laugh at him, that she would say something to make it all into nothing, as people did.

She did not laugh. She got up out of the rocking chair and came and stood on the step above him. He could not see her face in the dark. He felt her standing there.

Then she put out her hand and took hold of his wrist.

He did not move. Her hand was hard and dry, the hand of a woman who had milked cows and wrung the necks of chickens and scrubbed floors for twenty years, and it was not like the hand of the thin girl in the barn door. And yet it was the same. He knew that it was the same. She held his wrist and he sat still, and the leaves came down from the maple trees and the wind moved in the corn shocks out in the fields. Neither of them said anything at all.

After a while she let go.

"There's a bed made up in the front room," she said. "You'll be tired."

"Yes," he said.

She went into the house and he heard her moving about inside. Then a door closed and the house was still.

---

Tom Hartsel did not go in at once. He sat on the step. He did not think about anything. That is not quite true. He thought, but his thoughts were not like words. They were like the shapes of the corn shocks in the field, grey and indistinct, standing in rows and going away into the dark.

He had come to Lenville to ask her if she remembered. Now he had not asked her and he would never ask her. In the morning he would eat his breakfast and she would give him eggs from her forty hens, and they would talk about the wheat and the corn and the German Shultz, and he would walk back into town and take the train for Fort Wayne, where he had a customer. Perhaps he would write her a letter at Christmas. Perhaps she would write back. It would not matter. He knew now that there was nothing to ask. She had not forgotten. Nobody ever forgets. They only go on, and the thing stays in them, under everything, like a stone in a creek.

He got up stiffly, for his legs had gone to sleep, and he stood on the porch and looked out across the fields. He was a little drunk with something, though he had had nothing to drink. He thought that if he were a different kind of man, a poet or a preacher, he could go into the town in the morning and stand on the corner by Hagerty's hardware store and tell the people what he knew. He would tell them that they were not alone, that nobody was alone, that there was in every one of them a moment like the moment in the barn door, and that it was the only thing that mattered. But he was not that kind of man. He was a man who sold buckles. And besides, he did not quite know what it was that he knew. When he tried to put it into words, it went away from him, like a bird that flies up out of the grass when you go to look at it.

He went into the house and found the front room and undressed in the dark. The bed was cold and the sheets smelled of soap and of the cedar chest they had been kept in. He lay on his back. Somewhere in the house the clock in the kitchen ticked. Somewhere, in another room, his cousin Clara lay awake, or perhaps she slept. He did not know. He would never know. He lay with his hands at his sides and after a time he put one hand over the wrist of the other and held it there, lightly, and so he fell asleep.

When Ezra Hanby came home from the stave factory on the evening of the day his son had done the thing, he did not at first know anything had happened. He came along the road from the tracks the way he always came, walking slowly with his dinner pail swinging from one hand, and he was thinking of nothing at all. He was a tall man with stooped shoulders, and his hands were very large. All day the hands had been feeding hoop-poles into a machine, and now that the work was done they hung at his sides as though they did not belong to him and he did not know what to do with them. Sometimes when he was walking alone in the evening he would lift one of the hands and look at it. It was a queer thing to do and he knew it was queer. If anyone had seen him he would have been ashamed.

The house in which Ezra lived with his wife and the boy stood at the end of a street that ran out from the town toward the open country. Beyond the house there was a field of corn, and beyond the corn there was a strip of woods. In the summer evenings the boy, whose name was Teddy, went often to the edge of the corn and stood there looking. What he looked at no one knew. Perhaps he did not know himself. He was seven years old that summer, a thin boy with a large head and eyes that were too big for his face.

On that evening Ezra's wife met him at the kitchen door. She was a small woman who had once been pretty and was now tired. There was something in her face that Ezra did not understand, a kind of hardness, and at the same time a kind of fear. "You'll have to speak to him," she said. "I can't do anything with him. You'll have to speak to him tonight."

Ezra set the dinner pail on the shelf by the door. He did not ask at once what had happened. It was his way to wait. All his life he had waited for things to come to him, and they had come, and most of them had not been good things. He stood in the kitchen and the smell of the frying potatoes was in his nose, and he thought, "Now I am to be a father. Now I must be a father." The thought frightened him.

What had happened was a small thing. Anyone who has lived in a town like that one, or in any town, will know how small a thing it was. There was a blue sugar bowl on the top shelf of the cupboard, and in the sugar bowl Sarah Hanby kept the money she saved out of the household money, a few coins at a time, toward something she wanted. What she wanted was a new dress. She had not had a new dress in four years, and when she went to church on Sunday she sat near the back. On that afternoon the boy had climbed up on a chair and had taken a quarter from the bowl, and he had gone down into the town to Sinnings' store and had bought a tin whistle and a bag of licorice whips. When he came home his mouth was black with the licorice, and when his mother asked him where he had got the money he said he had found it in the road.

He said it twice. He said it, Sarah said, looking straight at her.

"I knew it right off," she told Ezra. "I went and looked in the bowl. He didn't even put the lid back on straight." Her voice was trembling. "It ain't the money," she said. "It's the lie. Him standing there telling it to my face."

Ezra nodded his head. He went to the wash basin on the bench by the door and began to wash his hands. He washed them for a long time, rubbing the soap into the cracks of the knuckles, and his wife stood watching him. He knew she wanted him to go at once and find the boy. She wanted him to be quick and angry and certain. That was what a man should be at such a time. He knew that. But the hands went on with the washing, slowly, and it seemed to him that if he could only go on washing them for a long time, until the light had gone out of the sky, something would happen and he would not have to do anything at all.

---

It is a strange thing about a man like Ezra Hanby. He had been a boy himself on a farm near the town of Clyde, and his own father had been a hard man. The father had been a German who came to Ohio when he was young and cleared forty acres of land with his own hands, and the work had made him hard. There was a leather strap that hung on a nail by the barn door, and when the boy Ezra did something wrong, or when the father thought he had done something wrong, which was not always the same, the father took down the strap. He did not say anything. That was the thing Ezra remembered best. The father never said anything at all. He took down the strap, and the boy went into the barn, and afterward the father hung the strap back on its nail and went to the house to eat his supper.

Ezra had not hated his father. That is what was strange. He had lain in the hay in the barn loft afterward, with the welts burning on his legs, and he had not hated him. He had wanted something from him. He did not know what it was. Lying in the hay and looking up at the light coming through the cracks between the boards, he had thought that some day his father would come up the ladder and sit down beside him and say something. What he would say Ezra could not imagine. He only knew that it would be something that would make everything plain. It would explain the strap and the silence, and the forty acres of stumps, and the mother who coughed all winter and died in the spring when Ezra was eleven. It would explain why the world was the way it was.

The father never came up the ladder. He died when Ezra was twenty, and he died without saying the thing.

After that Ezra went to work in the town, first in a livery stable and then in the stave factory, and he married Sarah, who was the daughter of a man who kept bees. When the boy was born Ezra stood in the doorway of the room where Sarah lay with the child, and he looked at the small red face and he made a vow. He did not say it aloud. He was not a man who could say things aloud. But in his heart he said, "I will not be like him. I will say the thing. When the time comes I will know how to say it."

And now the time had come, or a time had come, and he stood in his kitchen washing his hands.

---

"Where is he?" Ezra asked at last.

"In the woodshed. He's been there since three o'clock. I told him to stay there till you come."

Ezra dried his hands on the towel that hung on a roller beside the door. Then he went out of the kitchen and across the back yard. It was nearly dark. The light lay low and yellow across the cornfield, and the corn was so still that it seemed to be waiting. Somewhere down the road a dog was barking, and further away, toward the town, a man was calling to his horses. Ezra walked slowly. He had the feeling that everything in the world was watching him, the corn and the woods and the yellow light, and that they were all waiting to see what he would do.

The woodshed was a small building made of rough boards that had never been painted. Ezra opened the door and stood looking in. At first he could see nothing, and then he made out the shape of the boy sitting on the chopping block in the corner. The boy had his knees drawn up and his arms wrapped around them, and he did not move. The tin whistle lay on the ground at his feet.

"Come here," Ezra said.

The boy got up off the chopping block and came across the shed. He came slowly, and when he was near the door he stopped and stood with his head down. There was still a black smear of licorice at the corner of his mouth. Ezra looked at it. It seemed to him the saddest thing he had ever seen, that smear of black on the boy's face. He did not know why it should be sad. It made his throat tighten.

"Your mother says you took money out of the sugar bowl," Ezra said.

The boy said nothing.

"Did you take it?"

The boy nodded his head. He did not look up.

"And then you told her you found it in the road."

Again the boy nodded.

Ezra stood in the doorway. Behind him the light was going out of the sky, and the shed was full of shadows. He could smell the cut wood, a clean sharp smell, and under it the smell of earth. He thought that now he must say something. Now he must say the thing. He opened his mouth.

"You know better than that," he said.

The words came out of him and he heard them and they were not the words he wanted. They were only words, the kind of words any man would say. He tried again.

"Your mother," he said. "That money. She's been saving it." And then he stopped, because he did not know how to tell the boy about the dress, and about the four years, and about Sarah sitting at the back of the church on Sunday with her hands folded in her lap so that no one would see how the cuffs of her old dress were frayed. He did not know how to say any of it. It was all in him, a great deal of it, and it would not come out. It was like a thing that has been shut up in a dark room for a long time and has forgotten how to come out into the light.

There was a nail on the wall of the woodshed just inside the door. On the nail hung a piece of harness strap that Ezra had brought home from the livery stable years before, when he worked there. He had brought it home to mend a gate hinge, and he had never used it, and it had hung there ever since. Now he saw it. He had not thought of it before, but now he saw it, and the boy saw him looking at it.

---

What happened next was afterward a thing that Ezra Hanby could never quite explain, even to himself. For a long time he stood looking at the strap, and the boy stood looking at him, and neither of them moved. Ezra's hand came up. It was the right hand, the big one with the crack across the knuckle where a hoop-pole had once caught it in the machine. The hand came up slowly, as though it were going to take down the strap, and Ezra watched it come up. It seemed to him that the hand was not his own. It was his father's hand. It was the hand of the old German in the barn at Clyde, and it was going to do what that hand had always done, and there was nothing Ezra could do to stop it.

Then the boy began to cry.

He did not cry loudly. He stood there with his thin arms hanging at his sides and the tears ran down his face and made clean marks through the dust on his cheeks, and through the black smear at the corner of his mouth. He made no sound at all. And Ezra, standing in the doorway with his hand raised, saw that the boy was not crying because he was afraid of the strap. Or not only because of that. He was crying because of something else, something he could not have named, any more than his father could have named it. He was crying the way a man cries sometimes when he is alone and has come to the end of something.

Ezra's hand came down. It came down slowly, and it did not touch the strap. It came down and rested on the boy's head.

The hair was damp with sweat. It was very soft. Ezra had not touched the boy's hair in a long time, not since he was a baby, and he had forgotten how soft it was. He stood with his hand on the boy's head and he could feel the warmth of the head coming up into his palm, and something happened inside him. It was as though a door had been opened somewhere in a house where all the doors had been shut.

"Teddy," he said. And then he said nothing more for a while.

---

They stood like that in the woodshed until it was quite dark. Once Sarah came to the kitchen door and called out, "Ezra? Ezra, what are you doing out there?" and Ezra did not answer, and after a time she went back into the house. The dog down the road had stopped barking. A wind came up out of the west and moved through the corn, and the corn made a sound like people whispering.

At last Ezra sat down on the chopping block, and he drew the boy to him and stood him between his knees. He wanted to talk. All his life he had wanted to talk, and now he tried.

"When I was a boy," he said, and stopped. "When I was a boy there was a barn," he said. He could not see the boy's face now. It was too dark. He could only feel the thin shoulders under his hands. "There was a barn," he said again, "and a ladder up into the loft. And I used to lie up there in the hay and look at the cracks in the roof. The light come through them. In the afternoon the light come through them in long lines, and there was dust in the lines, and it went round and round."

He did not know why he was telling the boy this. It had nothing to do with the sugar bowl or the quarter or the lie. And yet it seemed to him that it had everything to do with them, if only he could make it plain.

"I used to lie there," he said, "and I'd think somebody was coming up the ladder. I'd lie there and listen for him."

The boy had stopped crying. He was standing very still between his father's knees, and Ezra could hear him breathing.

"Who was coming?" the boy asked.

Ezra did not answer at once. The question surprised him. He had not thought the boy would ask anything. He sat on the chopping block in the dark, and the wind went through the corn, and he thought about the question.

"Nobody," he said at last. "Nobody come."

It was not what he had meant to say. He had meant to say something about lies, how a lie is a thing that stands between people, how it makes a wall, how a man can spend his whole life on one side of a wall and never get over it. He had meant to say something about the mother and the dress. He had meant, perhaps, to say something about love, though he had never in his life said that word aloud and did not know if he could. None of it came. Only the barn, and the ladder, and the light coming through the cracks, and nobody coming.

But the boy put his hand up in the dark and touched his father's face. It was a small cold hand, and it was sticky with licorice, and it touched Ezra's cheek and stayed there.

---

When they went back into the house Sarah was sitting at the kitchen table with the lamp lit. The potatoes had gone cold in the skillet. She looked up when they came in, and she looked at the boy's face, and then she looked at Ezra. There was a question in her eyes. Ezra knew what the question was. She wanted to know if he had used the strap. She wanted to know if it was over and done with, so that they could eat their supper and go to bed and it would be finished.

Ezra did not answer the question. He went to the cupboard and took down the blue sugar bowl and set it on the table. Then he took a quarter out of his own pocket, out of the little leather purse where he kept the money for his tobacco, and he put the quarter into the boy's hand.

"Put it back," he said.

The boy climbed up on a chair beside the table. He held the quarter for a moment and looked at it in the lamplight. Then he dropped it into the sugar bowl, and it made a small sound against the other coins, and he put the lid back on, carefully, so that it sat straight.

"Now tell your mother," Ezra said.

The boy looked at his mother. His lips moved, but at first no sound came out of them. Ezra stood behind him and watched, and he thought, "He is like me. It is all shut up in him the way it is in me." He waited. The lamp flickered. A moth had got in through the screen door and was beating against the chimney.

"I didn't find it in the road," the boy said.

That was all. He did not say he was sorry. He did not say anything more. But Sarah Hanby put her two hands over her face and sat that way for a long time, and when she took them away her eyes were wet. She got up and went to the stove and began to warm the potatoes again, and her back was turned to them, and neither Ezra nor the boy could see her face.

---

That night after the boy had gone to bed Ezra went out and sat on the back step. It was a warm night and there were many stars. He sat with his big hands hanging between his knees and he looked out at the dark shape of the cornfield. He was thinking that he had not done the thing he had set out to do. He had not said what he meant to say. He had not punished the boy, not properly, not the way a father should. Tomorrow, perhaps, Sarah would say to him that he was too soft, that the boy would grow up wild, and she might be right. He did not know. He did not know anything for certain.

And yet he was not unhappy. That was the strange part of it. Sitting on the back step with the stars over him and the corn whispering, he felt a kind of quiet he had not felt since he was a very small child, before the barn and the strap and the forty acres of stumps. He lifted his right hand and looked at it in the starlight. It was the same hand. The crack across the knuckle was still there. But it seemed to him that something had gone out of it, or come into it. He could not tell which.

Inside the house, in the small room under the eaves, the boy lay awake. He was not thinking about the quarter or the licorice or the lie. He was thinking about a barn he had never seen, and a ladder, and long lines of light coming through the cracks in a roof, with the dust going round and round in them. He lay with his eyes open in the dark and he listened. He did not know what he was listening for. After a while he heard his father come in from the back step and close the kitchen door, and then he heard his father's slow heavy steps on the stairs, and they stopped outside his door, and stayed there for a long time, and then went on.

The boy fell asleep. Years afterward, when he was a grown man living in a city far from that town, he would sometimes wake in the night and lie listening in the same way, and he would not know why. It was something about a door, and footsteps that stopped outside it. It was something about a man who had wanted to say a thing and could not say it, and had said it anyway, with his hand.

One Sunday afternoon three boys sat on a log on the side of the hill that looked down into Coal Creek. From where they sat they could see the workers of the night shift idling in the sun on Main Street. From the coke ovens a thin line of smoke rose into the sky. A freight train heavily loaded crept round the hill at the end of the valley. It was spring and over even that hive of black industry hung a faint promise of beauty. In the town of Pickaway there lived a man named Will Hanby who kept the feed store at the corner of Mill Street and the Pike. He was a tall stooped man of thirty-four with long arms and a habit of rubbing the back of his neck with his hand when he was puzzled. In the town he was thought a steady fellow. Farmers who came in on Saturday afternoons to buy bran and oil meal stood about in his store and talked of the price of corn and of the weather, and Will stood behind the counter and listened and nodded his head. He did not talk much. When he did talk it was slowly, as though each word were a sack of feed that had to be lifted and carried and set down in its place.

Will had been married for six years to a woman named Ella Bunce, the daughter of a carpenter who had died of a fall from the roof of the Methodist church. She was a small dark woman with quick hands, and before her marriage she had trimmed hats in Mrs. Kerr's millinery shop on Main Street. In the town people said she had done well for herself. They said it on the porches in the evening and in the stores. "Will Hanby is a good provider," they said. "That Ella Bunce didn't have a thing and now look at her." The Hanbys lived in a white frame house on Cherry Street with a grape arbour at the back and a pump in the yard. There were no children.

On an evening in late September Will came home from the store and found the house dark. He went in at the kitchen door and lighted the lamp on the table. The stove was cold. A loaf of bread lay on the board with the knife beside it and there was a plate with a piece of cold meat on it covered with a cloth. Will stood in the middle of the kitchen with his hat in his hand. He did not sit down. For a long time he stood so, looking at the plate on the table, and then he put on his hat again and went out of the house and stood by the pump in the yard. The night was warm. Crickets sang in the grass by the fence and from somewhere over toward the railroad a dog barked. Will rubbed the back of his neck.

It was the third time in two weeks that this thing had happened. On the first night Ella had come in at ten o'clock and said she had been at her cousin's on Water Street, and Will had believed her. On the second night she said nothing at all. She came in and went up the stairs and he heard her moving about in the room overhead and then the creak of the bed. He had sat in the kitchen until after midnight, and when at last he went up she lay with her face to the wall, and he could not tell whether she slept.

Now as he stood by the pump in the darkness a strange thing happened to Will Hanby. His mind, that had always moved slowly, began to move fast. Pictures came into it. He saw his wife walking along a road in the dark with a man beside her. He could not see the man's face. He saw them stop under a tree and he saw the man put his hand on her arm. The pictures came one after another like the slides at the magic lantern show that had come once to the town hall when he was a boy, and he could not stop them. He gripped the handle of the pump with his hand. "I'll find out," he said aloud. "By God, I'll find out." The sound of his own voice in the yard startled him and he looked about to see if anyone had heard.

It is a thing that happens to men in small towns and perhaps everywhere. A man goes along for years, doing his work, eating and sleeping, going to the lodge on Thursday nights, and he thinks his life is a plain road that runs straight ahead of him like the Pike runs out of town toward the county seat. Then something happens. A door that he had not known was there swings open and he looks through and sees a room he had never been in. He is frightened. He would like to shut the door again and go on as before, but he cannot do it.

Will went back into the kitchen and sat down by the table. He did not eat. He sat with his long arms on the oilcloth and waited, and at a little after ten o'clock he heard Ella's step on the walk at the side of the house. She came in at the kitchen door and stopped when she saw him. She had on her grey dress, the one she wore to church, and her hat was in her hand. There was dust on the hem of her skirt. Her face was flushed and her eyes were bright, as though she had been walking fast, and when she saw him there by the lamp the brightness went out of them.

"You didn't eat," she said. She went to the table and lifted the cloth from the plate and put it down again. "I left it for you. I thought you would eat."

Will looked at the dust on her skirt. "Where have you been?" he asked. His voice came out hoarse and he cleared his throat. "Where do you go, Ella? I want to know where you go."

She went to the window and stood with her back to him, looking out into the yard. Her hands were busy with the hat. She turned it round and round, pulling at the ribbon. "I went walking," she said. "I went out the Pike and down along the tracks. I like to walk in the evening."

"Who with?" said Will.

She turned around quickly. "With nobody," she said. "With nobody at all. I went by myself."

Will got up from the table. He was a head taller than his wife and when he stood up in the low kitchen his head came near to the hanging lamp so that the light fell on his shoulders and left his face in shadow. He took a step toward her and stopped. He did not know what he meant to do. "A woman don't go walking out the Pike by herself at night," he said. "Not three times. Not a decent woman. Folks will talk. Maybe they're talking already. Maybe I'm the only man in town that don't know."

Ella laughed. It was not a pleasant laugh and it hurt him. "Don't know what?" she said. "What is there to know? You think I've got a man. I can see it in your face. You've been sitting there all evening thinking I've got a man out there somewhere in the dark." She threw the hat down upon a chair. "Well I haven't. I wish I had something as easy to tell you as that."

Will did not understand her. He stood rubbing the back of his neck and looking at her, and something in her face frightened him more than the thought of the man had frightened him. It was as though he looked at a stranger. He had seen her face every day for six years, bending over the stove, sitting across from him at the table, lying on the pillow beside him in the grey light of the morning, and now it was the face of a woman he did not know.

"Sit down, Ella," he said. "Sit down and tell me."

She did not sit down. She went to the stove and put her hand on it as though to see if it were warm, although she knew it was cold. "I don't know how to tell you," she said. "That's the trouble. If I could tell it I wouldn't have to go out there. I'd stay here and tell it to you and that would be the end of it." She stopped and bit her lip. "I go out and stand by the tracks," she said slowly. "There's a place past the grain elevator where the bank is high and you can see a long way both ways. I stand there and wait for the night freight to go through. It comes at nine-forty. Sometimes it's late. I stand there and it comes along out of the dark with the headlight shining on the rails, and it goes by so close I could reach out and touch it, and then it's gone, and I can hear it a long time going away toward Columbus. And then I come home."

Will stared at her. "That's all?" he said.

"That's all."

"You walk a mile and a half out the Pike to see a freight train go by?"

"Yes."

He sat down again at the table. His mind, that had been moving so fast, stopped altogether, and he sat with his hands spread out on the oilcloth and could think of nothing. Then the anger came back, only now it was a different kind of anger, a confused kind. He had been ready for a man. He had been ready to go out and find the man and fight him in the road. He could not fight a freight train. "I don't believe it," he said. "That's a crazy thing. Nobody does a thing like that."

"I do it," she said.

"But what for?" He raised his voice and struck the table with his fist so that the knife on the bread board jumped. "What for, Ella? You've got a good home. I give you everything. You've got the house and the arbour and the new carpet in the front room. I bought you the organ. You never play on it but I bought it for you. What do you want to go out there in the dark for, to look at a train?"

Ella came and stood across the table from him. Her small hands held to the back of the chair and he saw that the knuckles were white. "You see," she said. "I told you I couldn't say it. You think it's crazy. Maybe it is crazy. I don't know." She was silent a moment and then the words came out of her in a rush, as water comes out of a ditch when a farmer pulls the board away. "When I stand there and it goes by I think of all the places it goes. I think of the towns it goes through in the night with people asleep in them, and the cities, and the big lakes, and the men riding on it, the brakemen with their lanterns, and how they don't know me and never will know me and it don't matter to them whether I live or die. And it makes me feel—I can't tell you how it makes me feel. It makes me feel as though I were alive. In the daytime here I'm not alive. I get up and get breakfast and I sweep and I go down to Kerr's and buy thread and I come back and get supper and you come home and we eat and you read the Enquirer and go to sleep in the chair. And I sit and look at you. And I think, this is the way it's going to be. This is the way it's going to be until I'm old and dead. Nothing is going to happen, ever."

She stopped. Her breath came quick. Will sat looking at the plate of cold meat on the table and did not raise his eyes.

"I'm not a bad man to you," he said at last.

"No," she said. "No, you're not a bad man. That's what makes it so hard. If you were a bad man I could hate you. I could go away. Mrs. Truesdale went away from her man and went to Dayton, and everybody talked, but she went. I can't hate you. You're good. You're the best man in Pickaway, everybody says so. And I sit and look at you in the evening with the paper on your knees and your mouth open and I want to scream."

Will got up so suddenly that the chair fell over behind him. He did not pick it up. He walked to the door and stood looking out through the screen into the dark yard where the pump stood up like a man with one arm raised. A hot feeling had come into his throat and he could not speak. He thought of the days at the store, of lifting the sacks and carrying them out to the farmers' wagons, of keeping the books at night by the lamp in the back room so that there would be money for the house and the carpet and the organ. He had thought that was what a man did. He had thought she knew. He wanted to turn and say this to her, to tell her of the long days and of how he had thought of her through them, coming home at night to the lighted kitchen. But the words would not come. They lay in him like stones.

"Your mother was the same way," he said harshly, without turning around. "Folks used to say it. Old Bunce couldn't keep her home. Always wanting something. Always running somewhere."

He heard her draw in her breath behind him and he was sorry at once that he had said it. He had not meant to say it. It had come out of him of itself, out of the hurt place, and now it was said and he could not take it back.

"Yes," Ella said in a low voice. "Yes, she was. And she died in that house on Water Street with her hands all cracked from washing other people's clothes, and nobody ever came to see her but the preacher. She wanted something too and she never got it. That's what I'm afraid of, Will. That's what I go out there to the tracks for. I'm afraid of being like her."

Will turned around. She was standing by the table with her face in her hands. She was not crying. She stood quite still with her small hands over her face, and as he looked at her a great tenderness came over him, so that his knees went weak and he wanted to go to her and take her into his arms and hold her as one holds a child that has been frightened in the night. He took a step toward her. He thought, "If I hold her it will be all right. If I hold her she will know."

But when he came near and put his hand upon her shoulder she drew away. It was not much. It was only a little movement, a stiffening of her body under his hand, but he felt it and his hand dropped to his side. They stood so, close together by the table in the lamplight, and neither of them spoke. Outside the crickets went on singing. Far away, so faint it was hardly a sound at all, a train whistled for the crossing at Harrisburg.

Ella took her hands from her face and looked at him. Her eyes were dry. "You heard it?" she said.

"Yes," said Will.

"That's the ten-thirty passenger. It don't stop here. It goes right through." She laughed a little, and this time the laugh was not hard, only tired. "I know all of them. I know when every one of them goes through. It's a foolish thing for a woman to know."

Will picked up the chair that had fallen and set it in its place. He did it slowly and carefully, as though it mattered a great deal that the chair should stand straight. Then he stood with his hands on the back of it. "Maybe," he said, and stopped. He tried again. "Maybe next summer, after the wheat's in and business is slack, we could take the cars up to Sandusky. To the lake. A man was in the store said you can go out on a boat there. Out on the water."

Ella looked at him for a long time. A gentler look came into her face and for a moment he thought she would come around the table to him. Then she shook her head. "It wouldn't be the same," she said. "You don't understand, Will. You'd buy the tickets and you'd see that we got on the right car and you'd carry the valise and we'd go up there and look at the lake and come back. And it would be all right. It would be nice. But it wouldn't be the same thing at all."

"What would it be then?" he cried. "What do you want? Tell me what you want and I'll get it for you."

"I don't know," she said. "If I knew I'd tell you."

She picked up her hat from the chair and went to the stairway. At the foot of the stairs she stopped and stood with one hand on the rail, and without looking back at him she spoke again. "I'll not go out there any more if you don't want me to," she said. "I'll stay home. You won't need to wait up for me." Then she went up the stairs and he heard her step overhead and the door of the bedroom close.

Will stood a long time by the table. Then he blew out the lamp and went out at the kitchen door and sat on the step in the dark. The night had grown cool and a little wind came across the yard and stirred the dry leaves of the grape arbour so that they made a sound like whispering. He sat with his long arms on his knees. He thought of what she had said, going over it slowly in his mind as he would go over a column of figures in the account book, trying to make it come out right. It would not come out. There was something in it that he could not get hold of. "A freight train," he thought. "A freight train, by God." He wanted to laugh and could not.

He began to think of himself as a boy, when he had lived on his father's farm out the Pike beyond the place where Ella said she went to stand. He remembered that he too had gone at night sometimes to the top of the hill back of the barn and lain in the grass looking at the stars and thinking of the places he would see when he was a man. He had forgotten that. It was strange that he should have forgotten it. He had meant to go to Chicago. A man named Tom Pratt who worked for his father one summer had been to Chicago and had told him of it, of the streets that ran on and on and the lights at night, and he had lain in the grass and thought of going there. Then his father had died and there had been the farm to sell and the feed store had come up for sale cheap, and he had bought it, and the years had gone by.

"She thinks I'm a dead man," he said aloud in the darkness. "She thinks I never wanted nothing." The words hurt him and he sat with them a long time.

Overhead the light in the bedroom window went out. Will did not get up. He sat on the step until the cold came through his coat and the stars stood out sharp and many above the roofs of Cherry Street. Once he half rose, thinking he would go up to her and tell her about the hill back of his father's barn and about Tom Pratt and Chicago. He thought that if he could tell her that she would understand something. He did not know what. But when he stood up the thought went away from him, and the words with it, and he only stood in the dark yard by the pump with his hand on the back of his neck. After a while he went in and locked the door and climbed the stairs, walking softly so as not to wake her, although he knew she was not asleep.
