Here is an excerpt of Sherwood Anderson's writing, to show you their style:

One Sunday afternoon three boys sat on a log on the side of the hill that looked down into Coal Creek. From where they sat they could see the workers of the night shift idling in the sun on Main Street. From the coke ovens a thin line of smoke rose into the sky. A freight train heavily loaded crept round the hill at the end of the valley. It was spring and over even that hive of black industry hung a faint promise of beauty. The boys talked of the life of people in their town and as they talked thought each of himself. Although he had not been out of the valley and had grown strong and big there, Beaut McGregor knew something of the outside world. It isn't a time when men are shut off from their fellows. Newspapers and magazines have done their work too well. They reached even into the miner's cabin and the merchants along Main Street of Coal Creek stood before their stores in the afternoon and talked of the doings of the world. Beaut McGregor knew that life in his town was exceptional, that not everywhere did men toil all day black and grimy underground, that not all women were pale bloodless and bent. As he went about delivering bread he whistled a song. “Take me back to Broadway,” he sang after the soubrette in a show that had once come to Coal Creek. Now as he sat on the hillside he talked earnestly while he gesticulated with his hands. “I hate this town,” he said. “The men here think they are confoundedly funny. They don't care for anything but making foolish jokes and getting drunk. I want to go away.” His voice rose and hatred flamed up in him. “You wait,” he boasted. “I'll make men stop being fools. I'll make children of them. I'll——” Pausing he looked at his two companions. Beaut poked the ground with a stick. The boy sitting beside him laughed. He was a short well—dressed black—haired boy with rings on his fingers who worked in the town poolroom, racking the pool balls. “I'd like to go where there are women with blood in them,” he said. Three women came up the hill toward them, a tall pale brown-haired woman of twenty-seven and two fairer young girls. The black-haired boy straightened his tie and began thinking of a conversation he would start when the women reached him. Beaut and the other boy, a fat fellow, the son of a grocer, looked down the hill to the town over the heads of the newcomers and continued in their minds the thoughts that had made the conversation.

“Hello girls, come and sit here,” shouted the black-haired boy, laughing and looking boldly into the eyes of the tall pale woman. They stopped and the tall woman began stepping over the fallen logs, coming to them. The two young girls followed, laughing. They sat down on the log beside the boys, the tall pale woman at the end beside red-haired McGregor. An embarrassed silence fell over the party. Both Beaut and the fat boy were disconcerted by this turn to their afternoon's outing and wondered how it would turn out. The pale woman began to talk in a low tone. “I want to get away from here,” she said, “I wish I could hear birds sing and see green things grow.” Beaut McGregor had an idea. “You come with me,” he said. He got up and climbed over the logs and the pale woman followed. The fat boy shouted at them, relieving his own embarrassment by trying to embarrass them. “Where're you going—you two?” he shouted. Beaut said nothing. He stepped over the logs to the road and began climbing the hill. The tall woman walked beside him and held her skirts out of the deep dust of the road. Even on this her Sunday gown there was a faint black mark along the seams—the mark of Coal Creek. As McGregor walked his embarrassment left him. He thought it fine that he should be thus alone with a woman. When she had tired from the climb he sat with her on a log beside the road and talked of the black-haired boy. “He has your ring on his finger,” he said, looking at her and laughing. She held her hand pressed tightly against her side and closed her eyes. “The climbing hurts me,” she said. Tenderness took hold of Beaut. When they went on again he walked behind her, his hand upon her back pushing her up the hill. The desire to tease her about the black-haired boy had passed and he wished he had said nothing about the ring. He remembered the story the black-haired boy had told him of his conquest of the woman. “More than likely a mess of lies,” he thought. Over the crest of the hill they stopped and rested, leaning against a worn rail fence by the woods. Below them in a wagon a party of men went down the hill. The men sat upon boards laid across the box of a wagon and sang a song. One of them stood in the seat beside the driver and waved a bottle. He seemed to be making a speech. The others shouted and clapped their hands. The sounds came faint and sharp up the hill. In the woods beside the fence rank grass grew. Hawks floated in the sky over the valley below. A squirrel running along the fence stopped and chattered at them. McGregor thought he had never had so delightful a companion. He got a feeling of complete, good fellowship and friendliness with this woman. Without knowing how the thing had been done he felt a certain pride in it. “Don't mind what I said about the ring,” he urged, “I was only trying to tease you.” The woman beside McGregor was the daughter of an undertaker who lived upstairs over his shop near the bakery. He had seen her in the evening standing in the stairway by the shop door. After the story told him by the black-haired boy he had been embarrassed about her. When he passed her standing in the stairway he went hurriedly along and looked into the gutter. They went down the hill and sat on the log upon the hillside. A clump of elders had grown about the log since his visits there with Cracked McGregor so that the place was closed and shaded like a room. The woman took off her hat and laid it beside her on the log. A faint colour mounted to her pale cheeks and a flash of anger gleamed in her eyes. “He probably lied to you about me,” she said, “I didn't give him that ring to wear. I don't know why I gave it to him. He wanted it. He asked me for it time and again. He said he wanted to show it to his mother. And now he has shown it to you and I suppose told lies about me.” Beaut was annoyed and wished he had not mentioned the ring. He felt that an unnecessary fuss was being made about it. He did not believe that the black-haired boy had lied but he did not think it mattered. He began talking of his father, boasting of him. His hatred of the town blazed up. “They thought they knew him down there,” he said, “they laughed at him and called him 'Cracked.' They thought his running into the mine just a crazy notion like a horse that runs into a burning stable. He was the best man in town. He was braver than any of them. He went in there and died when he had almost enough money saved to buy a farm over here.” He pointed down the valley. Beaut began to tell her of the visits to the hillside with his father and described the effect of the scene on himself when he was a child. “I thought it was paradise,” he said. She put her hand on his arm and seemed to be soothing him like a careful groom quieting an excitable horse. “Don't mind them,” she said, “you will go away after a time and make a place for yourself out in the world.” He wondered how she knew. A profound respect for her came over him. “She is keen to guess that,” he thought. He began to talk of himself, boasting and throwing out his chest. “I'd like to have the chance to show what I can do,” he declared. A thought that had been in his mind on the winter day when Uncle Charlie Wheeler put the name of Beaut upon him came back and he walked up and down before the woman making grotesque motions with his hands as Cracked McGregor had walked up and down before him.

“I'll tell you what,” he began and his voice was harsh. He had forgotten the presence of the woman and half forgotten what had been in his mind. He sputtered and glared over his shoulder up the hillside as he struggled for words. “Oh to Hell with men!” he burst forth. “They are cattle, stupid cattle.” A fire blazed up in his eyes and a confident ring came into his voice. “I'd like to get them together, all of them,” he said, “I'd like to make them——” Words failed him and again he sat down on the log beside the woman. “Well I'd like to lead them to an old mine shaft and push them in,” he concluded resentfully.

On the eminence Beaut and the tall woman sat and looked down into the valley. “I wonder why we don't go there, mother and I,” he said. “When I see it I'm filled with the notion. I think I want to be a farmer and work in the fields. Instead of that mother and I sit and plan of the city. I'm going to be a lawyer. That's all we talk about. Then I come up here and it seems as though this is the place for me.” The tall woman laughed. “I can see you coming home at night from the fields,” she said. “It might be to that white house there with the windmill, You would be a big man and would have dust in your red hair and perhaps a red beard growing on your chin. And a woman with a baby in her arms would come out of the kitchen door to stand leaning on the fence waiting for you. When you came up she would put her arm around your neck and kiss you on the lips. The beard would tickle her cheek. You should have a beard when you grow older. Your mouth is so big.” A strange new feeling shot through Beaut. He wondered why she had said that and wanted to take hold of her hand and kiss her then and there. He got up and looked at the sun going down behind the hill far away at the other end of the valley. “We'd better be getting along back,” he said. The woman remained seated on the log. “Sit down,” she said, “I'll tell you something—something it's good for you to hear. You're so big and red you tempt a girl to bother you. First though you tell me why you go along the street looking into the gutter when I stand in the stairway in the evening.” Beaut sat down again upon the log, and thought of what the black-haired boy had told him of her. “Then it was true—what he said about you?” he asked.

“No! No!” she cried, jumping up in her turn and beginning to pin on her hat. “Let's be going.” Beaut sat stolidly on the log. “What's the use bothering each other,” he said. “Let's sit here until the sun goes down. We can get home before dark.” They sat down and she began talking, boasting of herself as he had boasted of his father.

“I'm too old for that boy,” she said; “I'm older than you by a good many years. I know what boys talk about and what they say about women. I do pretty well. I don't have any one to talk to except father and he sits all evening reading a paper and going to sleep in his chair. If I let boys come and sit with me in the evening or stand talking with me in the stairway it is because I'm lonesome. There isn't a man in town I'd marry—not one.” The speech sounded discordant and harsh to Beaut. He wished his father were there rubbing his hands together and muttering rather than this pale woman who stirred him up and then talked harshly like the women at the back doors in Coal Creek. He thought again as he had thought before that he preferred the black-faced miners drunk and silent to their pale talking wives. On an impulse he told her that, saying it crudely so that it hurt. Their companionship was spoiled. They got up and began to climb the hill, going toward home. Again she put her hand to her side and again he wished to put his hand at her back and push her up the hill. Instead he walked beside her in silence, again hating the town. Halfway down the hill the tall woman stopped by the road-side. Darkness was coming on and the glow of the coke ovens lighted the sky. “One living up here and never going down there might think it rather grand and big,” he said. Again the hatred came. “They might think the men who live down there knew something instead of being just a lot of cattle.” A smile came into the face of the tall woman and a gentler look stole into her eyes. “We get at one another,” she said, “we can't let one another alone. I wish we hadn't quarrelled. We might be friends if we tried. You have got something in you. You attract women. I've heard others say that. Your father was that way. Most of the women here would rather have been the wife of Cracked McGregor ugly as he was than to have stayed with their own husbands. I heard my mother say that to father when they lay quarrelling in bed at night and I lay listening.” The boy was overcome with the thought of a woman talking to him so frankly. He looked at her and said what was in his mind. “I don't like the women,” he said, “but I liked you, seeing you standing in the stairway and thinking you had been doing as you pleased. I thought maybe you amounted to something. I don't know why you should be bothered by what I think. I don't know why any woman should be bothered by what any man thinks. I should think you would go right on doing what you want to do like mother and me about my being a lawyer.” He sat on a log beside the road near where he had met her and watched her go down the hill. “I'm quite a fellow to have talked to her all afternoon like that,” he thought and pride in his growing manhood crept over him.

She put her hand on his arm and seemed to be soothing him like a careful groom quieting an excitable horse. “Don't mind them,” she said, “you will go away after a time and make a place for yourself out in the world.” He wondered how she knew. A profound respect for her came over him. “She is keen to guess that,” he thought. He began to talk of himself, boasting and throwing out his chest. “I'd like to have the chance to show what I can do,” he declared. A thought that had been in his mind on the winter day when Uncle Charlie Wheeler put the name of Beaut upon him came back and he walked up and down before the woman making grotesque motions with his hands as Cracked McGregor had walked up and down before him.

“I'll tell you what,” he began and his voice was harsh. He had forgotten the presence of the woman and half forgotten what had been in his mind. He sputtered and glared over his shoulder up the hillside as he struggled for words. “Oh to Hell with men!” he burst forth. “They are cattle, stupid cattle.” A fire blazed up in his eyes and a confident ring came into his voice. “I'd like to get them together, all of them,” he said, “I'd like to make them——” Words failed him and again he sat down on the log beside the woman. “Well I'd like to lead them to an old mine shaft and push them in,” he concluded resentfully.

On the eminence Beaut and the tall woman sat and looked down into the valley. “I wonder why we don't go there, mother and I,” he said. “When I see it I'm filled with the notion. I think I want to be a farmer and work in the fields. Instead of that mother and I sit and plan of the city. I'm going to be a lawyer. That's all we talk about. Then I come up here and it seems as though this is the place for me.” The tall woman laughed. “I can see you coming home at night from the fields,” she said. “It might be to that white house there with the windmill, You would be a big man and would have dust in your red hair and perhaps a red beard growing on your chin. And a woman with a baby in her arms would come out of the kitchen door to stand leaning on the fence waiting for you. When you came up she would put her arm around your neck and kiss you on the lips. The beard would tickle her cheek. You should have a beard when you grow older. Your mouth is so big.” A strange new feeling shot through Beaut. He wondered why she had said that and wanted to take hold of her hand and kiss her then and there. He got up and looked at the sun going down behind the hill far away at the other end of the valley. “We'd better be getting along back,” he said. The woman remained seated on the log. “Sit down,” she said, “I'll tell you something—something it's good for you to hear. You're so big and red you tempt a girl to bother you. First though you tell me why you go along the street looking into the gutter when I stand in the stairway in the evening.” Beaut sat down again upon the log, and thought of what the black-haired boy had told him of her. “Then it was true—what he said about you?” he asked.

“No! No!” she cried, jumping up in her turn and beginning to pin on her hat. “Let's be going.” Beaut sat stolidly on the log. “What's the use bothering each other,” he said. “Let's sit here until the sun goes down. We can get home before dark.” They sat down and she began talking, boasting of herself as he had boasted of his father.

“I'm too old for that boy,” she said; “I'm older than you by a good many years. I know what boys talk about and what they say about women. I do pretty well. I don't have any one to talk to except father and he sits all evening reading a paper and going to sleep in his chair. If I let boys come and sit with me in the evening or stand talking with me in the stairway it is because I'm lonesome. There isn't a man in town I'd marry—not one.” The speech sounded discordant and harsh to Beaut. He wished his father were there rubbing his hands together and muttering rather than this pale woman who stirred him up and then talked harshly like the women at the back doors in Coal Creek. He thought again as he had thought before that he preferred the black-faced miners drunk and silent to their pale talking wives. On an impulse he told her that, saying it crudely so that it hurt. Their companionship was spoiled. They got up and began to climb the hill, going toward home. Again she put her hand to her side and again he wished to put his hand at her back and push her up the hill. Instead he walked beside her in silence, again hating the town. Halfway down the hill the tall woman stopped by the road-side. Darkness was coming on and the glow of the coke ovens lighted the sky. “One living up here and never going down there might think it rather grand and big,” he said. Again the hatred came. “They might think the men who live down there knew something instead of being just a lot of cattle.” A smile came into the face of the tall woman and a gentler look stole into her eyes. “We get at one another,” she said, “we can't let one another alone. I wish we hadn't quarrelled. We might be friends if we tried. You have got something in you. You attract women. I've heard others say that. Your father was that way. Most of the women here would rather have been the wife of Cracked McGregor ugly as he was than to have stayed with their own husbands. I heard my mother say that to father when they lay quarrelling in bed at night and I lay listening.” The boy was overcome with the thought of a woman talking to him so frankly. He looked at her and said what was in his mind. “I don't like the women,” he said, “but I liked you, seeing you standing in the stairway and thinking you had been doing as you pleased. I thought maybe you amounted to something. I don't know why you should be bothered by what I think. I don't know why any woman should be bothered by what any man thinks. I should think you would go right on doing what you want to do like mother and me about my being a lawyer.” He sat on a log beside the road near where he had met her and watched her go down the hill. “I'm quite a fellow to have talked to her all afternoon like that,” he thought and pride in his growing manhood crept over him.

Write in third-person perspective. Match their diction, syntax, tone and voice as closely as you can. Do not paraphrase or reuse any of the author's content. Output only the piece itself with no title, preamble, or commentary.
column308:
When Will Ferris got off the train at Pickford he stood for a time on the station platform with his grip in his hand and looked about. It was late in October and the corn had been cut and stood in shocks in the fields that came down to the very edge of the town. A man with a wheelbarrow went along the platform pushing a trunk. Two boys sat on a baggage truck and swung their legs and looked at Will's clothes. He was a man of thirty-six then, a little heavy about the middle, and he wore a brown suit with a thin white stripe in it that he had bought in Cleveland the spring before. He had been gone from Pickford sixteen years. When he had left he had been a thin long-legged boy with big wrists and he had gone away on a night train, sitting by the window and crying a little in the dark where no one could see.

Now he did not know what to do with himself. He had written to his cousin Jesse that he would come but no one was there to meet him. He set the grip down and took out a cigar and lit it and then he took it out of his mouth and looked at it. "I'll walk out," he said aloud, and one of the boys on the baggage truck laughed. Will turned and glared at the boy and then he too laughed. He thought of himself as he had been, sitting on that same truck perhaps, swinging his legs and looking at travelling men who got off the trains, and he felt suddenly old and a little foolish.

The Ferris farm lay two miles out of town on the Medina road. Will walked out carrying his grip. The road was dusty and the dust got into the cuffs of his trousers and settled on his shoes. Once a farmer in a wagon came along and offered him a ride but Will shook his head. He wanted to walk. As he went along, things he had not thought of in years came back into his mind. There was a place where the road dipped down to cross a creek and where a sycamore tree grew. He remembered that he and Jesse had once caught a muskrat there in a trap and had sold the skin in town for thirty cents. They had quarrelled about the money and had fought in the road and Jesse had bloodied his nose. Afterward they had gone and sat together on the bridge with their feet hanging over the water and had not spoken for a long time. Then Jesse had given him all of the thirty cents. Will stopped on the bridge and looked down into the creek. The water was low and black leaves floated on it. "Jesse was a queer one," he thought. "He always gave in at the end."

Jesse Ferris was the son of Will's father's brother and the two boys had been born the same year. Will's mother had died when he was eight and after that he had lived at the farm with his uncle and aunt and his cousin. In the house the two boys slept together in a room under the roof. In the winter frost formed on the inside of the window and in the summer the room was so hot that they lay naked on top of the covers and talked half the night. It was there they had made their plans. They were going to Chicago together. Jesse was going to be a railroad engineer and Will was going to be something—he did not know what—something big. He used to lie in the dark and talk of it and wave his arms over his head until Jesse laughed at him. Jesse stammered when he talked and so he did not talk much. He lay on his back and listened and once in a while he said, "Y-you will, Will. You will all right."

When the boys were nineteen Jesse's father was kicked by a horse in the barn and lay for a year in the front room of the house and then died. Jesse stayed on the farm. Will went away. He had thought often in the years since that he had meant to write to Jesse and tell him how things were in the city but he had not done it. At first he had been ashamed because things were not going well with him and afterward, when he had begun to get on, he had been ashamed because so much time had passed. He had sent a Christmas card now and then. When Jesse married he had sent a clock.

It was nearly sundown when he came to the lane that led up to the house. He stopped at the gate. The house was smaller than he had remembered it. It needed paint. A woman came out of the kitchen door and threw a pan of water into the yard and then stood shading her eyes and looking at him. She was a thin woman with a long face and her hair was pulled back tight from her forehead. Will took off his hat. "I'm Will," he called. "Jesse's cousin. I wrote."

The woman did not come toward him. She stood in the door and wiped her hands on her apron. "He's out to the barn," she said. "He said you'd likely come today." Then she went back into the house and Will heard a door shut. He stood in the yard holding his hat and his grip. A dog came around the corner of the house and sniffed at his trousers and then lay down in the dust.

Will set his grip on the porch and went out to the barn. The barn door was open and inside it was nearly dark. He could smell the hay and the horses and the smell went into him and made him feel weak in the legs. He did not understand why it should be so. In the city he had sometimes thought of that smell and had said to men in the hotel lobbies that there was nothing like it, that a man raised on a farm never got it out of him, but he had said it the way men say such things, laughing and knocking the ashes off a cigar. Now he stood in the doorway and could not go in.

Jesse was milking. He sat on a three-legged stool with his head pressed against the flank of a red cow and the milk made a thin singing sound in the pail. He did not look up. "That you, Will?" he said.

"It's me," Will said.

Jesse finished milking the cow. He got up slowly and set the pail on a shelf out of reach of the cats and came toward the door wiping his hands on his overalls. He was a tall man, taller than Will, and very thin, and his shoulders were stooped. There was grey in his hair. His face was burned dark by the sun and there were deep lines at the corners of his eyes. He stood in front of Will and looked at him and Will put out his hand. Jesse took it. His hand was hard and dry and very large and he held Will's hand a long time without saying anything. Then he let go of it and laughed.

"You've got f-fat," he said.

Will laughed too. He wanted to say something about Jesse's grey hair but he did not. He put his hand on his own stomach and patted it. "It's the city living," he said. "Hotel food. You sit in a chair all day and talk and at night you sit in another chair and eat." He began to talk rapidly. He told Jesse that he was with the Atlas Harvester Company in Cleveland and that he had charge of the sales in three states. He had eleven men under him. He told how he travelled about and of the cities he had been in—Pittsburgh and Buffalo and Detroit and once New York. As he talked he walked up and down in the barn door and made motions with his hands and his voice got louder. Jesse leaned against a post and listened. Once he took a straw out of the manger and put it in his mouth and chewed on it. Will heard himself talking and could not stop. It was as though some other man were talking, some man he had met in a smoking car, and he was listening to him and thinking, "What a windbag the fellow is."

He stopped suddenly. Jesse had not said anything. The cow moved in her stall and a chain rattled. "Well," Will said, "that's how it is with me."

"I knew you'd get on," Jesse said. "I always said you would."

They went to the house together and ate supper in the kitchen. Jesse's wife, whose name was Martha, set the food on the table and then sat at the end of the table and ate without speaking. There were two children, a boy of ten and a girl of six or seven, and they stared at Will all through the meal. The boy had Jesse's long face and big hands. Once Will winked at the girl and she put her face down to her plate and began to cry and her mother took her out of the room. "She's bashful," Jesse said. Will felt that he had done something wrong. He tried to talk to Martha when she came back but she answered him in a word or two and got up and began to clear the table. "She don't hold with strangers," Jesse said afterward when they were alone, and then he added, "she's a good woman." He said it as though he were defending her against something Will had said and Will was puzzled and a little hurt.

After supper the two men went and sat on the front porch. It was cold and Jesse brought out an old coat and put it over Will's shoulders. The moon came up over the woods at the end of the pasture. Far off a dog was barking and Will heard a wagon going along the road toward town, the wheels grinding in the dust. He lit a cigar and offered one to Jesse and Jesse took it and turned it over in his fingers and then put it in the pocket of his shirt. "I'll smoke it Sunday," he said.

For a long time neither of them said anything. Will had thought that when he saw Jesse there would be a great deal to say. On the train coming down he had thought of it. He had thought they would talk of the old days and laugh together and that perhaps at the end he would tell Jesse things he had told no one. He did not know what the things were. There was something in him that wanted to be said and that he had carried about with him in the city for years. He had felt it at night in hotel rooms when he could not sleep and had got up and stood at the window looking down into a street where a man went along alone under the lights. He had felt it once in a restaurant in Pittsburgh when a woman at the next table had laughed in a certain way. It was a kind of hunger. He had thought that if he could come back to the farm and sit with Jesse in the dark the thing would come out of him and he would be done with it.

Now he sat on the porch and could think of nothing to say. Jesse sat with his hands on his knees looking at the moon.

"Do you remember the muskrat?" Will asked suddenly.

Jesse turned his head. "What muskrat?"

"The one we trapped down by the bridge. We fought over the money."

Jesse thought for a while. "No," he said, "I don't remember it." He shook his head slowly. "There was a lot of muskrats."

Will felt something like anger rise in him. It seemed to him that Jesse should remember. He began to tell about it, about the fight in the road and the blood running out of his nose and about sitting on the bridge afterward, and as he told it he laughed and slapped his knee. Jesse listened politely. "Maybe so," he said when Will had finished. "I don't remember it, though."

They were silent again. Will threw his cigar into the yard and watched the end of it glow and go out. He thought of Martha in the house and wondered if she were listening at the window. He thought that Jesse had grown dull, that the farm had done it to him, the years of getting up in the dark and milking and going out into the fields and coming back and eating and sleeping and getting up again. "He's like one of his own cows," he thought, and then he was ashamed of the thought and was glad it was dark so that Jesse could not see his face.

It was Jesse who spoke first. He spoke slowly, stopping often, and his stammer was worse than it had been at supper. Will had to lean toward him to hear.

"I w-went to Chicago once," Jesse said.

Will sat up. "You did? When?"

"Eight years ago. After the first baby. It was winter and there wasn't much to do." He stopped and rubbed his hands together. "I didn't tell nobody. I told Martha I was going to see about some hogs in Toledo. I got on the train at Pickford and I rode all night and in the morning I was there."

He was silent a long time. Will waited. The dog that had been lying in the yard got up and came onto the porch and lay down at Jesse's feet.

"I walked around," Jesse said. "All day I walked around. I went down by the railroad yards and I stood there and watched the engines. There was a man up in the cab of one of them, an old man with a white moustache, and he looked down at me standing there. I thought he was going to say something to me. I don't know what I thought he was going to say." He laughed, a short laugh, and put his hand down and touched the dog's head. "He didn't say anything. He just looked at me. I guess he thought I was some hick."

"What did you do then?" Will asked.

"I went and got a room in a hotel. It cost a dollar and a half. And I sat in it." Jesse's voice had dropped very low. "I sat on the bed all night and I didn't take my shoes off. There was a light outside the window that kept going off and on, red and then nothing and then red again. And I sat there and I thought, now you're here. Now you're here, Jesse. And I didn't know what I was there for." He stopped. "In the morning I went and got on the train and came home. I told Martha the hogs wasn't any good."

Will did not say anything. He could not. Something had come up into his throat and he sat with his hands gripping the arms of the chair. He thought of Jesse sitting on the bed in the hotel with his shoes on and the red light going off and on and it seemed to him that he had been in that room himself, that he had sat on that bed a hundred times. He wanted to get up and put his arms around his cousin. He wanted to tell him about the nights in the hotels and the man going along alone under the street lights and the woman laughing in the restaurant in Pittsburgh. He wanted to say, "It isn't any different there. It isn't any different anywhere." But the words would not come. He was afraid that if he began to speak he would cry, and that Martha would hear him, and that in the morning at breakfast she would look at him with her long face.

"I thought you'd be there," Jesse said. "In Chicago. I thought maybe I'd see you on the street."

"I never lived in Chicago," Will said. "I was always in Cleveland."

"I know it," Jesse said. "I knew it then. But I thought I'd see you anyway." He laughed again and stood up. The dog stood up too and stretched itself. "That's a fool thing," Jesse said. "I don't know why I told it."

He went into the house. Will heard him going up the stairs, his heavy shoes on the boards, and then a door closing. He sat alone on the porch. The moon had climbed high and the fields lay white under it and the corn shocks stood in rows like men waiting for something. Will looked at them for a long time. It seemed to him that he understood something, that a door had opened a little way in him and that if he could only get up and go through it he would be in a new place. He did not get up. After a while he grew cold and went in and climbed the stairs to the room under the roof where he and Jesse had slept as boys. There was a bed in it and a chair and on the wall a calendar from a feed store in Pickford. He lay down on the bed in his clothes and did not sleep. He thought of Jesse lying in the next room beside his thin wife and wondered if Jesse were awake too.

In the morning Jesse drove him to the train in a spring wagon. It was cold and there was frost on the fences. They did not talk on the way. At the station Will got down and took his grip out of the wagon and stood looking up at his cousin. Jesse held the reins in his big hands. The horse stamped and blew out its breath in a cloud.

"You come up and see me sometime," Will said. "Bring Martha and the children. I'd show you around."

"Maybe I will," Jesse said. "Maybe some winter."

The train came in. Will held up his hand and Jesse leaned down from the wagon and took it, and again he held it a long time. Then he let go and turned the horse and drove away up the street without looking back. Will got on the train and sat by the window. As the train pulled out he saw the spring wagon going along the Medina road, very small, and his cousin sitting in it with his shoulders bent forward.

"He's a good fellow, Jesse," Will said to himself. "A plain good fellow." He took out a cigar and bit off the end and then he did not light it. He sat holding it in his fingers and looking out at the fields going past, the corn shocks and the bare woods and the farmhouses with smoke going up from the chimneys. He thought of the room in the hotel in Chicago and the red light going off and on. He thought that he would write to Jesse when he got back to Cleveland, a long letter, and tell him everything. He began in his mind to compose the letter. "Dear Jesse," he began, and then he stopped. He did not know what came after that. The train ran on through the bright cold morning and a man across the aisle opened a newspaper and began to read, and Will Ferris sat with the unlit cigar in his fingers and the words he could not find going around and around in him like a bird shut in a barn.

Here is an excerpt of Sherwood Anderson's writing, to show you their style:

One Sunday afternoon three boys sat on a log on the side of the hill that looked down into Coal Creek. From where they sat they could see the workers of the night shift idling in the sun on Main Street. From the coke ovens a thin line of smoke rose into the sky. A freight train heavily loaded crept round the hill at the end of the valley. It was spring and over even that hive of black industry hung a faint promise of beauty. The boys talked of the life of people in their town and as they talked thought each of himself. Although he had not been out of the valley and had grown strong and big there, Beaut McGregor knew something of the outside world. It isn't a time when men are shut off from their fellows. Newspapers and magazines have done their work too well. They reached even into the miner's cabin and the merchants along Main Street of Coal Creek stood before their stores in the afternoon and talked of the doings of the world. Beaut McGregor knew that life in his town was exceptional, that not everywhere did men toil all day black and grimy underground, that not all women were pale bloodless and bent. As he went about delivering bread he whistled a song. “Take me back to Broadway,” he sang after the soubrette in a show that had once come to Coal Creek. Now as he sat on the hillside he talked earnestly while he gesticulated with his hands. “I hate this town,” he said. “The men here think they are confoundedly funny. They don't care for anything but making foolish jokes and getting drunk. I want to go away.” His voice rose and hatred flamed up in him. “You wait,” he boasted. “I'll make men stop being fools. I'll make children of them. I'll——” Pausing he looked at his two companions. Beaut poked the ground with a stick. The boy sitting beside him laughed. He was a short well—dressed black—haired boy with rings on his fingers who worked in the town poolroom, racking the pool balls. “I'd like to go where there are women with blood in them,” he said. Three women came up the hill toward them, a tall pale brown-haired woman of twenty-seven and two fairer young girls. The black-haired boy straightened his tie and began thinking of a conversation he would start when the women reached him. Beaut and the other boy, a fat fellow, the son of a grocer, looked down the hill to the town over the heads of the newcomers and continued in their minds the thoughts that had made the conversation.

“Hello girls, come and sit here,” shouted the black-haired boy, laughing and looking boldly into the eyes of the tall pale woman. They stopped and the tall woman began stepping over the fallen logs, coming to them. The two young girls followed, laughing. They sat down on the log beside the boys, the tall pale woman at the end beside red-haired McGregor. An embarrassed silence fell over the party. Both Beaut and the fat boy were disconcerted by this turn to their afternoon's outing and wondered how it would turn out. The pale woman began to talk in a low tone. “I want to get away from here,” she said, “I wish I could hear birds sing and see green things grow.” Beaut McGregor had an idea. “You come with me,” he said. He got up and climbed over the logs and the pale woman followed. The fat boy shouted at them, relieving his own embarrassment by trying to embarrass them. “Where're you going—you two?” he shouted. Beaut said nothing. He stepped over the logs to the road and began climbing the hill. The tall woman walked beside him and held her skirts out of the deep dust of the road. Even on this her Sunday gown there was a faint black mark along the seams—the mark of Coal Creek. As McGregor walked his embarrassment left him. He thought it fine that he should be thus alone with a woman. When she had tired from the climb he sat with her on a log beside the road and talked of the black-haired boy. “He has your ring on his finger,” he said, looking at her and laughing. She held her hand pressed tightly against her side and closed her eyes. “The climbing hurts me,” she said. Tenderness took hold of Beaut. When they went on again he walked behind her, his hand upon her back pushing her up the hill. The desire to tease her about the black-haired boy had passed and he wished he had said nothing about the ring. He remembered the story the black-haired boy had told him of his conquest of the woman. “More than likely a mess of lies,” he thought. Over the crest of the hill they stopped and rested, leaning against a worn rail fence by the woods. Below them in a wagon a party of men went down the hill. The men sat upon boards laid across the box of a wagon and sang a song. One of them stood in the seat beside the driver and waved a bottle. He seemed to be making a speech. The others shouted and clapped their hands. The sounds came faint and sharp up the hill. In the woods beside the fence rank grass grew. Hawks floated in the sky over the valley below. A squirrel running along the fence stopped and chattered at them. McGregor thought he had never had so delightful a companion. He got a feeling of complete, good fellowship and friendliness with this woman. Without knowing how the thing had been done he felt a certain pride in it. “Don't mind what I said about the ring,” he urged, “I was only trying to tease you.” The woman beside McGregor was the daughter of an undertaker who lived upstairs over his shop near the bakery. He had seen her in the evening standing in the stairway by the shop door. After the story told him by the black-haired boy he had been embarrassed about her. When he passed her standing in the stairway he went hurriedly along and looked into the gutter. They went down the hill and sat on the log upon the hillside. A clump of elders had grown about the log since his visits there with Cracked McGregor so that the place was closed and shaded like a room. The woman took off her hat and laid it beside her on the log. A faint colour mounted to her pale cheeks and a flash of anger gleamed in her eyes. “He probably lied to you about me,” she said, “I didn't give him that ring to wear. I don't know why I gave it to him. He wanted it. He asked me for it time and again. He said he wanted to show it to his mother. And now he has shown it to you and I suppose told lies about me.” Beaut was annoyed and wished he had not mentioned the ring. He felt that an unnecessary fuss was being made about it. He did not believe that the black-haired boy had lied but he did not think it mattered. He began talking of his father, boasting of him. His hatred of the town blazed up. “They thought they knew him down there,” he said, “they laughed at him and called him 'Cracked.' They thought his running into the mine just a crazy notion like a horse that runs into a burning stable. He was the best man in town. He was braver than any of them. He went in there and died when he had almost enough money saved to buy a farm over here.” He pointed down the valley. Beaut began to tell her of the visits to the hillside with his father and described the effect of the scene on himself when he was a child. “I thought it was paradise,” he said. She put her hand on his arm and seemed to be soothing him like a careful groom quieting an excitable horse. “Don't mind them,” she said, “you will go away after a time and make a place for yourself out in the world.” He wondered how she knew. A profound respect for her came over him. “She is keen to guess that,” he thought. He began to talk of himself, boasting and throwing out his chest. “I'd like to have the chance to show what I can do,” he declared. A thought that had been in his mind on the winter day when Uncle Charlie Wheeler put the name of Beaut upon him came back and he walked up and down before the woman making grotesque motions with his hands as Cracked McGregor had walked up and down before him.

“I'll tell you what,” he began and his voice was harsh. He had forgotten the presence of the woman and half forgotten what had been in his mind. He sputtered and glared over his shoulder up the hillside as he struggled for words. “Oh to Hell with men!” he burst forth. “They are cattle, stupid cattle.” A fire blazed up in his eyes and a confident ring came into his voice. “I'd like to get them together, all of them,” he said, “I'd like to make them——” Words failed him and again he sat down on the log beside the woman. “Well I'd like to lead them to an old mine shaft and push them in,” he concluded resentfully.

On the eminence Beaut and the tall woman sat and looked down into the valley. “I wonder why we don't go there, mother and I,” he said. “When I see it I'm filled with the notion. I think I want to be a farmer and work in the fields. Instead of that mother and I sit and plan of the city. I'm going to be a lawyer. That's all we talk about. Then I come up here and it seems as though this is the place for me.” The tall woman laughed. “I can see you coming home at night from the fields,” she said. “It might be to that white house there with the windmill, You would be a big man and would have dust in your red hair and perhaps a red beard growing on your chin. And a woman with a baby in her arms would come out of the kitchen door to stand leaning on the fence waiting for you. When you came up she would put her arm around your neck and kiss you on the lips. The beard would tickle her cheek. You should have a beard when you grow older. Your mouth is so big.” A strange new feeling shot through Beaut. “No! No!” she cried, jumping up in her turn and beginning to pin on her hat. “Let's be going.” Beaut sat stolidly on the log. “What's the use bothering each other,” he said. “Let's sit here until the sun goes down. We can get home before dark.” They sat down and she began talking, boasting of herself as he had boasted of his father.

“I'm too old for that boy,” she said; “I'm older than you by a good many years. I know what boys talk about and what they say about women. I do pretty well. Again the hatred came. “They might think the men who live down there knew something instead of being just a lot of cattle.” A smile came into the face of the tall woman and a gentler look stole into her eyes. “We get at one another,” she said, “we can't let one another alone. I heard my mother say that to father when they lay quarrelling in bed at night and I lay listening.” The boy was overcome with the thought of a woman talking to him so frankly. He looked at her and said what was in his mind. “I don't like the women,” he said, “but I liked you, seeing you standing in the stairway and thinking you had been doing as you pleased. I thought maybe you amounted to something. I don't know why you should be bothered by what I think. I don't know why any woman should be bothered by what any man thinks. I should think you would go right on doing what you want to do like mother and me about my being a lawyer.” He sat on a log beside the road near where he had met her and watched her go down the hill. “I'm quite a fellow to have talked to her all afternoon like that,” he thought and pride in his growing manhood crept over him.

They don't care for anything but making foolish jokes and getting drunk. I want to go away.” His voice rose and hatred flamed up in him. “You wait,” he boasted. “I'll make men stop being fools. Beaut and the other boy, a fat fellow, the son of a grocer, looked down the hill to the town over the heads of the newcomers and continued in their minds the thoughts that had made the conversation.

He thought it fine that he should be thus alone with a woman. When they went on again he walked behind her, his hand upon her back pushing her up the hill. The men sat upon boards laid across the box of a wagon and sang a song. One of them stood in the seat beside the driver and waved a bottle. He seemed to be making a speech. The others shouted and clapped their hands. The sounds came faint and sharp up the hill. In the woods beside the fence rank grass grew. Hawks floated in the sky over the valley below. A squirrel running along the fence stopped and chattered at them. McGregor thought he had never had so delightful a companion. He got a feeling of complete, good fellowship and friendliness with this woman. Without knowing how the thing had been done he felt a certain pride in it. “Don't mind what I said about the ring,” he urged, “I was only trying to tease you.” The woman beside McGregor was the daughter of an undertaker who lived upstairs over his shop near the bakery. He had seen her in the evening standing in the stairway by the shop door. After the story told him by the black-haired boy he had been embarrassed about her. When he passed her standing in the stairway he went hurriedly along and looked into the gutter. They went down the hill and sat on the log upon the hillside. A clump of elders had grown about the log since his visits there with Cracked McGregor so that the place was closed and shaded like a room. The woman took off her hat and laid it beside her on the log. A faint colour mounted to her pale cheeks and a flash of anger gleamed in her eyes. “He probably lied to you about me,” she said, “I didn't give him that ring to wear. I don't know why I gave it to him. He wanted it. He asked me for it time and again. He said he wanted to show it to his mother. And now he has shown it to you and I suppose told lies about me.” Beaut was annoyed and wished he had not mentioned the ring. He felt that an unnecessary fuss was being made about it. He did not believe that the black-haired boy had lied but he did not think it mattered. He began talking of his father, boasting of him. His hatred of the town blazed up. “They thought they knew him down there,” he said, “they laughed at him and called him 'Cracked.' They thought his running into the mine just a crazy notion like a horse that runs into a burning stable. He was the best man in town. He was braver than any of them. A profound respect for her came over him. “She is keen to guess that,” he thought. “I'll tell you what,” he began and his voice was harsh. He had forgotten the presence of the woman and half forgotten what had been in his mind. And a woman with a baby in her arms would come out of the kitchen door to stand leaning on the fence waiting for you. When you came up she would put her arm around your neck and kiss you on the lips. The beard would tickle her cheek. You should have a beard when you grow older. Your mouth is so big.” A strange new feeling shot through Beaut. The stave factory at Sand Ridge let its men go at six o'clock, and on summer evenings they came up Turner Street in twos and threes, their dinner pails swinging against their legs. Joe Wendell walked alone. He was a long thin man with stooped shoulders and a habit of holding his head to one side as though he were listening for something far off. In the factory he worked at the jointing machine, and the scream of it had got into his ears so that at night, when the town was quiet, he lay in bed and heard it still. He did not talk much to the other men. They thought him proud, but he was not proud. He had simply never learned the trick of talking easily, and when he tried it the words came out wrong and he was ashamed.

On this evening in July his wife met him at the gate. She was a small woman with a sharp nose and hands that were always red from the washtub, and when she was excited she pressed them together before her as though she were praying. She was pressing them together now. "It's Harry," she said. "He took the egg money off the clock shelf. Forty cents. And he went off with that old Ike Swartz down to the dam and didn't come home till the lamps were lit. I've been half crazy. I thought he was drowned."

Joe Wendell stood by the gate and looked past her at the house. It was a small house, painted once and not since, and it stood on a lot that ran back to the railroad tracks. A box elder grew by the kitchen door. Under the box elder, on an upturned bucket, sat his son. The boy was seven years old. He had his father's long face and his mother's way of looking out of the corners of his eyes, and he sat with his hands between his knees, very still, the way a rabbit sits in the grass when a dog has gone by.

"Where's he at now?" Joe asked, although he could see the boy plainly. He did not know why he asked it. He set his dinner pail on the gatepost and took off his hat and turned it round in his hands.

"Right there. I told him to sit there and wait for you. I told him you'd attend to him." The woman's voice rose. "You've got to do something, Joe. He'll grow up a thief. He'll grow up like that Swartz, loafing around the dam, never doing a lick of work. Forty cents. Do you know how many eggs that is?"

He did know. He knew to the egg. All the spring they had been saving, putting the dimes and nickels in a tin box behind the clock, and the money was to go for a pair of shoes for the boy against the time school started. It was a strange thing. The money stolen was money meant for the thief, and he thought of that and wanted to laugh and did not.

It isn't a time when a man can look at such things simply. In the old days, so the men said in the factory and at the barber shop on Saturday nights, a man knew what to do with a boy. You cut a switch and that was the end of it. Joe Wendell's own father had done so. He had been a big silent farmer over near Bidwell, and he had whipped Joe with a harness strap in the barn, not angrily but as a thing to be done, the way he would have drenched a sick calf. Joe remembered the smell of the barn and the dust floating in the light from the cracks between the boards. He remembered that after the whipping his father had gone on harnessing the team and had not looked at him, and that he, Joe, had gone out behind the straw stack and lain down on his face and wished his father dead. He had wished it all one summer. Then in the fall his father had died, kicked by a horse, and Joe had believed for years that his wishing had done it.

Now he stood at his own gate and the thing that had happened in the barn came back so plainly that he could smell it. His wife was still talking. He put his hat on and walked across the yard to where the boy sat.

The boy did not get up. He looked at his father's shoes. They were heavy shoes, cracked across the toes and white with sawdust, and the boy looked at them as though there were something written there that he must read.

"Well," Joe said. He cleared his throat. "Well, Harry."

The boy said nothing.

"Your mother says you took the money."

"Yes."

"What'd you do with it?"

The boy put his hand into the pocket of his overalls and brought out a small paper packet and held it up. His father took it and opened it. Inside were fishhooks, a dozen of them, bright and new, and a coil of green line. Joe stood holding them in the palm of his hand. They glittered in the evening light.

"Ike said I could have his old pole," the boy said suddenly, very fast, as though the words had been waiting a long time behind his teeth. "He said it was a good pole only the line was rotten. He said if I had hooks and line he'd show me how. He showed me. He showed me where the bass lay under the dam in the shade. He said the big ones come out at sundown. That's why I stayed. I wanted to see them come out. They didn't come out though. Ike said maybe tomorrow."

The words stopped. The boy looked up at his father for the first time, and then quickly down again at the shoes.

Joe Wendell's wife had come across the yard behind him. "You hear that?" she said. "Fishhooks. Forty cents for fishhooks. You hear him?"

"I hear him," Joe said. He closed his hand over the hooks and one of them pricked his palm. "You go in the house, Ella. I'll attend to this."

She looked at him and he saw that she did not believe he would. It was a look he knew. She had been looking at him so for nine years, ever since the first winter when he had been laid off at the factory and had sat by the stove all day and she had taken in washing. She did not say anything. She went into the house and the screen door slapped behind her.

"Come on," Joe said to the boy.

They went together to the woodshed at the back of the lot. It was a low building of rough boards with a sloping roof, and in it were the woodpile and the chopping block and a broken rocking chair that had belonged to Ella's mother. On a nail by the door hung a strap. It was an old razor strap, cracked and black, and it had never been used for anything. Ella had hung it there when the boy was three years old. "For when he needs it," she had said, and Joe had said nothing. Now he took it down from the nail and stood holding it in one hand and the fishhooks in the other.

The boy stood in the middle of the shed with his back very straight. His face was white. He did not cry. There was something in the way he stood that went through Joe Wendell like a pain. He thought the boy looked like a little soldier in a picture, waiting to be shot.

"Turn around," Joe said. His voice was harsh and strange to him.

The boy turned around. He put his hands on the chopping block and bent over a little, as he had seen the Halloran boys do it when their father whipped them in the alley. He had seen it many times. All the children on Turner Street had seen it. Old Halloran was a drinking man and he whipped his boys in the alley so the neighbors could hear, and the children gathered at the ends of the alley to watch, and afterward the Halloran boys swaggered and boasted of how many licks they had taken without bawling.

Joe Wendell raised the strap. He held it there over his head. The light came in through the cracks between the boards just as it had come into his father's barn, and the dust floated in it, and a wasp that had a nest up under the roof went droning back and forth. He stood so for what seemed a long time. Then he let his arm fall and sat down in the broken rocking chair.

"Turn around here," he said. "Look at me."

The boy turned. He did not understand. He stood by the chopping block and his lip began to tremble now, for the first time, as though not being whipped were harder to bear than the whipping would have been.

Joe did not know what he wanted to say. He looked at the strap across his knees and at the fishhooks in his hand. He thought he should talk to the boy about stealing, about how a man must work for what he has, about the eggs and the hens and his mother bending over the washtub. These were the things a father said. He had heard them said. But when he opened his mouth something else came out.

"I used to fish," he said. "When I was about your age. Over at Bidwell there was a creek ran through the bottom of my father's farm. Pickerel Creek, they called it. There was a hole under a sycamore tree where the water went round and round and was black, and there was a big fish in there. I never saw him. I used to think about him all the time. I used to go down there at night when I was supposed to be asleep."

He stopped. The boy was looking at him with his mouth a little open.

"I never caught him," Joe said. "I never even saw him." He laughed, a short laugh that was not a laugh at all. "Maybe there wasn't any fish."

He got up out of the rocking chair and walked to the door of the shed and stood looking out across the lot toward the railroad. A freight was going by, slowly, the cars clanking, and a brakeman sat on top of one of the cars with his legs hanging over the edge. The man had a red handkerchief about his neck. He was going somewhere. Joe watched him until the car went out of sight behind the coal sheds.

He was thinking of a great many things at once and could not get hold of any of them. He thought of the jointing machine and the scream of it. He thought of the nine years. He thought that every morning he got up in the dark and went to the factory and every evening he came home and ate his supper and sat on the back step and smoked his pipe and went to bed, and that this would go on, and that when he died the men at the factory would say, "Joe Wendell, he was a quiet fellow, kept to himself," and that would be all. He thought of old Ike Swartz sitting all day on the dam with his pole, a dirty old man whom the women of the town despised, and it came to him suddenly that he envied Ike Swartz. He had never thought of such a thing before. It frightened him.

He turned back into the shed. The boy had not moved.

"You hadn't ought to have took the money," Joe said. He said it loudly, as though he were saying it to someone else, to Ella or to the men at the factory. "That was your mother's money. That was for your shoes. You know that?"

"Yes."

"Then what'd you take it for?"

The boy did not answer. He looked at the floor. Then he said, very low, "I wanted to see them come out."

Joe Wendell felt something rise up in him that he could not name. It was partly anger and partly a kind of terrible tenderness and partly shame, and the three things were mixed together so that he did not know one from another. He thought the boy had looked into him and seen the thing he had kept hidden all his life, the night creek and the black water and the fish he had never seen, and he was afraid of the boy for knowing it. He wanted to take the boy in his arms. He wanted to tell him to go on, to go down to the dam every day, to sit there until the big fish came out, to never go into the factory, never. He wanted to say, "Don't be like me." He did not say any of it. He stood with the strap hanging from his hand, and then, without knowing that he was going to do it, he raised the strap and struck the boy once across the legs.

It was not a hard blow. The strap was old and limp and it made a flat sound against the overalls. But the boy cried out and stepped back against the woodpile and his face crumpled, and he began to cry at last, standing there with his fists against his eyes, crying with great gulping sobs that shook him all over.

Joe Wendell threw the strap down on the floor. He stood looking at it. Then he went out of the shed and across the lot and stood by the fence that ran along the railroad tracks. He held onto the fence with both hands. He could hear the boy crying in the shed, and after a time he could hear that the crying had stopped, and after another time he heard the boy come out of the shed and go across the yard and into the house. The screen door slapped.

It was dark when Joe went in. Ella had put his supper on the back of the stove and she set it before him without a word. He ate a little of it and pushed the plate away. She sat across from him with her red hands folded on the oilcloth.

"Did you whip him?" she asked.

"Yes."

"He didn't make much noise."

"He's a game one," Joe said. He was surprised to hear a kind of pride in his own voice.

She looked at him sharply, and then her face changed and grew softer. "I was scared," she said. "I thought he was drowned. I kept seeing him in the water. I don't know what I'd do." She got up suddenly and began clearing the table, rattling the dishes. With her back to him she said, "I'll get the shoes anyhow. I can take in the Thompsons' wash. Mrs. Thompson asked me."

Joe Wendell took the fishhooks out of his pocket and laid them on the table under the lamp. They glittered there. He looked at them for a long time.

Upstairs in the little room under the roof the boy lay on his cot and listened. The window was open and he could hear the frogs down by the tracks and, far off, the sound of a train whistling for the crossing at the edge of town. His legs did not hurt. It had not been much of a blow. He had cried more at Christmas when the Halloran boys took his sled. But he lay in the dark and felt the blow over and over, and it seemed to him that it had not been his father who struck him but someone else, someone who had come into the woodshed out of the light and dust and had stood for a moment where his father stood.

He thought of his father sitting in the rocking chair and saying, "Maybe there wasn't any fish." He thought of the way his father's voice had sounded then, not like a man's voice but like the voice of a boy. He did not understand it. He lay a long time trying to understand it. Below him he could hear his mother and father talking in the kitchen, their voices low and blurred, and once he heard his father laugh, the same short strange laugh, and then the voices stopped and there was only the sound of the frogs.

In the morning the fishhooks were lying on the chair beside his cot. He did not know who had put them there. He did not ask.

Years afterward, when he was a man and lived in a city and had himself become a father, Harry Wendell would remember that evening in the woodshed. He would remember it at strange times, sitting in a streetcar or lying awake at night with his wife breathing beside him. It was not the blow he remembered. He had forgotten that almost at once. It was his father standing in the door of the shed with the light behind him, looking out at the railroad, his long thin body bent a little, his head to one side as though he were listening for something far off. "I wonder what he was listening for," Harry Wendell would think. He never knew. His father had worked at the stave factory until the year he died, and he had never said anything more about the creek at Bidwell or the fish under the sycamore tree. But Harry Wendell knew, as surely as he knew anything in his life, that in that moment in the woodshed his father had wanted to say something to him, something of great importance, and that the words had not come, and that the blow had been struck instead of the words. And it seemed to him, when he thought of it, that this was the way of men, and that it was a sad thing, and that he himself was no different.
